events.summary: The army of Tarquinii defeated the consul C. Fabius and sacrificed 307 Roman prisoners in its forum; in 354 Rome retaliated by flogging and beheading 358 noble Tarquinienses in the Roman Forum.
events.detail: The ritual killing has been linked to Etruscan funerary iconography and the François Tomb fresco of Achilles slaughtering Trojan prisoners. The Elogia Tarquiniensia (inscriptions of the Spurinna family) may commemorate Etruscan leaders of these wars. Truce of 40 years in 351.
scholarship: Torelli, Elogia Tarquiniensia (1975)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998)

events.title: Lex Manlia de vicesima manumissionum
events.summary: The consul Cn. Manlius had his soldiers in camp at Sutrium vote, by tribes, a 5% tax on the value of manumitted slaves; the tribunes then made it a capital offence to convene an assembly away from Rome.
events.detail: The vicesima libertatis endured into the Empire, and its revenue (aurum vicesimarium) was stored as a reserve in the aerarium sanctius, opened in 209 during the Hannibalic war. The tax implies a significant slave population and frequent manumission already by the mid-4th century.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 181-185

events.title: Lex Duilia Menenia: interest capped at one-twelfth
events.summary: A tribunician law fixed the maximum rate of interest at one-twelfth (fenus unciarium), probably 8 1/3 % a year (or per ten-month year); in 347 it was halved to semunciarium.
events.detail: Tacitus says the Twelve Tables had already fixed the uncial rate, which complicates the tradition. A lex Genucia of 342 then banned interest altogether, a law impossible to enforce.

events.title: First plebeian dictator
events.summary: C. Marcius Rutilus became the first plebeian dictator, named his own plebeian master of horse, and defeated the Etruscans who had raided to the salt-works at the Tiber mouth; the people voted him a triumph over senatorial objections.
events.detail: Marcius went on to be the first plebeian censor (351) and held four consulships, a model of the plebeian noble whom the Licinio-Sextian settlement produced.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 123

events.title: Emergence of the Bruttii
events.summary: Diodorus dates to 356 the formation of the Bruttii in the toe of Italy, a people he describes as runaway slaves and herdsmen of the Lucanians, who took Terina, Hipponium and other Greek towns.
events.detail: The name was interpreted as 'rebels' in Lucanian (Strabo). The Bruttian confederacy, centred on Consentia, fought Alexander of Epirus in 331 and later allied with Pyrrhus and Hannibal.

events.title: First treaty between Rome and the Samnites
events.summary: Livy and Diodorus record a treaty of friendship (foedus) between Rome and the Samnite League in 354, probably fixing the Liris valley as the boundary between their spheres.
events.detail: The treaty reflects Rome's arrival on the borders of Campania after subduing the Volsci, Hernici and Aurunci. It was renewed in 341 after the First Samnite War. Tibur and Praeneste submitted to Rome the same year.
scholarship: Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 187-193
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998)

events.title: Hundred-year truce with Caere
events.summary: Caere, having joined Tarquinii, sued for peace and in memory of its help in 390 received a hundred-year truce.
events.detail: Gellius and Strabo say Caere was the first community to receive citizenship without the vote (civitas sine suffragio), and that the 'tabulae Caerites' (list of citizens without vote) took its name; whether this was a privilege of hospitium after 390 or a penalty imposed in 353 or 273 (when Caere lost half its territory) is debated.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973) 53-58
Humbert, Municipium et civitas sine suffragio (1978)
events.debate: Date and character of Caere's civitas sine suffragio.

events.title: Five-man debt commission (quinqueviri mensarii)
events.summary: Five commissioners set up tables in the Forum and settled debts by advancing state money against security or by valuing property for transfer to creditors.
events.detail: A pragmatic response to the debt crisis that the Licinio-Sextian laws had not resolved; Livy praises its fairness. It anticipates the triumviri mensarii of the Hannibalic war.

events.title: First plebeian censor
events.summary: C. Marcius Rutilus was elected the first plebeian censor despite patrician opposition; Tarquinii and Falerii received 40-year truces the same year.
events.detail: The lex Publilia of 339 later required one censor to be plebeian.

events.title: Valerius Corvus and the raven: battle against the Gauls
events.summary: In the Pomptine territory the military tribune M. Valerius fought a Gallic champion; a raven landed on his helmet and attacked the Gaul's face, and Valerius (henceforth Corvus) won; the consul L. Furius Camillus then routed the Gauls, who scattered to Apulia.
events.detail: Like the Torquatus duel, this is a family legend (the Valerii Corvini). In 350 M. Popillius Laenas had already defeated Gauls. Polybius (2.18.7-9) says that in this period the Gauls came again, the Romans met them, and the Gauls fled by night, after which there was peace for 13 years and then a formal peace treaty. The Latins refused troops this year, a sign of strain.

sides.strength: consular army of L. Furius Camillus

battle.significance: End of the series of 4th-century Gallic raids on Latium.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 237-255

events.title: Greek fleet raids the coast of Latium
events.summary: A Greek fleet harried the Laurentine coast and the mouth of the Tiber, skirmishing with the Gauls who also roamed the region; Livy guesses the ships came from Syracusan tyrants.
events.detail: Probably a Syracusan expedition under Dionysius II; Antium itself was a notorious pirate base until 338, and Strabo says complaints from Alexander and Demetrius Poliorcetes reached Rome about Antiate pirates.

events.title: Second treaty between Rome and Carthage
events.summary: A new treaty, in which Tyre and Utica joined Carthage, extended the forbidden zone to Mastia Tarseion in Spain and banned Romans from trading or founding cities in Sardinia and Libya, while Carthage might raid Latin towns not subject to Rome but must hand them over to Rome.
events.detail: Polybius gives the text without a date; Livy (7.27.2) and Diodorus (16.69.1) record a treaty in 348, the first known to them. Carthaginian Sicily and Carthage itself remained open to Roman traders. The clause allowing Carthage to keep captives and movables but surrender captured Latin towns to Rome reveals a Rome still claiming hegemony in Latium yet unable to protect it at sea. Mastia is usually placed near later Cartagena.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 345-349
Scardigli, I trattati romano-cartaginesi (1991)

events.title: Capua surrenders itself to Rome
events.summary: Attacked by the Samnites after Capua aided the Sidicini of Teanum, the Campanians appealed to Rome; when the Senate refused to break its treaty with the Samnites, the envoys made an unconditional deditio of Capua and its people, obliging Rome to defend its new property.
events.detail: Livy's story of a deditio is widely doubted as a pretext invented to excuse Rome's breach of the 354 treaty; but the appeal and Roman intervention began the century of Samnite wars. The Campanian aristocracy's links with Roman nobles (later intermarriage, the equites Campani) are a recurring factor.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 283-307
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 197-200
events.debate: Historicity of the deditio and of the whole war (Adcock and others doubted the First Samnite War entirely).

events.title: Battle of Mount Gaurus
events.summary: The consul M. Valerius Corvus defeated the Samnites in a hard-fought battle at Mount Gaurus above Cumae, the first battle between Rome and the Samnites.
events.detail: Livy's narrative (Samnites asking what fire burned in Roman eyes) is rhetorical; the victory nonetheless saved Campania for the Romans. The Fasti Triumphales record triumphs of both consuls over the Samnites in 343.

battle.significance: First Roman-Samnite battle; secures Campania.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 307-330

events.title: Decius Mus saves the army near Saticula
events.summary: The consul A. Cornelius Cossus' army was trapped in a valley near Saticula; the military tribune P. Decius Mus seized a height with a detachment, drew off the Samnites and broke out at night, enabling a Roman victory.
events.detail: Decius received the corona obsidionalis (grass crown) from the rescued army and an ox with gilded horns. The episode resembles later stories (the Caudine Forks reversed; the tribune Calpurnius Flamma in Sicily in 258).

battle.significance: Makes the reputation of Decius Mus.

events.title: Battle of Suessula
events.summary: Valerius Corvus surprised and destroyed the Samnite camp near Suessula; Livy claims 40,000 shields were collected and Carthage sent congratulations and a 25-pound gold crown for the Capitol.
events.detail: The Carthaginian embassy is often taken to reflect real diplomatic contact around the time of the 348 treaty. Faliscans asked to convert their truce into a treaty and the Latins turned their arms on the Paeligni.

battle.significance: Ends the active campaigning of the First Samnite War.

events.title: Mutiny of the Campanian garrison and the Genucian laws
events.summary: Roman troops wintering in Campania plotted to seize Capua and marched on Rome; the dictator Valerius Corvus reconciled them, and the tribune L. Genucius carried laws banning interest, forbidding re-election to the same office within ten years and holding two offices at once, and allowing both consuls to be plebeian.
events.detail: Livy confesses his sources disagree violently on the mutiny. From 342 one consul was regularly plebeian (both plebeian first in 172). The ten-year interval rule was often waived during the Samnite wars, and the Genucian package marks the effective end of the 'Struggle of the Orders' over the consulship.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 361-392

events.title: Peace and renewal of the Samnite treaty
events.summary: Rome renewed its 354 treaty with the Samnites and left them free to attack the Sidicini, effectively abandoning the cause for which it had fought; the Latins and Campanians, alarmed, prepared for war against Rome.
events.detail: The diplomatic about-turn is the strongest evidence that the 'First Samnite War' was a short, limited conflict.

events.title: Battle of Vesuvius (Veseris)
events.summary: The consuls T. Manlius Torquatus and P. Decius Mus defeated the Latins and Campanians near Mount Vesuvius on the road to Veseris; when the Roman left wavered, Decius devoted himself and the enemy to the gods of the underworld and charged to his death.
events.detail: Livy preserves the devotio formula, dictated by the pontifex M. Valerius ('Iane, Iuppiter, Mars pater, Quirine, Bellona, Lares, divi Novensiles, di Indigetes...'). Before the battle Torquatus had his own son beheaded for winning a single combat against the Tusculan Geminus Maecius in defiance of orders, the origin of the proverbial 'imperia Manliana'. Livy's set-piece description of the manipular legion (hastati, principes, triarii, rorarii, accensi; 'res ad triarios rediit') at this point is the classic but anachronistic source for the early manipular army. The site is disputed: near Vesuvius, or (Salmon) near Roccamonfina in Aurunca territory, which would better suit the strategic situation.
events.locName: Near the foot of Vesuvius, road to Veseris

sides.strength: two consular armies with Samnite allies (Livy)
sides.losses: heavy on the left; consul Decius killed

battle.significance: Breaks the Latin-Campanian coalition and decides the Latin War.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 405-480
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 206-208
Versnel, 'Two types of Roman devotio', Mnemosyne 29 (1976)
events.debate: Site; historicity of the first Decian devotio (the 295 devotio of his son is better attested and the father's may be a doublet).

events.title: Battle of Trifanum
events.summary: Torquatus caught the regrouped Latins and Campanians at Trifanum between Sinuessa and Minturnae and crushed them; the Latins surrendered and Campanian land (the ager Falernus) was confiscated.
events.detail: The Campanian equites (1,600) who had not revolted were rewarded with citizenship and a payment from the Campanian people; a bronze tablet recorded it in the temple of Castor at Rome.

battle.significance: Final field battle of the Latin War's first phase; ager Falernus annexed.

events.title: Leges Publiliae Philonis
events.summary: The plebeian dictator Q. Publilius Philo carried three laws: plebiscites to bind all citizens, the patrician senators' approval (patrum auctoritas) of centuriate laws to be given in advance, and one censor to be plebeian.
events.detail: The advance auctoritas turned a patrician veto into a formality, and was extended to elections by a lex Maenia of uncertain 3rd-century date. The plebiscite clause appears again in 287; whether the 339 law imposed conditions is debated.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 522-530
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 341-342

events.title: Battle of the Crimissus
events.summary: Timoleon of Corinth with about 12,000 men surprised a large Carthaginian army crossing the river Crimissus in western Sicily during a thunderstorm and destroyed it, including the 2,500-strong Sacred Band of Carthaginian citizens.
events.detail: The victory confirmed Timoleon's restoration of Greek Syracuse after the Dionysian tyranny and led to a treaty fixing the Halycus river as the Punic boundary. Plutarch and Diodorus date it to 341 or 339. Carthage afterwards relied more heavily on mercenaries rather than citizen troops abroad.
events.locName: River Crimissus, western Sicily (Belice or Freddo?)

sides.losses: 10,000 killed, 15,000 captured including the Sacred Band (Diodorus)

battle.significance: Halycus frontier; Greek revival in Sicily under Timoleon.

scholarship: Talbert, Timoleon and the Revival of Greek Sicily (1974)
events.debate: Year 341 or 339; river identity.

events.title: Battles of Pedum and the Astura
events.summary: The consul L. Furius Camillus defeated the last Latin army (Tiburtines, Praenestines, Veliterni, Lanuvini, Antiates) at Pedum while his colleague C. Maenius destroyed the Antiates and Lanuvini at the river Astura; both triumphed and received equestrian statues in the Forum.
events.detail: Camillus then took every Latin town by storm or surrender, ending the League's resistance and opening the way for the settlement of 338.

sides.strength: two consular armies (L. Furius Camillus, C. Maenius)

battle.significance: End of the Latin League as an independent power.

events.title: The settlement of 338: dissolution of the Latin League
events.summary: Rome dissolved the Latin League and dealt with each community separately: Lanuvium, Aricia, Nomentum and Pedum received full citizenship, Tusculum's was confirmed, Velitrae was punished, Antium became a citizen colony, Tibur and Praeneste remained allies minus land, and Capua, Fundi, Formiae, Cumae and Suessula received citizenship without the vote.
events.detail: The remaining Latins lost conubium, commercium and the right of assembly with one another, keeping these rights only with Rome. This divide-and-rule settlement created the graded system that underpinned Roman Italy: full citizens (cives optimo iure), citizens without suffrage (cives sine suffragio, with local self-government and military obligation), Latin colonies and allies (socii) bound by bilateral treaties to supply troops. It turned Rome from a city-state into a territorial state of perhaps 5,500 km2 and gave it a manpower base no Italian rival could match. Cornell calls it the true beginning of Roman imperialism.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 538-571
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 347-352
Sherwin-White, The Roman Citizenship (2nd ed. 1973) 38-58
events.debate: Whether civitas sine suffragio was a privilege or a burden at this date; the Campanian grant may be of 334 or 318.

events.title: The Rostra adorned with the beaks of Antium's ships
events.summary: The Antiate warships were burned or taken to Rome's dockyards, and their bronze beaks (rostra) were fixed to the speaker's platform in the Comitium, which thereafter took the name Rostra; a column was raised to C. Maenius.
events.detail: Antium, notorious for piracy, was forbidden the sea; a citizen colony was planted there. The Maenian column (columna Maenia) by the Comitium became a landmark where thieves and debtors were tried by the tresviri capitales. Maenius as censor in 318 added balconies (maeniana) over the Forum shops for watching games.

events.title: Citizen colony at Antium
events.summary: Antium received a garrison colony of Roman citizens (colonia maritima) while the Antiates were enrolled as citizens; in 317 they asked Rome for patroni to give them laws.
events.detail: One of the first coastal citizen colonies (with Ostia and later Tarracina 329, Minturnae and Sinuessa 296), small garrisons of c. 300 families guarding the coast and exempt from legionary service.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969) 70-81

events.title: Vestal Minucia buried alive; first plebeian praetor
events.summary: The Vestal Minucia, suspected for her elegant dress and convicted on a slave's evidence, was buried alive at the Campus Sceleratus by the Colline gate; the same year Q. Publilius Philo became the first plebeian praetor.
events.detail: Vestal executions cluster at moments of military or social crisis (483, 337, 266, 216, 114). Publilius Philo went on to be the first proconsul (326).
events.locName: Campus Sceleratus, by the Porta Collina

events.title: Latin colony at Cales
events.summary: After the Ausonian town of Cales was captured, 2,500 colonists were sent there, the first Latin colony founded after 338 and the first planted beyond Latium, controlling the route from Latium into northern Campania.
events.detail: The new-style Latin colony, with Latin rights but founded by Rome alone, became the principal instrument of Roman control: 19 more were founded by 263. Cales became famous for its black-gloss pottery (Calene ware) with relief medallions in the 3rd century.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969) 55-57

events.title: Alexander of Epirus campaigns in southern Italy
events.summary: Invited by Tarentum against the Lucanians and Messapians, Alexander the Molossian, uncle of Alexander the Great, campaigned from Apulia to Bruttium, took Heraclea, Sipontum, Consentia and Terina, and made a treaty of friendship with Rome (332).
events.detail: He fell out with Tarentum, planned to move the Italiote League's meeting place from Heraclea to Thurii, and was killed at Pandosia in 331. His campaign is the first of the great condottiere interventions (Cleonymus, Agathocles, Pyrrhus) that drew Rome into the affairs of Magna Graecia.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 665-690
Purcell, CAH VI2 (1994) ch. 9b

events.title: The 'dictator years' of the Varronian fasti
events.summary: The Fasti Capitolini insert four years (333, 324, 309, 301) in which a dictator and master of horse held office without consuls; Livy and the other annalists know nothing of them.
events.detail: They were almost certainly invented by Augustan-era (or late Republican) chronographers, together with the five-year anarchy of the 370s, to reconcile the Roman consular list with Greek synchronisms such as the sack of Rome in 387/386. As a result conventional Varronian dates before 300 are about four years too early relative to 'true' chronology: the Allia of 'Varronian 390' is probably 386. Modern handbooks retain Varronian dates for convenience while noting the problem. In this dataset all dates are Varronian.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 102-104
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 369-370
Drummond, CAH VII.2 (1989) 625-628
events.debate: The fictitious character of the dictator years is generally accepted; how the Varronian system arose is debated.

events.title: Tribus Maecia and Scaptia created
events.summary: Two new tribes on land confiscated from Latin cities in 338 brought the total to 29; the people of Acerrae received citizenship without vote.
events.detail: The Scaptia was probably on the old territory disputed between Ardea and Aricia (cf. P. Scaptius, 446).

events.title: Peace treaty with the Gauls
events.summary: Polybius records that after thirteen quiet years the Gauls, seeing Rome's growing power, made a formal peace, which they kept for thirty years until a new movement of Transalpine Gauls.
events.detail: Livy (8.20.2-3) reports that the Senones' threat in 329 proved empty. The treaty, probably with the Senones of the Adriatic coast, freed Rome to concentrate on the Samnites.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 185-186
events.debate: Exact date (c. 334-331).

events.title: The great poisoning trial of 331
events.summary: After many prominent men died of an apparent disease, a slave woman told the curule aedile Q. Fabius Maximus that matrons were brewing poisons; twenty were caught, two patrician women drank their own potions and died, and 170 were ultimately convicted.
events.detail: Livy reports it with reluctance as an act of 'madness' rather than malice; a dictator was named to drive the annual nail as expiation. It was the first trial for veneficium and resembles later mass prosecutions (Bacchanalia 186, poisonings 184 and 180).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 594-602

events.title: Death of Alexander of Epirus at Pandosia
events.summary: Alexander the Molossian, warned by Dodona to beware Pandosia and the Acheron (which he took to mean the places in Epirus), was trapped by Lucanians and Bruttians at the Italian Pandosia and killed crossing the river Acheron by a Lucanian exile.
events.detail: His body was mutilated and parts sent to Consentia; a woman of Consentia ransomed the remains and sent them to his wife Cleopatra (sister of Alexander the Great) and mother Olympias in Epirus.

battle.significance: Ends the first Epirote intervention in Italy.

events.title: Capture of Privernum
events.summary: Privernum, led by Vitruvius Vaccus of Fundi, revolted and was taken; when asked what punishment they deserved, a Privernate envoy replied 'what those deserve who think themselves worthy of liberty', and the Senate granted citizenship. A citizen colony of 300 was sent to Tarracina.
events.detail: Vaccus was executed, Privernum's walls demolished and its senate deported beyond the Tiber. The new tribe Oufentina (318) was formed partly on Privernate land.

sides.strength: two consular armies (L. Aemilius Mamercinus, C. Plautius Decianus)

battle.significance: Last Volscian revolt.

events.title: Latin colony at Fregellae
events.summary: Rome planted a Latin colony at Fregellae on the east bank of the Liris, on land the Samnites regarded as theirs, a provocation that helped cause the Second Samnite War.
events.detail: Fregellae was lost to the Samnites in 320, refounded in 313, and became one of the most prosperous Latin colonies until it revolted and was destroyed by the praetor L. Opimius in 125. Excavations have revealed its houses and a sanctuary of Aesculapius.
scholarship: Coarelli & Monti (eds.), Fregellae 1 (1998)
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 214-216

events.title: Siege of Neapolis and the first prorogation of command
events.summary: Q. Publilius Philo besieged Palaepolis and Neapolis, held by Samnite and Nolan garrisons; his command was extended into 326 'pro consule', the first prorogation of imperium, and the city was betrayed by the Greek leaders Charilaus and Nymphius.
events.detail: Neapolis received a favourable treaty (foedus aequum), supplying ships rather than troops, and remained a Greek city in name and language into the Empire. The prorogation became the key device for extending Roman commands beyond a year. The Samnite reaction to Rome's intervention was the formal start of the Second Samnite War; the Lucanians and Apulians allied with Rome in 326.

battle.significance: First promagistracy; Neapolis becomes a Roman ally.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 628-665
Frederiksen, Campania (1984) 208-212

events.title: Lex Poetelia Papiria: abolition of nexum
events.summary: After the moneylender L. Papirius flogged the debt-bondsman C. Publilius for refusing his advances, public outrage led to a law abolishing nexum: debtors could no longer pledge their persons, and creditors' claims lay against property, not bodies.
events.detail: Livy calls it 'a second beginning of liberty' for the plebs. Varro dates the law to the dictatorship of C. Poetelius (313). Its practical effect was to end debt-bondage as a labour supply, which several scholars (Finley, Hopkins) link to the growing use of chattel slaves captured in the Samnite wars.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 688-700
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 330-333
Finley, Ancient Slavery and Modern Ideology (1980)
events.debate: Date (326 or 313).

events.title: Battle of Imbrinium: Papirius Cursor and Fabius Rullianus
events.summary: While the dictator L. Papirius Cursor was in Rome renewing auspices, his master of horse Q. Fabius Rullianus attacked the Samnites at Imbrinium against orders and won; Papirius demanded his execution, and only the pleas of the army, Fabius' father and the people saved him.
events.detail: Livy cites Fabius Pictor here: Fabius burned the spoils so that the dictator could not use them in his triumph. The confrontation dramatises imperium versus popular appeal (provocatio) and the rivalry of two great generals of the Samnite wars.

battle.significance: Constitutional drama of dictatorial imperium.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998) 700-760

events.title: Alleged Roman embassy to Alexander the Great
events.summary: Arrian reports, citing Aristus and Asclepiades, that a Roman embassy reached Alexander at Babylon in 323 and that he foretold Rome's greatness; Arrian himself doubts it, noting that no Roman writer mentions it.
events.detail: Cleitarchus (per Pliny) also mentioned a Roman embassy. If real, it might relate to complaints about Antiate piracy (Strabo). Most scholars reject it as a later invention, though not all.

events.title: The Caudine Forks
events.summary: Deceived by Samnite soldiers disguised as shepherds into believing Luceria was under siege, the consuls T. Veturius Calvinus and Sp. Postumius Albinus marched through the Caudine pass, found both ends blocked, and surrendered their whole army to Gavius Pontius; the Romans passed under the yoke and gave 600 equites as hostages.
events.detail: Pontius' father Herennius advised either releasing the Romans unharmed or killing them all; his son chose the middle course of humiliation. The consuls swore a sponsio (personal guarantee), not a foedus. Livy claims the Senate repudiated it and handed over Postumius and the officers naked to the Samnites, Postumius kicking the fetial to make Rome's renewed war 'just' (since a Samnite had now struck a Roman), and that Rome won revenge at Luceria in 320. Many scholars (Salmon, Oakley) think the peace was in fact kept until 316, that Rome lost Fregellae and possibly Cales, and that the revenge narrative is patriotic fiction. The defeat drove military reform: Livy (8.8) and others associate the shift to manipular tactics and the scutum with the Samnite wars.
events.locName: Caudine Forks (Valle Caudina, between Arpaia and Montesarchio)

battle.significance: Greatest Roman humiliation of the Samnite wars; five-year peace; spur to Roman military reorganisation and the Via Appia strategy.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 1-160
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 225-232
events.debate: Site of the pass; whether the Senate repudiated the sponsio; historicity of Roman revenge in 320.

events.title: Recapture of Luceria (320)
events.summary: Livy has L. Papirius Cursor besiege and take Luceria, recover the 600 hostages and send 7,000 Samnites under the yoke in revenge for Caudium; Livy himself was unsure whether Papirius or Q. Aulius was in command.
events.detail: Probably a doublet of the genuine capture of Luceria in 314, when a Latin colony was founded. The Fasti Triumphales do record a triumph of Papirius over the Samnites in 319.

battle.significance: Patriotic revenge narrative; likely doublet.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 160-200
events.debate: Likely fictional or a doublet of 314.

events.title: Prefects for Capua; tribes Oufentina and Falerna
events.summary: Rome sent praefecti to Capua at the Campanians' request to give them laws, created the tribes Oufentina and Falerna (31 in all), and made alliances with Teanum Apulum and Canusium in Apulia.
events.detail: The praefecti Capuam Cumas, later elected, became the template for prefectures administering communities of cives sine suffragio. The Apulian alliances outflanked Samnium from the east.

events.title: Battle of Lautulae
events.summary: The dictator Q. Fabius Rullianus fought the Samnites at the Lautulae pass between Tarracina and Fundi; his master of horse Q. Aulius Cerretanus was killed, and Diodorus states plainly that the Romans were defeated, while Livy calls it indecisive.
events.detail: The defeat cut the coastal route to Campania and sparked a revolt among the Aurunci and part of the Campanian elite. Rome's response (Via Appia, colonies at Suessa, Pontiae, Interamna) was to secure the corridor permanently.
events.locName: Lautulae pass (Monte S. Biagio, near Terracina)

battle.significance: Samnites break into Latium; Campanian and Auruncan defections.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 290-310
events.debate: Livy's indecisive result vs Diodorus' Roman defeat.

events.title: Destruction of the Ausones
events.summary: The three Ausonian towns of Ausona, Minturnae and Vescia, which had joined the Samnites after Lautulae, were betrayed by young nobles and stormed at night; Livy says the Ausonian people were wiped out ('deleta Ausonum gens').
events.detail: Diodorus reports Roman victory near Tarracina in the same year. A Capuan conspiracy was investigated by the dictator C. Maenius; the Calavii brothers killed themselves. Roman citizen colonies followed at Minturnae and Sinuessa (296).

battle.significance: Annihilation of the Ausones; Liris corridor secured.

events.title: Latin colony at Luceria
events.summary: Captured Luceria received 2,500 Latin colonists, a bastion in northern Apulia behind Samnium, after the Senate debated destroying the town altogether.
events.detail: The far-flung Apulian colony embodied a strategy of encirclement. Luceria remained loyal during Hannibal's war and served as a base.

events.title: Colonies at Suessa Aurunca, Pontiae, Saticula and Interamna
events.summary: Latin colonies were founded at Suessa Aurunca and on the island of Pontiae (313), at Saticula (313) and at Interamna Lirenas (312), consolidating the Liris-Volturnus corridor; Fregellae was refounded.
events.detail: Together with Cales (334), Fregellae (328), Luceria (314) and the Via Appia (312), this ring of colonies isolated Samnium from Campania and Latium.
scholarship: Salmon, Roman Colonization under the Republic (1969)

events.title: Censorship of Appius Claudius Caecus
events.summary: Appius Claudius as censor enrolled sons of freedmen in the Senate, distributed the landless (humiles) across all tribes, built the Via Appia and Aqua Appia without senatorial approval, transferred the cult at the Ara Maxima from the gens Potitia to public slaves, and kept office beyond the 18-month limit.
events.detail: The consuls of 311 refused to recognise his Senate list. Legend said the Potitii died out within a year and Appius was later struck blind (hence Caecus). Modern views range from Appius as a 'popular' reformer seeking a clientele among the urban and commercial classes (Mommsen) to a Hellenising aristocrat building state infrastructure for war against Samnium (Humm, Oakley). His secretary Gnaeus Flavius published the legal formulas in 304.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus: la République accomplie (2005)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 349-415

events.title: Construction of the Via Appia
events.summary: Appius Claudius built the first great Roman highway, the Via Appia, 132 Roman miles from the Porta Capena to Capua, driving straight across the Alban Hills and the Pontine marshes (the 19-mile 'decennovium' stretch).
events.detail: Initially gravel (glarea); paving with basalt blocks came from 296 onward in sections. The road was a military lifeline to the newly won Campanian lands and the colonies on the Liris, avoiding the Lautulae pass. It was extended to Beneventum (after 268), Venusia and Tarentum, and Brundisium by the 190s. Statius called it 'regina viarum'.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)
Laurence, The Roads of Roman Italy (1999)

events.title: Construction of the Aqua Appia
events.summary: Rome's first aqueduct, built by Appius Claudius with his colleague C. Plautius (who found the springs, hence 'Venox'), ran 11,190 paces (c. 16.5 km), almost entirely underground, from springs off the Via Praenestina to the Forum Boarium.
events.detail: Only 60 paces near the Porta Capena ran on arches. Frontinus says Plautius resigned after 18 months but Appius remained in office to complete it and so the aqueduct bore his name alone. Its estimated daily discharge was some 73,000 m3 (Frontinus' 1,825 quinariae; conversions vary).
scholarship: Evans, Water Distribution in Ancient Rome (1994)
Ashby, The Aqueducts of Ancient Rome (1935)

events.title: Duoviri navales and elected military tribunes
events.summary: Plebiscites created two naval officers (duoviri navales) to equip and repair a fleet, and provided for 16 military tribunes for four legions to be elected by the people (lex Atilia Marcia).
events.detail: The duoviri navales attest a small Roman squadron, used in 310 for a raid on Nuceria from Pompeii that went badly, and in 282 off Tarentum. The four-legion army is standard from here on. The same year the guild of tibicines (flute-players), banned from feasting in the temple of Jupiter, went on strike and withdrew to Tibur until tricked back drunk in carts, a famous religious-comic episode (Ovid, Livy).
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 382-405

events.title: Battle of the Himeras river (Ecnomus)
events.summary: Hamilcar son of Gisgo defeated Agathocles of Syracuse near Gela at the Himeras river below the hill of Ecnomus; most Sicilian cities defected and Carthage besieged Syracuse.
events.detail: The defeat prompted Agathocles' audacious decision to carry the war to Africa.

battle.significance: Carthage besieges Syracuse; Agathocles invades Africa.

events.title: Etruscan siege of Sutrium
events.summary: With the end of the 40-year truce with Tarquinii, all the Etruscan cities except Arretium attacked the Roman colony at Sutrium; the consul Q. Aemilius Barbula and then Q. Fabius Rullianus defeated them before the walls.
events.detail: The siege opened the second front of the Second Samnite War and set up Fabius' march through the Ciminian forest.

battle.significance: Relief of the gateway colony of Etruria.

events.title: Agathocles invades Africa
events.summary: Blockaded in Syracuse, Agathocles slipped out with 60 ships and 14,000 men, landed on Cape Bon, burned his ships, and carried the war to Carthage's own territory for four years; a total solar eclipse on 15 August 310 BC occurred during the crossing.
events.detail: The eclipse (Diodorus 20.5.5, Justin 22.6) is a fixed point of Hellenistic chronology. Agathocles captured Tunis and dozens of towns, allied with Ophellas of Cyrene (whom he then murdered), and nearly took Carthage, which in panic sacrificed 200 noble children to Baal Hammon (Diodorus). The expedition collapsed in 307 when Agathocles abandoned his army, whose sons he left behind to be killed. It showed Rome that Carthage was vulnerable at home, a lesson applied by Regulus (256) and Scipio (204).
scholarship: Consolo Langher, Agatocle (2000)
Lancel, Carthage: A History (1995)

events.title: Fabius Rullianus crosses the Ciminian forest
events.summary: Q. Fabius Rullianus, after sending his brother, who had been educated at Caere and spoke Etruscan, to scout disguised as a shepherd, led his army through the dense Ciminian forest, until then 'more impassable than the forests of Germany were lately', and ravaged the untouched lands of central Etruria.
events.detail: The Senate, alarmed, sent envoys to forbid the crossing, but they arrived too late. The Camertes Umbri became Roman allies. Perusia, Cortona and Arretium sought a 30-year truce.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 450-500
Harris, Rome in Etruria and Umbria (1971)

events.title: Battle near Perusia
events.summary: Fabius defeated the Etruscan army near Perusia after crossing the Ciminian hills; Perusia, Cortona and Arretium, the leading cities of northern Etruria, asked for peace and received a 30-year truce.
events.detail: Livy reports another victory near Perusia in 309 (9.40.18-20), perhaps a doublet. Diodorus says Fabius' raid reached Umbria.

battle.significance: Thirty-year truce with the northern Etruscan cities.

events.debate: Possible doublet with 309.

events.title: First battle of Lake Vadimon
events.summary: The Etruscans, having raised an army under a lex sacrata (each man choosing a comrade), fought Rome at Lake Vadimon in the Tiber valley; Livy says it was the bloodiest Etruscan battle yet and broke the 'ancient wealth' of the Etruscans.
events.detail: Livy makes the dictator L. Papirius Cursor commander. The same small lake saw a decisive Roman victory over Etruscans and Boii in 283.
events.locName: Lake Vadimon (Laghetto di Bassano, near Orte)

sides.strength: Etruscan League army under lex sacrata

battle.significance: Breaks Etruscan League resistance; truces follow in 308.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 500-520

events.title: Battle of White Tunis
events.summary: Agathocles with about 13,500 men defeated a much larger Carthaginian citizen army under Hanno and Bomilcar near Tunis; Hanno fell and Bomilcar, contemplating a coup, withdrew.
events.detail: Carthage reacted with religious panic, sending offerings to Melqart at Tyre and sacrificing children. Bomilcar attempted a tyranny in 308 and was crucified.

battle.significance: Agathocles establishes himself in Africa.

events.title: Hernican revolt and citizenship for Anagnia
events.summary: Anagnia led the Hernici in revolt after Hernican volunteers were captured among Samnites; the consul Q. Marcius Tremulus crushed them, and Anagnia and others received citizenship without vote while the loyal Aletrium, Verulae and Ferentinum kept their autonomy and conubium by choice.
events.detail: Livy notes the loyal towns preferred their own laws to Roman citizenship, an important datum for how civitas sine suffragio was perceived. An equestrian statue of Marcius stood before the temple of Castor.

events.title: Third treaty between Rome and Carthage (the 'Philinus treaty')
events.summary: Livy records a third renewal of the Carthage treaty in 306; the pro-Carthaginian historian Philinus claimed a treaty by which Romans were to keep out of Sicily and Carthaginians out of Italy, which would make Rome's crossing to Messana in 264 a breach.
events.detail: Polybius denies such a treaty existed, saying no copy was in the archives. Modern opinion is split: many accept a 306 treaty with Philinus' spheres-of-influence clause (Cornell, Eckstein); others think Philinus misrepresented it or invented it. The issue bears directly on the 'war guilt' of the First Punic War.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 354-355
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998) 9-16
Serrati, 'Neptune's altars: the treaties between Rome and Carthage', CQ 56 (2006)
events.debate: Existence and content of the Philinus treaty.

events.title: Beginnings of Roman-Rhodian friendship
events.summary: Polybius says that by 167 Rhodes had cooperated with Rome for almost 140 years without a formal alliance, implying informal friendship from c. 306, perhaps tied to trade and anti-piracy interests.
events.detail: Rhodes had just resisted Demetrius Poliorcetes' great siege (305-304). The datum shows Rome's appearance in eastern Mediterranean diplomacy long before the Macedonian wars.

events.title: Battle of Bovianum
events.summary: Both consuls, L. Postumius Megellus and Ti. Minucius Augurinus, invaded Samnium; the Samnite commander Statius Gellius was captured, Bovianum (capital of the Pentri) was taken, and the Samnites sued for peace.
events.detail: Minucius died of wounds (or was replaced by M. Fulvius). Diodorus confirms the capture of Bovianum. Peace with the old treaty renewed followed in 304.

battle.significance: Ends the Second Samnite War.

events.title: End of the Second Samnite War
events.summary: The Samnites made peace and the old treaty was renewed; Rome emerged in control of Campania, the Liris valley and northern Apulia, with a girdle of colonies around Samnium.
events.detail: Treaties of alliance followed with the Marsi, Paeligni, Marrucini and Frentani (304) and the Vestini (302), extending Roman influence across the central Apennines to the Adriatic.

events.title: Annihilation of the Aequi
events.summary: After the Aequi refused Roman citizenship, the consuls P. Sempronius Sophus and P. Sulpicius Saverrio stormed 31 of their towns in 50 days, burning most and nearly exterminating the people.
events.detail: Livy's 'nomen Aequorum prope ad internecionem deletum' is followed by Latin colonies at Alba Fucens (303) and Carseoli (302 or 298) and a new tribe (Aniensis, 299) on their land. A scattered remnant, the Aequiculi, survived around Cliternia.
events.locName: Aequian highlands (upper Anio and Turano valleys)

battle.significance: End of the Aequi as a people.

events.title: Gnaeus Flavius publishes the legal formulas and calendar
events.summary: Cn. Flavius, son of a freedman and secretary to Appius Claudius, published the forms of legal action (legis actiones, the 'ius Flavianum') and posted the calendar of court days in the Forum, ending pontifical monopoly of legal knowledge; elected curule aedile, he dedicated a bronze shrine of Concord in the Graecostasis.
events.detail: Pliny says the shrine's inscription dated it 204 years after the dedication of the Capitoline temple, a key datum for the Capitoline era. Nobles snubbed him: when he visited a sick colleague, young nobles refused to rise, so he had his curule chair brought in. The publication, followed by the first public legal teaching of Ti. Coruncanius (c. 250s), began secular jurisprudence.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 607-650
Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)

events.title: Censorship of Q. Fabius Rullianus: urban tribes and the transvectio
events.summary: The censor Q. Fabius Rullianus confined the 'forensis turba' of freedmen and landless to the four urban tribes, reversing Appius Claudius, and instituted the annual parade of the equites on 15 July (transvectio equitum); for this he earned the cognomen Maximus.
events.detail: Confinement to four of 31 tribes minimised the voting power of the urban poor in tribal assemblies and remained the rule for freedmen (with variations) for the rest of the Republic.

events.title: Expedition of Cleonymus of Sparta
events.summary: Tarentum hired the Spartan prince Cleonymus against the Lucanians and Romans; he took Metapontum and campaigned among the Sallentini, was driven off by Roman forces according to Livy, then sailed up the Adriatic and was defeated by the Patavini near the Brenta.
events.detail: Livy, a Paduan, notes with pride that the prows of Cleonymus' ships still hung in Padua's temple of Juno. Diodorus places him in 303/302. The 'Lacinian treaty' between Rome and Tarentum may date from these years.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 41-60

events.title: Treaty with Tarentum: the Lacinian promontory clause
events.summary: Appian refers to 'ancient treaties' forbidding Roman ships to sail beyond the Lacinian promontory (Capo Colonna near Croton) into the Gulf of Tarentum; Rome's breach of this in 282 provoked the Tarentine attack.
events.detail: The date is unknown: c. 303 (after Cleonymus) is most often proposed, but the 330s (Alexander of Epirus) are possible.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 41-60
events.debate: Date of the treaty.

events.title: Latin colonies at Sora and Alba Fucens
events.summary: Rome sent 4,000 colonists to Sora on the upper Liris and 6,000 to Alba Fucens beside the Fucine lake in former Aequian land; Carseoli followed (302 per Velleius, 298 per Livy).
events.detail: Alba Fucens, with its 3 km polygonal walls and later Roman forum and basilica (Belgian excavations), became a prison for royal captives: Syphax, Perseus and Bituitus.

events.title: Lex Ogulnia: plebeians admitted to the priestly colleges
events.summary: The tribunes Q. and Cn. Ogulnius carried a law raising the pontiffs from four to eight and the augurs from four to nine, the new places reserved for plebeians.
events.detail: With this the last major patrician monopoly fell, apart from a few archaic priesthoods (rex sacrorum, the major flamines, the Salii) that stayed patrician. Livy gives Appius Claudius Caecus a speech against it and P. Decius Mus a speech for it. Control of the calendar, auspices and sacral law now passed to a mixed patricio-plebeian nobility; the first plebeian pontifex maximus, Ti. Coruncanius, followed c. 254.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 90-130
Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome I (1998) 64-68

events.title: Lex Valeria de provocatione (300)
events.summary: The consul M. Valerius Corvus carried a law forbidding magistrates to flog or execute a citizen who appealed to the people; Livy calls it the third such law, 'always brought by the same family'.
events.detail: Livy remarks that the only sanction was that violation would be 'improbe factum', a wicked act, showing how much early Roman law relied on social pressure. Most scholars regard this as the first historical lex de provocatione, the 509 and 449 laws being retrojections.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 130-145
Lintott, 'Provocatio', ANRW I.2 (1972)

events.title: Colony at Narnia; last tribes of the century
events.summary: After a long siege of the Umbrian town of Nequinum, Rome refounded it as the Latin colony of Narnia on a cliff above the Nar gorge, and created the tribes Aniensis and Teretina (33 in all).
events.detail: Narnia controlled the route into Umbria later followed by the Via Flaminia (220). The same year, Polybius says, Gauls joined by Etruscans plundered Roman territory and returned home unscathed.

events.title: Alliance with the Lucanians; outbreak of the Third Samnite War
events.summary: Lucanian envoys asked Rome for protection against a Samnite invasion and gave hostages; Rome ordered the Samnites out of Lucania, they refused, and the fetials declared war.
events.detail: The war rapidly widened into a coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls, the greatest challenge Rome had yet faced in Italy.

events.title: Campaign of L. Cornelius Scipio Barbatus
events.summary: The epitaph on Scipio Barbatus' sarcophagus in the Tomb of the Scipios claims he 'took Taurasia and Cisauna in Samnium, subdued all Lucania and brought back hostages'; Livy instead places the consul of 298 in Etruria fighting near Volaterrae.
events.detail: The peperino sarcophagus, now in the Vatican, with its Saturnian verse inscription (CIL I2 6-7) is the earliest substantial Roman elogium and a rare documentary check on Livy, revealing family claims and annalistic confusion side by side. Barbatus' son L. Scipio (cos. 259) took Corsica.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 154-170
Coarelli, 'Il sepolcro degli Scipioni', Dialoghi di Archeologia 6 (1972)
events.debate: Epitaph vs Livy.

events.title: Battle near Tifernum
events.summary: Q. Fabius Rullianus, consul for the fourth time, defeated a Samnite army that had tried to ambush him in a valley near Tifernum, while his colleague P. Decius Mus beat the Apulians at Maleventum.
events.detail: Livy offers the usual inflated casualty figures (3,400 killed, 830 captured, 23 standards). The location of Tifernum in Samnium (perhaps the Matese massif or the upper Biferno) is uncertain.

battle.significance: Roman pressure on central Samnium.

events.title: Appius Claudius Caecus vows the Temple of Bellona
events.summary: In a battle against Etruscans and Samnites Appius Claudius vowed a temple to Bellona, later built near the Circus Flaminius outside the pomerium; its anniversary was 3 June.
events.detail: Before the temple stood the columna bellica, over which the fetial hurled a spear into a plot deemed 'enemy territory' to declare war on distant foes; the Senate met there to receive returning generals and foreign envoys. Appius' elogium credits him with the vow.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Gellius Egnatius forms the anti-Roman coalition
events.summary: The Samnite leader Gellius Egnatius led an army north through the Apennines into Etruria and organised a grand coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls against Rome.
events.detail: The strategic boldness of the plan is clear even through Livy's narrative: by uniting Rome's enemies north of the Tiber with the Samnites, Egnatius aimed to force Rome to fight on one decisive field against superior numbers. The Roman response was to raise perhaps six legions and arm freedmen.
scholarship: Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 263-268

events.title: The Ogulnii set up the she-wolf and twins
events.summary: The curule aediles Cn. and Q. Ogulnius, using fines from moneylenders, set up statues of the infant Romulus and Remus under the she-wolf at the Ficus Ruminalis, placed bronze thresholds and vessels on the Capitol, and paved the road from the Porta Capena to the temple of Mars.
events.detail: The first securely dated monument of the twins legend, which appears on Romano-Campanian silver didrachms c. 269. (The Capitoline Wolf bronze, long thought Etruscan, has been radiocarbon-dated to the Middle Ages, and the twins were added in the Renaissance.) The same year a patrician woman, Verginia, excluded from the cult of Pudicitia Patricia for marrying a plebeian, founded an altar of Pudicitia Plebeia in her house on the Vicus Longus.
events.locName: Ficus Ruminalis by the Lupercal, Rome
scholarship: Wiseman, Remus: A Roman Myth (1995)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 250-270

events.title: Citizen colonies at Minturnae and Sinuessa
events.summary: Two small coastal citizen colonies of 300 families each were planted at Minturnae on the Liris mouth and at Sinuessa on the Massic coast, in former Ausonian land, though recruits were hard to find.
events.detail: Minturnae's castrum-style rectangular fort (c. 2.5 ha) is a classic example of the 'coloniae maritimae'; Marius hid in its marshes in 88.

events.title: Destruction of a Roman legion near Camerinum
events.summary: Before Sentinum, the Senones (with Samnites) annihilated a Roman legion under the propraetor L. Cornelius Scipio; Polybius places it near Camerinum, Livy near Clusium, and Livy notes some sources said the Gauls rode off with heads on their spears and hanging from their horses' chests.
events.detail: The disaster revealed the size of the coalition and caused the Romans to concentrate both consuls, Fabius and Decius, with four legions in Umbria.

sides.strength: one legion under L. Cornelius Scipio

battle.significance: Prelude to Sentinum.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 280-300
events.debate: Camerinum (Polybius) or Clusium (Livy).

events.title: Battle of Sentinum
events.summary: At Sentinum in Umbria the consuls Q. Fabius Rullianus and P. Decius Mus, with four legions and as many allies, defeated the Samnites under Gellius Egnatius and the Senonian Gauls; when Gallic chariots broke the Roman left, Decius devoted himself like his father, and the line held.
events.detail: Livy's figures (25,000 enemy dead, 8,000 captured; Romans 8,700 killed) are among the more plausible in his narrative. Duris of Samos, a contemporary, wrote that 100,000 died, the first Roman battle reported in a Greek historian. Fabius' wing wore down the Samnites, then took the Gauls in the rear; Gellius Egnatius fell. Diversionary attacks on Etruria had already drawn the Etruscans and Umbrians home. Fabius vowed a temple to Jupiter Victor. Sentinum decided the fate of Italy: the coalition never re-formed, and within 25 years Rome controlled the peninsula.

battle.significance: Decisive battle for the mastery of Italy; collapse of the Samnite-Gallic-Etruscan coalition.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 285-345
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 268-270
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 359-362

events.title: Temple of Venus Obsequens built from fines on adulteresses
events.summary: Q. Fabius Gurges as curule aedile fined matrons convicted of adultery (stuprum) and used the money to build a temple of Venus Obsequens near the Circus Maximus, Rome's first temple of Venus.
events.detail: The aedile's role in policing sexual morality and funding public buildings from fines is typical of the period (cf. the Ogulnii, 296). The same year the Fasti record plague and prodigies.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Victoria on the Palatine
events.summary: L. Postumius Megellus dedicated the temple of Victory on the Palatine, built as aedile from fines; in 204 the black stone of Magna Mater was housed there until her own temple was ready next door.
events.detail: The cult of the personified goddess Victoria reflects Hellenistic influence (Nike) at the height of the Samnite wars. Remains on the south-west Palatine have been identified.
scholarship: Ziolkowski, The Temples of Mid-Republican Rome (1992)

events.title: Battle of Aquilonia
events.summary: The consul L. Papirius Cursor (son of the dictator) crushed the Samnite 'linen legion' at Aquilonia, while his colleague Sp. Carvilius took Cominium; the Samnites had sworn its 16,000 picked men by gruesome oaths in a linen-roofed enclosure, executing those who refused.
events.detail: When the sacred chickens would not eat, the pullarius lied that the omens were favourable; Papirius said the falsehood fell on the reporter's head, and the man was killed by a stray javelin at the start of the battle. Papirius vowed a cup of mead to Jupiter Victor if he won. Livy's account of the Samnite oath (an old priest named Ovius Paccius, a ritual from ancient linen books) is consistent with Oscan religious practice. Papirius' triumph displayed 2,533,000 pounds of bronze from the sale of captives and 1,830 pounds of silver. The site is disputed (Monte Vairano near Campobasso, or near Lacedonia).

battle.significance: Final great field battle of the Samnite wars.

scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005) 380-440
Salmon, Samnium and the Samnites (1967) 182-186

events.title: Temple of Quirinus and Rome's first sundial
events.summary: L. Papirius Cursor dedicated the temple of Quirinus vowed by his father and decorated it with Samnite spoils; Pliny, citing Fabius Vestalis, says he set up the first sundial in Rome there.
events.detail: Pliny records an alternative tradition that the first sundial was brought from Catana in Sicily by M'. Valerius Messalla in 263, wrongly calibrated for Rome's latitude yet used for 99 years. The temple on the Quirinal was rebuilt by Augustus with 76 columns.

events.title: Census of 293: 262,321 citizens
events.summary: Livy records 262,321 citizens counted in the census of 293, the first of the mid-Republican figures generally treated as broadly reliable (adult males, including cives sine suffragio).
events.detail: Later figures: 287,222 (280/279), 271,224 (275), 292,234 (265). The dip after the Pyrrhic war suggests real losses. Rome's citizen manpower, plus the obligation of Latin and allied communities to send troops, gave it a military reserve of several hundred thousand by 225 (Polybius 2.24).
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower 225 BC - AD 14 (1971) 13-14
Scheidel, 'Human mobility in Roman Italy I', JRS 94 (2004)

events.title: Aesculapius brought from Epidaurus to the Tiber Island
events.summary: After a three-year plague and consultation of the Sibylline Books (293), envoys under Q. Ogulnius sailed to Epidaurus; a sacred snake boarded their ship and, at Rome, slipped overboard onto the Tiber Island, where a temple to Aesculapius was dedicated on 1 January.
events.detail: The island sanctuary became Rome's healing centre: sick slaves abandoned there were declared free by Claudius if they recovered. In the 1st century BC the island was faced with travertine in the shape of a ship, with a carved snake-and-staff relief still visible at its prow. The episode marks the culmination of the 4th-3rd century importation of Greek cults.
scholarship: Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome I (1998) 69-70

events.title: Execution of Gavius Pontius
events.summary: Q. Fabius Gurges, after a defeat retrieved with help from his father Rullianus as legate, beat the Samnites and led the captured C. Pontius in his triumph; Pontius, probably the Caudine victor (or his son), was then beheaded.
events.detail: Known only from the Livian epitome and late sources, the execution became a stock example of Roman ruthlessness, criticised as unworthy by later writers. Rullianus rode as legate beside his son's chariot.
events.debate: Whether the executed Pontius is the Caudine commander.

events.title: Latin colony at Venusia
events.summary: Rome founded at Venusia, on the border of Samnium, Apulia and Lucania, a Latin colony that Dionysius says numbered 20,000 colonists, the largest ever, splitting the Samnites from their southern neighbours.
events.detail: The figure may include families. Venusia controlled the Ofanto valley route to Tarentum; it sheltered survivors of Cannae in 216 and was the birthplace of Horace. The consul L. Postumius Megellus was later prosecuted for using his soldiers to clear his own estates.

events.title: Manius Curius conquers the Sabines and Praetuttii
events.summary: The consul M'. Curius Dentatus overran the Sabine country and the Praetuttii to the Adriatic in a single campaign; the Sabines received citizenship without vote (full citizenship in 268), and Rome's territory now crossed Italy from sea to sea.
events.detail: Curius allegedly boasted he had taken so much land that it would have been a desert, and so many men that they would have starved, had he not taken both. He refused more than the seven iugera allotted to each settler, saying a man not content with seven iugera was a dangerous citizen. Peace was concluded with the Samnites the same year, ending the Third Samnite War.
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 334-335

events.title: Curius drains the Lacus Velinus (Cascata delle Marmore)
events.summary: Curius Dentatus cut a channel through the travertine sill at Marmore to drain the Lacus Velinus near Reate into the Nar, creating the artificial waterfalls still known as the Cascata delle Marmore and reclaiming the plain of Rosea.
events.detail: The diversion caused centuries of litigation between Reate and Interamna (Terni) over flooding; Cicero represented Reate before a commission in 54 BC. Some date the work to Curius' censorship of 272.
events.debate: Date 290 or 272.

events.title: Latin colony at Hadria
events.summary: Hadria (Atri) in Praetuttian territory was made a Latin colony near the Adriatic, consolidating Curius' conquests; Castrum Novum on the coast may date from the same years.
events.detail: Hadria later minted its own heavy cast bronze (aes grave) with the legend HAT, and was the ancestral home of the emperor Hadrian's family.

events.title: Beginnings of Roman coinage: aes grave and the tresviri monetales
events.summary: The board of three moneyers (tresviri aere argento auro flando feriundo) is traditionally dated c. 289, around the time Rome began casting heavy bronze coins (aes grave) on a libral standard, after centuries of using raw bronze by weight (aes rude) and cast bars (aes signatum).
events.detail: The first Roman silver didrachms, with the legend ROMANO and types such as Mars/horse head, were struck c. 310-300 (Crawford dates the first to c. 280), probably at Neapolis or another Campanian mint, for use in the south. A Pomponius passage in the Digest dates the moneyers to the same reform as the tresviri capitales (c. 290). Coinage at Rome was thus a by-product of conquest and contact with the Greek south, not an archaic institution.
events.locName: Rome (mint by the temple of Juno Moneta, Arx)
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974) 35-46
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987) 1-15
events.debate: Exact date of the first moneyers and coins.

events.title: Mamertines seize Messana
events.summary: Campanian mercenaries discharged after Agathocles' death, calling themselves Mamertini ('sons of Mars'), were admitted to Messana as guests, massacred or expelled the men, took their wives and property, and made the city a base for raiding north-east Sicily.
events.detail: Their appeal to Rome (and to Carthage) in 264 against Hiero II of Syracuse triggered the First Punic War. Oscan-language coins of the Mamertines (legend MAMERTINΩN) and inscriptions survive.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 52-53
events.debate: Date 289 or 288.
tags: road to the First Punic War

events.title: Lex Hortensia and the last secession of the plebs
events.summary: After a debt crisis drove the plebs to secede to the Janiculum, the plebeian dictator Q. Hortensius carried a law making plebiscites binding on the whole Roman people without further sanction; the concilium plebis became Rome's main legislative body.
events.detail: The law is often called the formal end of the Struggle of the Orders. Pliny adds that it made the nundinae (market days) court days (fasti), so country people coming to market could settle lawsuits. Hortensius died in office. Most later Republican legislation, from the lex Aquilia (c. 286) to the Gracchan laws, passed as plebiscites. Paradoxically, the 'victory' integrated tribunes into the senatorial governing class, the arrangement that held until 133. Our sources are thin: the relevant books of Livy are lost and only the Periochae, Pliny and Gellius (citing the jurist Laelius Felix) survive.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 341-344
Hölkeskamp, Die Entstehung der Nobilität (1987)
Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 349-350
tags: end of the Struggle of the Orders

events.title: Battle of Arretium
events.summary: Senones, joined by Etruscans, besieged Rome's ally Arretium; the relieving army was destroyed and the praetor (or consul) L. Caecilius Metellus Denter killed with 13,000 men. Roman envoys sent to the Senones about prisoners were murdered.
events.detail: Polybius dates it ten years after Sentinum; Livy's epitome places it in 283 and Orosius gives the figure of 13,000 dead and 7 military tribunes. M'. Curius Dentatus, as replacement, then ravaged the Senonian lands.

battle.significance: Provokes the Roman destruction of the Senones.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 187-188
Williams, Beyond the Rubicon (2001)
events.debate: Year 284 or 283; Metellus praetor or consul.

events.title: Expulsion of the Senones; colony at Sena Gallica
events.summary: Rome invaded the ager Gallicus, killed or expelled the Senones, and planted a citizen colony at Sena Gallica on the Adriatic coast, the first Roman colony on Gallic land.
events.detail: Polybius says the Romans 'drove out the Senones and became masters of their country'. The ager Gallicus remained public land until C. Flaminius distributed it in 232, a step Polybius saw as a cause of the great Gallic war of 225.
events.locName: Sena Gallica (Senigallia) and the ager Gallicus

events.title: Second battle of Lake Vadimon
events.summary: Alarmed by the fate of the Senones, the Boii joined the Etruscans and marched on Rome; the consul P. Cornelius Dolabella annihilated them at Lake Vadimon, where, Polybius says, most of the Etruscans were cut down and very few Boii escaped.
events.detail: Pliny, citing the same lake, describes its floating islands. The victory ended the Etruscan cities' capacity for coordinated resistance.

sides.losses: most Etruscans killed; few Boii escaped

battle.significance: Ends the last Etruscan-Gallic coalition.

events.title: Battle near Populonia
events.summary: The Boii, with Etruscans, raised another army of young men the following year and were defeated again; they then sued for peace, which they kept for 45 years.
events.detail: Polybius gives no location; later accounts (Dio/Zonaras) place a defeat of Etruscans and Gauls near Populonia, the Etruscan iron-smelting port opposite Elba, under Q. Aemilius Papus.

sides.strength: consular army of Q. Aemilius Papus

battle.significance: Peace with the Boii for 45 years.

events.debate: Location.

events.title: Fabricius relieves Thurii
events.summary: Thurii, besieged by the Lucanians and Bruttians, appealed to Rome rather than Tarentum; the consul C. Fabricius Luscinus defeated the besiegers, and Rome garrisoned Thurii, Locri, Rhegium and Croton.
events.detail: The Thurians set up a statue and a golden crown for Fabricius. Rome's emergence as protector of Greek cities in the Gulf of Tarentum, against the Lacinian treaty, alarmed Tarentum.

battle.significance: Rome intervenes among the Italiote Greeks.

events.title: Tarentum attacks a Roman squadron and insults Rome's envoy
events.summary: Ten Roman ships under the duumvir L. Valerius sailed into the Gulf of Tarentum; the Tarentines, watching in their theatre, attacked, sank four and killed the commander, then expelled the Roman garrison from Thurii. When L. Postumius Megellus came to demand redress, his Greek was mocked and a drunk soiled his toga; he said the stain would be washed out in blood.
events.detail: The theatre scene and the toga story are later embellishments (Dionysius, Appian, Dio), but the casus belli is secure. In 281 the consul L. Aemilius Barbula ravaged Tarentine territory, and the Tarentines invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, who had earlier received Tarentine help.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

events.title: Tarentum invites Pyrrhus
events.summary: Facing the consul L. Aemilius Barbula's army, Tarentum and its Italian allies invited Pyrrhus of Epirus, offering a combined force of 350,000 foot and 20,000 horse (a boast); Pyrrhus sent Milo ahead with 3,000 men to garrison the citadel.
events.detail: Pyrrhus, recently expelled from Macedon and seeking a western empire, obtained ships from Antigonus Gonatas, money from Antiochus I and 5,000 Macedonian infantry plus elephants on loan from Ptolemy Keraunos for two years. Plutarch's dialogue between Pyrrhus and Cineas ('and then we shall rest') dates from this moment.
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Garoufalias, Pyrrhus, King of Epirus (1979)

events.title: The Campanian legion seizes Rhegium
events.summary: A Roman garrison of 4,000 Campanian citizen-soldiers under Decius Vibellius, sent to protect Rhegium against Pyrrhus, imitated the Mamertines across the strait, massacred or expelled the men and took the city for themselves.
events.detail: Rome could do nothing during the Pyrrhic War; the city was recaptured in 270.

events.title: Battle of Heraclea
events.summary: Pyrrhus defeated the consul P. Valerius Laevinus on the plain between Heraclea and Pandosia by the river Siris; the Roman cavalry and legions held the phalanx through seven charges until Pyrrhus' 20 elephants, never seen before by Romans, panicked the horses.
events.detail: Pyrrhus was nearly killed, having exchanged armour with his companion Megacles, who fell. Losses: Hieronymus of Cardia (via Plutarch) gives 7,000 Romans and just under 4,000 Pyrrhic dead; Dionysius gives 15,000 and 13,000. Lucanians, Bruttians, Messapians and Greek cities joined Pyrrhus; Locri expelled its Roman garrison. The Romans called the elephants 'Lucanian oxen' (boves Lucae). Pyrrhus was impressed by the Roman camp and order ('the discipline of these barbarians is not barbarous').
events.locName: Plain of the Siris near Heraclea (Policoro)

sides.strength: c. 25,000-30,000 including 20 elephants, Macedonian phalanx, Thessalian cavalry, Tarentines

battle.significance: First clash of legion and Hellenistic phalanx; first Roman encounter with war elephants.

scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 317-340
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

events.title: Pyrrhus marches on Rome
events.summary: After Heraclea, Pyrrhus advanced through Campania (failing to take Capua and Neapolis) up the Via Latina to Anagnia or Praeneste, perhaps within 60 km of Rome, but finding Laevinus reinforced and Coruncanius' army back from Etruria, he withdrew to winter in Tarentum.
events.detail: Plutarch says he came within 300 stades (c. 55 km) of Rome; Eutropius has him reach Praeneste. No Latin colony or ally defected, the first demonstration that Rome's Italian system held under pressure.

events.title: Cineas' embassy and the speech of Appius Claudius
events.summary: Pyrrhus sent his Thessalian orator Cineas to Rome with gifts and offers of peace if Rome left the Italiote Greeks free; as the Senate wavered, the old, blind Appius Claudius Caecus had himself carried to the Curia and declared Rome would not negotiate while a foreign army stood in Italy.
events.detail: Cicero knew a written version of the speech, the earliest Roman oration preserved in his day, and Ennius versified it ('quo vobis mentes, rectae quae stare solebant antehac, dementes sese flexere viai?'). Cineas reported that the Senate seemed to him an assembly of kings and that fighting Rome was like fighting a hydra. Fabricius led a counter-embassy about prisoners, refusing Pyrrhus' gifts; Pyrrhus released prisoners on parole for the Saturnalia, and all returned. Chronology (280 or 279) is debated.
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus (2005)
Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
events.debate: Date and sequence of embassies (280 or after Ausculum in 279).

events.title: Battle of Ausculum
events.summary: Pyrrhus fought the consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus over two days in rough ground near Ausculum in Apulia; on the second day he forced a battle on the plain and won, but at such cost that he reportedly said 'one more such victory and we are finished', the origin of 'Pyrrhic victory'.
events.detail: Hieronymus (via Plutarch) gives 6,000 Roman and 3,505 Pyrrhic dead; Dionysius gives a detailed order of battle with Italian and Greek contingents. Romans used anti-elephant wagons with spikes and fire-pots. A tradition (Cicero) has the third Decius Mus devote himself like his father and grandfather; Zonaras says Pyrrhus warned the Romans he would take Decius alive, and other sources say he survived. Pyrrhus was wounded by a javelin.

sides.strength: four legions plus allies, c. 40,000 (consuls P. Sulpicius Saverrio and P. Decius Mus)

battle.significance: The proverbial 'Pyrrhic victory'; Pyrrhus turns to Sicily.

scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 370-392
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)
events.debate: Third Decian devotio; outcome (Roman sources claim a draw or victory).

events.title: Fourth treaty between Rome and Carthage (against Pyrrhus)
events.summary: A Carthaginian admiral, Mago, arrived at Ostia with 120 ships to offer help; the resulting treaty, quoted by Polybius, renewed the earlier ones and provided that if either made an alliance with Pyrrhus it should reserve the right to help the other, with Carthage supplying ships for transport and combat but no obligation for crews to fight on land against their will.
events.detail: The Senate declined immediate naval help (Justin), but the treaty kept Rome and Carthage aligned while Pyrrhus turned to Sicily. A Carthaginian fleet ferried 500 Romans to Rhegium and burned timber Pyrrhus had collected.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 349-351
Hoyos, Unplanned Wars (1998)

events.title: Fabricius returns Pyrrhus' would-be poisoner
events.summary: Pyrrhus' physician (named Nicias or Cineas in some sources) offered the consul Fabricius to poison the king; Fabricius sent him back to Pyrrhus with a letter, and Pyrrhus released his Roman prisoners without ransom.
events.detail: An exemplum of Roman fides retold endlessly (Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Plutarch, Gellius citing Claudius Quadrigarius' text of the letter). It eased negotiations before Pyrrhus departed for Sicily.

events.title: Pyrrhus crosses to Sicily
events.summary: Invited by Syracuse, Acragas and Leontini against Carthage, which was besieging Syracuse, Pyrrhus left Milo in Tarentum and sailed with c. 8,000 foot and elephants from Locri to Tauromenium and Catana, lifted the siege of Syracuse and was hailed hegemon and king of Sicily.
events.detail: His claim rested partly on his marriage to Lanassa, daughter of Agathocles, and on his son Alexander, Agathocles' grandson. The Syracusan factions of Thoenon and Sosistratus handed him the city and its fleet of some 120-140 ships.

events.title: Pyrrhus storms Eryx
events.summary: Pyrrhus stormed the Carthaginian mountain stronghold of Eryx, being himself first onto the walls in Homeric style, and celebrated games to Heracles as he had vowed; Panormus also fell.
events.detail: By the end of 277 only Lilybaeum remained in Carthaginian hands. Eryx would later be the scene of Hamilcar Barca's long resistance (244-241).

battle.significance: Carthage reduced to Lilybaeum.

events.title: Pyrrhus fails before Lilybaeum
events.summary: Carthage, supplied by sea, offered Pyrrhus money and ships for peace; he demanded they evacuate Sicily entirely, then failed in a two-month siege of the impregnable sea-fortress of Lilybaeum.
events.detail: Pyrrhus then planned to invade Africa, demanded rowers and money from the Sicilian Greeks, and executed Thoenon; the cities turned against him, some inviting back the Carthaginians or Mamertines.

battle.significance: Turning point of Pyrrhus' Sicilian venture.

events.title: Naval battle in the Strait of Messina
events.summary: Recalled by his Italian allies, Pyrrhus sailed back to Italy and was attacked in the strait by a Carthaginian fleet, losing many ships; landing, he was harassed by 10,000 Mamertines, then took Locri and plundered the treasury of Persephone to pay his troops.
events.detail: A storm wrecked the ships carrying the temple treasure, which washed up at Locri; Pyrrhus, terrified, restored it (Dionysius, Livy 29.18 for the Locrian tradition). Pyrrhus' parting remark on Sicily, 'what a wrestling ground we leave for Carthaginians and Romans', is recorded by Plutarch.

sides.losses: many ships sunk or disabled (Plutarch: 70 ruined)

battle.significance: Pyrrhus returns to Italy weakened.

events.title: Battle of Beneventum (Maleventum)
events.summary: Pyrrhus attempted a night march to surprise the consul M'. Curius Dentatus near Maleventum, but lost his way in wooded hills and arrived at dawn exhausted; Curius drove back his troops and stampeded elephants into his own lines, and Pyrrhus abandoned Italy.
events.detail: Curius' triumph in 275 featured four captured elephants, the first seen in Rome, and spoils that paid for the Anio Vetus aqueduct. Ancient sources disagree whether it was a decisive defeat (Roman tradition) or a drawn engagement (Plutarch implies a Roman success but not a rout). Maleventum was renamed Beneventum as a better omen when colonised in 268. Pyrrhus left Milo in Tarentum and sailed home with 8,000 foot and 500 horse.

sides.strength: c. 20,000-25,000 with elephants and Samnite allies

battle.significance: Ends Pyrrhus' Italian venture; Rome becomes master of southern Italy.

scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957) 505-520
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)
events.debate: Decisiveness of the battle.

events.title: Census of 275 and the expulsion of Rufinus
events.summary: The census of 275 counted 271,224 citizens, down from 287,222 in 280/279; the censor C. Fabricius Luscinus expelled the twice-consul P. Cornelius Rufinus from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate.
events.detail: Rufinus, a capable general who had taken Croton in 277, was ancestor of Sulla. The anecdote became a staple of Roman moral nostalgia about early austerity, but it also shows that luxury silver was entering Rome with Greek contact.

events.title: Ptolemy II establishes friendship with Rome
events.summary: Impressed by Rome's defeat of Pyrrhus, Ptolemy II Philadelphus sent an embassy to Rome and a treaty of friendship (amicitia) was made; Rome returned an embassy of Q. Fabius Gurges, N. Fabius Pictor and Q. Ogulnius, who refused Ptolemy's personal gifts and deposited them in the treasury.
events.detail: The first formal Roman relationship with a Hellenistic great power. Lycophron's Alexandra, perhaps of these years (or a later interpolation), speaks of the descendants of Aeneas winning 'the sceptre and monarchy of land and sea'.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984) 673-678

events.title: Latin colonies at Paestum and Cosa; Caere punished
events.summary: Rome founded Latin colonies at Paestum (Greek Poseidonia, long ruled by Lucanians) and at Cosa on the Etruscan coast, on territory taken from Vulci; Caere lost half its territory after an abortive revolt.
events.detail: Cosa, excavated by the American Academy (F. E. Brown), is the type-site of the Latin colony: hilltop polygonal walls, grid, forum and Capitolium, harbour below. At Paestum the colonists built a forum and comitium beside the old Greek temples.
scholarship: Brown, Cosa: The Making of a Roman Town (1980)
Fentress (ed.), Cosa V (2003)

events.title: Death of Pyrrhus at Argos
events.summary: After a failed attack on Sparta, Pyrrhus fought his way into Argos at night; in the street fighting an old woman threw a roof tile from a housetop, stunning him, and a soldier of Antigonus Gonatas beheaded him.
