events.summary: Philip V sent Xenophanes of Athens to Hannibal and concluded an alliance. Polybius preserves the oath text, sworn before Zeus, Hera, Apollo, the daimon of Carthage, Heracles, Iolaus and other gods: mutual help, and if Rome made peace it must give up Corcyra, Apollonia, Epidamnus, Pharos, Dimale, the Parthini and Atintania, and restore Demetrius of Pharos' friends.
events.detail: The envoys were captured by the Roman fleet on their way back, revealing the treaty. Rome kept a fleet in the Adriatic under Marcus Valerius Laevinus, leading to the First Macedonian War. Livy's version (23.33), in which Philip promised to invade Italy and receive Greece, is generally considered annalistic exaggeration.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)
Barré, The God-List in the Treaty between Hannibal and Philip V (1983)
events.debate: The oath's god list appears to be a Greek rendering of a Punic formula and is valuable evidence for Carthaginian religion. Polybius' and Livy's terms differ substantially.

events.title: Death of Hiero II; Syracuse turns to Carthage
events.summary: Hiero II died at over ninety after 54 years of rule, his loyalty to Rome unshaken. His fifteen-year-old grandson Hieronymus switched to Carthage, was assassinated in 214 at Leontini, and in the turmoil the pro-Carthaginian Hippocrates and Epicydes, Syracusans born in Carthage, seized power.

events.title: Battle of Dertosa (Ibera)
events.summary: The Scipio brothers defeated Hasdrubal Barca near Ibera on the Ebro as he prepared to march to Italy. Hasdrubal used Hannibal's Cannae formation, but his weak Spanish centre broke first and the battle was a rout.
events.detail: Livy (23.28-29) is the only source. The victory prevented reinforcements reaching Hannibal for eight years and kept the Spanish front alive, one of the turning points of the war.

battle.significance: Stopped Hasdrubal's first attempt to join Hannibal.

events.debate: Date (215 or 216) and details rest only on Livy.

events.title: Hampsicora's revolt in Sardinia
events.summary: Sardinian chieftains under Hampsicora rose with Carthaginian help. Titus Manlius Torquatus defeated them and a Carthaginian force under Hasdrubal the Bald near Cornus; Hampsicora's son Hiostus was killed and Hampsicora took his own life.

sides.strength: c. 22,000 foot, 1,200 horse under T. Manlius Torquatus
Sardinians and a Carthaginian expeditionary force

battle.significance: Kept Sardinia, a grain source, in Roman hands.

events.title: Battle of Beneventum and the freeing of the volones
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, commanding legions largely of slave volunteers (volones), defeated Hanno near Beneventum after promising freedom to any who brought back an enemy head. He freed them all on the field; the feast that followed was painted on the walls of the temple of Libertas on the Aventine.

battle.significance: Showed that slave soldiers could fight; Livy's moralising set-piece on Roman freedom.

events.title: Philip V's failure at Apollonia
events.summary: Philip V sailed into the Adriatic with 120 lembi, took Oricum and besieged Apollonia. The praetor Marcus Valerius Laevinus retook Oricum and sent Quintus Naevius Crista into Apollonia, who surprised Philip's camp at night. Philip burned his ships at the mouth of the Aous and retreated overland, half-naked.

sides.strength: 2,000 men under Q. Naevius Crista plus fleet

battle.significance: Ended Philip's hopes of crossing to Italy.

events.debate: Only Livy narrates this; Polybius' account is lost.

events.title: Siege of Syracuse
events.summary: Marcellus and Appius Claudius Pulcher besieged Syracuse by land and sea. Archimedes' engines, catapults graded for range, cranes that lifted ships by the bow and dropped them, and the 'claw', repelled every assault. Marcellus settled for a blockade and in 212, during a festival of Artemis, scaled a weakly guarded stretch of the Epipolae walls. The island citadel of Ortygia fell later that year; Archimedes was killed by a Roman soldier in the sack.
events.detail: Polybius (8.3-7) and Plutarch (Marcellus 14-19) describe the engines; the legend that Archimedes burned Roman ships with mirrors first appears in much later writers (Lucian, Galen, Zonaras) and is doubted. Cicero found Archimedes' neglected tomb, marked with a sphere and cylinder, when quaestor in 75. Marcellus shipped the city's art to Rome, which Livy (25.40) calls the beginning of Roman admiration for Greek art and of the plundering of temples.

sides.strength: city militia, mercenaries and Carthaginian reinforcements under Himilco

battle.significance: Removed the last independent Greek power in Sicily and made the whole island Roman; began the flood of Greek art into Rome.

events.debate: Livy dates the start of the siege to 214, Polybius' sequence implies 213. The burning mirrors are almost certainly legend; experiments have produced mixed results.

events.title: Institution of the Ludi Apollinares
events.summary: Following the prophecies of the seer Marcius (carmina Marciana), which were said to have predicted Cannae, the Senate instituted games for Apollo to drive the enemy from Italy. They became annual in 208, held in July.

events.title: Tarentum betrayed to Hannibal
events.summary: Young Tarentine nobles, angered by the execution of Tarentine hostages who had tried to escape from Rome, let Hannibal into the city at night. The Roman garrison under Marcus Livius held the citadel for the next three years, and with it the harbour mouth.
events.detail: Polybius (8.24-34) gives a detailed narrative of the stratagem (the conspirators went out 'hunting' and returned with game each night to accustom the guards to opening the gate). Hannibal had his ships hauled across the city on wagons to get them out of the blocked harbour.

battle.significance: Hannibal's greatest gain in the south, but he never took the citadel.

events.debate: Polybius implies 213, Livy 212.

events.title: Fraud of the war contractors
events.summary: Contractors supplying the armies in Spain under a state guarantee against loss at sea sank old hulks loaded with worthless goods and claimed compensation. When tribunes prosecuted the ringleader Marcus Postumius of Pyrgi, the publicani rioted in the assembly; he and others went into exile.
events.detail: The episode (Livy 25.3-4) is the first known scandal of the companies of publicani, whose role expanded enormously as the state contracted out supply on credit in 215.

events.title: Battle of the Silarus
events.summary: Marcus Centenius Paenula, an ex-centurion who boasted he could beat Hannibal and was given 8,000 men, gathered as many volunteers and attacked Hannibal in Lucania. Fewer than 1,000 escaped.

battle.significance: Minor, but illustrates Roman overconfidence and the Senate's willingness to try anyone.

events.title: First battle of Herdonia
events.summary: Hannibal surprised the praetor Gnaeus Fulvius Flaccus near Herdonia in Apulia; of 18,000 Romans barely 2,000 escaped. Fulvius, accused of fleeing first, was later prosecuted and went into exile.

sides.strength: c. 18,000 under praetor Cn. Fulvius Flaccus

battle.significance: Another Roman disaster; Hannibal's last great field victory in open battle against a large army.

events.debate: The two battles of Herdonia (212 and 210) are suspiciously similar; De Sanctis and others suspected a doublet, though most now accept both.

events.title: Anabasis of Antiochus III
events.summary: Antiochus III led a seven-year expedition to the eastern satrapies, forcing Armenia, Parthia under Arsaces II and the Graeco-Bactrian king Euthydemus (after a two-year siege of Bactra) to acknowledge his supremacy, and renewing friendship with the Indian king Sophagasenus. He returned in 205/204 with 150 elephants and the title Megas, 'the Great'.
events.detail: Polybius (11.34.15-16) says the expedition made him seem worthy of royal power to Greeks as well as Asiatics. The prestige won here underlay his later confrontation with Rome.

events.title: Siege and fall of Capua
events.summary: Three Roman armies surrounded Capua with a double line of works. Hannibal failed to break the siege and marched on Rome to draw the besiegers off; they stayed. Capua surrendered in 211. Twenty-seven senators led by Vibius Virrius poisoned themselves at a last banquet; the proconsul Quintus Fulvius Flaccus executed 53 others. Capua lost its civic institutions and its land became ager publicus.
events.detail: For nearly two centuries Capua was administered by a prefect sent from Rome. The punishment was a terrible warning to Hannibal's other allies, whose defections now stalled.

sides.strength: Campanian forces and a Carthaginian garrison

battle.significance: Decisive turning point in Italy; Hannibal's inability to protect his allies became plain.

events.title: Hannibal at the gates
events.summary: Hannibal marched on Rome and camped by the Anio three miles from the city; he rode with cavalry up to the Colline Gate. Two consular armies plus the troops from Capua faced him and he withdrew. Livy says the land on which he was camped was sold at auction in Rome at full price during his stay.
events.detail: Polybius (9.5-7) says the march was a feint to relieve Capua and gives a direct route through Samnium; Livy (26.7-11), following Coelius, gives a different route by the Via Latina and adds a twice-repeated hailstorm that prevented battle. 'Hannibal ad portas' became a proverb.
events.debate: Polybius and Livy disagree on the route and on Hannibal's purpose; Livy reflects the dramatising Roman tradition.

events.title: Battle of the Upper Baetis: death of the Scipios
events.summary: The Scipio brothers divided their forces to attack three Carthaginian armies. Publius was overwhelmed near Castulo by Mago and Hasdrubal son of Gisco, joined by Numidian cavalry under the young Masinissa; 29 days later Gnaeus, deserted by his 20,000 Celtiberian mercenaries, was killed near Ilorci. Rome lost all of Spain south of the Ebro.
events.detail: The equestrian Lucius Marcius Septimus rallied the survivors north of the Ebro and, Livy says, won a night victory that may be largely invention. The lesson that Celtiberian mercenaries could be bought was not lost on Rome.

sides.losses: both commanders and most of both armies

battle.significance: Collapse of Roman Spain; led to the appointment of the younger Scipio in 210.

events.debate: Livy dates the disaster to 212; 211 is generally preferred. Ilorci is placed near Lorca by Pliny but may lie nearer Castulo. Marcius' victories as told by Livy (from Claudius Quadrigarius and Valerius Antias) are doubted.

events.title: Introduction of the denarius
events.summary: At the height of the war crisis Rome reformed its coinage, introducing the silver denarius (originally about 4.5 g, tariffed at 10 asses), with the quinarius and sestertius, a gold coinage and the victoriatus. The denarius became the standard silver coin of Rome for 450 years.
events.detail: Pliny (33.44) dated the first Roman silver to 269, and some scholars put the denarius in the 260s or 187. Excavations at Morgantina in Sicily found early denarii in a destruction layer associated with the Roman sack of 211, which with hoard evidence persuaded most numismatists (Crawford, RRC 44/5) to date the system to c. 211. The as was reduced to the sextantal standard (2 ounces) at about the same time.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)
Buttrey, 'The Morgantina Excavations and the Date of the Roman Denarius', Congresso Internazionale di Numismatica (1961)
events.debate: Date contested for a century (269, 187, c. 211); the Morgantina stratigraphy now makes c. 214-211 the consensus. The retariffing to 16 asses came c. 141.

events.title: Roman-Aetolian alliance
events.summary: Marcus Valerius Laevinus allied Rome with the Aetolian League against Philip V. The terms divided the spoils: captured cities and land would go to the Aetolians, movable property and captives to the Romans. Neither party could make a separate peace.
events.detail: A fragmentary copy of the treaty survives on a stone found at Thyrrheion in Acarnania (IG IX 1² 241), confirming Livy's summary (26.24). Greek opinion was shocked: Polybius (9.37-39, 11.5) records speeches condemning the Aetolians for selling Greeks to barbarians.
scholarship: Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
events.debate: The date (212 or 211) and whether Attalus, Sparta and Elis were original signatories are disputed.

events.title: Marcellus' ovation and the Syracusan spoils
events.summary: Denied a full triumph because his army remained in Sicily, Marcellus triumphed on the Alban Mount and celebrated an ovation in Rome, displaying paintings, statues and the riches of Syracuse. Livy says this began the Roman craze for Greek art and the despoiling of sacred and profane buildings alike.
events.detail: Marcellus dedicated much of the art in his temple of Honos and Virtus at the Porta Capena. Polybius (9.10) argues that Rome was wrong to strip conquered cities of art, which created envy and hatred. Marcellus kept only Archimedes' celestial globe for himself.

events.title: Scipio given the Spanish command as a privatus
events.summary: When no experienced commander would take the Spanish command, the people elected the 25-year-old Publius Cornelius Scipio, who had held only the aedileship, as proconsul with imperium. It was the first grant of consular imperium to a man who had never been consul or praetor.
events.detail: Livy (26.18-19) describes the comitia and Scipio's carefully cultivated aura of divine inspiration (daily visits alone to the Capitoline temple, rumours of a serpent father). Polybius (10.2-5) insists on his rational calculation instead. The appointment was a precedent for the extraordinary commands of the late Republic.
scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
events.debate: Polybius rejects the legends of divine favour, arguing Scipio exploited religion deliberately; Livy is ambivalent. Some scholars doubt the dramatic scene of no candidates coming forward.

events.title: Second battle of Herdonia
events.summary: Hannibal destroyed the army of the proconsul Gnaeus Fulvius Centumalus near Herdonia; Fulvius and eleven military tribunes were killed. Hannibal then burned Herdonia and moved its people to Metapontum and Thurii, a sign that he could no longer defend his Apulian allies.

sides.strength: c. 2 legions under Cn. Fulvius Centumalus

battle.significance: Tactical victory but strategic retreat: Hannibal was abandoning the cities he could not hold.

events.debate: Possible doublet of the battle of 212; Livy himself gives two casualty figures.

events.title: The sack of Aegina
events.summary: The Roman fleet under Publius Sulpicius Galba, with Aetolian allies, captured Aegina and enslaved its people. Under the treaty of 211 the island went to the Aetolians, who sold it to Attalus I of Pergamon for 30 talents.
events.detail: Polybius (9.42) records the Aeginetans begging to be allowed to ransom themselves and the Roman reply that they should have thought of that before. The episode became an argument in Greek debates on Roman brutality and the Aetolian 'betrayal' of Greeks.

battle.significance: Brought Pergamon an Aegean base and cemented its alliance with Rome.

events.title: Twelve Latin colonies refuse troops
events.summary: Twelve of the thirty Latin colonies (Ardea, Nepete, Sutrium, Alba, Carseoli, Sora, Suessa, Circeii, Setia, Cales, Narnia and Interamna) told the consuls they had neither men nor money left. The other eighteen, led by Fregellae, declared their loyalty and the Senate thanked them publicly.
events.detail: Livy (27.9-10) lists the colonies, a rare documentary-seeming passage. In 204 the twelve were punished with double levies and a new census on Roman lines. The episode shows how close Rome's manpower system came to breaking.
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)

events.title: The sacred reserve of gold opened
events.summary: The state opened the sanctius aerarium, the reserve built from the 5 percent tax on manumissions (vicesima libertatis) since 357, and drew out about 4,000 pounds of gold to pay for the war.

events.title: Capture of New Carthage
events.summary: Scipio marched from the Ebro to New Carthage in a week and stormed the Punic capital of Spain in a single day. While the walls were assaulted from the isthmus, a picked force waded across the lagoon at ebb, which Scipio had told his men Neptune had promised him, and climbed the undefended north wall.
events.detail: Polybius (10.8-15) explains that Scipio had learned from fishermen that the lagoon drained in the evening and insists the plan was rational, the Neptune story a morale device. The booty included 18 warships, the Carthaginian treasury and arsenal, 300 Spanish hostages whom Scipio returned to their families, and 2,000 artisans made public slaves to work in the arsenal. Scipio's restoration of a beautiful captive to her fiancé Allucius became a celebrated 'continence of Scipio'.

sides.strength: c. 1,000 soldiers under Mago plus 2,000 armed citizens

battle.significance: Gave Scipio the enemy's base, treasury and hostages, and won over many Iberian peoples.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
events.debate: Polybius dates it 209, Livy 210. The lagoon's tidal behaviour (the Mediterranean has negligible tides) has been explained by wind-driven seiche or a sluice.

events.title: Fabius recaptures Tarentum
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus, consul for the fifth time, recovered Tarentum through the treachery of the Bruttian garrison commander, who was in love with the sister of one of Fabius' soldiers. 30,000 Tarentines were enslaved and 3,000 talents of gold and silver taken; but Fabius left the statues of the gods, saying 'let us leave the Tarentines their angry gods'.
events.detail: Fabius did take a colossal bronze Heracles by Lysippus for the Capitol, beside which he set an equestrian statue of himself.

sides.strength: consular army and the citadel garrison

battle.significance: Hannibal arrived too late; his grip on the south was weakening.

events.title: Battle of Baecula
events.summary: Scipio attacked Hasdrubal Barca on a two-level plateau near Baecula, pinning him with light troops in front while he and Laelius led the heavy infantry up both flanks. Hasdrubal, judging the position lost, withdrew with his elephants, treasury and most of his army and marched for Italy.
events.detail: Livy (27.18) gives 8,000 enemy killed and 12,000 captured, probably exaggerated. Scipio's failure to stop Hasdrubal was criticised (Fabius made it a charge in 205). Scipio released Masinissa's nephew Massiva, a first contact with the Numidian. Since 2014 Spanish archaeologists have identified the battlefield at the Cerro de las Albahacas near Santo Tomé (Jaén) from scatters of sling bullets, nails and coins.
events.locName: Baecula (Cerro de las Albahacas, Santo Tomé, Jaén?)

battle.significance: Tactical success but failed to prevent Hasdrubal's march to Italy, which ended at the Metaurus.

scholarship: Bellón Ruiz et al., 'Baecula: arqueología de una batalla' (2015)
events.debate: Earlier candidates for the site lay near Bailén; the Santo Tomé identification rests on battlefield archaeology and is now widely accepted.

events.title: Death of Marcellus
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Titus Quinctius Crispinus rode out with 220 horsemen to reconnoitre a hill between their camps near Venusia and were ambushed by Numidians. Marcellus, aged about sixty and consul for the fifth time, was killed; Crispinus died of his wounds.
events.detail: Polybius (10.32) condemns Marcellus for behaving like a junior officer. Hannibal gave the body an honourable funeral and tried to use Marcellus' signet ring to trick Salapia with a forged letter, but Crispinus had warned the cities.

sides.losses: Marcellus killed, Crispinus mortally wounded, c. 40 killed

battle.significance: Both consuls lost in one year, a unique Roman calamity.

events.title: Livius Andronicus' hymn to Juno and the guild of poets
events.summary: After prodigies, the pontiffs ordered 27 maidens to process through the city singing a hymn to Juno Regina composed by Livius Andronicus. In his honour the state recognised a college of writers and actors (scribae et histriones) meeting at the temple of Minerva on the Aventine.
events.detail: Livy (27.37) notes the hymn might have seemed admirable to rough minds then but would be 'unpleasing and uncouth' if quoted now. The collegium is the first official recognition of literary professionals in Rome.

events.title: Battle of Grumentum
events.summary: The consul Gaius Claudius Nero fought an inconclusive but bloody action against Hannibal near Grumentum in Lucania, keeping him in the south as Hasdrubal descended into Italy.
events.detail: Livy (27.41-42) claims 8,000 Carthaginians killed; Polybius' account is lost. Hannibal then moved to Canusium to await news of his brother, which Nero intercepted.

battle.significance: Pinned Hannibal in the south.

events.debate: Livy's figures are probably exaggerated by annalists.

events.title: Battle of the Metaurus
events.summary: Capturing Hasdrubal's dispatch to Hannibal, the consul Gaius Claudius Nero secretly marched 7,000 picked men from Apulia to join his colleague Marcus Livius Salinator at Sena Gallica, about 400 km in six or seven days. Hasdrubal, realising from the double trumpet call that two consuls faced him, tried to withdraw, was caught at the Metaurus and killed with most of his army.
events.detail: Nero swung troops from the inactive Roman right round behind the line to fall on the Carthaginian right flank. He had Hasdrubal's head thrown in front of Hannibal's outposts; Livy has Hannibal say he recognised the fortune of Carthage. The victory ended any real chance of Carthaginian success in Italy. Horace (Odes 4.4) celebrates it as the salvation of Rome by the Claudii Nerones.
events.locName: River Metaurus (near Fossombrone or San Silvestro?)

sides.strength: c. 30,000 incl. Gauls, Ligurians and 10 elephants
sides.losses: c. 10,000 killed (Polybius); 56,000 killed and 5,400 captured (Livy, absurd)

battle.significance: Decisive: Hannibal withdrew into Bruttium and never again threatened central Italy.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)
events.debate: Livy's 56,000 Carthaginian dead is a notorious example of annalistic inflation, exceeding the size of Hasdrubal's army. The battle site along the lower Metauro valley is disputed.

events.title: Battle of Ilipa
events.summary: After days of drawn-up armies facing each other with the same dispositions, Scipio suddenly reversed his line one dawn, placing his Roman legions on the wings and his unreliable Spanish allies in the centre, and attacked before the enemy had eaten. His wings executed a complex wheeling manoeuvre and crushed the Carthaginian flanks while the Libyan centre stood idle. Carthaginian power in Spain collapsed.
events.detail: Polybius (11.20-24) admires the manoeuvre in detail; its exact drill is much debated by tacticians. A storm saved the routed Carthaginians from total annihilation. Hasdrubal son of Gisco fled to Gades and then to Africa.

battle.significance: Ended Carthaginian rule in Spain; Gades surrendered later that year.

scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
events.debate: Polybius' and Livy's Carthaginian numbers differ; Polybius' figure is generally thought high. Livy dates it to 207.

events.title: Mutiny at Sucro and the Ilergetan revolt
events.summary: While Scipio lay ill, 8,000 Roman soldiers at Sucro, unpaid and idle, mutinied and drove out their tribunes. Scipio paid them, summoned them to New Carthage, and executed the 35 ringleaders while the rest stood surrounded by loyal troops. Indibilis and Mandonius of the Ilergetes, who had rebelled on news of his illness, were crushed; Indibilis was killed in a renewed revolt in 205.

events.title: Founding of Italica
events.summary: After Ilipa, Scipio settled wounded veterans at a town he named Italica near the Baetis, the first Roman settlement in Spain and, centuries later, the home town of the families of Trajan and Hadrian.
events.detail: Appian (Iberica 38) is the source. Italica became a municipium and, under Hadrian, a colonia; its grand Hadrianic quarter and amphitheatre survive at Santiponce.

events.title: Surrender of Gades; Mago to the Balearics
events.summary: Mago Barca, ordered to take his fleet to Italy, failed in a raid on New Carthage, found Gades closed to him, and sailed for the Balearics, where he wintered at the harbour on Minorca that still bears his name (Portus Magonis, Mahón). Gades surrendered to Rome on terms that made it a federate ally (foedus Gaditanum).

events.title: Aetolians make a separate peace with Philip
events.summary: Abandoned by Rome, which sent no forces after 208, and having seen Philip sack their federal sanctuary at Thermum a second time (207), the Aetolians made peace with Philip on his terms. Rome regarded this as a breach of the 211 treaty, a grievance it remembered.

events.title: Peace of Phoenice
events.summary: Rome and Philip V ended the First Macedonian War at Phoenice in Epirus. Rome kept the Parthini, Dimale, Bargullum and Eugenium; Philip kept Atintania. Each side listed allies (adscripti) included in the peace.
events.detail: Livy's list (29.12) includes on the Roman side Ilium and Athens; many scholars regard these as later annalistic additions to justify the Second Macedonian War, though others defend them. The peace freed Rome to concentrate on Africa and left Philip free to turn to the Aegean.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
events.debate: Authenticity of the adscripti list (especially Ilium, Athens, Nabis of Sparta) is disputed.

events.title: Mago lands at Genua
events.summary: Mago sailed from Minorca with about 12,000 foot and 2,000 horse, took Genua and tried to raise the Ligurians and Gauls against Rome. Two years of manoeuvres in the north tied down several Roman armies.

events.title: Arrival of the Magna Mater
events.summary: Following a Sibylline oracle that a foreign enemy would be driven from Italy if the Idaean Mother were brought to Rome, an embassy obtained from Attalus I the black meteoric stone of Cybele from Pessinus (or Pergamon). It was received at Ostia in April 204 by Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica, chosen as the best man in Rome, and carried by matrons to the temple of Victoria on the Palatine.
events.detail: Legend says the ship ran aground in the Tiber and was freed by Claudia Quinta, whose chastity had been doubted. The cult's ecstatic Phrygian eunuch priests (galli) shocked Romans, who were forbidden to become galli; the Megalesia games began in 204, and the temple was dedicated in 191. The embassy also cemented the alliance with Pergamon that would shape Roman policy in Asia.
scholarship: Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome (1998)
Gruen, Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy (1990)
events.debate: Livy says the stone came from Pessinus; Varro says Pergamon, and Pessinus was not then under Attalus' control. Gruen reads the import as a Roman claim on Trojan ancestry and Hellenistic standing.

events.title: Recapture of Locri and the Pleminius scandal
events.summary: Scipio recovered Locri in 205 and left Quintus Pleminius in command. Pleminius and his troops plundered the treasury of Persephone's temple and committed atrocities; when two tribunes flogged him, he had them tortured to death. A Locrian embassy complained to the Senate in 204.
events.detail: Scipio's enemies, led by Fabius and Cato, used the affair to attack his command and his Hellenising lifestyle in Syracuse (Greek cloak and sandals, the gymnasium). A senatorial commission visited Sicily, found his army in excellent order and allowed him to proceed to Africa. Pleminius died in prison. Polybius cannot be checked here; Livy's narrative is long and dramatic.

events.title: Lex Cincia de donis et muneribus
events.summary: The tribune Marcus Cincius Alimentus carried a law forbidding advocates to accept fees or gifts for pleading cases and restricting large gifts generally except between close kin. Cato spoke for it in his youth.
events.detail: The law was still invoked under the emperors; Augustus and Claudius tried to enforce it (Tacitus, Annals 11.5-7).

events.title: Censorship of Claudius Nero and Livius Salinator
events.summary: The victors of the Metaurus, bitter personal enemies, held the censorship together. Each removed the other's public horse; Livius made aerarii of 34 of the 35 tribes for having first condemned and then elected him. A new tax on salt earned Livius the mocking cognomen Salinator.
events.detail: The farce (Livy 29.37) shows how personal enmities (inimicitiae) were fought out through office. They also let contracts for a salt monopoly at a fixed price, the first such regulation.
events.debate: The cognomen Salinator may in fact be older; Livy's etymology is suspect.

events.title: Cato brings Ennius to Rome
events.summary: Marcus Porcius Cato, returning from his quaestorship in Sicily and Africa by way of Sardinia, brought to Rome the Oscan-speaking, Greek-educated poet Quintus Ennius, who had been serving there as a centurion.
events.detail: Ennius became the father of Latin epic with the Annales in hexameters and the client of the Scipios and Fulvius Nobilior. Cato, ironically, later attacked Nobilior for taking poets on campaign.

events.title: Scipio lands in Africa; siege of Utica
events.summary: Scipio sailed from Lilybaeum with perhaps 25,000-35,000 men, including the disgraced legions of Cannae, and landed near the Fair Promontory west of Carthage. Masinissa joined him with a few hundred horsemen. A Carthaginian cavalry force under Hanno was destroyed, but a 40-day siege of Utica failed and Scipio wintered on a headland, the Castra Cornelia.
events.debate: Livy records divergent figures for Scipio's army, from 10,000 foot and 2,200 horse to 35,000 in all.

events.title: Burning of the camps
events.summary: While pretending to negotiate peace, Scipio sent spies disguised as slaves into the camps of Syphax and Hasdrubal son of Gisco near Utica. One night Laelius and Masinissa set fire to Syphax's camp of reed huts; as the Carthaginians ran out unarmed to help, Scipio fired their camp too. The two armies were destroyed.
events.detail: Polybius (14.1-6) praises the operation as the most brilliant of Scipio's career; modern readers note the bad faith in breaking off negotiations he had encouraged. Polybius gives Hasdrubal 30,000 foot and 3,000 horse and Syphax 50,000 foot and 10,000 horse; Livy (30.6) claims 40,000 killed and 5,000 captured.

battle.significance: Destroyed the field armies of Carthage and Syphax at one stroke.

events.debate: Ancient army sizes are inflated; the ethics of the ruse were debated already in antiquity.

events.title: The secret pact of Philip V and Antiochus III
events.summary: After the death of Ptolemy IV left a child king in Egypt, Philip V and Antiochus III allegedly agreed to divide the Ptolemaic overseas possessions between them. Antiochus attacked Coele-Syria; Philip seized Ptolemaic and independent cities in the Aegean and the Straits.
events.detail: Polybius (15.20) condemns the pact as monstrous and calls the subsequent ruin of both kings Fortune's punishment. Rhodian and Pergamene envoys reported it at Rome in 201, and Roman fear of a combined Hellenistic bloc is one explanation offered for the Second Macedonian War.
scholarship: Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Errington, 'The Alleged Syro-Macedonian Pact and the Origins of the Second Macedonian War', Athenaeum 49 (1971)
events.debate: Errington and Magie argued that the pact was Rhodian propaganda; Eckstein argues forcefully that it was real and that it created a 'power-transition crisis' in the Hellenistic system to which Rome reacted.

events.title: Battle of the Great Plains
events.summary: Hasdrubal and Syphax raised a new army, stiffened by 4,000 newly arrived Celtiberian mercenaries, on the Great Plains of the Bagradas. Scipio's Roman and Italian cavalry and Masinissa's Numidians routed both wings; the Celtiberians, with no hope of pardon, died fighting where they stood.

battle.significance: Led Carthage to recall Hannibal and Mago.

events.title: Capture of Syphax; Sophonisba
events.summary: Laelius and Masinissa pursued Syphax into his kingdom and defeated him; his horse was wounded and he was captured. Cirta opened its gates. Masinissa married Syphax's wife Sophonisba, daughter of Hasdrubal son of Gisco, but when Scipio demanded her surrender as a captive, Masinissa sent her poison, which she drank.
events.detail: The Sophonisba story (Livy 30.12-15, Appian, Diodorus) became a favourite of Renaissance and later tragedians. Masinissa was rewarded with a crown, ivory sceptre and the title of king, and later took Syphax's realm.

battle.significance: Removed Carthage's chief African ally and made Masinissa master of Numidia.

events.title: Mago defeated in Insubrian territory
events.summary: The praetor Publius Quinctilius Varus and the proconsul Marcus Cornelius Cethegus defeated Mago's army in Insubrian territory. Mago, wounded in the thigh, withdrew to the Ligurian coast and sailed for Africa on the recall order, dying of his wound off Sardinia.

sides.strength: 4 legions under P. Quinctilius Varus and M. Cornelius Cethegus

battle.significance: Ended the Carthaginian presence in northern Italy.

events.debate: Some sources (Nepos, Zonaras) say Mago survived; Livy reports he died at sea.

events.title: Hannibal leaves Italy
events.summary: Recalled to defend Carthage, Hannibal sailed from Croton in autumn 203 after fifteen years in Italy, landing at Leptis Minor. Before leaving he set up at the temple of Hera Lacinia a bronze tablet in Punic and Greek recording his deeds and army numbers, which Polybius read.
events.detail: Livy (30.20) says Hannibal left in a rage, cursing himself for not marching on Rome after Cannae, and Diodorus claims he massacred Italian soldiers who refused to follow him; the massacre story is probably Roman propaganda.
events.debate: The massacre at the temple of Hera is widely doubted.

events.title: Battle of Zama
events.summary: In the final battle of the war, Scipio arranged his maniples in columns with lanes through which Hannibal's 80 elephants were funnelled harmlessly. Laelius and Masinissa drove off the Carthaginian cavalry. The Roman infantry broke Hannibal's first two lines; the decisive struggle with his third line of Italian veterans was ended when the Roman and Numidian cavalry returned and fell on its rear.
events.detail: Polybius (15.5-16) is the main source; he records the meeting of Hannibal and Scipio before the battle, in speeches that are his own compositions. Carthaginian losses were about 20,000 killed and nearly as many captured; Roman losses about 1,500. Hannibal escaped to Hadrumetum and advised Carthage to accept peace. The name 'Zama' comes from Nepos and later writers; Polybius places the battle near 'Margaron' and Livy near Naraggara.

sides.strength: c. 29,000 Romans and Italians plus Masinissa's 6,000 foot and 4,000 horse

sides.losses: c. 20,000 killed and as many captured (Polybius)

battle.significance: Ended the Second Punic War and Carthage's career as a great power.

scholarship: Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Lancel, Hannibal (1995)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)
events.debate: Site disputed (Polybius' Margaron, Livy's Naraggara, Nepos' Zama; Zama Regia itself is placed at Jama or Seba Biar). Conventional date 19 October rests on Livy's mention of an eclipse and is uncertain. Some scholars doubt that Hannibal's third line consisted of Italian veterans.

events.title: The armistice broken
events.summary: During an armistice while a Carthaginian embassy was in Rome, a Roman supply convoy was driven ashore by a storm in the Gulf of Carthage and the Carthaginians seized it. When Roman envoys protested, their ship was attacked on the way back. Scipio resumed the war.

events.title: Battle of Chios
events.summary: Philip V's fleet was badly mauled off Chios by the combined fleets of Rhodes and Attalus I. Polybius says Philip lost 92 decked ships and 70 lembi, and 9,000 men, far more than his enemies; Attalus was nearly captured. Philip claimed victory because he held the field.
events.detail: Philip then defeated the Rhodians at Lade and ravaged Pergamene territory. Rhodes and Attalus appealed to Rome in autumn 201, setting in motion the Second Macedonian War.

sides.losses: 92 decked ships and 70 lembi lost; 3,000 Macedonians and 6,000 rowers killed (Polybius)

battle.significance: Weakened Macedonian sea power and provoked the appeal to Rome.

events.debate: Polybius' loss figures, from Rhodian sources (Zeno of Rhodes, whom he criticises elsewhere), may be inflated.

events.title: Peace treaty ending the Second Punic War
events.summary: Carthage kept its African territory within the 'Phoenician trenches' and its own laws, but surrendered all warships except ten triremes, all elephants, and all prisoners and deserters; paid 10,000 talents over fifty years; gave 100 hostages chosen by Scipio; agreed to wage no war outside Africa and none in Africa without Roman permission; and restored to Masinissa all that had belonged to him or his ancestors.
events.detail: The open-ended Masinissa clause was a time bomb: it gave the Numidian king licence to nibble Carthaginian territory for fifty years, ultimately provoking the Third Punic War. Five hundred Punic warships were towed out and burned, a sight Livy says moved the Carthaginians like the burning of the city itself. Deserters were executed, Latin ones beheaded, Roman ones crucified.

events.title: Scipio's triumph; the cognomen Africanus
events.summary: Scipio returned and celebrated a magnificent triumph, depositing 123,000 pounds of silver in the treasury and giving each soldier 400 asses. He was the first Roman general to take a cognomen from a conquered land, Africanus, whether given by his soldiers, his friends or popular favour.
events.detail: Polybius (16.23) says Syphax was led in the procession and died soon after; Livy says he died at Tibur before the triumph. Scipio refused, Livy says, offers of perpetual consulship and dictatorship and statues in the Comitium and on the Capitol.
events.debate: Polybius and Livy disagree on whether Syphax walked in the triumph.

events.title: Battle of Panium
events.summary: Antiochus III decisively defeated the Ptolemaic army under the Aetolian mercenary general Scopas at Panium near the sources of the Jordan, using elephants and cataphract cavalry led by his son Antiochus. Coele-Syria and Judaea passed permanently to the Seleucids.
events.detail: Polybius (16.18-19) criticises Zeno of Rhodes' account of the battle. Josephus records Antiochus' charter of privileges to the Jews of Jerusalem, who had welcomed him.

battle.significance: Ended a century of Ptolemaic rule in Coele-Syria and Judaea.

events.title: Rome votes for war with Philip
events.summary: The consul Publius Sulpicius Galba proposed war against Philip V. The comitia centuriata, war-weary after 17 years against Hannibal, rejected it almost unanimously; after a speech by Sulpicius warning that Philip would otherwise invade Italy like Pyrrhus, a second vote approved it. The young envoy Marcus Aemilius Lepidus delivered the ultimatum to Philip at the siege of Abydos.
events.detail: Livy (31.6-8) is the source for the double vote. The ultimatum demanded that Philip make war on no Greek state and submit his disputes with Attalus to arbitration, terms that treated him as a subordinate. The causes of the war are the classic battleground of the imperialism debate: Holleaux saw fear of the Philip-Antiochus pact; Harris aggressive expansionism; Gruen a reluctant Rome drawn in by Greek appeals; Eckstein the systemic crisis of the Hellenistic state system.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, Rome Enters the Greek East (2008)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XXXI-XXXIII (1973)
Rich, Declaring War in the Roman Republic (1976)
events.debate: Why Rome fought is fiercely debated. Livy's account of the first vote shows that the people did not share the Senate's enthusiasm; Polybius emphasises the Rhodian and Pergamene appeals and Philip's aggression.

events.title: Siege of Abydos
events.summary: Philip V besieged Abydos on the Hellespont. When the walls were breached, the citizens resolved to kill their women and children and burn their property if the city fell; their magistrates surrendered instead, but the populace carried out the mass suicide when Philip entered. Philip gave them three days to die.
events.detail: Polybius (16.30-34) compares the Abydenes to the Phocians and Acarnanians of old. It was here that Marcus Aemilius Lepidus delivered Rome's ultimatum.

sides.strength: citizens of Abydos with Rhodian and Pergamene help

battle.significance: Gave Philip the Straits, but sealed his reputation for savagery in Greek opinion.

events.title: Athens declares war on Philip; Attica ravaged
events.summary: After two Acarnanian youths were executed for straying into the Eleusinian Mysteries, Acarnania and Philip attacked Attica. Athens declared war, abolished the two tribes named after Antigonus and Demetrius and ordered the destruction of all Antigonid statues and inscriptions. Philip ravaged the Attic countryside, burning the Academy, the Lyceum and the sanctuaries and tombs around the city.

events.title: Battle of Cremona
events.summary: Insubres, Boii and Cenomani, led by a Carthaginian officer named Hamilcar who had stayed in Italy, sacked Placentia and besieged Cremona. The praetor Lucius Furius Purpureo crushed them; Hamilcar was killed. Livy claims 35,000 Gauls killed or captured.

sides.strength: praetorian army under L. Furius Purpureo

battle.significance: Opened the final Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul.

events.debate: Livy's numbers are typical annalistic exaggeration.

events.title: Battle of the Aous
events.summary: Philip V held the narrow gorge of the Aous (Aoi Stena) for weeks against the new consul Titus Quinctius Flamininus. A shepherd sent by the pro-Roman Epirote chief Charops guided 4,000 Romans over the mountains in three nights to a height above the Macedonian camp; attacked from front and rear, Philip abandoned the pass with the loss of 2,000 men.
events.locName: Aoi Stena, gorge of the Aous (Vjosë) near Këlcyrë

battle.significance: Opened Thessaly to the Romans and brought the Achaeans over to Rome.

events.title: Conference of Nicaea
events.summary: Flamininus and Philip negotiated on the shore of the Malian Gulf near Nicaea, Philip speaking from the prow of his ship. Flamininus arranged that the matter be referred to the Senate, where his friends ensured negotiations would fail if his command was prorogued, or succeed if he was to be replaced. It was prorogued.
events.detail: Polybius (18.1-12) records the sharp exchanges in detail, including Philip's taunt to the Aetolians about their own conduct. The episode shows a Roman general manipulating war and peace for his own career.
scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)

events.title: The Leges Porciae on provocatio
events.summary: One or more laws proposed by members of the Porcian gens extended the citizen's right of appeal (provocatio) against magistrates, in particular protecting Roman citizens from flogging, including outside Rome and in military contexts.
events.detail: Three Porcian laws are mentioned by Cicero (De re publica 2.54). Their authors are usually identified as Publius Porcius Laeca (tribune 199), Cato the Elder (consul 195) and Lucius Porcius Licinus (consul 184). A denarius of P. Laeca (RRC 301/1, c. 110 BC) shows a citizen appealing against a magistrate with the legend PROVOCO.
scholarship: Lintott, 'Provocatio: From the Struggle of the Orders to the Principate', ANRW I.2 (1972)
Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)
events.debate: Dates, authorship and content are uncertain; the laws are dated anywhere between 199 and 184.

events.title: The Achaean League joins Rome
events.summary: At a stormy assembly at Sicyon, the Achaean strategos Aristaenus persuaded the League to abandon its long alliance with Macedon and join Rome. Some cities, including Dyme, Megalopolis and Argos, walked out; Argos then handed itself to Philip, who gave it to Nabis of Sparta.

events.title: Battle of Cynoscephalae
events.summary: On the misty 'Dog's Head' hills of Thessaly, an encounter battle between Flamininus and Philip V developed piecemeal. Philip's right wing phalanx charged downhill and pushed back the Roman left; Flamininus attacked the Macedonian left as it was still deploying, using elephants, and broke it. An unnamed military tribune then took 20 maniples from the victorious Roman right and attacked the rear of the Macedonian right phalanx, which collapsed. Macedonian soldiers raising their sarissas in surrender were cut down by Romans who did not understand the signal.
events.detail: Polybius (18.18-27) gives the battle in detail and follows it (18.28-32) with his famous comparison of legion and phalanx: the phalanx is irresistible on level ground and from the front but inflexible, while the legion can fight anywhere and in any formation. Each army numbered about 25,000. The Macedonians lost 8,000 killed and 5,000 captured, the Romans 700. The Aetolian cavalry played a part, and their claim to the victory infuriated Flamininus.

sides.strength: c. 26,000 incl. 6,000 Aetolians and Athamanians, 20 elephants

battle.significance: Ended the Second Macedonian War; Polybius' showcase for the superiority of the legion over the phalanx.

scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius II (1967)
Hammond, 'The Campaign and the Battle of Cynoscephalae in 197 BC', JHS 108 (1988)
events.debate: Livy (33.10) notes that Valerius Antias claimed 40,000 Macedonian dead and Claudius Quadrigarius 32,000, while he himself follows Polybius' 8,000, an explicit example of Livy correcting annalistic inflation with Polybius. The battlefield's exact location is debated.

events.title: Two Spanish provinces and six praetors
events.summary: The number of praetors was raised to six so that two could be sent annually to govern Hispania Citerior (the east coast north of New Carthage) and Hispania Ulterior (the Baetis valley), with boundaries fixed by the praetors of that year.
events.detail: The decision marks Rome's commitment to permanent rule in Spain, motivated in part by silver and by the need to suppress constant warfare. It was followed immediately by a great revolt. Livy (32.28.11) says the praetors were ordered to fix the boundary.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae: Spain and the Development of Roman Imperialism, 218-82 BC (1986)

events.title: Revolt in Spain; death of Sempronius Tuditanus
events.summary: Most of southern and eastern Spain rose against Roman rule, the Turdetani under the chieftain Culchas and the cities of Malaca and Sexi among them. The praetor of Citerior, Gaius Sempronius Tuditanus, was defeated and died of his wounds.

events.title: Battle of the Mincius
events.summary: The consul Gaius Cornelius Cethegus defeated the Insubres and Cenomani on the Mincius after secretly persuading the Cenomani to change sides during the battle. The Carthaginian Hamilcar was captured (in one version) and Cethegus triumphed.

sides.strength: consular army under C. Cornelius Cethegus

battle.significance: Broke the Insubrian coalition; the Cenomani became loyal allies.

events.debate: Livy reports that Hamilcar had already been killed at Cremona in 200 according to other sources.

events.title: Flamininus proclaims the freedom of the Greeks
events.summary: At the Isthmian Games of 196, a herald announced that the Senate and Flamininus declared free, ungarrisoned, untaxed and governed by their own laws the Greek peoples formerly subject to Philip. The crowd's shouts were so loud, Plutarch says, that crows flying overhead fell stunned into the stadium.
events.detail: The peace terms (Polybius 18.44): Philip evacuated all Greek cities in Europe and Asia, surrendered his fleet except five ships and the royal 'sixteen', paid 1,000 talents (half at once) and sent his son Demetrius as a hostage. Whether 'freedom' was sincere philhellenism, propaganda directed at Antiochus, or a Roman form of patronage (libertas under Roman fides) is a central question of the period; the 'fetters of Greece' (Demetrias, Chalcis, Acrocorinth) were evacuated in 194.
scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)
Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Dmitriev, The Greek Slogan of Freedom and Early Roman Politics in Greece (2011)
events.debate: Badian saw Realpolitik behind philhellenism; Gruen stressed Roman adoption of Greek diplomatic language; Dmitriev traces the slogan's Hellenistic precedents.

events.title: Conference of Lysimachia
events.summary: Roman commissioners met Antiochus III at Lysimachia in Thrace, which he was rebuilding, and told him to keep his hands off the autonomous cities of Asia and out of Europe. Antiochus replied that Asia was none of Rome's business, any more than he meddled in Italy, and that Thrace was his by inheritance from Seleucus I's victory over Lysimachus.
events.detail: The exchange (Polybius 18.49-52) frames the cold war that turned hot in 192. Rumours of Ptolemy V's death broke up the meeting.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

events.title: Creation of the tresviri epulones
events.summary: A law of the tribune Gaius Licinius Lucullus created a new priestly college of three epulones to organise the sacred banquet (epulum Iovis) at the Ludi Romani and Plebeii, relieving the overburdened pontiffs. It became one of the four great colleges (later septemviri).

events.title: Repeal of the Lex Oppia
events.summary: Two tribunes, Marcus Fundanius and Lucius Valerius, proposed repealing the wartime Lex Oppia. Roman women filled the streets and the approaches to the Forum to lobby men for repeal, the first recorded women's demonstration in Rome. The consul Cato spoke against; the law was repealed.
events.detail: Livy (34.1-8) gives Cato a speech on the dangers of female luxury and assertiveness and Valerius a reply; both speeches are Livy's own compositions and reflect Augustan concerns with moral legislation. The episode is a key text in the history of Roman women.
events.debate: The speeches are Livy's invention; whether Cato really spoke is uncertain.

events.title: Cato in Spain: the battle of Emporiae
events.summary: The consul Cato landed at Emporiae with two legions, sent away his ships to force his men to fight, and defeated a large Iberian army in a dawn attack, using his reserve to break the enemy centre. He then disarmed the tribes north of the Ebro and, by sending sealed letters to all cities to be opened the same day, had their walls demolished simultaneously.
events.detail: Cato boasted that he had taken more towns than he had spent days in Spain (Plutarch). His speeches and the Origines were Livy's sources and are full of self-praise; he also organised the taxation of the iron and silver mines, a major source of Roman revenue.

sides.strength: 2 legions, allies and Spanish auxiliaries, c. 25,000

battle.significance: Pacified north-east Spain; Cato triumphed in 194.

events.debate: Livy (34.15.9) notes that Valerius Antias put the enemy dead at 40,000; Cato's own self-aggrandising account is the ultimate source.

events.title: War against Nabis: siege of Sparta
events.summary: A Panhellenic coalition led by Flamininus, with Achaeans, Macedonians, Rhodians and Pergamenes, took Gythium and attacked Sparta itself. Nabis, whose revolutionary regime had freed helots and redistributed land, sued for peace: he kept Sparta but surrendered Argos and the coastal towns, his fleet and hostages.
events.detail: Livy (34.22-41) presents Nabis as a tyrant; Polybius (13.6-8) tells of his 'Apega', an iron maiden built in the likeness of his wife. Flamininus' moderation in leaving Nabis in place angered the Achaeans and Philopoemen.

battle.significance: Freed Argos but left Nabis in power.

events.debate: Hostile sources dominate the image of Nabis; modern scholars see a social reformer in the line of Agis and Cleomenes.

events.title: Hannibal's suffeteship and flight
events.summary: Elected suffete in 196, Hannibal broke the power of the oligarchic court of 104 judges by making membership annual and reformed the state finances so that the Roman indemnity could be paid without extra taxes. His enemies denounced him at Rome for plotting with Antiochus; when a Roman embassy arrived in 195 he fled by night to Tyre and then to Antiochus at Ephesus.

events.title: Eight citizen colonies on the coasts of southern Italy
events.summary: Rome planted eight citizen colonies of 300 families each at Puteoli, Volturnum, Liternum, Salernum, Buxentum, Sipontum, Tempsa and Croton, on land confiscated from communities that had sided with Hannibal.
events.detail: Puteoli grew into the greatest port of Italy within a century. Several of these small colonies failed, and Sipontum and Buxentum were reported deserted by 186 (Livy 39.23).

events.title: Flamininus' triumph and Roman withdrawal from Greece
events.summary: Flamininus evacuated the last Roman garrisons from Greece, including Acrocorinth, Chalcis and Demetrias, and celebrated a three-day triumph displaying Macedonian armour, bronze and marble statues, silver and gold, including 14,514 gold coins called Philippei. Freed Roman captives sold as slaves in Greece after Cannae, ransomed by the Achaeans, marched behind his chariot with shaved heads.
events.detail: Flamininus had gold staters struck in Greece with his own portrait, the first living Roman on a coin. Greek cities created cults for him with Roma.
scholarship: Crawford, Roman Republican Coinage (1974)

events.title: Lex Sempronia extends usury limits to allies
events.summary: Because Roman creditors evaded the limits on interest by lending through Latin and Italian allies not bound by Roman law, a plebiscite of the tribune Marcus Sempronius Tuditanus applied Roman laws on loans to dealings with allies.

events.title: Emporium and Porticus Aemilia
events.summary: The curule aediles Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Aemilius Paullus built an emporium on the Tiber below the Aventine and a vast portico outside the Porta Trigemina; the Porticus Aemilia was rebuilt in concrete in 174, one of the earliest large concrete structures.
events.detail: Remains in the Testaccio district, about 487 m long, have traditionally been identified as the Porticus Aemilia, though some argue they belong to the Navalia (ship sheds).
events.debate: Identification of the Testaccio ruins with the Porticus Aemilia has been challenged (Navalia hypothesis).

events.title: Battle of Mutina
events.summary: The consul Lucius Cornelius Merula fought a hard battle against the Boii near Mutina, claiming 14,000 Gauls killed. His legates accused him of letting the enemy escape and blocked his triumph.

sides.strength: consular army under L. Cornelius Merula

battle.significance: Part of the grinding final war against the Boii.

events.title: Latin colonies at Copia (Thurii) and Vibo Valentia
events.summary: Rome founded Latin colonies at Thurii, renamed Copia (193), and at Hipponium, renamed Vibo Valentia (192), in the Bruttian south, the last Latin colonies in southern Italy.

events.title: Antiochus III lands at Demetrias
events.summary: Invited by the Aetolians, who named him their commander and 'liberator of Greece', Antiochus crossed to Demetrias in autumn 192 with only 10,000 foot, 500 horse and 6 elephants. Rome declared war. Antiochus wintered at Chalcis, where he married a young Chalcidian woman, which Roman tradition mocked as idleness.
events.detail: Hannibal, at Antiochus' court, urged an attack on Italy itself with a fleet, but was distrusted. The small force suggests Antiochus expected a negotiated outcome or mass Greek defections, neither of which came.
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

events.title: Murder of Nabis; Sparta joins the Achaean League
events.summary: The Aetolians, seeking to seize Sparta as a base for Antiochus, sent Alexamenus with 1,000 men as 'allies'; he murdered Nabis during a review. The Spartans rose and killed the Aetolians, and Philopoemen brought Sparta into the Achaean League.

events.title: Battle of Thermopylae
events.summary: Antiochus fortified the pass of Thermopylae against the consul Manius Acilius Glabrio, leaving Aetolians to hold the mountain paths. Cato, as a legate, led a force by night over the heights of Callidromus, surprised the Aetolian guard and appeared above Antiochus' camp. The Seleucid army broke; Antiochus fled to Chalcis with 500 men and sailed for Asia.
events.detail: Cato's self-glorifying account (Plutarch, Cato 13-14) was Livy's source; it echoes Persian outflanking of Leonidas in 480.

sides.losses: almost the whole army, according to Livy

battle.significance: Drove Antiochus out of Europe after a single campaign.

events.title: Dedication of the temple of Magna Mater
events.summary: The praetor Marcus Junius Brutus dedicated the temple of the Great Mother on the Palatine, thirteen years after the goddess's arrival. Plautus' comedy Pseudolus was staged at the dedication games, as its production notice (didascalia) records.
events.detail: Excavations on the Palatine have found terracotta figurines of Attis in the temple's earliest deposits, showing the Phrygian cult was present from the start.

events.title: Battle of Corycus
events.summary: The Roman fleet of Gaius Livius Salinator, with Eumenes II of Pergamon, defeated the Seleucid admiral Polyxenidas off Cape Corycus near Erythrae, sinking 10 and capturing 13 ships.

battle.significance: Gave the allies the initiative in the Aegean.

events.title: Siege of Heraclea Trachinia
events.summary: After Thermopylae, Acilius Glabrio besieged and stormed the Aetolian stronghold of Heraclea near Mount Oeta, then besieged Naupactus until Flamininus arranged a truce.

battle.significance: Forced the Aetolians to negotiate.

events.title: The Aetolians and the meaning of deditio
events.summary: Aetolian envoys led by Phaeneas agreed to entrust themselves to the 'faith of the Romans' (in fidem). When Acilius then demanded the surrender of individuals and threatened to put the envoys in chains, Phaeneas protested that this was not Greek custom. Acilius replied that by Roman usage those who gave themselves into Roman fides were at Rome's absolute disposal.
events.detail: Polybius (20.9-10) uses the scene to explain the gulf between the Greek understanding of pistis as a reciprocal relationship and the Roman deditio in fidem as unconditional surrender. It is a central text for Roman diplomatic concepts.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Eckstein, 'Glabrio and the Aetolians: A Note on Deditio', TAPA 125 (1995)

events.title: Final defeat of the Boii
events.summary: The consul Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica defeated the Boii in a great battle and forced their surrender, confiscating half their territory for Roman colonists. Livy claims 28,000 Boii killed. Nasica's triumph, opposed by a tribune, was granted; its spoils included 1,471 gold torques.
events.detail: The submission of the Boii ended Gallic independence south of the Po. Strabo (5.1.6) says the Boii were expelled and migrated to the Danube, but the Po valley names and archaeology show many remained under Roman rule.

battle.significance: Completed the Roman conquest of Cisalpine Gaul south of the Po.

events.debate: Strabo's claim of total expulsion of the Boii is contradicted by later evidence.

events.title: Battle of the Eurymedon (Side)
events.summary: A Rhodian fleet under Eudamus defeated the Seleucid Phoenician fleet commanded by Hannibal and Apollonius off Side in Pamphylia. It was Hannibal's only recorded naval command, and his defeat prevented the Phoenician squadrons from joining the main Seleucid fleet.

battle.significance: Kept the Phoenician fleet out of the Aegean.

events.title: Battle of Myonessus
events.summary: The Roman praetor Lucius Aemilius Regillus with Rhodian allies defeated Polyxenidas off Myonessus near Teos. The Rhodian fire-pots, braziers slung on poles from the bows, were decisive. The Seleucids lost 42 ships, and Antiochus abandoned Lysimachia, leaving the Hellespont open.

sides.strength: 58 Roman and 22 Rhodian ships under L. Aemilius Regillus

battle.significance: Gave Rome command of the Aegean and allowed the Scipios to cross into Asia unopposed.

events.title: Antiochus' peace offer and Africanus' son
events.summary: As the Scipios crossed into Asia, Antiochus offered to pay half the Roman war costs and abandon Lampsacus, Smyrna and Alexandria Troas, and offered Africanus, through the envoy Heraclides, the return without ransom of his captured son. Africanus refused to treat but advised Antiochus not to fight. The king returned the son anyway.

events.title: Battle of Magnesia
events.summary: On the plain near Magnesia-ad-Sipylum, Lucius Cornelius Scipio, with Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus effectively in command while Africanus lay ill at Elaea, defeated Antiochus III's huge multi-ethnic army. Eumenes II's light troops stampeded the scythed chariots back into the Seleucid left, and his cavalry broke it. Antiochus' cataphracts on the right routed a Roman legion and charged to the Roman camp, but too late; the Seleucid phalanx, attacked on all sides and disordered by its own panicking elephants, was destroyed.
events.detail: Livy (37.38-44, from Polybius) catalogues the Seleucid army: 16,000 phalangites in ten blocks with elephants between, cataphracts, Galatians, Arab camel-archers, Cretans, Cappadocians and others, 72,000 in all. Livy gives Seleucid losses as 50,000 foot and 3,000 horse and Roman losses as 300 foot, 24 horse and 25 of Eumenes' men, figures many scholars consider propaganda. The date fell in December 190 or January 189 by the Roman calendar, which was then several weeks ahead of the seasons.

sides.strength: c. 30,000 (4 legions and allies, Pergamenes, Achaeans) plus 16 African elephants
c. 72,000 (Livy) with 54 Indian elephants and scythed chariots
sides.losses: 50,000 foot, 3,000 horse killed, 1,400 captured (Livy; probably inflated)

battle.significance: Destroyed Seleucid power west of the Taurus and made Rome the arbiter of the whole Hellenistic world.

scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)
Bar-Kochva, The Seleucid Army (1976)
Briscoe, A Commentary on Livy XXXIV-XXXVII (1981)
events.debate: Seleucid numbers and losses are disputed; Bar-Kochva accepts Livy's order of battle (from Polybius) but not the loss figures. The role of Domitius is attested by Livy; Africanus' absence spared him the risk of a defeat.

events.title: Decree of Aemilius Paullus at Lascuta
events.summary: On 19 January 189 Lucius Aemilius Paullus, as propraetor in Hispania Ulterior, decreed that the 'slaves of the Hastenses' living in the Turris Lascutana should be free and keep the land and town they held, as long as the Roman people and Senate wished.
events.detail: The bronze tablet, found near Alcalá de los Gazules (Cádiz) and now in the Louvre (CIL II 5041 = ILS 15), is the oldest Latin document from Spain and the oldest original Roman magisterial decree to survive. It shows a governor intervening in local dependency relations to break the power of a hostile city.
events.locName: Turris Lascutana (near Alcalá de los Gazules)

events.title: Siege of Ambracia
events.summary: The consul Marcus Fulvius Nobilior besieged Ambracia, formerly Pyrrhus' capital. When the Romans dug a mine, the defenders countermined and drove them out by filling the tunnel with smoke from burning feathers blown with a bellows. The city surrendered on terms; Fulvius removed its statues and paintings, including statues of the Muses, which he set up in his temple of Hercules Musarum in Rome.
events.detail: Polybius (21.27-28) describes the mine warfare in detail. Ennius accompanied Fulvius and wrote a play, Ambracia, on the campaign, which Cato attacked as unseemly. The Senate later ruled that the looting had been improper.

battle.significance: Forced the Aetolians to accept peace.

events.title: Peace with the Aetolian League: the maiestas clause
events.summary: The Aetolians made peace on harsh terms: an indemnity of 500 talents, surrender of hostages and of the cities taken by Rome since 192, and the obligation to 'preserve the empire and majesty of the Roman people' and to have the same friends and enemies. It was the first Roman treaty with a Greek state to contain the maiestas clause.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

events.title: Manlius Vulso's Galatian war: Mount Olympus
events.summary: Without clear authorisation from the Senate, the consul Gnaeus Manlius Vulso marched against the Galatians, Antiochus' allies. He stormed the Tolistobogii on their refuge of Mount Olympus with massed slingers and archers, then defeated the Tectosages on Mount Magaba near Ancyra. Livy claims 40,000 captives.
events.detail: Polybius (21.38) tells the story of Chiomara, wife of a Galatian chief, who had a Roman centurion who had raped her beheaded and brought his head to her husband. Manlius' campaign was criticised at Rome as private war for plunder.

battle.significance: Crushed Galatian raiding power and handed Eumenes a secure kingdom; brought vast booty to Rome.

events.title: Latin colony at Bononia
events.summary: A Latin colony of 3,000 settlers was founded at Bononia (Bologna) on land taken from the Boii; cavalrymen received 70 iugera, others 50.

events.title: Treaty of Apamea
events.summary: Antiochus III gave up all territory west of the Taurus, paid 15,000 talents (the largest indemnity in ancient history), surrendered his elephants and all warships but ten, which were not to sail west of Cape Sarpedon, and gave 20 hostages including his son Antiochus. He also had to hand over Hannibal and other enemies of Rome, who escaped.
events.detail: The commissioners of ten under Manlius Vulso divided the territory: Eumenes II received most of Asia Minor north of the Maeander, Rhodes received Lycia and Caria south of the river; Greek cities that had backed Rome were declared free. Rome took no territory, a sign of its preferred style of hegemony through client states.
scholarship: Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

events.title: Full citizenship for Formiae, Fundi and Arpinum
events.summary: A tribunician law gave Formiae, Fundi and Arpinum, communities of citizens without the vote (cives sine suffragio), full voting citizenship, enrolling them in the tribes Aemilia and Cornelia. Arpinum later produced Marius and Cicero.

events.title: Death of Antiochus III
events.summary: Short of money for the Apamea indemnity, Antiochus III attempted to plunder the treasury of the temple of Bel in Elymais and was killed by the local population. His son Seleucus IV succeeded.

events.title: The trials of the Scipios
events.summary: Cato and the tribunes Quintus and Quintus Petillius demanded an account of 500 talents received from Antiochus. Africanus tore up his brother's account books in the Senate. Later, prosecuted himself, he reminded the people that it was the anniversary of Zama and led them up to the Capitol to give thanks, leaving the accusers alone. He withdrew to his villa at Liternum. Lucius Scipio was condemned to a fine; the tribune Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, though an enemy, vetoed his imprisonment.
events.detail: Livy (38.50-60) admits that his sources contradict each other hopelessly on dates, charges, tribunes and outcomes, and quotes divergent versions of Valerius Antias. The trials marked the end of Scipionic dominance and a reassertion of collective senatorial control over over-mighty individuals.
scholarship: Scullard, Roman Politics 220-150 BC (1951)
Gruen, 'The Fall of the Scipios', in Malkin & Rubinsohn (eds.), Leaders and Masses in the Roman World (1995)
events.debate: Chronology (187 or 184) and the sequence of trials are irrecoverable; Livy himself despairs. Scullard's model of 'Scipionic' and 'Catonian' factions has been heavily criticised.

events.title: Manlius Vulso's triumph and 'the origin of foreign luxury'
events.summary: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso, after a fight in the Senate over his unauthorised Galatian war, triumphed with Asiatic booty. Livy says his army introduced to Rome bronze dining couches, costly coverlets and tapestries, one-legged tables, female lute and harp players at dinners, and cooks, who rose from the cheapest of slaves to the most valued.
events.detail: Livy (39.6.7-9), probably following Piso Frugi, dates the beginning of Roman luxury to this triumph; other moralists chose 146 (Sallust) or 133. The topos of decline through eastern wealth is itself an important Roman historiographical idea.

events.title: Via Aemilia
events.summary: The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus built a road from Ariminum to Placentia along the foot of the Apennines, binding the newly conquered Po plain to Rome. His colleague Gaius Flaminius built a road from Bononia across the Apennines to Arretium.
events.detail: The Via Aemilia gave its name to the region (Aemilia, modern Emilia-Romagna) and fixed the line of colonies at Bononia, Mutina, Parma and Placentia.

events.title: The Bacchanalia affair
events.summary: Alerted by the courtesan Hispala Faecenia and her young lover Publius Aebutius, the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus revealed to the Senate a secret Bacchic cult accused of nocturnal orgies, forged wills and murders. A special inquiry pursued it across Italy: over 7,000 people were said to be implicated, and many were executed. The Senate's decree permitted Bacchic worship only with its permission, in groups of no more than five, with no common fund or male priests.
events.detail: Livy's lurid narrative (39.8-19) contrasts with the dry bronze copy of the senatus consultum de Bacchanalibus found at Tiriolo in Bruttium in 1640 (CIL I² 581, now Vienna), addressed to the allied communities of the ager Teuranus. Interpretations range from genuine moral panic to the Senate's assertion of authority over religion throughout allied Italy (Gruen), the suppression of a cross-class, cross-gender organisation outside elite control (Pailler, North) and a pretext for intervention in allied affairs.
events.locName: Rome and Italy (copy found at Tiriolo, Calabria)
scholarship: Gruen, Studies in Greek Culture and Roman Policy (1990)
Pailler, Bacchanalia (1988)
Beard, North & Price, Religions of Rome (1998)
events.debate: The decree is dated to the Nones of October (7 October) 186. How far Livy's account reflects real events rather than a moralising novella, and why the Senate acted, are long debated.

events.title: First athletic contests and wild-beast hunt at Rome
events.summary: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior celebrated votive games for his Aetolian victory lasting ten days, at which Rome saw for the first time Greek athletic contests and a venatio, a hunt of lions and panthers. Many Greek actors came to honour him.

events.title: Censorship of Cato
events.summary: Cato and Lucius Valerius Flaccus held the most famous censorship in Roman history. Cato expelled seven senators, among them the ex-consul Lucius Quinctius Flamininus for killing a Gallic noble at a banquet to amuse a boy lover, took the public horse from Lucius Scipio Asiaticus, assessed luxury goods, slaves and carriages at ten times their value and taxed them, cut off private pipes illegally drawing public water, demolished buildings encroaching on public land, and let public contracts at harsh prices.
events.detail: Valerius was made princeps senatus. Cato's severity earned him a statue in the temple of Salus with an inscription praising him for restoring the Roman state when it was tottering (Plutarch, Cato 19). He also cleaned and extended the sewers. The censorship became the archetype of the censor as moral guardian.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)

events.title: Basilica Porcia, the first basilica in Rome
events.summary: Cato as censor bought two houses and four shops by the Curia and built the Basilica Porcia, the first known basilica in Rome, a covered hall for business and courts. The tribunes of the plebs later used it as their headquarters. It burned with the Curia in 52 BC.
events.detail: The basilica form, probably adapted from Hellenistic stoas and halls, spread rapidly: Basilica Aemilia (179), Basilica Sempronia (169) and Basilica Opimia (121).

events.title: Death of Scipio Africanus
events.summary: Scipio Africanus died in voluntary exile at his villa at Liternum, aged about 52. He reportedly asked to be buried there rather than in ungrateful Rome; Valerius Maximus quotes the epitaph 'Ingrata patria, ne ossa quidem mea habes'.
events.detail: Livy (39.52) records disagreement over the year (187 to 183) and the place of burial, noting monuments at both Liternum and the Tomb of the Scipios. Seneca visited the villa and its small dark bath (Epistles 86).
events.debate: Polybius places his death in the same year as Hannibal's and Philopoemen's (183); Valerius Antias put it earlier.

events.title: Death of Hannibal
events.summary: After Apamea Hannibal fled via Crete (where, Nepos says, he hid his treasure in amphorae filled with lead) to Armenia and then to Prusias I of Bithynia, for whom he won a naval battle against Eumenes by hurling jars of snakes onto the enemy ships. When Flamininus came as envoy and Prusias agreed to surrender him, Hannibal took poison at Libyssa, saying, according to Livy, 'let us relieve the Romans of their long anxiety'.
events.detail: Nepos (Hannibal 13) notes that Atticus dated his death to 183, Polybius to 182 and Sulpicius Blitho to 181.
events.debate: Year (183, 182 or 181) disputed in antiquity; Flamininus' role was criticised even by Romans (Plutarch).

events.title: Death of Philopoemen
events.summary: The seventy-year-old Achaean general Philopoemen, 'the last of the Greeks', was captured by rebel Messenians and forced to drink poison in prison. The young Polybius carried his funeral urn in the procession to Megalopolis.

events.title: Colonies of Parma, Mutina and Saturnia; Potentia and Pisaurum
events.summary: A burst of colonisation in the north and on the Adriatic: citizen colonies at Potentia and Pisaurum (184), Parma and Mutina with 2,000 settlers each and Saturnia (183), and Graviscae (181). Unlike earlier Latin colonies these were citizen colonies with substantial allotments.

events.title: Founding of Aquileia
events.summary: A Latin colony of 3,000 infantry families was founded at Aquileia at the head of the Adriatic to block Gallic migrations and Istrian raids; it was reinforced with 1,500 more families in 169. It was the last Latin colony founded in Italy and grew into one of the great cities of the Empire.
events.detail: Its foundation followed the expulsion of a group of 12,000 Transalpine Gauls who had tried to settle nearby in 186-183.

events.title: Discovery and burning of the 'Books of Numa'
events.summary: Workmen digging on land of the scribe Lucius Petillius at the foot of the Janiculum found two stone chests, one inscribed as the coffin of King Numa, the other containing books on pontifical law in Latin and on Pythagorean philosophy in Greek. The urban praetor judged them subversive of religion and, with the Senate's approval, burned them in the Comitium.
events.detail: The episode reflects the contemporary belief, rejected by Livy and Cicero on chronological grounds, that Numa was Pythagoras' pupil, and Roman anxiety about Greek philosophy.

events.title: Lex Cornelia Baebia de ambitu
events.summary: The consuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus carried the first known law against electoral bribery (ambitus), reflecting the escalating cost of competition for office. A related Lex Baebia provided for four and six praetors in alternate years, but was soon abandoned.

events.title: Battle of Aebura
events.summary: In the First Celtiberian War the praetor Quintus Fulvius Flaccus defeated a Celtiberian army near Aebura in Carpetania and in 180 fought his way through an ambush at the Manlian Pass. Livy claims 23,000 enemy killed at Aebura.

sides.strength: praetorian army under Q. Fulvius Flaccus

battle.significance: Opened the way for Gracchus' settlement.

events.title: Lex Villia Annalis
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Villius carried a law fixing the minimum ages at which each magistracy could be held. It probably also required an interval of two years (biennium) between curule offices and made the praetorship a prerequisite for the consulship, regularising the cursus honorum.
events.detail: The law responded to the meteoric careers of the war generation (Scipio, Flamininus) and to fierce electoral competition. Under Sulla's later revision the minimum ages were 30 for the quaestorship, 39 for the praetorship and 42 for the consulship; the original Villian ages are inferred rather than attested.
scholarship: Astin, The Lex Annalis before Sulla (1958)
Evans & Kleijwegt, 'Did the Romans like Young Men?', ZPE 92 (1992)
events.debate: The exact age limits of the Villian law are not stated by any source and are reconstructed from known careers.

events.title: Pestilence and poisoning trials
events.summary: A severe epidemic struck Rome and Italy between 182 and 180, killing a consul (Gaius Calpurnius Piso), a pontifex maximus and many others. Suspicion of poisoning led to special inquiries; Livy says 3,000 were condemned in 180, among them Piso's widow Hostilia, accused of poisoning her husband to make her son consul.

events.title: Deportation of the Apuan Ligurians to Samnium
events.summary: After years of Ligurian warfare, the proconsuls Publius Cornelius Cethegus and Marcus Baebius Tamphilus forcibly moved 40,000 Apuan Ligurians with their women and children to public land in Samnium, giving them 150,000 sesterces for equipment. Another 7,000 followed. The deportees formed two communities, the Ligures Baebiani and Ligures Corneliani.
events.detail: The Ligures Baebiani were still a distinct community three centuries later: a bronze alimentary table of Trajan (AD 101) found at Macchia di Circello records loans to its landowners.
events.locName: Samnium (Ligures Baebiani, Macchia di Circello) from the Apuan Alps

events.title: Tiberius Gracchus' settlement of Celtiberia
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus (father of the Gracchi), praetor in Citerior 180-178, combined victories with negotiation. His treaties fixed tribute and military service obligations, settled landless Celtiberians, forbade the founding of new fortified towns, and founded Gracchurris on the upper Ebro. The peace held for 25 years.
