events.detail: Polybius (25.1) mocked claims that Gracchus had taken 300 towns, saying many were mere forts. The ban on new walled towns was the legal pretext for the war with Segeda in 154.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)

events.title: Censorship of Lepidus and Nobilior: Basilica Aemilia and Pons Aemilius
events.summary: The censors Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Marcus Fulvius Nobilior, publicly reconciled from bitter enmity at the Senate's urging, built the Basilica Aemilia et Fulvia on the north side of the Forum, a fish market, a harbour and the piers of the first stone bridge over the Tiber, the Pons Aemilius, whose arches were completed in 142. They also reorganised voting in the tribal assembly by region, status and class.
events.detail: The Basilica, rebuilt by later Aemilii into the first century AD, preserves the family name. The voting reform (Livy 40.51.9) is obscure.

events.title: Death of Philip V; accession of Perseus
events.summary: Philip V, who had rebuilt Macedonian strength since 196, died at Amphipolis in 179, haunted, as the tradition has it, by the execution in 180 of his pro-Roman younger son Demetrius on charges brought by his elder son Perseus, supported by a letter from Flamininus later said to be forged. Perseus succeeded and renewed the treaty with Rome.
events.detail: Polybius (23.10) treats the Demetrius affair as a tragedy sent by the Furies. Roman historians portrayed Perseus as planning war from the start; modern scholars see a cautious king whose popularity in Greece alarmed Rome and Eumenes.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)
events.debate: Whether the letter incriminating Demetrius was forged is uncertain.

events.title: Second Istrian War: siege of Nesactium
events.summary: After the Istrians captured a Roman camp at the Timavus in 178 (its garrison was found drunk on the captured wine when retaken), the consul Gaius Claudius Pulcher besieged Nesactium and took it by diverting the river that supplied it. King Aepulo and the defenders killed their families and themselves. Istria submitted.

sides.strength: consular army under C. Claudius Pulcher

battle.significance: Ended Istrian independence.

events.title: Gracchus' war in Sardinia: 'Sardi venales'
events.summary: The consul Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus crushed a rising of the Ilienses and Balari in Sardinia in 177-176, killing or capturing 80,000 according to the tablet he dedicated in the temple of Mater Matuta. So many captives were sold that 'Sardi venales' ('Sardinians for sale', i.e. cheap goods) became a proverb.
events.detail: Livy (41.28.8-10) quotes the dedicatory tablet, which bore a map of Sardinia with depictions of the battles, an early example of a Roman triumphal map.

battle.significance: Broke Sardinian resistance for a generation; flooded the slave market.

events.title: Citizen colony at Luna
events.summary: A citizen colony of 2,000 settlers was founded at Luna on land taken from the Ligurians at the mouth of the Magra; it later became famous for the white marble of the nearby Apuan quarries (Carrara).

events.title: Expulsion of two Epicurean philosophers
events.summary: In the consulship of Lucius Postumius, two Epicureans, Alcaeus and Philiscus, were expelled from Rome for corrupting the young with the doctrine of pleasure.
events.debate: The date depends on identifying the consul Postumius (173 or 155).

events.title: The Statellates affair
events.summary: The consul Marcus Popillius Laenas attacked the Ligurian Statellates, who had never fought Rome, and after they surrendered sold 10,000 of them into slavery. The Senate ordered their freedom and restitution; Popillius defied it. In 172 the tribunes passed a Lex Marcia for an inquiry, but Popillius' brother, the new consul, obstructed it and the case collapsed.

events.title: Both consuls plebeian for the first time
events.summary: Gaius Popillius Laenas and Publius Aelius Ligus were elected consuls for 172, the first time both consuls were plebeians. The Fasti Capitolini note 'ambo primi de plebe'. The Licinio-Sextian requirement that one consul be plebeian (367) had never been matched by a rule requiring a patrician.

events.title: Eumenes' denunciation of Perseus and the attack at Delphi
events.summary: Eumenes II came to Rome in person and denounced Perseus to the Senate for war preparations, his marriage alliance with the Seleucids and his intrigues in Greece. On his way home he was nearly killed by a rockfall at Delphi engineered, it was said, by Perseus' agents. The Senate decided on war.
events.detail: Livy (42.11-18) gives Eumenes' speech. Polybius (22.18) said the true causes of the war went back to Philip's resentment; modern scholars see Rome as determined to eliminate a revived Macedon regardless of Perseus' conduct.

sources.w: Roman letter to the Amphictyons on Perseus

scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
events.debate: A Roman indictment of Perseus inscribed at Delphi (Syll.³ 643) lists the official charges. The degree of Perseus' aggression is disputed.

events.title: Carteia, the first Latin colony outside Italy
events.summary: More than 4,000 men, sons of Roman soldiers and Spanish women, who as children of unions without conubium had no citizenship, petitioned the Senate for a town. They were settled at Carteia near the Strait of Gibraltar as a Latin colony 'of freedmen' (libertinorum), together with the existing inhabitants who wished to join.
events.detail: Carteia is the first Latin colony founded outside Italy and a revealing glimpse of the social consequences of long Roman service in Spain.

events.title: Spanish envoys accuse Roman governors
events.summary: Envoys from both Spanish provinces complained to the Senate of the greed of Roman magistrates. The praetor appointed panels of five senatorial recuperatores for each case, and patrons for the Spaniards, among them Cato, Aemilius Paullus and Scipio Nasica. One ex-governor was acquitted and two, Publius Furius Philus and Marcus Matienus, went into exile before verdict.
events.detail: The Senate also forbade Roman officials to fix the price of grain or to station prefects in Spanish towns to collect money. The procedure prefigured the permanent extortion court of 149.
scholarship: Richardson, Hispaniae (1986)
Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

events.title: Battle of Callinicus
events.summary: Perseus caught the consul Publius Licinius Crassus' cavalry and light troops near the hill of Callinicus outside Larissa and routed them, but did not commit his phalanx to exploit the victory. He then offered peace on the terms of his father's treaty; the Romans, true to their custom of never negotiating after a defeat, refused.
events.detail: Polybius (27.8) uses the Roman refusal to illustrate a national characteristic: they were most unyielding in defeat. Greek sympathy for Perseus after the battle alarmed Rome.

sides.strength: cavalry and light infantry of P. Licinius Crassus' army
sides.losses: c. 200 cavalry and 2,000 infantry killed, 600 captured (Livy)

battle.significance: Perseus' only major victory; his failure to follow it up and Rome's refusal to negotiate set the pattern of the war.

events.title: Lex Voconia
events.summary: The tribune Quintus Voconius Saxa carried a law, supported by the elderly Cato, forbidding citizens of the first census class to institute a woman as heir and limiting legacies so that no legatee received more than the heirs.
events.detail: The law aimed to stop great fortunes passing to women; it was evaded by trusts (fideicommissa) and by not registering in the census. Cicero (Verrines 2.1.104-114) shows Verres' manipulation of it; St Augustine still found it unjust.

events.title: Marcius Philippus crosses into Pieria
events.summary: The consul Quintus Marcius Philippus led his army over a difficult pass near Lake Ascuris, lowering elephants down cliffs on ramps, and descended into Pieria behind Perseus' lines at Tempe. Perseus panicked and abandoned the passes, but recovered as Marcius' supplies failed. The Achaean cavalry commander that year, Polybius, met Marcius as an envoy.

events.title: Battle of Pydna
events.summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus faced Perseus on the plain near Pydna. On the evening before, the military tribune Gaius Sulpicius Gallus had predicted a lunar eclipse to calm the troops. Next afternoon a skirmish over a runaway pack animal at the river escalated into battle. The Macedonian phalanx advanced irresistibly at first, but as it crossed uneven ground gaps opened; Roman maniples pushed into them and the phalangites, helpless at close quarters with their long sarissas, were massacred. Perseus fled with the cavalry.
events.detail: Paullus told Polybius he had never seen anything more terrifying than the advancing phalanx (Polybius 29.17). Livy gives 20,000 Macedonian dead and 11,000 captured; Plutarch, citing Paullus' son-in-law Scipio Nasica, puts Roman losses at about 100. The battle confirmed Polybius' analysis of legion versus phalanx. At Delphi Paullus took over a pillar prepared for a statue of Perseus and topped it with his own equestrian statue; its frieze, the earliest Roman historical relief, shows the loose horse that started the battle.

battle.significance: Ended the Antigonid monarchy; Macedon was dismembered and the Hellenistic world recognised Roman supremacy.

sources.w: Monument of Aemilius Paullus at Delphi

scholarship: Hammond, 'The Battle of Pydna', JHS 104 (1984)
Kähler, Der Fries vom Reiterdenkmal des Aemilius Paullus in Delphi (1965)
events.debate: The battle date is fixed by the lunar eclipse of 21 June 168 (Julian), which Livy (44.37.8) places on 3 September by the Roman calendar, showing the civil calendar was about 2.5 months ahead of the seasons. Exact site uncertain.

events.title: The Day of Eleusis
events.summary: Antiochus IV, having occupied much of Egypt in the Sixth Syrian War, was besieging Alexandria when the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas met him at Eleusis, a suburb of the city, and handed him the Senate's decree ordering him out of Egypt. When the king asked for time to consult, Popillius drew a circle in the sand around him with his vine staff and told him to answer before stepping out of it. Antiochus complied and withdrew from Egypt and Cyprus.
events.detail: Polybius (29.27) says Popillius acted with such confidence because news of Pydna had just arrived. The episode, famous as 'the circle of Popillius', showed that the word of a single Roman senator could now stop a Hellenistic great power in its tracks.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)
Morkholm, Antiochus IV of Syria (1966)
events.debate: The Book of Daniel refers to the 'ships of Kittim' turning back the king of the north; Antiochus' subsequent measures in Jerusalem (167) have been linked to his humiliation.

events.title: Third Illyrian War: Genthius surrenders at Scodra
events.summary: Genthius, king of the Illyrians, allied with Perseus for a promised subsidy of 300 talents (mostly never paid) and imprisoned Roman envoys. The praetor Lucius Anicius Gallus defeated him in a campaign of thirty days and besieged him in Scodra, where Genthius surrendered. He was led in Anicius' triumph.

battle.significance: Ended the Ardiaean kingdom; Illyria divided into three tributary districts.

events.title: Surrender of Perseus at Samothrace
events.summary: Perseus fled with his treasure to the sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace. Blockaded by the praetor Gnaeus Octavius' fleet and abandoned by his Cretan guards, who made off with his gold, he surrendered with his children. Paullus received him with courtesy and wept, Plutarch says, at the reversal of fortune.

events.title: Triumph of Aemilius Paullus
events.summary: Aemilius Paullus' triumph lasted three days: 250 wagons of statues and paintings, then armour, then coin, and finally Perseus walking with his children before the chariot. Five days before, Paullus' 14-year-old son had died, and three days after it his 12-year-old son died too; his two elder sons had been adopted into other families (one became Scipio Aemilianus). Paullus told the people that Fortune had taken her due from his house rather than from the state.
events.detail: Paullus kept nothing for himself except Perseus' library, which he gave to his sons. His soldiers, angry at their share of the booty, nearly blocked the triumph, inspired by Servius Sulpicius Galba. Perseus died in captivity at Alba Fucens a few years later.

events.title: Macedonia divided into four republics
events.summary: At Amphipolis, Aemilius Paullus and ten commissioners proclaimed the Macedonians free, abolished the monarchy and divided the kingdom into four autonomous republics (merides) with capitals at Amphipolis, Thessalonica, Pella and Pelagonia. Intermarriage and land purchase across their borders were forbidden, the royal gold and silver mines closed, the cutting of ship timber banned, and tribute fixed at half what had been paid to the kings. The royal officials and their sons over fifteen were deported to Italy.
events.detail: Illyria was similarly divided into three districts. Livy (45.18) presents the closure of the mines as protecting the Macedonians from Roman publicani. The mines reopened in 158. The settlement aimed to make Macedon harmless without the cost of direct rule; it lasted until Andriscus.
scholarship: Gruen, The Hellenistic World and the Coming of Rome (1984)

events.title: The sack of Epirus
events.summary: On the Senate's orders, Aemilius Paullus punished the Molossians of Epirus, who had sided with Perseus. Roman detachments entered seventy towns simultaneously on a fixed day, collected all valuables, then sacked the towns and enslaved 150,000 people. The proceeds paid the army's donative.
events.detail: Polybius (30.15, preserved by Strabo 7.7.3) and Livy (45.34) record the figures. It was one of the largest enslavements in ancient history and a calculated act of terror; Harris uses it as evidence for Roman brutality and for the economic motive of plunder and slaves.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Ziolkowski, 'Urbs direpta, or how the Romans sacked cities', in Rich & Shipley (eds.), War and Society in the Roman World (1993)
events.debate: The figure of 150,000 may be inflated but is taken seriously by most historians; it fed the slave economy of Italy.

events.title: The thousand Achaean hostages; Polybius in Rome
events.summary: Denounced by the pro-Roman Achaean politician Callicrates, about 1,000 leading Achaeans suspected of sympathy for Perseus were deported to Italy and detained without trial in Etruscan towns for sixteen years. One of them, the former cavalry commander Polybius of Megalopolis, was allowed to stay in Rome, where he became the mentor and friend of the young Scipio Aemilianus and began his Histories.
events.detail: When the 300 survivors were finally released in 150, Cato remarked that the Senate was spending a whole day debating whether some old Greeks should be buried by Italian or Achaean undertakers. The detention embittered Achaean politics and contributed to the war of 146.

events.title: Roman citizens freed from direct tax
events.summary: The Macedonian booty deposited by Paullus was so large that the tributum, the direct property tax paid by Roman citizens to fund war, was no longer levied from 167. Citizens of Italy paid no direct tax again until 43 BC.
events.detail: Pliny (33.56) says Paullus deposited 300 million sesterces; Velleius gives 200 million and Livy's figure (45.40) is lower. The end of tributum shows how empire paid for itself and shifted the fiscal burden to provincials.
events.debate: The booty totals vary by source; the tributum was technically suspended, not abolished.

events.title: Terence's first comedy
events.summary: Publius Terentius Afer, a former slave from North Africa, staged the Andria at the Megalesian games of 166. His five other comedies followed until 160, the Adelphoe and a second attempt at the Hecyra being performed at the funeral games of Aemilius Paullus.
events.detail: Terence adapted Menander and Apollodorus with a polished style admired by the Scipionic circle; rumours that Scipio Aemilianus or Laelius wrote his plays circulated in his lifetime and he answered them in his prologues.

events.title: Rhodes punished: Delos made a free port
events.summary: Rhodes had tried to mediate between Rome and Perseus, which the Senate took as an affront. Rome stripped Rhodes of Lycia and Caria and gave Delos to Athens as a customs-free port. Rhodian harbour dues fell, according to Rhodian envoys, from a million drachmas a year to 150,000.
events.detail: Polybius (30.31) records the envoys' complaint. Delos became the great slave market of the Aegean, where 10,000 slaves could change hands in a day (Strabo 14.5.2). Rhodes became a formal ally in 164.

events.title: Escape of Demetrius from Rome
events.summary: Demetrius, son of Seleucus IV, held as a hostage in Rome since 178, was repeatedly refused permission by the Senate to claim the Seleucid throne after the death of Antiochus IV. With the help of his friend Polybius, who planned the escape, he slipped out of Rome during a hunting party, sailed from Ostia on a Carthaginian ship and seized the throne as Demetrius I Soter.
events.detail: Polybius (31.11-15) tells the story in the first person, one of the most vivid passages of his work.

events.title: Masinissa seizes the Emporia
events.summary: Masinissa occupied the fertile coastal Emporia region of the Lesser Syrtis, claiming it as ancestral land under the 201 treaty. A Roman embassy, Polybius says, ruled in his favour as always, and Carthage lost the towns and paid 500 talents for the revenues.
events.detail: Polybius (31.21) admits that Carthage had the better case but that Roman arbiters favoured Masinissa. Repeated encroachments over the next decade drove Carthage to the war of 150.
events.debate: The date may be 162 or 161; Livy's epitomes place a later dispute in 157.

events.title: Roman treaty with Judas Maccabaeus
events.summary: Judas Maccabaeus, leader of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucids, sent Eupolemus and Jason to Rome and obtained a treaty of friendship and alliance. The Senate wrote warning Demetrius I not to oppress the Jews, Rome's friends.
events.detail: The text of the treaty is given in 1 Maccabees 8 and Josephus. It was a cheap way to weaken the Seleucids and had no immediate practical effect (Judas was killed in 160), but it began a relationship that ended with Pompey's capture of Jerusalem in 63.
events.debate: Authenticity of the treaty text was once doubted but is now generally accepted, though its wording has been adapted. The Hasmonean polity formally dates from c. 140; the polity tag here anticipates it.

events.title: Senatus consultum expelling philosophers and rhetors
events.summary: A decree of the Senate in the consulship of Gaius Fannius Strabo and Marcus Valerius Messalla authorised the praetor Marcus Pomponius to ensure that no philosophers or rhetoricians remained in Rome.
events.detail: Suetonius and Gellius quote the decree's wording. Like the expulsion of the Epicureans and the reaction to Carneades, it shows a conservative senatorial anxiety about Greek education that never stopped the elite from employing Greek teachers.

events.title: Lex Fannia sumptuaria
events.summary: A sumptuary law of the consul Gaius Fannius Strabo limited the cost of dinners to 100 asses on certain festival days, 30 asses on ten other days a month and 10 asses on ordinary days, restricted the number of guests and forbade serving more than one hen, which must not be fattened.
events.detail: Lucilius mocked the law's 'miserable hundred asses'. Pliny (10.139) notes that the hen clause led Romans to fatten capons instead, a classic example of sumptuary law evasion.

events.title: Death of Aemilius Paullus
events.summary: Lucius Aemilius Paullus died after a long illness. His estate was so modest that his widow's dowry could barely be repaid. At his funeral games, organised by his sons Fabius Aemilianus and Scipio Aemilianus, Terence's Adelphoe was staged.

events.title: Censorship of Scipio Nasica Corculum; the first water clock
events.summary: As censor, Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum removed from the Forum all statues of magistrates set up without the authority of the people or Senate, and installed Rome's first public water clock under cover, so that the hour could be told on cloudy days and at night. A Lex Cornelia Fulvia against electoral bribery carried death or exile.

events.title: Dalmatian War: capture of Delminium
events.summary: The Dalmatae, accused of attacking Roman allies Issa and the Daorsi and of insulting Roman envoys, were attacked in 156 by Gaius Marcius Figulus, who failed. In 155 Scipio Nasica Corculum took their stronghold of Delminium by shooting bundles of burning pitch-soaked tow into the town with catapults. Polybius says the Senate wanted to keep Italian soldiers from going soft in peace.

battle.significance: Brought the Dalmatae temporarily to submission; Nasica triumphed.

events.title: Ptolemy VIII bequeaths Cyrene to Rome
events.summary: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II, then king of Cyrene and at war with his brother Ptolemy VI, published a will leaving his kingdom to Rome if he died without heirs, to deter assassination and secure Roman support. The will was inscribed in stone at Cyrene.
events.detail: The inscription (SEG IX 7), found in 1929, is the first known royal bequest to Rome and a model for the wills of Attalus III (133), Ptolemy Apion (96) and Nicomedes IV (74). Ptolemy VIII outlived its purpose and it never took effect.

events.title: The embassy of the philosophers
events.summary: Athens, fined 500 talents for sacking Oropus, sent the heads of three philosophical schools to Rome to plead its case: Carneades of the Academy, Diogenes of Babylon of the Stoa and Critolaus of the Peripatos. Their lectures enthralled Roman youth. Carneades spoke one day in praise of justice and the next against it, arguing that if Rome practised justice it would have to return its empire and go back to huts.
events.detail: Cato urged the Senate to decide quickly and send them home before they corrupted the young (Plutarch, Cato 22). The fine was reduced to 100 talents. The episode is a landmark in the reception of Greek philosophy at Rome; Cicero later reworked Carneades' arguments in De re publica 3.

events.title: Lusitanian raids into Ulterior
events.summary: Lusitanians under Punicus raided Roman Ulterior, defeating the praetors Manius Manilius and Lucius Calpurnius Piso with 6,000 Roman dead. Their successor Caesarus defeated Lucius Mummius in 153. The Lusitanian War, with intervals, lasted until 139.

events.title: The first stone theatre demolished
events.summary: The censors Marcus Valerius Messalla and Gaius Cassius Longinus began a permanent stone theatre near the Palatine. On the motion of Scipio Nasica Corculum the Senate ordered it pulled down as harmful to public morals, sold the materials, and for a time forbade seating at plays within a mile of Rome.
events.detail: Rome had no permanent theatre until Pompey's of 55 BC, which was disguised as an approach to a temple of Venus Victrix.

events.title: Consular year begins on 1 January
events.summary: Because of the emergency in Spain, the consuls of 153 took office on 1 January instead of 15 March, so that Quintus Fulvius Nobilior could reach Spain earlier in the campaigning season. The date stuck, and 1 January became the start of the Roman civil year and eventually of ours.

events.title: Nobilior's defeats: the Vulcanalia and the elephants at Numantia
events.summary: When Segeda of the Belli enlarged its walls in breach of the Gracchan treaties, Quintus Fulvius Nobilior marched with nearly 30,000 men. On 23 August, the feast of the Vulcanalia, the Segedan Carus ambushed his column and killed 6,000 Romans; the day was afterwards held unlucky. Nobilior then attacked the Arevaci at Numantia with ten elephants sent by Masinissa; one was struck by a stone, panicked, and stampeded the others through the Roman ranks, and 4,000 more Romans fell.

sides.strength: c. 30,000 under Q. Fulvius Nobilior with 10 elephants
sides.losses: 6,000 in the ambush and 4,000 at Numantia (Appian)

sides.strength: Belli, Titthi and Arevaci; 20,000 foot, 5,000 horse under Carus

battle.significance: Beginning of twenty years of humiliations for Rome in Celtiberia.

events.title: Cato's embassy to Carthage: 'Carthago delenda est'
events.summary: Cato served on an embassy to arbitrate between Carthage and Masinissa and was alarmed by Carthage's prosperity, manpower and arms. Back in Rome he dropped fresh figs from his toga in the Senate, saying they had been picked three days ago in Carthage, and ended every speech, whatever the subject, by declaring that Carthage must be destroyed. Scipio Nasica Corculum answered each time that Carthage must be preserved, as a check on Roman decadence.
events.detail: The exact formula 'Carthago delenda est' is a later standardisation; Plutarch gives the Greek sense. Whether Rome's motive in 149 was fear, greed, Masinissa's ambitions or Catonian ideology is debated: Harris stresses aggression, Astin traces the debate inside the Senate, and others note that Carthage had nearly finished paying the indemnity in 151.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)
Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
events.debate: The date (153 or 152) and Nasica's motives are debated; the figs story is probably authentic in substance.

events.title: Foundation of Corduba
events.summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus founded Corduba on the Baetis, the first Roman settlement of its kind in the south and later the capital of Baetica, home of the two Senecas and Lucan. In 152, as consul, Marcellus made a negotiated peace with the Celtiberians that the Senate initially rejected.
events.detail: Polybius (35.2-4) describes the Senate's refusal of Marcellus' peace and the 'fiery war' in Spain; Marcellus nevertheless concluded it on his own terms.
events.debate: Strabo does not date the foundation: it may belong to Marcellus' praetorship (169/168) or to his third consulship (152).

events.title: Levy crisis and the ban on second consulships
events.summary: Terrified by reports of Celtiberian warfare, young Romans evaded the levy for Spain and tribunes imprisoned the consuls Lucius Licinius Lucullus and Aulus Postumius Albinus for refusing exemptions. The 34-year-old Scipio Aemilianus shamed the young nobles by volunteering as military tribune. About this time a law, supported by Cato, forbade anyone to hold the consulship twice.
events.detail: Polybius (35.4) was in Rome and describes the panic. The iteration ban explains why Aemilianus' election in 134 required a special exemption.
events.debate: The date of the law against iteration (c. 152-151) is inferred.

events.title: Lucullus' massacre at Cauca
events.summary: Without provocation or authorisation, Lucius Licinius Lucullus attacked the Vaccaei. Cauca surrendered, paying 100 talents and giving hostages; Lucullus then sent troops inside and massacred the adult males, about 20,000. At Intercatia Scipio Aemilianus killed a Spanish champion in single combat and was first over the wall, winning the mural crown; at Pallantia Lucullus failed.
events.detail: Appian (Iberica 52) says Lucullus was never brought to account. The episode, with Galba's massacre a year later, fuelled the movement for an extortion court.

battle.significance: A byword for Roman bad faith in Spain.

events.title: Galba's massacre of the Lusitanians
events.summary: Servius Sulpicius Galba, praetor in Ulterior, promised the Lusitanians good land if they laid down their arms, divided them into three groups, disarmed them and then had them slaughtered. Suetonius gives 30,000 victims. Among the few survivors was a young herdsman named Viriathus.
events.detail: Prosecuted in 149 by the tribune Lucius Scribonius Libo, with the 85-year-old Cato speaking against him in his last speech, Galba won acquittal by tearfully presenting his young children and an orphaned ward to the people. Cicero thought him the greatest orator of his age. The scandal helped carry the Lex Calpurnia.

battle.significance: Produced Viriathus and a decade of war.

events.title: Carthage's war with Masinissa
events.summary: Provoked beyond endurance, Carthage raised an army under Hasdrubal and fought Masinissa, now 88 and still riding without a saddle, near Oroscopa. Surrounded in a hilltop camp, starved and diseased, the Carthaginians surrendered, but Gulussa's Numidian cavalry massacred them as they left disarmed. Scipio Aemilianus, in Africa to obtain elephants for Lucullus, watched from a hill.
events.detail: By waging war without Roman permission Carthage breached the treaty of 201, giving Rome its pretext. Appian gives 58,000 Carthaginians, few of whom returned.

sides.strength: 25,400 foot and 400 horse plus later levies (Appian)
sides.losses: most of the army killed after surrender

battle.significance: Carthage's breach of the 201 treaty became Rome's casus belli.

events.title: Rome declares war; the Carthaginian surrender and the final demand
events.summary: Rome declared war on Carthage. Utica had already surrendered to Rome. Carthage too made a formal deditio, handing over 300 children of noble families as hostages and then, at the consuls' demand, 200,000 sets of armour and 2,000 catapults. Only then did the consuls Manius Manilius and Lucius Marcius Censorinus announce the Senate's final condition: the Carthaginians must abandon their city and resettle at least 80 stades (about 15 km) from the sea. Carthage refused and prepared to fight.
events.detail: In desperation the Carthaginians freed slaves, worked day and night in the temples making weapons, and, the tradition says, cut off women's hair for catapult cords. Polybius (36.2-9) records the debate among Greeks over whether Rome had acted justly; Appian (Libyca 74-93) preserves Censorinus' speech arguing that a city by the sea breeds dangerous ambitions.
scholarship: Harris, War and Imperialism in Republican Rome (1979)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Miles, Carthage Must Be Destroyed (2010)
events.debate: Polybius 36.9 reports four Greek views on the morality of Rome's conduct. Modern debate pits Roman fear and Catonian ideology against greed for land and plunder and the desire to forestall Masinissa.

events.title: Lex Calpurnia de repetundis: the first permanent criminal court
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi carried a law creating a standing court (quaestio perpetua) under a praetor, with a jury of senators, to hear claims by provincials and allies for the recovery of money illegally taken by Roman magistrates (pecuniae repetundae).
events.detail: Cicero (Brutus 106) calls it the first such law. Its procedure was civil rather than penal: restitution, not punishment. It became the model for the system of standing criminal courts that Gaius Gracchus (who transferred juries to the equites), Sulla and Augustus developed, and the control of the repetundae juries became one of the great political battlegrounds of the late Republic.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)
Richardson, 'The Purpose of the Lex Calpurnia de repetundis', JRS 77 (1987)
events.debate: J. S. Richardson argued that the law served Roman interests in controlling governors more than provincial redress.

events.title: Death of Cato the Elder
events.summary: Cato died at about 85, in the year the war he had demanded began. In his last months he spoke against Galba and was still writing the Origines, the first history of Rome in Latin prose, which omitted the names of generals and recorded the deeds of the Roman people as a whole (and the name of a brave Carthaginian elephant, Surus).

events.title: Siege of Carthage
events.summary: For three years Rome besieged Carthage, a city of perhaps 200,000 behind a triple wall across the isthmus. The consuls of 149 failed: Censorinus breached the wall but was repulsed, and his fleet was burned by fireships. Only the military tribune Scipio Aemilianus distinguished himself. In 147 Aemilianus, now consul, cut the city off by land and built a great mole across the harbour mouth; the Carthaginians dug a new channel and sailed out a fleet built in secret, but delayed and lost the chance. In spring 146 Laelius stormed the Cothon and the Romans fought for six days from house to house up the streets to the Byrsa.
events.detail: Appian (Libyca 94-135), based on Polybius, who was present, is the main account. Excavations have revealed the circular naval harbour with ship sheds for some 170 ships and the 'Quartier Hannibal' on the Byrsa slope, destroyed in 146 and buried under Roman terracing.

sides.strength: c. 80,000 in 149 (Appian; probably exaggerated), later c. 40,000
citizens, freed slaves and field army

battle.significance: Ended Carthage as a state after some 670 years.

scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Lancel, Carthage (1992)
Hurst, Excavations at Carthage: The British Mission II.1, The Circular Harbour, North Side (1994)

events.title: Andriscus, the false Philip
events.summary: Andriscus, a man of humble origin from Adramyttium who claimed to be Philip, son of Perseus, escaped from Roman custody, raised Thracian support and was proclaimed king in Macedonia, reuniting the four republics. In 148 he defeated and killed the praetor Publius Juventius Thalna and briefly controlled Thessaly.

events.title: Second battle of Pydna
events.summary: The praetor Quintus Caecilius Metellus, supported by the fleet of Attalus II, defeated Andriscus near Pydna. Andriscus fled to Thrace, where the chief Byzes handed him over. Metellus took the cognomen Macedonicus. Macedonia was thereafter governed directly as a Roman province.

battle.significance: Ended Macedonian independence for good; led to the province of Macedonia.

events.title: Viriathus' victory at Tribola
events.summary: Viriathus, chosen leader by Lusitanians surrounded by the praetor Gaius Vetilius, ordered his men to scatter and later regroup while he held off the Romans with a thousand horsemen. He then lured Vetilius' army into an ambush in thickets near Tribola. Vetilius was captured and killed by a Lusitanian who thought the fat old man not worth ransoming; 6,000 of his 10,000 men escaped.

battle.significance: Launched Viriathus' eight-year career of victories.

events.title: Scipio Aemilianus elected consul under age
events.summary: Scipio Aemilianus, aged about 37 and standing only for the aedileship, was demanded as consul by a popular movement frustrated with the failures at Carthage. The presiding consul cited the Lex Villia; the tribunes threatened to take the elections from the consuls; the Senate had the law suspended for a year. The people also assigned him Africa by vote instead of the lot.
events.detail: The episode set a precedent for popular intervention in the allocation of commands, exploited later by Marius and others.
scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)

events.title: Capture of Nepheris
events.summary: In winter 147/146 Scipio Aemilianus sent Laelius and Gulussa to destroy the Carthaginian field army under Diogenes at Nepheris, the base that supplied the besieged city. Appian claims 70,000 killed, including non-combatants, and 10,000 captured. Nepheris fell after a 22-day siege.

sides.strength: Roman troops and Numidians under Gulussa

battle.significance: Removed Carthage's last external support.

events.title: Destruction of Carthage
events.summary: After six days of street fighting, 50,000 men, women and children came down from the Byrsa and were spared to be sold. Some 900 Roman deserters burned themselves in the temple of Eshmun. Hasdrubal surrendered and knelt before Scipio; his wife, cursing him, killed their children and threw herself into the flames. The city burned for days. Watching it, Scipio wept and quoted Homer's lines on the fall of Troy, saying to Polybius that he feared the same fate would one day befall Rome.
events.detail: A Senate commission of ten ordered the city razed, cursed the site, and made its territory Roman public land. Before the assault, according to Macrobius (3.9), Scipio performed an evocatio inviting the tutelary deity of Carthage to come to Rome. The story that the Romans sowed salt in the ruins is a modern invention, first found in the 19th century (Ridley). Carthage was refounded as a Roman colony by Caesar and Augustus.
scholarship: Ridley, 'To Be Taken with a Pinch of Salt: The Destruction of Carthage', CPh 81 (1986)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
events.debate: The salting of Carthage is a myth; the curse on the site is attested. Sallust and others dated the moral decline of Rome to the removal of the Carthaginian threat (metus Punicus) in this year.

events.title: Creation of the province of Africa
events.summary: Carthage's territory became the province of Africa, governed from Utica, which with six other towns that had sided with Rome (Hadrumetum, Leptis Minor, Thapsus, Achulla, Usalis and Teudalis) became a free city. The boundary with Numidia was marked by a ditch, the fossa regia. Carthage's libraries were given to the Numidian kings, except Mago's 28 books on agriculture, which the Senate had translated into Latin.
events.detail: Mago's treatise, translated under the direction of Decimus Junius Silanus, became the foundation of Roman agronomy and was cited by Varro, Columella and Pliny.

sources.r: CIL I² 585 = Crawford, Roman Statutes no. 2

events.title: Battle of Scarpheia
events.summary: The Achaean League, under its strategos Critolaus, rejected Roman demands to detach Sparta, Corinth, Argos and other cities and declared war, nominally on Sparta. Quintus Caecilius Metellus marched south from Macedonia and caught the Achaean army at Scarpheia in Locris; Critolaus disappeared in the rout, perhaps drowned in the marshes or by poison.
events.detail: Polybius, whose account survives in fragments (38.9-18), blamed the Achaean leaders' demagoguery and the masses' folly, a judgement shaped by his own position as friend of Rome.

sides.losses: heavy; 1,000 Arcadians later destroyed at Chaeronea

battle.significance: Destroyed the Achaean field army.

events.debate: Polybius' hostility to Critolaus and Diaeus colours the tradition; Pausanias says Critolaus was never found.

events.title: Battle of Corinth (Leucopetra)
events.summary: The consul Lucius Mummius, with 23,000 foot and 3,500 horse, defeated the last Achaean army under Diaeus, reinforced by 12,000 freed and armed slaves, on the Isthmus at Leucopetra. Diaeus fled to Megalopolis, killed his wife and poisoned himself.

sides.strength: 23,000 foot, 3,500 horse plus Cretan archers and Pergamenes (Pausanias)

battle.significance: Ended Greek independence.

events.title: Sack of Corinth
events.summary: Mummius entered Corinth, killed the men, sold the women and children into slavery and, on the Senate's orders, razed the city. Its art treasures were shipped to Rome and distributed to Italian towns. Polybius, who was present, saw soldiers playing dice on famous paintings thrown on the ground, among them Aristides' Dionysus.
events.detail: Mummius, a 'new man', became a byword for philistinism: Velleius (1.13.4) says he warned the shippers that if they lost any of the paintings and statues they would have to replace them with new ones. The Achaean League was dissolved and Greece placed under the supervision of the governor of Macedonia; Polybius helped the commissioners frame new constitutions and was honoured with statues across the Peloponnese. Corinth lay in ruins until Caesar's colony of 44.
events.debate: Archaeology shows some continued occupation at Corinth after 146, so the destruction was not total. Pliny's story that 'Corinthian bronze' was an alloy formed when the city burned is fanciful.

events.title: Province of Macedonia and the Via Egnatia
events.summary: After Andriscus, Macedonia became a permanent Roman province, with responsibility for supervising Greece and defending the northern frontier against Thracians and Scordisci. Within a few years the proconsul Gnaeus Egnatius built the Via Egnatia from Dyrrachium and Apollonia across the Balkans to Thessalonica, later extended to the Hebrus and Byzantium.
events.detail: A bilingual milestone of Egnatius found near Thessalonica and published in 1974 dates the road to c. 145-120. The province's era was reckoned from 148.

sources.w: Bilingual milestone of Cn. Egnatius near Thessalonica

events.debate: Whether the province dates from 148 or 146, and the exact date of the road, are debated.

events.title: Temple of Jupiter Stator: the first marble temple in Rome
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus built a temple of Jupiter Stator, designed by the Greek architect Hermodorus of Salamis and the first temple in Rome built entirely of marble, beside a rebuilt temple of Juno Regina, within a new colonnade, the Porticus Metelli. In front he set Lysippus' bronze group of the 25 Companions of Alexander who fell at the Granicus, taken from Dion in Macedonia.
events.debate: Construction may have begun after Metellus' triumph of 146 and finished somewhat later.

events.title: Triumph of Mummius 'Achaicus'
events.summary: Lucius Mummius triumphed over Achaea and Corinth, taking the cognomen Achaicus, the first new man to earn a victory title. He dedicated a temple to Hercules Victor, whose dedicatory inscription survives, and distributed Corinthian statues to towns in Italy and as far as Spain, many with his name inscribed.
events.detail: The surviving dedication (CIL I² 626) reads that Achaea was captured and Corinth destroyed under his leadership and auspices. Inscribed bases of Mummian dedications have been found at Italica, Parma, Nursia and elsewhere.

sources.w: Dedication of L. Mummius to Hercules Victor

events.title: Construction of the Aqua Marcia
events.summary: The praetor Quintus Marcius Rex was given 180 million sesterces to repair the old aqueducts and build a new one, the Aqua Marcia, bringing cold, clear water some 91 km from the upper Anio valley, the last 10 km on high arches. When the decemvirs found a Sibylline objection to bringing water to the Capitol, the Senate overrode it.
events.detail: Frontinus (De aquis 1.7) gives the figures. The Marcia was the longest and most admired of Rome's aqueducts, and its water was considered the best; Pliny calls it the most famous water in the world.
events.locName: Rome, from the upper Anio valley

events.title: Appius Claudius' triumph and his Vestal daughter
events.summary: Denied a triumph over the Alpine Salassi, the consul Appius Claudius Pulcher triumphed at his own expense. When a tribune tried to drag him from the chariot, his daughter Claudia, a Vestal Virgin, climbed in beside him; the tribune dared not touch her, and the procession reached the Capitol.

events.title: Censorship of Scipio Aemilianus
events.summary: As censor with the lenient Lucius Mummius, Scipio Aemilianus took a severe line on morals. At the closing lustrum he reportedly changed the traditional prayer asking the gods to make the Roman state better and greater, saying it was great and good enough, and asked them instead to preserve it for ever. The arches of the Pons Aemilius were completed.
events.debate: The prayer story may be a later invention reflecting the 'limits of empire' theme.

events.title: Erisane: Servilianus capitulates to Viriathus
events.summary: While Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus besieged Erisane, Viriathus slipped into the town by night, attacked the Roman siege lines and drove the army into a gorge where it was trapped. Viriathus let the Romans go on terms: peace, recognition of the Lusitanians' land, and Viriathus' status as a friend of the Roman people. The Roman people ratified the treaty.
events.detail: Within months the next governor, Quintus Servilius Caepio, persuaded the Senate to let him renew the war.

battle.significance: The high point of Viriathus' career: Rome recognised him as amicus populi Romani.

events.title: Lex Gabinia tabellaria: the secret ballot
events.summary: The tribune Aulus Gabinius carried a law introducing the secret written ballot (tabella) in elections, replacing oral voting announced to officials. It was followed by the Lex Cassia (137) for trials before the people, the Lex Papiria (131) for legislation and the Lex Coelia (107) for treason trials.
events.detail: Cicero (De legibus 3.35) regarded the ballot laws as destroying the authority of the optimates over voters. They reduced aristocratic control of the clientele and helped make the populares politics of the Gracchi possible.
scholarship: Yakobson, 'Secret Ballot and its Effects in the Late Roman Republic', Hermes 123 (1995)

events.title: Astrologers and Jews expelled from Rome
events.summary: The praetor peregrinus Gnaeus Cornelius Hispalus ordered the Chaldaean astrologers to leave Rome and Italy within ten days, and also expelled Jews who, the epitome says, tried to corrupt Roman morals with the cult of 'Jupiter Sabazius', and removed their private altars.
events.detail: The passage survives only in two epitomes of Valerius Maximus (1.3.3); the reference to Sabazius may be a confusion with the Jewish divine title Sabaoth. It is the earliest notice of Jews in Rome.
events.debate: Whether the expelled were Jews, worshippers of the Phrygian Sabazius or both is debated.

events.title: Murder of Viriathus
events.summary: Quintus Servilius Caepio bribed three of Viriathus' envoys, Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, who stabbed him in the throat as he slept in his armour. The Lusitanians burned him on a great pyre and held funeral games with 200 pairs of fighters at his tomb. When the assassins came for their reward, later tradition says, they were told Rome did not approve of soldiers killing their general.
events.detail: Viriathus' career made him a hero of Iberian and Portuguese national memory. His successor Tautalus soon surrendered, and Decimus Junius Brutus settled the Lusitanian veterans at Valentia (138).
events.debate: The phrase usually quoted ('Rome does not pay traitors') is not ancient in that form; the refusal of reward is reported by Eutropius and Orosius.

events.title: Tribunes imprison the consuls over the levy
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Curiatius, angered by the consuls' refusal to grant exemptions from service in Spain, had the consuls Decimus Junius Brutus and Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica thrown into prison. Curiatius gave Nasica the mocking nickname Serapio, after a sacrificial attendant he resembled. Grain prices and the levy were becoming flashpoints of popular politics.

events.title: Foundation of Valentia
events.summary: Decimus Junius Brutus gave land and a town, Valentia, to those who had fought under Viriathus. Excavations at L'Almoina in Valencia have found the earliest Roman buildings and a foundation-period deposit consistent with that date.

events.title: Brutus Callaicus crosses the River of Forgetfulness
events.summary: Decimus Junius Brutus campaigned north through Lusitania into Gallaecia, crossing the Durius (Douro). At the Limia, which local belief held to be the Lethe, river of forgetfulness, his soldiers refused to cross; Brutus seized a standard, crossed, and called each man by name from the far bank. He reached the Minius and, Florus says, saw the sun sink into the Ocean. He took the cognomen Callaicus.

events.title: Surrender of Mancinus at Numantia
events.summary: The consul Gaius Hostilius Mancinus, panicked by a false rumour of approaching Cantabri and Vaccaei, abandoned his camp near Numantia at night and was trapped with 20,000 men. The Numantines would only negotiate with his quaestor, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, whose father they trusted. The treaty saved the army, recognised Numantine independence, and was sworn by Mancinus and his officers.
events.detail: The Senate repudiated the treaty. Plutarch (Tiberius Gracchus 5-7) argues that the humiliation of seeing his treaty disowned set Tiberius against the Senate leadership, a contributing cause of the crisis of 133.

battle.significance: The low point of Roman arms in Spain; the repudiated treaty radicalised Tiberius Gracchus.

events.title: Lex Cassia tabellaria
events.summary: The tribune Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravilla extended the secret ballot to trials before the popular assemblies, except cases of treason (perduellio).

events.title: Mancinus handed over to the Numantines
events.summary: To free Rome from the oath of the repudiated treaty, the Senate decreed that Mancinus be surrendered to the Numantines. The fetial priests delivered him naked and bound before the town gate; the Numantines refused to accept him, saying that the guilt for broken faith could not be shifted onto one man. After a day he was taken back, later had a statue of himself made showing him in that state, and even resumed a public career.
events.detail: The case was debated by jurists for centuries: whether a man surrendered and refused had lost his citizenship (postliminium).

events.title: Outbreak of the First Servile War
events.summary: In Sicily, where great estates were worked by masses of slaves, many recently enslaved in Rome's wars, slaves of the cruel Damophilus of Enna rose under Eunus, a Syrian slave and prophet who breathed fire by hiding a nutshell of burning sulphur in his mouth. They took Enna, massacred their masters and proclaimed Eunus king under the name Antiochus. Cleon, a Cilician herdsman, raised the slaves of the Agrigentum region and joined him.
events.detail: Diodorus (34/35.2), deriving from Posidonius, is the main source, in Byzantine excerpts. Eunus struck bronze coins inscribed BA ANTIO with Demeter and an ear of grain. Numbers are uncertain: Livy's epitome gives 70,000 rebels, Diodorus 200,000. Several praetors and consuls were defeated.
scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World, 140 B.C.-70 B.C. (1989)
Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
events.debate: The start date (136 or 135, or even 140s) is uncertain; Diodorus' figures are inflated; how far the revolt aimed at a Hellenistic-style kingdom rather than abolition of slavery is debated.

events.title: Siege of Numantia
events.summary: Elected consul for 134 by special exemption from the law against second consulships, Scipio Aemilianus restored discipline to the demoralised army in Spain, expelling 2,000 prostitutes and the traders, and then encircled Numantia with a continuous wall about 9 km long, linking seven camps and towers, with the Duero blocked by booms of spiked timbers. Some 60,000 men, including Numidians under the young Jugurtha, besieged 4,000-8,000 Numantines. After fifteen months of starvation and cannibalism the city surrendered in summer 133; many inhabitants killed themselves. Scipio kept fifty for his triumph, sold the rest and razed the town.
events.detail: Appian (Iberica 84-98), from Polybius, who was present, is the main narrative. The Numantine Rhetogenes broke out with five friends to seek help from Lutia, whose young men wanted to come; Scipio cut off the right hands of 400 of them. Adolf Schulten's excavations (1905-1912) uncovered the Roman camps and circumvallation, the most complete Roman siege works of the Republic before Alesia. Gaius Marius, Jugurtha, the satirist Lucilius and the historian Sempronius Asellio served in the army. Scipio took the cognomen Numantinus and triumphed in 132.
events.locName: Numantia (Cerro de la Muela, Garray, Soria)

battle.significance: Ended the Celtiberian wars; Numantia became the symbol of Iberian resistance.

scholarship: Schulten, Numantia: Die Ergebnisse der Ausgrabungen 1905-1912 (1914-1931)
Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)
Dobson, The Army of the Roman Republic: The Second Century BC, Polybius and the Camps at Numantia (2008)
events.debate: Dobson's re-examination of Schulten's camps questions some of Schulten's camp plans and dates. Figures for the defenders vary widely.

events.title: Attalus III bequeaths Pergamon to Rome
events.summary: Attalus III of Pergamon, the last of his dynasty, died in spring 133 leaving a will that bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman people, while the city of Pergamon itself was to be free. When the will reached Rome, Tiberius Gracchus proposed that the royal treasure be used to equip the new smallholders of his land law and that the people, not the Senate, decide on the cities of the kingdom.
events.detail: A Pergamene decree (OGIS 338) issued soon after the king's death confirms the will and extends citizenship to various groups to secure the city against the rising of Aristonicus, an illegitimate son of Eumenes II who claimed the throne as Eumenes III and rallied the poor and slaves as 'Heliopolitans', with the Stoic Blossius of Cumae as adviser. The war lasted until 129, when Manius Aquillius organised the province of Asia, which became the richest source of Roman revenue.

sources.w: Pergamene decree on the will of Attalus III

scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire: The Development of the Roman Imperium in the East from 148 to 62 B.C. (1995)
Sherwin-White, Roman Foreign Policy in the East (1984)
events.debate: Why Attalus made the bequest (fear of social revolution, ensuring the cities' freedom, or Roman pressure) is unknown. Some modern scholars doubt Attalus' reputation for eccentricity (gardening in poisonous plants, studying sculpture), which comes from hostile sources.

events.title: Tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus
events.summary: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus, tribune from 10 December 134, used the concilium plebis to pass an agrarian law over senatorial opposition, deposed a vetoing colleague, and sought immediate re-election. Ancient and modern writers alike treat the year as the start of the Republic's century of crisis.
events.detail: Tiberius was grandson of Scipio Africanus through his mother Cornelia and brother-in-law of Scipio Aemilianus. Plutarch preserves a story from Gaius' pamphlet that Tiberius conceived the law while travelling through Etruria to Numantia in 137 and seeing the land worked by imported slaves. His backers were heavyweights: Appius Claudius Pulcher (princeps senatus, his father-in-law), Publius Mucius Scaevola (consul 133) and Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus. The novelty lay less in the law than in the methods: bypassing the senate, removing a tribune, and claiming the Pergamene bequest for the people.
scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
Bernstein, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus: Tradition and Apostasy (1978)
Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)
events.debate: Was Tiberius a reformer responding to real rural depopulation (Brunt) or did he exaggerate a manpower crisis (Rich, Historia 1983)? Archaeological survey of the ager Romanus and Etruria does not show the wholesale disappearance of small farms that Appian and Plutarch imply.

events.title: Lex Sempronia agraria
events.summary: Tiberius Gracchus' land law enforced the old limit of 500 iugera on holdings of public land (ager publicus), with extra allowances for sons, and redistributed the surplus to poor citizens in small inalienable lots, administered by a three-man commission.
events.detail: The limit itself was old (attributed to the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367), but had long gone unenforced. Appian (BC 1.9-11) gives 500 iugera plus 250 for each of two sons; possessors kept the retained land rent-free in perpetuity. New allotments, perhaps of 30 iugera, paid a vectigal and could not be sold. The commissioners (tresviri agris iudicandis adsignandis) were Tiberius, his brother Gaius and Appius Claudius Pulcher; after 133 they continued working, and boundary stones naming the commissioners survive from Campania, Lucania and the Hirpini. The census rose from 318,823 (131/0) to 394,736 (125/4), which may reflect the distributions. Italian allies who occupied ager publicus lost land without gaining allotments, a grievance that fed straight into the citizenship question.
scholarship: Roselaar, Public Land in the Roman Republic (2010)
Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
events.debate: Whether allies were entitled to allotments and how large the lots were is disputed; the law's text does not survive, and the later lex agraria of 111 (CIL I2 585) is the main documentary witness to its effects.

events.title: Deposition of the tribune Marcus Octavius
events.summary: When his colleague Marcus Octavius persistently vetoed the agrarian bill, Tiberius had the plebeian assembly vote him out of office, arguing that a tribune who acted against the people forfeited his office. It was without precedent.
events.detail: Appian and Plutarch describe the tribes voting in turn; when 17 of the 35 had voted for removal Tiberius paused and begged Octavius to relent, then completed the vote. Octavius was dragged from the rostra. Tiberius' argument that a tribune derived his authority from the people and could lose it was coherent popular theory, but to opponents it destroyed the veto, the main brake within the tribunate, and made the assembly's will unlimited.
scholarship: Morstein-Marx, Mass Oratory and Political Power in the Late Roman Republic (2004)

events.title: Murder of Tiberius Gracchus
events.summary: During the assembly to elect tribunes for 132, at which Tiberius sought re-election, the pontifex maximus Scipio Nasica led senators and their clients up the Capitol and clubbed Tiberius and some 300 supporters to death. The bodies were thrown into the Tiber.
events.detail: The consul Scaevola refused to act without legal process, so Nasica called on those who wished to save the state to follow him, his toga drawn over his head in priestly fashion. The weapons were broken benches and staves: no swords. This was the first political killing within the city in living memory and, as Appian notes, set the pattern for those that followed. In 132 the consuls Popillius Laenas and Rupilius ran a special court that executed or exiled Tiberius' associates; Nasica was sent on an embassy to Asia to remove him from popular anger and died at Pergamon.
scholarship: Lintott, Violence in Republican Rome (1968)

events.title: Revolt of Aristonicus in Asia
events.summary: Aristonicus, an illegitimate son of Eumenes II, claimed the Attalid throne as Eumenes III and resisted the Roman inheritance, drawing on slaves and the rural poor whom he called Heliopolitai, citizens of the Sun.
events.detail: He minted cistophori in his regnal name, and Blossius of Cumae, Tiberius Gracchus' Stoic adviser, joined him. The utopian label rests on Strabo and Diodorus; modern scholars see him primarily as a dynastic pretender exploiting social discontent. He held out until 129.
events.debate: The Heliopolitai as a social-revolutionary programme versus a dynastic war is debated.

events.title: Rupilius ends the Sicilian slave war
events.summary: The consul Publius Rupilius starved out the rebel stronghold of Tauromenium, where the defenders were reduced to eating their children, and then took Enna through betrayal; Cleon fell fighting. Eunus fled with his bodyguard and was found hiding in a cave; he died in prison at Morgantina. Over 20,000 rebels were crucified or killed. Rupilius then drew up a charter for the province, the Lex Rupilia.
events.detail: Lead sling bullets inscribed with the name of Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul of 133, have been found at Enna, documenting the earlier Roman siege attempts.

battle.significance: Ended the First Servile War; Sicilian agriculture was reorganised under the Lex Rupilia.

scholarship: Bradley, Slavery and Rebellion in the Roman World (1989)

events.title: Lex Rupilia for Sicily
events.summary: After the slave war, Rupilius and a senatorial commission issued a charter (lex data) for Sicily, regulating which courts heard disputes between Sicilians, Romans and cities. Cicero still cites it in the Verrines sixty years later.

events.title: Lex Papiria tabellaria
events.summary: The tribune Gaius Papirius Carbo extended the written secret ballot to legislative assemblies, completing the series begun by the lex Gabinia (139, elections) and lex Cassia (137, trials).
events.detail: Cicero (De legibus 3.35) regarded the ballot laws as undermining aristocratic influence. Carbo also proposed allowing tribunes to stand for immediate re-election, which failed, opposed by Scipio Aemilianus.

events.title: Battle of Leucae
events.summary: The consul Publius Licinius Crassus Mucianus was defeated and killed by Aristonicus near Leucae. Captured, he provoked a Thracian guard into killing him rather than be paraded alive.

battle.significance: Demonstrated that the Asian inheritance would have to be conquered and delayed the province's organisation by two years.

events.title: Siege of Stratonicea and capture of Aristonicus
events.summary: Marcus Perperna (consul 130) besieged Aristonicus in Stratonicea and starved him into surrender. Aristonicus was taken to Rome and strangled in prison.

battle.significance: Ended Attalid resistance; Perperna died before his triumph and Manius Aquillius (consul 129) completed the settlement.

events.title: Organisation of the province of Asia
events.summary: Manius Aquillius and a ten-man senatorial commission organised the Attalid kingdom as the province of Asia, giving Phrygia to Mithridates V of Pontus and parts of Lycaonia to the sons of Ariarathes of Cappadocia. It became Rome's richest province.
events.detail: Aquillius' milestones (the earliest Roman road markers in Asia, in Latin and Greek) mark a road system radiating from Pergamon. The sale of Phrygia to Pontus was later alleged to have been bought with bribes, and Gaius Gracchus attacked it; the senate revoked the grant after Mithridates V's death in c. 120, a grievance Mithridates VI never forgot.
scholarship: Kallet-Marx, Hegemony to Empire (1995)

events.title: Death of Scipio Aemilianus
events.summary: Scipio Aemilianus, who had taken up the Italian allies' complaints against the land commission and had the commission's judicial powers transferred to the consul, was found dead in bed the morning he was due to speak. No inquiry was held.
events.detail: Rumour accused his wife Sempronia (the Gracchi's sister), Cornelia, Carbo and Fulvius Flaccus. Natural death is quite possible. The episode marks the moment the agrarian question became an Italian question: allies who possessed ager publicus had no vote and could only appeal to Roman patrons.
events.debate: Murder or natural death; ancient authors themselves were divided.

events.title: Lex Iunia expels non-citizens from Rome
events.summary: The tribune Marcus Iunius Pennus carried a law expelling non-citizens from the city, aimed at Italians who had come to lobby against the land commission. Gaius Gracchus spoke against it.

events.title: Census registers 394,736 citizens
events.summary: The census of 125/4 counted 394,736 adult male citizens, up from 318,823 in 131/0. The jump of nearly a quarter is commonly linked to the Gracchan allotments, which required citizen status and may have encouraged poor men to register.
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)
events.debate: Real population growth, better registration, or both? Brunt saw registration effects; the figures are also subject to textual corruption.

events.title: Fulvius Flaccus proposes citizenship for the allies
events.summary: The consul Marcus Fulvius Flaccus, a land commissioner, proposed giving allies citizenship or alternatively the right of appeal (provocatio). The senate side-stepped it by sending him to help Massalia against the Saluvii, which began the Roman conquest of southern Gaul.

events.title: Revolt and destruction of Fregellae
events.summary: Fregellae, the leading Latin colony on the Liris, revolted after Flaccus' bill failed. The praetor Lucius Opimius took it through the treachery of Quintus Numitorius Pullus and razed it; Fabrateria Nova was founded nearby in 124.
events.detail: Fregellae had been loyal through Hannibal's war. Excavation shows a prosperous town with Hellenistic houses and a sanctuary of Aesculapius abruptly destroyed. The revolt's isolation shows the allies were not yet ready for concerted action; its brutal suppression anticipated Opimius' role in 121.

battle.significance: First armed allied revolt over citizenship; a warning of the Social War three decades later.

events.note: Fregellae was a Latin colony; both sides are given as 'rome' because no separate polity is defined for it.

events.title: Metellus conquers the Balearic Islands
events.summary: Quintus Caecilius Metellus (consul 123) subdued the Balearic islanders, ostensibly for piracy, protecting his ships against their famous slingers with stretched hides, and settled 3,000 Romans from Iberia at Palma and Pollentia. He took the cognomen Balearicus.

events.title: Tribunates of Gaius Gracchus
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus, tribune in 123 and 122, passed the most ambitious legislative programme of the Republic: subsidised grain, equestrian juries, Asian tax farming at Rome, protection of citizens from summary execution, colonies, roads and army reforms.
events.detail: Gaius was a better orator than his brother (Cicero thought him the most gifted of all) and turned to face the people in the Forum rather than the Curia. His laws created constituencies: the urban plebs (grain), the equites (juries and Asian contracts), soldiers (free clothing), contractors (roads, granaries). Re-elected for 122, he sailed to Africa for 70 days to found Junonia, during which the senate's tribune Livius Drusus outbid him. His citizenship bill failed and he lost the election for 121.
scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
events.debate: Whether Gaius had a coherent plan to reshape the state (Mommsen) or reacted to events; the chronology of his laws between 123 and 122 is uncertain.

events.title: Lex Sempronia frumentaria
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus' grain law guaranteed every citizen in Rome a monthly ration of grain at 6 1/3 asses per modius, below the market price, and built public granaries. Every later popularis grain law built on it.
events.detail: The price was fixed, not free; Clodius made it free in 58. Cicero tells of the ex-consul Piso Frugi, an opponent, queueing for his ration because, he said, if Gracchus was distributing his property he wanted his share (Tusc. 3.48).

events.title: Gracchan jury law and the lex repetundarum
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus transferred the juries of the extortion court (quaestio de repetundis) from senators to equites. The surviving bronze law on extortion (Tabula Bembina, CIL I2 583), usually identified with the lex Acilia of 123/2, shows the details: 450 jurors, none of them senators, and generous rewards for successful prosecutors.
events.detail: Appian says the change made equites masters of the senate; governors now feared juries drawn from the business class that profited from provincial taxation. The control of the juries became the most fought-over question of the next fifty years: Caepio 106, Glaucia c. 101, Drusus 91, Sulla 81, Aurelius Cotta 70.
events.debate: Whether the lex Acilia is Gaius' own law or a colleague's, and whether Plutarch's version (adding equites to the senate) is a confusion with Drusus in 91.

events.title: Lex Sempronia on the taxes of Asia
events.summary: Gaius Gracchus ordered that the tithe of the new province of Asia be auctioned by the censors at Rome in large five-year contracts. This created the great companies of publicani whose interests shaped Roman policy in the East for a century.
scholarship: Badian, Publicans and Sinners (1972)

events.title: Lex Sempronia de capite civis
events.summary: Gaius' law forbade capital sentences on citizens without the people's authorisation and made any magistrate who executed a citizen without trial liable to prosecution. Popillius Laenas, who had punished Tiberius' followers in 132, went into exile.
events.detail: The law framed the arguments of 121, 63 and 58: Opimius' defence in 120, Cicero's execution of the Catilinarians and his exile under the lex Clodia all turned on whether the senatus consultum ultimum overrode it.

events.title: Foundation of Aquae Sextiae
events.summary: Gaius Sextius Calvinus, having destroyed the Saluvian oppidum at Entremont, founded a Roman garrison post at the hot springs below it, the first permanent Roman settlement in Transalpine Gaul.
events.detail: Entremont, with its sculptures of heroes holding severed heads, was sacked c. 123; its destruction layer matches the literary record.

events.title: Foundation of Colonia Junonia at Carthage
events.summary: Under the lex Rubria Gaius Gracchus and Fulvius Flaccus founded a colony of 6,000 settlers on the site of Carthage, the first Roman colony outside Italy. Reports that wolves tore up the boundary markers were used against it, and the colony was formally abolished, though the allotments survived.
events.note: Settlers kept their land; the lex agraria of 111 deals with their holdings.

events.title: Livius Drusus outbids Gaius Gracchus
events.summary: With senatorial backing the tribune Marcus Livius Drusus proposed twelve colonies of 3,000 poor citizens each, the abolition of rent on Gracchan allotments and a ban on flogging Latin soldiers. The colonies were never founded, but the proposals drained Gaius' support.

events.title: Gaius Gracchus' citizenship bill defeated
events.summary: Gaius proposed full citizenship for Latins and Latin rights for other Italian allies. The consul Fannius asked the plebs whether, if they gave the Latins the vote, they expected to find room at the games and festivals, and the bill failed.
events.debate: Appian and Plutarch differ on the scope; the bill's failure showed that the Roman plebs would not share its privileges.

events.title: First senatus consultum ultimum
events.summary: After a supporter of Gaius killed the consul Opimius' attendant Quintus Antyllius, the senate decreed that the consul should see that the state suffered no harm (videret consul ne quid res publica detrimenti caperet). Opimius used it as authority to attack the Gracchans on the Aventine.
events.detail: This was the first use of the decree modern scholars call the senatus consultum ultimum. It conferred no new legal power; it signalled senatorial backing for force and a promise to defend the magistrate afterwards. It was used again in 100, 88/83, 77, 63, 62, 52, 49, 48, 47 and 43. Whether it could override the citizen's right of appeal was never resolved.
scholarship: Lintott, The Constitution of the Roman Republic (1999)

events.title: Death of Gaius Gracchus and the Aventine massacre
events.summary: Opimius, with senators, equites and Cretan archers, stormed the Aventine where Fulvius Flaccus had occupied the temple of Diana. Flaccus and his son were killed; Gaius fled across the Tiber and had his slave Philocrates kill him in the grove of Furrina. Some 3,000 followers were executed afterwards.
events.detail: Opimius had offered Gaius' head's weight in gold; Plutarch says the man who brought it had filled it with lead and it weighed 17 2/3 pounds. Opimius then rebuilt the temple of Concord, and someone carved beneath the dedication that a work of madness had made a temple of Concord. The Gracchi became martyrs: Plutarch says the people set up statues to them and offered sacrifices at the places of their deaths.

events.title: Opimius restores the temple of Concord
events.summary: By senatorial decree Opimius rebuilt the temple of Concord at the foot of the Capitol and added the Basilica Opimia beside it. The graffito 'Vecordiae opus aedem facit Concordiae' summed up popular opinion.
events.detail: The temple later hosted the senate meeting of 5 December 63 that condemned the Catilinarians.

events.title: Battle of Vindalium
events.summary: The proconsul Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus defeated the Allobroges at Vindalium, where the Sulga (Sorgue) meets the Rhône. His elephants panicked the Gallic horses; 20,000 Gauls were said to have been killed.
events.detail: Suetonius (Nero 2) says Ahenobarbus afterwards rode through the province on an elephant escorted by his troops, a scene of triumphal display remembered in his family.
events.locName: Confluence of the Sorgue and Rhône

battle.significance: Broke the Allobroges and opened the Rhône corridor to Roman control.

events.title: Battle of the Isara
events.summary: Quintus Fabius Maximus, grandson of Aemilius Paullus, crushed a huge army of Arverni and Allobroges under the Arvernian king Bituitus near the Isère. Bituitus, famous for his silver chariot and hounds, was later seized at a parley by Ahenobarbus and interned at Alba Fucens.
events.detail: Ancient totals of 120,000 to 130,000 Gauls killed against 15 Roman dead are fantastical, but the victory ended Arvernian hegemony in southern Gaul. Fabius took the name Allobrogicus and, with Ahenobarbus, set up stone trophy towers on the battlefields, a novelty Florus remarks on.
events.locName: Confluence of the Isère and Rhône

battle.significance: Destroyed the Arvernian hegemony and led directly to the creation of the province of Transalpine Gaul.

events.debate: Casualty figures are rhetorical.

events.title: Trial and acquittal of Opimius
events.summary: Prosecuted before the people for killing citizens without trial, Opimius argued that the senate's decree justified him and was acquitted. His defender was Gaius Papirius Carbo, once a Gracchan ally, now consul.
events.detail: The acquittal gave the senatus consultum ultimum practical force. Opimius was convicted in 109 by the Mamilian commission for taking Jugurtha's bribes and died in exile at Dyrrachium.

events.title: Marius' tribunate and the lex Maria
events.summary: As tribune Gaius Marius passed a law narrowing the gangways (pontes) by which voters passed to cast their ballots, to prevent aristocrats from inspecting votes, and threatened to have the consul Cotta arrested when the senate opposed it. He then surprised everyone by vetoing a grain bill.

events.title: Foundation of Narbo Martius
events.summary: A citizen colony was founded at Narbo, championed by the young orator Lucius Licinius Crassus against senatorial objection. It anchored the new province of Transalpine Gaul and the road to Spain.
events.detail: Narbo was the first citizen colony outside Italy that survived (Junonia having been abolished). The Via Domitia, built by Ahenobarbus, ran through it; a milestone naming Gnaeus Domitius as imperator, found at Treilles near Narbonne, is the oldest Roman milestone known in Gaul.

events.title: Construction of the Via Domitia
events.summary: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus built the road linking Italy to Spain along the Mediterranean coast of Gaul, from the Alps via Nemausus and Narbo to the Pyrenees. Pompey later fortified its Pyrenean pass with his trophies (71).
events.note: Date of construction c. 120-118; Cicero mentions its upkeep in the 70s.

events.title: Death of Micipsa and partition of Numidia
events.summary: King Micipsa, son of Masinissa, left Numidia jointly to his sons Adherbal and Hiempsal and to his adopted nephew Jugurtha, a veteran of Numantia with friends among the Roman nobility. Jugurtha had Hiempsal murdered at Thirmida within a year.
events.detail: In 116 a senatorial commission led by Opimius divided the kingdom: Jugurtha got the richer, more populous west; Adherbal the east with Cirta and its ports. Sallust says the commissioners were bought.

events.title: Trial of the Vestals and human sacrifice in the Forum Boarium
events.summary: After a prodigy in which a girl riding on horseback was struck dead by lightning, three Vestals, Aemilia, Licinia and Marcia, were accused of unchastity. The pontiffs condemned only Aemilia; a special tribunal under Lucius Cassius Longinus Ravilla condemned the other two in 113. Two Gauls and two Greeks were buried alive in the Forum Boarium, and a temple was vowed to Venus Verticordia.
events.detail: This was the last recorded Roman human sacrifice of this ritual type (also performed in 228 and 216). Cassius was the judge famous for asking 'cui bono?'. The affair shows religious anxiety about the Cimbri and the political use of religious courts: the tribunal was set up by a tribune's law over pontifical jurisdiction.

events.title: Battle of Noreia
events.summary: The consul Gnaeus Papirius Carbo, trying to protect the Taurisci of Noricum, Roman guest-friends, ambushed the migrating Cimbri after negotiating their withdrawal, and was routed. Only a storm saved his army from annihilation.
events.detail: This was the first Roman encounter with the Cimbri, a people whose origin the ancients placed in Jutland. Carbo was later prosecuted by Marcus Antonius and killed himself. Noreia's site is unknown; the Magdalensberg and sites near Neumarkt in Styria have been proposed.

battle.significance: Opened twelve years of Cimbrian warfare and exposed Roman treachery as counterproductive.

events.title: Siege of Cirta and the massacre of the Italians
events.summary: Jugurtha besieged Adherbal in Cirta for months while senatorial embassies came and went. The Italian traders defending the city persuaded Adherbal to surrender on terms; Jugurtha tortured him to death and massacred the adult Numidians and Italian merchants (negotiatores) alike.
events.detail: The killing of Italici, men with links to the equestrian business class, made war unavoidable: the tribune-elect Gaius Memmius whipped up the people and the senate assigned Numidia to the consul of 111, Bestia.

battle.significance: Turned a dynastic dispute into a Roman war.

events.note: Both sides are Numidian; Adherbal's faction is given as numidia.

events.title: Jugurtha in Rome and the murder of Massiva
events.summary: After Bestia granted Jugurtha lenient terms, the tribune Memmius summoned him to Rome under safe conduct to testify against the nobles he had bribed. Another tribune, Baebius, forbade him to speak. While in Rome Jugurtha had his cousin Massiva, a rival claimant, assassinated by his agent Bomilcar and was expelled.
events.detail: Leaving the city, Jugurtha is said to have looked back and called Rome a city for sale and doomed to perish if it found a buyer. Sallust built his whole monograph around this theme of aristocratic venality.
scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)

events.title: Lex agraria of 111
events.summary: An agrarian law, preserved on the reverse of the bronze Tabula Bembina (CIL I2 585), converted Gracchan allotments and permitted holdings of ager publicus into private land free of rent and halted further distribution. It effectively wound up the Gracchan programme in Italy and regulated public land in Africa and at Corinth.
events.detail: It is the longest surviving Republican statute text. Appian's account (BC 1.27) of three post-Gracchan laws, first allowing sale of allotments, then stopping distribution, then abolishing rent, is usually reconciled with it.
scholarship: Lintott, Judicial Reform and Land Reform in the Roman Republic (1992)

events.title: Capitulation of Aulus Albinus at Suthul
