events.summary: Lepidus, who had brought 14 legions from Africa and received the surrender of Sextus' army, claimed Sicily for himself. Octavian walked into his camp almost alone and the legions deserted to him. Lepidus, in mourning clothes, begged for mercy; he was stripped of his triumviral power but allowed to keep the office of pontifex maximus and lived under guard at Circeii until 13 or 12 BC.
events.detail: Octavian, now master of 40 legions, received the sacrosanctity of a tribune for life and an ovation. Rome would have two masters, not three.

events.title: Battle of Naulochus
events.summary: Some 300 ships a side met off Naulochus. Agrippa's heavier ships used the harpax, a grapnel fired from a catapult and reeled in by winch, to drag enemy ships alongside for boarding. Sextus lost 28 ships sunk and almost all the rest captured, burned or run ashore, escaping with 17 to the East. Agrippa received a naval crown, a golden wreath decorated with ships' prows.
events.detail: Octavian, Suetonius reports, was so deeply asleep before the battle that friends had to wake him to give the signal, a story enemies used to mock his courage. Sextus was captured and executed at Miletus in 35 by Antony's officer Marcus Titius.

battle.significance: Destroyed Sextus' sea power; ended the last Pompeian resistance.

scholarship: Welch, Magnus Pius: Sextus Pompeius and the Transformation of the Roman Republic (2012)

events.title: Antony's Parthian campaign and the siege of Phraaspa
events.summary: Antony invaded Media Atropatene through Armenia with 16 legions and perhaps 100,000 men, leaving his siege train of 300 wagons with two legions under Oppius Statianus. The Parthian king Phraates IV and the Median king destroyed the train and its escort while Artavasdes of Armenia withdrew his cavalry. Unable to take Phraaspa without engines, Antony retreated in October across mountains in 27 days and 18 battles.
events.detail: Plutarch puts the losses at 20,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry, half to disease, with 8,000 more dying of cold on the march through Armenia to the sea. Antony decimated cohorts that fled. Cleopatra brought clothing and money to Leuke Kome. Octavian's propaganda made the failure, and Antony's dependence on Cleopatra, a central theme.

sides.strength: 16 legions, 10,000 Gallic and Spanish horse, allies; c. 100,000 (Plutarch)
sides.losses: c. 24,000 in the retreat plus c. 8,000 on the march home; 10,000 with the siege train

battle.significance: Antony's military reputation was badly damaged; the East was not conquered.

events.debate: Site of Phraaspa (near Maragheh or Takht-e Soleyman); size of Antony's army.

events.title: Octavian's Illyrian war: the siege of Metulum
events.summary: To give his legions work and himself military glory, Octavian campaigned in Illyricum in 35-33. At Metulum, capital of the Iapydes, he was wounded when a siege bridge collapsed; the defenders burned the town and themselves. He took Siscia on the Save and later recovered standards lost by Gabinius in 48.

battle.significance: Gave Octavian a military record to set against Antony's.

events.title: The Donations of Alexandria
events.summary: After capturing Artavasdes of Armenia, Antony staged a triumph-like procession in Alexandria and then, on silver thrones in the gymnasium, proclaimed Cleopatra Queen of Kings and Caesarion, as Caesar's true son, King of Kings. Alexander Helios was given Armenia, Media and Parthia (yet to be conquered), Cleopatra Selene Cyrenaica and Libya, and the infant Ptolemy Philadelphus Phoenicia, Syria and Cilicia.
events.detail: Coins of Antony and Cleopatra hail her as queen of kings and of her sons who are kings. In Rome the proclamation of Caesarion directly challenged Octavian's status as Caesar's son, and the celebration of a 'triumph' outside Rome was presented as treason.
scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra (2010)

events.title: Agrippa's aedileship
events.summary: Though a former consul, Agrippa took the junior office of aedile and spent lavishly on the city: he repaired the aqueducts and built the Aqua Julia, sailed through the Cloaca Maxima on a boat after cleaning it, set up 700 basins and 105 fountains, and provided free baths, barbers, oil and lotteries. It was a campaign to win the urban plebs for Octavian.

events.title: The rupture of 32: Antony's will and the oath of Italy
events.summary: When the consuls Sosius and Ahenobarbus attacked Octavian in the senate, he came with armed men; the consuls and over 300 senators fled to Antony. Antony divorced Octavia. Plancus and Titius defected and revealed Antony's will, which Octavian seized illegally from the Vestals and read to the senate: it recognised Caesarion, left legacies to Cleopatra's children and asked for burial in Alexandria.
events.detail: The whole of Italy then swore an oath of personal allegiance to Octavian, followed by the western provinces; Augustus later claimed in the Res Gestae that 'all Italy swore in my words of its own accord'. Some 700 senators fought on his side. The legality of Octavian's position after the triumvirate lapsed is murky; this oath was its substitute.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Osgood, Caesar's Legacy (2006)

events.title: War declared on Cleopatra
events.summary: Octavian had war declared on Cleopatra alone, not Antony, to frame the coming civil war as a foreign war. He performed the archaic fetial rite himself, hurling a bloodied spear into a plot of 'enemy' ground by the temple of Bellona. Antony was stripped of his consulship for 31 and his powers.

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.summary: Antony and Cleopatra's fleet, bottled up in the Ambracian Gulf through summer by Agrippa's blockade and weakened by disease and desertion, came out to break through. After hours of fighting, Cleopatra's squadron of 60 ships hoisted sail and fled through a gap with the war chest; Antony followed in a fast ship. The rest of the fleet fought on and was burned or surrendered; the land army of 19 legions surrendered a week later.
events.detail: Plutarch gives Antony some 230 large warships after burning those he could not crew, and 5,000 dead. That the ships carried their sails, unusual for battle, suggests that escape was planned (Tarn). Agrippa, who had taken Methone and Leucas in the spring, commanded at sea; Octavian's lighter Liburnian ships proved nimbler. Octavian founded Nicopolis on his camp site and built a memorial whose sockets for 35 captured rams survive. The battle became the foundation myth of the regime, embroidered by Virgil and Propertius, though as a fight it was modest.
events.locName: mouth of the Ambracian Gulf, off Actium

sides.strength: c. 400 ships (lighter), 8 legions embarked or ashore
c. 230 warships incl. 60 Egyptian, 19 legions ashore
sides.losses: c. 5,000 killed; fleet and army surrendered

battle.significance: Decided the last civil war of the Republic.

scholarship: Tarn, JRS 21 (1931)
Gurval, Actium and Augustus (1995)
Murray & Petsas, Octavian's Campsite Memorial for the Actian War (1989)
Lange, Res Publica Constituta (2009)
events.debate: Was Cleopatra's flight treachery, panic or a planned breakout? Most moderns accept a planned breakout, as Tarn argued.

events.title: Fall of Alexandria and death of Antony
events.summary: Octavian advanced on Egypt from Syria while Cornelius Gallus came from Cyrene. Antony won a cavalry skirmish near the hippodrome on 31 July, but the next day his fleet and cavalry went over to Octavian. Told falsely that Cleopatra was dead, he stabbed himself and was hauled up into her mausoleum to die in her arms. 1 August became a holiday at Rome.
events.detail: Octavian's men took Cleopatra alive by a ruse. Antony's son Antyllus was killed at the statue of Caesar where he had taken refuge; Caesarion, lured back from flight towards India, was executed, Octavian's adviser Areius having observed that too many Caesars were not good.

sides.strength: remnant forces; fleet and cavalry defected

battle.significance: Ended the war and the Ptolemaic dynasty.

events.title: Death of Cleopatra
events.summary: Learning that Octavian meant to lead her in his triumph, Cleopatra VII, last Ptolemaic ruler and the last Hellenistic monarch of note, killed herself with her maids Iras and Charmion, probably about 10 or 12 August. The asp brought in a basket of figs is the version Plutarch reports along with others; he admits no one knew the truth, and poison is equally possible.
events.detail: She was 39 and had reigned for 21 years. Octavian, Plutarch says, admired her nobility and buried her beside Antony. In his triumph her effigy was carried with an asp. Her daughter Cleopatra Selene married Juba II of Mauretania.
scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra (2010)
Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)
events.debate: Method of death (asp or poison) and exact date.

events.title: Annexation of Egypt
events.summary: Egypt became a Roman possession under an equestrian prefect answerable to Octavian; senators and leading equites were forbidden to enter it without his permission. Its first prefect, the poet-soldier Gaius Cornelius Gallus, crushed a revolt in the Thebaid and boasted of it on a trilingual stele at Philae (29), and fell from favour and killed himself in 26.
events.detail: Ptolemaic treasure paid off Octavian's armies and the land bought for veterans; interest rates at Rome fell from 12 to 4 per cent, Dio says. Egypt's grain fed Rome for centuries. Octavian visited Alexander's tomb, accidentally breaking the nose of the mummy, and declined to see the Ptolemies, saying he had come to see a king, not corpses.

events.title: Octavian's triple triumph
events.summary: On 13, 14 and 15 August Octavian triumphed over Illyricum, Actium and Egypt; in the Egyptian procession Cleopatra's effigy with the asp and her children Alexander Helios and Cleopatra Selene were displayed. He dedicated the temple of the Deified Julius on 18 August, its speakers' platform adorned with rams from Actium, and the rebuilt senate house, the Curia Julia, with an altar and statue of Victory, on 28 August. The doors of the temple of Janus had been closed earlier that year, signalling peace throughout the empire for the first time since 235.

events.title: Marcus Crassus denied the spolia opima
events.summary: Marcus Licinius Crassus, grandson of the triumvir and proconsul of Macedonia, killed Deldo, king of the Bastarnae, with his own hands and claimed the right to dedicate the spolia opima to Jupiter Feretrius, the rarest honour in Roman arms. He was refused, it seems because he did not hold independent command; Livy reports that Augustus produced the linen corslet of Cossus proving that only a consul could claim it.
events.detail: Crassus triumphed in 27 but disappeared from public life. Historians see the episode as Octavian refusing to let any other general outshine him.
scholarship: Rich, Chiron 26 (1996)
events.debate: Whether the corslet story was fabricated for the occasion.

events.title: Census of 28 and the restoration of laws
events.summary: As consuls with Agrippa, Octavian held the first census in 42 years, registering 4,063,000 citizens, and purged the senate, removing perhaps 190 members. He annulled the illegal measures of the triumviral period by edict from the end of 28, and an aureus of that year proclaims that he restored to the Roman people their laws and rights.
events.detail: The leap from 910,000 in 70/69 to over 4 million is among the most debated numbers in ancient demography: either women and children were now counted (the 'low count', Beloch and Brunt) or Italy's free population was far larger than usually thought (the 'high count', Lo Cascio).
scholarship: Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971)
Rich & Williams, Numismatic Chronicle 159 (1999)
events.debate: Low count versus high count of the Italian population.

events.title: Division of the provinces between princeps and Senate
events.summary: The settlement of 27 BC divided provinces into those of the princeps (Hispania Tarraconensis and Lusitania, the Gauls, Syria, Cyprus and Egypt) and 'public' provinces assigned by lot to proconsuls (Africa, Asia, Achaea, Macedonia, Illyricum, Crete-Cyrene, Bithynia-Pontus, Sardinia, Baetica, Sicily).
events.detail: Imperial provinces were governed by legati Augusti of senatorial rank (Egypt by an equestrian prefect, from which senators were barred even from visiting without permission), public provinces by ex-consuls (Africa, Asia) or ex-praetors serving a year. Dio says the arrangement was designed to keep the armed provinces under Augustus while appearing to share power; but Africa and Illyricum, both proconsular, still had legions. In 22 BC Augustus returned Cyprus and Gallia Narbonensis to the Senate as pacified; Illyricum passed to him c. 11 BC when it became a war zone, and Dalmatia and Pannonia stayed imperial. The ten-year term was renewed in 18 BC (five years), 13 BC, 8 BC, AD 3 and AD 13, producing the decennalia festivals.
scholarship: Millar, 'The emperor, the Senate and the provinces', JRS 56 (1966)

events.title: The settlement of 27 BC
events.summary: On 13 January 27 Octavian, consul for the seventh time, announced to the senate that he was returning the res publica to the senate and people. In the choreographed response the senate pressed on him a ten-year command over a large provincia including Spain, Gaul, Syria and Egypt, where most of the legions were, while the other provinces were governed by proconsuls chosen by lot. He was voted the oak-leaf civic crown for his door and laurels for its posts.
events.detail: In the Res Gestae (34) he claims that from then on he exceeded all others in auctoritas but had no more power (potestas) than his colleagues in each magistracy. A golden shield in the Curia (a marble copy survives at Arles) praised his virtue, clemency, justice and piety. Ovid dates the restoration of the provinces to the Ides of January. Syme's verdict that the Republic was 'restored' as a façade over a military monarchy set the modern debate; others stress the genuine attempt to rebuild consensus.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Millar, JRS 63 (1973)
Lange, Res Publica Constituta (2009)
Rich & Williams, Numismatic Chronicle 159 (1999)
events.debate: Restored republic or veiled monarchy? Debate on what 'res publica restituta' meant to contemporaries.

events.title: First constitutional settlement; Octavian becomes Augustus
events.summary: On 13 January 27 BC Octavian announced to the Senate that he was transferring the res publica to the Senate and people; the Senate begged him to retain a large provincial command, and on 16 January voted him the name Augustus, the oak-leaf corona civica over his door, laurels on his doorposts and a golden shield (clupeus virtutis) in the Curia.
events.detail: This was the formal birth of the Principate. Augustus kept his consulship (held every year until 23 BC) and received for ten years a single 'province' comprising Spain, Gaul, Syria and Egypt, where most legions were stationed, governed through legati Augusti pro praetore. Res Gestae 34 claims that after this he 'excelled all in auctoritas but had no more potestas than his colleagues in each magistracy'. The name Augustus, with its religious overtones (augur, augere), was preferred to Romulus. A gold aureus of 28 BC (British Museum, acquired 1995) reading LEGES ET IVRA P(opulo) R(omano) RESTITVIT shows the restoration theme already in play the year before; the Fasti Praenestini record the oak crown 'because he restored the res publica to the Roman people'. Cassius Dio's account (53.2-22) is written in the light of the Severan monarchy and treats the whole as a sham.
scholarship: Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)
Millar, 'Triumvirate and Principate', JRS 63 (1973)
Rich and Williams, 'Leges et iura p.R. restituit', Numismatic Chronicle 159 (1999)
events.debate: Whether 'res publica restituta' meant restoration of the Republic or simply of constitutional normality after the triumviral period is much debated; the term itself appears in the Laudatio Turiae and the Fasti Praenestini, not in the Res Gestae.

events.title: Octavian receives the name Augustus
events.summary: Three days later, on the motion of Lucius Munatius Plancus, the senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, 'the revered one', with associations of augury and sanctity. He had considered Romulus but rejected it for its overtones of kingship and fratricide. The date is conventionally taken as the end of the Republic and the start of the Principate.

events.title: Triumph of Marcus Licinius Crassus and the spolia opima controversy
events.summary: Crassus, grandson of the triumvir, triumphed 'ex Thraecia et Geteis' after campaigns of 29-28 BC in which he killed Deldo, king of the Bastarnae, with his own hand. His claim to dedicate the spolia opima in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius was blocked on the ground that he had not fought under his own auspices.
events.detail: Livy (4.20.5-11) records that Augustus told him he had seen, in the restored temple of Jupiter Feretrius, the linen corslet of Aulus Cornelius Cossus inscribed to show that Cossus had won the spolia as consul, not military tribune, which would establish that only a commander with his own auspices could dedicate them. Crassus also took the title imperator, a privilege then being restricted to the princeps and his family. Crassus disappears from the record afterwards. Dessau and Syme saw a deliberate snub to a rival; Rich (1996) argues the issue was invented later or exaggerated.
scholarship: Rich, 'Augustus and the spolia opima', Chiron 26 (1996)
events.debate: How far the Cossus episode was manufactured to block Crassus is contested.

events.title: Augustus holds a census of the Gauls at Narbo
events.summary: On his way to Spain Augustus convened an assembly at Narbo and ordered a census of the Three Gauls, the first systematic registration of persons and property for tribute in the lands conquered by Caesar.
events.detail: Livy's Periocha 134 reports the conventus at Narbo and the census; Dio adds that Augustus organised the Gauls administratively, a task completed by the division into Aquitania, Lugdunensis and Belgica, usually dated 16-13 BC. Later censuses in Gaul (12 BC under Drusus, AD 14-16 under Germanicus, AD 61 and 83) were moments of tension; the census of 12 BC coincided with unrest and the dedication of the altar at Lugdunum.

events.title: Battle of Vellica
events.summary: Opening victory of Augustus's Cantabrian campaign, fought 'under the walls of Vellica' after the Cantabri descended from their hill forts to meet the Roman columns.
events.detail: Florus says the Cantabri were defeated beneath Vellica and fled to the 'very lofty' Mons Vindius, believing the ocean would rise to it before Roman arms, where they were besieged into starvation. Augustus may not have commanded in person on the day; Suetonius (Aug. 20) says he conducted only two wars personally after Actium, the Dalmatian and Cantabrian, and Dio records a thunderbolt narrowly missing his litter during a night march, which led him to dedicate the temple of Jupiter Tonans on the Capitol (22 BC).
events.locName: Vellica, near Aguilar de Campoo (Monte Cildá?)

sides.strength: Several legions in three columns (numbers unknown)

sides.losses: heavy; survivors fled to Mons Vindius

battle.significance: Broke Cantabrian field resistance and drove them into hill-top refuges that the Romans then blockaded.

events.debate: Vellica is usually placed at Monte Cildá near Olleros de Pisuerga, but this is not secure.

events.title: Siege of Aracillum
events.summary: Cantabrian stronghold besieged by the Roman columns in 26 BC and taken after a long resistance; it became the type-site for Roman siege archaeology in the Cantabrian war.
events.detail: Florus calls it Aracelium and says it resisted strongly; Orosius gives Racilium. Archaeologists have identified Roman siege works around the Iron Age hillfort of La Espina del Gallego (Cantabria), with three Roman camps (El Cildá, Cueto del Avellanosa, El Cincho), which many now equate with Aracillum, though the older candidate Aradillos near Reinosa still has supporters.

sides.strength: Probably more than one legion with auxiliaries

battle.significance: Consolidated the Roman hold on the upper Besaya valley, the main north-south route through Cantabria.

scholarship: Peralta Labrador, Los cántabros antes de Roma (2003)

events.title: Downfall and suicide of Cornelius Gallus
events.summary: Gaius Cornelius Gallus, poet, friend of Virgil and first prefect of Egypt, was renounced by Augustus for boastful self-promotion and indiscreet talk; after the Senate voted his condemnation and exile he killed himself.
events.detail: Gallus had suppressed a revolt in the Thebaid and set up a trilingual stele at Philae (dated 15 April 29 BC; ILS 8995) claiming to have taken an army beyond the First Cataract 'where neither the Roman people nor the kings of Egypt had borne arms', and inscribed his deeds on the pyramids. The renuntiatio amicitiae by the princeps was followed by prosecutions in the Senate, showing how imperial disfavour could translate into legal ruin. A papyrus from Qasr Ibrim, published in 1979, preserves lines of his love-elegies, previously known only from one pentameter.
scholarship: Anderson, Parsons and Nisbet, 'Elegiacs by Gallus from Qasr Ibrîm', JRS 69 (1979)
events.debate: Jerome dates his death to 27 BC; Dio places it in 26.

events.title: Siege of Marib (Marsiaba)
events.summary: Climax of Aelius Gallus's expedition to Arabia Felix: the Roman army besieged the Sabaean capital for six days and withdrew for lack of water, two days' march from the 'land of aromatics'.
events.detail: Strabo reports that in the only real battle the Romans lost two men against 10,000 Arabs, and that the expedition's losses came from disease, heat and thirst, blaming the treachery of the Nabataean vizier Syllaeus. Augustus's Res Gestae (26.5) claims the army reached Mariba in the land of the Sabaeans. The expedition yielded geographical knowledge and showed that conquest of South Arabia was impractical; Rome turned to controlling the Red Sea trade instead, which boomed after Egypt's annexation (Strabo saw 120 ships a year sailing from Myos Hormos to India).

sides.strength: c. 10,000 at the start, much reduced by disease
sides.losses: few in battle; many to disease

battle.significance: Ended Roman ambitions to conquer the incense lands; no Roman army returned to South Arabia.

events.debate: Whether Syllaeus truly sabotaged the expedition or became Strabo's scapegoat is debated; Syllaeus was executed in Rome c. 6 BC for other crimes.

events.title: Siege of Lancia
events.summary: The Astures, descending in three columns along the Astura (Esla) to attack Roman camps, were betrayed by the Brigaecini; Publius Carisius pre-empted them and besieged the survivors in Lancia, which he took but spared.
events.detail: Florus says Carisius had to restrain his soldiers from burning the town, keeping it intact 'as a better monument of Roman victory'. Lancia lies at Villasabariego (León), where excavations have found a Roman town overlying the Asturian oppidum. Carisius founded Emerita and struck coins at a mint in the north-west showing captured Cantabro-Asturian weapons (caetra shields, double-axes).

sides.strength: Army of Lusitania (legions V Alaudae and X Gemina probable)

battle.significance: Broke Asturian resistance in the plains; Augustus closed the temple of Janus for the second time.

events.title: Destruction of the Salassi and foundation of Augusta Praetoria
events.summary: Aulus Terentius Varro Murena crushed the Salassi of the Val d'Aosta, who had controlled the Alpine passes and gold-washing for generations; 36,000 were sold at auction at Eporedia, and the colony of Augusta Praetoria was founded with 3,000 praetorian veterans.
events.detail: Strabo says 8,000 of those sold were men of fighting age and that the buyers were forbidden to free them for 20 years. The colony (Aosta) retains its Augustan walls, gate (Porta Praetoria) and arch. Control of the Great and Little St Bernard opened direct routes to the Rhone and upper Rhine, indispensable for the coming German wars.

events.title: Foundation of Augusta Emerita
events.summary: Publius Carisius settled discharged veterans (emeriti) of legions V Alaudae and X Gemina on the Anas (Guadiana), creating the colony that became capital of Lusitania.
events.detail: Mérida preserves one of the best ensembles of Roman architecture in the West: the theatre (dedicated by Agrippa, 16-15 BC), amphitheatre (8 BC), the 60-arch Guadiana bridge, two aqueducts (Los Milagros, San Lázaro) and the Proserpina reservoir. Its coinage under Carisius depicts the city gate.

events.title: Annexation of Galatia
events.summary: When king Amyntas was killed fighting the Homonadenses of the Taurus, Augustus did not appoint a successor but turned his large kingdom (Galatia, Lycaonia, Pisidia, parts of Pamphylia) into a province under a legate at Ancyra.
events.detail: Galatia was the first of the great Augustan annexations of client kingdoms, setting a pattern of absorbing them on the death of the ruler. It was expanded with Paphlagonia (6/5 BC) and Pontus Galaticus (3/2 BC) and colonised with veteran colonies in Pisidia (Antioch, Lystra, Cremna, Comama, Olbasa, Parlais), linked by the Via Sebaste (6 BC). The best-preserved copy of the Res Gestae, in Latin and Greek, survives on the temple of Rome and Augustus at Ancyra (Monumentum Ancyranum).
scholarship: Mitchell, Anatolia I (1993)

events.title: Agrippa dedicates the first Pantheon
events.summary: Marcus Agrippa completed the Pantheon on the Campus Martius as part of a complex with the Saepta Julia (dedicated 26 BC) and the Baths of Agrippa. The inscription still on Hadrian's rebuilding, M. AGRIPPA L.F. COS. TERTIUM FECIT, refers to his third consulship in 27 BC.
events.detail: Dio says Agrippa wished to install a statue of Augustus inside and name the building after him; Augustus declined, so statues of Julius Caesar stood inside and of Augustus and Agrippa in the porch. The original was rebuilt after fires of 80 and c. 110, and Hadrian's version (c. 118-128) is the building that survives. Excavations by Beltrami in the 1890s were taken to show a south-facing Agrippan temple; work in 1996-97 suggests the original faced north on the same axis, though its plan (rectangular or circular) is still debated.
scholarship: Marder and Wilson Jones (eds), The Pantheon: From Antiquity to the Present (2015)

events.title: Battle of Pselchis
events.summary: Gaius Petronius, prefect of Egypt, routed a Kushite army three times his size near Pselchis (Dakka) in Lower Nubia, reversing the Kushite capture of Syene, Elephantine and Philae.
events.detail: Strabo says the Kushites were poorly armed, with large oxhide shields, axes, pikes and swords; some fled into the town, others into the desert, others swam to an island. Petronius then stormed Primis and marched on Napata, the residence of the queen's son, which he razed. He sent a thousand captives to Augustus. The Meroë head of Augustus, buried beneath the threshold of a victory shrine, is the Kushite counter-memorial of the same war.

battle.significance: Restored the southern frontier of Egypt and led to the peace of Samos.

events.debate: Whether the battle belongs to late 25 or 24 BC is uncertain; Petronius's prefecture is usually dated 25-21 BC.

events.title: Second constitutional settlement: tribunicia potestas and imperium maius
events.summary: After a near-fatal illness (when he handed his signet ring to Agrippa and state papers to his consular colleague Piso), Augustus resigned the consulship on 1 July 23 BC and received instead the tribunician power for life, numbered annually, and a proconsular imperium overriding that of governors in all provinces.
events.detail: The tribunicia potestas gave him the right to convene Senate and assemblies, propose laws, veto and protect citizens, without holding the office (as a patrician he could not be tribune). It became the dating system of the reign and the core power of every later emperor. He also obtained the right to bring the first motion at any Senate meeting and retained his imperium inside the pomerium. Giving up continuous consulships doubled the number of consular places available to senators. Augustus's physician Antonius Musa cured him by cold baths and was rewarded with a statue and gold ring; the same cure failed to save Marcellus months later.
scholarship: Rich, Cassius Dio: The Augustan Settlement (1990)
Crook, CAH X2 (1996), ch. 2
events.debate: Whether Augustus received imperium maius in 23 BC (Dio) or only later is debated; the edicts of Cyrene (7-6 BC) show him intervening in a public province. Tacitus called tribunicia potestas the 'summi fastigii vocabulum' devised by Augustus.

events.title: Conspiracy of Fannius Caepio and Murena
events.summary: Following the trial of Marcus Primus, governor of Macedonia, who claimed he had attacked the Odrysians on Augustus's or Marcellus's orders, a plot against Augustus was alleged; Fannius Caepio and a Murena (probably Varro Murena, Primus's advocate) were condemned in absence and killed.
events.detail: Augustus appeared uninvited at Primus's trial and denied giving instructions; Murena's insolent questioning ('What are you doing here, who summoned you?') was remembered. Several jurors voted for acquittal of the conspirators, and Augustus responded with a law that votes in such cases be open. Caepio's slave who betrayed him was paraded with a placard; another who defended him was rewarded. The episode is commonly linked to the political crisis and constitutional reshaping of 23 BC.
scholarship: Swan, 'The consular fasti of 23 B.C. and the conspiracy of Varro Murena', HSCP 71 (1966)
events.debate: Dio dates it to 22 BC; many scholars prefer 23. Whether the consul of 23 BC, who disappears from the Fasti, was the conspirator Murena is disputed. Maecenas reportedly leaked the danger to his wife Terentia, Murena's sister, cooling his relationship with Augustus.

events.title: Death of Marcellus
events.summary: Marcus Claudius Marcellus, Augustus's nephew and son-in-law (married to Julia in 25 BC) and presumed heir, died at Baiae aged 19, the first to be buried in the Mausoleum of Augustus.
events.detail: Marcellus had been allowed to stand for office ten years early and gave lavish games as aedile in 23 BC. Rumour blamed Livia; Dio rejects this given the epidemic of that year. Virgil's lament at the end of Aeneid 6 ('tu Marcellus eris') reportedly made Octavia faint when he recited it before her (Donatus, Vita Vergilii 32). Augustus named the theatre near the Circus Flaminius after him and Octavia built a library in his memory. Julia was then married to Agrippa.

events.title: Augustan reform of the base-metal coinage
events.summary: Around 23 BC the mint at Rome resumed production under the tresviri monetales and introduced a new token coinage: brass (orichalcum) sestertii and dupondii and copper asses and quadrantes, alongside the gold aureus and silver denarius.
events.detail: The system (1 aureus = 25 denarii = 100 sestertii = 400 asses) lasted, with modifications, until the third century. Brass, a zinc-copper alloy, was valued above copper, so sestertius and dupondius (yellow) were distinguished from the as (red) by colour, the dupondius later by a radiate crown. The SC on base-metal issues probably acknowledges senatorial authorisation. Precious-metal production soon shifted to Lugdunum (from c. 15 BC), close to the Rhine armies. Moneyers' names disappear from coins after c. 4 BC.
scholarship: Sutherland, Roman Imperial Coinage I2 (1984)
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)
events.debate: The exact date (23 or 19 BC) and the meaning of SC on bronze are debated.

events.title: Augustus refuses the dictatorship and takes the cura annonae
events.summary: During famine, plague and floods in 23-22 BC the Roman crowd tried to force the dictatorship and a perpetual consulship on Augustus. He knelt and bared his breast in refusal but accepted charge of the grain supply, ending the shortage within days at his own expense.
events.detail: Res Gestae 5 records both the refusal and the cura annonae. In the same year Augustus had censors elected, Paullus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Munatius Plancus, the last pair of private citizens to hold the office; the platform collapsed on the first day, an omen. The grain supply was later placed under an equestrian praefectus annonae (by AD 14), one of the great prefectures.

events.title: Return of the Parthian standards
events.summary: Under threat of Tiberius's army in Armenia and Augustus's presence in Syria, Phraates IV returned the standards and surviving prisoners taken from Crassus at Carrhae (53 BC), from Decidius Saxa (40 BC) and from Antony (36 BC). The diplomatic success was trumpeted as a military victory.
events.detail: Simultaneously Tiberius crowned Tigranes III king of Armenia. The standards were first placed in a small temple of Mars Ultor on the Capitol and later in the temple of Mars Ultor in the Forum of Augustus (2 BC). The scene of a Parthian handing a standard to a Roman figure occupies the centre of the cuirass of the Prima Porta statue, and coins of 19-16 BC proclaim SIGNIS RECEPTIS with a kneeling Parthian; Horace and Propertius celebrated it. Around 10 BC Phraates sent four sons with their families to Rome as hostages, partly to protect himself from his queen Musa, an Italian slave-girl gifted by Augustus, who later had him murdered (2 BC) to enthrone her son Phraataces.
scholarship: Rich, 'The Parthian Honours', PBSR 66 (1998)
events.debate: Whether a Parthian arch was built in the Forum, and where, remains disputed.

events.title: Peace of Samos with Kush
events.summary: Kushite envoys, escorted by Petronius's officers to Augustus wintering on Samos, obtained everything they asked, including remission of the tribute Petronius had imposed.
events.detail: The frontier was fixed at Hiera Sykaminos (Maharraqa), with the Dodekaschoinos as a Roman military zone. The generosity reflects Augustus's preference for stable frontiers and the low value of Lower Nubia. The peace held, with minor exceptions (a Neronian exploration party reached Meroë and the Sudd c. 61-63), until the Blemmyes troubles of the third century.

events.title: Herod begins rebuilding the Jerusalem Temple
events.summary: In the eighteenth year of his reign (20/19 BC) Herod began the reconstruction of the Second Temple, doubling the Temple Mount platform with vast retaining walls (including the Western Wall) to about 144,000 square metres.
events.detail: To avoid profaning the sanctuary, 1,000 priests were trained as masons; the shrine itself took 18 months, the porticoes eight years, and work continued until c. AD 63, only seven years before its destruction. The Royal Stoa ran along the southern edge. A Greek warning inscription forbidding Gentiles to pass the balustrade on pain of death was found in 1871 (OGIS 598), confirming Josephus's description. Some ashlars of the retaining walls weigh over 500 tonnes.

events.title: Triumph of Cornelius Balbus over the Garamantes
events.summary: Lucius Cornelius Balbus the Younger, proconsul of Africa, triumphed over the Garamantes after capturing their capital Garama in the Fezzan. He was the first man born outside Italy (at Gades) to triumph, and the last person outside the imperial family ever to do so.
events.detail: Pliny lists the names of towns and peoples carried in the procession, including Cidamus (Ghadames) and Garama, and notes that the route over the mountains was unknown before. Balbus used his spoils to build the Theatre of Balbus and its crypta in the Campus Martius (dedicated 13 BC). After this, generals received only triumphal ornaments (ornamenta triumphalia); the Fasti Triumphales on the Arch of Augustus end with Balbus.

events.title: Agrippa opens the Aqua Virgo
events.summary: Agrippa's aqueduct, about 21 km long and almost entirely underground, brought spring water to the Campus Martius to supply his baths. It still feeds the Trevi Fountain.
events.detail: Frontinus says the name came from a young girl who showed the source to soldiers searching for water. It is the only ancient Roman aqueduct to have functioned almost continuously to the present (restored by Pope Nicholas V in 1453 as the Acqua Vergine). Agrippa as aedile in 33 BC had already overhauled Rome's water system, creating 700 basins, 500 fountains and 130 reservoirs, and his slave water-gang of 240 was bequeathed to Augustus and then made public.

events.title: Death of Virgil
events.summary: Publius Vergilius Maro died at Brundisium after falling ill in Greece, where he had met Augustus at Athens. He asked that the unfinished Aeneid be burned; Augustus ordered Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca to publish it without additions.
events.detail: The Aeneid's half-lines and inconsistencies betray its incomplete state. Its epitaph, supposedly composed by Virgil himself, ran 'Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenent nunc Parthenope; cecini pascua rura duces'. The poem became the school text of the Latin West for the rest of antiquity and was quoted on graffiti at Pompeii and on writing tablets at Vindolanda.

events.title: Execution of Egnatius Rufus
events.summary: Marcus Egnatius Rufus, who had won popularity as aedile by running a private fire brigade of his slaves, tried to stand for the consulship of 19 BC illegally; when the consul Sentius Saturninus refused his candidacy he was accused of plotting against Augustus and executed.
events.detail: Velleius, deeply hostile, presents him as a gladiator rather than a senator. The affair, during Augustus's absence in the East, and riots over consular elections led the Senate to send for Augustus; on his return Dio says he received consular power for life (54.10.5), a passage whose reliability is debated. Fire-fighting remained a political issue until Augustus created the vigiles in AD 6.

events.title: Agrippa ends the Cantabrian War
events.summary: A last revolt by Cantabrian slaves who had escaped from Roman owners and killed them was crushed by Agrippa, who had to overcome his own soldiers' reluctance; virtually all men of military age were killed and the rest forced from their mountains into the plains.
events.detail: Dio notes that Agrippa declined a triumph and did not even report his success to the Senate, a sign of the new etiquette that triumphal honours belonged to the princeps. He degraded legio I Augusta, stripping it of its title. The pacified north-west was reorganised around new towns, Asturica Augusta (Astorga), Lucus Augusti (Lugo) and Bracara Augusta (Braga), and its gold fields were exploited by hydraulic mining (ruina montium) on a massive scale.

events.title: Lex Julia de maritandis ordinibus and Lex Julia de adulteriis coercendis
events.summary: Augustus used his tribunician power to carry laws penalising celibacy and childlessness among the propertied classes and making adultery a public crime tried before a standing court (quaestio).
events.detail: The marriage law required men aged 25-60 and women aged 20-50 to be married, restricted the capacity of the unmarried to inherit, forbade senators and their descendants to marry freedwomen, actresses or prostitutes, and rewarded parents of three children (ius trium liberorum) with privileges such as faster careers and, for women, freedom from guardianship. The adultery law obliged a husband to divorce an adulterous wife on pain of prosecution for pimping (lenocinium), allowed a father to kill a daughter and her lover caught in his house, and imposed relegation to separate islands and confiscations. Horace's Carmen Saeculare (17 BC) prays for the success of the 'patrum decreta super iugandis feminis'. The laws were revised by the lex Papia Poppaea in AD 9. Both Augustus's daughter and granddaughter were later exiled under the adultery law.
scholarship: Treggiari, Roman Marriage (1991)
Edwards, The Politics of Immorality in Ancient Rome (1993)
events.debate: Propertius 2.7 celebrates the withdrawal of a law that would have forced him to marry, often taken as evidence of a failed attempt c. 28 BC, though this is contested. The demographic effectiveness of the laws was doubted already by Tacitus (Ann. 3.25).

events.title: Lectio senatus of 18 BC
events.summary: Augustus purged the Senate from about 800 to 600 members after a chaotic system of co-optation failed; Suetonius says he presided wearing a breastplate under his toga and a sword, with ten senators around his chair.
events.detail: This was the second Augustan purge after that of 29-28 BC (from about 1,000 to 800). A minimum census for senators was fixed, probably at 1 million sesterces, with Augustus subsidising worthy but poor members. A third revision followed in 11 BC and a committee of three (tresviri legendi senatus) in AD 4.

events.title: Secular Games of 17 BC
events.summary: Augustus and Agrippa, as magistri of the quindecimviri sacris faciundis, celebrated the Ludi Saeculares over three nights and days (31 May-3 June), proclaiming the beginning of a new age. Horace's Carmen Saeculare was sung by 27 boys and 27 girls on the Palatine and the Capitol.
events.detail: A long inscription recording the protocol (the Acta of the games, CIL VI 32323) was found in 1890 near the Tiber at the site of the Tarentum, giving prayers to the Moirai, Ilithyiae, Terra Mater, Jupiter, Juno, Apollo and Diana and naming 110 matrons. The calculation of a 110-year saeculum was itself a scholarly construction of the jurist Ateius Capito. Shortly afterwards Augustus adopted Agrippa's sons Gaius and the newborn Lucius as his own, signalling the dynastic purpose of the new age.
scholarship: Feeney, Literature and Religion at Rome (1998)
Schnegg-Köhler, Die augusteischen Säkularspiele (2002)

events.title: Clades Lolliana
events.summary: The Sugambri, Usipetes and Tencteri crucified Roman traders in their territory, crossed the Rhine, ambushed Roman cavalry and routed the legate Marcus Lollius, capturing the eagle of legio V Alaudae.
events.detail: Velleius calls it a defeat 'of greater disgrace than damage'; Suetonius pairs it with the Varian disaster as Augustus's only two serious and ignominious defeats, both in Germany. Augustus came to Gaul in person (16-13 BC), the Germans withdrew and gave hostages, and the episode led directly to Drusus's offensives across the Rhine from 12 BC. Lollius later served as guardian to Gaius Caesar in the East and was disgraced for taking bribes from the Parthians (AD 2).

sides.losses: Unknown; the eagle of V Alaudae captured

battle.significance: Triggered the Augustan offensive into Germany and Augustus's three-year stay in Gaul.

events.debate: Dio dates it to 16 BC; the Livian tradition (Obsequens) may imply 17. Site unknown.

events.title: Drusus and Tiberius conquer the Raeti and Vindelici
events.summary: In a pincer campaign Drusus advanced from Italy up the Adige valley and over the Alps while Tiberius came from Gaul, fought a naval battle on Lake Constance and joined his brother near the source of the Danube, subduing the Raeti and Vindelici in a single summer.
events.detail: Horace (Odes 4.14) dates the decisive victory to the anniversary of the fall of Alexandria (1 August); Odes 4.4 compares Drusus to an eagle. Dio says the Romans deported most of the strongest men, leaving enough to farm. The Augustan legionary base at Dangstetten on the upper Rhine and the early camp at Augsburg-Oberhausen belong to this phase. Raetia was later governed by an equestrian prefect and procurator with its capital at Augusta Vindelicum.

events.title: Incorporation of Noricum
events.summary: The Celtic kingdom of Noricum, long a trading partner of Rome, was absorbed in 16-15 BC after the Norici joined Pannonians in raiding Istria; it was governed by an equestrian prefect and from Claudius as a procuratorial province.
events.detail: The hill-town on the Magdalensberg, with its Roman traders' quarter and inscriptions recording the export of Noric iron and steel (ferrum Noricum, praised by Ovid and Horace), was the centre of the region until Claudius founded Virunum in the plain below. Velleius treats the annexation as part of the Alpine war of 15 BC. Noricum received no legion until the Marcomannic Wars (legio II Italica, at Lauriacum).

events.title: Agrippa settles the Bosporan Kingdom
events.summary: Agrippa brought a fleet to Sinope to dislodge the usurper Scribonius from the Bosporan throne and installed Polemon I of Pontus as king, married to the Bosporan queen Dynamis.
events.detail: On this eastern tour (16-13 BC) Agrippa visited Jerusalem with Herod (15 BC), sacrificing a hecatomb in the Temple, and in 14 BC heard the complaints of Ionian Jews, confirming their privileges, a speech Nicolaus of Damascus preserved through Josephus. Dynamis soon broke with Polemon and ruled alone, issuing gold staters with Augustus's portrait. Agrippa declined the triumph voted for the Bosporan success.

events.title: Ara Pacis Augustae
events.summary: The Senate voted the Altar of Augustan Peace on 4 July 13 BC to mark Augustus's return from Gaul and Spain; it was dedicated on 30 January 9 BC, Livia's birthday, on the Campus Martius beside the Via Flaminia.
events.detail: Its marble precinct walls carry the most famous relief programme of the age: a procession of the imperial family, priests and magistrates (including Agrippa, Livia, Tiberius, Antonia and the children Gaius and Lucius), mythological panels (Aeneas or Numa sacrificing, Romulus and Remus, Roma, and the so-called Tellus panel), and a lower register of acanthus scrolls teeming with small animals. Fragments were found in 1568 and 1859; the monument was excavated in 1903 and in 1937-38 using ground-freezing beneath the Palazzo Fiano, then reassembled for Mussolini's Augustan bimillennium beside the Mausoleum. Richard Meier's pavilion replaced the fascist shelter in 2006.
events.locName: Campus Martius, Rome (original site under Palazzo Fiano)
scholarship: Zanker, The Power of Images in the Age of Augustus (1988)
Rossini, Ara Pacis (2006)
events.debate: The identity of the female figure on the 'Tellus' panel (Tellus, Italia, Pax or Venus) and of the sacrificer (Aeneas or Numa) are classic debates.

events.title: Dedication of the Theatre of Marcellus
events.summary: Augustus dedicated the stone theatre begun by Julius Caesar near the Circus Flaminius in the name of his dead nephew Marcellus; it held perhaps 11,000-20,000 spectators.
events.detail: Its superimposed Doric and Ionic arcades on a radial concrete substructure anticipated the Colosseum. Pliny says a tame tiger was exhibited in a cage at its dedication, the first in Rome. In the Middle Ages it became a fortress of the Pierleoni and Savelli, and Baldassare Peruzzi built the Palazzo Orsini (Savelli) into its upper cavea in the 1520s.
events.debate: Dio places the dedication in 13 BC, Pliny's evidence implies 11 BC.

events.title: Death of Agrippa
events.summary: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa died in Campania shortly after returning from Pannonia, aged about 51. Augustus delivered the funeral oration and buried him in his own Mausoleum.
events.detail: Agrippa had held the tribunician power and imperium since 18 BC, a virtual co-regent. A Greek translation of part of Augustus's laudatio survives on a papyrus (P.Köln VI 249), published in 1970, which mentions the grant to him of imperium greater than that of any provincial governor. His posthumous son Agrippa Postumus was born weeks later. His death forced Augustus to rely on his stepsons; Tiberius was compelled to divorce Vipsania Agrippina, whom he loved, and marry the widowed Julia (11 BC).
scholarship: Koenen, 'Die Laudatio Funebris des Augustus für Agrippa auf einem neuen Papyrus', ZPE 5 (1970)

events.title: Augustus becomes pontifex maximus
events.summary: On the death of the former triumvir Lepidus, who had kept the chief pontificate in exile at Circeii since 36 BC, Augustus was elected pontifex maximus by a crowd that Res Gestae claims was larger than any ever seen in Rome.
events.detail: Rather than live in the official domus publica on the Via Sacra, he made part of his Palatine house public and dedicated a shrine of Vesta there (28 April 12 BC), joining the cult of the hearth of the state to his own household. As pontifex maximus he had over 2,000 anonymous prophetic books burned and deposited an edited set of Sibylline books in the temple of Apollo Palatinus. Every emperor until Gratian held the office.

events.title: Altar of Rome and Augustus at Lugdunum
events.summary: Drusus dedicated an altar of Rome and Augustus at the confluence of the Rhône and Saône outside Lugdunum, where delegates of the sixty civitates of the Three Gauls met each year on 1 August under an elected Gallic priest.
events.detail: The first priest was the Aeduan Gaius Julius Vercondaridubnus. The concilium Galliarum became a forum for provincial elites, who later built an amphitheatre on the site (AD 19); the martyrs of 177 died there. The altar appears on the 'ROM ET AVG' asses minted at Lugdunum. It was a model for an altar of the Ubii at Cologne (Ara Ubiorum) intended for the future province of Germany.
events.debate: Livy's Periocha and Dio date the dedication to 12 BC, but Suetonius says Claudius was born at Lugdunum on 1 August 10 BC, the very day the altar was dedicated. Solutions include a two-stage inauguration.

events.title: Battle of Arbalo
events.summary: Returning from the Weser in 11 BC, Drusus's army was trapped by the Germans in a narrow defile at Arbalo and nearly destroyed, but the overconfident attackers came to close quarters in disorder and were beaten.
events.detail: Pliny the Elder cites the battle as a case where an evil omen (a swarm of bees settling on a tent-rope in Drusus's camp) proved false, for the battle was 'most fortunate'. After it Drusus built a fort at the confluence of the Lippe and Eliso (Aliso) and another among the Chatti on the Rhine. It is the only named battle of Drusus's campaigns.

battle.significance: Allowed Drusus to extricate his army and fortify the Lippe line.

events.title: Death of Drusus the Elder
events.summary: After reaching the Elbe, Drusus was injured when his horse fell on his leg and died about 30 days later in his summer camp, aged 29. Tiberius rode some 200 miles in a day and a night from Ticinum to reach him before he died.
events.detail: Tiberius walked before the body all the way to Rome. Drusus was cremated on the Campus Martius and buried in the Mausoleum; the Senate granted him and his descendants the hereditary cognomen Germanicus, and erected a marble arch with trophies on the Via Appia. A cenotaph (tumulus honorarius) was raised at Mogontiacum, around which the legions held annual ceremonies; the 'Drususstein' in Mainz citadel is traditionally identified with it. Dio reports that at the Elbe a superhuman woman told him in Latin to turn back as the end of his deeds and life was near. The pseudo-Ovidian Consolatio ad Liviam laments him.

events.title: Tiberius deports 40,000 Sugambri across the Rhine
events.summary: Succeeding his dead brother in Germany, Tiberius forced the Sugambri to submit; their envoys, including leading nobles, were arrested and killed themselves, and some 40,000 Sugambri and Suebi were transplanted to the left bank of the Rhine.
events.detail: The resettled Sugambri became the Cugerni around Vetera (Xanten). Suetonius records the deportation as an example of Augustan practice. Augustus himself came to the Rhine, and Tiberius received a triumph (celebrated 1 January 7 BC) and a second consulship. Dio says Augustus refused to treat with the Sugambri unless they sent envoys, then detained them.

events.title: Sextilis renamed Augustus; calendar error corrected
events.summary: A senatus consultum renamed the month Sextilis 'Augustus' because Augustus had begun his first consulship and conquered Egypt in it. Augustus also corrected the Julian calendar, which the pontiffs had misapplied by intercalating every third year instead of every fourth.
events.detail: Macrobius preserves the text of the decree (Sat. 1.12.35). Since 45 BC the pontiffs, using inclusive counting, had inserted twelve leap days in 36 years instead of nine; Augustus suspended intercalation for about twelve years so that the calendar was back in step by AD 8. The exact years of the triennial leap days are reconstructed differently by modern chronologers, which affects the conversion of some Roman dates of 45-9 BC.
scholarship: Bennett, 'The Early Augustan Calendars in Rome and Egypt', ZPE 142-147 (2003-2004)

events.title: Division of Rome into 14 regions and the vici
events.summary: Augustus reorganised the city of Rome into fourteen regiones subdivided into vici (265 by AD 73), each under four annually elected vicomagistri, mostly freedmen, who tended the crossroads shrines of the Lares Augusti and the Genius of Augustus.
events.detail: The reform turned neighbourhood cult into a vehicle of loyalty and gave freedmen honoured public roles; surviving compital altars, such as that of the vicus Sandaliarius (2 BC) in the Uffizi, show the Lares holding laurel branches. The regions also structured fire-fighting (two per cohort of vigiles from AD 6), grain distribution and later the fourth-century Regionary Catalogues. Augustus also enlarged the city's boundary with the regions extending beyond the Servian wall.
scholarship: Lott, The Neighborhoods of Augustan Rome (2004)

events.title: Edicts of Augustus at Cyrene
events.summary: A marble stele found in the agora of Cyrene in 1926 preserves five edicts of Augustus (7/6-4 BC) regulating juries, citizen privileges and provincial justice in this senatorial province, ending with the senatus consultum Calvisianum on extortion trials.
events.detail: The edicts set up mixed juries of Greeks and Romans for capital cases involving Greeks, require Greek holders of Roman citizenship to continue performing local liturgies, and send cases of treason to the governor. The SC Calvisianum (4 BC) created a fast procedure in which five senators chosen by lot could assess restitution for provincials claiming extortion by a governor, without a full criminal trial. They show the princeps intervening in a public province, the practical meaning of his imperium maius.
scholarship: Oliver, 'On the edicts of Augustus at Cyrene', Historia 18 (1969)
Sherk, Roman Documents from the Greek East (1969) no. 31

events.title: Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie
events.summary: The Senate and people erected a monumental trophy on the Via Julia Augusta above Monaco, recording that under Augustus's leadership and auspices all the Alpine peoples from the Adriatic to the Tyrrhenian had been brought under Roman rule; 45 peoples are named.
events.detail: The inscription is dated by Augustus's seventeenth acclamation and fourteenth tribunician power (7/6 BC). Pliny copied the full text (NH 3.136-137), allowing its reconstruction from fragments; the list begins with the Triumpilini and Camunni and ends with the peoples of the Maritime Alps. The monument, about 35 m high, was quarried in the Middle Ages and partly restored in 1929-1933 by Jules Formigé with funds from the American Edward Tuck.

events.title: Tiberius withdraws to Rhodes
events.summary: Just after receiving the tribunician power for five years and a mission to Armenia, Tiberius insisted on retiring to Rhodes, where he spent nearly eight years as a private scholar, alienated from Augustus.
events.detail: Motives were debated even in antiquity: disgust with his wife Julia, resentment at the rapid promotion of Gaius and Lucius, a wish to avoid seeming their rival, or exhaustion (Suetonius gives several). Augustus complained publicly of desertion; Tiberius's tribunician power lapsed in 1 BC and he came close to danger when Gaius's entourage suggested killing him. He returned in AD 2 with Augustus's permission on condition he take no part in public affairs. On Rhodes he befriended the astrologer Thrasyllus, who remained his confidant until 36.

events.title: Gaius and Lucius Caesar hailed principes iuventutis
events.summary: Augustus held his twelfth and thirteenth consulships (5 and 2 BC) to introduce his adopted sons to public life. Each was designated consul at fourteen to take office five years later, and the equestrian order hailed each as princeps iuventutis with silver shields and spears.
events.detail: The Lugdunum denarius showing the two youths with shields, spears and priestly implements (C L CAESARES AVGVSTI F COS DESIG PRINC IVVENT) is one of the commonest Roman silver coins. The Maison Carrée at Nîmes was rededicated to them as 'principes iuventutis'. Res Gestae 14 records the honours. Their deaths in AD 2 and 4 wrecked Augustus's succession plans.

events.title: Quirinius's war against the Homonadenses
events.summary: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, probably as legate of Galatia or Syria, reduced the Homonadenses of the Taurus, who had killed king Amyntas, starving out 44 strongholds and settling 4,000 captives in nearby towns; he received triumphal ornaments.
events.detail: Strabo describes their homeland as a fertile hollow surrounded by cliffs. The war secured the new Pisidian colonies and the Via Sebaste. Its date (between c. 12 BC and AD 1) and Quirinius's province at the time are disputed, a question entangled with the census of Luke 2.

events.title: Death of Herod and partition of his kingdom
events.summary: Herod died at Jericho in spring 4 BC, after executing three of his sons. Augustus largely confirmed his will: Archelaus became ethnarch of Judaea, Samaria and Idumaea, Herod Antipas tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, and Philip tetrarch of the north-eastern territories.
events.detail: Josephus dates the death shortly after a lunar eclipse and before Passover; the partial eclipse of 13 March 4 BC fits, though some argue for the total eclipse of 10 January 1 BC, a debate that also bears on the chronology of Jesus's birth. Risings across the kingdom on Herod's death were crushed by Publius Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria, who crucified 2,000 rebels. Macrobius reports Augustus's quip that it was better to be Herod's pig than his son.
events.debate: Date of Herod's death (4 BC conventional; 1 BC minority view).

events.title: Roman town at Waldgirmes on the Lahn
events.summary: A civilian Roman town with stone-founded forum and basilica was laid out around 4 BC at Lahnau-Waldgirmes, 100 km east of the Rhine, and abandoned peacefully around AD 9. It is the clearest archaeological proof that a province of Germania was being built.
events.detail: Excavations from 1993 found a forum with a gilded bronze equestrian statue of Augustus, whose life-size horse head was recovered from a well in 2009; native Germanic potters and Roman houses coexisted. Dendrochronology dates the wells to 4/3 BC. The finds confirm Dio's statement (56.18) that the Romans held parts of Germany, that cities were being founded and the barbarians adapting to Roman ways, before Varus's attempt to impose tribute too quickly.
scholarship: Becker and Rasbach, Waldgirmes (2015)

events.title: Augustus hailed Pater Patriae
events.summary: On 5 February 2 BC the Senate, equites and whole people, on a motion by Valerius Messalla Corvinus, saluted Augustus as Father of his Country; he answered in tears that his prayers were fulfilled.
events.detail: Res Gestae 35, the culminating chapter, records that the title was inscribed in the vestibule of his house, in the Curia Julia and in the Forum of Augustus beneath the quadriga erected to him by decree of the Senate. Suetonius quotes Messalla's formula and Augustus's reply. The title had been given informally before (Cicero, Caesar) and became standard for emperors, who usually accepted it after an interval.

events.title: Dedication of the Forum of Augustus and Temple of Mars Ultor
events.summary: Augustus dedicated his forum, built on private land bought from war booty, with the temple of Mars the Avenger vowed at Philippi. Its colonnades held statues of Aeneas, Romulus, the Julian ancestors and the 'summi viri' of the Republic with elogia.
events.detail: Here the Senate debated war and triumphs, governors set out for their provinces and youths assumed the toga virilis; the recovered Parthian standards were deposited in the temple. Caryatids copying the Erechtheion and a 33-metre fire wall separating it from the Subura survive. The celebrations included a naumachia in a basin across the Tiber (1,800 by 1,200 Roman feet) in which 3,000 men refought Salamis, and the slaughter of 260 lions in the Circus. Gaius Caesar was sent east about this time.
scholarship: Zanker, Forum Augustum (1968)
Spannagel, Exemplaria principis (1999)
events.debate: Ovid places the dies natalis of Mars Ultor on 12 May; Velleius and Dio imply 1 August 2 BC. One view takes 12 May as the date of the earlier Capitoline shrine of 20 BC.

events.title: Exile of Julia, daughter of Augustus
events.summary: Augustus denounced his daughter Julia to the Senate by letter for adulteries and sent her to the island of Pandateria; her mother Scribonia went with her. Iullus Antonius, son of Mark Antony, was forced to suicide, and other noble lovers were exiled.
events.detail: Those named include Sempronius Gracchus, Appius Claudius Pulcher, Quinctius Crispinus and a Scipio. Pliny the Elder mentions a plot against Augustus's life in connection with Julia, and many scholars (Syme, Levick) argue the scandal concealed a political conspiracy around her and Iullus in favour of her sons and against Tiberius. She was moved to Rhegium after five years and died there in AD 14, shortly after Tiberius cut her allowance.
scholarship: Levick, 'The fall of Julia the Younger', Latomus 35 (1976)
events.debate: Moral scandal versus political conspiracy.

events.title: Lex Fufia Caninia and Lex Aelia Sentia
events.summary: Two laws restricted manumission: the lex Fufia Caninia (2 BC) capped the number of slaves freed by will on a sliding scale to a maximum of 100; the lex Aelia Sentia (AD 4) required a master to be 20 and the slave 30 for a formal manumission conferring citizenship, unless justified before a council.
events.detail: Aelia Sentia also created the degraded status of dediticii for freed slaves who had been chained, branded or tortured, barring them from citizenship and from living near Rome, and annulled manumissions in fraud of creditors. Gaius's Institutes (1.13-46) are the main source. The laws aimed at controlling the influx of new citizens rather than stopping manumission, which remained common.

events.title: Death of Lucius Caesar
events.summary: Lucius Caesar, Augustus's younger adopted son, died at Massilia of a sudden illness while on his way to the Spanish armies, aged 18.
events.detail: His death, and that of Gaius 18 months later, produced the Pisan decrees (cenotaphia Pisana, ILS 139-140), which preserve the honours voted by the colony of Pisa, including annual rites and the closing of temples on the anniversary, a rich source for municipal loyalism. Tacitus reports rumours that Livia was responsible.

events.title: Gaius Caesar meets Phraataces on the Euphrates
events.summary: Augustus's grandson and heir met the Parthian king Phraataces (Phraates V) on an island in the Euphrates; the Parthian renounced claims to Armenia, and the two dined on each bank in turn.
events.detail: Velleius Paterculus, serving as a military tribune, witnessed it. At the meeting Phraataces revealed that Gaius's guardian Marcus Lollius had taken bribes from eastern kings; Lollius died soon after, perhaps by suicide, and Tiberius's partisan Sulpicius Quirinius replaced him. Gaius then installed Ariobarzanes of Media as king of Armenia, leading to the siege of Artagira where he was wounded.

events.title: Death of Gaius Caesar
events.summary: Gaius Caesar, wounded by treachery at the siege of Artagira in Armenia on 9 September AD 3, lost heart, asked to retire to private life, and died at Limyra in Lycia on his way back to Italy, aged 23.
events.detail: His cenotaph at Limyra survives. The deaths of both grandsons left Augustus with no alternative to Tiberius; within four months he adopted him. Pisa decreed annual mourning on 21 February. Velleius blames Gaius's flatterers for his decline.

events.title: Augustus adopts Tiberius and Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Augustus adopted Tiberius, saying 'I do this for the sake of the state', and on the same day his last grandson Agrippa Postumus. Tiberius in turn was required to adopt his nephew Germanicus, though he had a son of his own, Drusus.
events.detail: Tiberius received tribunician power for ten years and command in Germany. The formula 'hoc rei publicae causa facio' was read by hostile writers as a sign of Augustus's reluctance. The arrangement fixed the double line of succession (Claudian through Tiberius, Julian through Germanicus, husband of Augustus's granddaughter Agrippina) that shaped dynastic politics until Nero.

events.title: Tiberius's immensum bellum in Germany
events.summary: Tiberius's campaigns of AD 4-5 subdued the Cananefates, Chattuarii, Bructeri and Cherusci, wintered the army at the source of the Lippe, then crushed the Langobardi and reached the Elbe, where a fleet that had sailed round from the Rhine through the North Sea met the army.
events.detail: Velleius, an eyewitness, calls it an 'immense war' and describes an old German who paddled across the Elbe in a dugout to touch Tiberius and declare it the happiest day of his life. Res Gestae 26.4 claims the fleet sailed east from the Rhine mouth to the land of the Cimbri (Jutland), 'where no Roman had gone before', and that the Cimbri, Charydes and Semnones sent envoys. The legionary base at Anreppen on the upper Lippe, built of timber in AD 4-5, matches the winter quarters.

events.title: Creation of the aerarium militare
events.summary: Augustus created a military treasury to pay discharge bonuses to veterans, endowing it with 170 million sesterces of his own money and funding it permanently from a new 5% tax on inheritances (vicesima hereditatium) and a 1% sales tax.
events.detail: The previous year service terms were set at 20 years (plus reserve) for legionaries and 16 for praetorians, with cash discharge bonuses of 12,000 sesterces for legionaries and 20,000 for praetorians replacing land grants, which had driven the confiscations of the triumviral age. The inheritance tax, levied only on citizens and exempting close kin and small estates, provoked strong senatorial opposition; Augustus invited alternative proposals and threatened a property tax instead. Three ex-praetors (praefecti aerarii militaris) administered the fund. The cost of the standing army, perhaps half of state revenue, was now institutionalised.
scholarship: Corbier, L'aerarium Saturni et l'aerarium militare (1974)

events.title: Judaea becomes a Roman province; census of Quirinius
events.summary: After Jewish and Samaritan complaints against Archelaus, Augustus deposed him and exiled him to Vienne in Gaul; Judaea, Samaria and Idumaea were placed under an equestrian prefect, Coponius, while Quirinius, legate of Syria, took a census for tribute.
events.detail: The census provoked the resistance of Judas the Galilean and a Pharisee named Saddok, who taught that paying tribute to Rome meant accepting slavery and acknowledging a master other than God; Josephus calls their movement the 'fourth philosophy' and traces the later Zealots and Sicarii to it. The prefects resided at Caesarea, commanded auxiliary troops recruited from Caesarea and Sebaste, and appointed high priests. Luke 2.1-2 dates the birth of Jesus to this census 'when Quirinius was governing Syria', which conflicts with Matthew's dating under Herod, who died in 4 BC; attempts to harmonise the two remain unconvincing to most historians.
events.debate: Historicity and date of the Lucan census.

events.title: Creation of the vigiles
events.summary: After a serious fire Augustus established seven cohorts of vigiles, recruited from freedmen, each responsible for two of the fourteen regions, under an equestrian praefectus vigilum. They fought fires and patrolled the streets at night.
events.detail: Each cohort had about 500 men (later 1,000) with specialists such as siphonarii (pump operators), aquarii, centonarii (with fire blankets) and doctors. Service in the vigiles brought freedmen of Junian Latin status full citizenship after six years (later three, under a lex Visellia of AD 24). The excubitorium of the seventh cohort in Trastevere, with its graffiti, survives. The same year saw famine, the expulsion of gladiators and slaves for sale to 100 miles from Rome, and Augustus's appointment of two consulars to oversee the grain supply.
scholarship: Rainbird, 'The fire stations of imperial Rome', PBSR 54 (1986)

events.title: Outbreak of the Great Illyrian Revolt
events.summary: As Tiberius advanced from Carnuntum with twelve legions to attack Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom in Bohemia, the Daesitiates of Dalmatia, mustered as auxiliaries, rose under Bato, and the Breuci of Pannonia under another Bato and Pinnes marched on Sirmium. Tiberius had to abandon the Bohemian war and make peace with Maroboduus.
events.detail: The planned pincer (Sentius Saturninus from Mainz, Tiberius from the Danube) was within days of contact when the revolt broke out; Velleius claims Maroboduus was saved only by it. Roman traders and veterans were massacred, Salona was attacked (the Daesitiate Bato was wounded there), and raids reached Macedonia. Rome enrolled freedmen as soldiers, levied extraordinary taxes, and Augustus told the Senate the enemy could be at Rome in ten days.

events.title: Battle near Sirmium
events.summary: Aulus Caecina Severus, governor of Moesia, marched to save Sirmium and defeated the Breuci near the city, but with heavy losses, and soon had to return to Moesia to repel Dacian and Sarmatian raids.
events.detail: Dio's brief account is the only source. The relief of Sirmium kept the key crossing of the Sava in Roman hands; the rebels then joined forces on Mons Almus (Fruška Gora) north of the city, where Rhoemetalces's Thracian cavalry skirmished with them.

battle.significance: Saved Sirmium for Rome in the first weeks of the revolt.

events.title: Battle of the Volcaean Marshes
events.summary: Caecina Severus and Plautius Silvanus, bringing five legions with auxiliaries and Thracian cavalry from the east to join Tiberius, were ambushed by the two Batos near the Volcaean marshes; the cavalry and auxiliaries broke but the legions rallied and won.
events.detail: Velleius, who served in the war, says the legions saved the day 'by their own courage' after the Thracian cavalry of king Rhoemetalces was routed, the alae fled and cohorts turned; several senior officers, including a camp prefect and military tribunes, were killed. After the battle Tiberius had ten legions, more than 70 auxiliary cohorts, 14 alae, more than 10,000 veteran reservists and many volunteers at Siscia, which Velleius says was the largest army assembled since the civil wars; Tiberius judged it too large to supply and sent part away.
events.locName: Volcaean marshes, between the Sava and Drava (near Cibalae?)

battle.significance: Allowed the eastern army to join Tiberius at Siscia, concentrating overwhelming Roman forces.

events.title: Exile of Agrippa Postumus
events.summary: Augustus disowned his last grandson, Agrippa Postumus, for his 'savage' and unmanageable character, banishing him first to Surrentum and then, by senatorial decree, permanently to the island of Planasia under military guard.
events.detail: The ancient sources describe him as brutish but not criminal; modern historians suspect political motives, perhaps connected to the conspiracies around his sister Julia the Younger (exiled in AD 8) and her husband Aemilius Paullus. Tacitus reports a rumour that Augustus secretly visited him on Planasia shortly before his death. He was killed immediately after Augustus died in AD 14.

events.title: Surrender of the Breuci at the Bathinus river
events.summary: Worn down by famine and Tiberius's devastation, the Pannonians laid down their arms at the river Bathinus. The Breucian Bato, who had betrayed his colleague Pinnes to the Romans and been rewarded, was captured and executed soon after by the Daesitiate Bato.
events.detail: The Fasti record 3 August as the day of a victory of Tiberius in Illyricum, often linked to this surrender. Only the Dalmatian highlands remained in revolt into AD 9.

events.title: Relegation of Ovid to Tomis
events.summary: Augustus relegated the poet Ovid by personal edict to Tomis on the Black Sea, for 'a poem and a mistake' (carmen et error). The poem was the Ars Amatoria; the mistake has never been identified.
events.detail: Ovid's exile poetry (Tristia, Epistulae ex Ponto) gives a vivid, if literary, picture of a frontier town raided by Getae and Sarmatians across the frozen Danube. He kept his property and citizenship (relegatio, not exilium) and died at Tomis c. AD 17, his appeals to Augustus and Tiberius unanswered. The same year Julia the Younger was banished to Trimerus for adultery with Decimus Junius Silanus; many link Ovid's 'error' to her circle. No contemporary source other than Ovid mentions the exile, and a minority has even doubted it took place.
events.debate: The nature of Ovid's error; the authenticity of the exile (Fitton Brown 1985) is a fringe but persistent question.

events.title: Battle of the Teutoburg Forest (Varian Disaster)
events.summary: Publius Quinctilius Varus, leading legions XVII, XVIII and XIX with auxiliaries and a long baggage train to winter quarters, was lured by the Cheruscan Arminius, a Roman citizen and equestrian commanding auxiliaries, into a multi-day running fight in forest and bog where the army was annihilated.
events.detail: Segestes had warned Varus of Arminius's plans the night before. Rain, broken terrain and the column's strung-out baggage favoured the Germans. Varus and senior officers killed themselves; the cavalry commander Numonius Vala fled and was cut down; the camp prefect Ceionius surrendered. Prisoners were sacrificed in groves, tribunes and centurions on altars, and the three eagles taken. Varus's head was sent to Maroboduus, who forwarded it to Augustus. Augustus dismissed his German bodyguard, let his hair and beard grow for months and cried 'Quinctilius Varus, give back my legions!'; the three legion numbers were never used again. The Kalkriese site, discovered by the amateur Tony Clunn in 1987, has yielded over 6,000 military finds, a turf rampart with drainage, mule bones and the silver face-mask of a cavalry helmet; coins end about AD 9 and many carry the VAR countermark. At Xanten the cenotaph of the centurion Marcus Caelius of legio XVIII (CIL XIII 8648) records that he 'fell in the Varian war'.

sides.strength: 3 legions, 3 alae, 6 cohorts: c. 15,000-20,000 soldiers plus camp followers
Cherusci, Bructeri, Marsi, Chatti and others; unknown

battle.significance: Ended Augustus's attempt to make Germany between Rhine and Elbe a province; fixed the Rhine as the frontier and became a founding myth of German nationalism (Hermannsdenkmal, 1875).

scholarship: Wells, The Battle That Stopped Rome (2003)
Wolters, Die Schlacht im Teutoburger Wald (2008)
events.debate: Kalkriese as the site of the final stage is widely but not universally accepted; some argue it was a battle of Germanicus's campaigns (AD 15-16) instead. Dio's multi-day narrative and Tacitus's description of successive camps are hard to fit to one site.

events.title: Siege of Aliso
events.summary: After the Varian disaster the Germans besieged the Lippe fortress of Aliso. Its commander, the camp prefect Lucius Caedicius, held out until supplies failed, then broke out on a stormy night with soldiers, women and children and reached the Rhine.
events.detail: Dio says the defenders' archers repulsed assaults and the Germans tried to starve them; the garrison slipped past two German posts but was detected at the third, and was saved by trumpeters sounding the signal for a relief force, which made the Germans fall back. Lucius Asprenas, Varus's nephew, secured the Rhine crossings with two legions and prevented a German advance into Gaul.

battle.significance: The breakout preserved a remnant and denied the Germans a second triumph.

events.debate: Aliso has been identified with Haltern, Oberaden, Anreppen and other Lippe sites.

events.title: Siege of Raetinium
events.summary: Germanicus besieged the Dalmatian stronghold of Raetinium; the defenders set fire to the outer town as the Romans broke in, trapping many attackers, and withdrew to the citadel, which later fell.
events.detail: Dio describes the stratagem in detail. Germanicus then took Seretium and Splonum; at Arduba the women, refusing surrender, threw their children and themselves into the flames or the river.

battle.significance: Part of the methodical reduction of the Dalmatian hill-forts in AD 9.

events.title: Siege of Andetrium and surrender of Bato
events.summary: Tiberius besieged the Daesitiate Bato in the rock fortress of Andetrium near Salona. Bato negotiated his own surrender; the garrison fought on and was stormed, ending the Great Illyrian Revolt.
events.detail: Asked by Tiberius why his people had rebelled, Bato replied that Rome sent 'wolves, not dogs or shepherds' to guard its flocks. Tiberius spared him and he lived out his life at Ravenna. The victory was announced in Rome only days before news arrived of Varus's disaster in Germany, which overshadowed the celebrations.

battle.significance: Ended the most dangerous revolt of Augustus's reign.

events.title: Lex Papia Poppaea
events.summary: The consuls Marcus Papius Mutilus and Quintus Poppaeus Secundus, both themselves unmarried and childless as Dio wryly notes, carried a law revising the Augustan marriage legislation of 18 BC, refining the incentives for parenthood and the inheritance penalties for the unmarried and childless.
events.detail: Lapsed legacies (caduca) of those incapable of inheriting went first to heirs with children and ultimately to the treasury, making the law a source of revenue and of informers (delatores). Before its passage Augustus harangued the unmarried and married equites in separate assemblies (Dio 56.1-10). Juristic commentaries on 'the lex Julia et Papia' fill whole books of the Digest; Constantine repealed the penalties on celibacy in 320.

events.title: Tiberius's Pannonian and Dalmatian triumph
events.summary: Tiberius celebrated his postponed triumph over the Pannonians and Dalmatians; before mounting the Capitol he dismounted and knelt before Augustus. He spared the rebel leader Bato and gave him a residence at Ravenna.
events.detail: The Gemma Augustea, a sardonyx cameo in Vienna, is often interpreted as showing Tiberius stepping from a chariot before an enthroned Augustus and Roma, above Roman soldiers raising a trophy over captives, and may commemorate this triumph. Tiberius fed the people at 1,000 tables and gave each citizen 300 sesterces. In 13 his tribunician power was renewed and he received imperium equal to Augustus's in the provinces.

events.title: Death of Augustus
events.summary: Augustus died at Nola, in the room where his father had died, aged 75, after a journey to Campania and Beneventum with Tiberius.
