events.summary: The new emperor Philip made peace with Shapur, paying 500,000 denarii (aurei, according to the ŠKZ) and apparently recognising Persian influence in Armenia, while Roman coins proclaimed PAX FUNDATA CUM PERSIS.
events.detail: The ŠKZ calls Philip a tributary. Roman writers say he later reneged on the Armenian clause. Philip also founded Philippopolis (Shahba) in his native Trachonitis and deified his father Marinus.

events.title: Philip celebrates Rome's millennium
events.summary: On 21 April 248 Philip staged the Ludi Saeculares for the thousandth anniversary of Rome's foundation, with games in which, according to later tradition, a thousand pairs of gladiators and exotic animals collected by Gordian III appeared.
events.detail: Coins carry SAECULUM NOVUM. The celebration coincided with Gothic and Carpic invasions and military revolts, an irony later Christian tradition, which also made Philip the first Christian emperor (Eusebius, HE 6.34), exploited. The Christian claim is generally rejected.
events.debate: Philip's Christianity is a later legend; the animal list in the HA is suspect.

events.title: Revolts of Pacatianus and Jotapianus
events.summary: In 248 Tiberius Claudius Marinus Pacatianus was proclaimed by the Danube legions and Jotapianus, claiming kinship with Severus Alexander, rose in Syria or Cappadocia; both were soon killed by their own troops.
events.detail: Philip's offer to resign was answered by the senator Decius, who predicted the usurpers would fall; Philip then sent Decius to the Danube, where the troops proclaimed him instead. Pacatianus' coins, minted at Viminacium, are dated 'year 1001 of Rome'.

events.title: Battle of Verona
events.summary: Decius, proclaimed by the Danubian army, marched into Italy and defeated and killed Philip near Verona; Philip's son Philip II was murdered by the Praetorians in Rome.

battle.significance: Brought the Danubian Decius to power.

events.debate: Location (Verona vs Beroea in Macedonia, a scribal confusion) and date (September or October 249) debated.

events.title: Plague of Cyprian
events.summary: A pandemic, probably originating in Ethiopia and reaching Alexandria by 249, swept the empire for over a decade; Bishop Cyprian of Carthage describes bloody diarrhoea, vomiting, eye haemorrhage, gangrene of the limbs and loss of hearing and sight.
events.detail: Dionysius of Alexandria reports the city's population so reduced that the number of men aged 14 to 80 equalled those aged 40 to 70 in earlier times. The emperors Hostilian (251) and probably Claudius II (270) died of plague. Kyle Harper has argued for a viral haemorrhagic fever (filovirus) and an empire-wide mortality crisis, which others think overstated. The epidemic coincided with the worst military defeats of the century and may have hampered recruitment and tax.
scholarship: Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Harper, 'Pandemics and passages to late antiquity', JRA 28 (2015)
Huebner, 'The Plague of Cyprian: A revised view', Klio (2021)
events.debate: Pathogen unknown (smallpox, measles, filovirus proposed); scale contested.

events.title: Decius' edict of universal sacrifice
events.summary: Decius ordered every inhabitant of the empire to sacrifice to the gods, taste the sacrificial meat and obtain a certificate (libellus) from local commissioners; Christians who refused were imprisoned or executed, including Pope Fabian (20 January 250).
events.detail: Over forty libelli survive on papyrus from Egypt, including one for a priestess of Petesouchos, showing the order applied to everyone, not just Christians. The measure was probably a supplicatio for the empire's welfare tied to Decius' Trajanic-traditionalist programme rather than a targeted persecution, but its effect on the Church was severe: mass lapses, purchased certificates (libellatici), and bitter disputes over readmitting the lapsed that produced the Novatianist schism. Origen was tortured at Caesarea and died a few years later.

sources.w: Libelli of 250 (over 40 surviving papyri from Egypt)

scholarship: Rives, 'The Decree of Decius and the Religion of Empire', JRS 89 (1999)
Knipfing, 'The Libelli of the Decian Persecution', HTR 16 (1923)
events.debate: Whether Decius intended to target Christians is debated; Rives argues for a universalising religious policy.

events.title: Siege and sack of Philippopolis
events.summary: The Gothic king Cniva besieged Philippopolis in Thrace, whose governor Lucius Priscus, despairing of help from Decius, proclaimed himself emperor and allied with the Goths; the city fell and Ammianus says 100,000 people were killed or captured.
events.detail: A Vienna palimpsest (the 'Scythica Vindobonensia', identified in 2014) preserves fragments of Dexippus describing this campaign in Thrace, including speeches by Decius. Priscus was declared a public enemy and soon disappeared.

battle.significance: First sack of a major Balkan city by the Goths.

scholarship: Martin and Grusková, 'Scythica Vindobonensia', WS 127 (2014)

events.title: Battle of Beroe (Augusta Traiana)
events.summary: Cniva surprised Decius' army in camp near Beroe-Augusta Traiana, routing it and forcing the emperor to retreat to Moesia to regroup, leaving Philippopolis to its fate.

battle.significance: Left Thrace open to the Goths.

events.title: Battle of Abritus
events.summary: Decius and his son Herennius Etruscus were killed when Cniva's Goths lured the Roman army into a marsh near Abritus in Moesia Inferior; Decius was the first emperor to die fighting a foreign enemy, and his body was never found.
events.detail: Herennius was killed by an arrow early in the fighting; Decius reportedly told the troops that the loss of one soldier did not matter. Cniva placed part of his army behind a swamp; the Romans pursuing into it were trapped. Byzantine sources (Zosimus, Zonaras) accuse the governor Trebonianus Gallus of treachery, a claim many moderns doubt. Gallus, proclaimed emperor, allowed the Goths to withdraw with their booty and prisoners and promised an annual subsidy. A large fortified Roman camp excavated near Razgrad and coin hoards in the area have been linked to the battle.

sides.losses: very heavy; emperor and heir killed

battle.significance: First Roman emperor killed by a foreign enemy; symbol of the third-century nadir.

scholarship: Bursche, 'The battle of Abritus, the imperial treasury and aurei in Barbaricum', NC 173 (2013)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
events.debate: Date (June or July 251), Gallus' alleged treachery, and Gothic identity of Cniva's force (perhaps a mixed coalition) debated. Lactantius gloats over the persecutor's unburied corpse.

events.title: Novatianist schism at Rome
events.summary: When Cornelius was elected bishop of Rome in March 251 and favoured readmitting the lapsed after penance, the learned presbyter Novatian had himself consecrated rival bishop, founding a rigorist church that survived for centuries.
events.detail: Cyprian at Carthage backed Cornelius after hesitation and held councils on the lapsed. The Novatianists ('Cathari') spread across the empire; Constantine later tolerated them, and their bishops attended Nicaea. Novatian's De Trinitate is the first major Latin Trinitarian treatise from Rome.

events.title: Battle of Barbalissos
events.summary: Opening his second war, Shapur I destroyed a Roman army of 60,000 (his figure) at Barbalissos on the Euphrates, then overran Syria and Cappadocia; the ŠKZ lists 37 captured cities.
events.detail: Shapur's pretext was Roman interference in Armenia, where the Arsacid king (probably Khosrov II) was murdered and his son Tiridates fled to Rome. Barbalissos opened the road to Antioch.

battle.significance: Left the Roman East defenceless.

events.debate: Date 252 or 253; known only from Shapur's inscription.

events.title: Shapur I sacks Antioch
events.summary: Shapur took and sacked Antioch, the third city of the empire, guided (according to Ammianus and the Thirteenth Sibylline Oracle) by a renegade Antiochene councillor named Mariades; thousands were deported to Persia.
events.detail: Ammianus has the people of Antioch watching a mime in the theatre when an actor's wife cried 'Am I dreaming, or are the Persians here?'. Deportees from Antioch peopled Gundeshapur and Bishapur and helped to spread Christianity in Persia. Shapur later executed Mariades.

battle.significance: The greatest humiliation inflicted on Rome in the East to that date.

events.debate: Date 253 or 256; some argue for two captures (253 and 260).

events.title: Uranius Antoninus defends Emesa
events.summary: Lucius Julius Aurelius Sulpicius Severus Uranius Antoninus, priest of Elagabal at Emesa, led local resistance to Shapur and struck gold and silver coins as emperor in 253-254.
events.detail: Malalas records a priest of Aphrodite (Sampsigeramus) driving off Shapur from Emesa with slingers; the identification with Uranius is widely accepted. His local defence anticipates the larger role of Odaenathus of Palmyra.

events.title: Aemilianus overthrows Gallus; Valerian seizes power
events.summary: Aemilius Aemilianus, governor of Moesia, won a victory over the Goths, was proclaimed emperor and invaded Italy; Trebonianus Gallus and his son Volusian were killed by their own men near Interamna. Three months later Aemilianus met the same fate near Spoletium as Valerian approached with the Rhine army.
events.detail: Valerian, a senior senator in his sixties, made his son Gallienus co-Augustus, dividing responsibility between East (Valerian) and West (Gallienus), a pattern for later joint rule.

events.title: Sasanian siege of Dura-Europos
events.summary: Shapur's army besieged and destroyed the Roman frontier fortress of Dura-Europos on the Euphrates; excavations revealed siege mines and countermines in which some twenty Roman soldiers and one Persian died, perhaps the earliest archaeological evidence of chemical warfare.
events.detail: Simon James has argued that the Persians filled the Roman countermine with toxic smoke from burning bitumen and sulphur crystals, killing the Romans who broke in. To strengthen the wall the defenders had buried the street behind it with an earthen ramp, which preserved the synagogue with its painted biblical cycle, the Christian house-church with the earliest datable baptistery, and the Mithraeum. The city was abandoned after its fall.

battle.significance: Its ramp-buried buildings are among the most important finds of Roman archaeology.

scholarship: James, 'Stratagems, Combat, and Chemical Warfare in the Siege Mines of Dura-Europos', AJA 115 (2011)
James, The Roman Military Base at Dura-Europos (2019)
events.debate: Date of fall 256 or 257 from coin and graffiti evidence.

events.title: Gothic and Boranoi sea raids: Pityus and Trapezus
events.summary: Using ships commandeered from the Bosporan Kingdom, Boranoi and Goths raided the eastern Black Sea, taking Pityus at the second attempt and storming Trapezus, whose large garrison fled by night.
events.detail: Zosimus describes the raiders climbing the walls with tree trunks against the hillside and carrying off immense booty and captives. Gregory Thaumaturgus' Canonical Epistle deals with Christian captives and collaborators after these raids in Pontus. In 258 another fleet raided the Propontis and sacked Chalcedon, Nicomedia and Nicaea.

events.title: Valerian's persecution of the clergy
events.summary: Valerian's first edict (257) ordered clergy to sacrifice and banned Christian meetings and cemeteries; a second (258) ordered execution of bishops, priests and deacons and confiscated property of Christian senators and equestrians.
events.detail: Victims included Pope Sixtus II, beheaded with deacons in the catacomb of Callixtus on 6 August 258, the deacon Lawrence (later legend: the gridiron), and Cyprian of Carthage. Unlike Decius, Valerian targeted the Church's leadership and property, implying awareness of its institutional strength.

events.title: Martyrdom of Cyprian of Carthage
events.summary: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage, was beheaded at the villa Sexti outside Carthage before a large crowd after a trial before the proconsul Galerius Maximus, the first African bishop to be martyred.
events.detail: The Acta Proconsularia record his reply 'Deo gratias' to the sentence. His letters and treatises (De Unitate Ecclesiae, De Lapsis) are the most important sources for third-century church organisation and the plague and persecutions.

events.title: Battle of Mediolanum
events.summary: Gallienus defeated a vast Alamannic army (Zonaras says 300,000) near Milan with a force of 10,000, after the invaders had crossed the Alps and reached the outskirts of Rome, where the Senate armed the plebs.
events.detail: The invasion forced Gallienus to concentrate cavalry in northern Italy, often seen (with caution) as the origin of a mobile cavalry reserve under Aureolus based at Milan.

battle.significance: Saved Italy from the first major barbarian invasion since the Cimbri.

events.debate: Date 259 or 260; numbers absurd.

events.title: Battle at Augusta Vindelicum
events.summary: On 24-25 April 260 the Raetian governor Marcus Simplicinius Genialis, with soldiers and local levies, defeated Semnones or Juthungi returning from Italy laden with booty and freed 'many thousands of Italian captives', as recorded on a victory altar found in Augsburg in 1992.
events.detail: The altar is dated by the consuls of 260 'Postumus Augustus and Honoratianus', showing that Raetia had joined Postumus' Gallic Empire. It is a rare contemporary document of the invasions and of a provincial army acting without the emperor.

battle.significance: Epigraphic snapshot of invasion, captives and the Gallic secession.

scholarship: Bakker, 'Raetien unter Postumus', Germania 71 (1993)
Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome (2007)

events.title: Revolts of Ingenuus and Regalianus on the Danube
events.summary: Ingenuus, governor of Pannonia, was proclaimed emperor and defeated by Gallienus' cavalry commander Aureolus at Mursa; his successor as usurper, Regalianus, struck coins at Carnuntum before being killed after Sarmatian (Roxolani) attacks.
events.detail: Regalianus' coins, crude overstrikes on older denarii, include issues for his wife Sulpicia Dryantilla. Both revolts reflect frontier armies' demand for an emperor on the spot.
events.debate: Date 258 or 260 for Ingenuus.

events.title: Battle of Mursa (260)
events.summary: Gallienus and his cavalry commander Aureolus crushed the usurper Ingenuus near Mursa; Ingenuus was killed or drowned himself.

battle.significance: Early display of Gallienus' mobile cavalry.

events.title: Battle of Edessa and capture of Valerian
events.summary: Shapur I defeated Valerian between Carrhae and Edessa and captured him, the only Roman emperor ever taken prisoner by a foreign enemy, along with his praetorian prefect, senators and, by Shapur's count, an army of 70,000.
events.detail: Valerian's army was already weakened by plague. Roman sources suggest he was seized during negotiations; the ŠKZ says Shapur captured him 'with his own hands'. Valerian died in captivity; Christian writers (Lactantius) relished stories that Shapur used him as a mounting block and had his skin stuffed and hung in a temple. The reliefs at Naqsh-e Rustam and Bishapur show Shapur on horseback holding Valerian by the wrist while Philip kneels. Roman prisoners built the Band-e Kaisar dam at Shushtar. Shapur's army then ravaged Cilicia and Cappadocia before Odaenathus and Ballista harried it on its return.

battle.significance: Nadir of Roman prestige; precipitated the Gallic and Palmyrene secessions.

scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu (1991)
Potter, The Roman Empire at Bay (2014)
Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009)
events.debate: Circumstances (battle vs treacherous parley) and exact year (260, possibly 259) disputed.

events.title: Usurpation of the Macriani
events.summary: After Valerian's capture, his finance official Fulvius Macrianus and the prefect Ballista had Macrianus' sons Macrianus Minor and Quietus proclaimed emperors in the East; the Macriani invaded the Balkans in 261 and were destroyed by Aureolus, while Odaenathus of Palmyra killed Quietus and Ballista at Emesa.

events.title: Postumus founds the Gallic Empire
events.summary: Marcus Cassianius Latinius Postumus, commander on the Rhine, quarrelled with Gallienus' son Saloninus and his guardian Silvanus over booty, besieged them in Colonia Agrippinensis and had them killed; he then ruled Gaul, Germany, Britain, Spain and briefly Raetia for nine years.
events.detail: The Gallic Empire had its own consuls, praetorian guard and Senate (probably at Trier or Cologne) and never tried to march on Rome; Postumus presented himself as defender of the Rhine (coins: RESTITVTOR GALLIARVM, HERCVLI DEVSONIENSI). Drinkwater characterises it as a Roman regime born of regional needs rather than Gallic separatism. Gallienus' attempt to retake it c. 265 failed when he was wounded besieging Postumus.
scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)

events.title: Gallienus' rescript restoring Christian property
events.summary: Gallienus ended his father's persecution and restored churches and cemeteries to the bishops, effectively recognising the Church as a property-holding body; peace for Christians lasted until 303.
events.detail: Eusebius quotes Gallienus' rescript to Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria and others. The forty years of peace saw large churches built in cities like Nicomedia, opposite the imperial palace.

events.title: Odaenathus' counter-offensives against Persia
events.summary: Septimius Odaenathus of Palmyra, acting as Gallienus' commander in the East, recovered Mesopotamia including Carrhae and Nisibis and twice advanced to Ctesiphon (262 and c. 266), taking the title King of Kings while Gallienus called him 'corrector totius Orientis'.
events.detail: Odaenathus' mixed army of Palmyrene cataphracts and archers with Roman remnants restored Roman authority in the East without a Roman emperor present. Gallienus celebrated a Persian triumph and took the title Persicus Maximus. Palmyra's power, built on caravan trade, now became a quasi-dynastic regional monarchy, the base for Zenobia's later bid.
scholarship: Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Andrade, Zenobia: Shooting Star of Palmyra (2018)
events.debate: Number and dates of expeditions to Ctesiphon disputed; the official meaning of corrector totius Orientis is uncertain.

events.title: Gallienus excludes senators from military command
events.summary: Aurelius Victor reports that Gallienus forbade senators to serve in the army, after which legionary commands and most frontier governorships passed to equestrian professionals (praefecti legionis, praesides), many of them risen from the ranks.
events.detail: Epigraphy shows senatorial legionary legates disappearing in the 260s, confirming a real shift, though Victor's language of an edict may oversimplify a gradual process. Combined with the Danubian origins of the officer corps, this produced the soldier-emperors Claudius, Aurelian, Probus and Diocletian, and separated civil and military careers, a separation Diocletian and Constantine made systematic.
scholarship: De Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)
Christol, Essai sur l'évolution des carrières sénatoriales (1986)
events.debate: Whether there was a formal edict (Victor) or a de facto trend is disputed.

events.title: Herulian sack of Athens
events.summary: A great seaborne invasion of Heruli and Goths, reported as 500 ships, broke into the Aegean, sacking Byzantium's suburbs, Cyzicus, the islands, Corinth, Argos, Sparta and Athens; the Athenian historian Dexippus then led 2,000 men in guerrilla resistance from the olive groves.
events.detail: Destruction layers in the Athenian Agora and the construction of the 'Post-Herulian Wall' from spoliated monuments mark the event archaeologically. A Roman fleet under Cleodamus and Athenaeus engaged the invaders, and the speech attributed to Dexippus survives in fragments (FGrH 100 F 28) and the new Vienna palimpsests. The raiders then moved north into Thrace and Macedonia, where Gallienus met them at the Nestus.

sides.strength: part of a fleet of 500 ships (Syncellus)

battle.significance: Ended classical Athens' urban continuity; the Agora was abandoned behind a reduced circuit.

scholarship: Frantz, The Athenian Agora XXIV: Late Antiquity (1988)
Mallan and Davenport, 'Dexippus and the Gothic invasions', JRS 105 (2015)
events.debate: Date 267 or 268; Dexippus' own role probably self-glorifying.

events.title: Siege of Mediolanum and murder of Gallienus
events.summary: While besieging his rebellious cavalry commander Aureolus in Milan, Gallienus was lured from his tent at night by a false alarm and killed by a conspiracy of his officers, including Heraclianus, Marcianus and probably Claudius and Aurelian.
events.detail: Claudius was proclaimed and Aureolus, who surrendered, was killed. The Senate in Rome reacted by killing Gallienus' relatives and partisans until Claudius ordered his predecessor's deification to placate the army. Gallienus' reputation was blackened by senatorial tradition (the HA presents him as a frivolous aesthete), but modern scholars credit him with surviving fifteen years of simultaneous crises and with patronage of Plotinus and a Hellenic cultural revival.

battle.significance: Brought the 'Illyrian emperors' to power.

events.title: Battle of Lake Benacus
events.summary: Claudius II defeated the Alamanni, who had crossed into Italy during the siege of Milan, near Lake Garda; the Epitome claims half the enemy were killed.

battle.significance: Secured northern Italy for the new emperor.

events.title: Battle of the Nestus
events.summary: Gallienus defeated the Herulian raiders on the river Nestus in Thrace and accepted the surrender of their leader Naulobatus, who received consular insignia, an early example of enrolling a barbarian chief in Roman service.

battle.significance: Partially checked the great raid before Gallienus turned to deal with Aureolus.

events.debate: Date 267 or 268.

events.title: Battle of Naissus
events.summary: Claudius II crushed a huge Gothic army near Naissus in Moesia Superior, earning the title Gothicus Maximus; survivors were pursued through the Balkans, starved and dissolved by plague, and many captives were settled as farmers or enrolled in the army.
events.detail: The HA inflates the invaders to 320,000 men and 2,000 ships. Zosimus describes a battle where the Romans were initially driven back but then attacked the Goths from an unexpected route. Recent work on the Dexippus palimpsests has prompted some (e.g. Grusková, Martin) to redate parts of the sequence and to reattribute the victory to Gallienus in 268; the traditional attribution to Claudius in 269 remains the majority view.

sides.strength: imperial field army with Dalmatian cavalry

battle.significance: Broke the great Gothic invasions; the Goths made no major attack for half a century.

scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Mallan and Davenport, JRS 105 (2015)
events.debate: Date (268 or 269) and commander (Gallienus or Claudius) debated; HA figures are fiction.

events.title: Revolt of Laelianus and murder of Postumus
events.summary: Ulpius Cornelius Laelianus revolted at Mogontiacum; Postumus took the city but, forbidding his troops to sack it, was murdered by them. The soldier Marius ruled briefly before Victorinus took power.

events.title: Siege of Augustodunum
events.summary: Autun, capital of the Aedui, appealed to Claudius II and declared for the central empire; Victorinus besieged it for seven months and sacked it, a destruction still lamented by the orator Eumenius in a panegyric of 298.

battle.significance: Showed that Claudius would not intervene in Gaul.

events.title: Zenobia's forces take Egypt and Asia Minor
events.summary: Ruling for her son Vaballathus after Odaenathus' murder, Zenobia sent her general Zabdas with 70,000 men into Egypt, defeating the prefect Tenagino Probus, and pushed Palmyrene control through Asia Minor as far as Ancyra and the borders of Bithynia.
events.detail: Vaballathus' titles evolved from 'King of Kings and corrector totius Orientis' to Augustus in 272; Alexandrian coins dated by the regnal years of both Aurelian and Vaballathus suggest a period of uneasy co-rule. Zenobia's court attracted the rhetorician Cassius Longinus, and she claimed descent from Cleopatra. Whether she aimed at independence or at a share of the empire is still debated.
scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia (2018)
Hartmann, Das palmyrenische Teilreich (2001)
Southern, Empress Zenobia (2008)

events.title: Death of Claudius II; Quintillus and Aurelian
events.summary: Claudius II died of plague at Sirmium early in 270; his brother Quintillus was recognised by the Senate but abandoned by his troops within weeks, and the cavalry commander Aurelian took power.
events.detail: Claudius' reputation was later inflated by Constantinian propaganda, which invented his descent from Constantius I, and the HA life is a panegyric. Quintillus' reign may have lasted 17 days or several months.

events.title: Battle of Placentia
events.summary: Juthungi (or Alamanni and Marcomanni) invading Italy ambushed Aurelian's army in woods near Placentia and inflicted a severe defeat, causing panic in Rome.
events.detail: The defeat prompted the consultation of the Sibylline Books and the decision to wall Rome. Dexippus' fragment preserves negotiations in which Juthungian envoys demanded the subsidies they had formerly received.

battle.significance: Triggered the building of the Aurelian Walls.

events.debate: Identity of invaders (Juthungi, Alamanni, Marcomanni) and the date (270 or 271) debated.

events.title: Battle of Fanum Fortunae
events.summary: Aurelian defeated the invaders on the Metaurus near Fanum Fortunae, the river where Hasdrubal had died in 207 BC, as they marched along the Via Flaminia toward Rome.

battle.significance: Turned the invaders back from Rome.

events.title: Battle of Ticinum
events.summary: Aurelian annihilated the retreating invaders on the plain of Ticinum (Pavia), ending the threat to Italy.

battle.significance: Ended the last great barbarian invasion of Italy for over a century.

events.title: Revolt of the moneyers in Rome
events.summary: The workers of the Rome mint, led by the rationalis Felicissimus and facing exposure for embezzling silver, rose in revolt; Aurelian suppressed them in fighting on the Caelian hill in which, according to the sources, 7,000 soldiers died.
events.detail: The scale suggests that senatorial opponents and the urban plebs joined the moneyers. Aurelian closed the Rome mint temporarily and executed several senators. The episode was linked to the deeply debased antoninianus, which Aurelian set out to reform.

events.title: Construction of the Aurelian Walls
events.summary: Aurelian began a new circuit of brick-faced concrete walls around Rome, 19 km long, about 6-8 m high, with 381 towers and 18 main gates, finished under Probus; it was the first city wall built since the Republic and enclosed the whole fourteen-region city.
events.detail: Built largely by civic guilds rather than soldiers, the wall incorporated existing structures such as the Pyramid of Cestius, the Castra Praetoria and stretches of aqueduct. It was raised to double height under Maxentius and Honorius (c. 401-403). Its construction marks a psychological shift: Rome itself now needed defending, a sign, as many scholars note, of the inward turn of the late empire. Many Gallic, Spanish and Italian cities built reduced circuits from spolia in the same decades.
scholarship: Todd, The Walls of Rome (1978)
Dey, The Aurelian Wall and the Refashioning of Imperial Rome (2011)

events.title: Aurelian defeats the Goths beyond the Danube
events.summary: Marching east against Zenobia, Aurelian crossed the Danube and defeated a Gothic force, killing their leader Cannabaudes with 5,000 men, and took the title Gothicus Maximus.

battle.significance: Secured the lower Danube before the eastern campaign.

events.debate: Cannabaudes known only from the HA; some identify him with Cniva.

events.title: Abandonment of Trajanic Dacia
events.summary: Aurelian withdrew the army and administration from Trajan's province north of the Danube and created a new Dacia (later Dacia Ripensis and Dacia Mediterranea) south of the river, carved out of Moesia, with its capital at Serdica.
events.detail: Eutropius and the HA say he evacuated the Roman population too; archaeology shows considerable continuity of settlement and Christian finds north of the Danube, which feeds the long-running and politically charged debate between Romanian scholars (continuity of a Daco-Roman population) and Hungarian scholars (re-immigration from the south in the Middle Ages). Roman control of Dacia had already eroded under Gallienus, with coinage and inscriptions ending around 260. Legion XIII Gemina moved to Ratiaria and V Macedonica to Oescus.
events.locName: Dacia north of the Danube; new Dacia with capital Serdica
scholarship: Bichir, Archaeology and History of the Carpi (1976)
Ellis, 'Dacians, Sarmatians and Goths', in Shepherd and Mattingly (eds.) (1996)
events.debate: Date (271, 272-275, or gradually from Gallienus), the extent of evacuation and Daco-Roman continuity are disputed.

events.title: Aurelian takes Tyana
events.summary: Tyana in Cappadocia, held for Palmyra, was betrayed by a citizen named Heraclammon; Aurelian forbade a sack, saying he would leave 'not a dog alive' and then ordering the dogs killed instead, and the clemency induced other cities to surrender.
events.detail: The HA adds that the ghost of Apollonius of Tyana appeared to Aurelian to plead for his city, a story revealing the HA's interest in Apollonius. Aurelian executed the traitor.

battle.significance: Opened the Cilician Gates; clemency won over Asia Minor.

events.title: Battle of Immae
events.summary: Near Antioch, Aurelian's cavalry feigned flight before Zabdas' heavy-armoured Palmyrene cataphracts, wore them out in the heat and then turned and destroyed them.
events.detail: Zabdas retreated into Antioch and then slipped away by night after parading a lookalike of Aurelian in chains. Aurelian entered Antioch and won over the population with an amnesty.

sides.strength: Dalmatian and Moorish light cavalry and infantry

battle.significance: Broke Palmyrene power in Syria's north.

events.title: Battle of Emesa
events.summary: Zenobia and Zabdas made a stand with 70,000 men on the plain before Emesa; the Roman cavalry was routed by the cataphracts, but Aurelian's legionary infantry, including clubmen from Palestine, broke the Palmyrene line, and Zenobia fled to Palmyra.
events.detail: Aurelian attributed the victory to the sun god of Emesa, whom he believed had appeared to rally his troops, an episode tied to his later promotion of Sol Invictus in Rome.

sides.strength: field army incl. Palestinian clubmen, Moesian and Pannonian legions

battle.significance: Decisive defeat of the Palmyrene army.

events.title: Siege of Palmyra and capture of Zenobia
events.summary: Aurelian besieged Palmyra, harassed by desert Arabs; Zenobia tried to escape on a female camel to seek Persian help but was captured on the Euphrates, and the city surrendered.
events.detail: Zenobia was brought to Emesa for trial, where she blamed her advisers; the philosopher Longinus was executed. Her fate is variously told: paraded in Aurelian's triumph in golden chains and then pensioned at a villa at Tibur (HA), or dying en route (Zosimus). Shapur I had died around this time and no Persian help came.

battle.significance: Ended the Palmyrene Empire.

events.debate: HA letters between Aurelian and Zenobia are fabrications.

events.title: Aurelian decides the Paul of Samosata case
events.summary: Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, deposed by a synod in 268 for heresy (adoptionism) but kept in his church house under Palmyrene protection, was evicted when the Christians appealed to Aurelian, who ruled the building should go to those in communion with the bishops of Italy and Rome.
events.detail: The first known case of an emperor arbitrating a church dispute, a precedent for Constantine. Paul was accused of behaving like a ducenarius procurator, with a throne and choir of women singing his praises.

events.title: Second Palmyrene revolt and the sack of Palmyra
events.summary: Palmyra rose again under Septimius Antiochus, massacring its Roman garrison of 600 archers; Aurelian returned at speed, sacked the city and reduced it to a garrison town, ending its role in the caravan trade. A related rising in Egypt under Firmus was crushed.
events.detail: Diocletian later built a legionary camp (Legio I Illyricorum) on the site of the Temple of Allat. Aurelian restored the Temple of Bel, damaged in the sack, and used Palmyrene treasure for his temple of Sol.
events.debate: Firmus is known chiefly from the HA and his significance may be exaggerated.

events.title: Aurelian dedicates the temple of Sol Invictus
events.summary: Aurelian dedicated a great temple of the Sun on the Campus Agrippae in Rome, staffed it with a new college of pontifices Solis and instituted games (agon Solis) every four years; 25 December is attested in the Chronograph of 354 as the Natalis Invicti.
events.detail: Whether Aurelian himself fixed the festival on 25 December, and whether the Christian Christmas borrowed it or vice versa, is debated (Hijmans argues the 25 December Sol festival is not attested before 354). The Sol cult provided a unifying imperial religion that Constantine's early coinage continued until about 325.
scholarship: Hijmans, Sol: The Sun in the Art and Religions of Rome (2009)
Berrens, Sonnenkult und Kaisertum (2004)
events.debate: Date of the dedication and the relationship to Christmas are disputed.

events.title: Battle of Châlons (Catalaunian Fields)
events.summary: Aurelian defeated the army of the Gallic Empire at the Catalaunian Fields near Châlons-en-Champagne; the Gallic emperor Tetricus I, according to a widely repeated story, had secretly arranged to desert his own army, which fought on with heavy losses.
events.detail: Tetricus and his son walked in Aurelian's triumph and were then pardoned; Tetricus became corrector of Lucania. Gaul, Britain and Spain returned to the central empire after fourteen years. The carnage was remembered: Eutropius notes how heavily the Gallic legions suffered.

battle.significance: Reunified the empire.

events.debate: The tale of Tetricus' betrayal may be propaganda; date late winter/spring 274.

events.title: Aurelian's triumph as Restitutor Orbis
events.summary: Aurelian celebrated a spectacular triumph over Palmyra and Gaul, with Zenobia and Tetricus displayed among captives, and was hailed Restitutor Orbis ('restorer of the world').
events.detail: The HA's description (elephants, tigers, Goths, Alans, Franks, captured Amazons, Zenobia in golden chains) is embroidered but probably reflects a real show. Aurelian's coinage also introduced the title deus et dominus natus, a step toward the openly sacral monarchy of the Tetrarchs.

events.title: Aurelian's coin reform
events.summary: Aurelian reopened and reorganised the mints and issued a heavier radiate with a fixed silver content of about 5%, marked XXI or KA (in Greek), probably signifying 20 units of bronze to 1 of silver, together with a new aureus at 50 to the pound.
events.detail: The reform restored a measure of confidence and standardisation after the debasement nadir of 268-270 (when antoniniani contained around 1-2% silver), but prices in Egyptian papyri jumped sharply around 274-276, perhaps because the new coin was retariffed upward against older coin. Aurelian also standardised mint-marks and reorganised the mint network (Rome, Milan, Siscia, Serdica, Cyzicus, Antioch, Lugdunum, Tripolis). The meaning of XXI is one of the classic debates in Roman numismatics.
scholarship: Estiot, Ripostiglio della Venèra III (1995)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy 300 BC to AD 700 (1996)
Rathbone, 'Monetisation, not price-inflation, in third-century AD Egypt?' (1996)
events.debate: Meaning of XXI (1:20 alloy ratio vs value of 20 sestertii or 2 denarii) and the reform's effect on prices are disputed.

events.title: Assassination of Aurelian at Caenophrurium
events.summary: Marching against Persia, Aurelian was murdered at Caenophrurium in Thrace by officers duped by his secretary Eros, who forged a list of men marked for execution.
events.detail: An interregnum of several weeks followed (exaggerated by the HA into six months), after which the elderly Marcus Claudius Tacitus was chosen. The HA's story that the army deferred to the Senate is a senatorial fantasy.
events.debate: The HA's long interregnum is fictional.

events.title: Death of Mani in prison at Gundeshapur
events.summary: The prophet Mani, who had enjoyed Shapur I's patronage, was imprisoned by Bahram I under pressure from the Zoroastrian priest Kartir and died in chains at Bet Lapat (Gundeshapur) after 26 days.
events.detail: Manichaeism, a dualist synthesis of Christian, Zoroastrian and Buddhist elements, spread to Roman Egypt, Syria and North Africa (where Augustine was a hearer for nine years) and along the Silk Road to China. Kartir's inscriptions boast of persecuting Jews, Buddhists, Christians, Manichaeans and others. Diocletian's edict against the Manichaeans followed in 297 or 302.

events.title: Deaths of Tacitus and Florianus; Probus emperor
events.summary: Tacitus, after a campaign against Goths or Heruli in Asia Minor, died or was killed at Tyana in mid-276; his half-brother Florianus seized power but was killed by his own troops at Tarsus after a standoff with Probus, proclaimed by the eastern army.

events.title: Probus restores Gaul and the Rhine
events.summary: Probus drove Franks, Alamanni, Burgundians and Vandals out of Gaul, recovered (by his own count) 60 or 70 cities, crossed the Rhine, and settled tens of thousands of captives in the provinces.
events.detail: Zosimus tells of Frankish prisoners settled on the Black Sea who seized ships, raided Greece, Sicily (sacking Syracuse) and Africa, and sailed home through the Strait of Gibraltar. Probus is also credited with allowing vines to be planted in Gaul, Pannonia and Moesia, and using soldiers to plant vineyards near Sirmium.
events.debate: The campaign is not really part of the Gallic Empire war; listed here for the Rhine context. Numbers of cities are rhetorical.

events.title: Siege of Cremna: the Isaurian bandit Lydius
events.summary: The Isaurian brigand Lydius held the Pisidian hill city of Cremna against Probus' general Terentius Marcianus, expelling useless mouths and growing grain inside; he was killed by a disaffected artillerist, and excavation has revealed the Roman siege mound and the defenders' counter-wall.

battle.significance: Archaeologically documented Roman siege; shows endemic Isaurian banditry.

scholarship: Mitchell, Cremna in Pisidia (1995)

events.title: Blemmyes occupy Coptos and Ptolemais
events.summary: The Blemmyes, nomads of the Eastern Desert, seized Coptos and Ptolemais Hermiou in Upper Egypt; Probus' generals recovered them and Probus celebrated a triumph that included Blemmye captives.

events.title: Revolts of Saturninus, Proculus and Bonosus
events.summary: Probus faced the usurpation of Julius Saturninus in Syria or Egypt, and of Proculus at Lugdunum and Bonosus at Colonia Agrippinensis in the West; all were suppressed.
events.debate: The HA lives of these men are almost wholly fictional.

events.title: Murder of Probus at Sirmium
events.summary: Probus was killed by soldiers at Sirmium, allegedly resentful at being made to drain marshes and plant vines, after the praetorian prefect Marcus Aurelius Carus had been proclaimed emperor in Raetia.

events.title: Carus' Persian campaign and death
events.summary: Exploiting Sasanian dynastic strife under Bahram II, Carus invaded Mesopotamia with his son Numerian, took Seleucia and Ctesiphon, and died in his camp beyond the Tigris in July or August 283, reportedly struck by lightning.
events.detail: The lightning story was taken as a divine warning that no emperor should pass Ctesiphon, a superstition still current in Julian's time. Carus never consulted the Senate on his accession, a sign of the Senate's irrelevance; his sons Carinus (West) and Numerian (East) succeeded.
events.debate: Whether Carus died of illness, lightning or murder by the prefect Aper is uncertain.

events.title: Diocletian proclaimed emperor at Nicomedia
events.summary: After Numerian was found dead in his closed litter on the march back from Persia, the army near Nicomedia chose Diocles, commander of the protectores domestici, who personally ran through the praetorian prefect Arrius Aper before the assembled troops.
events.detail: Diocles, a Dalmatian of humble origin, took the name Gaius Aurelius Valerius Diocletianus. The HA preserves a story that a Druidess in Gaul had prophesied he would become emperor after killing a boar (aper). His accession, counted from 20 November 284, became the start of the 'Era of Diocletian' (Era of the Martyrs) used by Egyptian Christians and the Coptic calendar.
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Williams, Diocletian and the Roman Recovery (1985)
Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (2004)

events.title: Battle of the Margus
events.summary: Diocletian met Carinus, the legitimate western emperor, on the Margus (Morava) near its confluence with the Danube; Carinus' army was winning when he was murdered by one of his own officers, allegedly a tribune whose wife he had seduced, leaving Diocletian sole emperor.
events.detail: Diocletian retained Carinus' praetorian prefect Aristobulus and most officials, a conciliatory move that contrasted with earlier purges and helped consolidate the regime.
events.locName: River Margus near Margum, Moesia Superior

battle.significance: Last battle of the 'military anarchy'; Diocletian became sole ruler.

events.debate: Date spring or summer 285.

events.title: Maximian raised to Caesar and Augustus
events.summary: Diocletian appointed his fellow Pannonian officer Maximian as Caesar in 285 and as Augustus in 286, creating a dyarchy in which Diocletian took the name Jovius and Maximian Herculius, divine patronage expressing seniority.
events.detail: Maximian was sent to Gaul to suppress the Bagaudae and protect the Rhine, while Diocletian took the Danube and East. The Jovian/Herculian theology, celebrated in the panegyrics of 289 and 291, gave the new collegiate monarchy a sacral foundation independent of dynastic descent.
events.debate: Date of Maximian's elevation to Augustus (1 April 286 or later in 286) and whether he was ever Caesar debated.

events.title: Maximian suppresses the Bagaudae
events.summary: Maximian crushed the Bagaudae, bands of rural rebels in Gaul led by Aelianus and Amandus, who had taken advantage of the collapse of order.
events.detail: The Bagaudae reappear in Gaul and Spain in the fifth century. Older Marxist scholarship saw a peasant revolution; more recent work (Drinkwater) stresses local self-help, banditry and aristocratic leadership. Later tradition placed their stronghold at Saint-Maur-des-Fossés near Paris.
scholarship: Drinkwater, 'Patronage in Roman Gaul and the problem of the Bagaudae', in Wallace-Hadrill (ed.), Patronage in Ancient Society (1989)

events.title: Carausius seizes Britain
events.summary: Mausaeus Carausius, a Menapian commander of the Channel fleet based at Gesoriacum, accused of letting Frankish and Saxon pirates raid in order to seize their loot, was condemned by Maximian and proclaimed himself emperor in Britain and northern Gaul.
events.detail: Carausius' coinage was of unusually good silver and full of Virgilian allusions: RSR (Redeunt Saturnia Regna) and INPCDA (Iam nova progenies caelo demittitur alto), the most literary legends in Roman coinage. He also struck coins of 'Carausius et fratres sui', claiming collegiality with Diocletian and Maximian.
scholarship: Casey, Carausius and Allectus: The British Usurpers (1994)
de la Bédoyère, 'Carausius and the marks RSR and I.N.P.C.D.A.', NC 158 (1998)
events.debate: Date 286 or 287.

events.title: Maximian's failed naval expedition against Carausius
events.summary: A fleet built by Maximian to invade Britain in 289 failed, the panegyrist of 291 hinting at bad weather; for a few years Carausius was tolerated de facto.

events.title: Codex Gregorianus and Codex Hermogenianus
events.summary: The jurists Gregorius and Hermogenianus, working in Diocletian's chancery, compiled the first collections of imperial constitutions (mostly rescripts), the Gregorianus (c. 291-292, from Hadrian onward) and the Hermogenianus (c. 295, Diocletian's own rescripts of 293-294).
events.detail: These private but semi-official codes were the models for the Theodosian Code (438) and Justinian's Codex (529/534), into which much of their content passed. Diocletian's reign is the best-documented in rescripts of any emperor, over 1,200 surviving, reflecting the emperor's role as dispenser of law to ordinary petitioners, including women and slaves.
scholarship: Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (1996, rev. 2000)
Connolly, Lives Behind the Laws (2010)

events.title: Creation of the Tetrarchy
events.summary: On 1 March 293 Maximian appointed Constantius (Chlorus) as his Caesar at Milan and Diocletian appointed Galerius at Sirmium (or Nicomedia), creating a college of two Augusti and two Caesars bound by adoption and marriage.
events.detail: Constantius married Maximian's (step)daughter Theodora, setting aside Helena, mother of Constantine; Galerius married Diocletian's daughter Valeria. Each ruler had his own court, army and prefect, but laws were issued in all four names and the empire remained one. Capitals at Trier, Milan, Sirmium, Thessalonica, Antioch and Nicomedia replaced Rome as centres of government. The word 'Tetrarchy' is modern. Whether Diocletian planned it as a system (with automatic succession and retirement) from the start or improvised it is a central debate; Kolb sees a planned system, while Barnes, Rees and others see more ad hoc arrangements later systematised in Lactantius' narrative.
scholarship: Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Rees, Diocletian and the Tetrarchy (2004)
Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)
events.debate: Planned system or improvisation; place of Galerius' proclamation; whether the Caesars were appointed in 293 or earlier (Galerius possibly in 287 per some).

events.title: Siege of Gesoriacum
events.summary: Constantius, newly made Caesar, blockaded Carausius' continental base at Boulogne with a mole across the harbour mouth and forced its surrender, cutting the usurper off from Gaul.

battle.significance: Isolated Britain and precipitated Carausius' murder.

events.title: Carausius murdered by Allectus
events.summary: After the loss of Boulogne, Carausius was killed by his finance minister (rationalis) Allectus, who ruled Britain for three more years and built a large palace in London, perhaps the structure found under Cannon Street.

events.title: Diocletian's provincial reorganisation and the dioceses
events.summary: Diocletian roughly doubled the number of provinces from about 50 to about 100, separated civil governors from military commanders (duces), included Italy in the provincial system, and grouped provinces into twelve dioceses under vicarii responsible to the praetorian prefects.
events.detail: The Laterculus Veronensis (Verona List), a seventh-century copy of a list dated c. 303-314, gives the twelve dioceses: Oriens, Pontica, Asiana, Thraciae, Moesiae, Pannoniae, Britanniae, Galliae, Viennensis, Italia, Hispaniae and Africa. Smaller provinces made revolts harder and taxation more intrusive. Italy lost its fiscal privileges (except the suburbicarian region around Rome, whose status is debated), being divided into provinces under correctores. Recent work (Zuckerman) dates the dioceses to c. 313-314 under Constantine and Licinius rather than to Diocletian.
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982), ch. 12-13
Zuckerman, 'Sur la liste de Vérone et la province de Grande Arménie', TravMém 14 (2002)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964)
events.debate: The date of the dioceses (c. 297 vs c. 313-314) and the exact list of provinces are disputed.

events.title: Strata Diocletiana and the fortified eastern frontier
events.summary: Diocletian built or rebuilt a chain of forts along a military road from north-east Arabia through Damascus and Palmyra to Sura on the Euphrates, marked by milestones naming the Strata Diocletiana.
events.detail: The programme, along with new legions (by now smaller units of perhaps 1,000-2,000 men) and quadriburgia, reflects the tetrarchic investment in frontier defence that Zosimus contrasts with Constantine's withdrawal of troops into cities.
events.locName: Syrian desert from Bostra to Sura via Palmyra
scholarship: Bowersock, Roman Arabia (1983)
Parker, Romans and Saracens (1986)

events.title: Diocletian's currency reform
events.summary: Around 294 Diocletian created a unified empire-wide coinage: a gold aureus at 60 to the pound, a near-pure silver argenteus at 96 to the pound (reviving Neronian standards), and a large silver-washed bronze 'nummus' (modern 'follis') with the GENIO POPVLI ROMANI reverse, struck at mints marked in a uniform system.
events.detail: Local civic coinages in the East, including Alexandria's tetradrachms, ended (Alexandria by 296-297). The reform did not stop inflation, partly because the state paid and taxed in its own fiduciary coins while gold and silver were hoarded; the doubling of the face value of the nummus in September 301 (Aphrodisias currency edict) and the Price Edict of late 301 were responses.
events.locName: Imperial mints (about 15, from London to Alexandria)
scholarship: Sutherland, RIC VI (1967)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
events.debate: Exact date (293-296) and denominational values debated.

events.title: Galerius defeats the Carpi; mass resettlement
events.summary: After victories by Galerius, the Carpi of the eastern Carpathians were transplanted wholesale into the empire and settled in Pannonia, a large-scale deportation of the type the Tetrarchs used to repopulate land and supply recruits.
events.debate: Dates of the Carpic victories range 295-297 (Diocletian took Carpicus Maximus several times).

events.title: Diocletian's palace at Spalatum
events.summary: Diocletian built a fortified retirement palace near Salona on the Dalmatian coast, a 215 x 180 m enclosure combining fortress plan, residence, mausoleum (now Split cathedral) and temple (now baptistery), which became the nucleus of the city of Split.
events.detail: The peristyle with its arcuated colonnades and the palace's courtly architecture influenced late antique and Renaissance taste (Robert Adam's 1764 publication). Comparable tetrarchic palace-mausolea are Galerius' Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad) and the Thessalonica complex.
scholarship: Wilkes, Diocletian's Palace, Split (1986)

events.title: Constantius recovers Britain
events.summary: Constantius' praetorian prefect Asclepiodotus landed in fog, slipping past Allectus' fleet off the Isle of Wight, burned his boats and defeated and killed Allectus somewhere in southern Britain; Constantius' squadron reached London and saved it from Frankish mercenaries.
events.detail: The famous gold medallion from the Arras (Beaurains) hoard shows Constantius on horseback before a kneeling Londinium with the legend REDDITOR LVCIS AETERNAE ('restorer of the eternal light').

battle.significance: Ended the ten-year Britannic secession.

events.title: Battle of Callinicum (Galerius' defeat)
events.summary: Narseh, who had seized the Persian throne in 293, invaded Roman Armenia and Mesopotamia; Galerius, attacking with too small a force, was defeated between Callinicum and Carrhae.
events.detail: Ammianus and others tell that Diocletian, in his carriage at Antioch, made Galerius walk a mile in front of it in his purple, a humiliation that Galerius turned into a determination to win; the story's meaning (punishment or ceremonial) is debated.

battle.significance: Prompted the reinforcement of Galerius with Danubian troops for the decisive campaign of 298.

events.debate: Date 296 or 297.

events.title: Diocletian's new tax system (capitatio-iugatio and the indiction)
events.summary: An edict of the prefect of Egypt Aristius Optatus dated 16 March 297 announces a new empire-wide assessment of land (iuga) and people (capita) to calculate annual requisitions in kind, set in a regular budget, the indiction.
events.detail: The system rationalised the improvised levies (annona) of the third century into a predictable annual tax, eventually reassessed on a fifteen-year indiction cycle that became a standard dating system into the Middle Ages (first cycle counted from 312). Assessment units varied regionally (iugum in Syria, millena in Italy, centuria in Africa). Lactantius' complaint that there were more tax collectors than taxpayers reflects the expanded bureaucracy, perhaps 30,000 officials in the fourth century.
scholarship: Carrié, 'Dioclétien et la fiscalité', AnTard 2 (1994)
Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
events.debate: Whether capitatio and iugatio were separate or merged taxes, and how uniform the system was, remain debated.

events.title: Revolt of Domitius Domitianus and siege of Alexandria
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Domitianus, with his corrector Aurelius Achilleus, revolted in Egypt in 297, perhaps provoked by the new tax census; Diocletian came in person, besieged Alexandria for eight months, cut the aqueducts, and after its fall vowed to kill until the blood reached his horse's knees.
events.detail: According to the legend, his horse stumbled at the city gate, staining its knees, and the grateful Alexandrians set up a statue of the horse. The tall column known as 'Pompey's Pillar' was erected in honour of Diocletian around 298, probably for his provision of grain to the city. Busiris and Coptos, which had joined the revolt, were razed.

battle.significance: Ended the last major revolt of Roman Egypt; followed by Diocletian's reorganisation of Egypt into separate provinces.

events.debate: Relationship of Domitianus and Achilleus (same revolt, successive leaders) and chronology (297-298) disputed.

events.title: Diocletian withdraws from the Dodecaschoenus
events.summary: Visiting Upper Egypt, Diocletian withdrew the frontier from the Dodecaschoenus to Philae and the First Cataract, settling Nobatae in the evacuated zone as a buffer against the Blemmyes and paying both peoples annual subsidies.
events.detail: Procopius records the arrangement, including shared temples at Philae for the Isis cult, which continued until Justinian closed them c. 537.

events.title: Galerius' victory in Armenia
events.summary: With a new army of Danubian veterans, Galerius advanced through Armenia, personally reconnoitred the Persian camp and fell on Narseh by surprise, routing his army and capturing his treasury, harem, wife Arsane and children.
events.detail: Galerius' arch at Thessalonica depicts the battle, including a duel-like encounter between Galerius and Narseh. Galerius then advanced down the Tigris through Media and Adiabene and possibly took Ctesiphon. The captured royal women became the key bargaining chip in the peace of 299.
events.locName: Armenia, probably between Satala and Erzurum

battle.significance: Greatest Roman victory over the Sasanians before Heraclius.

scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)
Dodgeon and Lieu (1991)
events.debate: Site unknown; 'Satala' is a convenient modern label. Date 298 (some 297).

events.title: Battles of Lingones and Vindonissa
events.summary: Constantius, nearly captured and hauled over the walls of Lingones (Langres) by a rope, defeated the Alamanni outside the city the same day, killing 60,000 according to Eutropius, and won a second victory near Vindonissa.

battle.significance: Secured the upper Rhine for a generation.

events.debate: Date 298 or 302.

events.title: Baths of Diocletian in Rome
events.summary: Maximian began, in Diocletian's name, the largest baths ever built in Rome, covering 13 hectares on the Viminal, dedicated 305-306; Michelangelo converted the frigidarium into the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli.

events.title: Peace of Nisibis
events.summary: Diocletian's envoy Sicorius Probus imposed terms on Narseh: Persia ceded five regions beyond the Tigris (Arzanene, Moxoene, Zabdicene, Rehimene and Corduene), recognised Roman control of Armenia (border at Zintha) and Iberia, and accepted Nisibis as the sole point of trade exchange.
events.detail: Peter the Patrician, our main source, preserves the negotiations: the Persian envoy Apharban called Rome and Persia the two eyes of the world. The treaty gave Rome its best eastern frontier ever and forty years of peace, until Shapur II reopened war. Jovian's surrender of the Transtigritane regions and Nisibis in 363 reversed it.
scholarship: Blockley, 'The Romano-Persian peace treaties of AD 299 and 363', Florilegium 6 (1984)
Winter, Die sasanidisch-römischen Friedensverträge des 3. Jahrhunderts n. Chr. (1988)
events.debate: The list of five regions differs between Peter and Ammianus; date 298 or 299.

events.title: Currency edict of 301 (Aphrodisias)
events.summary: An edict, known from an inscription at Aphrodisias and effective 1 September 301, retariffed the coinage, apparently doubling the face value of the nummus and the argenteus, a revaluation that preceded the Price Edict by three months.
events.debate: Exact values in the damaged text are disputed.

events.title: Edict on Maximum Prices
events.summary: Issued between 20 November and 9 December 301 in the names of all four Tetrarchs, the Edictum de pretiis rerum venalium fixed maximum prices and wages for over 1,200 goods and services, from wheat and wine to lion skins, freight charges and a lawyer's fee, on pain of death.
events.detail: Its preamble denounces the 'unbridled greed' of profiteers who follow the armies. Known from over 130 fragments of inscriptions, mostly from the Greek East (Aphrodisias, Stratonicea, Tegea and elsewhere), with prices in 'denarii communes'. Examples: a modius castrensis of wheat 100 denarii; farm labourer 25 denarii a day with keep; a pound of purple silk 150,000. Lactantius says it caused goods to disappear from markets and much bloodshed, and was soon abandoned. Modern historians value it as the single richest economic document from antiquity, while debating whether its figures reflect real prices.
events.locName: Issued probably from Nicomedia; copies across the eastern provinces

sources.w: Edictum Diocletiani de pretiis rerum venalium

scholarship: Lauffer, Diokletians Preisedikt (1971)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)
Crawford and Reynolds, 'The Aphrodisias copy of Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices', ZPE 26 (1977)
events.debate: Whether the edict was ever seriously enforced, and whether it was applied in the West, are disputed; Lactantius is hostile.

events.title: Conversion of Armenia under Tiridates III
events.summary: King Tiridates III of Armenia, restored by Rome, accepted Christianity through the preaching of Gregory the Illuminator, who was consecrated bishop at Caesarea in Cappadocia; Armenia claims to be the first Christian kingdom.
events.detail: Armenian tradition (Agathangelos) dates the conversion to 301, after Gregory's thirteen years in a pit at Khor Virap and the king's transformation into a boar. Most modern scholars prefer c. 314, after the Edict of Milan and Galerius' and Maximinus' persecutions, which Eusebius says included a war by Maximinus against Christian Armenians.
scholarship: Garsoïan, in Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times I (1997)
events.debate: Date 301 (tradition) vs c. 314 (most scholars).

events.title: Diocletian's edict against the Manichaeans
events.summary: Diocletian ordered the leaders of the Manichaeans burned with their books and their followers executed or sent to the mines, condemning the sect as a Persian import that corrupted the 'modest and tranquil Roman people'.
events.locName: Rescript to the proconsul of Africa
events.debate: Date 297 or 302 depends on the identification of the proconsul Julianus and Diocletian's itinerary.

events.title: The Great Persecution begins
events.summary: On the feast of the Terminalia, 23 February 303, soldiers demolished the church of Nicomedia, visible from the palace; the next day an edict ordered churches destroyed, scriptures surrendered and burned, Christian meetings banned and Christians of rank stripped of privileges.
events.detail: Three further edicts followed: arrest of clergy, release of clergy who sacrificed, and (spring 304) a general order for all to sacrifice. Lactantius blames Galerius and an oracle of Apollo at Didyma for the decision. Enforcement varied enormously: Constantius in Gaul and Britain went no further than pulling down some churches, while the East under Galerius and Maximinus Daia suffered persecution until 311 and, intermittently, 313. Eusebius' Martyrs of Palestine counts some 90 executions there. The surrender of scriptures created the 'traditores' problem that split the African church into Donatists and Catholics.
scholarship: de Ste. Croix, 'Aspects of the Great Persecution', HTR 47 (1954)
Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Corcoran, 'Before Constantine', in Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006/2012)
events.debate: Lactantius and Eusebius are partisan Christian sources writing after the persecutors' defeat; Galerius' role may be exaggerated to exculpate Diocletian or vice versa. Numbers of martyrs are uncertain.

events.title: Diocletian's vicennalia in Rome
events.summary: Diocletian visited Rome, probably for the only time, to celebrate his twentieth anniversary and a joint triumph with Maximian; the Decennalia base of the Tetrarchs in the Forum survives. Irritated by Roman freedom of speech, he left in December before taking up his consulship.

events.title: Abdication of Diocletian and Maximian
events.summary: On 1 May 305 Diocletian at Nicomedia and Maximian at Milan simultaneously abdicated; Constantius and Galerius became Augusti, and the new Caesars were Galerius' protégés Severus and Maximinus Daia, passing over Constantine and Maxentius, the sons of emperors.
events.detail: Lactantius describes the assembled army at Nicomedia expecting Constantine to be named and being astonished when Galerius pushed forward Maximinus. Diocletian retired to Spalatum to grow cabbages (as he later told Maximian, who urged him to resume power in 308). The voluntary abdication of a Roman emperor was unprecedented; the exclusion of dynastic heirs proved fatal to the system within eighteen months.
events.locName: Hill three miles from Nicomedia; Mediolanum

events.title: Synod of Elvira
events.summary: Nineteen Spanish bishops, including Ossius of Corduba, met at Iliberris (Granada) and issued 81 canons, the earliest surviving disciplinary code of a church council, including clerical celibacy, bans on images painted on church walls and on marriage of Christian girls to Jews or pagans.

sources.w: Canons of the Council of Elvira

events.debate: Date anywhere from c. 295 to 314; the canon collection may be a later compilation (Meigne, Vilella).

events.title: Constantine proclaimed at Eboracum
events.summary: Constantius I died at York after a campaign against the Picts, and his army, prompted by the Alamannic king Crocus, proclaimed his son Constantine Augustus; Galerius grudgingly recognised him as Caesar.
events.detail: Constantine had escaped Galerius' court in 305, reportedly hamstringing the post-horses behind him. His accession broke the tetrarchic principle of merit-appointment in favour of heredity and began the dynasty that ruled until 363.

events.title: Maxentius seizes Rome
events.summary: Angered by Galerius' plan to extend the census and taxation to the city of Rome and to abolish the Praetorian Guard, the Praetorians and people proclaimed Maximian's son Maxentius princeps, and Maximian came out of retirement to support him.
events.detail: Maxentius styled himself 'conservator urbis suae' and lavished building on Rome: the Basilica Nova, the rebuilt Temple of Venus and Roma, and the villa, circus and mausoleum on the Via Appia.

events.title: Severus' invasion of Italy and death
events.summary: Severus, sent by Galerius against Maxentius, advanced on Rome but his troops, many of them former soldiers of Maximian, deserted; he fled to Ravenna, surrendered on promise of his life, and was later killed or forced to suicide at Tres Tabernae.

events.title: Galerius' failed invasion of Italy
events.summary: Galerius marched on Rome in summer 307 but, finding the city too large and well defended to besiege and his troops wavering, retreated, allowing his army to plunder Italy on the way.

events.title: Constantine marries Fausta and is made Augustus by Maximian
events.summary: At Trier, Maximian gave his daughter Fausta to Constantine in marriage and named him Augustus, an alliance celebrated in a panegyric (Pan. Lat. 7(6)) that describes a painting of the betrothal at Aquileia.

events.title: Conference of Carnuntum
events.summary: Galerius summoned Diocletian from retirement to Carnuntum; Maximian was forced to abdicate again, Licinius was made Augustus of the West directly, Constantine was demoted to Caesar, and Maxentius was declared a public enemy.
events.detail: Diocletian refused to resume power, replying that if Maximian could see the cabbages he grew at Salona he would never urge it. An altar to Mithras 'fautor imperii sui' dedicated by the emperors at Carnuntum survives. The settlement failed at once: Maximinus Daia and Constantine both claimed the Augustan title in 309-310.

events.title: Revolt of Domitius Alexander in Africa
events.summary: Lucius Domitius Alexander, vicarius of Africa, rebelled against Maxentius, cutting Rome's grain supply; Maxentius' praetorian prefect Rufius Volusianus crushed him around 310 and sacked Carthage and Cirta.
events.detail: Cirta was rebuilt by Constantine and renamed Constantina (Constantine, Algeria). The famine in Rome during the revolt weakened Maxentius' popularity.

events.title: Basilica Nova of Maxentius
events.summary: Maxentius built the vast Basilica Nova on the Velia with three cross-vaulted bays over a 25 m-wide nave, the last great vaulted civic building of pagan Rome, completed by Constantine, who placed his colossal seated statue (whose head and hand survive in the Capitoline Museums) in a new apse.

events.title: Constantine introduces the solidus
events.summary: Around 309-310, at the Trier mint, Constantine began striking a lighter gold coin at 72 to the Roman pound (c. 4.5 g), the solidus, which became the stable standard of the late Roman and Byzantine world for some 700 years.
events.detail: Funded partly by confiscated temple treasures after 324, the solidus circulated in large volumes and taxes were increasingly commuted into gold (adaeratio), creating, in Jairus Banaji's analysis, a gold-based aristocracy and a deep divide between gold-holders and those paid in debased bronze. Its fineness was maintained until the eleventh century, earning it the nickname 'dollar of the Middle Ages'.
scholarship: Banaji, Agrarian Change in Late Antiquity (2001)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)
Bruun, RIC VII (1966)
events.debate: Date (309 or 310) and whether introduced initially only in Constantine's territories (extended east after 324).

events.title: Revolt and death of Maximian at Massilia
events.summary: Living at Constantine's court, Maximian proclaimed himself emperor again at Arles while Constantine was on the Rhine; Constantine marched south, besieged him in Massilia and Maximian was forced to hang himself.
events.detail: Lactantius adds a second plot in which Maximian tried to murder Constantine in bed and killed a eunuch substitute. Constantine then abandoned his Herculian descent and claimed descent from Claudius II, announced in the panegyric of 310.

events.title: Constantine's 'pagan vision' at Grand
events.summary: The panegyrist of 310 describes Constantine visiting a temple of Apollo (probably at Grand in the Vosges), where he saw Apollo with Victory offering him laurel wreaths each bearing the sign XXX, foretelling a thirty-year reign.
events.detail: Peter Weiss argued that what Constantine actually saw was a solar halo phenomenon, later reinterpreted as the Christian vision reported by Eusebius; others keep the 310 and 312 visions distinct. Constantine's coinage honoured Sol Invictus as 'comes' until the early 320s.
scholarship: Weiss, 'The vision of Constantine', JRA 16 (2003)
Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power (2011)
events.debate: Identification of the temple; relation to the later Christian vision.

events.title: Galerius' edict of toleration and death
events.summary: Dying of a horrible disease (Lactantius describes his body consumed by worms), Galerius issued an edict, posted at Nicomedia on 30 April 311, ending the persecution and permitting Christians to 'exist again and hold their meetings' on condition they pray to their god for the emperors' safety; he died days later.
events.detail: The edict acknowledges failure: many Christians had neither returned to the gods nor worshipped their own god. Maximinus Daia complied only briefly and resumed persecution in late 311 with petitions from cities requesting the expulsion of Christians (an inscription from Arycanda survives).
events.debate: Lactantius' gloating account of Galerius' illness is a stock 'death of the persecutor' motif.

events.title: Outbreak of the Donatist schism
events.summary: The consecration of Caecilian as bishop of Carthage by Felix of Abthugni, accused of being a traditor in the persecution, was rejected by Numidian bishops, who elected Majorinus and then Donatus; the African church split into two hierarchies for over a century.
events.detail: The dissidents appealed to Constantine in 313, prompting the Council of Rome (313) and Council of Arles (314), both of which upheld Caecilian. Constantine's attempt at coercion (317-321) failed and he conceded toleration. The Donatists, rigorist and rooted in Numidia, saw themselves as the church of martyrs; violent rural partisans, the Circumcellions, later attached themselves to the movement. The schism lasted until the conference of Carthage in 411 and beyond.
scholarship: Frend, The Donatist Church (1952)
Shaw, Sacred Violence (2011)
events.debate: Date of Caecilian's election (307/8 or 311/312) disputed.

events.title: Constantine's vision and the Christian sign
events.summary: Before the battle against Maxentius, Constantine was, according to Lactantius, told in a dream to mark 'the heavenly sign of God' on his soldiers' shields; Eusebius, writing after Constantine's death and claiming the emperor's own sworn account, describes a cross of light in the sky with the words 'by this conquer' (touto nika) followed by a dream and the making of the labarum.
events.detail: The two Christian accounts differ in timing, content and the sign (a staurogram or chi-rho). Neither panegyrist of 313 nor of 321 mentions Christ. Modern explanations range from a genuine religious experience to a solar halo seen in 310 and reinterpreted (Weiss), to retrospective propaganda. What is not in doubt is that from 312 Constantine favoured the Church: restitution of property, exemption of clergy from curial duties (313), grants to bishops and building the Lateran basilica. The chi-rho appears on Constantine's helmet on a silver medallion from Ticinum of c. 315.
scholarship: Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power (2011)
Weiss, JRA 16 (2003)
Van Dam, Remembering Constantine at the Milvian Bridge (2011)
Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006/2012)
events.debate: Lactantius and Eusebius are partisan; their versions are inconsistent. The sincerity and timing of Constantine's conversion are among the most contested questions in Roman history.

events.title: Battle of the Milvian Bridge
events.summary: On the sixth anniversary of his accession, Maxentius left the Aurelian Walls, crossed the Tiber on a pontoon bridge beside the cut Milvian Bridge and drew up with the river at his back near Saxa Rubra; Constantine's cavalry routed his wings, the army collapsed toward the river, the pontoon gave way and Maxentius drowned.
events.detail: Lactantius says Maxentius had consulted the Sibylline Books, which foretold that 'the enemy of the Romans' would die that day. His body was recovered and his head paraded through Rome on a spear and sent to Africa. The Praetorians, who had fought hardest, were disbanded and their camp demolished. Constantine entered Rome on 29 October but, notably, apparently did not climb the Capitol to sacrifice to Jupiter (a much-debated silence). The Senate voted him the senior Augustan title and an arch. The battle became the founding myth of Christian empire.
events.locName: Milvian Bridge and Saxa Rubra, north of Rome

sides.strength: c. 40,000 (modern estimate); Zosimus claims 90,000 foot, 8,000 horse
Zosimus claims 170,000 foot, 18,000 horse (impossible); Praetorians, Italian and African troops

battle.significance: Gave Constantine the West and Rome; traditionally the turning point toward a Christian empire.

scholarship: Van Dam, Remembering Constantine at the Milvian Bridge (2011)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)
events.debate: Zosimus' numbers are fantastical; the precise topography (Saxa Rubra vs the bridge itself) and the Sibylline story are uncertain. Eusebius compares the drowning to Pharaoh in the Red Sea.

events.title: Battle of Turin
events.summary: After storming Segusio at the foot of the Alps, Constantine met Maxentius' heavily armoured cavalry (clibanarii) on the plain west of Turin; his men opened ranks and clubbed the armoured riders down with iron-bound maces, and Turin shut its gates on the fleeing Maxentians.

sides.strength: perhaps 40,000 (panegyric of 313 says under a quarter of his army, c. 25,000-40,000)

battle.significance: Opened the Po valley; Milan welcomed Constantine.

events.title: Siege and battle of Verona
events.summary: Constantine besieged Verona, held by Maxentius' praetorian prefect Ruricius Pompeianus, who broke out to bring a relief army; Constantine defeated and killed him in a night battle, after which Verona and Aquileia surrendered.
events.detail: The panegyrist of 313 records that Constantine fought in person and was rebuked by his officers for risking himself, and that the captured Maxentian soldiers were chained with fetters made from their own swords.

battle.significance: Destroyed Maxentius' northern army, leaving Rome exposed.

events.title: Abolition of the Praetorian Guard
events.summary: Constantine dissolved the Praetorian cohorts and the equites singulares Augusti, who had fought for Maxentius, demolished the internal walls of the Castra Praetoria, and replaced them with the new scholae palatinae, cavalry guard regiments attached to the emperor's person.
events.detail: The equites singulares' cemetery on the Via Labicana was built over by the basilica of Saints Marcellinus and Peter and the mausoleum of Helena, and their barracks on the Caelian by the Lateran basilica, a pointed reuse of the losers' property for Christian building.

events.title: Foundation of the Lateran Basilica
events.summary: Constantine gave the bishop of Rome the Lateran property and built the Basilica Constantiniana (later St John Lateran) over the barracks of the disbanded horse guard, a five-aisled basilica about 100 m long, the first great church of Rome and cathedral of its bishop.
events.detail: The Liber Pontificalis lists its endowments of gold and silver fittings and estates. Constantine's churches in Rome were placed mostly on imperial land at the edges of the city (Lateran, St Peter's on the Vatican, St Paul's, the cemetery basilicas), leaving the monumental core to its traditional cults.
scholarship: Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City (1980)
Krautheimer, Three Christian Capitals (1983)

events.title: Constantine's military reorganisation
events.summary: Constantine developed a permanent mobile field army (comitatenses) separate from the frontier forces (ripenses, later limitanei), created the commands of magister peditum and magister equitum, and stripped the praetorian prefects of military authority, turning them into the highest civil officials.
events.detail: Zosimus accuses Constantine of withdrawing troops from the frontiers into cities, softening them and exposing the borders. Modern scholars (Jones, Elton, Southern and Dixon) see the field army as an outgrowth of tetrarchic comitatus forces and Gallienus' cavalry, and doubt Zosimus' moralising. Germanic recruitment into the army and officer corps grew, and the new auxilia palatina units (Cornuti, Brachiati) took names and shield designs recorded in the Notitia Dignitatum.
scholarship: Jones, The Later Roman Empire (1964)
Elton, Warfare in Roman Europe AD 350-425 (1996)
Southern and Dixon, The Late Roman Army (1996)
events.debate: Dating of the comitatenses/limitanei division and Zosimus' hostile interpretation.

events.title: The 'Edict of Milan'
events.summary: Meeting at Milan in February 313, where Licinius married Constantine's half-sister Constantia, the two Augusti agreed on a policy of religious freedom for all and restoration of confiscated church property; the text survives as a letter issued by Licinius at Nicomedia on 13 June 313.
events.detail: The document grants 'to Christians and to all others free power to follow the religion each one wishes, so that whatever divinity there is in the heavenly seat may be favourable to us'. Strictly it was not an edict and not issued at Milan; Lactantius gives the Latin text and Eusebius a Greek translation. It ended persecution in the East and established the principle of state restitution to the churches as corporate bodies.
events.debate: Its legal form (edict, rescript, letter) and whether Constantine had already issued a similar measure in the West are debated.

events.title: Battle of Tzirallum (Campus Ergenus)
events.summary: Maximinus Daia crossed into Europe and took Byzantium and Heraclea, but Licinius, with about 30,000 men against 70,000, defeated him on the Campus Ergenus near Tzirallum; Lactantius says an angel dictated a prayer to Licinius that his soldiers recited before battle.

battle.significance: Left the empire divided between two Augusti, Constantine and Licinius.

events.debate: Lactantius' numbers and angelic prayer are part of his providential narrative.

events.title: Death of Maximinus Daia at Tarsus
events.summary: Fleeing to Asia Minor, Maximinus issued his own toleration edict and died at Tarsus in summer 313, of poison or disease; Licinius then killed his family and the families of Galerius, Severus and Diocletian, including Diocletian's widow Prisca and daughter Valeria.

events.title: Council of Arles
