events.summary: Constantine summoned bishops from across the West, including three from Britain (York, London and probably Lincoln), to Arles to judge the Donatist appeal; they upheld Caecilian and issued canons, including one threatening excommunication for soldiers who threw down their arms in peacetime.
events.detail: The first council called by an emperor, it set the pattern for Nicaea. The British bishops' signatures are the earliest firm evidence for an organised church in Britain.

sources.w: Canons of the Council of Arles (314)

events.title: Arch of Constantine dedicated
events.summary: For his decennalia in 315 the Senate dedicated a triple arch beside the Colosseum, celebrating victory over the 'tyrant' Maxentius; it reused reliefs from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius with heads recut as Constantine, together with a contemporary frieze of the campaign of 312.
events.detail: Its inscription attributes the victory to 'instinctu divinitatis' (by the prompting of the divinity), a famously ambiguous phrase acceptable to pagans and Christians. The stylistic contrast between the second-century spolia and the squat Constantinian frieze is a textbook case in debates about 'decline' versus deliberate late antique aesthetics.
scholarship: Elsner, 'From the culture of spolia to the cult of relics', PBSR 68 (2000)

events.title: Battle of Cibalae
events.summary: In the first war between Constantine and Licinius, Constantine with 20,000 men defeated Licinius' 35,000 in a day-long battle in the narrow ground between a hill and a marsh near Cibalae in Pannonia; Licinius retreated to Sirmium and then Thrace.
events.detail: The war began after a failed plan to make Bassianus, husband of Constantine's half-sister Anastasia, Caesar of a buffer zone in Italy and Illyricum. Licinius raised his officer Valens as co-Augustus.

battle.significance: Constantine gained the initiative in the Balkans.

events.debate: Date 316 (now standard) vs older 314.

events.title: Battle of Mardia
events.summary: Constantine and Licinius fought an indecisive battle at Campus Mardiensis in Thrace in late 316 or early 317; the peace concluded at Serdica gave Constantine all the Balkans except Thrace (the dioceses of Pannonia and Moesia).
events.detail: Licinius' co-emperor Valens was deposed and executed as part of the settlement.

battle.significance: Led to a negotiated peace and redistribution of the Balkans.

events.title: Crispus, Constantine II and Licinius II made Caesars
events.summary: At Serdica on 1 March 317 Constantine's sons Crispus (about 12-17) and the infant Constantine II and Licinius' infant son Licinius II were proclaimed Caesars, sealing the peace and establishing hereditary succession for both houses.

events.title: Arius and the beginning of the Arian controversy
events.summary: Arius, presbyter of the Baucalis church in Alexandria, taught that the Son was created by the Father and that 'there was when he was not'; Bishop Alexander condemned him at a synod of about 100 Egyptian bishops, but Arius found support from Eusebius of Nicomedia and other Lucianist bishops in the East.
events.detail: Arius set his teaching to popular songs (the Thalia), sung by sailors and millers. The dispute fused theology with rivalries between sees (Alexandria, Nicomedia, Antioch) and quickly became an imperial problem when Constantine gained the East in 324. 'Arianism' is a polemical label: many later 'Arians' had little to do with Arius, and modern scholars (Hanson, Williams, Ayres) prefer to speak of a fourth-century debate about the Trinity.
scholarship: Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988)
Williams, Arius: Heresy and Tradition (1987/2001)
Ayres, Nicaea and its Legacy (2004)
events.debate: Start date 318 or 320/321.

events.title: Old St Peter's Basilica begun
events.summary: Constantine built a vast five-aisled basilica over the reputed tomb of the apostle Peter on the Vatican hill, levelling part of the hillside and burying a pagan necropolis to centre the building on the second-century aedicula.
events.detail: Excavations under the Vatican in 1940-1949 exposed the necropolis and the 'Tropaion of Gaius'. The basilica, about 120 m long, was a funerary hall and martyrium rather than a cathedral and stood until its demolition from 1506.
events.debate: Start date (c. 319-322 or after 324) debated.

events.title: Constantine's law on the 'venerable day of the Sun'
events.summary: Constantine ordered that magistrates, city people and craftsmen rest on the 'venerable day of the Sun' (dies Solis), while allowing farmers to work; a July 321 law permitted manumissions and emancipations on that day.
events.detail: The religiously neutral language (Sun, not Lord's day) suited both Christians and solar worshippers, and the law founded the Western legal tradition of Sunday rest.

events.title: Battle of the Hellespont
events.summary: Crispus with Constantine's fleet of 200 smaller warships defeated Licinius' admiral Abantus (Amandus) with 350 triremes in the Hellespont over two days, a storm on the second day wrecking much of the enemy fleet.
events.detail: The victory broke the blockade of the straits and allowed Constantine to supply the siege of Byzantium and ferry his army to Asia. It was the last major naval battle in the Mediterranean between Roman fleets until the fifth century.

battle.significance: Opened the straits; prerequisite for Chrysopolis.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople (324)
events.summary: Constantine, now openly fighting under the labarum, crossed the Hebrus with a small detachment upstream and fell on Licinius' fortified camp near Adrianople, winning a major victory; Licinius retreated to Byzantium.
events.detail: Zosimus gives Licinius 150,000 foot and 15,000 horse against Constantine's 120,000 foot and 10,000 horse, figures much inflated. Constantine was wounded in the thigh. Eusebius presents the war as a crusade against Licinius' renewed harassment of Christians.

battle.significance: Drove Licinius out of Thrace.

events.title: Battle of Chrysopolis
events.summary: Constantine crossed the Bosporus and crushed Licinius' army, reinforced by Gothic auxiliaries under Alica, at Chrysopolis opposite Byzantium; Licinius fled to Nicomedia and surrendered on the plea of his wife Constantia.
events.detail: Licinius had proclaimed his magister officiorum Martinianus co-emperor. The victory reunited the empire under one ruler for the first time since 285; within weeks, on 8 November 324, Constantine marked out the new city on the site of Byzantium.

sides.losses: very heavy; Zosimus says scarcely 30,000 of 130,000 escaped (exaggerated)

battle.significance: Made Constantine sole emperor; led to the foundation of Constantinople.

events.title: Foundation of Constantinople
events.summary: On 8 November 324 Constantine traced the boundary of a greatly enlarged city on the site of Byzantium, about four times its former size, as his eponymous residence and 'New Rome'.
events.detail: The site commanded the Bosporus crossing between the Danube and Euphrates fronts. Philostorgius tells that Constantine walked the line with spear in hand and, asked how far he would go, replied 'until he who walks ahead of me stops'. Construction drew on spolia from across the East: the Serpent Column from Delphi, statues for the Baths of Zeuxippus, and a porphyry column in the oval Forum of Constantine topped by a statue of the emperor as Sol or Apollo. Whether Constantine intended a new capital, a Christian city, or another tetrarchic residence is debated; the city received a Senate (of lower rank until Constantius II) and free grain dole (80,000 rations) from 332.
scholarship: Dagron, Naissance d'une capitale (1974)
Krautheimer, Three Christian Capitals (1983)
Bassett, The Urban Image of Late Antique Constantinople (2004)
events.debate: Date of foundation 324 (standard) and the city's original character (Christian or not) disputed.

events.title: First Council of Nicaea
events.summary: Constantine convened some 250-300 bishops (later tradition: 318) at Nicaea in Bithynia, opening the council in person in the imperial palace; it condemned Arius, adopted a creed declaring the Son 'homoousios' (of the same substance) with the Father, set rules for the date of Easter and issued twenty canons.
events.detail: Only two bishops, Secundus of Ptolemais and Theonas of Marmarica, refused to sign and were exiled with Arius; Eusebius of Nicomedia signed but balked at the anathemas. Ossius of Corduba probably presided. The canons regulated the ranks of Alexandria, Rome and Antioch (canon 6), honour for Jerusalem (7), readmission of Novatianists (8) and banned self-castrated clergy (1). The term homoousios, probably suggested by Ossius or the emperor himself, later became the rallying point of Nicene orthodoxy, but in 325 it was a compromise and its acceptance lasted only a few years. Eusebius of Caesarea, a participant, wrote a letter to his church explaining why he signed.
scholarship: Ayres, Nicaea and its Legacy (2004)
Hanson, The Search for the Christian Doctrine of God (1988)
Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
events.debate: Number of bishops, president, and the significance of homoousios at the time are debated; Athanasius' later accounts are partisan.

events.title: Execution of Licinius at Thessalonica
events.summary: Spared at first and sent to Thessalonica, Licinius was executed in spring 325, accused of plotting with barbarians; his son Licinius II was killed in 326.

events.title: Execution of Crispus and death of Fausta
events.summary: In 326 Constantine had his eldest son Crispus, Caesar and victor of the Hellespont, executed at Pola in Istria; shortly afterwards the empress Fausta died, reportedly suffocated in an overheated bath.
events.detail: No contemporary source explains why. Later writers (Zosimus, Zonaras) tell of Fausta falsely accusing Crispus of seducing her, a Phaedra story; others suggest adultery between them, or Fausta's attempt to secure the succession for her own sons. Both were subjected to damnatio memoriae. Zosimus claims Constantine's guilt drove him to Christianity, a pagan polemic Sozomen explicitly refutes.
scholarship: Woods, 'On the death of the empress Fausta', G&R 45 (1998)
Barnes, Constantine (2011)
events.debate: Motive unknown; Woods suggests Fausta died from a botched abortion in a hot bath.

events.title: Helena's pilgrimage and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre
events.summary: Constantine ordered Bishop Macarius to demolish the Hadrianic temple over the supposed tomb of Christ in Jerusalem and build a basilica; his mother Helena toured the Holy Land in 326-328 founding churches at Bethlehem and on the Mount of Olives. The Holy Sepulchre was dedicated in September 335.
events.detail: The legend of Helena finding the True Cross is first attested in Ambrose's funeral oration for Theodosius (395), not in Eusebius. Constantine's building programme created the Christian Holy Land and the practice of pilgrimage (the Bordeaux Pilgrim's itinerary of 333 survives).
scholarship: Hunt, Holy Land Pilgrimage in the Later Roman Empire (1982)
Drijvers, Helena Augusta (1992)

events.title: Confiscation of temple treasures and the chrysargyron
events.summary: After 324 Constantine's agents stripped temples of gold and silver, bronze doors and cult statues, funding the new gold coinage and Constantinople, and he introduced the collatio lustralis (chrysargyron), a tax on merchants and craftsmen paid every five years, and the collatio glebalis on senators.
events.detail: The anonymous author of De Rebus Bellicis links the temple gold to the debasement of social values, saying it swelled the houses of the powerful while the poor suffered. Libanius and Zosimus attack the chrysargyron as falling cruelly on the poor; it was abolished by Anastasius in 498.

events.title: Constantine's Danube bridge at Oescus
events.summary: Constantine opened a bridge of about 2.4 km across the Danube between Oescus and Sucidava, the longest bridge of the ancient world, reasserting Roman power north of the river in the old Dacian lands.

events.title: Dedication of Constantinople
events.summary: On 11 May 330 the new city was formally dedicated with forty days of celebrations; the anniversary was marked annually in the Hippodrome by a procession of a gilded statue of Constantine holding a figure of the city's Tyche.
events.detail: Later legend added that the Palladium of Rome was buried under the porphyry column, with Christian relics. The dedication has traditionally been taken as the birth of the Byzantine Empire, although contemporaries saw the city as an imperial residence within a single Roman empire. Constantinople had perhaps 30,000-90,000 inhabitants by 337 and some 300,000-400,000 by 500.

events.title: Constantine's Gothic war and treaty
events.summary: Intervening for the Sarmatians against the Tervingi, Constantine's son Constantine II won a great victory on 20 April 332, said to have killed 100,000 Goths through hunger and cold; the ensuing treaty made the Tervingi allies who supplied troops in return for subsidies and trading rights.
events.detail: The treaty, whose exact terms are disputed (whether the Goths became foederati in the later sense), kept the lower Danube quiet for a generation and fostered Gothic Christianisation and Romanisation; the son of the Gothic king Ariaric was sent as a hostage to Constantinople.
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
events.debate: Nature of the foedus of 332 (equal alliance or subjection) is debated.

events.title: Constantine's law on fugitive coloni
events.summary: A law of 30 October 332 ordered that a colonus found on another's land be returned to the estate of his origin, and permitted fugitive coloni to be chained like slaves, a key text in the history of the 'tied colonate'.
events.detail: Older scholarship saw the beginning of serfdom here. Since the 1980s (Carrié, Sirks, Grey) the colonate has been reinterpreted as a fiscal device for registering tax liability rather than a uniform legal status binding peasants to the soil.
scholarship: Carrié, 'Le colonat du Bas-Empire: un mythe historiographique?', Opus 1 (1982)
Grey, 'Contextualizing colonatus', JRS 97 (2007)
Sirks, 'The colonate in Justinian's reign', JRS 98 (2008)
events.debate: Meaning of the colonate (proto-serfdom vs fiscal registration).

events.title: Settlement of 300,000 Sarmatians
events.summary: When the Sarmatian 'Argaragantes' were overthrown by their armed slaves (the Limigantes), Constantine received more than 300,000 Sarmatian refugees and distributed them across Thrace, Scythia, Macedonia and Italy.
events.debate: The figure of 300,000 is suspect.

events.title: Council of Tyre and the first exile of Athanasius
events.summary: A council at Tyre, dominated by Eusebius of Nicomedia's allies, tried Athanasius of Alexandria on charges including violence against Melitian clergy, the breaking of a chalice and the murder of Bishop Arsenius (who was produced alive); Athanasius fled to Constantinople and Constantine exiled him to Trier after he was accused of threatening the Alexandrian grain fleet.
events.detail: Athanasius would be exiled five times under four emperors (335-337, 339-346, 356-362, 362-363, 365-366), and his polemical writings shaped the later picture of an 'Arian' conspiracy.
scholarship: Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)

events.title: Death of Arius at Constantinople
events.summary: On the eve of his planned readmission to communion at Constantinople, Arius died suddenly in a public latrine; his opponents (Athanasius, Socrates) saw divine judgement, comparing his end to Judas' bursting asunder.

sources.w: Epistula ad Serapionem de morte Arii

events.debate: Poisoning has been suspected; the account is polemical.

events.title: Baptism and death of Constantine
events.summary: Preparing a war against Shapur II, Constantine fell ill, was baptised by Eusebius of Nicomedia at the villa of Achyron near Nicomedia, and died at Pentecost, 22 May 337, aged about 65; he was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople amid cenotaphs of the twelve apostles.
events.detail: Deathbed baptism was common for those holding power that involved bloodshed. Constantine was deified by the Roman Senate as divus with a coin showing him ascending to heaven in a chariot, while the Church called him isapostolos, 'equal to the apostles'. No successor was named Augustus for over three months, during which a purge of the family took place.

events.title: Massacre of the Constantinian princes
events.summary: In the summer of 337 the army at Constantinople murdered Constantine's half-brothers Julius Constantius and Flavius Dalmatius, his nephews the Caesar Dalmatius and Hannibalianus ('King of Kings and of the Pontic peoples'), the patrician Optatus and the prefect Ablabius, leaving only Constantine's three sons and two small boys, Gallus and Julian.
events.detail: The soldiers claimed they would accept only Constantine's sons. Julian later blamed Constantius II directly; Eusebius and Christian writers present it as the army's spontaneous will. On 9 September 337 Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans were proclaimed Augusti, and in 338 they met in Pannonia (Viminacium) to divide the empire: Constantine II the West beyond the Alps, Constans Italy, Africa and Illyricum, Constantius the East.
scholarship: Burgess, 'The summer of blood: the Great Massacre of 337', DOP 62 (2008)
events.debate: Constantius II's degree of responsibility is debated; Burgess argues he organised it.

events.title: First siege of Nisibis by Shapur II
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis for some 63 or 70 days; the city held, its defence later credited by Syriac tradition to the prayers of Bishop Jacob of Nisibis, who reportedly sent a plague of gnats against the Persian elephants.
events.detail: The Syriac poet Ephrem, a deacon of Nisibis, wrote hymns (Carmina Nisibena) on the three sieges. Jacob's role and the gnats belong to hagiography; the siege date may be 337 or 338.

battle.significance: Opened 25 years of Persian attempts on Roman Mesopotamia.

events.title: Constantine II killed invading Italy
events.summary: Constantine II, claiming seniority and resentful of his share, invaded Constans' territory and was ambushed and killed near Aquileia (at the river Alsa) in spring 340; Constans took over the whole West.

events.title: Ulfilas consecrated bishop of the Goths
events.summary: Ulfilas (Wulfila), a Goth descended from Cappadocian captives of the 250s raids, was consecrated 'bishop of the Christians in the Getic land' by Eusebius of Nicomedia, probably at the Dedication Council of Antioch; he devised a Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible, omitting, it was said, the Books of Kings as too warlike.
events.detail: Expelled in a persecution by the Tervingian leadership around 347-348, he settled with his flock near Nicopolis ad Istrum. His Homoian theology made 'Arian' Christianity the faith of the Goths, Vandals and other Germanic peoples, a confessional divide with Nicene Romans that shaped the post-Roman kingdoms. The Codex Argenteus in Uppsala preserves much of his Gospel text.
scholarship: Heather and Matthews, The Goths in the Fourth Century (1991)
events.debate: Date 336 or 341.

events.title: Constans' winter crossing to Britain
events.summary: Constans crossed the Channel from Boulogne in midwinter 343, an unusual feat celebrated by Firmicus Maternus, apparently to deal with trouble on the northern frontier involving the areani (frontier scouts) or with Picts and Scots.

events.title: Council of Serdica
events.summary: Called by Constans and Constantius to settle the Athanasian dispute, the council split on arrival: about 90 western bishops under Ossius met in Serdica, restored Athanasius and Marcellus of Ancyra and gave the bishop of Rome a right to hear appeals, while some 80 eastern bishops withdrew to Philippopolis and excommunicated Julius of Rome and Ossius.
events.detail: The schism of East and West over doctrine and authority, preceded by the eastern Dedication Council of Antioch (341) with its four creeds, made the Trinitarian question a lever in relations between the imperial brothers; Constans threatened war to restore Athanasius, who returned to Alexandria in 346.
scholarship: Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)
events.debate: Date 342 or 343.

events.title: Shapur II's persecution of Christians
events.summary: Shapur II imposed a double tax on Christians and, when Catholicos Simeon bar Sabba'e of Seleucia-Ctesiphon refused to collect it, had him executed with many clergy at Karka d-Ledan, beginning a 'Great Persecution' in Persia that lasted intermittently until Shapur's death in 379.
events.detail: Persian Christians were suspected as a fifth column after Constantine's conversion and his letter to Shapur claiming protection of them. The Syriac Acts of the Persian Martyrs record thousands of victims, a number modern scholars treat with caution.

sources.w: Acts of the Persian Martyrs (Martyrdom of Simeon)

scholarship: Smith, Constantine and the Captive Christians of Persia (2016)
events.debate: Date 339, 341 or 344 for Simeon's death.

events.title: Night battle of Singara
events.summary: Constantius II's army stormed Shapur's camp near Singara and appeared victorious, but in the disordered night fighting the Persians counterattacked and inflicted heavy losses; Shapur's heir Narseh was captured and killed.
events.detail: Julian's panegyric presents it as a Roman victory spoiled by indiscipline; Festus and Ammianus' allusions treat it as a defeat. Ammianus says Constantius fought nine major battles against Persia without a decisive success.

battle.significance: Bloodiest battle of Constantius' Persian war; neither side gained ground.

events.debate: Date 344 or 348; outcome disputed.

events.title: Usurpation of Magnentius and death of Constans
events.summary: At a birthday banquet at Augustodunum, the comes Flavius Magnentius, of part-Frankish or British origin, appeared in purple and was acclaimed emperor by officers alienated from the unpopular Constans, who fled and was killed by Gaiso near Helena (Elne) in the Pyrenees.
events.detail: Magnentius, though probably pagan-tolerant, used the chi-rho as a large reverse type on his bronzes (with alpha and omega), possibly the first use of a Christian symbol as the sole design of a coin. He controlled Gaul, Britain, Spain, Africa and Italy.

events.title: Third siege of Nisibis
events.summary: Shapur II besieged Nisibis for about four months (his second attempt had failed in 346), damming the Mygdonius river and releasing the floodwater against the walls, which partly collapsed; the defenders under Lucillianus built a new wall behind the breach overnight and repelled the attack with Persian elephants bogged in mud.
events.detail: Ephrem and Julian's panegyric describe the flooding vividly. News of nomad attacks on his eastern frontier forced Shapur to withdraw, freeing Constantius to march west against Magnentius.

sides.strength: royal army with elephants and Indian contingents

battle.significance: Nisibis' successful defence preserved Roman Mesopotamia until 363.

events.title: Vetranio and Nepotianus
events.summary: On 1 March 350 the old general Vetranio was proclaimed in Illyricum, apparently at the instigation of Constantina, sister of Constantius, to block Magnentius; in June Constantine's nephew Nepotianus seized Rome with gladiators for 28 days before Magnentius' officer Marcellinus killed him and massacred his supporters. Vetranio abdicated before Constantius' army at Naissus on 25 December 350 and retired to Prusa.

events.title: Battle of Mursa
events.summary: Constantius II defeated Magnentius on the Drava near Mursa in one of the bloodiest battles in Roman history: Zonaras reports 30,000 of Constantius' 80,000 and 24,000 of Magnentius' 36,000 killed. Constantius' heavily armoured cavalry (cataphracts and clibanarii) turned Magnentius' left.
events.detail: Eutropius judged that the losses weakened Roman manpower for foreign wars; Constantius spent the battle in a martyr's shrine with the Homoian bishop Valens of Mursa, who announced victory as revealed by an angel. Magnentius fled to Aquileia and then Gaul. The general Silvanus defected with his troops to Constantius before the battle.

battle.significance: Decided the civil war; remembered as a catastrophic bleeding of Roman military manpower.

events.debate: Casualty figures from Zonaras are probably exaggerated.

events.title: Battle of Mons Seleucus and death of Magnentius
events.summary: After Constantius forced the Alpine passes, Magnentius was defeated at Mons Seleucus in the Cottian Alps; abandoned by his troops, he killed his family and committed suicide at Lugdunum on 10 August 353, and his brother Decentius hanged himself at Senones.
events.detail: Constantius' notary Paulus 'Catena' ('the Chain') then conducted savage treason trials in Britain, described by Ammianus.

battle.significance: Left Constantius sole emperor.

events.title: The Chronograph of 354
events.summary: The calligrapher Furius Dionysius Filocalus produced an illustrated almanac for a wealthy Christian Roman, Valentinus, combining the pagan festival calendar, consular fasti, a list of popes, the earliest list of Christian feasts (Depositio Martyrum, including 25 December as Christ's birth), a city chronicle and the regionary catalogue of Rome.
events.detail: It illustrates the easy coexistence of pagan and Christian culture among the Roman elite in the mid-fourth century and is a fundamental source for chronology and topography.
scholarship: Salzman, On Roman Time (1990)
Burgess, 'The Chronograph of 354', JLA 6 (2013)

events.title: Execution of the Caesar Gallus
events.summary: Constantius Gallus, Caesar at Antioch since 351, ruled by terror (Ammianus' extant narrative opens with his excesses, including a lynching of the governor of Syria during a famine); summoned west, he was arrested and beheaded near Pola.

events.title: Usurpation of Silvanus at Cologne
events.summary: Silvanus, Frankish magister militum in Gaul, framed by a forged letter at court, proclaimed himself emperor at Cologne; after 28 days he was murdered in a chapel by soldiers suborned by Ursicinus, whose staff included Ammianus Marcellinus.
events.detail: Ammianus, an eyewitness participant, gives the court intrigue in detail. The Franks then sacked Cologne in the confusion.

events.title: Julian made Caesar and sent to Gaul
events.summary: Constantius summoned his last male relative, the philosophy student Julian, from Athens, married him to his sister Helena and proclaimed him Caesar at Milan, sending him to Gaul with a small force and close supervision.
events.detail: Ammianus records Julian muttering a line of Homer about 'purple death' as he was robed. Julian had been secretly initiated into Neoplatonic theurgy by Maximus of Ephesus around 351.

events.title: Constantius II visits Rome
events.summary: Constantius entered Rome on 28 April 357 for his vicennalia in a triumphal adventus, motionless in his carriage 'as if a statue'; he admired the Forum of Trajan, erected the obelisk of Thutmose III (now the Lateran obelisk) in the Circus Maximus and removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house.
events.detail: Ammianus' description is a classic set-piece of late Roman imperial ceremony and of senatorial Rome's self-image.

events.title: Battle of Argentoratum (Strasbourg)
events.summary: Julian, with 13,000 men, defeated an Alamannic coalition of seven kings under Chnodomar, perhaps 35,000 strong, near Strasbourg; 243 Romans and 4 tribunes fell against some 6,000 Alamanni killed on the field and many more drowned in the Rhine. Chnodomar was captured.
events.detail: Ammianus' account, the most detailed of any late Roman battle, describes the Roman cavalry breaking before the Alamannic infantry until Julian rallied them in person, and the Batavi and Reges and the Cornuti and Bracchiati units holding the line with the barritus war cry. The army acclaimed Julian Augustus on the field, which he refused. The victory secured the Rhine and made Julian's reputation.

sides.losses: 6,000 killed on the field, many more drowned

battle.significance: The most complete late Roman battle narrative; restored the Rhine frontier.

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome (2007)
Elton, Warfare in Roman Europe (1996)
events.debate: Ammianus, an admirer of Julian, may minimise Roman losses and inflate enemy numbers.

events.title: Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia and the Homoian creed
events.summary: Constantius convened twin councils, some 400 western bishops at Ariminum and about 160 eastern at Seleucia in Isauria; under pressure, both accepted a creed saying the Son was 'like (homoios) the Father according to the Scriptures', banning the term ousia. A council at Constantinople ratified it in January 360.
events.detail: Jerome's famous line, 'the whole world groaned and was astonished to find itself Arian', refers to this settlement. The Homoian creed, preceded by the 'Blasphemy of Sirmium' of 357, was the official faith of the eastern empire until 378 and of Ulfilas' Goths.

events.title: Siege of Amida
events.summary: Shapur II, invading with allied Chionites under King Grumbates and guided by the Roman defector Antoninus, besieged Amida for 73 days; Ammianus Marcellinus, inside the city, describes the death of Grumbates' son before the walls, siege towers, sallies by Gallic legionaries, plague and the final storming via a collapsed siege mound.
events.detail: Seven legions and other troops were trapped in the city; the garrison commander Aelianus and tribunes were crucified, and Ammianus escaped through a postern by night. The delay cost Shapur the campaigning season. Ammianus' account (books 18-19) is one of the great eyewitness siege narratives of antiquity.

sides.strength: royal army with Chionite, Albanian and Segestani allies and elephants
seven legions and citizens, c. 20,000 in the city (Ammianus)
sides.losses: city stormed; garrison killed or captured

battle.significance: Persian victory, but costly delay that saved the rest of Mesopotamia that year.

scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)
Kelly, Ammianus Marcellinus: The Allusive Historian (2008)

events.title: Julian proclaimed Augustus at Paris
events.summary: Ordered to send his best auxiliary units east for the Persian war, Julian's troops at Lutetia, many recruited on the promise of never serving beyond the Alps, mutinied and raised him on a shield as Augustus, crowning him with a soldier's torque in place of a diadem.
events.detail: Julian claimed he had been forced. Negotiations with Constantius failed, and in 361 Julian marched east down the Danube with remarkable speed, his men sailing from Raetia to Sirmium, while Constantius moved west from Antioch. Aquileia held out for Constantius.

events.title: Siege of Singara
events.summary: Shapur took Singara with a ram that broke a newly repaired stretch of wall, deporting its garrison, legions I Flavia and I Parthica, and the inhabitants to Persia.

sides.strength: legions I Flavia and I Parthica, cavalry and citizens

battle.significance: Loss of a key Roman base in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Sieges of Bezabde
events.summary: Shapur stormed Bezabde on the Tigris, defended by three legions (II Flavia, II Armeniaca and II Parthica), and garrisoned it; Constantius' autumn counter-siege failed in the rains.

battle.significance: Persia gained a bridgehead in the Transtigritane regions ceded in 299.

events.title: Death of Constantius II at Mopsucrenae
events.summary: Marching against Julian, Constantius died of fever at Mopsucrenae in Cilicia aged 44, reportedly naming Julian his successor on his deathbed after being baptised by the Homoian bishop Euzoius; civil war was averted.

events.title: Julian's restoration of paganism
events.summary: Sole emperor from December 361, Julian reopened temples and restored sacrifices, recalled exiled bishops of all factions (to let Christians quarrel, Ammianus says), purged the palace staff, and tried to create a pagan priestly hierarchy imitating Christian charity.
events.detail: His edict of 17 June 362 required teachers to be approved by city councils, and a circular explained that Christians could not honestly teach Homer and Hesiod while despising their gods; Ammianus, a pagan admirer, condemned it as harsh, 'to be buried in eternal silence'. Julian wrote treatises Against the Galilaeans and hymns to King Helios and the Mother of the Gods. Christian sources (Gregory of Nazianzus' invectives) cast him as 'the Apostate'.
scholarship: Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978)
Smith, Julian's Gods (1995)
Teitler, The Last Pagan Emperor (2017)

events.title: Julian at Antioch: the Daphne fire and the Misopogon
events.summary: Wintering at Antioch, Julian alienated the Christian and pleasure-loving city with his sacrifices, his beard and price controls during a grain shortage; when the temple of Apollo at Daphne burned on 22 October 362, he blamed Christians and closed the cathedral. Lampooned by the Antiochenes, he replied with the satirical Misopogon ('Beard-Hater').
events.detail: Julian had ordered the removal of the relics of the martyr Babylas from Apollo's sanctuary, and the fire followed the translation of the relics.

events.title: Siege of Maiozamalcha
events.summary: Marching down the Euphrates, Julian took the fortress-town of Pirisabora and then stormed Maiozamalcha near Ctesiphon by mining under the walls, Roman soldiers emerging inside a house while the defenders watched the assault on the walls.

battle.significance: Cleared the approach to Ctesiphon.

events.title: Battle of Ctesiphon (363)
events.summary: Julian's army made a night crossing of the Tigris under fire and defeated the Persian army under the Surena before the walls of Ctesiphon, killing 2,500 for about 70 Roman losses (Ammianus); but Julian judged the city too strong to besiege.
events.detail: Julian then burned his river fleet of over 1,000 ships, so that the 20,000 men needed to haul it upstream could fight, and struck inland toward the Persian interior hoping to meet Procopius' northern army, a decision Ammianus and later writers regarded as fatal.

battle.significance: Tactical victory that brought no strategic result.

events.title: Battle near Samarra and death of Julian
events.summary: Retreating north up the Tigris under constant Persian harassment, Julian rushed into a skirmish without his breastplate and was struck by a cavalry spear that pierced his liver; he died that night in his tent, discussing the soul with the philosophers Maximus and Priscus.
events.detail: The killer was never identified: Libanius suggested a Christian Roman soldier, while Persian and other sources credit a Persian or Saracen. The Christian legend has Julian cry 'You have won, Galilean'. His death left the army stranded deep in enemy territory; the next day the officers chose Jovian, a Christian guards officer.
events.locName: Near Samarra (Toummara/Maranga region), on the Tigris

sides.losses: significant, incl. generals Merena and Nohodares (Ammianus)

battle.significance: Death of the last pagan emperor; ended the Constantinian dynasty and forced the peace of 363.

events.debate: Identity of the killer; site of the battle.

events.title: Jovian's peace with Shapur II
events.summary: Trapped without supplies near Dura on the Tigris, Jovian accepted a thirty-year peace ceding five Transtigritane regions, Nisibis, Singara and Castra Maurorum, and abandoning Rome's alliance with Armenia; the citizens of Nisibis were evacuated, weeping, to Amida.
events.detail: Ammianus, who marched in the retreat, calls it a shameful peace without precedent in Roman history. Ephrem the Syrian left Nisibis for Edessa. The treaty created the frontier that lasted, with modifications, until the sixth century, and exposed Armenia to Persian conquest.
scholarship: Blockley, Florilegium 6 (1984)
Lightfoot, 'Facts and fiction: the third siege of Nisibis', Historia 37 (1988)

events.title: Julian's attempt to rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem
events.summary: Julian ordered the Jewish Temple rebuilt under the supervision of Alypius of Antioch, to falsify Christian prophecy; Ammianus reports that 'fearful balls of fire' burst from the foundations, burning workmen, and the project was abandoned, probably also because of the earthquake of 19 May 363 and Julian's death.
events.debate: Cause of the fires (gas in cisterns, earthquake, miracle in Christian accounts).

events.title: Death of Jovian at Dadastana
events.summary: Jovian died on his way to Constantinople at Dadastana on the Bithynian-Galatian border, apparently from charcoal fumes from a brazier in a freshly plastered bedroom, after a reign of eight months in which he restored Christian privileges.

events.title: Valentinian I and Valens become emperors
events.summary: The army at Nicaea chose Valentinian, a Pannonian guards officer, as emperor on 26 February 364; on 28 March at the Hebdomon outside Constantinople he made his younger brother Valens co-Augustus, and at Mediana near Naissus they divided the court, army and empire, Valentinian taking the West and Valens the East.
events.detail: The division of army units and officials between the brothers, recorded by Ammianus, anticipated the permanent split of 395 and gave many units paired seniores and iuniores names in the Notitia Dignitatum. Valentinian's court was based mainly at Trier and Milan, Valens' at Constantinople, Antioch and Marcianople.
scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire: Valens and the Roman State in the Fourth Century AD (2002)

events.title: The Cretan earthquake and tsunami
events.summary: A massive earthquake off western Crete, estimated at magnitude 8 or more, uplifted the western end of the island by up to 9 m and sent a tsunami across the eastern Mediterranean; Ammianus describes the sea withdrawing at Alexandria and ships being hurled onto rooftops.
events.detail: The anniversary was commemorated at Alexandria as a 'day of horror' into the sixth century. Geological evidence of the uplift is visible on the Cretan coast; destruction across Crete, Cyprus, Sicily and Libya was later conflated in literary sources.
events.locName: Off western Crete; tsunami at Alexandria and across the eastern Mediterranean
scholarship: Kelly, 'Ammianus and the great tsunami', JRS 94 (2004)
Shaw et al., 'Eastern Mediterranean tectonics and tsunami hazard inferred from the AD 365 earthquake', Nature Geoscience 1 (2008)

events.title: Revolt of Procopius
events.summary: Procopius, a maternal relative of Julian rumoured to have been designated his successor, emerged from hiding and was proclaimed emperor in Constantinople while Valens was away; he won over units passing through Thrace by displaying Constantius II's widow Faustina and her infant daughter, last of the Constantinian line.
events.detail: He gained Thrace, Bithynia and support from the Gothic Tervingi, who sent 3,000 men; this later gave Valens his pretext for the Gothic war of 367.

events.title: Damasus and Ursinus: the papal election riots
events.summary: After the death of Pope Liberius, rival factions elected Ursinus and Damasus as bishop of Rome; in the fighting, Damasus' supporters stormed the basilica of Sicininus and, Ammianus reports, 137 corpses were found there in a single day.
events.detail: Ammianus observes drily that the wealth of the Roman see, its gifts from matrons and its bishops riding in carriages and dining better than kings made the office worth killing for. Damasus prevailed with the support of the urban prefect, and went on to promote the cult of martyrs with verse inscriptions carved by Filocalus.

events.title: Battles of Thyatira and Nacolia
events.summary: Valens defeated Procopius' general Gomoarius at Thyatira in Lydia, and in May 366 at Nacolia in Phrygia Procopius' remaining troops deserted after his commander Agilo defected; Procopius was betrayed and beheaded on 27 May 366.

sides.strength: Thracian and palatine units, Gothic auxiliaries

battle.significance: Ended the last Constantinian bid for power.

events.title: Gratian proclaimed Augustus at Ambiani
events.summary: After a serious illness, Valentinian raised his eight-year-old son Gratian directly to Augustus (not Caesar) before the army at Ambiani (Amiens), securing the dynasty; the poet Ausonius became his tutor.

events.title: The 'Barbarian Conspiracy' in Britain
events.summary: In 367 Picts, Attacotti and Scotti attacked Britain while Franks and Saxons raided Gaul; the count of the Saxon Shore Nectaridus was killed and the dux Fullofaudes ambushed. Valentinian sent Count Theodosius (the Elder), who recovered London and restored order in 368-369.
events.detail: Ammianus calls it a 'barbarica conspiratio'; the frontier scouts (areani) were accused of collusion and disbanded. A province, Valentia, was created or renamed. The scale of the crisis is debated: some archaeologists see little destruction, but signal stations on the Yorkshire coast may date from the restoration.
scholarship: Esmonde Cleary, The Ending of Roman Britain (1989)
events.debate: Whether it was a coordinated 'conspiracy' and how much damage it caused.

events.title: Battle of Solicinium
events.summary: Valentinian and Gratian led a punitive expedition across the Rhine after the Alamanni sacked Mogontiacum during a Christian festival; the Alamanni held a steep hill at Solicinium but were driven off with heavy losses after Valentinian nearly fell in an ambush.
events.detail: Valentinian then built an intensive system of forts, burgi and river crossings along the Rhine and Danube (369-374), the last great Roman frontier programme in the West.
events.locName: Solicinium (unidentified; perhaps near Rottenburg am Neckar or Heidelberg)

battle.significance: Punitive victory followed by major fortification programme.

events.title: Treason and magic trials at Rome and Antioch
events.summary: At Rome the prefect of the annona Maximinus (later praetorian prefect) prosecuted senators and their wives for adultery and magic with torture; at Antioch in 371-372 a séance using a magic tripod that spelled out THEOD as the next emperor's name led to the execution of the notary Theodorus and many others, and burnings of books.
events.detail: Ammianus, who was in Antioch and burned some of his own papers, gives a horrified account. The trials show the reach of imperial fear of divination in a precarious dynasty.
scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

events.title: Valens' Gothic war and the treaty on the Danube
events.summary: After three years of campaigns north of the Danube (367-369) against the Tervingi, hampered by floods in 368, Valens met the Tervingian 'judge' Athanaric on a boat in midstream, since Athanaric had sworn never to set foot on Roman soil; trade was restricted to two Danube towns and subsidies ended.
events.detail: Themistius' Oration 10 celebrates the peace as philanthropy. The treaty treated the Goths as an independent people. Athanaric followed it with a persecution of Gothic Christians (369-372), whose martyrs include Saba the Goth.
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

events.title: Revolt of Firmus in Mauretania
events.summary: Firmus, son of the Moorish prince Nubel, rebelled after a dispute with the rapacious comes Africae Romanus; Count Theodosius waged a hard campaign through Mauretania until Firmus hanged himself to avoid capture.
events.detail: Firmus had Donatist support, and his brother Gildo, who fought for Rome, later held Africa (386-398). The campaign typifies the late Roman reliance on Moorish princes as both allies and rebels.

events.title: Ambrose elected bishop of Milan
events.summary: Ambrose, governor of Aemilia-Liguria, intervened to calm the crowds at the disputed election to succeed the Homoian bishop Auxentius, and was himself acclaimed bishop by the people, according to legend after a child cried 'Ambrose bishop'; he was baptised and consecrated within a week.
scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan: Church and Court in a Christian Capital (1994)
events.debate: Date 373 or 374.

events.title: Death of Valentinian I at Brigetio
events.summary: After campaigning against the Quadi, who had invaded Pannonia in 374 after the murder of their king Gabinius by a Roman officer, Valentinian received a Quadic embassy at Brigetio, flew into a rage at their insolence and died of a stroke.
events.detail: Five days later the officers proclaimed his four-year-old son Valentinian II Augustus at Aquincum without consulting Gratian, who accepted the fait accompli. Count Theodosius was executed at Carthage early in 376 in murky circumstances; his son, the future Theodosius I, retired to Spain.

events.title: The Goths cross the Danube
events.summary: Driven by the Huns, who had destroyed the Greuthungian kingdom of Ermanaric and defeated Athanaric's Tervingi on the Dniester, a large body of Tervingi under Alavivus and Fritigern petitioned Valens for land and were admitted across the Danube, probably near Durostorum, in exchange for military service; the Greuthungi under Alatheus and Saphrax crossed without permission.
events.detail: Ammianus describes the crossing in boats, rafts and hollowed tree trunks, and the corrupt Roman officers Lupicinus and Maximus extorting the starving Goths, selling them dog meat in exchange for their children as slaves. Numbers are unknown: Eunapius' 200,000 is a guess; modern estimates for the Tervingi range from 15,000 to 20,000 warriors with families. Valens welcomed the prospect of recruits, which Ammianus regards as fatal optimism.
scholarship: Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007)
events.debate: Numbers of Goths and the role of the Huns (Heather) versus Roman policy and the internal politics of the Goths (Kulikowski, Halsall).

events.title: Lupicinus' banquet and the battle of Marcianople
events.summary: At a banquet at Marcianople the comes Lupicinus tried to seize or murder Fritigern and Alavivus; Fritigern escaped, rallied the Goths and destroyed Lupicinus' army nine miles from the city, beginning the Gothic war.

battle.significance: Turned the Gothic settlement into open war.

events.debate: Date late 376 or early 377.

events.title: Battle of Ad Salices
events.summary: Roman forces under Richomeres, Profuturus and Trajanus fought the Goths behind their wagon-laager at Ad Salices ('By the Willows') in the Dobruja; the battle was bloody and indecisive, and Ammianus says the bones of the dead still whitened the field years later.

sides.strength: Gothic warriors behind the wagon circle

battle.significance: Showed the Goths could not be easily contained.

events.title: Battle of Argentaria
events.summary: Gratian's generals Nannienus and Mallobaudes, king of the Franks and comes domesticorum, destroyed the Lentienses, an Alamannic people who had crossed the frozen Rhine, near Argentaria (Horbourg near Colmar); Ammianus says only 5,000 of 40,000 escaped.
events.detail: The campaign delayed Gratian's march east to help Valens, a factor in Valens' decision to fight at Adrianople without waiting.

battle.significance: Delayed Gratian's eastern march.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.summary: Valens, refusing to wait for Gratian, marched out from Adrianople in the August heat and attacked Fritigern's wagon camp; while negotiations dragged on, Roman units engaged prematurely, the returning Greuthungian cavalry of Alatheus and Saphrax struck the Roman left, and the infantry, crushed together so they could not draw swords, were annihilated. Valens died and two-thirds of the army perished.
events.detail: Ammianus counts the dead as including the generals Trajanus and Sebastianus, 35 tribunes and the former magister Equitius' relatives; he compares it to Cannae. Valens' body was never found; one story has him burned alive in a farmhouse. Modern estimates put the Roman army at 15,000-30,000 and losses at 10,000-20,000. The Goths failed to take Adrianople and Constantinople, where an Arab contingent of Queen Mavia's Saracens horrified them by drinking the blood of a slain Goth. Magister Julius ordered the massacre of Gothic recruits in the eastern provinces. Older views of Adrianople as a victory of cavalry over infantry, ushering in medieval warfare (Oman), are now rejected. Its consequences were political: Goths settled as an autonomous force within the empire.
events.locName: About 13 km north of Hadrianopolis (Edirne), Thrace

sides.losses: two-thirds of the army (Ammianus); emperor killed

sides.strength: Tervingi, Greuthungi and Alans; perhaps 15,000-20,000 warriors

battle.significance: Death of an emperor and destruction of the eastern field army; led to the settlement of Goths inside the empire.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Burns, 'The battle of Adrianople: a reconsideration', Historia 22 (1973)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
events.debate: Army sizes, battlefield location and the long-term military significance are disputed. Christian sources (Orosius) saw the 'Arian' emperor's death as divine punishment.

events.title: Theodosius made Augustus at Sirmium
events.summary: Gratian recalled Theodosius, son of the executed Count Theodosius, from his Spanish estates, gave him a command against the Goths and Sarmatians and proclaimed him Augustus of the East at Sirmium, together with the dioceses of Dacia and Macedonia.
events.detail: Theodosius rebuilt the eastern army by mass recruitment including barbarians, based himself at Thessalonica, and after a serious illness was baptised there in 380 by the Nicene bishop Acholius.

events.title: Edict of Thessalonica (Cunctos populos)
events.summary: Theodosius, Gratian and Valentinian II decreed that all peoples should follow the faith 'which the divine apostle Peter delivered to the Romans' as taught by Damasus of Rome and Peter of Alexandria, belief in the one deity of Father, Son and Holy Spirit; others were 'demented and insane' heretics.
events.detail: The edict, addressed to the people of Constantinople, defined orthodoxy by communion with named bishops and laid the legal foundation for Nicene Christianity as the state religion. On entering Constantinople in November 380 Theodosius expelled the Homoian bishop Demophilus and installed Gregory of Nazianzus.
scholarship: Errington, Roman Imperial Policy from Julian to Theodosius (2006)
events.debate: Whether the edict was an empire-wide religious law or a specific measure for Constantinople is debated (Errington).

events.title: First Council of Constantinople
events.summary: About 150 eastern bishops, summoned by Theodosius, reaffirmed the Nicene faith, condemned Macedonians (who denied the divinity of the Spirit) and others, and in canon 3 gave the bishop of Constantinople 'precedence of honour after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome'.
events.detail: Gregory of Nazianzus presided briefly after Meletius' death and then resigned amid quarrels; Nectarius, an unbaptised senator, succeeded him. The expanded creed attributed to this council (the 'Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed', the Nicene Creed of modern liturgies) is first attested at Chalcedon in 451. Canon 3 began the long rivalry of Constantinople with Alexandria and Rome.

sources.w: Canons of the Council of Constantinople (381)

events.title: Theodosius' treaty with the Goths
events.summary: On 3 October 382, after Theodosius' generals had contained but not defeated the Goths, the magister Saturninus made peace: the Goths were settled in northern Thrace and along the Danube as a people under their own leaders, providing troops under their own commanders while remaining legally autonomous.
events.detail: Themistius' Oration 16 justifies the peace as turning enemies into farmers and allies. The arrangement, whose exact terms are unrecorded, is often seen as the first settlement of an intact barbarian people on Roman soil, a precedent for the federate kingdoms of the fifth century. Heather and Kulikowski stress how much it was a compromise forced by Roman weakness. Athanaric had already come to Constantinople in January 381 and died there, receiving a state funeral.
events.locName: Constantinople; settlement in Thrace and Moesia
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Errington, 'Theodosius and the Goths', Chiron 26 (1996)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
events.debate: Terms of the foedus (autonomy, land vs tax shares) are unknown and debated.

events.title: Usurpation of Magnus Maximus and death of Gratian
events.summary: Magnus Maximus, a Spanish officer serving in Britain and a relative of Theodosius, was proclaimed emperor by the British army and crossed to Gaul; Gratian's troops deserted near Paris, and Gratian was caught and killed at Lugdunum on 25 August 383.
events.detail: Gratian had alienated the army by favouring his Alan bodyguard. Maximus ruled Gaul, Britain and Spain from Trier and was recognised by Theodosius in 384. Welsh legend (Macsen Wledig, 'The Dream of Macsen') made him an ancestor of Welsh dynasties; Gildas blamed him for stripping Britain of troops.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

events.title: The Altar of Victory controversy
events.summary: In 382 Gratian removed the Altar of Victory from the Senate house and cut state funding of the pagan cults and the Vestals; in 384 the urban prefect Symmachus petitioned Valentinian II for its restoration in his Third Relatio, and Ambrose answered with two letters ensuring the request failed.
events.detail: Symmachus' plea, 'one cannot reach so great a mystery by one road alone', is a classic statement of religious pluralism. Gratian had also refused the title pontifex maximus (the exact date is debated, possibly 383 or later per Cameron).
scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)

events.title: Execution of Priscillian at Trier
events.summary: Priscillian, an ascetic bishop of Avila accused by Spanish bishops of Manichaeism and sorcery, was tried before Magnus Maximus at Trier and beheaded with several followers, including the noblewoman Euchrotia, the first Christians executed by Christian authorities for heresy.
events.detail: Martin of Tours and Ambrose protested; Martin refused communion with the accusing bishops Ithacius and Hydatius. Priscillianism survived in Galicia into the sixth century.
scholarship: Chadwick, Priscillian of Avila (1976)
Burrus, The Making of a Heretic (1995)
events.debate: Date 385 or 386.

events.title: Ambrose and the Milan basilica conflict
events.summary: The empress mother Justina and the court of Valentinian II demanded a basilica in Milan for Homoian worship; Ambrose and his congregation occupied the church through Holy Week of 386, singing antiphonal hymns, while troops surrounded it, and the court backed down. Weeks later Ambrose discovered the bodies of the martyrs Gervasius and Protasius and installed them under the altar of his new basilica.
events.detail: Augustine, then teacher of rhetoric at Milan, witnessed the events (Confessions 9.7) and was baptised by Ambrose at Easter 387. Ambrose's hymns introduced congregational singing to the West.
scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)

events.title: The Riot of the Statues at Antioch
events.summary: A new tax levy, perhaps for Theodosius' decennalia, provoked Antioch's crowd to smash the statues and portraits of the emperor and his family; facing imperial vengeance, the city was saved by the embassy of Bishop Flavian and the intercession of monks, while the young priest John Chrysostom preached his 21 Homilies on the Statues.
events.detail: Libanius' orations on the riot provide a pagan view. The episode illustrates the crime of lèse-majesté against images and the rising intercessory power of bishops and holy men in cities.
scholarship: Browning, 'The riot of AD 387 in Antioch', JRS 42 (1952)

events.title: Partition of Armenia between Rome and Persia
events.summary: Theodosius and Shapur III agreed to divide Armenia: the Persian zone (Persarmenia), about four-fifths of the kingdom, under Khosrov IV, and a smaller Roman zone in the west under Arsaces III, ending decades of struggle since Shapur II had captured King Arsaces II and Rome's protégé Pap had been murdered by a Roman officer (374/375).
events.detail: The partition brought nearly a century and a half of relative peace between the two empires. The Roman Arsacid kingdom was absorbed after Arsaces III's death around 390.
scholarship: Greatrex and Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)
Blockley, East Roman Foreign Policy (1992)
events.debate: Date 384 or 387.

events.title: Battle of Siscia
events.summary: After Magnus Maximus invaded Italy in 387, driving Valentinian II and Justina to Thessalonica, Theodosius marched west; at Siscia on the Save his Hunnic, Alan and Gothic horse archers swam the river and routed Maximus' army.
events.detail: Theodosius had married Valentinian's sister Galla, sealing the alliance. His army included large barbarian contingents, some of whom Maximus had tried to suborn.

sides.strength: eastern army with Gothic, Hunnic and Alan auxiliaries

battle.significance: Opened the road to Italy.

events.title: Battle of Poetovio and death of Magnus Maximus
events.summary: Theodosius defeated Maximus' brother Marcellinus at Poetovio; Maximus was surrounded at Aquileia, handed over by his own troops, and executed on 28 August 388. His son Victor was killed in Gaul by the Frankish general Arbogast.
events.detail: Theodosius restored Valentinian II in the West under the supervision of Arbogast and stayed in Italy until 391, the period of his clashes with Ambrose.

battle.significance: Ended Maximus' regime; Theodosius effectively ruled the whole empire.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

events.title: The Callinicum synagogue affair
events.summary: Christians at Callinicum on the Euphrates, incited by their bishop, burned a synagogue and a Valentinian gnostic chapel; Theodosius ordered the bishop to rebuild the synagogue, but Ambrose refused to celebrate the Eucharist in the emperor's presence until he withdrew the order.

events.title: Massacre of Thessalonica and Theodosius' penance
events.summary: After the people of Thessalonica lynched the Gothic magister militum Butheric, who had jailed a popular charioteer for homosexual assault, troops were turned on the crowd in the hippodrome and some 7,000 were killed (Theodoret); Ambrose, in a private letter, required Theodosius to do public penance before readmitting him to communion.
events.detail: Later church historians dramatised the scene into Ambrose barring Theodosius at the cathedral door, an archetype for medieval church-state relations. Modern scholars (McLynn) see a carefully staged reconciliation that benefited both men. The casualty figure and the emperor's personal responsibility are uncertain.
scholarship: McLynn, Ambrose of Milan (1994)

events.title: Obelisk of Theodosius raised in the Hippodrome
events.summary: The prefect Proclus re-erected an obelisk of Thutmose III, brought from Karnak, on the spina of the Hippodrome of Constantinople in 32 days, as its Latin and Greek inscriptions boast; the marble base shows Theodosius and his family in the kathisma receiving tribute.

sources.w: Base of the Obelisk of Theodosius

events.title: Ammianus Marcellinus completes his Res Gestae
events.summary: Ammianus Marcellinus, a Greek-speaking former protector from Antioch living in Rome, completed his Latin history in 31 books from Nerva to the death of Valens (378); books 14-31, covering 353-378, survive and are the finest narrative history of late antiquity.
events.detail: Ammianus served on the staff of Ursicinus, escaped from Amida in 359 and marched with Julian into Persia; his work combines eyewitness reports, digressions (on Persia, the Huns, Roman society) and moral judgement. He admires Julian while criticising his superstition and school law, and is restrained about Christianity. Historians consider him the most reliable narrator of the fourth century, though Barnes (1998) and Kelly have stressed his literary artifice and selective silences.
scholarship: Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)
Barnes, Ammianus Marcellinus and the Representation of Historical Reality (1998)
Kelly, Ammianus Marcellinus: The Allusive Historian (2008)
events.debate: Date of completion (c. 390-391); identification of Libanius' correspondent.

events.title: Destruction of the Serapeum and the Theodosian decrees
events.summary: Theodosius' laws of 24 February and 16 June 391 banned sacrifice and visits to temples; in Alexandria, rioting between pagans and Christians led by Bishop Theophilus ended with the destruction of the great Serapeum and its cult statue by Bryaxis, with imperial permission. A law of 8 November 392 banned all forms of pagan cult, even private household worship.
events.detail: Rufinus describes a soldier striking the statue's jaw with an axe while the crowd waited for the sky to fall. The Serapeum's 'daughter library' may already have been dispersed. The laws were not uniformly enforced, and pagan cult persisted in many places into the sixth century, but the decrees mark the legal end of public paganism.
scholarship: Hahn, Emmel and Gotter (eds.), From Temple to Church (2008)
Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
events.debate: Date of the Serapeum's destruction (391 or 392).

events.title: Death of Valentinian II; Eugenius proclaimed
events.summary: Valentinian II, aged 21 and humiliated by his magister militum Arbogast, who had torn up his letter of dismissal, was found hanged at Vienne; on 22 August Arbogast, unable as a Frank to take the throne himself, proclaimed the rhetor and court official Eugenius emperor.
events.detail: Whether Valentinian was murdered or took his own life was disputed even at the time; Ambrose's funeral oration hedges. Eugenius, a nominal Christian, restored funding to pagan cults at the request of the senatorial aristocracy led by Virius Nicomachus Flavianus, though Alan Cameron argues that the 'pagan revival' of 393-394 has been exaggerated.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)

events.title: End of the ancient Olympic Games (traditional)
events.summary: The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally said to have ended after the 293rd Olympiad in 393, under Theodosius' anti-pagan legislation, though no law specifically abolishing them is known.
events.detail: The Byzantine historian Cedrenus dates the end to Theodosius I, while a scholion to Lucian attributes the burning of the temple of Zeus to Theodosius II. Archaeological finds at Olympia (including a bronze victor list running to 385) and later evidence suggest that some form of the games continued into the fifth century.
scholarship: Remijsen, The End of Greek Athletics in Late Antiquity (2015)
events.debate: The date 393 is a modern convention; games probably continued until c. 420-430.

events.title: Battle of the Frigidus
events.summary: Theodosius forced the Julian Alps and attacked Eugenius and Arbogast on the river Frigidus (Vipava) on 5-6 September 394; on the first day his 20,000 Gothic federates under Gainas and Alaric were thrown back with heavy losses, but on the second a violent bora wind blew dust into the western army's faces and turned its missiles back, and part of Arbogast's force defected. Eugenius was captured and beheaded; Arbogast killed himself two days later.
events.detail: Christian writers (Rufinus, Ambrose, Orosius, Augustine) and the pagan poet Claudian alike celebrated the miraculous wind, Claudian's lines ('O nimium dilecte deo') later quoted by Augustine. Eugenius' army reportedly marched under statues of Jupiter and banners of Hercules; Flavianus committed suicide. The battle was framed as the last stand of paganism, a construction Cameron and others contest. The heavy Gothic losses (10,000 according to Orosius, who welcomed them) embittered Alaric. Theodosius died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the empire to his sons Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West under Stilicho's guardianship, a division that proved permanent.

sides.strength: eastern army with c. 20,000 Gothic federates
western army with Frankish and Alamannic contingents

battle.significance: Last time the whole empire was united under one emperor; traditionally the victory of Christianity over paganism.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans
Panegyric on the Third Consulship of Honorius

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
Kulikowski, The Tragedy of Empire: From Constantine to the Destruction of Roman Italy (2019)
events.debate: The religious framing of the battle; the wind as a natural bora vs miracle; numbers.

events.title: Death of Theodosius I and division of the empire
events.summary: Theodosius I died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving the East to Arcadius (about 17) and the West to Honorius (10). It was meant as a collegiate division within one empire, but the two courts never again had a single ruler with real power over both.
events.detail: Nothing in 395 was formally partitioned: law was still issued in the joint names of both Augusti, consuls were shared, and contemporaries spoke of one res publica. The real fault lines were human and fiscal. Stilicho, magister militum and husband of Theodosius's niece Serena, claimed that the dying emperor had entrusted both sons to him, a claim the eastern court under the praetorian prefect Rufinus rejected. The dispute over the prefecture of Illyricum (the dioceses of Dacia and Macedonia, prime recruiting ground) poisoned relations for fifteen years and gave Alaric room to play one court against the other. The West inherited the longer and more exposed frontiers and a smaller, more aristocratically captured tax base; the East had Egypt's grain and a defensible capital.
events.debate: Whether 395 was a 'division' at all is a modern framing. Kaldellis stresses continuity of a single Roman polity; Heather and others see 395 as the start of diverging fiscal-military systems. Stilicho's claim to guardianship of Arcadius rests on Claudian, his court poet.
scholarship: Cameron, Claudian (1970)
Cameron & Long, Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

events.title: Murder of the prefect Rufinus at the Hebdomon
events.summary: Gainas's returning eastern troops, saluting Arcadius at the Hebdomon parade ground outside Constantinople, surrounded and hacked to death the praetorian prefect Rufinus; his head and right hand were paraded through the city.
events.detail: Claudian, writing for Stilicho, makes Rufinus a monster; it is likely Stilicho arranged the killing. The beneficiary was not Stilicho but the eunuch grand chamberlain Eutropius, who now dominated Arcadius.

events.title: Composition of the Historia Augusta
events.summary: The Historia Augusta, a collection of imperial biographies from Hadrian to Carinus (117-284) purporting to be by six authors writing under Diocletian and Constantine, was in fact written by a single author around the 390s, as Hermann Dessau showed in 1889.
events.detail: The lives of the major emperors to Caracalla draw on a good source (probably Marius Maximus and an 'Ignotus'), but the later lives and those of usurpers and minor figures are increasingly fictional, with invented documents, letters, speeches and bogus authorities (Syme counted dozens of fake historians). For the third century, where other narratives are thin, it is both indispensable and treacherous: historians use it only where corroborated by coins, inscriptions or other texts. A gap covering 244-260 is either a lacuna or a deliberate fiction. Syme saw a 'rogue grammarian' amusing himself; Cameron and others place it in the context of pagan senatorial culture c. 395-400.
scholarship: Dessau, 'Über Zeit und Persönlichkeit der Scriptores Historiae Augustae', Hermes 24 (1889)
Syme, Ammianus and the Historia Augusta (1968)
Syme, Emperors and Biography (1971)
Rohrbacher, The Play of Allusion in the Historia Augusta (2016)
Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)
events.debate: Date (from c. 360 to c. 410; most now c. 395-400), purpose (hoax, satire, pagan propaganda) and the value of the early lives.

events.title: Alaric's Goths revolt and ravage the Balkans and Greece
events.summary: The Gothic federates who had bled at the Frigidus (394) rose under Alaric, marched to the walls of Constantinople, then turned into Thessaly and Greece, sacking Corinth, Argos and Sparta in 395-396. Athens was spared, probably by payment.
events.detail: Alaric's grievance was status and pay: he wanted a regular Roman command, not to lead expendable auxiliaries. Stilicho marched east with the combined army of both halves but was ordered by Arcadius to send the eastern units home; under Gainas they returned to Constantinople and murdered Rufinus. Zosimus's lurid account of the Greek devastation, with Christian monks opening Thermopylae, reflects pagan polemic. Eleusis was destroyed and the Mysteries ended in this period.
events.debate: Whether Alaric was already 'king of the Visigoths' in 395 is doubtful; Kulikowski and Heather see the Gothic people being forged in these years around his leadership rather than pre-existing.
scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Heather, Goths and Romans 332-489 (1991)

events.title: Stilicho traps Alaric at Pholoe
events.summary: Stilicho landed at Corinth and hemmed Alaric's Goths in on the Pholoe plateau in Elis, but Alaric slipped away to Epirus. Eutropius had the eastern senate declare Stilicho a public enemy, and soon gave Alaric an eastern command in Illyricum.

battle.significance: Showed the cost of the two courts' rivalry: Stilicho was ordered off eastern soil and Alaric was rewarded with the magisterium per Illyricum, the official post he would seek ever after.

events.debate: Zosimus says Stilicho let Alaric escape through negligence and debauchery; Claudian implies a political deal or eastern interference. Modern views lean to the latter.

events.title: Battle of the Ardalio: fall of Gildo
events.summary: Gildo, the Moorish comes Africae who had transferred Africa's allegiance to Constantinople and stopped the grain to Rome, was routed between Theveste and Ammaedara by his own brother Mascezel, sent by Stilicho with about 5,000 veterans. Gildo fled and killed himself at Thabraca.
events.detail: Gildo had murdered Mascezel's sons, so Stilicho chose an avenger. The Senate formally declared Gildo hostis publicus, a revival of republican procedure that Claudian celebrates in De Bello Gildonico. Gildo's vast estates were confiscated into a special treasury, the comitiva Gildoniaci patrimonii, still in the Notitia Dignitatum. Mascezel himself drowned soon afterward; Zosimus claims Stilicho's guards pushed him off a bridge.
events.locName: River Ardalio, between Theveste and Ammaedara

battle.significance: Restored the African grain supply to Rome and the West's control of its richest provinces for another generation.

events.debate: Orosius frames the victory as a miracle after Mascezel prayed at Capraria with monks; numbers are hagiographical.

events.title: Consulship and fall of the eunuch Eutropius
events.summary: Eutropius, Arcadius's grand chamberlain and a former slave, became the first eunuch consul in 399, to western outrage; Claudian's In Eutropium is pure venom. By August the revolt of Tribigild in Phrygia and Gainas's pressure forced his dismissal; he took sanctuary in Hagia Sophia, was exiled to Cyprus and executed at Chalcedon.
events.debate: The West refused to recognise his consulship; the fasti show divergence. Chrysostom preached over the cowering Eutropius in the cathedral.

events.title: Massacre of Gainas's Goths in Constantinople
events.summary: After months in which the Gothic general Gainas dominated the capital, the citizens rose on 12 July 400 while he was outside the walls and slaughtered his Gothic troops, reportedly about 7,000, many burned alive in a church near the palace where they had fled.
events.detail: The episode inspired Synesius's allegory De Providentia and fed the long modern argument over an 'anti-German' party at the eastern court. Cameron and Long dismantled the idea of a coherent ideological faction; the massacre was opportunistic urban violence against a resented garrison.

battle.significance: Ended the threat of a barbarian generalissimo controlling the eastern court.

scholarship: Cameron & Long, Barbarians and Politics at the Court of Arcadius (1993)

events.title: Fravitta destroys Gainas's rafts on the Hellespont
events.summary: Trying to cross from the Thracian Chersonese to Asia on improvised rafts, Gainas's army was shattered by the Liburnian galleys of Fravitta, a pagan Goth loyal to Rome. Gainas fled north of the Danube, where the Hun Uldin killed him and sent his head to Constantinople (arrived 3 January 401).

sides.strength: fleet of Liburnian galleys under Fravitta

battle.significance: First appearance of a Hunnic ruler, Uldin, acting as a diplomatic partner of Constantinople.

events.title: Alaric invades Italy
events.summary: Displaced from his Illyrian command after the fall of Eutropius, Alaric crossed the Julian Alps in November 401 while Stilicho was fighting Vandals and Alans in Raetia. He besieged Aquileia and threatened Milan, where Honorius was cut off until Stilicho returned with troops stripped from the Rhine and Britain.

events.title: Battle of Pollentia
events.summary: On Easter Sunday 402 Stilicho attacked Alaric's camp at Pollentia in Liguria, gambling that the Christian Goths would not expect battle on the feast. The fight was bloody and inconclusive, but Alaric's camp, treasure, wife and children were captured, forcing him to negotiate.
events.detail: Stilicho's Alan contingent under Saul opened the attack and suffered heavily; Saul was killed. Claudian claims a crushing victory; Orosius, writing after Stilicho's disgrace, condemns the sacrilege of fighting on Easter and says the Goths won the fight. Alaric withdrew toward the Po valley under a truce, which he soon broke.

sides.strength: western field army with Alan federates; perhaps 15,000-20,000

battle.significance: A tactical draw but strategic success: Alaric lost his baggage and hostages, and his army began to fray.

events.debate: Claudian (pro-Stilicho) and Orosius (anti-Stilicho) give opposite verdicts; Jordanes's Gothic victory is late and derivative.

events.title: Battle of Verona
events.summary: When Alaric broke the Pollentia truce and moved on Raetia or Gaul, Stilicho caught him near Verona and defeated him; desertions followed and Alaric withdrew to the Balkans with a much reduced following. Stilicho let him go, apparently wanting him as an ally against the East.

battle.significance: Ended Alaric's first invasion of Italy; Honorius celebrated a triumph in Rome in 404, the last imperial triumph held in the old capital.

events.debate: The year is disputed between summer 402 and 403.

events.title: The western court moves to Ravenna
events.summary: Shaken by the siege of Milan, Honorius moved the court to Ravenna around the end of 402. Protected by marshes and with the fleet base at Classis giving access to the Adriatic and Constantinople, Ravenna remained the western capital until 476 and the seat of Odoacer, Theodoric and the exarchs.
scholarship: Deliyannis, Ravenna in Late Antiquity (2010)
events.debate: The move was gradual; Milan remained important and the date of the formal transfer is debated (402-408).

events.title: Second exile of John Chrysostom
events.summary: Deposed by the Synod of the Oak (403) under Theophilus of Alexandria, recalled after an earthquake frightened the empress Eudoxia, then exiled again in June 404 after sermons read as attacks on her silver statue, John Chrysostom left Constantinople. That night Hagia Sophia and the senate house burned. He died on a forced march at Comana in 407.

sources.w: Dialogue on the Life of John Chrysostom

events.debate: The famous 'Herodias' sermon attributed to John may be spurious; the conflict was as much about episcopal jurisdiction and Alexandrian rivalry as about the empress.

events.title: Radagaisus invades Italy
events.summary: A large Gothic-led force under the pagan king Radagaisus crossed the Alps from the middle Danube in late 405 and spread through northern Italy, one of several shock waves set off by Hunnic expansion west of the Carpathians.
events.debate: Zosimus's 400,000 and Orosius's 200,000 are fantasies; Heather suggests 20,000 warriors with families. Heather links Radagaisus, the Rhine crossing and later Hunnic movements as a single migration crisis; Halsall downplays external pressure.

events.title: Battle of Faesulae: destruction of Radagaisus
events.summary: Radagaisus besieged Florence; Stilicho, with 30 numeri plus Uldin's Huns and Sarus's Goths, relieved the city and blockaded the invaders on the heights of Faesulae until hunger broke them. Radagaisus was executed on 23 August 406; 12,000 of his best men were enrolled in the Roman army and so many captives were sold that slaves went for a solidus a head.

sides.strength: 30 numeri (Zosimus), plus Hunnic and Gothic auxiliaries

sides.losses: army surrendered; 12,000 drafted, the rest enslaved

battle.significance: Stilicho's last great victory. The 12,000 recruits later joined Alaric after Stilicho's fall, swelling the force that sacked Rome.

events.debate: Augustine and Orosius use the pagan Radagaisus's defeat to answer claims that Christianity weakened Rome.
events.detail: The survivors were rescued by the arrival of the consul Lucius Aemilius Papus. The Gauls, laden with plunder, decided to withdraw along the coast.

events.title: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
events.summary: On the last day of 406 (per Prosper) Hasding and Siling Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the Rhine near Mainz after defeating Frankish federates who killed the Hasding king Godigisel. For three years they plundered Gaul, then in 409 crossed into Spain; the Hasdings under Gaiseric would end in Carthage.
events.detail: Jerome's letter 123 lists the victims: Mainz sacked and thousands massacred in the church, Worms destroyed, Reims, Amiens, Arras, Tournai, Speyer and Strasbourg taken. The Rhine frontier had been thinned by Stilicho's withdrawals to fight Alaric and Radagaisus. The crisis also triggered the British army's proclamation of Constantine III. The image of a frozen Rhine is a modern embellishment not found in the sources.
events.debate: Kulikowski argued for 31 December 405, reading Zosimus's chronology against Prosper; most still prefer 406. Whether the invaders were pushed by the Huns (Heather) or drawn by opportunity and Roman politics (Halsall, Goffart) is central to the 'fall vs transformation' debate.
scholarship: Kulikowski, 'Barbarians in Gaul, usurpers in Britain', Britannia 31 (2000)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West 376-568 (2007)
Goffart, Barbarian Tides (2006)

events.title: Constantine III proclaimed in Britain
