Later legend has him unable to pass the gate on horseback in imperial regalia until he dismounted and walked barefoot. The feast of the Exaltation of the Cross acquired this story.
events.locName: Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem
events.debate: Date debated: 21 March 630 is preferred by most; Zuckerman argues for 629. Some contemporaries interpreted the moment eschatologically, and some scholars connect it with Heraclius's later order for the forced baptism of Jews (632), whose extent is disputed.
scholarship: Drijvers, 'Heraclius and the restitutio crucis', in Reinink & Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (2002)
Zuckerman, 'Heraclius and the return of the Holy Cross', Travaux et Mémoires 17 (2013)

events.title: Death of Muhammad
events.summary: Muhammad died at Medina on 8 June 632 (traditional date). Abu Bakr was chosen as his successor (khalifa) and spent 632-633 suppressing the Ridda, the defection of Arabian tribes, uniting the peninsula under Medina for the first time and creating the forces that would be turned on Syria and Iraq.
events.debate: The Doctrina Jacobi nuper baptizati (written c. 634) mentions a prophet 'appearing with the Saracens' as if still alive, prompting debate about the traditional chronology.

events.title: Monoenergism: the Pact of Union at Alexandria
events.summary: Cyrus, Heraclius's appointee as patriarch of Alexandria, united the Chalcedonians and the Theodosian miaphysites on 3 June 633 on the formula that Christ acted through 'one theandric energy', a compromise devised by Patriarch Sergius and the emperor. The monk Sophronius protested, and in 634 Sergius forbade further talk of energies.

sources.w: ACO ser. 2, II (Acts of the Sixth Council)

scholarship: Booth, Crisis of Empire: Doctrine and Dissent at the End of Late Antiquity (2014)
Allen (ed.), Sophronius of Jerusalem and Seventh-Century Heresy (2009)

events.title: Battle of Dathin
events.summary: Near Gaza on 4 February 634, an Arab army under Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan defeated a Roman force under the candidatus Sergius, perhaps dux of Palestine; Sergius was killed. The Syriac Chronicle of 640 by Thomas the Presbyter notes 'a battle between the Romans and the Arabs of Muhammad' with 4,000 Palestinian villagers killed, the first securely dated event of the conquest in a non-Muslim source.

sides.strength: Arab army under Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan
local Roman forces under the candidatus Sergius
sides.losses: commander killed; 4,000 villagers killed (Thomas the Presbyter)

battle.significance: Opened southern Palestine to the conquerors.

scholarship: Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)
Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

events.title: Khalid ibn al-Walid's desert crossing
events.summary: Ordered by Abu Bakr to reinforce the armies in Syria, Khalid led perhaps 500-800 picked men from Iraq across the waterless desert between Qurraqir and Suwa in about five days, watering camels in advance and slaughtering some to drink the water stored in their stomachs, according to tradition. He appeared near Damascus at Marj Rahit around Easter 634, took Bosra and joined the other commanders.
events.debate: The route and timing are reconstructed from contradictory Arabic traditions; Donner discusses at least four route variants.
scholarship: Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

events.title: Battle of Ajnadayn
events.summary: The united Arab armies, including Khalid, defeated a Roman army in southern Palestine at Ajnadayn, between Ramla and Beit Guvrin, traditionally on 30 July 634. Arab tradition names its commander as 'Artabun'; Theodore, Heraclius's brother, may have been in command in the region. Palestine's open country fell to the invaders; cities held out behind their walls.

sides.strength: Roman field army of Palestine, size unknown (Arab sources: 100,000)

battle.significance: The first major pitched-battle victory of the conquests in Syria.

events.debate: Date (July 634 or 635), location and commanders are all disputed; some suggest Ajnadayn and Fahl have been confused in the tradition.

events.title: Battle of Fahl (Pella)
events.summary: Roman troops who had flooded the Jordan valley around Baysan to block the Arabs were defeated near Pella (Fahl) in January 635, a battle the tradition calls 'the Day of the Mud'. Jordan and the Galilee fell, and the road to Damascus was open.

battle.significance: Secured the Jordan valley and isolated Damascus.

events.title: Surrender of Damascus
events.summary: After a six-month blockade, Damascus surrendered in September 635 on terms negotiated, according to tradition, by Mansur ibn Sarjun, the city's fiscal official and grandfather of John of Damascus: security of life, property and churches in return for tribute. Khalid is said to have entered by force at the east gate at the same time Abu Ubayda entered by treaty at the west.

battle.significance: Gave the conquerors the main city of interior Syria; abandoned briefly before Yarmuk, it was reoccupied in 636 and became the Umayyad capital in 661.

events.debate: The tale of the two gates is an etiological explanation for the city being treated partly as conquered by force and partly by treaty.

events.title: Battle of the Yarmuk
events.summary: Heraclius gathered a great army in 636 under the Armenian Vahan, the sakellarios Theodore Trithyrios, and the Ghassanid king Jabala ibn al-Ayham, which forced the Arabs to abandon Damascus and Emesa. The Arabs concentrated on the plateau near the Yarmuk river, and after weeks of skirmishing and some six days of battle, traditionally ending on 20 August 636, the Roman army was routed, many trapped against the ravine of the Wadi al-Ruqqad.
events.detail: Arab sources inflate the Roman army to 100,000-240,000; modern estimates range from 15,000-40,000 Romans against 20,000-40,000 Arabs. Kaegi stresses Roman command friction (Vahan was briefly proclaimed emperor by his troops according to one source), unpaid and mutinous soldiers, the defection or wavering of Christian Arab allies, and Arab mastery of mobile warfare on terrain they chose. Heraclius, at Antioch, left Syria; Baladhuri preserves his farewell from a height: 'Peace be upon you, Syria, and what a fine land you are for the enemy.' The whole of Syria south of the Taurus was lost within four years.
events.locName: Yarmuk river and Wadi al-Ruqqad, Golan / Hauran

sides.strength: perhaps 15,000-40,000 (Arab sources: 100,000-240,000), incl. Armenians and Ghassanids

battle.significance: One of the most consequential battles in history: it ended Roman rule in Syria and Palestine after seven centuries and opened the way to Egypt and Mesopotamia.

events.debate: Date (Arab sources give dates from 634 to 636), sequence, and numbers are all disputed; Arabic accounts are later reconstructions with literary topoi (sandstorms, oaths, women fighting in the rear).
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)
Jandora, 'The battle of the Yarmuk: a reconstruction', Journal of Asian History 19 (1985)

events.title: Heraclius abandons Syria
events.summary: After the Yarmuk, Heraclius left Antioch for Constantinople. Arab tradition has him say from a height on his way north: 'Peace be upon you, Syria, and what a fine country this is for the enemy.' He withdrew garrisons behind the Taurus and created a depopulated buffer, a zone of raids that would define the Arab-Byzantine frontier for three centuries.
events.debate: The farewell is a literary topos; Kaegi notes that Heraclius continued to direct defence from Anatolia.
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

events.title: Surrender of Jerusalem to Umar
events.summary: Blockaded since 636, Jerusalem under Patriarch Sophronius surrendered in 637 or early 638 on condition that the caliph Umar come in person to accept it. Tradition tells of Umar arriving in a simple patched cloak, touring the Holy Sepulchre but praying outside so that Muslims would not claim it, and clearing the Temple Mount. Sophronius, who had lamented the 'Saracens' in his Christmas sermon of 634, died soon after.

battle.significance: The holy city of Christianity passed to Muslim rule, which lasted, apart from 1099-1187 and 1229-1244, until 1917.

events.debate: The 'Covenant of Umar' text granted to Jerusalem's Christians is a later composition; the date of surrender (636, 637 or 638) is disputed.

events.title: Plague of Amwas
events.summary: A wave of the Justinianic plague struck the Arab armies in Syria and Palestine in 638-639, named for their camp at Emmaus (Amwas). Arab tradition says 25,000 died, including the commanders Abu Ubayda and Yazid ibn Abi Sufyan, whose brother Mu'awiya succeeded him in Syria.
scholarship: Conrad, 'Umar at Sargh: the evolution of an Umayyad tradition on flight from the plague', in Leder (ed.), Story-telling in the Framework of Non-fictional Arabic Literature (1998)

events.title: The Ecthesis: Monotheletism decreed
events.summary: Drafted by Patriarch Sergius and posted in the narthex of Hagia Sophia in 638, Heraclius's Ecthesis forbade discussion of 'one or two energies' and declared that Christ had a single will. Councils in Constantinople accepted it; Rome rejected it, and its condemnation at the Sixth Ecumenical Council in 680-681 made Heraclius a posthumous heretic in Chalcedonian eyes.

sources.w: ACO ser. 2, I (Lateran Council of 649), text of the Ecthesis

scholarship: Booth, Crisis of Empire (2014)

events.title: Amr ibn al-As invades Egypt
events.summary: With perhaps 4,000 men and only the reluctant approval of Umar, Amr ibn al-As crossed from Palestine into Egypt in December 639, reaching al-Arish at the Feast of Sacrifice. He took Pelusium after a siege of about a month, then Bilbays, and marched on the fortress of Babylon at the apex of the Delta.
scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (1902; 2nd ed. Fraser, 1978)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

events.title: Arab conquest of Roman Mesopotamia
events.summary: After Antioch and northern Syria fell in 637-638, Iyad ibn Ghanm crossed the Euphrates and in 639-640 took the cities of the Jazira, Raqqa, Edessa, Harran, Amida, Dara and Resaina, mostly by treaty. Edessa surrendered on terms that the Arabs would keep its walls and churches, and pay tribute.

events.title: Battle of Heliopolis
events.summary: Reinforced by 4,000 or more men under al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, Amr drew the Roman army of Egypt under Theodore into battle near Heliopolis in July 640, using a concealed detachment that attacked from the rear. The Roman force broke; part fled to the fortress of Babylon, part to Alexandria.

sides.strength: Roman field army of Egypt under Theodore, perhaps 15,000-20,000

battle.significance: Decided the fate of Egypt in the field; the rest was sieges and negotiation.

events.title: Fall of Caesarea Maritima
events.summary: The capital of Palaestina Prima, supplied by sea, held out for years against blockade until Mu'awiya took it by storm in 640 or 641, reportedly guided by a Jewish informer through an aqueduct. The last Roman city in Palestine fell; the tradition says 7,000 defenders were killed.

battle.significance: Completed the conquest of Palestine.

events.title: Death of Heraclius
events.summary: Heraclius died on 11 February 641 aged about 66, of a disease Nikephoros describes as dropsy, which some contemporaries saw as punishment for his uncanonical marriage to his niece Martina. He left the empire jointly to Constantine III, his son by Fabia-Eudocia, and Heraclonas, his son by Martina, with Martina to be honoured as 'mother and empress'. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles.
events.detail: His reign is the hinge between late antiquity and the middle Byzantine world: the triumph over Persia in 628 and the loss of Syria, Palestine, Mesopotamia and much of Egypt within a decade of it; the end of Latin in government; the crisis of Constantinople's food supply; and the failure of Monoenergism and Monotheletism to reunite the churches. Theodosius I had died in 395 ruling from the Atlantic to the Euphrates; Heraclius died holding Anatolia, the Balkan coasts, Africa, parts of Italy and a collapsing Egypt.
scholarship: Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Reinink & Stolte (eds.), The Reign of Heraclius (610-641): Crisis and Confrontation (2002)
Haldon, The Empire That Would Not Die (2016)

events.title: Surrender of the fortress of Babylon
events.summary: Besieged since September 640, the Roman fortress of Babylon (Old Cairo), guarding the Nile crossing at the head of the Delta, surrendered on 9 April 641, Easter Monday, after news of Heraclius's death and the recall of the patriarch Cyrus had undermined resistance. Amr founded the camp-city of Fustat beside it.

battle.significance: Gave the Arabs control of the Nile and Upper Egypt; Fustat became the capital of Islamic Egypt.

scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (2nd ed. 1978)

events.title: Treaty of Alexandria
events.summary: Restored to Alexandria by the new regime, Patriarch Cyrus agreed with Amr on 8 November 641 to surrender Egypt: an armistice of eleven months, a poll tax of two dinars per adult man, protection of churches, and evacuation of the Roman army by sea. The last Roman troops left Alexandria in September 642, ending nearly 700 years of Roman rule in Egypt.
events.debate: The famous story of Amr burning the Library of Alexandria on Umar's orders first appears in thirteenth-century writers (Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi, Ibn al-Qifti) and is rejected by historians; the library had long since ceased to exist in its Ptolemaic form. A Roman fleet briefly retook Alexandria in 645-646.
scholarship: Butler, The Arab Conquest of Egypt (2nd ed. 1978)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

events.title: Constantine III, Heraclonas and the fall of Martina
events.summary: Constantine III, consumptive, died after a reign of about three months (May 641), amid rumours that Martina had poisoned him. Martina and Heraclonas governed briefly, but the army under Valentinus and the people of Constantinople forced the coronation of Constantine III's son Constans II in September, and in late 641 Martina's tongue and Heraclonas's nose were slit and they were exiled to Rhodes, the first use of such mutilation to disqualify a ruler.
events.debate: Exact dates in 641 are uncertain; Constantine III's death is placed between April and May, Martina's fall in September-November.

people.name: Romulus
people.summary: Legendary founder and first king of Rome, son of Mars and the Vestal Rhea Silvia, suckled with his twin Remus by a she-wolf; tradition gives him a reign of 753-716 and a disappearance in a storm on the Campus Martius, after which he was worshipped as Quirinus.
people.detail: The twins legend is attested in Greek sources from the 4th-3rd century and monumentalised at Rome by the Ogulnii in 296. Romulus' 'institutions' (Senate of 100, curiae, the asylum, the rape of the Sabines, joint rule with Titus Tatius) are etiological reconstructions. Wiseman argues Remus was added in the 4th century to reflect patrician-plebeian power-sharing.
people.death: vanished in a storm during a review on the Campus Martius (legend); alternatively murdered by senators
scholarship: Wiseman, Remus: A Roman Myth (1995)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 57-80

people.name: Numa Pompilius
people.summary: Second king in the Roman tradition, a Sabine from Cures credited with founding Rome's religious institutions under the guidance of the nymph Egeria.
people.detail: The Calpurnii, Pomponii, Pinarii and Aemilii later claimed descent from his sons. The supposed 'books of Numa' discovered in 181 BC were burned as subversive.

people.name: Servius Tullius
people.summary: Sixth king, of slave or captive birth in Roman tradition and identified in an Etruscan tradition (Claudius' Lyons speech) with the adventurer Mastarna; credited with the census, centuriate assembly, tribes, the temple of Diana on the Aventine and a city wall.
people.detail: Murdered at the instigation of his daughter Tullia and her husband Tarquinius Superbus; Tullia drove her carriage over his body in the Vicus Sceleratus. The 'Servian' constitution as described by Livy is a 4th-3rd century system projected back. His patronage of Fortuna and Mater Matuta at the Forum Boarium (Sant'Omobono temples, 6th century) is archaeologically plausible.
people.death: murdered at the instigation of Tarquinius Superbus and Tullia
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 130-141, 173-197

people.name: Tarquinius Superbus
people.summary: Seventh and last king of Rome in tradition, a tyrant who extended Roman power over Latium, began the Capitoline temple and was expelled c. 509, after which he sought restoration through Veii, Tarquinii, Porsenna and the Latins before dying in exile at Cumae.
people.detail: His reign shows Rome at its archaic peak: hegemony over Latium (reflected in the 509 Carthage treaty), colonies at Signia and Circeii, the Cloaca and Circus works, and the purchase of the Sibylline Books. The 'tyrant' portrait borrows from Greek models (Periander's poppy-lopping lesson to Thrasybulus reappears in the capture of Gabii).
people.death: died in exile at Cumae, at the court of Aristodemus
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-239

people.name: Lucretia
people.fullName: Lucretia, wife of L. Tarquinius Collatinus
people.summary: Roman matron whose rape by Sextus Tarquinius and subsequent suicide, after summoning her father and husband to swear vengeance, triggered the expulsion of the kings.
people.detail: Her story is a Roman exemplum of pudicitia and the paradigm of tyranny overthrown through outrage to a woman, repeated in Verginia (449). Livy's version dramatises it like a tragedy.

people.name: Lucius Junius Brutus
people.summary: Legendary liberator of Rome and first consul, Tarquin's nephew who feigned dullness (brutus) to survive, led the revolt after Lucretia's death, executed his own sons for plotting a Tarquin restoration, and died in single combat with Arruns Tarquinius at the Silva Arsia.
people.detail: The later plebeian Iunii, including Caesar's assassin, claimed descent despite the tradition that his only sons were executed; Dionysius notes the problem. His statue stood on the Capitol among the kings, holding a drawn sword.
people.death: killed in a cavalry duel with Arruns Tarquinius at the Silva Arsia

people.name: Tarquinius Collatinus
people.summary: Husband of Lucretia and colleague of Brutus as first consul; forced to resign and go into exile at Lavinium because he bore the hated name of Tarquin.
people.detail: His expulsion illustrates the archaic idea of a whole gens tainted by the regnum; Sp. Lucretius and then Publicola replaced him.

people.name: Publius Valerius Publicola
people.summary: Co-founder of the Republic, four times consul, who demolished his own grand house on the Velia when suspected of aiming at kingship, lowered the fasces before the people and is credited with the first law of appeal (provocatio).
people.detail: Plutarch paired him with Solon. The Lapis Satricanus (c. 500) naming the companions of 'Poplios Valesios' may refer to him. The Valerian family tradition, inflated by the annalist Valerius Antias, accounts for much of his legend.
people.death: died poor and was buried at public expense within the city
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 1-7

people.name: Lars Porsenna
people.summary: Etruscan king of Clusium who attacked Rome c. 508, nominally to restore Tarquin; Roman legend has him withdraw out of admiration for Roman heroism, but Tacitus and Pliny indicate he captured the city and imposed terms.
people.detail: Varro (in Pliny) described his fantastic tomb at Clusium with a labyrinth and pyramids, likely a fiction. His son Arruns was killed at Aricia by Latins and Cumaeans, ending his power in Latium.
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 215-218

people.name: Horatius Cocles
people.summary: One-eyed (cocles) hero who held the Pons Sublicius against Porsenna's army while it was demolished behind him, then swam the Tiber in armour.
people.detail: Polybius (6.55) tells a version in which he drowns, as an example of Roman self-sacrifice. A statue in the Comitium, probably of Vulcan or an unrelated lame figure, was explained by his story. Rewarded with as much land as he could plough in a day.

people.name: Mucius Scaevola
people.summary: Young Roman who infiltrated Porsenna's camp to kill him, stabbed the wrong man, and when captured thrust his right hand into a brazier to show Roman contempt for pain, earning the name Scaevola ('left-handed').
people.detail: The legend explained the cognomen of the plebeian Mucii Scaevolae, a great jurist family of the late Republic, and the 'Prata Mucia' across the Tiber.

people.name: Cloelia
people.summary: Roman girl given as hostage to Porsenna who led other girls in escaping across the Tiber; returned by Rome under the treaty, she was released by Porsenna in admiration with a group of hostages of her choosing.
people.detail: An equestrian statue of her stood at the top of the Sacra Via, a rare honour for a woman; it may originally have represented a goddess (Venus Equestris).

people.name: Aristodemus of Cumae
people.summary: Cumaean general who defeated the Etruscans in 524 and, leading the Cumaean contingent, destroyed Arruns Porsenna's army at Aricia c. 504; he then seized power as tyrant of Cumae and sheltered the exiled Tarquinius Superbus.
people.detail: Nicknamed Malakos ('the effeminate', or 'the soft'), he allegedly raised boys as girls to prevent a new aristocracy. He seized Roman grain ships in 492 as Tarquin's heir. Overthrown and killed by the sons of the exiles he had murdered. Dionysius' detailed narrative is thought to derive from a local Cumaean chronicle.
people.death: killed in an uprising of returned exiles
scholarship: Alföldi, Early Rome and the Latins (1965) 56-72

people.name: Aulus Postumius Albus
people.summary: Dictator who won the battle of Lake Regillus against the Latins (499 or 496), taking the cognomen Regillensis; he vowed the temples of Castor and of Ceres, Liber and Libera.
people.detail: His son dedicated the temple of Castor in 484. The Postumii were one of the great patrician houses of the early Republic.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 10-11

people.name: Octavius Mamilius

roles.t: Leader (dictator?) of Tusculum and of the Latin League army

people.summary: Leading man of Tusculum and son-in-law of Tarquinius Superbus, who raised the Latin League against Rome and was killed at Lake Regillus.
people.detail: The Mamilii of Tusculum later became Roman citizens and reached the consulship (from 265). Their family legend traced them to Telegonus, son of Odysseus and Circe.
people.death: killed at the battle of Lake Regillus

people.name: Spurius Cassius
people.summary: Three times consul, author of the Foedus Cassianum with the Latins (493) and the treaty with the Hernici (486), dedicator of the temple of Ceres; condemned and executed for aiming at kingship after proposing the first agrarian law.
people.detail: His career is the centre of the 'adfectatio regni' pattern. That the later Cassii were plebeians while he was consul raises the question whether the early consulship was open to non-patricians.
people.death: executed for adfectatio regni (by the quaestors or by his father)
scholarship: Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995) 269-270, 299-301

people.name: Coriolanus
people.summary: Patrician hero of the capture of Corioli (493) who opposed the plebs during the famine of 492-491, was exiled, and led the Volsci against Rome (c. 488) until his mother Veturia and wife Volumnia persuaded him to turn back.
people.detail: Livy reports conflicting traditions on his death: killed by the Volsci for his failure, or (Fabius Pictor) living on into old age in exile, lamenting that 'exile is more wretched for an old man'. Plutarch's life, the basis of Shakespeare's play, pairs him with Alcibiades. His historicity is doubtful.
people.death: uncertain: killed by the Volsci, or died in old age in exile
scholarship: Cornell, 'Coriolanus: myth, history and performance', in Braund & Gill (eds.), Myth, History and Culture in Republican Rome (2003)

people.name: Menenius Agrippa
people.summary: Consul of 503 who, according to tradition, ended the first secession by telling the plebs the fable of the limbs that starved themselves by refusing to feed the belly.
people.detail: The fable has Greek and Near Eastern parallels (Aesop, an Egyptian papyrus) and was probably attached to him later. He died so poor that the plebs paid for his funeral.
people.death: natural causes; buried at public expense

people.name: Appius Claudius Sabinus
people.summary: Sabine noble Attus Clausus of Regillum who migrated to Rome c. 504 with a large clientele, founded the patrician Claudii and as consul in 495 took a hard line against debtors.
people.detail: The archetype of Claudian arrogance (superbia) in Livy's portrayal of the family. His descendants include the decemvir (451), Caecus (312) and, through adoption and marriage, the emperors Tiberius and Claudius.

people.name: Cincinnatus
people.summary: Patrician called from his small farm across the Tiber to be dictator in 458, who rescued a consular army from the Aequi on the Algidus and resigned after sixteen days; dictator again at 80 in 439 during the Maelius affair.
people.detail: His poverty was explained by a heavy fine paid for his son Caeso, a violent opponent of the tribunes. He became the supreme exemplum of civic virtue for Romans and later for the American founders (the Society of the Cincinnati). The 458 narrative is legendary.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 39, 56

people.name: Appius Herdonius
people.summary: Sabine leader who seized the Capitol in 460 with some 2,500 exiles and slaves, calling slaves to revolt, and was killed when the Romans and Tusculans retook it.
people.detail: An example of the archaic condottiere with a personal war band, like Attus Clausus or the Fabii.
people.death: killed in the recapture of the Capitol

people.name: Appius Claudius the Decemvir
people.summary: Leading member of both decemvirates who drafted the Twelve Tables; in the second year his rule became tyrannical and his attempt to seize Verginia led to the decemvirs' fall.
people.detail: Livy portrays him as the archetypal Claudian tyrant. Whether the second decemvirate was really oppressive or became the scapegoat for the anti-plebeian conubium clause is debated.
people.death: suicide (or death) in prison awaiting trial
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I 45-48

people.name: Verginia
people.summary: Plebeian girl whom the decemvir Appius Claudius tried to seize by having a client claim her as his slave; her father, the centurion L. Verginius, stabbed her in the Forum to save her honour, triggering the second secession.
people.detail: A conscious doublet of Lucretia, her story ends the decemvirate as Lucretia's ended the monarchy.
people.death: killed by her father in the Forum

people.name: Gaius Canuleius
people.summary: Tribune of 445 who carried the law allowing intermarriage between patricians and plebeians and campaigned to open the consulship to plebeians.
people.detail: Livy's speech for him (4.3-5) is one of the great set pieces on the equality of citizens, appealing to Rome's history of admitting outsiders (Numa, Tarquinius Priscus, Servius).

people.name: Spurius Maelius
people.summary: Wealthy plebeian eques who distributed grain during the famine of 440-439 and was killed by Servilius Ahala for allegedly plotting kingship.
people.detail: His razed house site, the Aequimaelium, remained an open space below the Capitol used as a livestock market. Cicero repeatedly cites his death as just tyrannicide.

people.name: Servilius Ahala
people.summary: Master of horse to Cincinnatus in 439 who killed Spurius Maelius in the Forum; exiled later for the deed according to some sources, then recalled.
people.detail: His dagger became a symbol of tyrannicide: Marcus Brutus, Caesar's assassin, displayed Ahala's portrait alongside L. Brutus' on his coins (c. 54 BC) through his Servilian mother.

people.name: Aulus Cornelius Cossus
people.summary: Patrician who killed Lars Tolumnius of Veii in combat and dedicated the second spolia opima in the temple of Jupiter Feretrius.
people.detail: Augustus' claim to have read 'consul' on Cossus' linen corslet served to deny the honour to M. Licinius Crassus in 29-27 BC.
scholarship: Rich, 'Augustus and the spolia opima', Chiron 26 (1996)

people.name: Lars Tolumnius
people.summary: King of Veii who encouraged Fidenae to revolt and whose order (or misunderstood dice-game remark) led to the murder of four Roman envoys; killed by Cossus in battle.
people.detail: A Tolumnius family is attested in Etruscan inscriptions at Veii (a 6th-century dedication by Karcuna Tulumnes in the Portonaccio sanctuary), which lends the name authenticity.
people.death: killed in single combat by A. Cornelius Cossus

people.name: Camillus
people.summary: Conqueror of Veii (396), exiled over the booty, recalled as dictator during the Gallic sack, and celebrated as 'second founder of Rome'; five times dictator and four times triumphator.
people.detail: His legend grew enormously, especially his rescue of Rome from the Gauls (unknown to Polybius) and his role in the compromise of 367. Much of the Camillus saga was shaped in the late Republic, perhaps with Sulla or Caesar in mind (Momigliano, Bruun). Plutarch's Life is the main narrative. He died in the plague of 365.
scholarship: Momigliano, 'Camillus and Concord', CQ 36 (1942)
Bruun, 'What every man in the street used to know: M. Furius Camillus, Italic legends and Roman historiography', in Bruun (ed.), The Roman Middle Republic (2000)

people.name: Brennus
people.summary: Chief of the Senonian Gauls who besieged Clusium, won at the Allia and sacked Rome; at the weighing of the ransom he threw his sword on the scales with the words 'vae victis'.
people.detail: The name may be a title or a borrowing from the Brennus who attacked Delphi in 279. Only Livy and Plutarch name him for 390.

people.name: Marcus Manlius Capitolinus
people.summary: Consul of 392 who, woken by Juno's geese, repelled the Gallic night attack on the Capitol; later champion of debtors, condemned for aiming at kingship and thrown from the Tarpeian Rock.
people.detail: His cognomen Capitolinus perhaps derived from his house on the Capitol rather than his heroism. The prohibition on later Manlii using the praenomen Marcus is attested.
people.death: executed by being thrown from the Tarpeian Rock
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997) 476-567

people.name: Titus Manlius Torquatus
people.summary: Won the torque of a Gallic champion in single combat at the Anio (361); as consul in 340 executed his own son for fighting against orders, then defeated the Latins at Vesuvius and Trifanum.
people.detail: 'Manliana imperia' became proverbial for harsh discipline. As a youth he had defended his father, L. Manlius Imperiosus, against a tribune by threatening him with a knife.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. II (1998)

people.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus
people.summary: Won his cognomen in a duel with a Gaul aided by a raven (349), won the first battles against the Samnites at Mount Gaurus and Suessula (343), calmed the mutiny of 342 and carried the lex Valeria of 300; consul six times between 348 and 299 and said to have lived to 100.
people.detail: Cicero (De Senectute) cites his 46-year span between first and sixth consulships and 21 curule offices as a model of active old age. The Valerian annalist Valerius Antias likely embroidered his career.
scholarship: Broughton, MRR I

people.name: Gaius Licinius Stolo
people.summary: Plebeian tribune who with L. Sextius pushed through the Licinio-Sextian laws of 367 on the consulship, debt and public land, after a decade of re-election.
people.detail: Livy tells that he was spurred by his wife Fabia, jealous of her sister married to a patrician consular tribune whose lictor knocked at the door. In 357 he was fined 10,000 asses under his own law for holding 1,000 iugera with his emancipated son. The cognomen Stolo ('sucker', a shoot) was explained by his care in pruning vines.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. I (1997)

people.name: Lucius Sextius Lateranus
people.summary: Colleague of Licinius in the tribunate and first plebeian consul (366).
people.detail: His consulship marks the formal admission of plebeians to supreme magistracy, though plebeian tenure was not continuous until 342.

people.name: Gaius Marcius Rutilus
people.summary: First plebeian dictator (356) and first plebeian censor (351), four times consul; the model plebeian noble of the post-367 order.
people.detail: His son C. Marcius Rutilus Censorinus, censor twice (294, 265), carried the law against iterating the censorship.

people.name: Publius Decius Mus (consul 340)
people.summary: Plebeian military tribune who saved the army at Saticula in 343 and as consul devoted himself to the gods of the underworld at the battle of Vesuvius in 340, dying to secure victory over the Latins.
people.detail: The first of three Decii credited with devotio (his son 295, grandson perhaps 279), a family tradition whose first instance may be a projection of the second.
people.death: killed charging the enemy after his devotio at the battle of Vesuvius

people.name: Publius Decius Mus (consul 295)
people.summary: Four times consul and colleague of Fabius Rullianus, who argued for the lex Ogulnia (300) and at Sentinum (295), when the Gallic chariots broke his wing, devoted himself to death in imitation of his father.
people.detail: His devotio is attested in Livy, Polybius' contemporary-era chronology and was celebrated by the dramatist Accius in a praetexta, 'Decius'.
people.death: killed after his devotio at Sentinum
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. IV (2005)

people.name: Quintus Publilius Philo
people.summary: Plebeian statesman of many firsts: author of the Publilian laws (339), first plebeian praetor (337), and first holder of prorogued command (proconsul at Neapolis, 326).
people.detail: Four consulships and a censorship make him one of the founders of the patricio-plebeian nobility.

people.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor
people.summary: Leading patrician general of the Second Samnite War, five times consul and twice dictator, famous for his speed (Cursor), his appetite, and his severity toward his master of horse Fabius Rullianus in 325.
people.detail: Livy (9.16-19) uses him as the Roman who could have matched Alexander the Great, in a celebrated digression on what would have happened had Alexander invaded Italy. The capture of Luceria in 320 credited to him is suspect.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005) 184-261

people.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor (consul 293)
people.summary: Son of the dictator; won the battle of Aquilonia (293) against the Samnite linen legion, dedicated the temple of Quirinus with Rome's first sundial, and in his second consulship received the surrender of Tarentum (272).
people.detail: His Aquilonia triumph brought vast bronze and silver into the treasury; the spoils decorated the temple of Quirinus and the Forum.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus
people.summary: The dominant Roman general of the Samnite wars: five times consul, victor at Imbrinium (325), the Ciminian forest and Perusia (310) and Sentinum (295), censor who confined freedmen to the urban tribes and earned the cognomen Maximus (304).
people.detail: Defeated at Lautulae (315). Served as legate to his son Gurges in 292 and rode beside his chariot in the triumph. Great-grandfather (or grandfather) of the Cunctator. His career was surely embellished by Fabius Pictor, the first Roman historian and a member of his gens.
scholarship: Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vols. II-IV

people.name: Spurius Postumius Albinus (consul 321)
people.summary: Consul who surrendered at the Caudine Forks in 321 and, in Livy's version, urged the Senate to repudiate the sponsio and hand him over to the Samnites, whereupon he kicked the fetial to manufacture a just cause for war.
people.detail: The cognomen Caudinus appears in some sources. The handing-over (deditio noxae) was repeated with Mancinus in Spain in 137.

people.name: Gavius Pontius
people.summary: Samnite general who trapped and humiliated the Roman army at the Caudine Forks (321); a Pontius, probably he, was captured and beheaded after the triumph of Fabius Gurges in 291.
people.detail: His father Herennius Pontius is said to have been a friend of the philosopher Archytas and to have advised either releasing the Romans with honour or killing them all. Cicero imagines Pontius wishing he had been born when Romans took bribes.
people.death: executed at Rome after Fabius Gurges' triumph (if the same man)

people.name: Appius Claudius Caecus
people.summary: Censor of 312 who built the Via Appia and Aqua Appia, reformed Senate and tribe lists in favour of freedmen's sons and the landless, and in blind old age rallied the Senate against making peace with Pyrrhus; the first Roman author known by name.
people.detail: He wrote a collection of moral sayings in Saturnian verse ('faber est suae quisque fortunae', each man is the architect of his own fortune), a speech against Pyrrhus that Cicero read, and supposedly a treatise on legal actions; he is credited with orthographic reform (replacing intervocalic s with r, e.g. Valesius to Valerius). His elogium (ILS 54) lists three interreges, two praetorships, two consulships, a dictatorship and the censorship, and the vow of the temple of Bellona.
people.death: natural causes in old age, blind
scholarship: Humm, Appius Claudius Caecus: la République accomplie (2005)
Oakley, A Commentary on Livy Books VI-X, vol. III (2005)

people.name: Gnaeus Flavius
people.summary: Son of a freedman and secretary to Appius Claudius who published the forms of legal action and the court calendar (304) and, to the nobility's fury, was elected curule aedile.
people.detail: He dedicated a bronze shrine to Concord in the Graecostasis, vowed without the Senate's approval; the episode produced a law requiring Senate or tribune consent for dedications. Livy draws on the annalist Licinius Macer and on Piso for his story.

people.name: Quintus Ogulnius Gallus
people.summary: Plebeian tribune who with his brother Gnaeus carried the lex Ogulnia (300) opening the priesthoods; as aedile set up the she-wolf and twins at the Ficus Ruminalis (296); led the embassy that brought Aesculapius to Rome and the embassy to Ptolemy II; consul 269.
people.detail: A neat example of a plebeian noble whose career spans religious reform, monument-building and Hellenistic diplomacy in the generation before the Punic Wars.

people.name: Gellius Egnatius
people.summary: Samnite general who led an army into Etruria in 296 and forged the coalition of Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Senonian Gauls; killed at Sentinum.
people.detail: The Egnatii were a prominent Samnite family; Marius Egnatius led the Samnites in the Social War (90-89).

people.name: Scipio Barbatus
people.summary: Consul of 298, first occupant of the Tomb of the Scipios on the Via Appia, whose sarcophagus epitaph claims victories in Samnium (Taurasia, Cisauna) and the subjugation of Lucania, contradicting Livy's account.
people.detail: Great-grandfather of Scipio Africanus. The epitaph, in Saturnian verse, praises him as 'brave and wise, whose appearance matched his virtue'. Livy has him serve as legate at Sentinum and propraetor in 295 (the commander of the legion destroyed at Camerinum was 'L. Scipio').
scholarship: Coarelli, 'Il sepolcro degli Scipioni', Dialoghi di Archeologia 6 (1972)

people.name: Manius Curius Dentatus
people.summary: Plebeian 'new man' who conquered the Sabines and Praetuttii (290), defeated Pyrrhus at Beneventum (275), drained the Lacus Velinus and as censor began the Anio Vetus aqueduct; the paragon of rustic incorruptibility.
people.detail: Samnite envoys found him roasting turnips at his hearth and were told he preferred ruling those who had gold to having it. He won two triumphs (Samnites and Sabines in 290, Pyrrhus in 275) and an ovation over the Lucanians. Cato the Elder admired his farmhouse near Reate.
people.death: died in office as a commissioner for the Anio Vetus
scholarship: Forsythe, A Critical History of Early Rome (2005) 334-335

people.name: Quintus Hortensius
people.summary: Plebeian dictator appointed during the last secession of the plebs (to the Janiculum) who carried the lex Hortensia making plebiscites binding on all citizens; he died in office.
people.detail: Almost nothing else is known; the relevant books of Livy are lost.

people.name: Lucius Caecilius Metellus Denter
people.summary: First consul of the plebeian Caecilii Metelli (284), killed with much of his army when relieving Arretium from the Senones.
people.detail: Polybius calls the Roman commander a praetor; Livy's epitome and Orosius report 13,000 dead. The Metelli became one of the most powerful families of the later Republic.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Dolabella (consul 283)
people.summary: Consul who destroyed the Boii and Etruscans at Lake Vadimon (283) and helped clear the Senones from the ager Gallicus.
people.detail: Ancestor of the later Cornelii Dolabellae, including Cicero's son-in-law.

people.name: Lucius Postumius Megellus
people.summary: Three times consul, victor at Bovianum (305), dedicator of the temple of Victoria (294), and the envoy whose toga was soiled by a Tarentine in 282, promising that the stain would be washed out with blood.
people.detail: Known for arrogance: he triumphed in 294 without Senate approval and in 291 used 2,000 soldiers to clear woodland on his estate, for which he was fined.

people.name: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus
people.summary: New man from Aletrium who relieved Thurii (282), negotiated with Pyrrhus over prisoners refusing his gifts, returned the king's would-be poisoner (278) and as censor expelled P. Cornelius Rufinus from the Senate for owning ten pounds of silver plate.
people.detail: With Curius Dentatus he became the late Republic's emblem of poor but incorruptible early Romans (Cicero, Virgil 'parvoque potentem Fabricium'). He was so poor that the state provided his daughters' dowries.

people.name: Publius Valerius Laevinus
people.summary: Consul defeated by Pyrrhus at Heraclea (280) when the elephants routed his cavalry; he regrouped and shadowed Pyrrhus' march on Rome.
people.detail: Plutarch reports that he refused Pyrrhus' offer of arbitration, saying the Romans neither accepted him as judge nor feared him as enemy.

people.name: Tiberius Coruncanius
people.summary: New man from Tusculum, consul in 280 who triumphed over Vulsinii and Vulci and shielded Rome against Pyrrhus' advance; the first plebeian pontifex maximus and the first to give public instruction in law.
people.detail: Pomponius' history of jurisprudence (Digest 1.2.2.35, 38) names him as the first to profess law publicly, building on Flavius' publication. No writings survived.

people.name: Cineas
people.summary: Thessalian orator, reputedly a pupil of Demosthenes, who served Pyrrhus as diplomat; Pyrrhus said Cineas had won more cities by words than he by arms. He led the 280/279 peace embassy to Rome.
people.detail: He reportedly learned the names of Roman senators and equites within a day of arriving. He epitomised Aeneas Tacticus' work on siegecraft. Plutarch's dialogue in which he asks Pyrrhus what he will do after conquering Italy, Sicily and Carthage is the classic critique of limitless ambition.

people.name: Pyrrhus
people.fullName: Pyrrhus son of Aeacides, king of the Molossians and Epirus
people.summary: Hellenistic king of Epirus, kinsman of Alexander the Great, who answered Tarentum's call in 280, defeated Rome at Heraclea and Ausculum, conquered most of Carthaginian Sicily, and after the check at Beneventum (275) returned to Greece, dying in street fighting at Argos.
people.detail: A hostage at Ptolemy I's court, he married Ptolemy's stepdaughter Antigone and later Agathocles' daughter Lanassa. He wrote a manual on tactics and memoirs; Hannibal rated him among the greatest generals. His Italian war established Rome's reputation in the Greek world (Ptolemy II's embassy, 273) and gave Rome its first experience of a professional Hellenistic army and elephants.
people.death: stunned by a roof tile thrown by an old woman at Argos and beheaded by a soldier of Antigonus Gonatas
scholarship: Lévêque, Pyrrhos (1957)
Garoufalias, Pyrrhus, King of Epirus (1979)
Kent, A History of the Pyrrhic War (2020)

people.name: Gelon
people.summary: Deinomenid tyrant of Gela and then Syracuse, which he made the greatest Greek city of the west by mass transfers of population; victor over Carthage at Himera (480).
people.detail: He offered the mainland Greeks 200 triremes and 28,000 men against Xerxes on condition of command (Herodotus). Dionysius of Halicarnassus' story that he sent grain to Rome in 492 is an anachronism criticised by Dionysius himself.

people.name: Hiero I
people.summary: Brother and successor of Gelon who crushed the Etruscan fleet off Cumae (474) and was patron of Pindar, Bacchylides, Simonides and Aeschylus.
people.detail: His dedicated Etruscan helmets from the Cumae spoils survive from Olympia. He founded Aetna (Catana) for his son.

people.name: Dionysius I
people.summary: Tyrant of Syracuse for 38 years who fought four wars with Carthage (destroying Motya in 397), crushed the Italiote League at the Elleporus (389), took Rhegium (387), raided Pyrgi (384) and founded Adriatic outposts.
people.detail: He pioneered artillery, quinqueremes and great siege trains; wrote tragedies (one won at the Lenaea in 367); employed Celtic and Iberian mercenaries and allied with the Gauls who had sacked Rome (Justin 20.5). Plato's visits to Syracuse involved his son and successor.
people.death: natural causes (allegedly hastened by his physicians)
scholarship: Caven, Dionysius I: War-Lord of Sicily (1990)

people.name: Timoleon
people.fullName: Timoleon son of Timodemus of Corinth
people.summary: Corinthian liberator who expelled Dionysius II and other Sicilian tyrants, defeated Carthage at the Crimissus (341 or 339) and resettled Greek Sicily with thousands of colonists before retiring.
people.detail: Plutarch paired him with Aemilius Paullus. He went blind in his last years and was buried at public expense in Syracuse, with a gymnasium called the Timoleonteum.
scholarship: Talbert, Timoleon and the Revival of Greek Sicily (1974)

people.name: Alexander of Epirus
people.fullName: Alexander I son of Neoptolemus, king of the Molossians
people.summary: Brother of Olympias and uncle and brother-in-law of Alexander the Great, who campaigned in southern Italy for Tarentum (334-331), made a treaty with Rome, and was killed at Pandosia in Bruttium.
people.detail: Livy (8.24) and Justin report his saying that his nephew had fought women in Asia while he fought men in Italy. Installed by Philip II, he married Philip's daughter Cleopatra in 336 at the wedding where Philip was murdered.
people.death: killed crossing the Acheron at Pandosia

people.name: Archytas of Tarentum
people.summary: Pythagorean philosopher, mathematician and statesman who led Tarentum, head of the Italiote League, at the height of its power, and rescued Plato from Dionysius II in 361.
people.detail: He solved the problem of doubling the cube, worked on harmonics and mechanics (a flying wooden dove is attributed to him), and was elected general seven years running despite a legal limit, never defeated. Cicero has the Samnite Herennius Pontius converse with him.
people.death: drowned or shipwrecked off Apulia (Horace, Odes 1.28)
scholarship: Huffman, Archytas of Tarentum (2005)

people.name: Agathocles
people.summary: Potter's son turned tyrant of Syracuse who invaded Carthaginian Africa (310-307), took the royal title (304), intervened in southern Italy against the Bruttians and seized Corcyra, and married his daughter Lanassa to Pyrrhus.
people.detail: His Campanian mercenaries, discharged at his death, became the Mamertines who seized Messana. Polybius cited Scipio Africanus' admiration for Agathocles and Dionysius as men who combined daring with intelligence. He renounced restoring Syracusan democracy on his deathbed (Diodorus).
scholarship: Consolo Langher, Agatocle (2000)

people.name: Cleonymus of Sparta
people.summary: Spartan prince, passed over for the throne, who was hired by Tarentum against the Lucanians and Romans (303-302) and after setbacks raided the Adriatic coast until defeated by the Patavini.
people.detail: He later invited Pyrrhus to attack Sparta in 272, a campaign that preceded Pyrrhus' death at Argos.

people.name: Hiero II
people.summary: Syracusan officer of Pyrrhus' army who became general, defeated the Mamertines at the Longanus and was acclaimed king; he assisted Rome at Rhegium (270), fought Rome briefly in 264-263, and then reigned for half a century as Rome's most loyal ally.
people.detail: Polybius praises his moderation. His tax law (lex Hieronica) was adopted by Rome for Sicily. Patron of Archimedes, and builder of the giant ship Syracusia and the great altar of Syracuse.
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius I (1957) 54-56

people.name: Archimedes
people.summary: The greatest mathematician of antiquity, whose war machines held Marcellus at bay during the siege of Syracuse; killed by a Roman soldier in the sack of 212, reportedly while drawing figures in the sand. Cicero found his tomb, marked with a sphere inscribed in a cylinder, in 75 BC.
people.death: killed by a Roman soldier during the sack of Syracuse

people.name: Hannibal son of Gisco
people.summary: Carthaginian commander who defended Agrigentum (262-261), captured Scipio Asina at Lipara (260) but lost at Mylae; crucified by his own officers after the defeat off Sulci (258).
people.death: crucified by his own men in Sardinia

people.name: Xanthippus
people.summary: Spartan mercenary officer who reorganised the Carthaginian army and destroyed Regulus at Tunes (255), then left Carthage; later stories of his murder by jealous Carthaginians are dubious.

people.name: Adherbal
people.summary: Carthaginian admiral who destroyed Publius Claudius Pulcher's fleet at Drepana in 249, the only great Carthaginian naval victory of the war.

people.name: Carthalo
people.summary: Carthaginian admiral who in 249 harried the Roman convoy of Junius Pullus and manoeuvred it onto a lee shore where a storm destroyed it; raided the Italian coast in 248.

people.name: Hamilcar Barca
people.summary: Father of Hannibal, Hasdrubal and Mago. Undefeated commander in Sicily (247-241) at Heircte and Eryx, saviour of Carthage in the Mercenary War, and founder of the Barcid dominion in Spain from 237, where he drowned in 229/228. His nickname Barca probably means 'lightning'.
people.detail: Polybius (3.9-10) makes 'the wrath of Hamilcar', inflamed by the loss of Sardinia, the first cause of the Second Punic War, a view now often thought too personal. Hoyos sees him as building a Barcid power base in Spain in cooperation with the home government.
people.death: drowned crossing a river while retreating from Helice
scholarship: Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)

people.name: Hanno the Great

roles.t: General in Africa and in the Mercenary War

people.summary: Leader of the landed aristocracy at Carthage and rival of the Barcids; conqueror of territory in Africa, initially unsuccessful commander in the Mercenary War, and in Roman tradition the advocate of peace with Rome who opposed Hannibal's war.
people.debate: Livy's speeches of Hanno against the Barcids may reflect Roman interpretations more than Carthaginian politics.

people.name: Mathos
people.summary: Libyan soldier who with Spendius led the mercenary and Libyan revolt against Carthage (241-238); after his defeat he was dragged through the streets of Carthage and tortured to death.
people.death: executed at Carthage after a triumph-like procession

people.name: Hasdrubal the Fair
people.summary: Son-in-law of Hamilcar Barca and his successor in Spain (229-221), who expanded Carthaginian power by diplomacy and marriage to an Iberian princess, founded New Carthage and concluded the Ebro treaty with Rome. Murdered by a Celt.
people.death: assassinated by a Celtic servant at New Carthage

people.name: Hannibal Barca
people.summary: Rome's most dangerous enemy. Commander in Spain from 221, he took Saguntum, crossed the Alps in 218 and destroyed Roman armies at the Trebia, Trasimene and Cannae, then held out in southern Italy for thirteen more years until recalled to Africa and defeated by Scipio at Zama (202). As suffete (196) he reformed Carthage's finances and courts, then fled to Antiochus III, lost a naval battle at the Eurymedon, and finally took poison in Bithynia to avoid extradition.
people.detail: Polybius admired his generalship and noted that his multi-ethnic army never mutinied in sixteen years; Livy portrays him as brilliant but cruel and faithless ('perfidia plus quam Punica'). Modern debate centres on his strategy: whether he expected Rome's Italian alliance to collapse after Cannae, why he did not march on Rome, and whether his grand strategy was ever realistic given Roman manpower (Lazenby, Goldsworthy, Hoyos, Lancel). No portrait is certainly identified, though Barcid coins from Spain may show him.
people.death: suicide by poison at Libyssa, Bithynia, to avoid extradition to Rome
scholarship: Lancel, Hannibal (1995)
Hoyos, Hannibal's Dynasty (2003)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)
Goldsworthy, The Punic Wars (2000)

people.name: Hasdrubal Barca
people.summary: Hannibal's younger brother, commander in Spain from 218, defeated by the Scipios at Dertosa (215) but victorious over them in 211; checked by Africanus at Baecula (208), he slipped away to Italy across the Alps and was destroyed and killed at the Metaurus (207).
people.death: killed at the Metaurus; his head thrown into Hannibal's camp

people.name: Mago Barca
people.summary: Youngest brother of Hannibal; led the ambush at the Trebia, fought at Cannae and brought news of it to Carthage, served in Spain (211-206), held Minorca (Port Mahón bears his name), landed at Genua (205) and died of wounds on the voyage home in 203.
people.death: died of a thigh wound at sea off Sardinia
people.debate: Nepos and Zonaras report a different end.

people.name: Hasdrubal son of Gisco
people.summary: Carthaginian commander in Spain (214-206) who shared in the defeat of the Scipios (211) and lost at Ilipa (206); father of Sophonisba, he won Syphax for Carthage but lost both their armies to Scipio's night attack and at the Great Plains (203). He committed suicide or was killed by a mob in 202.

people.name: Hanno son of Bomilcar
people.summary: Hannibal's nephew (Appian) and officer who outflanked the Volcae at the Rhône crossing (218), probably commanded the right at Cannae, and fought the Romans in southern Italy, losing at Beneventum (214).
people.debate: It is not certain that all actions attributed to 'Hanno' in southern Italy belong to the same man.

people.name: Maharbal
people.summary: Hannibal's cavalry commander who captured the Roman vanguard after Trasimene and destroyed Centenius' cavalry; Livy has him tell Hannibal after Cannae, 'you know how to win, not how to use a victory'.
people.debate: The famous remark appears only in Livy and may be invented; Polybius gives Maharbal no such role at Cannae.

people.name: Hasdrubal (Cannae)
people.summary: Commander of Hannibal's Spanish and Celtic heavy cavalry on the left at Cannae, who routed the Roman horse, rode behind the Roman army to scatter the allied cavalry and then charged the rear of the legions.

people.name: Hasdrubal the Boetharch
people.summary: Carthaginian general defeated by Masinissa in 150 and condemned to death to appease Rome, then recalled to lead the defence of Carthage (149-146). He tortured Roman prisoners on the walls, surrendered on the Byrsa and was spared to live in Italy; his wife killed herself and their children.

people.name: Sophonisba
people.fullName: Sophonisba (Saphanba'al) daughter of Hasdrubal son of Gisco
people.summary: Carthaginian noblewoman married to Syphax to bind him to Carthage; after his capture she married Masinissa, who, ordered by Scipio to give her up as a captive, sent her poison, which she drank.

people.name: Syphax
people.summary: King of the western Numidian Masaesylii, courted by both Rome and Carthage; married Sophonisba and sided with Carthage, lost his army in Scipio's night attack (203) and was captured by Laelius and Masinissa. He died a prisoner in Italy.
people.death: died in captivity at Tibur (Livy) or after Scipio's triumph (Polybius)

people.name: Masinissa
people.summary: Massylian prince who fought for Carthage in Spain, switched to Rome in 206, helped win the Great Plains and Zama, and was made king of all Numidia. For fifty years he used the 201 treaty to annex Carthaginian territory, provoking the Third Punic War. He fathered a son at 86 and led his army at 88; Scipio Aemilianus divided his kingdom among his sons.
people.detail: Polybius (36.16) admired his vigour and claimed he transformed Numidia into a land of settled agriculture, though archaeology suggests agriculture was already established. His monumental tomb is perhaps the Medracen or El-Khroub mausoleum near Cirta.

people.name: Indibilis
people.summary: Chief of the Ilergetes of north-east Spain, captured at Cissa (218), then a shifting ally of Carthage and Rome; with his brother Mandonius he revolted against Scipio in 206 and was killed in battle in 205.
people.death: killed in battle against the Romans

people.name: Teuta
people.summary: Widow of King Agron and regent of the Illyrian kingdom whose fleets raided Epirus and the Adriatic; Rome's war on her in 229-228 brought Roman armies to the Balkans for the first time. Polybius' portrait of her as an irrational woman is hostile.

people.name: Demetrius of Pharos
people.summary: Greek-Illyrian dynast who betrayed Corcyra to Rome in 229, was rewarded with a principality, then defied Rome and was driven out in 219. At Philip V's court he urged war on Rome; he was killed attacking Messene in 214.
people.death: killed in an assault on Messene

people.name: Genthius
people.summary: Last Ardiaean king (c. 181-168), who allied with Perseus for a subsidy that never fully arrived and was conquered by Anicius in thirty days; led in triumph and interned at Iguvium.

people.name: Viridomarus
people.summary: King of the Gaesatae killed in single combat by Marcellus at Clastidium (222), whose armour was dedicated as the last spolia opima.

people.name: Aneroestes
people.summary: King of the Gaesatae who with Concolitanus led the great Gallic invasion of 225; after Telamon he fled and killed himself with his companions.

people.name: Philip V
people.summary: Antigonid king of Macedon (221-179), the 'darling of Greece' turned tyrant in Polybius' account. He allied with Hannibal (215), fought Rome in the First (214-205) and Second (200-197) Macedonian Wars, was beaten at Cynoscephalae, and then cooperated with Rome against Antiochus while quietly rebuilding his kingdom. His last years were darkened by the execution of his son Demetrius.
people.detail: Polybius traces his moral decline from 215 (the sack of Messene, the advice of Demetrius of Pharos). Walbank's biography reassessed him as an able ruler whose ambitions collided with Rome's emerging hegemony.
scholarship: Walbank, Philip V of Macedon (1940)

people.name: Perseus
people.summary: Last king of Macedon (179-168). Popular among Greek commoners and allied by marriage to the Seleucids, he alarmed Rome and Eumenes; defeated at Pydna (168), he surrendered at Samothrace, walked in Paullus' triumph and died in captivity at Alba Fucens.
people.death: died in captivity at Alba Fucens, perhaps by starvation or sleep deprivation

people.name: Andriscus
people.summary: Fuller from Adramyttium who claimed to be a son of Perseus, seized Macedonia with Thracian help in 149, killed a Roman praetor and was defeated by Metellus in 148; led in Metellus' triumph and executed.

people.name: Antiochus III
people.summary: Seleucid king (222-187) who lost at Raphia (217), restored the empire's eastern satrapies in his anabasis (212-205), took Coele-Syria at Panium (200), and crossed into Europe. Invited by the Aetolians, he fought Rome and was defeated at Thermopylae (191) and Magnesia (190/189); by the Treaty of Apamea he lost Asia Minor and paid 15,000 talents. Killed plundering a temple in Elymais.
people.detail: Polybius thought him vigorous in youth and feeble in age. Grainger and others see his war with Rome as a misjudgement born of a different understanding of legitimate spheres, not a planned bid for world power.
people.death: killed by locals while robbing the temple of Bel in Elymais
scholarship: Grainger, The Roman War of Antiochus the Great (2002)

people.name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
people.summary: Son of Antiochus III, hostage in Rome after Apamea, king from 175. He conquered most of Egypt in the Sixth Syrian War until the Roman envoy Popillius Laenas drew a circle round him at Eleusis (168). His suppression of Jewish worship in Jerusalem provoked the Maccabean revolt.
scholarship: Morkholm, Antiochus IV of Syria (1966)

people.name: Demetrius I Soter
people.summary: Son of Seleucus IV, hostage in Rome from 178, who escaped in 162 with Polybius' help and seized the Seleucid throne; killed fighting the Roman-backed pretender Alexander Balas.

people.name: Ptolemy IV Philopator
people.summary: King of Egypt (221-204), victor over Antiochus III at Raphia (217) with an army including 20,000 native Egyptian phalangites; Polybius depicts him as dissolute, ruled by his ministers Sosibius and Agathocles.

people.name: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II
people.summary: Younger brother and rival of Ptolemy VI, king of Cyrene from 163 and of Egypt from 145; in 155 he published a will leaving Cyrene to Rome, the first known royal bequest to the Roman people. Scipio Aemilianus' embassy saw him in 139 and mocked his corpulence.

people.name: Attalus I
people.summary: King of Pergamon (241-197) who won fame by defeating the Galatians, allied with Rome against Philip V, bought Aegina, helped bring the Magna Mater to Rome and urged the Second Macedonian War; he collapsed while addressing the Boeotians and died soon after.

people.name: Eumenes II
people.summary: King of Pergamon (197-159), Rome's chief ally in Asia, whose cavalry and light troops decided Magnesia and who gained most of Seleucid Asia Minor at Apamea; builder of the Great Altar and library of Pergamon. He denounced Perseus at Rome (172) but lost Roman favour after 168.

people.name: Attalus III
people.summary: Last Attalid king (138-133), reputed by hostile sources to have neglected government for botany, poisons and sculpture; on his death he bequeathed his kingdom to the Roman people.

people.name: Aristonicus
people.summary: Illegitimate son of Eumenes II who claimed the Attalid throne after the bequest of 133, minted coins as Eumenes III and rallied the poor and slaves as 'Heliopolitans'; defeated the consul Crassus Mucianus (130) but was captured by Perperna and strangled in a Roman prison.

people.name: Nabis
people.summary: Last independent king of Sparta (207-192), a revolutionary who freed helots and redistributed property; Rome and the Achaeans warred on him in 195. Murdered by the Aetolians in 192.

people.name: Philopoemen
people.summary: Eight times strategos of the Achaean League, who reformed its army on Macedonian lines, killed the Spartan tyrant Machanidas at Mantinea (207), annexed Sparta (192) and tried to keep the League independent of Rome; called 'the last of the Greeks'. Captured and poisoned by the Messenians.
people.death: forced to drink poison by the Messenians

people.name: Polybius
people.fullName: Polybius son of Lycortas, of Megalopolis
people.summary: Achaean statesman and cavalry commander (169) deported to Rome as a hostage in 167, where he became mentor to Scipio Aemilianus. He witnessed the destruction of Carthage (146) and helped reorganise Greece after the fall of Corinth. His Histories, in 40 books (1-5 complete), explained how Rome came to dominate the known world in under 53 years (220-167) and is the main source for this whole era.
people.detail: Polybius insisted on autopsy (he walked Hannibal's route over the Alps), documents (he read the Rome-Carthage treaties and Hannibal's Lacinian inscription) and political experience, and attacked rivals such as Timaeus, Phylarchus and Fabius Pictor. His analysis of the Roman 'mixed constitution' (book 6) and his comparison of legion and phalanx (book 18) are foundational. His closeness to the Scipios and his Achaean loyalties colour his judgements; Livy used him extensively for eastern affairs, sometimes translating him almost word for word.
people.death: said to have died at 82 after a fall from his horse
scholarship: Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius, 3 vols (1957-1979)
Walbank, Polybius (1972)
Eckstein, Moral Vision in the Histories of Polybius (1995)

people.name: Critolaus
people.summary: Achaean strategos in 147/146 who rejected Roman demands, suspended debt collection and led the League into war with Rome; vanished after his defeat at Scarpheia.
people.death: disappeared after Scarpheia, perhaps drowned or by poison

people.name: Diaeus
people.summary: Achaean strategos who succeeded Critolaus in 146, freed and armed slaves, and was defeated by Mummius at Leucopetra; he killed his wife and poisoned himself at Megalopolis.

people.name: Carneades
people.summary: Head of the sceptical New Academy at Athens, whose lectures for and against justice during the embassy of 155 dazzled Roman youth and alarmed Cato.

people.name: Diogenes of Babylon
people.summary: Head of the Stoa at Athens and member of the philosophers' embassy of 155; teacher of Panaetius, who later brought Stoicism into the circle of Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Critolaus of Phaselis
people.summary: Head of the Peripatetic school at Athens and member of the philosophers' embassy to Rome in 155; not to be confused with the Achaean general of 146.

people.name: Judas Maccabaeus
people.summary: Leader of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucids from 166, who rededicated the Temple in Jerusalem (164, the origin of Hanukkah) and concluded a treaty of friendship with Rome (161); killed at Elasa in 160.

people.name: Viriathus
people.summary: Lusitanian shepherd and survivor of Galba's massacre (150) who led a guerrilla war from 147 to 139, defeating a series of Roman praetors and consuls and forcing Fabius Servilianus to recognise him as a friend of the Roman people (140). Murdered by his own envoys, bribed by Caepio.
people.detail: Diodorus (33.1, 7, 21), following Posidonius, idealises him as a man of simple virtue. He became a national hero of Portugal and Spain.
people.death: stabbed in his sleep by three of his envoys bribed by Q. Servilius Caepio

people.name: Eunus
people.summary: Syrian slave from Apamea owned at Enna, a prophet and wonder-worker who led the great Sicilian slave revolt from c. 135, took the royal name Antiochus and minted coins; captured in 132, he died in prison at Morgantina.

people.name: Appius Claudius Caudex
people.summary: Consul in 264 who led the first Roman army across the Straits of Messina, beginning the First Punic War; probably a son of Appius Claudius Caecus.

people.name: Manius Valerius Messalla
people.summary: Consul in 263 who forced Hiero II into alliance, took the cognomen Messalla from Messana, displayed the first battle painting in the Curia and brought a Catanian sundial to Rome; censor 252.

people.name: Gaius Duilius
people.summary: Novus homo, consul in 260, victor of Mylae, Rome's first naval triumph; honoured with the Columna Rostrata and a torch and flute player to escort him home at night. Censor 258.

people.name: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Asina
people.summary: Son of Scipio Barbatus; consul 260, captured with his squadron at Lipara and nicknamed Asina; ransomed, he took Panormus as consul again in 254 and triumphed.

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio
people.summary: Son of Scipio Barbatus and brother of Asina; consul 259, captured Aleria in Corsica and dedicated a temple to the Tempestates; censor 258. His verse epitaph survives in the Tomb of the Scipios.

people.name: Aulus Atilius Calatinus
people.summary: Consul 258 and 254, captor of Panormus, and in 249 the first dictator to lead an army outside Italy. His epitaph called him by common consent the foremost man of Rome.

people.name: Marcus Atilius Regulus
people.summary: Consul 256, victor at Ecnomus and Adys, whose harsh terms to Carthage were rejected; defeated and captured by Xanthippus at Tunes in 255. Roman legend made him a martyr of fides who returned to Carthage to die under torture.
people.detail: Polybius (1.35) treats him as an example of the instability of fortune and knows nothing of the embassy and torture, which appear in later Roman writers (Cicero, Horace, Livy's epitome). Diodorus' story of his widow's revenge on Carthaginian prisoners suggests the torture legend arose to justify her actions.
people.death: died in Carthaginian captivity, c. 250; torture story probably legend
people.debate: Embassy and torture legend versus Polybius' silence.

people.name: Lucius Caecilius Metellus
people.summary: Victor at Panormus (250) who captured and paraded the Carthaginian elephants; consul 251 and 247, pontifex maximus from 243, dictator 224. Blinded rescuing the Palladium from the burning temple of Vesta in 241.
people.detail: His son's funeral eulogy, quoted by Pliny (7.139-140), lists the ten greatest things a Roman could achieve and claims he achieved them all: first warrior, best orator, bravest general, greatest commands, highest honour, supreme wisdom, foremost senator, great wealth honestly gained, many children, and fame. It is a key text of Roman aristocratic values.

people.name: Publius Claudius Pulcher
people.summary: Consul 249, who threw the sacred chickens overboard before losing the fleet at Drepana; mocked the Senate by naming his freedman dictator, and was condemned and fined. Died before 246.

people.name: Gaius Lutatius Catulus
people.summary: Consul 242, who trained the new privately funded fleet and destroyed the Carthaginian relief fleet at the Aegates Islands on 10 March 241, ending the First Punic War; negotiated the treaty that bears his name.

people.name: Gaius Flaminius
people.summary: The most controversial politician of the inter-war years: as tribune (232) he distributed the ager Gallicus, as praetor (227) he was first governor of Sicily, as consul (223) he defeated the Insubres and triumphed against the Senate's will, and as censor (220) he built the Via Flaminia and Circus Flaminius. He supported the Lex Claudia. Killed at Lake Trasimene in his second consulship.
people.detail: The hostile tradition, rooted in Fabius Pictor and amplified by Livy, portrays him as an impious demagogue who despised the auspices. Modern scholars see a successful novus homo with a strong popular base, and the senatorial verdict as partly retrospective scapegoating for Trasimene.
people.death: killed by an Insubrian horseman at Lake Trasimene
scholarship: Feig Vishnia, State, Society and Popular Leaders in Mid-Republican Rome (1996)

people.name: Marcus Claudius Marcellus
people.summary: Five times consul, winner of the last spolia opima at Clastidium (222), defender of Nola, conqueror of Syracuse (212) and the most aggressive Roman commander against Hannibal; Posidonius called him the sword of Rome to Fabius' shield. Killed in an ambush near Venusia in his fifth consulship.
people.detail: His removal of Syracusan art to Rome was remembered as the start of Roman passion for Greek art. He dedicated a double temple of Honos and Virtus. Plutarch's Life, paired with Pelopidas, preserves much of the family tradition.
people.death: killed in a Numidian ambush near Venusia

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus
people.summary: Five times consul and twice dictator, the architect of the strategy of attrition against Hannibal after Trasimene, which earned him the name Cunctator ('Delayer'). He recovered Tarentum in 209, became princeps senatus, and opposed Scipio's invasion of Africa.
people.detail: Nicknamed Verrucosus for a wart on his lip and Ovicula ('little lamb') as a mild child. He was augur for 62 years. Ennius' line 'one man by delaying restored the state to us' fixed his reputation. His opposition to Scipio, whom he saw as reckless and Hellenising, is sometimes read as factional rivalry.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus
people.summary: Consul 219, victor in the Second Illyrian War over Demetrius of Pharos, and consul 216, killed at Cannae. Roman tradition, shaped by his descendants and Polybius' patrons, made him the cautious consul overruled by his rash plebeian colleague Varro.
people.debate: Polybius' favourable portrait reflects his friendship with Paullus' grandson Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Gaius Terentius Varro
people.summary: Novus homo, consul 216, who commanded on the day of Cannae and escaped. The Senate thanked him for not despairing of the Republic, and he held commands and embassies for years afterwards, which casts doubt on the hostile tradition that he alone caused the disaster.
people.debate: Livy's claim that he was a butcher's son is aristocratic slander.

people.name: Marcus Minucius Rufus
people.summary: Consul 221 (Istrian war); master of horse to Fabius in 217, then raised to equal imperium by the Lex Metilia and nearly destroyed at Gerunium; killed at Cannae. An altar he dedicated to Hercules calls him dictator.

people.name: Tiberius Sempronius Longus
people.summary: Consul 218, recalled from preparing an invasion of Africa at Lilybaeum to face Hannibal in the north, and defeated at the Trebia.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Scipio
people.summary: Father of Africanus. As consul 218 he missed Hannibal at the Rhône but sent his army on to Spain, was wounded at the Ticinus, and from 217 fought in Spain alongside his brother Gnaeus until both were killed in 211.
people.death: killed near Castulo in the battle of the Upper Baetis

people.name: Gnaeus Cornelius Scipio Calvus
people.summary: Consul 222 (captured Mediolanum), who from 218 led the Roman war in Spain, winning at Cissa, the Ebro and Dertosa; killed at Ilorci in 211 after his Celtiberian mercenaries deserted.

people.name: Scipio Africanus
people.summary: The general who won the Second Punic War. Given the Spanish command at 25 as a privatus, he took New Carthage, won at Baecula and Ilipa and drove Carthage from Spain; as consul (205) he invaded Africa, destroyed the armies of Syphax and Hasdrubal, and defeated Hannibal at Zama (202). Later censor and princeps senatus, legate to his brother against Antiochus, and target of political trials, he died in self-imposed exile at Liternum.
people.detail: Polybius, writing for Scipio's adoptive grandson and drawing on Laelius, insists that Scipio's successes came from calculation and that he only exploited the popular belief in his divine inspiration. Livy preserves the legends: daily visits to the Capitoline temple, a serpent father like Alexander. His career strained republican norms (command without office, consulship under age, a cognomen from a conquered land) and he became the model for later great men. Polybius' and Livy's portraits both shaped the Renaissance image of the virtuous general.
people.death: died at his villa at Liternum
scholarship: Scullard, Scipio Africanus: Soldier and Politician (1970)
Lazenby, Hannibal's War (1978)

people.name: Gaius Laelius
people.summary: Scipio Africanus' lifelong friend and lieutenant: commander of the fleet at New Carthage, of the cavalry at Zama, captor of Syphax; consul 190. In old age he gave Polybius his eyewitness account of Scipio.

people.name: Gaius Laelius Sapiens
people.summary: Son of Africanus' friend and the closest friend of Scipio Aemilianus, whom he served at Carthage (stormed the Cothon, took Nepheris); consul 140. A cultivated orator and Stoic sympathiser, he is the speaker of Cicero's De amicitia.

people.name: Gaius Claudius Nero
people.summary: Consul 207, whose secret forced march north from Apulia brought about the destruction of Hasdrubal at the Metaurus; censor 204 with his enemy Livius Salinator. Ancestor of the Claudii Nerones and so of the emperor Tiberius.

people.name: Marcus Livius Salinator
people.summary: Consul 219 and victor in the Second Illyrian War, then convicted of unfairly dividing booty and retired in bitterness; recalled, he was consul again in 207 and shared the victory of the Metaurus. As censor in 204 he feuded with his colleague Nero.

people.name: Quintus Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Four times consul (237, 224, 212, 209), dictator 210 and conqueror of Capua (211), where he executed the Campanian senators, by tradition before the Senate's letter of clemency could be opened.

people.name: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus
people.summary: Master of horse 216, consul 215 and 213, who led the slave legions (volones) to victory at Beneventum (214) and freed them; killed in an ambush in Lucania in 212.
people.death: killed in an ambush in Lucania

people.name: Marcus Valerius Laevinus
people.summary: Commander in the Adriatic who checked Philip V at Apollonia (214), concluded the alliance with the Aetolians (211) and, as consul 210, completed the conquest of Sicily by taking Agrigentum.

people.name: Publius Sulpicius Galba Maximus
people.summary: Consul 211 and commander in the First Macedonian War (sack of Aegina); as consul again in 200 he persuaded the reluctant comitia to vote for war on Philip V. Dictator 203.

people.name: Titus Quinctius Flamininus
people.summary: Consul at about 30 in 198, victor at the Aous and Cynoscephalae, and proclaimer of the freedom of the Greeks at the Isthmian Games of 196. Fluent in Greek, he was worshipped in Greek cities and was the first living Roman shown on a coin. In 183 he pressed Prusias to surrender Hannibal.
people.detail: Badian's study framed him as an adroit manipulator for whom philhellenism served Realpolitik and personal ambition; Polybius admired his diplomatic skill. His brother Lucius was expelled from the Senate by Cato.
scholarship: Badian, Titus Quinctius Flamininus: Philhellenism and Realpolitik (1970)

people.name: Manius Acilius Glabrio
people.summary: Novus homo and consul 191, who defeated Antiochus III at Thermopylae and besieged the Aetolians at Heraclea and Naupactus; vowed the temple of Pietas, which held the first gilded equestrian statue in Rome. His candidacy for the censorship in 189 was destroyed by charges of embezzlement backed by Cato.

people.name: Lucius Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus
people.summary: Younger brother of Africanus, consul 190, nominal victor at Magnesia over Antiochus III and holder of the cognomen Asiaticus. Prosecuted for misappropriating Seleucid money, fined, and deprived of his public horse by Cato in 184.

people.name: Gnaeus Manlius Vulso
