people.summary: Consul 189, who campaigned against the Galatians without clear authorisation and supervised the Treaty of Apamea. His troops' Asiatic booty was blamed by Livy for introducing luxury to Rome.

people.name: Marcus Fulvius Nobilior
people.summary: Consul 189, conqueror of Ambracia and peacemaker with the Aetolians, patron of Ennius, who accompanied his campaign. He built the temple of Hercules Musarum with the looted Muses and a calendar with commentary, and as censor 179 the Basilica Aemilia et Fulvia.

people.name: Scipio Nasica
people.summary: Son of Gnaeus Scipio Calvus, judged the 'best man' in Rome and chosen to receive the Magna Mater at Ostia in 204; as consul 191 he completed the subjugation of the Boii.

people.name: Scipio Nasica Corculum
people.summary: Son of Nasica (cos. 191) and son-in-law of Africanus; distinguished at Pydna, consul 162 and 155 (took Delminium), censor 159, pontifex maximus from 150. He had the first stone theatre demolished and opposed Cato's call to destroy Carthage, arguing that fear of Carthage kept Rome disciplined.

people.name: Cato the Elder
people.summary: Novus homo from Tusculum who rose by talent and self-advertisement to consul (195) and censor (184). Hero of Thermopylae (191), scourge of the Scipios, prosecutor or defendant in some 44 trials, champion of old Roman frugality against Greek luxury (while learning Greek himself), author of the first Latin prose history (Origines), the earliest surviving Latin prose work (De agri cultura) and some 150 published speeches. He spent his last years demanding the destruction of Carthage.
people.detail: Cato's writings fixed the image of the stern, self-made Roman for posterity. His De agri cultura describes a slave-run estate of 100-240 iugera producing wine and oil for market, a document of the agrarian transformation of Italy. Astin argues that his anti-Hellenism was selective and political rather than a blanket rejection of Greek culture.
scholarship: Astin, Cato the Censor (1978)

people.name: Lucius Valerius Flaccus
people.summary: Patrician patron who launched Cato's career, his colleague as consul (195) and censor (184), and princeps senatus from 184 until he died in the plague of 180.

people.name: Marcus Aemilius Lepidus
people.summary: Envoy who delivered Rome's ultimatum to Philip V at Abydos (200); consul 187 (Via Aemilia) and 175, censor 179, pontifex maximus from 180 and princeps senatus from 179, the most honoured senator of his generation. A later family coin shows him crowning Ptolemy V as guardian.
people.debate: The guardianship of Ptolemy V is attested only by Valerius Maximus and a late coin and may be family legend.

people.name: Lucius Aemilius Paullus Macedonicus
people.summary: Son of the consul killed at Cannae; governor of Ulterior (decree of Lascuta, 189), consul 182 and 168, victor of Pydna over Perseus, executor of the sack of Epirus and reorganiser of Macedonia. His triumph of 167 brought enough booty to end the citizen property tax; his two younger sons died around it. Father of Scipio Aemilianus and Fabius Aemilianus by adoption.
people.detail: Polybius, tutor to his sons, portrays him as the model of old Roman virtue and incorruptibility; at his death his estate barely covered his widow's dowry. He was also a connoisseur who took Perseus' library and erected a monument at Delphi.

people.name: Scipio Aemilianus
people.fullName: Publius Cornelius Scipio Aemilianus Africanus Numantinus
people.summary: Natural son of Aemilius Paullus, adopted by Africanus' son; fought at Pydna at 17, won the mural crown at Intercatia, destroyed Carthage (146) as consul under age, and as consul again in 134 besieged and razed Numantia. Patron of Polybius, Panaetius, Terence, Lucilius and the so-called Scipionic circle. Censor 142. He died suddenly in 129 amid the Gracchan crisis, rumour said by murder.
people.detail: Polybius was his mentor and companion at Carthage, and Cicero made him the ideal statesman of De re publica. His career, with dispensations from age limits and the iteration ban, illustrates the tension between republican rules and the demand for proven commanders. He opposed the Gracchan land commission's work on behalf of the Italian allies. 'Scipionic circle' as a cultural programme is largely Cicero's construction.
people.death: found dead in his bed in 129; murder suspected but never proven
scholarship: Astin, Scipio Aemilianus (1967)

people.name: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Macedonicus
people.summary: Praetor who defeated Andriscus at Pydna (148) and the Achaeans at Scarpheia (146); builder of the first marble temple in Rome (Jupiter Stator) and the Porticus Metelli; consul 143 in Spain, censor 131. He died having seen four sons reach the consulship, a byword for good fortune.

people.name: Lucius Mummius Achaicus
people.summary: Novus homo, praetor in Ulterior (153), consul 146, destroyer of Corinth, first new man to earn a victory cognomen. Remembered both as an honest administrator in Greece and as a philistine who threatened to make shippers replace lost masterpieces. Censor 142 with Scipio Aemilianus.

people.name: Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus
people.summary: Tribune who protected Lucius Scipio from prison despite personal enmity; governor of Citerior who made the lasting Gracchan treaties with the Celtiberians and founded Gracchurris; consul 177 (Sardinian war) and 163, censor 169. He married Cornelia, daughter of Africanus, and fathered the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus.

people.name: Servius Sulpicius Galba
people.summary: Praetor in Ulterior who massacred the disarmed Lusitanians in 150; prosecuted in 149 with Cato against him, he was acquitted by parading his weeping children. Cicero rated him the finest orator of his day. Consul 144.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus
people.summary: Adopted into the Fabii; consul 142, who campaigned against Viriathus and, trapped at Erisane in 140, concluded the peace recognising him as a friend of the Roman people.

people.name: Quintus Servilius Caepio
people.summary: Consul 140 and brother of Servilianus, who repudiated his brother's peace, renewed the war and procured the murder of Viriathus by bribing his envoys (139).

people.name: Gaius Hostilius Mancinus
people.summary: Consul 137 who surrendered his army of 20,000 to the Numantines. The Senate disowned his treaty and in 136 had him handed over naked and bound by the fetials; the Numantines refused him. He commissioned a statue of himself in that state.

people.name: Decimus Junius Brutus Callaicus
people.summary: Consul 138, imprisoned by a tribune over the levy; founder of Valentia for Viriathus' veterans and conqueror of Gallaecia, where he led his men across the dreaded 'Lethe'. Patron of the tragic poet Accius.

people.name: Gaius Popillius Laenas
people.summary: Consul 172 (with the first all-plebeian college) and 158, who as envoy in 168 drew a circle around Antiochus IV at Eleusis and forced him out of Egypt.

people.name: Lucius Anicius Gallus
people.summary: Praetor 168 who conquered Genthius' Illyria in thirty days; at his triumphal games he made famous Greek flute-players fight like boxers to amuse the crowd (Polybius 30.22). Consul 160.

people.name: Lucius Licinius Lucullus
people.summary: Consul 151, imprisoned by tribunes over the levy, who then waged an unauthorised war on the Vaccaei and massacred the surrendered men of Cauca. He built a temple of Felicitas with Mummius' Greek statues.

people.name: Manius Manilius
people.summary: Consul 149 and commander at the beginning of the siege of Carthage; one of the founders of Roman civil law (Ulpian lists him with Brutus and Scaevola) and a speaker in Cicero's De re publica.

people.name: Lucius Marcius Censorinus
people.summary: Consul 149 who delivered to the disarmed Carthaginians the order to abandon their city, and then failed in his assaults on the walls. Censor 147.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi
people.summary: Tribune 149 who created the first standing court for extortion (Lex Calpurnia), consul 133 against the Sicilian slaves, censor 120, opponent of Gaius Gracchus and author of moralising Annales that dated the onset of luxury to 154.

people.name: Publius Rupilius
people.summary: Consul 132, friend of Scipio Aemilianus, who crushed the Sicilian slave revolt at Tauromenium and Enna and gave Sicily the Lex Rupilia; he prosecuted the followers of Tiberius Gracchus and died soon after his brother failed in a consular election.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Pictor
people.summary: Senator who served in the Gallic war of 225 and was sent to Delphi after Cannae; author, in Greek, of the first history of Rome by a Roman, presenting Rome's case to the Hellenistic world and blaming the Second Punic War on Barcid ambition. Polybius used and criticised him.
scholarship: Dillery, 'Quintus Fabius Pictor and Greco-Roman Historiography at Rome', in Miller et al. (eds.), Vertis in usum (2002)

people.name: Livius Andronicus
people.summary: Greek from Tarentum, probably brought to Rome as a captive and freed by a Livius; staged the first Latin tragedy and comedy at the Ludi Romani of 240, translated the Odyssey into Saturnian verse (Odusia) and composed the state hymn of 207.

people.name: Ennius
people.summary: Poet from Rudiae in Calabria, speaking Oscan, Greek and Latin ('three hearts'); brought to Rome by Cato, patronised by Fulvius Nobilior and the Scipios, granted citizenship in 184. His Annales, in Latin hexameters, told Roman history from Aeneas to his own day and was the national epic until Virgil.
scholarship: Skutsch, The Annals of Quintus Ennius (1985)

people.name: Plautus
people.summary: Umbrian from Sarsina, the most popular comic dramatist of Rome; 21 comedies adapted from Greek New Comedy survive, full of song, wordplay and Roman references (Miles Gloriosus, Pseudolus, Menaechmi, Amphitruo).

people.name: Terence
people.summary: Former slave from Carthaginian Africa who wrote six polished comedies after Menander and Apollodorus (166-160), close to the circle of Scipio Aemilianus and Laelius; he died on a journey to Greece.
people.debate: His birth date (195 or 185) is uncertain.

people.name: Tiberius Gracchus
people.summary: Grandson of Scipio Africanus and son of the twice-consul Ti. Sempronius Gracchus, he carried the agrarian law of 133 through the plebeian assembly, deposed a vetoing colleague and was clubbed to death on the Capitol while seeking re-election.
people.detail: As quaestor in 137 he negotiated the treaty that saved Mancinus' army at Numantia, which the senate repudiated, a humiliation some ancient writers saw as his motive. His speeches, quoted by Plutarch and Appian, framed the land question as the plight of soldiers who had 'not a clod of earth to call their own'. Whether a sincere reformer or ambitious noble, he made the tribunate and the popular assembly instruments of policy against the senate.
people.death: clubbed to death on the Capitol by senators led by Scipio Nasica during the tribunician elections, summer 133
scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)
Bernstein, Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus (1978)

people.name: Gaius Gracchus
people.summary: Younger brother of Tiberius and the greatest orator of his generation, he passed a sweeping legislative programme in two tribunates (123-122): subsidised grain, equestrian juries, Asian tax contracts, colonies, roads and protection against summary execution. He died in the first use of the senatus consultum ultimum.
people.detail: Cicero considered him the most gifted orator Rome had produced. A dream in which Tiberius told him he could not escape the same fate was reported by Cicero from Gaius' own account. His laws reshaped Roman politics for a century, binding the equites and urban plebs into politics as distinct interests.
people.death: had his slave Philocrates kill him in the grove of Furrina as Opimius' forces closed in, 121
scholarship: Stockton, The Gracchi (1979)

people.name: Cornelia
people.summary: Daughter of Scipio Africanus and mother of the Gracchi, she bore twelve children of whom three survived, refused a marriage offer from Ptolemy VIII, and became the model Roman matron, famous for calling her sons her jewels.
people.detail: Her statue, set up in the Porticus Metelli, had a base inscribed 'Cornelia, daughter of Africanus, mother of the Gracchi' (CIL VI 31610). Fragments of letters ascribed to her in Cornelius Nepos urge Gaius not to stand for the tribunate; their authenticity is disputed. She retired to Misenum and kept a cultured household.
people.death: natural causes at Misenum, date uncertain (after 121)

people.name: Marcus Octavius
people.summary: Tribune in 133 and friend of Tiberius Gracchus, he vetoed the agrarian bill, himself possessing much public land, and was removed from office by a vote of the plebeian assembly, an unprecedented act.

people.name: Scipio Nasica Serapio
people.summary: Pontifex maximus and leader of the senatorial attack that killed Tiberius Gracchus on the Capitol in 133. Sent to Asia on an embassy to remove him from popular hatred, he died at Pergamon.
people.detail: As consul in 138 he had been briefly imprisoned by tribunes over the levy. His nickname Serapio, from a resemblance to a pig dealer, was given him by a tribune. He was the first pontifex maximus to leave Italy.

people.name: Opimius

roles.t: Head of the commission dividing Numidia

people.summary: Destroyer of Fregellae as praetor and, as consul in 121, the first magistrate to act under a senatus consultum ultimum, killing Gaius Gracchus and Fulvius Flaccus and executing thousands of their followers. Acquitted in 120, he was condemned in 109 for taking Jugurtha's bribes.
people.detail: The vintage of his consular year, the Opimian wine of 121, became legendary; Pliny says some of it survived, thick as honey, almost two centuries later.
people.death: in exile at Dyrrachium, date unknown

people.name: Fulvius Flaccus
people.summary: Gracchan ally who proposed citizenship for the Italians as consul in 125, conducted the first Roman campaign beyond the Alps for Massalia, and took the extraordinary step for an ex-consul of serving as tribune with Gaius Gracchus in 122.
people.death: killed with his son while hiding in a bath-house after the Aventine was stormed, 121

people.name: Marcus Livius Drusus (tribune 122)
people.summary: Senatorial tribune who outbid Gaius Gracchus in 122 with proposals for twelve colonies and rent-free allotments, splitting Gaius' following. As consul and proconsul he triumphed over the Scordisci in Macedonia. Father of the tribune of 91.

people.name: Jugurtha

roles.t: Commander of Numidian contingent at Numantia

people.summary: Grandson of Masinissa and adopted son of Micipsa, he served under Scipio at Numantia, seized all Numidia by murdering his co-heirs, massacred Italian traders at Cirta and fought Rome for seven years, exposing the venality of the Roman nobility. Betrayed by Bocchus to Sulla, he was paraded in Marius' triumph.
people.detail: Sallust portrays him as brilliant, charming and ruthless, a mirror held up to Roman decline. His war made the careers of Marius and Sulla and was the immediate occasion of the enrolment of the capite censi.
people.death: starved to death in the Tullianum at Rome after Marius' triumph, January 104
scholarship: Paul, A Historical Commentary on Sallust's Bellum Jugurthinum (1984)

people.name: Metellus Numidicus
people.summary: Incorruptible aristocrat who restored discipline to the Roman army in Numidia (109-108) and beat Jugurtha at the Muthul, only to be superseded by his own legate Marius. As censor he tried to expel Saturninus and Glaucia from the senate; in 100 he refused Saturninus' oath and went into exile until 98.

people.name: Bocchus I
people.summary: Father-in-law of Jugurtha, he joined him against Rome in 108 for the promise of a third of Numidia, then after defeats in 106 negotiated with Sulla and handed Jugurtha over in 105, receiving western Numidia. In 91 he dedicated a gilded group of the surrender on the Capitol.

people.name: Scaurus
people.summary: From an impoverished patrician family, he became consul in 115 and princeps senatus for a quarter-century, the archetypal senatorial grandee, suspected of taking Jugurtha's bribes, builder of the stone Milvian Bridge and the Via Aemilia Scauri. He wrote an autobiography in three books.
people.detail: Accused in 90 of inciting the Italian allies, he answered: 'Varius of Sucro says Scaurus incited the allies to revolt; Scaurus denies it. Which of the two do you believe, citizens?', and was acquitted. Sallust depicts him as clever and corrupt; Cicero revered him.

people.name: Marius
people.summary: A novus homo of equestrian family from Arpinum, he married into the patrician Julii (he was Julius Caesar's uncle by marriage), won the Jugurthine War, destroyed the Cimbri and Teutones in an unprecedented run of five consecutive consulships, and was credited with recruiting the landless poor into the legions. Driven out by Sulla in 88, he returned with Cinna in 87 and died early in his seventh consulship.
people.detail: He was the first great beneficiary of the army's new dependence on its commander, but a clumsy politician: in 100 he turned on his ally Saturninus, and in 88 his greed for the Mithridatic command provoked Sulla's march on Rome. The massacres of 87 darkened his memory. Caesar restored his trophies in 65 and built his own popularity on Marius' name.
scholarship: Evans, Gaius Marius: A Political Biography (1994)
Matthew, On the Wings of Eagles (2010)

people.name: Caepio (consul 106)
people.summary: Consul in 106, he restored senatorial juries and sacked Tolosa, whose sacred treasure disappeared. His refusal to cooperate with the novus homo Mallius Maximus produced the catastrophe of Arausio (105). Stripped of command, condemned in 103 and exiled.
people.death: in exile at Smyrna, date unknown

people.name: Catulus (consul 102)
people.summary: Cultured aristocrat, poet and memoirist who shared the victory of Vercellae with Marius and disputed the credit. He vowed the round temple of Fortuna Huiusce Diei (Temple B, Largo Argentina). An enemy of Marius, he was proscribed in 87.
people.death: suicide by charcoal fumes in a freshly plastered room to avoid Marius' vengeance, 87

people.name: Boiorix
people.summary: King of the Cimbri who led them at Arausio and killed the captured legate Aurelius Scaurus; Plutarch says he rode up to the Roman camp before Vercellae to challenge Marius to fix a day and place for battle.
people.death: killed in the battle of Vercellae, 30 July 101

people.name: Saturninus
people.summary: Radical tribune and ally of Marius who passed land grants for veterans, a cheap grain law and the first law on maiestas. His use of violence, culminating in the murder of a consular candidate, led to the senatus consultum ultimum of 100 and his death in the Curia.
people.death: stoned to death with roof tiles in the Curia Hostilia, where he had been confined after surrendering, December 100

people.name: Manius Aquillius
people.summary: Marius' colleague in 101, he ended the Second Sicilian Slave War, killing Athenion in single combat. As envoy in Asia in 89 he pushed Nicomedes IV to attack Pontus, starting the First Mithridatic War.
people.death: handed to Mithridates by Mytilene and executed at Pergamon by molten gold poured down his throat, 88

people.name: Rutilius Rufus
people.summary: Stoic pupil of Panaetius, jurist and historian, he fought at the Muthul, introduced gladiatorial drill as consul after Arausio, and as Scaevola's legate in Asia protected provincials from the publicani, for which an equestrian jury convicted him of extortion in 92. He lived out his exile honoured at Smyrna.
people.death: natural causes in exile at Smyrna, after 78

people.name: Crassus the orator
people.summary: The greatest orator of his generation and Cicero's model, protagonist of the De oratore. He championed the colony at Narbo, as consul passed the lex Licinia Mucia expelling false citizens and as censor banned Latin rhetoric schools. He backed Drusus in 91.
people.death: pleurisy days after a passionate speech against the consul Philippus, September 91

people.name: Scaevola Pontifex
people.summary: Jurist who wrote the first systematic treatise on Roman civil law in 18 books, a model governor of Asia whose edict Cicero copied, and pontifex maximus. Cicero studied law with him and his cousin the augur.
people.death: murdered at the temple of Vesta on the orders of the younger Marius, 82

people.name: Marcus Livius Drusus (tribune 91)
people.summary: Son of Gaius Gracchus' opponent, he tried in 91 to reconcile everyone with a package of senatorial juries, colonies and citizenship for the Italians, and was assassinated, which triggered the Social War. His nephew Cato the Younger grew up in his house.
people.detail: Asked what he would leave his heirs, he reportedly said a house so built that all could see what he did. Dying, he asked when the Republic would again have a citizen like him.
people.death: stabbed by an unknown assassin in the atrium of his house, autumn 91
scholarship: Mouritsen, Italian Unification (1998)

people.name: Poppaedius Silo

roles.t: Consul of the Italian confederation (Marsic group)

people.summary: Marsic leader, friend of Drusus, and the most dangerous Italian general of the Social War; Plutarch tells how, staying with Drusus, he dangled the child Cato out of a window when the boy refused to support Italian citizenship.
people.death: killed in battle against Mamercus Aemilius in Apulia, 88

people.name: Papius Mutilus

roles.t: Consul of the Italian confederation (Samnite group)

people.summary: Samnite commander of the southern Italian forces in the Social War, he overran Campania in 90 and later fought for the Marians. His coins in Oscan bear his name and the title embratur (imperator).
people.death: suicide at Teanum after his wife refused to admit him while he was proscribed, 80

sources.r: Italian allied issues with legend Mutil embratur

people.name: Pompeius Strabo
people.summary: Picene magnate and father of Pompey, he took Asculum in 89, passed the lex Pompeia giving Latin rights to the Transpadanes, and in 87 played both sides between Cinna and the senate. Hated for his greed, he died during the siege of Rome.
people.death: died in camp in 87, by lightning according to one tradition, by plague in another; the crowd dragged his body from its bier

people.name: Sulpicius
people.summary: Brilliant orator (a speaker in Cicero's De oratore) who as tribune in 88 tried to distribute the new Italian citizens across all tribes and transferred the Mithridatic command from Sulla to Marius, provoking Sulla's march on Rome.
people.death: betrayed by a slave and killed near Laurentum; his head displayed on the Rostra, 88

people.name: Sulla

roles.t: Dictator legibus scribundis et rei publicae constituendae

people.summary: Impoverished patrician who captured Jugurtha, won the Social War in the south, and as consul in 88 became the first Roman to march on Rome. He defeated Mithridates in Greece, returned to win a second civil war in 83-82, proscribed his enemies and as dictator rebuilt the constitution around a strengthened senate before retiring voluntarily.
people.detail: He called himself Felix, the Fortunate, and in Greek Epaphroditus, favoured of Aphrodite. Ancient writers saw a split personality: charming, cultivated and dissolute in youth, merciless in power. His memoirs, in 22 books, shaped later accounts. His settlement collapsed within a decade, but its institutions (standing courts, a 600-member senate, the cursus rules) lasted, and his example of a general taking the state by force haunted every later crisis.
people.death: haemorrhage at his villa near Puteoli, 78; state funeral and cremation in the Campus Martius
scholarship: Keaveney, Sulla: The Last Republican (2nd ed. 2005)
Santangelo, Sulla, the Elites and the Empire (2007)

people.name: Cinna
people.summary: Consul four years running (87-84), he championed the new Italian citizens, was driven from Rome, returned with Marius and the army from Nola, and dominated the 'Cinnanum tempus', a period of uneasy normality before Sulla's return. His daughter Cornelia married Julius Caesar.
people.death: killed by mutinous troops at Ancona while preparing to cross to Illyricum, 84

people.name: Carbo
people.summary: Leader of the Marian regime after Cinna's death, three times consul. He lost the war of 82 in the north and fled to Africa and Sicily.
people.death: captured on Cossyra and executed by Pompey at Lilybaeum, 82

people.name: Marius the Younger
people.summary: Son (perhaps adopted nephew) of Marius, elected consul at 26 in 82 for the magic of the name. Beaten by Sulla at Sacriportus, he ordered the murder of leading senators in Rome before being besieged in Praeneste.
people.death: suicide in a tunnel under Praeneste as the town surrendered, 82

people.name: Pontius Telesinus
people.summary: Samnite general who led the last Italian army against Sulla, marching on Rome itself and nearly winning at the Colline Gate, crying that the wolves must be destroyed in their lair.
people.death: killed at the battle of the Colline Gate, 1 November 82

people.name: Mithridates VI
people.fullName: Mithridates VI Eupator Dionysus, king of Pontus
people.summary: King of Pontus for 57 years and Rome's most persistent enemy, he built an empire around the Black Sea, overran Asia in 88 and ordered the massacre of the Italians there, and fought three wars against Sulla, Lucullus and Pompey. The Greek East saw him as a liberator for a time.
people.detail: Pliny says he spoke the 22 languages of his subjects; he experimented with poisons and antidotes until, the story goes, poison would not kill him. Cicero called him the greatest king after Alexander. He fought on into his late sixties, planning, it was said, to invade Italy from the north.
people.death: had his Gallic bodyguard Bituitus kill him at Panticapaeum after his son Pharnaces' revolt, 63
scholarship: McGing, The Foreign Policy of Mithridates VI Eupator (1986)
Mayor, The Poison King (2010)

people.name: Archelaus
people.summary: Cappadocian Greek, Mithridates' leading general, who conquered Greece in 88, held the Piraeus against Sulla and lost the battles of Chaeronea and Orchomenus. He negotiated the preliminaries of Dardanus with Sulla; suspected of treachery by Mithridates, he went over to the Romans in 83. His son became priest-king of Comana and husband of Berenice IV.

people.name: Fimbria
people.summary: Violent Marian officer who had the consul Flaccus murdered and took over his army, beat Mithridates' son at the Rhyndacus, sacked Ilium and nearly captured Mithridates. Abandoned by his troops when Sulla arrived.
people.death: suicide in the sanctuary of Asclepius at Pergamon, 85

people.name: Metellus Pius
people.summary: Earned his cognomen Pius by campaigning for his exiled father's recall. He held out against the Marians, joined Sulla in 83, won at Faventia, and fought Sertorius for eight years in Spain, cautiously and in the end successfully. His death in 63 opened the pontificate to Caesar.

people.name: Sertorius
people.summary: From Nursia in the Sabine hills, he fought at Arausio, spied among the Cimbri in Gallic dress, lost an eye in the Social War, and as the last Marian commander built a Romano-Iberian state in Spain that defeated Metellus and Pompey for years. He was murdered by his own officers.
people.detail: Plutarch's admiring Life (from Sallust) presents a humane, gifted commander with a counter-senate in exile, a school for Iberian nobles at Osca, and a white fawn sent by Diana; the Iberians called him a new Hannibal. Modern debate asks whether he was a Roman patriot fighting the Sullan regime or a warlord drifting into separatism.
people.death: stabbed at a banquet at Osca by Perperna and other officers, 73 or 72
scholarship: Konrad, Plutarch's Sertorius (1994)
Spann, Quintus Sertorius and the Legacy of Sulla (1987)

people.name: Perperna
people.summary: Marian praetor who brought the remnant of Lepidus' army to Sertorius, resented his subordination, and murdered him. Beaten by Pompey in his first battle, he tried to buy his life with Sertorius' correspondence.
people.death: executed by Pompey, who burned Sertorius' letters unread, 72

people.name: Lepidus (consul 78)
people.summary: Enriched in the Sullan proscriptions, he turned against Sulla's system as consul in 78 and led an armed revolt in 77 that Catulus and Pompey crushed. Father of the triumvir.
people.death: died in Sardinia after his defeat, 77

people.name: Lucullus

roles.t: Quaestor (the only officer to follow Sulla to Rome)
Proquaestor and fleet commander in the East

people.summary: Sulla's most loyal officer and literary executor, he relieved Cyzicus, conquered Pontus, routed Tigranes at Tigranocerta and relieved the Asian cities of Sullan debt, but was undone by his soldiers' mutiny and the hostility of the equites, and superseded by Pompey. He spent his last years in proverbial luxury.
people.detail: Pliny credits him with bringing the cherry tree to Italy from Cerasus. His gardens on the Pincian (horti Luculliani), his fishponds at Misenum and Naples, his library open to scholars, and his banquets ('Lucullus dines with Lucullus') became bywords. Cicero made him a speaker in his Academica.
people.death: natural causes after a period of mental decline, c. 57/56

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

scholarship: Keaveney, Lucullus: A Life (1992)

people.name: Tigranes the Great
people.summary: Raised as a hostage at the Parthian court, he made Armenia an empire stretching to Syria, called himself King of Kings and built Tigranocerta. Son-in-law and ally of Mithridates, he was routed by Lucullus in 69 and submitted to Pompey in 66, keeping Armenia as a client kingdom.

people.name: Spartacus
people.summary: Thracian, perhaps once a soldier in Roman service, enslaved and trained as a gladiator at Capua, he led the breakout of 73 and an army of runaway slaves that defeated several Roman armies, including both consuls of 72, before Crassus crushed it in 71.
people.detail: Plutarch calls him more Hellenic than Thracian in intelligence and gentleness; Appian says he shared booty equally. There is no evidence he aimed to abolish slavery. Since Marx, who called him the finest fellow in all ancient history, he has been a modern political icon.
people.death: killed fighting in the final battle on the upper Silarus, 71; body never found
scholarship: Shaw, Spartacus and the Slave Wars (2001)
Strauss, The Spartacus War (2009)

people.name: Crixus
people.summary: Gallic gladiator who broke out of Capua with Spartacus and led the Gauls and Germans of the slave army; he separated from Spartacus and was destroyed near Mount Garganus.
people.death: killed near Mount Garganus by the praetor Arrius, 72

people.name: Crassus
people.summary: The richest man in Rome, who built his fortune buying proscribed estates and burning houses cheaply, won the Colline Gate for Sulla, crushed Spartacus, and used loans and legal advocacy to place much of the senate in his debt. Partner of Pompey and Caesar in the 'First Triumvirate', he sought military glory against Parthia and died after Carrhae.
people.detail: Plutarch puts his landed wealth at over 7,000 talents and quotes him saying no one was rich who could not keep an army on his income. He escaped the Marian massacres by hiding for eight months in a seaside cave in Spain. His death removed the balance between Caesar and Pompey.
people.death: killed in a scuffle at a parley with the Parthians after the defeat at Carrhae, 53
scholarship: Ward, Marcus Crassus and the Late Roman Republic (1977)

people.name: Pompey

roles.t: Raised a private army for Sulla

people.summary: Son of Pompeius Strabo, he raised an army at 23, won his name Magnus under Sulla, triumphed three times over three continents, cleared the sea of pirates in three months, conquered and reorganised the East, and held three consulships, one without colleague. Allied with Caesar from 60, married to his daughter Julia, he drifted to the optimates after her death and led their cause in the civil war, losing at Pharsalus.
people.detail: His career was built on extraordinary commands outside the normal cursus, and in that sense he did more than anyone to undermine the Republic he finally defended. He wanted to be the first man by the senate's free consent rather than by force, and never quite understood that this was not on offer. He built Rome's first stone theatre and governed his provinces through legates, both precedents for the Principate.
people.death: stabbed by Achillas and Lucius Septimius while landing at Pelusium, Egypt, 28 September 48

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

scholarship: Seager, Pompey the Great (2nd ed. 2002)
Gelzer, Pompeius (1949)

people.name: Verres

roles.t: Quaestor (deserted Carbo with the pay chest)

people.summary: Governor of Sicily whose plunder of art, grain tithes and justice was exposed by Cicero in 70, making Cicero's name. He fled into exile at Massilia before the trial's end.
people.death: killed in the proscriptions of 43, reportedly for refusing to surrender his Corinthian bronzes to Antony

people.name: Hortensius
people.summary: The leading advocate in Rome until Cicero beat him in the Verres case, famous for his florid 'Asiatic' style, prodigious memory and luxury: Varro says he was the first to serve peacock at dinner and kept fishponds where he wept over a dead lamprey. Later Cicero's friend and fellow-optimate.

people.name: Gabinius

roles.t: Legate of Pompey in the East

people.summary: Pompey's man, author of the lex Gabinia of 67, consul in 58 when Cicero was exiled, governor of Syria who restored Ptolemy XII in defiance of the senate. Condemned for extortion in 54, he was recalled by Caesar and fought for him in Illyricum.
people.death: died of illness at Salona while commanding for Caesar in Illyricum, 47

people.name: Catiline

roles.t: Officer under Pompeius Strabo at Asculum

people.summary: Patrician of a declining family, a Sullan killer during the proscriptions, he failed three times to win the consulship and in 63 organised a conspiracy of indebted nobles, ruined Sullan veterans and the dispossessed, which Cicero exposed. He died fighting at Pistoria.
people.detail: Sallust makes him a monster of ambition and depravity with a fierce courage; Cicero's invective defines him. Modern historians stress the real debt crisis of the 60s and the programme of debt cancellation (tabulae novae) he offered.
people.death: killed at the battle of Pistoria, January 62
scholarship: Rawson, Cicero (1975)

people.name: Lentulus Sura
people.summary: Ex-consul expelled from the senate in 70, he won a second praetorship and became the leader of the Catilinarian plotters in Rome, believing a Sibylline prophecy that three Cornelii would rule. Stepfather of Mark Antony.
people.death: strangled in the Tullianum by order of the consul Cicero, 5 December 63

people.name: Cicero
people.summary: Equestrian from Arpinum who became Rome's greatest orator and its best-documented individual, consul in 63 when he suppressed Catiline, exiled in 58, wavering in the civil war, and in 44-43 leader of the senate against Antony in the Philippics. He was proscribed and killed.
people.detail: Over 900 of his letters (to Atticus, his brother Quintus, friends, and Brutus), 58 speeches and a shelf of philosophical and rhetorical works survive. The letters are the single most important near-contemporary evidence for the period: unguarded, dated, and partisan. His vanity and indecision are notorious; his commitment to government by consensus of the propertied classes (concordia ordinum, consensus omnium bonorum) was genuine. Through Petrarch and the Renaissance his style became the model of Latin prose.
people.death: killed near his villa at Formiae by soldiers under Herennius and Popillius Laenas, 7 December 43; head and hands displayed on the Rostra
scholarship: Rawson, Cicero (1975)
Mitchell, Cicero: The Ascending Years (1979)
Lintott, Cicero as Evidence (2008)

people.name: Cato the Younger
people.summary: Great-grandson of Cato the Elder and a Stoic, he made inflexible adherence to principle a political weapon: he swung the senate to execute the Catilinarians, filibustered against Caesar and Pompey, and opposed every extraordinary command until he backed Pompey's sole consulship. His suicide at Utica after Thapsus made him the martyr of the Republic.
people.detail: As tribune he expanded the grain dole to win the plebs from Caesar. Cicero complained that he spoke as if in Plato's Republic rather than Romulus' sewer. His half-sister Servilia was Brutus' mother; his daughter Porcia married Bibulus and then Brutus.
people.death: suicide at Utica, April 46, tearing open his wound after doctors bandaged it

people.name: Clodius
people.summary: Patrician of the Claudii who spelled his name in plebeian fashion, profaned the Bona Dea rites, had himself adopted into a plebeian family to become tribune, and in 58 passed free grain, restored the collegia, exiled Cicero and annexed Cyprus. His street organisation dominated Rome until Milo's men killed him.
people.detail: Long portrayed (from Cicero) as the triumvirs' hired thug, he is now seen as an independent popularis with real support among the urban plebs. His sister Clodia is usually identified with Catullus' Lesbia. His widow Fulvia later married Curio and Antony.
people.death: killed on the Via Appia near Bovillae by Milo's retinue, 18 January 52
scholarship: Tatum, The Patrician Tribune: Publius Clodius Pulcher (1999)

people.name: Milo
people.summary: Optimate tribune who fought Clodius with gangs of gladiators, worked for Cicero's recall, and killed Clodius in 52. Convicted despite Cicero's defence, he went into exile at Massilia.
people.death: killed near Compsa leading a revolt in southern Italy with Caelius, 48

people.name: Bibulus
people.summary: Caesar's constantly overshadowed colleague as aedile, praetor and consul. In 59 he declared that he was watching the sky for omens and stayed home, rendering Caesar's laws religiously void. He failed to stop Caesar crossing the Adriatic in 48. Husband of Cato's daughter Porcia.
people.death: died of illness and exhaustion while commanding the fleet off Corcyra, 48

people.name: Julius Caesar
people.summary: Patrician of an old but undistinguished family, nephew by marriage of Marius and son-in-law of Cinna, he rose as a popularis, formed the alliance with Pompey and Crassus, conquered Gaul in eight years, crossed the Rubicon in 49, defeated the Pompeians in Spain, Greece, Egypt, Asia, Africa and Spain again, and ruled as dictator until he was assassinated on the Ides of March 44.
people.detail: His reforms as dictator included the Julian calendar, the enfranchisement of Transpadane Gaul, colonies at Corinth and Carthage, a reduced grain dole, debt relief and a senate of 900. His Commentaries are both literary masterpieces and political propaganda. His policy of clemency (clementia) towards defeated citizens was admired and resented: to be pardoned implied a master. The question whether he sought monarchy or simply a pre-eminence the system could not accommodate is the central historiographical question of the period, from Mommsen's hero to Syme's party leader and Morstein-Marx's popular politician defending his dignitas.
people.death: stabbed 23 times by senators in the curia of Pompey, 15 March 44
scholarship: Gelzer, Caesar: Politician and Statesman (1968)
Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (2006)
Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (2021)
Syme, The Roman Revolution (1939)

people.name: Julia
people.summary: Caesar's only legitimate child, married to Pompey in 59 to seal the alliance; ancient writers agree that the marriage was a genuinely happy one and that her death in childbirth in 54 loosened the bond between the two men.
people.death: in childbirth, late summer 54; buried in the Campus Martius by popular demand

people.name: Vatinius
people.summary: Caesar's tribune in 59 who carried the lex Vatinia giving him Gaul and Illyricum. Mocked by Cicero (In Vatinium) for his scrofulous appearance, and later defended by him under pressure. He triumphed over Illyricum in 42.

people.name: Labienus

roles.t: Caesar's legate pro praetore in Gaul

people.summary: Picene tribune who prosecuted Rabirius and restored popular election of priests in 63, then Caesar's ablest lieutenant throughout the Gallic War, often in independent command (Sabis, Treveri, Lutetia). In 49 he joined Pompey, his old patron, and fought Caesar to the end.

people.name: Quintus Cicero

roles.t: Legate of Caesar in Gaul and Britain
Legate of his brother in Cilicia

people.summary: Marcus' younger brother, a hot-tempered but able soldier who held his camp against the Nervii in 54. The election handbook (Commentariolum petitionis) addressed to Marcus in 64 is attributed to him, its authenticity debated.
people.death: killed in the proscriptions with his son, 43

people.name: Ariovistus

roles.t: King of the Suebi in Gaul

people.summary: Germanic king invited into Gaul by the Sequani and Arverni against the Aedui; he won at Magetobriga, settled 120,000 Germans in Alsace and was named a friend of the Roman people in 59. Caesar defeated him in 58.
people.death: died by 54, after his defeat (Caesar BG 5.29)

people.name: Diviciacus

roles.t: Vergobret and druid of the Aedui

people.summary: Aeduan noble and druid who addressed the senate in 61 asking help against Ariovistus, stayed with Cicero (who discusses his augury in De divinatione), and was Caesar's chief Gallic ally in 58-57, interceding for his brother Dumnorix.

people.name: Dumnorix
people.summary: Diviciacus' ambitious brother, who controlled Aeduan tolls, backed the Helvetii and refused to go to Britain in 54, fleeing Caesar's camp.
people.death: cut down by Caesar's cavalry, crying that he was a free man of a free state, 54

people.name: Ambiorix
people.summary: King of the Eburones who destroyed a legion and five cohorts at Atuatuca in 54 by false promises of safe conduct. Caesar devastated his territory in 53 and invited neighbours to plunder it, but Ambiorix escaped with four horsemen and disappears from history; today he is a Belgian national hero with a statue at Tongeren.

people.name: Cassivellaunus

roles.t: War leader of the British coalition

people.summary: British king north of the Thames chosen to lead resistance to Caesar in 54. He used chariot tactics and scorched earth, lost his oppidum, and accepted terms brokered by Commius, including tribute and hostages.

people.name: Vercingetorix

roles.t: King and commander of the Gallic coalition

people.summary: Arvernian noble whose father Celtillus had been killed for aiming at kingship. In 52 he united most of Gaul against Caesar, used scorched earth, beat Caesar at Gergovia and was besieged and forced to surrender at Alesia. Gold staters bearing his name survive.
people.detail: Caesar portrays him as a capable and charismatic commander who imposed discipline by terror. The surrender scene with arms laid at Caesar's feet is from later writers. Nineteenth-century France made him a national hero; Napoleon III's colossal statue stands on Mont Auxois.
people.death: executed in the Tullianum after Caesar's Gallic triumph, 46

people.name: Commius

roles.t: King of the Atrebates (installed by Caesar)
Commander of the relief army at Alesia

people.summary: Made king of the Atrebates by Caesar and used as his envoy to Britain, he joined the great revolt in 52 and was one of the four commanders of the relief army at Alesia. After surviving an assassination attempt by Caesar's officer Volusenus, he swore never again to come into the presence of a Roman and fled to Britain, where coins of a Commios are found.

people.name: Publius Crassus

roles.t: Caesar's cavalry commander and legate in Gaul
Officer in his father's Parthian campaign

people.summary: Younger son of the triumvir, a cultured and admired young officer who saved the day against Ariovistus and conquered Aquitania in 56. He brought 1,000 Gallic cavalry east and died leading a breakout at Carrhae.
people.death: killed (or had himself killed) at Carrhae; his head was displayed on a lance before his father's army, 53

people.name: Surena
people.summary: Head of the great Suren clan, which had the hereditary right to crown the Arsacid king, he was barely 30 when he destroyed Crassus' army at Carrhae, using horse archers resupplied by a camel train. Plutarch describes his effeminate make-up and a baggage train of 200 wagons of concubines.
people.death: executed by King Orodes II out of jealousy, c. 52

people.name: Orodes II
people.summary: Arsacid king who seized the throne from his brother Mithridates III and reigned during Carrhae and the invasions of 51 and 40. Grief at the death of his son Pacorus at Gindarus broke him.
people.death: murdered by his son and successor Phraates IV, c. 37

people.name: Curio

roles.t: Caesarian commander in Sicily and Africa

people.summary: Brilliant, dissolute young optimate whose vast debts Caesar paid; as tribune in 50 he blocked every attempt to recall Caesar unless Pompey also disarmed, carrying the senate 370 to 22. For his father's funeral games he built two wooden theatres that pivoted to form an amphitheatre with the audience still seated (Pliny).
people.death: killed fighting at the Bagradas against Juba's army, refusing to flee, August 49

people.name: Domitius Ahenobarbus (consul 54)

roles.t: Pompeian commander at Corfinium and Massilia

people.summary: Brother-in-law of Cato and implacable enemy of Caesar, designated to succeed him in Gaul. Captured and released at Corfinium, he defended Massilia and fought at Pharsalus. Great-great-grandfather of the emperor Nero.

people.name: Metellus Scipio
people.fullName: Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio Nasica
people.summary: A Scipio Nasica adopted by Metellus Pius, father-in-law of Pompey from 52, he commanded the Pompeian centre at Pharsalus and the army in Africa beaten at Thapsus.
people.death: stabbed himself on board ship off Hippo Regius when intercepted, telling his captors 'the commander is well', 46

people.name: Juba I
people.summary: King of Numidia who hated Caesar, who had once pulled his beard in a lawsuit at Rome. He destroyed Curio's army at the Bagradas in 49 and fought with the Pompeians at Thapsus. Numidia was then annexed as Africa Nova, with Sallust as first governor.
people.death: killed in a suicide pact with Petreius after Thapsus, 46

people.name: Ptolemy XII Auletes
people.summary: The 'Flute-player', an illegitimate son of Ptolemy IX, he bought Roman recognition in 59 for 6,000 talents, was expelled by the Alexandrians in 58, and was restored by Gabinius in 55, borrowing ruinously from the banker Rabirius Postumus. Father of Cleopatra VII.

people.name: Ptolemy XIII

roles.t: King of Egypt with Cleopatra VII

people.summary: Brother and co-ruler of Cleopatra, whose regents had Pompey murdered in 48 and fought Caesar in the Alexandrian War.
people.death: drowned in the Nile when his boat sank after the battle of the Nile, 47

people.name: Cleopatra VII
people.summary: Last ruler of the Ptolemaic dynasty and the only Ptolemy, Plutarch says, who learned Egyptian. She allied herself with Caesar, by whom she had a son, Caesarion, and then with Antony, by whom she had three children, and sought to rebuild Ptolemaic power in the East through Roman partners. Defeated with Antony at Actium, she killed herself in 30.
people.detail: Hostile Augustan propaganda made her a decadent eastern seductress; Plutarch stresses her intelligence and conversation over her beauty. Her portraits on coins show a strong aquiline profile. She administered Egypt competently in a time of famine and civil war.
people.death: suicide at Alexandria, probably c. 10-12 August 30, by asp bite or poison
scholarship: Roller, Cleopatra: A Biography (2010)
Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)

people.name: Caesarion

roles.t: Proclaimed King of Kings at the Donations of Alexandria

people.summary: Son of Cleopatra, claimed as Caesar's son, a claim Caesar may have tacitly allowed and Octavian's side denied. Proclaimed King of Kings in 34, he was a direct threat to Octavian's position as Caesar's heir.
people.death: executed on Octavian's orders after being lured back to Alexandria, 30

people.name: Pharnaces II
people.fullName: Pharnaces II, king of the Bosporus
people.summary: Son of Mithridates VI who led the revolt that drove his father to suicide in 63 and was rewarded by Pompey with the Bosporan kingdom. In 48 he invaded Pontus, beat Domitius Calvinus at Nicopolis, and was routed by Caesar at Zela in a single afternoon.
people.death: killed fighting his rebel governor Asander in the Bosporus, 47

people.name: Deiotarus

roles.t: King of Galatia (and part of Pontus)

people.summary: Loyal Galatian ally of Rome in the Mithridatic wars, rewarded by Pompey, he raised two legions on the Roman model, fought for Pompey at Pharsalus and then for Caesar at Nicopolis. Accused before Caesar by his grandson of plotting murder, he was defended by Cicero (Pro rege Deiotaro, 45).

people.name: Gnaeus Pompeius the Younger

roles.t: Commander of the Pompeian Egyptian squadron

people.summary: Elder son of Pompey, a fierce and brutal commander who raised the Spanish rising of 46-45 and commanded at Munda.
people.death: hunted down and killed near Lauro after Munda; his head displayed at Hispalis, April 45

people.name: Mark Antony
people.summary: Grandson of the orator Marcus Antonius and son of Antonius Creticus, he was Caesar's cavalry officer, tribune in 49, commander of the left at Pharsalus and consul in 44. After the Ides he seized Caesar's papers and funds, fought the senate at Mutina, formed the triumvirate, won Philippi, and ruled the East, where his alliance and marriage with Cleopatra and his failed Parthian campaign gave Octavian the material for war. Defeated at Actium, he killed himself at Alexandria.
people.detail: Our image of him comes overwhelmingly from Cicero's Philippics and Augustan propaganda, filtered through Plutarch's Life, Shakespeare's source. He was a brave and popular soldier, a reasonable administrator of the East, and a reluctant enemy of Octavian until 33.
people.death: suicide at Alexandria after the defection of his fleet and cavalry, 1 August 30
scholarship: Pelling, Plutarch: Life of Antony (1988)
Goldsworthy, Antony and Cleopatra (2010)

people.name: Lepidus
people.summary: Son of the rebel consul of 78, Caesar's master of horse in 44, he joined Antony after Mutina and became the third triumvir, holding Spain and then Africa. When he claimed Sicily in 36 his troops deserted to Octavian and he was stripped of power, keeping only the chief priesthood.

people.name: Brutus

roles.t: Quaestor in Cilicia (under his father-in-law Appius Claudius)
Governor of Cisalpine Gaul for Caesar

people.summary: Son of Servilia (Cato's half-sister) and of the Brutus killed by Pompey in 77, adopted by his uncle Servilius Caepio, he fought for Pompey, was pardoned and promoted by Caesar, and led the conspiracy of the Ides, claiming descent from the Brutus who expelled the kings. He lost the second battle of Philippi and killed himself.
people.detail: Cicero's letters reveal that Brutus lent money to the city of Salamis in Cyprus at 48 per cent interest and had a prefect besiege its council to collect. He wrote philosophy (De virtute) and was admired by Cicero, who dedicated the Brutus and other works to him. His EID MAR denarius is the most famous Roman coin.
people.death: suicide after the second battle of Philippi, falling on a sword held by his friend Strato, 23 October 42
scholarship: Tempest, Brutus: The Noble Conspirator (2017)

people.name: Cassius

roles.t: Liberator commander in Syria and Asia

people.summary: Survivor of Carrhae who saved Syria from the Parthians in 52-51, Pompeian admiral, pardoned by Caesar, and the driving force behind the conspiracy. In 43 he seized Syria, took Rhodes and joined Brutus at Philippi.
people.death: suicide in the first battle of Philippi, believing the battle lost, October 42

people.name: Decimus Brutus

roles.t: Caesar's fleet commander against the Veneti and at Massilia

people.summary: One of Caesar's most trusted officers, named in his will as a secondary heir, he nonetheless joined the conspiracy and fetched Caesar to the senate on the Ides. Besieged by Antony at Mutina, he was relieved in 43 but abandoned by his troops.
people.death: killed by a Gallic chieftain, Camilus, on Antony's orders while fleeing to Macedonia, September 43

people.name: Fulvia
people.summary: Wife in turn of Clodius, Curio and Antony, and the most politically active Roman woman of her age. She organised Clodius' funeral riot, defended Antony's interests in Rome in 43, and with Lucius Antonius raised war against Octavian in 41. Her portrait may appear on coins as Victory, and a Phrygian city briefly took her name.
people.death: illness at Sicyon, 40, after fleeing Italy

people.name: Lucius Antonius
people.summary: Mark Antony's younger brother, who as consul in 41 championed the dispossessed Italian landowners against Octavian and was besieged in Perusia. Spared, he was sent to govern Spain, where he died.
people.death: died in Spain, probably soon after 40

people.name: Octavia
people.summary: Octavian's sister, married first to Gaius Claudius Marcellus (consul 50) and then, to seal the treaty of Brundisium, to Antony, for whom she mediated the treaty of Tarentum. Antony divorced her in 32; she raised his children by Fulvia and Cleopatra with her own. Through her daughters she was ancestress of Caligula, Claudius and Nero.

people.name: Sextus Pompey

roles.t: Pompeian officer in Africa and Spain
Prefect of the fleet and sea coast (by senatorial decree)

people.summary: Pompey's younger son, he escaped Munda, rebuilt a Pompeian force in Spain, was appointed naval commander by the senate in 43 and, proscribed, made Sicily a refuge for the proscribed and runaway slaves, starving Rome with his blockade. Recognised at Misenum in 39, he was crushed by Agrippa at Naulochus in 36.
people.detail: He styled himself son of Neptune on his coins. Augustan writers branded him a pirate leader of slaves; Welch reinterprets him as the last defender of a republican legitimacy.
people.death: captured in Asia and executed at Miletus by Antony's officer Marcus Titius, 35
scholarship: Welch, Magnus Pius (2012)

people.name: Ventidius Bassus
people.summary: From Picenum, led as a child captive in Pompeius Strabo's triumph of 89, he made a living contracting mules and carriages for magistrates, rose under Caesar and Antony, and as Antony's legate drove the Parthians out of Syria, killing Pacorus at Gindarus. He celebrated the first Roman triumph over Parthia, 27 November 38.

people.name: Quintus Labienus

roles.t: Envoy of Brutus and Cassius to Parthia
Commander of Parthian forces in Asia Minor

people.summary: Son of Titus Labienus, sent by the liberators to seek Parthian help, he stayed after Philippi and in 40 led a Parthian army through Syria and Asia Minor, calling himself imperator Parthicus on coins showing a saddled Parthian horse.
people.death: captured and killed in Cilicia after his defeat by Ventidius, 39

people.name: Pacorus
people.summary: Son and co-regent of Orodes II, he invaded Syria in 51 and again in 40, when he took Jerusalem and installed Antigonus as king. Popular in Syria for his justice, Dio says.
people.death: killed at the battle of Gindarus, 38

people.name: Phraates IV
people.summary: Murdered his father Orodes and his brothers to take the throne, destroyed Antony's siege train and repelled his invasion of Media in 36, and later in 20 returned the standards lost at Carrhae to Augustus.
people.death: poisoned by his wife Musa and son Phraataces, 2 BC

people.name: Artavasdes II
people.summary: Son of Tigranes the Great, a Hellenised king who wrote Greek tragedies. He advised Crassus to invade through Armenia, then married his sister to the Parthian prince; Crassus' head arrived at his court during a performance of the Bacchae. He deserted Antony in 36 and was captured in 34, paraded in silver chains at Alexandria.

people.name: Varro

roles.t: Pompey's legate in the pirate war
Director of Caesar's planned public library

people.summary: The most learned Roman, author of some 74 works in over 600 books, of which On the Latin Language (partly) and On Agriculture survive. A Pompeian who surrendered to Caesar in Spain, he was chosen by Caesar to organise Rome's first public library, was proscribed in 43 but protected, and lived to nearly 90. His Antiquities fixed the Varronian chronology still used for early Rome.

people.name: Sallust
people.summary: From Amiternum, expelled from the senate in 50, restored by Caesar, he enriched himself as governor of Africa Nova and retired to write the Bellum Catilinae, the Bellum Jugurthinum and the Histories (78-67, fragmentary). His theme is the moral decline of the Roman nobility after 146; his style, archaic and abrupt, consciously imitates Thucydides and Cato.
people.detail: He is a source for the Jugurthine War, Catiline, Sertorius, Lepidus and Spartacus, and a historian whose moralising framework (avarice and ambition) shaped the very idea of a 'fall of the Republic'. His gardens (horti Sallustiani) became imperial property.

people.name: Lucretius
people.summary: Author of De rerum natura, a six-book hexameter poem expounding Epicurean atomism and arguing that fear of the gods and of death is groundless. Almost nothing is known of his life; Jerome's story that a love potion drove him mad and that he wrote in lucid intervals is unreliable. Cicero read the poem in 54.
people.death: died c. 55-50; Jerome's tale of suicide is doubtful

people.name: Catullus

roles.t: Staff member of Memmius in Bithynia

people.summary: From Verona, the leading 'new poet' (neoteric) whose 116 surviving poems include love poems to 'Lesbia', usually identified with Clodia, sister of Clodius, and abusive verses on Caesar and his engineer Mamurra. Caesar, Suetonius says, accepted his apology and invited him to dinner the same day.

people.name: Augustus
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Divi filius Augustus (born Gaius Octavius)
people.summary: Founder of the Principate. Great-nephew and adopted son of Julius Caesar, he won the civil wars at Actium (31 BC) and then, through the settlements of 27 and 23 BC, built a monarchy disguised as a restored Republic that lasted, in its essentials, for three centuries.
people.detail: His power rested on control of the armies and of Egypt, on tribunicia potestas and imperium maius, and on an auctoritas cultivated through building (he claimed to have found Rome brick and left it marble), religion, moral legislation and an all-pervasive visual programme. He doubled the size of the empire, created a standing professional army with fixed terms and a military treasury, and organised Rome's city administration. His long search for an heir (Marcellus, Agrippa, Gaius and Lucius, finally Tiberius) dominated his reign. Sources: his own Res Gestae, Suetonius's Life, Dio books 51-56, Velleius (adulatory), Tacitus Annals 1 (hostile). Modern views range from Syme's ruthless faction-leader to Zanker's master of images.
people.death: natural causes at Nola, 19 August AD 14; deified 17 September

people.name: Livia

roles.t: Augusta and priestess of Divus Augustus

people.summary: Wife of Augustus for 52 years and mother of Tiberius and Drusus by her first husband Tiberius Claudius Nero. The most influential woman of the early Principate, granted sacrosanctity (35 BC) and adopted into the Julian family as Julia Augusta by Augustus's will.
people.detail: Tacitus and Dio cast her as a poisoner who cleared the way for Tiberius by eliminating Marcellus, Gaius, Lucius, Postumus and even Augustus; modern scholars largely reject these charges, seeing a powerful patron and adviser. She managed huge estates and a household of over a thousand slaves and freedmen known from the columbarium of her staff. Her villa at Prima Porta produced the garden frescoes and the Augustus of Prima Porta. Claudius deified her in 42.

people.name: Agrippa

roles.t: Holder of tribunicia potestas and imperium maius

people.summary: Augustus's lifelong friend, admiral and right-hand man, victor of Naulochus and Actium, builder of the Pantheon, the Aqua Virgo and the Baths of Agrippa, husband of Julia and father of Gaius, Lucius, Agrippina the Elder and Agrippa Postumus.
people.detail: Of obscure equestrian family, he declined triumphs to avoid overshadowing Augustus. In the principate he governed the East (23-21, 16-13 BC), ended the Cantabrian war (19 BC) and settled the Bosporus (14 BC). He compiled a world map (orbis pictus) displayed in the Porticus Vipsania, used by Pliny. His powers from 18 BC made him effectively co-regent and designated successor.

people.name: Julia the Elder
people.summary: Augustus's only child, married successively to Marcellus, Agrippa (five children) and Tiberius, and the instrument of his dynastic policy. Exiled to Pandateria in 2 BC for adultery and possibly conspiracy; she died at Rhegium soon after her father.
people.death: starvation or neglect at Rhegium, AD 14

people.name: Marcellus
people.summary: Augustus's nephew and first son-in-law, married to Julia in 25 BC and widely seen as heir; his early death at 19 was lamented by Virgil in Aeneid 6 and commemorated by the Theatre of Marcellus.

people.name: Maecenas

roles.t: Augustus's agent in Rome and Italy

people.summary: Etruscan-born equestrian friend and agent of Augustus who never held office, managing Rome in his absences and patronising Virgil, Horace and Propertius, so that his name became a byword for literary patronage.
people.detail: His influence waned after 23 BC, perhaps because of his wife Terentia's link to the Murena conspiracy. Seneca mocked his effeminate prose style and luxury. His gardens on the Esquiline included the 'auditorium of Maecenas'. He left his estate to Augustus.

people.name: Drusus the Elder
people.summary: Younger son of Livia and brother of Tiberius, conqueror of Raetia (15 BC) and the first Roman general to reach the Elbe (9 BC). Popular and reputedly republican in sympathy, he died after a riding accident in Germany; his sons were Germanicus and Claudius.
people.death: complications after a fall from his horse in Germany, 9 BC

people.name: Gaius Caesar
people.summary: Eldest son of Agrippa and Julia, adopted by Augustus in 17 BC and groomed as heir. He met the Parthian king on the Euphrates in AD 2, was wounded at Artagira in Armenia, and died at Limyra.
people.death: after a wound received at Artagira, at Limyra, 21 February AD 4

people.name: Lucius Caesar
people.summary: Younger son of Agrippa and Julia, adopted by Augustus with his brother; he died suddenly at Massilia on his way to Spain, honoured with the cenotaph decrees of Pisa.

people.name: Agrippa Postumus
people.fullName: Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa Postumus (Agrippa Julius Caesar)
people.summary: Posthumous son of Agrippa, adopted by Augustus in AD 4 alongside Tiberius but disowned and exiled to Planasia in AD 7 for his violent temper; killed immediately after Augustus's death.

people.name: Julia the Younger
people.summary: Granddaughter of Augustus, wife of Lucius Aemilius Paullus; exiled to the island of Trimerus in AD 8 for adultery with Decimus Silanus, the same year as Ovid's banishment, and died there twenty years later.

people.name: Tiberius
people.fullName: Tiberius Julius Caesar Augustus (born Tiberius Claudius Nero)

roles.t: Commander in the Alps, Illyricum and Germany

people.summary: Son of Livia and stepson of Augustus, the greatest general of his generation (Raetia, Pannonia, Germany, the Illyrian revolt), adopted in AD 4 and emperor from 14 to 37. His reign was fiscally prudent and militarily cautious but darkened by treason trials, the ascendancy of Sejanus and his withdrawal to Capri.
people.detail: Tacitus's portrait of a dissembling tyrant whose true nature emerged as restraints fell away has shaped his image; Velleius, who served under him, gives the opposite view. Modern historians (Levick, Seager) stress his genuine respect for senatorial forms, his reluctance and his isolation. He left 2,700 million sesterces in the treasury.
people.death: at Misenum, 16 March 37, possibly smothered by Macro

people.name: Germanicus

roles.t: Commander in the East with imperium maius

people.summary: Son of Drusus the Elder, adopted by Tiberius in AD 4, husband of Augustus's granddaughter Agrippina and father of Caligula. Hugely popular, he quelled the Rhine mutiny of 14, campaigned in Germany (14-16), and died in Antioch convinced he had been poisoned by Piso.
people.detail: He also wrote poetry, including a Latin version of Aratus's Phaenomena that survives. His death became the founding grievance of his family's feud with Tiberius. Tacitus idealises him, though his campaigns achieved little at great cost.
people.death: illness, alleged poisoning, near Antioch, 10 October AD 19

people.name: Agrippina the Elder
people.summary: Daughter of Agrippa and Julia, wife of Germanicus and mother of nine children including Caligula and Agrippina the Younger. Proud of her Augustan blood, she saved the Rhine bridge in 15, carried Germanicus's ashes to Rome, and was exiled by Tiberius to Pandateria, where she starved to death.

people.name: Drusus the Younger
people.summary: Tiberius's only son, who suppressed the Pannonian mutiny of 14 and was designated successor after Germanicus's death; poisoned, according to later revelations, by his wife Livilla and Sejanus.

people.name: Antonia Minor
people.summary: Daughter of Mark Antony and Octavia, widow of Drusus the Elder and mother of Germanicus, Livilla and Claudius. Respected for her virtue and influence, she warned Tiberius of Sejanus's plot in 31.
people.death: in 37, perhaps by suicide or poison under Caligula

people.name: Sejanus
people.summary: Equestrian from Volsinii who, as praetorian prefect, concentrated the guard in one camp, became Tiberius's indispensable minister after the emperor withdrew to Capri, and destroyed Agrippina's family before being himself destroyed in October 31.
people.detail: Whether he aimed at the throne, at regency for a Julio-Claudian minor, or simply at survival is disputed. The 'Sejanus affair' generated a wave of prosecutions and a lasting literary topos (Juvenal 10, Ben Jonson's Sejanus).

people.name: Livilla
people.summary: Sister of Germanicus and Claudius, wife of Drusus the Younger, alleged lover of Sejanus and accomplice in poisoning her husband; she died after the revelations of 31, starved by her mother Antonia according to Dio.

people.name: Macro
people.summary: Praetorian prefect who executed Sejanus's downfall in 31, allegedly smothered the dying Tiberius, and backed Caligula's accession, only to be forced to suicide by him in 38.

people.name: Tiberius Gemellus
people.summary: Grandson of Tiberius and co-heir in his will, set aside by the Senate in favour of Caligula, who adopted him and then forced him to kill himself, probably late in 37.

people.name: Caligula
people.summary: Son of Germanicus and Agrippina, nicknamed 'Little Boot' by the Rhine soldiers. After a popular start his reign became notorious for cruelty, extravagance and demands for divine honours; he was murdered by praetorian officers after less than four years.
people.detail: The sources (Seneca, Philo, Suetonius, Dio) are uniformly hostile and contain much anecdote (the horse Incitatus as consul, the seashells). Modern accounts (Barrett, Winterling) present an autocrat who exposed the hypocrisy of the Augustan system by humiliating the Senate openly, rather than a madman.

people.name: Drusilla
people.summary: Favourite sister of Caligula, named his heir during his illness of 37, and after her death the first Roman woman deified (as Diva Drusilla).

people.name: Cassius Chaerea
people.summary: Praetorian tribune and veteran of the Rhine mutiny of 14 who, repeatedly mocked by Caligula with effeminate watchwords, led his assassination; Claudius had him executed.

people.name: Claudius
people.summary: Son of Drusus the Elder, kept from public life by his disabilities, made emperor by the praetorians in 41. His reign saw the conquest of Britain, annexations of Mauretania, Lycia and Thrace, the harbour at Portus, liberal grants of citizenship and the rise of freedman secretaries such as Narcissus and Pallas.
people.detail: A learned antiquarian, he wrote histories of the Etruscans and Carthaginians (lost) and tried to add three letters to the Latin alphabet. Ancient writers depict him as dominated by wives and freedmen; modern assessments (Levick, Osgood) credit him with energetic centralising administration. His speech on Gallic senators survives on the Lyon Tablet.

people.name: Messalina
people.summary: Third wife of Claudius and mother of Britannicus and Octavia, depicted by Tacitus and Juvenal as insatiable and murderous; executed after her public 'marriage' to Gaius Silius in 48.
people.death: executed in the Gardens of Lucullus, 48

people.name: Narcissus
people.summary: Freedman secretary of Claudius, immensely rich and powerful, who shamed the invasion army of 43 into embarking and engineered Messalina's fall; forced to suicide on Nero's accession.

people.name: Agrippina the Younger
people.summary: Daughter of Germanicus, sister of Caligula, fourth wife of Claudius and mother of Nero, whom she brought to the throne. The first living wife of an emperor called Augusta, she shared power openly in Nero's first years until he had her murdered.
people.detail: Her lost memoirs were a source for Tacitus and Pliny. She founded Cologne as a colony (Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium) in her birthplace in 50. Ancient tradition credits her with poisoning Claudius.
people.death: murdered on Nero's orders at Baiae, March 59

people.name: Britannicus
people.summary: Son of Claudius and Messalina, named for his father's British conquest, displaced by Nero's adoption and poisoned at dinner in 55, just before he turned fourteen.

people.name: Claudia Octavia
people.summary: Daughter of Claudius and Messalina, married to Nero in 53, divorced and murdered on Pandateria in 62 so that he could marry Poppaea; heroine of the tragedy Octavia.

people.name: Nero
people.fullName: Nero Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus (born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus)
people.summary: Last Julio-Claudian emperor, son of Agrippina the Younger. Guided early by Seneca and Burrus, he later murdered his mother, wives and rivals, performed publicly as singer and charioteer, rebuilt Rome after the fire of 64 and persecuted Christians. Revolts in Gaul and Spain and the desertion of the guard drove him to suicide.
people.detail: Popular with the urban plebs and in the Greek East (several 'false Neros' appeared after his death), he was execrated by the senatorial tradition. Champlin's Nero (2003) reads his conduct as calculated showmanship. Christian tradition made him the Antichrist.

people.name: Poppaea Sabina
people.summary: Wife of Otho, then mistress and (62) wife of Nero; Josephus calls her a 'God-fearer' sympathetic to Jews. She died pregnant, supposedly after Nero kicked her, and was deified.

people.name: Seneca
people.summary: Stoic philosopher, tragedian and statesman from Corduba, exiled to Corsica by Claudius (41-49), recalled by Agrippina to tutor Nero and co-director of government with Burrus until 62; forced to suicide after the Pisonian conspiracy.
people.detail: His works include the Moral Letters to Lucilius, dialogues (De ira, De clementia, De brevitate vitae), Natural Questions, nine tragedies and the satire Apocolocyntosis. His vast wealth (300 million sesterces) and loans in Britain sat uneasily with his preaching; critics such as Suillius Rufus attacked his hypocrisy.

people.name: Burrus
people.summary: Gallic equestrian from Vasio, praetorian prefect appointed through Agrippina, who with Seneca guided Nero's early government; his death in 62, perhaps by poison, removed a key restraint.

people.name: Tigellinus
people.summary: Nero's notorious praetorian prefect and organiser of his entertainments and repressions after 62, blamed for the second outbreak of the Great Fire; he abandoned Nero in 68 and was forced to suicide by Otho.

people.name: Corbulo
people.summary: The outstanding general of the mid-first century, famous for harsh discipline. He crushed the Chauci (47), conquered Armenia for Nero (58-60) and negotiated the Rhandeia settlement (63); Nero ordered him to die in 67.
people.detail: Tacitus's narrative of the Armenian war appears to draw on Corbulo's own memoirs. His daughter Domitia Longina married Domitian. His troops' exploits were remembered by the Flavian generals who had served under him.

people.name: Varus
people.summary: Senator related by marriage to Augustus, governor of Africa and Syria (where he crushed the revolt after Herod's death), whose attempt to impose Roman law and tribute in Germany ended in the destruction of three legions in AD 9.
people.detail: Velleius calls him a man of mild character, more suited to camp leisure than war, who 'came poor to rich Syria and left rich Syria poor'. Modern scholars see him more as the victim of an unworkable policy and of Arminius's betrayal.
people.death: suicide during the Varian disaster, September AD 9

people.name: Arminius

roles.t: Commander of Cheruscan auxiliaries in Roman service

people.summary: Cheruscan noble, Roman citizen and equestrian, who led the ambush that destroyed Varus's legions in AD 9, fought Germanicus to a standstill (15-16), defeated Maroboduus (17), and was murdered by his own kinsmen for aspiring to kingship.
people.detail: Tacitus calls him 'without doubt the liberator of Germany'. His wife Thusnelda, daughter of the pro-Roman Segestes, was captured and paraded in Germanicus's triumph with their son. From the sixteenth century he became 'Hermann', a German national hero, culminating in the Hermannsdenkmal near Detmold (1875).

people.name: Segestes
people.summary: Pro-Roman Cheruscan noble who warned Varus of Arminius's plot, was besieged by Arminius (who had abducted his daughter Thusnelda) and rescued by Germanicus in 15, and watched his daughter paraded in the triumph of 17.

people.name: Inguiomerus
people.summary: Uncle of Arminius and Cheruscan war-leader who pressed the attack on Caecina's camp at Pontes Longi (15), escaped from Idistaviso (16), and later defected to Maroboduus.

people.name: Maroboduus
people.summary: Roman-educated king who led the Marcomanni to Bohemia and built a powerful kingdom with an army of 70,000 foot and 4,000 horse; Rome's planned attack on him in AD 6 was aborted by the Illyrian revolt. Defeated by Arminius and expelled, he spent 18 years in exile at Ravenna.

people.name: Bato the Daesitiate

roles.t: Leader of the Great Illyrian Revolt

people.summary: Leader of the Dalmatian Daesitiates who began the Great Illyrian Revolt in AD 6, executed his Breucian namesake for treachery, and surrendered to Tiberius at Andetrium in 9, famously blaming Rome's 'wolves' for the rising. He was interned at Ravenna.
people.death: in comfortable internment at Ravenna, date unknown

people.name: Bato the Breucian
people.summary: Leader of the Pannonian Breuci in the Great Illyrian Revolt who betrayed his fellow leader Pinnes to the Romans in AD 8 and was then captured and executed by Bato the Daesitiate.

people.name: Caecina Severus
people.summary: Veteran commander who fought forty campaigns: he relieved Sirmium and fought at the Volcaean Marshes in the Illyrian revolt and led Germanicus's lower army, narrowly escaping at Pontes Longi (15).

people.name: Plautius Silvanus
people.summary: Consul of 2 BC, governor of Galatia, who brought eastern legions to the Illyrian war and fought at the Volcaean Marshes; his family tomb survives near Tibur.

people.name: Sentius Saturninus
people.summary: Consul of 19 BC who resisted Egnatius Rufus's candidacy, governed Syria, and commanded the Rhine army that was to strike Maroboduus from the west in AD 6.

people.name: Lucius Caedicius
people.summary: Camp prefect who held the fort of Aliso after the Varian disaster and led its garrison and civilians in a night breakout to the Rhine.

people.name: Nonius Asprenas
people.summary: Nephew of Varus whose two legions on the upper Rhine secured the river crossings after the disaster of AD 9 and prevented panic spreading to Gaul; accused of seizing the dead men's property.

people.name: Velleius Paterculus

roles.t: Cavalry prefect and legate under Tiberius

people.summary: Officer who served with Gaius Caesar in the East and Tiberius in Germany and Illyricum, and whose brief Roman history (published AD 30) is an eyewitness but adulatory source for Tiberius and Sejanus.

people.name: Gnaeus Calpurnius Piso
people.summary: Proud aristocrat appointed governor of Syria alongside Germanicus's eastern command, accused of poisoning him and of trying to recover his province by force; he killed himself during his trial, recorded in the senatus consultum de Cn. Pisone patre.

people.name: Plancina
people.summary: Wife of Gnaeus Piso and friend of Livia, suspected of poisoning Germanicus with the help of a notorious poisoner, Martina; pardoned at Livia's request in 20 but forced to suicide in 33.

people.name: Tacfarinas
people.summary: Numidian deserter from Roman auxiliary service who organised the Musulamii and Moorish tribes into units trained in Roman fashion and waged guerrilla war in Africa for seven years, until killed at Auzea.

people.name: Junius Blaesus
people.summary: Uncle of Sejanus who faced the Pannonian mutiny of 14 and fought Tacfarinas, becoming the last man outside the imperial family to be hailed imperator by his troops; he fell with his nephew.

people.name: Publius Cornelius Dolabella
people.summary: Proconsul of Africa who ended the war of Tacfarinas at Auzea in 24 but was refused triumphal ornaments to spare Sejanus's uncle Blaesus.

people.name: Gaius Silius
people.summary: Commander of the upper Rhine army who crushed Sacrovir's revolt in 21; prosecuted for treason in 24 as a friend of Germanicus's family, he killed himself. Father of Messalina's lover of the same name.

people.name: Julius Sacrovir
people.summary: Aeduan noble and Roman citizen who led the Gallic revolt of 21, seizing Augustodunum; defeated by Gaius Silius, he burned himself and his companions in a villa.

people.name: Seius Tubero
people.summary: Half-brother (or adoptive brother) of Sejanus who commanded the cavalry under Germanicus in 16 and was suffect consul in 18.

people.name: Poppaeus Sabinus
people.summary: Long-serving governor of Moesia, Achaea and Macedonia (24 years, Tacitus says, because he was 'equal to his tasks and no more'), who suppressed the Thracian revolt of 26; grandfather of Poppaea Sabina.

people.name: Lucius Apronius
people.summary: Commander who decimated a cowardly cohort in the war against Tacfarinas and later failed against the Frisian revolt of 28, losing 900 men at Baduhenna Wood.

people.name: Cremutius Cordus
people.summary: Historian of the civil wars and Augustus prosecuted in 25 for praising Brutus and Cassius; he starved himself and his books were burned, but his daughter Marcia saved copies.
