people.name: Ptolemy of Mauretania
people.summary: Last king of Mauretania, son of Juba II and Cleopatra Selene and thus grandson of Antony and Cleopatra. He helped Rome defeat Tacfarinas but was killed by his cousin Caligula, and his kingdom was annexed.

people.name: Archelaus of Cappadocia
people.summary: Client king of Cappadocia for over fifty years, appointed by Antony, whose summons to Rome and death in 17 led Tiberius to annex his kingdom.

people.name: Rhoemetalces I
people.summary: Client king of Thrace whose cavalry fought for Rome in the Great Illyrian Revolt, notably at the Volcaean Marshes.

people.name: Amyntas of Galatia
people.summary: Client king installed by Antony who deserted to Octavian before Actium; killed by the Homonadenses in 25 BC, after which his kingdom became the province of Galatia.

people.name: Herod the Great
people.summary: Idumaean-born client king of Judaea, installed by Rome in 40/37 BC, a loyal friend of Antony and then of Augustus and Agrippa. He was a prodigious builder (the Temple, Caesarea, Masada, Herodium, Machaerus) and a ruthless dynast who executed his wife Mariamme and three sons.

people.name: Quirinius
people.summary: New man from Lanuvium who subdued the Homonadenses, advised Gaius Caesar in the East, and as legate of Syria carried out the census of Judaea in AD 6 mentioned in Luke's Gospel.

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.summary: Equestrian prefect of Judaea who provoked Jewish protests by bringing military standards into Jerusalem and using Temple funds for an aqueduct, ordered the crucifixion of Jesus, and was recalled after a massacre of Samaritans. A dedicatory inscription from Caesarea confirms his title.

people.name: Jesus of Nazareth
people.summary: Galilean Jewish teacher and healer proclaiming the kingdom of God, crucified in Jerusalem under Pontius Pilate around 30 or 33; the movement of his followers became Christianity.

people.name: Paul of Tarsus
people.summary: Diaspora Jew and Roman citizen, persecutor turned apostle, whose missions in Asia Minor and Greece and whose letters, the earliest Christian documents, shaped Gentile Christianity. Tradition places his execution in Rome under Nero.

people.name: Peter the Apostle
people.summary: Galilean fisherman and leading disciple of Jesus, later a missionary; early tradition (1 Clement, Ignatius, Dionysius of Corinth) places his martyrdom in Rome under Nero, and his tomb was venerated on the Vatican hill.

people.name: Philo of Alexandria
people.summary: Jewish Platonist philosopher and exegete of Alexandria who led the Jewish embassy to Caligula in 39/40; his In Flaccum and Embassy to Gaius are eyewitness sources for the crisis of 38-41.

people.name: Agrippa I
people.summary: Grandson of Herod, raised in Rome with the imperial princes, friend of Caligula and Claudius; he dissuaded Caligula from desecrating the Temple, mediated Claudius's accession, and ruled all Herod's kingdom until his sudden death.

people.name: Agrippa II

roles.t: King of Chalcis and northern territories

people.summary: Son of Agrippa I, client king with authority over the Temple, who tried to prevent the revolt of 66, fought on the Roman side, and supplied Josephus with information. His sister Berenice was Titus's lover.

people.name: Publius Petronius
people.summary: Legate of Syria ordered by Caligula to set up the emperor's statue in the Jerusalem Temple; he delayed in the face of mass protest and was spared execution only by Caligula's death.

people.name: Aulus Plautius
people.summary: Commander of the Claudian invasion of Britain and its first governor, awarded the last ovatio granted to a non-imperial general (47). His wife Pomponia Graecina was tried for a 'foreign superstition', possibly Christianity.

people.name: Hosidius Geta
people.summary: Officer who campaigned against the Moors in 42 and won the second day of the Medway battle in 43, receiving triumphal ornaments before reaching the consulship.

people.name: Caratacus
people.summary: Son of Cunobelinus who led British resistance against Rome for eight years, from the Medway to Wales; betrayed by Cartimandua in 51 and pardoned by Claudius after his celebrated speech in Rome.

people.name: Togodumnus
people.summary: Brother of Caratacus and joint leader of British resistance in 43; he died shortly after the Romans crossed the Thames.
people.death: died of wounds or in battle, 43

people.name: Togidubnus

roles.t: Client king (rex magnus) in southern Britain

people.summary: British client king whom Tacitus says remained loyal 'down to our own times'; an inscription from Chichester (RIB 91) calls him 'great king of Britain'. The Fishbourne palace is often associated with him.

people.name: Ostorius Scapula
people.summary: Second governor of Britain, who disarmed the allied tribes (provoking an Icenian revolt), founded the colony at Camulodunum and defeated Caratacus, but died exhausted by the Silurian war.

people.name: Suetonius Paullinus
people.summary: First Roman to cross the Atlas mountains (42), conqueror of Mona and victor over Boudica (60/61); in 69 he advised Otho against giving battle at Bedriacum.

people.name: Boudica

roles.t: Queen and war-leader of the Iceni

people.summary: Widow of the Icenian client king Prasutagus who, after being flogged and her daughters raped by Roman officials, led the great revolt of 60/61 that destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before her defeat by Suetonius Paullinus.
people.detail: Dio describes her as tall, with a harsh voice and a mass of tawny hair to her hips, wearing a great gold torc. Tacitus gives her a speech presenting her as avenging lost liberty and the outraged bodies of her daughters. She became a British national icon in the Victorian era (Thomas Thornycroft's statue on Westminster Bridge).
people.death: poison (Tacitus) or illness (Dio) after defeat, 60 or 61

people.name: Prasutagus
people.summary: Wealthy client king of the Iceni who left half his kingdom to Nero in the hope of protecting his family; Roman officials treated the kingdom as conquered, provoking his widow Boudica's revolt.

people.name: Cartimandua
people.summary: Pro-Roman queen of the Brigantes who handed Caratacus over to Rome in 51; after she replaced her husband Venutius with his armour-bearer, Venutius overthrew her in 69 and Rome evacuated her.

people.name: Julius Classicianus
people.summary: Gallic-born procurator sent to Britain after the Boudican revolt, who reported that Paullinus's reprisals were prolonging the war; his tombstone, found in London, is in the British Museum (RIB 12).

people.name: Quintus Veranius
people.summary: First governor of Lycia, whose road-building is recorded on the Stadiasmus Patarensis; he died in his first year as governor of Britain, boasting in his will that he would have conquered the island in two more years.

people.name: Gallio
people.summary: Elder brother of Seneca, proconsul of Achaea before whom Paul was accused at Corinth (Acts 18); the Delphi inscription naming him fixes Pauline chronology. He perished after the Pisonian conspiracy.

people.name: Cassius Longinus
people.summary: Leading jurist of the Sabinian school, descendant of the tyrannicide Cassius, who argued for executing Pedanius Secundus's 400 slaves in 61; exiled by Nero in 65 and recalled by Vespasian.

people.name: Gaius Calpurnius Piso
people.summary: Popular, generous aristocrat chosen by the conspirators of 65 as Nero's replacement; when the plot was betrayed he opened his veins, his will flattering Nero to protect his wife.

people.name: Lucan
people.summary: Nephew of Seneca and author of the epic Pharsalia (Bellum Civile) on the war of Caesar and Pompey; banned from publishing by a jealous Nero, he joined the Pisonian conspiracy and was forced to die aged 25, reciting his own verses.

people.name: Petronius
people.summary: Nero's 'arbiter of elegance', probably the author of the Satyricon. Denounced by Tigellinus, he slowly bled to death amid conversation and light verse, sending Nero a catalogue of the emperor's debaucheries.

people.name: Thrasea Paetus
people.summary: Stoic senator from Patavium whose silent opposition (walking out of the Senate after Agrippina's murder) made him the emblem of senatorial independence; condemned in 66, his death closes the surviving Annals.

people.name: Nymphidius Sabinus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect who detached the guard from Nero in June 68 by promising a huge donative in Galba's name, then tried to seize power himself and was killed by the praetorians.

people.name: Gessius Florus
people.summary: Procurator of Judaea whose extortion and seizure of Temple funds, followed by a massacre in Jerusalem, Josephus blames for provoking the revolt of 66.

people.name: Cestius Gallus
people.summary: Legate of Syria whose withdrawal from Jerusalem in 66 turned into the rout at Beth Horon; he died, 'by fate or weariness' says Tacitus, early in 67.

people.name: Caesennius Paetus
people.summary: General who capitulated to Vologases at Rhandeia in 62; pardoned with a joke by Nero, he later, as Vespasian's governor of Syria, annexed Commagene (72).

people.name: Tiridates I
people.summary: Brother of Vologases I and Zoroastrian magus, installed in Armenia by Parthia, driven out by Corbulo, and finally crowned by Nero in Rome in 66 under the Rhandeia compromise, founding the Arsacid dynasty of Armenia.

people.name: Vologases I
people.summary: Arsacid king who installed his brother Tiridates in Armenia, forced Paetus's capitulation at Rhandeia, accepted the compromise of 63, and later offered Vespasian 40,000 mounted archers in 69.

people.name: Antiochus IV of Commagene
people.summary: Richest of the client kings, restored to Commagene by Caligula, an ally in the Armenian and Jewish wars, deposed in 72 on a charge of plotting with Parthia; his grandson Philopappus became an Athenian archon and Roman consul.

people.name: Plautius Silvanus Aelianus
people.summary: Neronian legate of Moesia whose funerary inscription near Tibur (ILS 986) records his settling of over 100,000 Transdanubians in the province, intervention in the Crimea and grain shipments to Rome.

people.name: Virgil
people.summary: Poet from near Mantua, author of the Eclogues, Georgics and Aeneid, Rome's national epic, which made Aeneas's mission and Augustus's destiny one story; he died before completing the Aeneid.

people.name: Horace
people.summary: Freedman's son from Venusia who fought for Brutus at Philippi and became, through Maecenas, the lyric voice of the Augustan age (Odes, Epodes, Satires, Epistles, Ars Poetica) and composer of the Carmen Saeculare.

people.name: Ovid
people.summary: Equestrian poet from Sulmo, author of the Amores, Ars Amatoria, Metamorphoses and Fasti, relegated by Augustus to Tomis in AD 8 for 'a poem and a mistake'; he died in exile.

people.name: Aelius Gallus
people.summary: Second prefect of Egypt, friend of Strabo, who led the failed expedition to Arabia Felix in 26-25 BC.

people.name: Cornelius Gallus
people.summary: Elegiac poet and friend of Virgil, Octavian's general at the conquest of Egypt and its first prefect, whose self-glorifying inscriptions led to his disgrace and suicide.

people.name: Gaius Petronius
people.summary: Prefect of Egypt who repelled the Kushite invasion, sacked Napata (24 BC) and relieved Primis.

people.name: Amanirenas
people.summary: Kushite queen, probably the one-eyed 'Candace' of Strabo, who with prince Akinidad attacked Roman Egypt in 25 BC and secured favourable terms at Samos; the Meroë head of Augustus is a trophy of her war.

people.name: Publius Carisius
people.summary: Augustan legate who defeated the Astures and took Lancia (25 BC) and founded Augusta Emerita; his harshness provoked a renewed revolt.

people.name: Varro Murena
people.summary: Brother-in-law of Maecenas who destroyed the Salassi (25 BC) and is usually identified with the Murena executed for conspiracy in 23/22 BC.

people.name: Marcus Licinius Crassus (cos. 30 BC)
people.summary: Grandson of the triumvir who defeated the Bastarnae and Getae and killed king Deldo in single combat, but was denied the spolia opima; he triumphed in July 27 BC and then vanishes.

people.name: Marcus Lollius
people.summary: First governor of Galatia, defeated by the Sugambri in 16 BC with the loss of an eagle, later guardian of Gaius Caesar in the East, disgraced for taking bribes.

people.name: Maelo
people.summary: Sugambrian leader named in the Res Gestae (32) as a king who came to Augustus as a suppliant; probably a leader of the attack on Lollius in 16 BC.

people.name: Cornelius Balbus the Younger
people.summary: Native of Gades who conquered the Garamantes and celebrated the last triumph of a non-imperial Roman (19 BC); builder of the Theatre of Balbus.

people.name: Silius Nerva
people.summary: Governor of Illyricum who subdued the Camunni and Vennii and repelled Norican and Pannonian raiders in 16 BC, paving the way for the incorporation of Noricum.

people.name: Galba
people.summary: Elderly aristocrat of ancient nobility, governor of Tarraconensis, who rebelled against Nero in April 68 and became the first emperor not of the Julio-Claudian house. His parsimony and severity alienated the praetorians, and he was murdered after seven months.

people.name: Piso Licinianus
people.summary: Austere young noble, descended from Crassus and Pompey, adopted by Galba on 10 January 69 and killed with him five days later.
people.death: murdered at the temple of Vesta, 15 January 69

people.name: Otho
people.summary: Nero's companion and first husband of Poppaea, exiled to govern Lusitania, who backed Galba, then murdered him and reigned for three months before killing himself after defeat at Bedriacum, a death admired even by his detractors.

people.name: Vitellius
people.summary: Son of Claudius's powerful minister Lucius Vitellius, proclaimed by the Rhine legions in January 69; his generals defeated Otho, but his reign, remembered for gluttony, collapsed before the Flavian advance and he was lynched in Rome.

people.name: Salvius Titianus
people.summary: Otho's elder brother, nominal commander of the Othonian army at the first battle of Bedriacum, pardoned by Vitellius.

people.name: Fabius Valens
people.summary: Ambitious legate who first hailed Vitellius at Cologne, led the larger Vitellian column into Italy and won Bedriacum; captured at sea while trying to raise Gaul, he was executed at Urbinum.

people.name: Caecina Alienus
people.summary: Flamboyant Vitellian general who crossed the Alps with the upper German army, won Bedriacum, then tried to defect to Vespasian before the second battle and was arrested by his men; executed by Titus in 79 for alleged conspiracy.

people.name: Vindex
people.summary: Aquitanian noble of royal descent and senator who raised Gaul against Nero in March 68 and proposed Galba as emperor; his army was destroyed by Verginius Rufus at Vesontio and he killed himself.

people.name: Verginius Rufus
people.summary: Commander who defeated Vindex but twice refused the throne offered by his legions; he lived to 83, honoured with a state funeral at which Tacitus spoke and an epitaph boasting he had claimed power for his country, not himself.

people.name: Antonius Primus
people.summary: Gallic-born adventurer, once condemned for forgery, who led the Danubian legions into Italy for Vespasian, won the second battle of Bedriacum and took Rome, only to be sidelined by Mucianus. Martial knew him in retirement at Tolosa.

people.name: Mucianus
people.summary: Governor of Syria who persuaded Vespasian to bid for power, marched the Syrian army west, and ran Rome in Vespasian's name in 70; also a writer on natural wonders quoted by Pliny.

people.name: Flavius Sabinus
people.summary: Elder brother of Vespasian and long-serving prefect of Rome, who negotiated Vitellius's abdication, was besieged on the Capitol and killed when it burned.

people.name: Vespasian
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Vespasianus Augustus (Titus Flavius Vespasianus)

roles.t: Legate of legio II Augusta in Britain

people.summary: Son of a Sabine tax-collector, a capable general in Britain and Judaea, proclaimed emperor in 69. He restored finances and order after the civil wars, rebuilt the Capitol, began the Colosseum and Temple of Peace, extended Latin rights to Spain, and founded the Flavian dynasty.
people.detail: Tacitus notes he was the only emperor changed for the better by power. Known for earthy humour (the tax on urine, 'money does not smell') and frugality. The Lex de imperio Vespasiani preserves the legal grant of his powers.

people.name: Titus
people.summary: Elder son of Vespasian, conqueror of Jerusalem (70), feared as a ruthless praetorian prefect but remembered as emperor as 'the delight of the human race' for his generosity during the Vesuvius eruption and the fire and plague of 80; he inaugurated the Colosseum and died after two years.

people.name: Domitian
people.summary: Younger son of Vespasian, an autocratic and capable administrator who raised army pay, campaigned against the Chatti, Dacians and Sarmatians, built extensively (the Palatine palace, the stadium, the Arch of Titus) and enforced morals as perpetual censor; increasingly suspicious after 89, he executed senators and was murdered by his household.
people.detail: The senatorial sources (Tacitus, Pliny, Suetonius, Dio) portray a tyrant who demanded the title 'dominus et deus'; modern scholarship (Jones, Southern) credits efficient provincial administration and sound coinage. His damnatio memoriae erased his name from many inscriptions.

people.name: Domitia Longina
people.summary: Daughter of Corbulo, wife of Domitian, briefly exiled for an alleged affair with the actor Paris, and said to have known of the plot against her husband; she lived honoured into Hadrian's reign.

people.name: Berenice
people.summary: Herodian princess, sister of Agrippa II, who tried to stop Florus's massacre in 66 and became Titus's lover; she came to Rome in 75 but Titus, under popular pressure, sent her away on becoming emperor ('invitus invitam').

people.name: Tiberius Julius Alexander
people.summary: Nephew of Philo from a wealthy Alexandrian Jewish family who abandoned Judaism for an equestrian career; as prefect of Egypt he crushed Jewish riots in Alexandria (66), first proclaimed Vespasian (1 July 69), and served as Titus's second-in-command at Jerusalem.

people.name: Josephus

roles.t: Flavian client and historian in Rome

people.summary: Priestly aristocrat of Jerusalem who commanded rebel forces in Galilee, surrendered at Jotapata after predicting Vespasian's rule, served the Romans as interpreter at the siege of Jerusalem, and wrote in Rome the Jewish War, Jewish Antiquities, Life and Against Apion.
people.detail: His works are the principal source for Judaea from the Maccabees to 74 and include famous passages on John the Baptist, James and (in partly interpolated form) Jesus. Regarded by many Jews as a traitor and preserved by Christians, he remains indispensable and carefully self-justifying.

people.name: John of Gischala
people.summary: Galilean rival of Josephus who escaped to Jerusalem when Gischala fell, allied with the Zealots, and controlled the Temple during the siege of 70; he surrendered and was condemned to life imprisonment.

people.name: Simon bar Giora
people.summary: Radical rebel leader with messianic-royal pretensions who fought at Beth Horon, raised a peasant army, held the Upper City during the siege, emerged from the ruins in royal robes, and was executed at the Flavian triumph.
people.death: executed in Rome at the triumph, 71

people.name: Eleazar ben Simon
people.summary: Priestly leader of the Zealot faction, prominent in the defeat of Cestius Gallus and in control of the inner Temple until John of Gischala's men seized it at Passover 70.

people.name: Eleazar ben Yair

roles.t: Leader of the Sicarii at Masada

people.summary: Kinsman of Menahem and leader of the Sicarii at Masada, to whom Josephus attributes the speeches persuading the defenders to choose death over slavery.

people.name: Lucilius Bassus
people.summary: Admiral who brought the Ravenna fleet over to Vespasian in 69, then as legate of Judaea took Herodium and Machaerus before dying in office.

people.name: Flavius Silva
people.summary: Legate of Judaea who besieged and took Masada with legio X Fretensis; an inscription from his home town Urbs Salvia, where he built the amphitheatre, records his career.

people.name: Julius Civilis

roles.t: Batavian prince and Roman auxiliary commander

people.summary: Batavian noble of royal blood, a Roman citizen who had served 25 years in the auxilia and been twice arrested for treason, who led the Batavian revolt of 69-70; his fate after the negotiations with Cerialis is unknown. Rembrandt painted him.

people.name: Julius Classicus
people.summary: Treveran noble claiming royal descent, commander of an auxiliary cavalry unit, who proclaimed the Imperium Galliarum in 70 and made Roman legions swear allegiance to it.

people.name: Veleda
people.summary: Seeress of the Bructeri who lived in a tower on the Lippe and was consulted by intermediaries; she foretold the Batavian successes of 69, received captured Roman prisoners and a flagship, and was later captured and taken to Italy (a Greek satirical inscription from Ardea mocks her).

people.name: Munius Lupercus
people.summary: Commander of the besieged legions at Vetera, who surrendered in March 70 and was sent as a gift to the seeress Veleda but killed on the journey.

people.name: Petillius Cerialis
people.summary: Probably Vespasian's son-in-law; a dashing, reckless commander who lost legio IX's infantry to Boudica, crushed the Batavian revolt in 70 and conquered the Brigantes as governor of Britain.

people.name: Frontinus
people.summary: Governor of Britain who subdued the Silures, served in Domitian's Chattan war, and as water commissioner under Nerva wrote De aquaeductu, the key technical source on Rome's aqueducts, as well as the Strategemata.

people.name: Agricola
people.summary: Senator from Forum Iulii (Fréjus), father-in-law of Tacitus, whose seven-year governorship of Britain carried Roman arms to Mons Graupius and the Orkneys. Recalled by Domitian, he lived in quiet retirement; Tacitus's biography is his monument.
people.detail: Tacitus credits him with Romanising the British elite through baths, porticoes and banquets, 'which the ignorant called civilisation though it was part of their enslavement' (Agr. 21). The account is panegyric and much of the archaeology of his campaigns remains disputed.
people.death: illness, 23 August 93, with rumours of poison

people.name: Calgacus
people.summary: Caledonian leader at Mons Graupius, known only from Tacitus, who gives him the most famous anti-imperial speech in Latin literature ('they make a desert and call it peace').

people.name: Tacitus
people.summary: Senator, orator and the greatest Roman historian, author of the Agricola, Germania, Dialogus, Histories and Annals, whose dark, ironic analysis of the Principate from Tiberius to Domitian has dominated the modern understanding of the period.

people.name: Pliny the Elder

roles.t: Prefect of the fleet at Misenum

people.summary: Equestrian officer and polymath from Comum, friend of Vespasian, author of the 37-book Natural History and of lost histories of the German wars and of his own times; he died at Stabiae during the eruption of Vesuvius.
people.death: asphyxiated at Stabiae during the eruption of Vesuvius, 79

people.name: Pliny the Younger
people.summary: Nephew and adopted son of Pliny the Elder, lawyer and senator, whose nine books of literary letters, tenth book of correspondence with Trajan and Panegyricus are windows on senatorial life, the Vesuvius eruption and early Christianity.

people.name: Martial
people.summary: Epigrammatist from Bilbilis in Spain whose Book of Spectacles celebrates the Colosseum's opening and whose twelve books of epigrams depict Flavian Rome with wit and obscenity; he returned to Spain in 98.

people.name: Helvidius Priscus
people.summary: Stoic senator, son-in-law of Thrasea Paetus, exiled under Nero and executed under Vespasian for his defiant opposition; his son, also Helvidius, was executed by Domitian in 93.

people.name: Epictetus
people.summary: Phrygian-born former slave of Nero's freedman Epaphroditus, Stoic teacher expelled from Rome in 93, who taught at Nicopolis; his pupil Arrian recorded his Discourses and Handbook, admired by Marcus Aurelius.

people.name: Cornelius Fuscus
people.summary: Equestrian who declared for Vespasian in 69, Domitian's praetorian prefect, killed with much of his army invading Dacia in 86 or 87.
people.death: killed in battle in Dacia, 86 or 87

people.name: Oppius Sabinus
people.summary: Governor of Moesia killed when the Dacians crossed the frozen Danube in the winter of 85/86, opening Domitian's Dacian war.

people.name: Tettius Julianus
people.summary: Disciplinarian governor of Upper Moesia who defeated Decebalus at Tapae in 88.

people.name: Vezinas
people.summary: Dacian noble, second in rank to Decebalus, who survived the battle of Tapae in 88 by pretending to be dead and escaping at night.

people.name: Antonius Saturninus
people.summary: Governor of upper Germany proclaimed emperor at Mainz on 1 January 89; his German allies were stopped by a thaw on the Rhine and he was defeated and killed by Lappius Maximus.

people.name: Lappius Maximus
people.summary: Governor of lower Germany who crushed Saturninus's revolt in 89 and burned the rebel's papers to spare those compromised; rewarded with a second consulship (95).

people.name: Rabirius
people.summary: Domitian's architect, praised by Martial, designer of the Palatine palace (Domus Flavia and Domus Augustana), dedicated in 92.

people.name: Flavius Clemens
people.summary: Domitian's cousin, father of the emperor's designated heirs, executed for 'atheism' in 95, perhaps for Jewish or Christian sympathies; his wife Flavia Domitilla was exiled.

people.name: Decebalus
people.summary: King of Dacia who defeated Cornelius Fuscus, made a profitable peace with Domitian (89), resisted Trajan in two wars (101-102, 105-106), and killed himself rather than be captured; his head was displayed in Rome.
people.detail: Dio describes him as shrewd in strategy, knowing when to attack and when to retreat, skilled at ambushes. He used Roman engineers to fortify his Orăștie mountain capital. A 40-metre rock sculpture of his face (1994-2004) overlooks the Danube at the Iron Gates.

people.name: Nerva
people.summary: Elderly senator and jurist, a survivor who had won triumphal honours for helping suppress the Pisonian conspiracy, chosen as emperor on Domitian's murder; after a praetorian mutiny he adopted Trajan, beginning the era of the 'adoptive emperors'.

people.name: Casperius Aelianus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect under Domitian and again under Nerva, who led the guard's mutiny of 97 demanding the execution of Domitian's assassins; Trajan had him executed.

people.name: Trajan
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Nerva Traianus Augustus (Marcus Ulpius Traianus)
people.summary: First emperor born in a province, at Italica in Baetica; conqueror of Dacia (101-106) and of Armenia and Mesopotamia (114-116), annexer of Arabia, builder of the Forum, Column, Markets and Baths of Trajan, the Danube bridge and Portus's hexagonal basin, and creator of the alimenta. The Senate named him Optimus.
people.detail: Remembered as the model good emperor: later emperors were wished 'luckier than Augustus, better than Trajan', and medieval legend placed him in Paradise (Dante). His eastern conquests overreached and were abandoned by Hadrian. Sources are thin: Dio's epitome, Pliny's Panegyricus and letters, the Column.
people.death: stroke at Selinus in Cilicia, August 117

people.name: Plotina
people.summary: Wife of Trajan, admired for modesty and Epicurean learning, who championed Hadrian and announced his deathbed adoption, a story Dio suspected she staged.

people.name: Lusius Quietus
people.summary: Moorish chieftain whose cavalry fought in Trajan's Dacian and Parthian wars; he retook Nisibis and Edessa, crushed the Jews of Mesopotamia, became consul and governor of Judaea, and was executed in 118 as one of the four consulars.

people.name: Licinius Sura
people.summary: Spanish senator and Trajan's closest adviser, who helped secure his adoption and served in the Dacian wars; Trajan honoured him with a public funeral and baths on the Aventine.

people.name: Laberius Maximus
people.summary: General of the First Dacian War who captured Decebalus's sister and a strong fortress; later exiled to an island on suspicion of plotting.

people.name: Apollodorus of Damascus
people.summary: Syrian Greek architect and engineer of Trajan's Danube bridge, Forum, Markets, Baths and probably the Column; he wrote a treatise on siege engines (Poliorcetica). Dio claims Hadrian exiled and executed him for criticising his designs.

people.name: Tiberius Claudius Maximus
people.summary: Cavalry scout who brought the head of Decebalus to Trajan; his self-composed tombstone from near Philippi narrates a career from legionary cavalryman to decurion.

people.name: Pompeius Longinus
people.summary: Roman commander in Dacia treacherously captured by Decebalus in 105; he took poison so that he could not be used to extract concessions from Trajan.
people.death: suicide by poison in Dacian captivity, 105

people.name: Cornelius Palma
people.summary: Governor of Syria who annexed Nabataea as the province of Arabia in 106; executed in 118 as one of the four consulars.

people.name: Osroes I
people.summary: Arsacid king whose deposition of the Armenian king provoked Trajan's invasion; he fled from Ctesiphon in 116, losing his daughter and throne to the Romans, and later regained power.

people.name: Parthamaspates
people.summary: Son of Osroes's rival, crowned by Trajan at Ctesiphon in 116; rejected by the Parthians, he was given a lesser kingdom by Hadrian.

people.name: Marcius Turbo

roles.t: Commander against the Jewish revolt in Egypt and Cyrene

people.summary: Equestrian general who suppressed the Jewish revolts in Egypt and Cyrenaica, later governed Dacia and Pannonia together, and served Hadrian as praetorian prefect.

people.name: Attianus
people.summary: Hadrian's former guardian and Trajan's praetorian prefect, who with Plotina announced Hadrian's adoption and was blamed for the execution of the four consulars.

people.name: Hadrian
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Traianus Hadrianus Augustus (Publius Aelius Hadrianus)
people.summary: Trajan's cousin and ward from Italica, who abandoned the eastern conquests, consolidated the frontiers (Hadrian's Wall, the German palisade), spent half his reign touring the provinces, codified the praetor's edict, rebuilt the Pantheon, created the Panhellenion and his villa at Tibur, and crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt.
people.detail: A passionate philhellene (the first emperor to wear a full beard), poet, amateur architect and lover of the youth Antinous, he was admired and feared; his relations with the Senate never recovered from the execution of the four consulars, and his last years were marred by illness and executions.

people.name: Sabina
people.summary: Great-niece of Trajan and wife of Hadrian in an unhappy, childless marriage; she travelled with him to Britain and Egypt (her companion Julia Balbilla carved poems on the Colossus of Memnon) and was deified after her death.

people.name: Antinous
people.summary: Bithynian youth from Claudiopolis, Hadrian's beloved, who drowned in the Nile in 130; Hadrian founded Antinoopolis and made him a god, producing one of the most widespread cults and portrait types of antiquity.

people.name: Platorius Nepos
people.summary: Friend of Hadrian and governor of Britain who began the construction of Hadrian's Wall; his name appears on building inscriptions from milecastles.

people.name: Salvius Julianus
people.fullName: Lucius Octavius Cornelius Publius Salvius Julianus Aemilianus
people.summary: North African jurist who codified the praetor's edict for Hadrian and wrote the 90-book Digesta, one of the most influential works of Roman law.

people.name: Simon bar Kokhba
people.summary: Leader of the Second Jewish Revolt, hailed by Rabbi Akiva as messiah ('son of the star'), later called Bar Koziba ('son of the lie') in rabbinic texts; his own letters survive from the Judaean desert caves.
people.death: killed at the fall of Betar, 135

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.summary: Leading sage of the generation, foundational for the Mishnah's legal method, who according to the Jerusalem Talmud hailed Bar Kosiba as messiah; tradition says he was flayed by the Romans for teaching Torah.

people.name: Tineius Rufus
people.summary: Governor of Judaea at the outbreak of the Bar Kokhba revolt, remembered in rabbinic tradition as Turnus Rufus, persecutor of Akiva.

people.name: Julius Severus
people.summary: Hadrian's best general, transferred from Britain to Judaea, who crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt by attrition and received triumphal ornaments.

people.name: Arrian
people.summary: Greek senator from Nicomedia, pupil of Epictetus (whose Discourses he recorded), governor of Cappadocia who repelled the Alans in 135, and author of the Anabasis of Alexander, the Indica, the Periplus of the Black Sea and the Order of Battle against the Alans.

people.name: Lucius Aelius Caesar
people.fullName: Lucius Aelius Caesar (born Lucius Ceionius Commodus)
people.summary: Elegant, consumptive aristocrat adopted by Hadrian as heir in 136; he died on 1 January 138, and his young son became the emperor Lucius Verus.

people.name: Antoninus Pius
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Augustus Pius (Titus Aurelius Fulvus Boionius Arrius Antoninus)
people.summary: Wealthy senator of Gallic (Nemausus) origin adopted by Hadrian in 138 on condition he adopt Marcus and Lucius. His 23-year reign, spent entirely in Italy, was the most peaceful of the Principate, marked by the Antonine Wall, legal humanity and a full treasury.
people.detail: Marcus's portrait of him (Meditations 1.16) is the fullest sketch of an ideal ruler from someone who knew him intimately: patient, thorough, frugal, courteous, indifferent to flattery. The lack of narrative sources leaves his reign almost without events, which Gibbon took as the mark of a happy age.

people.name: Faustina the Elder
people.summary: Wife of Antoninus Pius and aunt of Marcus Aurelius, deified after her death in 140 and commemorated by the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina and the girls' charity of the puellae Faustinianae.

people.name: Marcus Aurelius
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus (born Marcus Annius Verus)
people.summary: Philosopher-emperor, adopted at Hadrian's behest, who shared power with Lucius Verus, faced the Parthian war, the Antonine Plague, the Marcomannic Wars and the revolt of Avidius Cassius, and spent most of his last decade on the Danube writing the Meditations. He broke with adoption by making his son Commodus co-emperor.
people.detail: Educated by Fronto in rhetoric and by Junius Rusticus in Stoicism; his correspondence with Fronto survives in a palimpsest. His reign saw Christian martyrdoms (Justin, Lyon) under the existing legal framework. His equestrian statue on the Capitol and his column in the Campus Martius survive. Dio judged his death the end of a golden age.
people.death: illness, possibly plague, at Vindobona or Sirmium, 17 March 180

people.name: Lucius Verus
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus (born Lucius Ceionius Commodus)
people.summary: Son of Lucius Aelius Caesar, co-emperor with Marcus from 161, nominal commander of the victorious Parthian war (162-166) waged by his generals; he married Marcus's daughter Lucilla and died of a stroke while returning from the Danube.

people.name: Faustina the Younger
people.summary: Daughter of Antoninus Pius, wife of Marcus Aurelius and mother of at least thirteen children, including Commodus and Lucilla; she accompanied Marcus on campaign (hailed 'mother of the camp') and died at Halala, suspected by hostile sources of encouraging Avidius Cassius.
people.death: natural causes at Halala, Cappadocia, winter 175/176

people.name: Lucilla
people.summary: Daughter of Marcus Aurelius, married to Lucius Verus at Ephesus in 164 and then to Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus; resentful of Commodus's wife's precedence, she organised the failed assassination attempt of 182 and was exiled and killed.

people.name: Commodus
people.fullName: Imperator Caesar Lucius Aelius Aurelius Commodus Augustus
people.summary: Son of Marcus Aurelius, the first emperor 'born in the purple' to a reigning emperor. He ended the Marcomannic Wars by treaty, left government to favourites (Perennis, Cleander), survived conspiracies, increasingly identified himself with Hercules and fought in the arena, and was strangled on the last night of 192.
people.detail: Dio, a senator under him, and Herodian give lurid portraits; the Historia Augusta is worse. Modern historians (Hekster) read his Hercules persona as a deliberate appeal to the plebs and army over the Senate's head. His death ended the Antonine dynasty and began the civil wars of 193.
people.death: strangled in his bath by the wrestler Narcissus, 31 December 192

people.name: Avidius Cassius
people.summary: Syrian-born general, son of an equestrian secretary of Hadrian, famed for brutal discipline, who sacked Seleucia and Ctesiphon (165), suppressed the Bucoli (172) and held a supreme command over the East until his proclamation as emperor in 175 on a false rumour of Marcus's death.
people.death: murdered by a centurion after three months as usurper, July 175

people.name: Statius Priscus
people.summary: Experienced general who rose from the equestrian militia, transferred from Britain to Cappadocia, and recaptured and destroyed Artaxata in 163.

people.name: Sedatius Severianus
people.summary: Gallic-born governor of Cappadocia who, encouraged by the oracle of Alexander of Abonuteichos, marched into Armenia and lost his army and his life at Elegeia in 161.

people.name: Martius Verus
people.summary: General of the Parthian war who later as governor of Cappadocia stayed loyal to Marcus during Cassius's revolt and burned the rebel's correspondence; consul for the second time in 179.

people.name: Vologases IV
people.summary: Arsacid king who invaded Armenia and Syria in 161 and lost Seleucia, Ctesiphon and northern Mesopotamia to the generals of Lucius Verus.

people.name: Lollius Urbicus
people.summary: Berber-born senator from Tiddis in Numidia who served in the Bar Kokhba war, reconquered southern Scotland and built the Antonine Wall, and later presided as city prefect over the trial in Apuleius's circle.

people.name: Aelius Aristides
people.summary: Greek orator of the Second Sophistic from Mysia, author of the panegyric To Rome, the Sacred Tales recording his dream-cures by Asclepius, and a lament for Eleusis sacked by the Costoboci.

people.name: Ptolemy
people.summary: Alexandrian astronomer, geographer and mathematician, author of the Almagest, Geography, Tetrabiblos and Harmonics, whose models dominated science for fourteen centuries.

people.name: Justin Martyr
people.summary: Greek-speaking philosopher from Samaria who converted to Christianity, taught in Rome, wrote two Apologies and the Dialogue with Trypho, and was beheaded under the city prefect Junius Rusticus.

people.name: Galen

roles.t: Physician to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus

people.summary: Physician of Pergamon, trained on gladiators, who became court doctor to Marcus Aurelius and Commodus; his vast output (about a sixth of all surviving Greek literature before 350) includes the key descriptions of the Antonine Plague and, in De indolentia, the loss of his library in the fire of 192.

people.name: Gaius
people.summary: Mysterious jurist known only by his praenomen, perhaps teaching in the East, author of the Institutes (c. 161), the one classical Roman legal work to survive almost complete, rediscovered in Verona in 1816.

people.name: Herodes Atticus
people.fullName: Lucius Vibullius Hipparchus Tiberius Claudius Atticus Herodes
people.summary: Fabulously rich Athenian sophist, tutor of Marcus Aurelius and consul in 143, benefactor of the Odeion in Athens, the Panathenaic stadium and the nymphaeum at Olympia; he chose the holders of Marcus's Athenian chairs.

people.name: Blandina
people.summary: Slave woman martyred at Lyon in 177, whose endurance under days of torture is the centre of the letter of the churches of Vienne and Lyon.
people.death: killed in the amphitheatre at Lyon, 177

people.name: Ballomar
people.summary: King of the Marcomanni who led the eleven-tribe embassy to the governor of Pannonia in 166/167 and is probably the leader of the invasion of Italy in 170.

people.name: Marcus Claudius Fronto

roles.t: Governor of the three Dacias and Upper Moesia

people.summary: Veteran of the Parthian war who governed the combined Dacian and Moesian command and died fighting Germans and Iazyges in 170; a statue in Trajan's Forum honoured him (ILS 1098). Not to be confused with the orator Fronto.

people.name: Claudius Pompeianus

roles.t: Senior commander in the Marcomannic Wars

people.summary: Syrian-born general from Antioch, Marcus's chief commander and son-in-law (husband of Lucilla), who drove the invaders from Italy in 170, advanced Pertinax, opposed Commodus's peace and twice refused the throne.

people.name: Valerius Maximianus
people.summary: Equestrian officer from Poetovio, adlected into the Senate, whose career inscription from Diana Veteranorum records that he killed Valao, king of the Naristi, with his own hand; he commanded the winter camp at Laugaricio.

people.name: Perennis
people.summary: Praetorian prefect who effectively ran the government for Commodus after 182, until a delegation of the British army accused him of conspiring to make his son emperor.
people.death: handed over to the soldiers and killed, 185

people.name: Cleander
people.summary: Phrygian former slave who rose to dominate Commodus's court, selling magistracies (25 consuls in one year), until a grain riot forced Commodus to sacrifice him.

people.name: Ulpius Marcellus
people.summary: Austere, sleepless governor of Britain sent by Commodus to repel the northern invasion of the early 180s; Dio describes his relentless discipline.

people.name: Maternus
people.summary: Deserter who led bands of soldiers and brigands through Gaul and Spain and plotted to kill Commodus at the Hilaria; betrayed and beheaded (Herodian).

people.name: Marcia
people.summary: Freedwoman and mistress of Commodus, said to favour Christians (she secured the release of confessors from the Sardinian mines), who organised his murder with Laetus and Eclectus; she was executed by Didius Julianus.

people.name: Pertinax

roles.t: Prefect of a cohort in Syria
Governor of Moesia, Dacia, Syria, Britain

people.summary: Son of a freedman from Alba Pompeia who rose through equestrian and then senatorial commands under Marcus Aurelius, governed four provinces, and was made emperor on the night Commodus was strangled (31 December 192). He reigned 87 days.
people.detail:
Pertinax tried to restore Antonine austerity: he sold Commodus's luxuries at auction, cut court spending and promised the Praetorians less than they expected. On 28 March 193 some 200 to 300 guardsmen stormed the palace and killed him; the guard then sold the throne to Didius Julianus. Septimius Severus took his name, deified him and staged a magnificent funeral to present himself as the avenger, a claim Cassius Dio, who witnessed it, describes in detail.

In Britain (185-187) he had nearly been killed suppressing a legionary mutiny, which earned him a reputation for severity with soldiers that the Praetorians remembered.
people.death: killed by mutinous Praetorians in the palace on 28 March 193

people.name: Didius Julianus
people.summary: Wealthy Milanese senator raised in Marcus Aurelius' household who bought the throne from the Praetorians on 28 March 193 and was killed in the palace on 1 June after 66 days, as Severus approached Rome.
people.death: killed in the palace on the Senate's order, 1 June 193

people.name: Septimius Severus
people.summary: African senator from Lepcis Magna (born 11 April 145) who won the civil wars of 193-197, sacked Ctesiphon, created the province of Mesopotamia and founded the Severan dynasty; he died campaigning in Britain.
people.detail: Severus spoke Latin with an African accent and had Punic-speaking relatives. His reign raised army pay, enlarged the garrison of Rome, gave equestrians new commands (the Parthian legions, Mesopotamia), and saw the classic age of Roman jurisprudence under Papinian, Ulpian and Paul. His second wife Julia Domna of Emesa, chosen, it was said, because her horoscope promised she would marry a king, presided over an intellectual circle. Gibbon called him the principal author of the decline of the empire; modern assessments (Birley) emphasise his administrative competence and the continuity of his government.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Birley, Septimius Severus: The African Emperor (1971, 2nd ed. 1988)

people.name: Pescennius Niger
people.summary: Italian equestrian-born senator and governor of Syria proclaimed emperor in April 193; popular in Rome but slow to act, he was defeated at Cyzicus, Nicaea and Issus and killed fleeing toward Parthia.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Clodius Albinus
people.summary: Aristocrat from Hadrumetum, governor of Britain, who accepted the rank of Caesar from Severus in 193, proclaimed himself Augustus when sidelined, and died after the battle of Lugdunum.
people.death: killed or suicide after the battle of Lugdunum, 19 February 197; his corpse was trampled by Severus' horse

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Julia Domna
people.summary: Daughter of the high priest of Elagabal at Emesa, wife of Septimius Severus and mother of Caracalla and Geta, honoured as 'mater castrorum et senatus et patriae'; she patronised a circle of intellectuals including Philostratus, whom she commissioned to write the Life of Apollonius of Tyana.
people.detail: She handled petitions and correspondence for Caracalla and was in Antioch when he was murdered. Her sister Julia Maesa and nieces Soaemias and Mamaea carried the dynasty on through Elagabalus and Severus Alexander, the most politically powerful set of women in Roman imperial history.
people.death: starved herself to death at Antioch after Caracalla's murder, 217
scholarship: Levick, Julia Domna: Syrian Empress (2007)

people.name: Caracalla
people.fullName: Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus (born Lucius Septimius Bassianus)
people.summary: Elder son of Severus, nicknamed after the Gallic hooded cloak he favoured; he murdered his brother Geta, issued the Constitutio Antoniniana (212), introduced the antoninianus, built the great baths and was assassinated near Carrhae during a Parthian war.
people.detail: Caracalla cultivated the soldiers, raising their pay by half, and modelled himself on Alexander the Great, raising a Macedonian phalanx. Dio, who knew him, portrays a paranoid, cruel ruler; his massacre at Alexandria and purge after Geta's murder confirm the brutality. His portraits, with a scowling turn of the head, deliberately projected menace.
people.death: assassinated by Julius Martialis near Carrhae, 8 April 217

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Geta
people.summary: Younger son of Severus, joint emperor with Caracalla from 211; murdered by his brother in their mother's arms in December 211 and subjected to one of the most thorough damnationes memoriae known.
people.death: murdered on Caracalla's orders in the palace, December 211

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Plautianus
people.summary: Fellow Lepcitane and perhaps kinsman of Severus, praetorian prefect with near-total power, father-in-law of Caracalla; he was killed in the palace in January 205 after a probably fabricated plot charge.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Papinian
people.summary: Regarded by later Romans as the greatest of the jurists; author of Quaestiones and Responsa, prefect under Severus, executed by Caracalla in 212, according to tradition for refusing to justify the murder of Geta.
people.detail: The Law of Citations of 426 made Papinian the decider when other authorities were evenly split. Justinian's law students in their third year were called 'Papinianistae'.

people.name: Ulpian
people.summary: Jurist from Tyre whose vast output (commentaries Ad Edictum, Ad Sabinum) supplied about one-third of Justinian's Digest; as Severus Alexander's praetorian prefect he was murdered by the Praetorians.
people.detail: His definitions (justice as 'constans et perpetua voluntas ius suum cuique tribuendi'; the distinction of public and private law; the emperor 'legibus solutus') shaped European legal thought.
people.death: murdered by Praetorians in the palace, probably 223
scholarship: Honoré, Ulpian: Pioneer of Human Rights (2nd ed. 2002)

people.name: Cassius Dio

roles.t: Governor of Africa, Dalmatia and Pannonia Superior

people.summary: Senator from Nicaea whose 80-book Greek Roman History, from Aeneas to 229, is a contemporary witness for Commodus and the Severans, surviving for this period mainly in Byzantine epitomes.
scholarship: Millar, A Study of Cassius Dio (1964)

people.name: Herodian
people.summary: Greek historian, probably from the East and of modest official rank, whose eight books cover 180-238; vivid and moralising but chronologically vague, he is the main narrative source for 235-238.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Kemezis, Greek Narratives of the Roman Empire under the Severans (2014)

people.name: Macrinus
people.summary: Mauretanian equestrian lawyer from Caesarea who had Caracalla killed and became the first emperor not of senatorial rank; he bought peace from Parthia after Nisibis and lost the throne to Elagabalus' supporters.
people.death: captured in Cappadocia and executed, June 218

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Elagabalus
people.fullName: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (born Varius Avitus Bassianus)
people.summary: Teenage priest-emperor from Emesa who promoted his sun god Elagabal above Jupiter, married a Vestal, and scandalised Rome; murdered with his mother by the Praetorians.
people.detail: Ancient accounts of his sexual life, including a wish to be called empress, are now read partly as invective, though Dio is contemporary. The HA life is largely fantasy.
people.death: killed by the Praetorians with his mother Soaemias, March 222

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Icks, The Crimes of Elagabalus (2011)

people.name: Julia Maesa
people.summary: Sister of Julia Domna and grandmother of Elagabalus and Severus Alexander; she organised the coup of 218 with her fortune and later engineered the replacement of Elagabalus by Alexander.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Julia Mamaea
people.summary: Mother and dominant adviser of Severus Alexander; she invited Origen to Antioch for theological discussion and was blamed by Herodian for her son's timidity and avarice. Killed with him in 235.
people.death: murdered with Severus Alexander near Mogontiacum, 235

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Severus Alexander
people.fullName: Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander (born Bassianus Alexianus)
people.summary: Last Severan emperor, ruling from age 13 under his mother Mamaea and a council of senators; faced the new Sasanian threat and Germanic invasions and was murdered by his soldiers on the Rhine.
people.detail: The HA's idealised portrait (his household shrine with Christ, Abraham and Orpheus) is fiction, but the reign saw relative calm in government and law.
people.death: murdered by mutinous soldiers at Vicus Britannicus near Mogontiacum, March 235

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Artabanus IV
people.summary: Last Arsacid great king (often numbered V), who fought Macrinus to a bloody draw at Nisibis in 217 but was defeated and killed by Ardashir at Hormozgan in 224.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Vologaeses V
people.summary: Arsacid king who backed Niger, besieged Nisibis in 197 and lost Ctesiphon to Severus' invasion of 197-198.

people.name: Ardashir I
people.summary: Founder of the Sasanian Empire; overthrew Artabanus IV in 224, built Ardashir-Khwarrah, attacked Roman Mesopotamia (230, 237-240) and captured Hatra with his son Shapur.
people.detail: Later Persian tradition (Karnamag-i Ardashir) made him a legendary hero and ideal king; the Testament of Ardashir circulated as a mirror for princes in Islamic times.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

scholarship: Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)

people.name: Shapur I

roles.t: King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran

people.summary: The most successful foreign enemy of third-century Rome: he defeated Gordian III at Misiche (244), sacked Antioch, destroyed Dura and captured Valerian at Edessa (260), recording his deeds in the trilingual ŠKZ inscription and the rock reliefs of Naqsh-e Rustam and Bishapur.
people.detail: He settled Roman captives in new cities in Khuzestan and Persis, patronised Mani, and took the expanded title 'King of Kings of Iran and non-Iran' (Eran ud Aneran).
scholarship: Huyse, Die dreisprachige Inschrift Šābuhrs I. an der Ka'ba-i Zardušt (1999)
Canepa, The Two Eyes of the Earth (2009)

people.name: Maximinus Thrax
people.summary: A gigantic soldier of humble Balkan origin (the 'Thracian' label may be a slur), proclaimed by the Rhine army in 235; he campaigned deep into Germany (Harzhorn) and on the Danube but never visited Rome, and his fiscal exactions provoked the revolts of 238.
people.detail: Herodian and the HA present him as a barbarous peasant; in fact he had a long equestrian career. His reign is the conventional start of the soldier-emperors.
people.death: murdered by his own troops at the siege of Aquileia, 238

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Gordian I
people.summary: Octogenarian aristocratic proconsul of Africa proclaimed at Thysdrus in 238; after his son fell at Carthage he hanged himself, having reigned about three weeks.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Gordian II
people.fullName: Marcus Antonius Gordianus Sempronianus Romanus Africanus
people.summary: Son and co-emperor of Gordian I, killed leading the Carthaginian militia against Capelianus' legion.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Pupienus
people.summary: Senior senator and soldier chosen by the Senate as co-emperor with Balbinus in 238; murdered by the Praetorians after 99 days.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Balbinus
people.summary: Patrician senator co-elected with Pupienus in 238; he governed Rome during street fighting while Pupienus went north, and was killed with him by the Praetorians.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

people.name: Gordian III
people.summary: Grandson of Gordian I, emperor at 13; under his prefect and father-in-law Timesitheus he campaigned against Shapur I, winning at Rhesaina but dying after the defeat at Misiche in 244.
people.death: died in Mesopotamia early 244, from battle wounds (Persian version) or murdered (Roman version)

people.name: Timesitheus
people.summary: Career equestrian administrator, attested on inscriptions through a long series of procuratorships, whose daughter Tranquillina married Gordian III; as prefect he directed the Persian war until his death from illness in 243.

people.name: Philip the Arab
people.summary: From Trachonitis in Arabia, he succeeded Gordian III, made a costly peace with Shapur, celebrated Rome's millennium in 248 and was defeated and killed by Decius near Verona.
people.detail: Later Christian tradition made him the first Christian emperor; most historians reject this. He founded Philippopolis (Shahba) in his homeland.

people.name: Decius
people.summary: Pannonian senator from Budalia near Sirmium who took the name Trajan, ordered universal sacrifice (250), and became the first emperor killed by a foreign enemy, at Abritus against Cniva's Goths.
people.death: killed in battle at Abritus, June 251

people.name: Herennius Etruscus
people.summary: Elder son and co-emperor of Decius, killed by an arrow at Abritus shortly before his father.

people.name: Cniva
people.summary: Gothic leader who besieged Novae, defeated Decius at Beroe, took Philippopolis and destroyed the Roman army at Abritus in 251; known chiefly from Jordanes and Dexippus.

people.name: Trebonianus Gallus
people.summary: Governor proclaimed after Abritus who paid the Goths to leave; his reign saw plague and Persian invasion, and he was murdered by his troops when Aemilianus invaded Italy.
people.death: killed by his own soldiers at Interamna, 253

people.name: Aemilianus
people.summary: Moorish-born governor of Moesia who beat the Goths, was proclaimed emperor, overthrew Gallus and was himself murdered after about three months near Spoletium.
people.death: killed by his own troops near Spoletium, 253

people.name: Valerian
people.summary: Elderly aristocratic senator who took power in 253 and shared it with his son Gallienus; he persecuted the clergy (257-258) and was captured by Shapur I at Edessa in 260, dying in captivity.
people.death: died in Persian captivity at an unknown date

people.name: Gallienus
people.summary: Son of Valerian who held the core empire through fifteen years of invasions, secessions (Postumus, Palmyra) and usurpations; credited with a mobile cavalry force, excluding senators from army commands and ending the persecution.
people.detail: He was initiated at Eleusis, patronised Plotinus (who sought his support for a philosophers' city, Platonopolis, in Campania) and promoted a Hellenising revival in portraiture and coinage. Senatorial historiography and the HA vilified him as frivolous; modern historians (de Blois, Potter) see a resourceful ruler in impossible circumstances.
people.death: murdered by his officers outside Milan, September 268
scholarship: De Blois, The Policy of the Emperor Gallienus (1976)

people.name: Postumus
people.summary: Probably a Batavian, commander on the Rhine, who founded the Gallic Empire in 260 and defended Gaul, Britain and Spain for nine years without attempting to take Rome.
people.death: killed by his own troops at Mogontiacum after refusing them its sack, 269
scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)

people.name: Victorinus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect of Postumus who became Gallic emperor, sacked Augustodunum after a seven-month siege and was murdered at Cologne, reportedly by an officer whose wife he had seduced.

people.name: Tetricus I
people.summary: Senatorial governor of Aquitania proclaimed Gallic emperor in 271 with the backing of Victorinus' mother Victoria; defeated by Aurelian at Châlons in 274, he walked in the triumph and was given an Italian governorship.

people.name: Odaenathus

roles.t: King of Kings; corrector totius Orientis

people.summary: Palmyrene noble and Roman senator who harried Shapur's army after Valerian's capture, crushed the Macriani's Quietus at Emesa, and led two counter-offensives to Ctesiphon as Gallienus' eastern commander.
people.death: assassinated at Emesa with his son Herodianus by a relative, Maeonius, 267

people.name: Zenobia
people.summary: Widow of Odaenathus, who ruled for her son Vaballathus and extended Palmyrene power over Egypt and most of Asia Minor (270-271) before defeat by Aurelian at Immae and Emesa and capture in 272.
people.detail: Ancient sources romanticised her as a chaste huntress-queen claiming descent from Cleopatra. Her end is variously told: death on the journey to Rome, or exhibition in Aurelian's triumph and retirement at Tibur, where descendants were known in the fourth century.
scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia (2018)
Southern, Empress Zenobia (2008)

people.name: Vaballathus
people.fullName: Lucius Julius Aurelius Septimius Vaballathus Athenodorus
people.summary: Son of Odaenathus and Zenobia in whose name Palmyra ruled the East; his coins first paired him with Aurelian, then proclaimed him Augustus in 272.

people.name: Zabdas
people.summary: Zenobia's general who conquered Egypt in 270 and commanded at Immae and Emesa.

people.name: Claudius II Gothicus
people.summary: Illyrian officer who succeeded Gallienus after joining the plot against him; defeated the Alamanni at Lake Benacus and the Goths at Naissus, and died of plague at Sirmium.
people.detail: Constantine later claimed descent from him, so the HA and fourth-century sources inflate his virtues.

people.name: Quintillus
people.summary: Brother of Claudius II, recognised by the Senate on his death, but deserted when the army acclaimed Aurelian; died after a short reign, perhaps by suicide at Aquileia.

people.name: Aurelian
people.summary: Danubian cavalry general nicknamed 'manu ad ferrum' (hand on hilt) who in five years drove the Juthungi from Italy, reconquered Palmyra and the Gallic Empire, abandoned Dacia, walled Rome, reformed the coinage and established Sol Invictus as an imperial cult; titled Restitutor Orbis.
people.death: murdered by his officers at Caenophrurium, 275
scholarship: Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

people.name: Tacitus
people.summary: Elderly emperor chosen after Aurelian's murder; the HA's claims of senatorial election and kinship with the historian are fiction. He campaigned against Gothic raiders in Asia Minor and died at Tyana.

people.name: Florianus
people.summary: Praetorian prefect and half-brother of Tacitus who seized power on his death; killed by his troops at Tarsus after about three months, facing Probus.
people.death: killed by his own troops at Tarsus, 276

people.name: Probus
people.summary: Born at Sirmium, he restored the Rhine and Gaul after the invasions of 275-276, crushed several usurpers, finished the Aurelian Walls and encouraged viticulture in the provinces; killed by his soldiers at Sirmium.
people.death: murdered by his soldiers at Sirmium, 282

people.name: Carus
people.summary: Probably from Narbo, he took power from Probus, made his sons Caesars, invaded Persia and took Ctesiphon, dying in his camp in 283, reportedly struck by lightning.
people.death: died in his camp beyond the Tigris, 283

people.name: Carinus
people.summary: Elder son of Carus who ruled the West; defeated the usurper Julianus at Verona but was murdered by his own officers during the battle of the Margus against Diocletian.
people.death: murdered by one of his officers at the Margus, 285

people.name: Numerian
people.summary: Younger son of Carus, a poet, who led the army back from Persia; found dead in his litter near Nicomedia, blamed on his father-in-law Aper.
people.death: died in his litter near Nicomedia, 284, probably murdered

people.name: Uranius Antoninus
people.fullName: Lucius Julius Aurelius Sulpicius Severus Uranius Antoninus
people.summary: Priest of Elagabal at Emesa who organised resistance to Shapur I and struck coins as emperor in 253-254.

people.name: Ingenuus
people.summary: Governor of Pannonia who claimed the purple after Valerian's capture (or in 258) and was defeated by Aureolus at Mursa.
people.death: killed or drowned himself after Mursa, 260

people.name: Aureolus
people.summary: Dacian-born ex-shepherd who led Gallienus' mobile cavalry, defeating Ingenuus and the Macriani, then rebelled at Milan in 268 in favour of Postumus and finally for himself.
people.death: surrendered to Claudius II and killed, 268

people.name: Dexippus

roles.t: Archon basileus and eponymous archon of Athens

people.summary: Athenian aristocrat, historian of the Gothic wars (Scythica) and a world Chronicle, who led Athenian resistance after the Herulian sack of 267/268; new fragments recovered from a Vienna palimpsest since 2014 have expanded his text.
scholarship: Mecella, Dexippo di Atene (2013)
Martin and Grusková, WS 127 (2014)

people.name: Cyprian
people.summary: Wealthy rhetorician converted c. 246, bishop of Carthage through the Decian persecution, the plague that bears his name and the disputes over the lapsed and baptism; beheaded under Valerian.
people.detail: His De Unitate Ecclesiae, letters and councils made the African church a model of episcopal collegiality; his clash with Pope Stephen over rebaptism of heretics foreshadowed later Roman claims.
scholarship: Brent, Cyprian and Roman Carthage (2010)

people.name: Origen

roles.t: Head of the catechetical school of Alexandria

people.summary: Alexandrian Christian scholar, author of the Hexapla, the treatise On First Principles and Against Celsus, who taught at Caesarea after a break with his bishop; tortured in the Decian persecution, he died at Tyre around 253.
people.detail: His allegorical exegesis and speculative theology shaped Eastern thought; Eusebius was his admirer, but several of his doctrines were condemned in 553.
people.death: after torture under Decius, at Tyre, c. 253

people.name: Plotinus
people.summary: Founder of Neoplatonism, born in Egypt, who taught in Rome from 244 to 269 under the patronage of Gallienus and Salonina; his treatises were edited by his pupil Porphyry as the Enneads.

people.name: Cassius Longinus
people.summary: Platonist philosopher and critic, teacher of Porphyry at Athens, who became an adviser to Zenobia and was executed by Aurelian after Palmyra's fall.
people.death: executed by Aurelian at Emesa, 272 or 273

people.name: Paul of Samosata
people.summary: Bishop of Antioch condemned in 268 for teaching that Christ was a man indwelt by the Logos; his refusal to leave the church house led to Aurelian's ruling of 272.

people.name: Mani
people.summary: Babylonian prophet, raised among the Elchasaite baptists, who founded Manichaeism around 240, enjoyed Shapur I's favour, and died in prison under Bahram I.
people.death: died in chains at Bet Lapat, c. 274-277
scholarship: Gardner and Lieu, Manichaean Texts from the Roman Empire (2004)

people.name: Diocletian
people.summary: Dalmatian soldier of low birth who ended the 'military anarchy', created the Tetrarchy, doubled the provinces, reformed taxation and coinage, issued the Price Edict, began the Great Persecution and became the first emperor to abdicate voluntarily.
people.detail: His court introduced adoratio (prostration) and a more elaborate sacral ceremonial, though the contrast between 'Principate' and 'Dominate' is now seen as overdrawn. Lactantius, hostile, portrays a fearful, greedy ruler driven by Galerius; pagan sources praise him as father of a golden age. His reforms, extended by Constantine, set the framework of the late Roman state for three centuries.
people.death: natural causes (or suicide, according to some sources) at Spalatum, probably 3 December 311 or 312
scholarship: Barnes, The New Empire of Diocletian and Constantine (1982)
Williams, Diocletian and the Roman Recovery (1985)
Kolb, Diocletian und die Erste Tetrarchie (1987)
Corcoran, The Empire of the Tetrarchs (2000)

people.name: Maximian
people.summary: Pannonian soldier and Diocletian's co-Augustus in the West, who suppressed the Bagaudae, fought Franks and Moors and campaigned in Africa (297-298); he abdicated unwillingly in 305, returned to support his son Maxentius, then turned on him and finally on his son-in-law Constantine.
people.death: forced to hang himself at Massilia, 310

people.name: Constantius I
people.summary: Illyrian officer, father of Constantine by Helena, Caesar in the West from 293; he took Boulogne, reconquered Britain (296), defeated the Alamanni and enforced the persecution only lightly. He died at York after a Pictish campaign.
people.detail: The nickname Chlorus ('pale') is Byzantine. Constantinian propaganda invented his descent from Claudius II.

people.name: Galerius
people.summary: Herdsman's son from Dacia Ripensis, Caesar under Diocletian; defeated Narseh in Armenia (298), was the driving force of the Great Persecution according to Lactantius, dominated the Second Tetrarchy, and issued the edict of toleration on his deathbed.
people.detail: His palace and arch at Thessalonica and his birthplace villa, Felix Romuliana (Gamzigrad), named for his mother Romula, survive.
people.death: illness (probably cancer) in 311, after issuing the edict of toleration
scholarship: Leadbetter, Galerius and the Will of Diocletian (2009)

people.name: Helena
people.summary: Mother of Constantine, of humble origin from Drepanum in Bithynia (renamed Helenopolis), possibly a stablemaid; set aside by Constantius I in 289 or 293, she was made Augusta in 324 and toured the Holy Land in 326-328, founding churches.
people.detail: The legend that she found the True Cross appears only in the 390s. Her porphyry sarcophagus is in the Vatican Museums.
people.death: natural causes, c. 329, probably at Nicomedia; buried in Rome on the Via Labicana
scholarship: Drijvers, Helena Augusta (1992)

people.name: Severus II
people.summary: Galerius' friend made Caesar in 305 and Augustus on Constantius' death; deserted by his army in Italy, he surrendered to Maximian and was killed.
people.death: killed or forced to suicide at Tres Tabernae, 307

people.name: Maximinus Daia
people.summary: Galerius' nephew, ruler of the Diocese of Oriens and Egypt, the most determined persecutor, who sponsored anti-Christian 'Acts of Pilate' and a pagan priestly hierarchy; defeated by Licinius at Tzirallum.

people.name: Maxentius
people.summary: Son of Maximian, excluded from the Tetrarchy in 305, who seized Rome in 306, repelled Severus and Galerius, and built extensively in the city; defeated and drowned at the Milvian Bridge.
people.detail: Christian sources paint him as a tyrant, but he tolerated Christians and restored church property in Rome and Africa. His son Romulus died in 309 and was buried in the mausoleum on the Via Appia.
people.death: drowned in the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge, 28 October 312

people.name: Licinius
people.summary: Galerius' comrade from Dacia, made Augustus at Carnuntum (308); defeated Maximinus Daia (313), co-authored the 'Edict of Milan', and ruled the East until his defeats by Constantine in 316 and 324.
people.detail: Eusebius, after 324, depicts him as a renewed persecutor who expelled Christians from his household and army; the extent of this is debated.

people.name: Constantia
people.summary: Half-sister of Constantine married to Licinius at Milan in 313; she obtained her husband's life after Chrysopolis and later sympathised with Arius and Eusebius of Nicomedia.

people.name: Constantine the Great
people.summary: Son of Constantius I and Helena, born at Naissus on 27 February; proclaimed at York (306), he won the West at the Milvian Bridge (312), the whole empire at Chrysopolis (324), convened Nicaea (325), founded Constantinople (324-330), introduced the solidus and made Christianity the favoured religion of the emperor.
people.detail: Constantine's religion remains the great question of his reign: Eusebius' Christian hero, Zosimus' murderer turning to Christ for absolution, or a pragmatist steering from Sol toward the Christian God. He killed his eldest son and wife in 326, legislated harshly (molten lead for complicit nurses in abduction cases), and built a dynastic monarchy undermining the Tetrarchy's collegiality. Barnes sees an early and sincere Christian; Drake a consensus-seeking politician; Potter and Lenski stress continuity with tetrarchic government.
people.death: illness near Nicomedia after baptism, 22 May 337
scholarship: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Barnes, Constantine: Dynasty, Religion and Power (2011)
Drake, Constantine and the Bishops (2000)
Lenski (ed.), Cambridge Companion to the Age of Constantine (2006/2012)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

people.name: Fausta
people.summary: Daughter of Maximian, married to Constantine in 307, mother of Constantine II, Constantius II and Constans; she died in 326, reportedly in an overheated bath, soon after the execution of her stepson Crispus.
people.death: suffocated or scalded in a bath, 326

people.name: Crispus
people.summary: Constantine's eldest son by Minervina, pupil of Lactantius, Caesar in Gaul and victor over Licinius' fleet in the Hellespont (324); executed by his father at Pola in 326 for unknown reasons.

people.name: Constantine II
people.summary: Eldest son of Constantine and Fausta, victor over the Goths in 332; as Augustus he claimed seniority over his brothers and was killed invading Constans' territory.
people.death: killed in an ambush near Aquileia, 340

people.name: Constans
people.summary: Youngest son of Constantine, ruler of the West after 340, a Nicene supporter of Athanasius who campaigned against Franks and crossed to Britain in winter 343; overthrown by Magnentius.
people.death: killed at Helena (Elne) in the Pyrenees, 350

people.name: Constantius II
people.summary: Son of Constantine who ruled the East for 24 years against Shapur II, won the civil war against Magnentius at Mursa (351), promoted Homoian Christianity and the Senate of Constantinople, and died marching against his cousin Julian.
people.detail: Ammianus, though hostile to his suspicious court of eunuchs and informers, describes his dignity and self-control; Athanasius and Hilary attacked him as an Arian Antichrist.
scholarship: Barnes, Athanasius and Constantius (1993)
Henck, 'Constantius ho philoktistes?', DOP 55 (2001)

people.name: Constantius Gallus
people.summary: Julian's half-brother, survivor of the 337 massacre, Caesar at Antioch who governed violently with his wife Constantina; recalled and executed by Constantius.

people.name: Magnentius
people.summary: Officer of barbarian descent born at Samarobriva (Amiens), proclaimed at Autun in 350; defeated at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353).

people.name: Vetranio
people.summary: Aged, reputedly illiterate general proclaimed in Illyricum in March 350 to forestall Magnentius; he abdicated before Constantius at Naissus in December and lived out his life at Prusa.

people.name: Silvanus
people.summary: Frankish officer who deserted Magnentius before Mursa, commanded in Gaul, and was driven to usurpation by court intrigue in 355; killed after 28 days.

people.name: Julian
people.summary: Nephew of Constantine and survivor of the massacre of 337, raised a Christian but secretly a Neoplatonist; as Caesar he won at Strasbourg (357) and restored the Rhine, was proclaimed Augustus at Paris (360), attempted to restore traditional cults and died on campaign in Persia.
people.detail: Julian left orations, satires (the Caesars, Misopogon), hymns and letters, making him the best-documented emperor in his own words. His school law and anti-Christian measures earned him the name 'Apostate'; for Libanius and Ammianus he was a hero with flaws. Gibbon and later writers made him a figure of romantic fascination.
people.death: mortally wounded by a spear near Samarra, 26 June 363
scholarship: Bowersock, Julian the Apostate (1978)
Tougher, Julian the Apostate (2007)
Teitler, The Last Pagan Emperor (2017)

people.name: Jovian
people.summary: Christian guards officer chosen after Julian's death; he extricated the army by ceding Nisibis and the Transtigritane regions to Shapur II and died eight months later.
people.death: asphyxiated by fumes at Dadastana, 17 February 364

people.name: Valentinian I
people.summary: Pannonian officer from Cibalae, emperor of the West, who fought the Alamanni (Solicinium 368), fortified the Rhine and Danube, sent Count Theodosius to Britain and Africa and died of rage at a Quadic embassy.
people.detail: Ammianus depicts a capable but irascible ruler who kept two man-eating bears, Innocence and Gold Nugget, near his bedroom. He was religiously tolerant despite his Nicene faith.

people.name: Valens
people.summary: Younger brother of Valentinian and emperor of the East; defeated Procopius (366) and the Tervingi (367-369), supported Homoian Christianity, admitted the Goths in 376 and died at Adrianople.
people.death: killed at Adrianople, 9 August 378; body never found
scholarship: Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)

people.name: Procopius
people.summary: Cilician relative of Julian, commander of the northern army in 363, who seized Constantinople in 365 claiming Constantinian legitimacy; betrayed and executed.

people.name: Gratian
people.summary: Son of Valentinian I, Augustus at eight; won at Argentaria (378), appointed Theodosius, removed the Altar of Victory and ended state funding of pagan cults, and was overthrown by Magnus Maximus.

people.name: Valentinian II
people.summary: Son of Valentinian I and Justina, proclaimed at four; expelled from Italy by Maximus (387), restored by Theodosius under Arbogast's control, and found hanged at Vienne.

people.name: Justina
people.summary: Widow of Magnentius and then wife of Valentinian I, mother of Valentinian II and Galla; a Homoian Christian who clashed with Ambrose over the basilicas of Milan in 385-386.

people.name: Count Theodosius
people.summary: Spanish general, father of Theodosius I, who restored Britain after 367, fought the Alamanni and suppressed Firmus in Mauretania; executed at Carthage early in 376 after Valentinian's death.

people.name: Theodosius I
people.summary: Spaniard from Cauca, made Augustus in 379 to retrieve the Gothic disaster; settled the Goths by treaty (382), made Nicene Christianity the state religion (380-381), defeated Magnus Maximus (388) and Eugenius at the Frigidus (394), and was the last emperor to rule both halves of the empire.
people.detail: His anti-pagan laws of 391-392, his penance after Thessalonica and his relations with Ambrose made him 'the Great' in Christian historiography. He died at Milan on 17 January 395, leaving Arcadius and Honorius under Stilicho.
scholarship: Williams and Friell, Theodosius: The Empire at Bay (1994)
McLynn, 'Genere Hispanus', in Gillett (ed.) (2005)
Errington, Roman Imperial Policy from Julian to Theodosius (2006)

people.name: Magnus Maximus
people.summary: Spanish officer in Britain proclaimed in 383; overthrew Gratian, ruled from Trier, executed Priscillian, invaded Italy in 387 and was defeated by Theodosius.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

people.name: Arbogast
people.summary: Frankish general who dominated Valentinian II, set up Eugenius as emperor in 392 and lost at the Frigidus.
people.death: suicide two days after the Frigidus, September 394

people.name: Eugenius
people.summary: Teacher of rhetoric and magister scrinii raised to the throne by Arbogast in 392; his toleration of pagan senators made the Frigidus campaign appear a religious war.

people.name: Firmus
people.summary: Moorish prince who revolted against the comes Africae Romanus and was hunted down by Count Theodosius.

people.name: Carausius
people.summary: Menapian sailor and fleet commander who seized Britain and northern Gaul, issuing high-quality coinage with Virgilian legends; murdered by Allectus.
scholarship: Casey, Carausius and Allectus (1994)

people.name: Allectus
people.summary: Carausius' finance officer and murderer, who ruled Britain until defeated by Asclepiodotus.
