Cassius advanced down the Euphrates, won at Dura and Sura, and in 165 sacked Seleucia on the Tigris despite its submission, and burned the palace at Ctesiphon. In 166 he crossed into Media. Lucian's satirical 'How to Write History' mocks the flood of sycophantic histories of this war; Fronto's letters and Principia Historiae offer the court view.

phases.t: Parthian invasion; Elegeia
Reconquest of Armenia
Mesopotamian offensive; Seleucia and Ctesiphon
Media; triumph in Rome

wars.name: Marcomannic Wars
wars.outcome: Rome restores the Danube frontier after near-catastrophe; Marcus's plans for provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia abandoned by Commodus in the peace of 180
wars.summary: A generation of war along the middle Danube, beginning with an incursion of Langobardi and Obii in 166/167 and culminating in the first barbarian invasion of Italy for nearly three centuries, when Marcomanni and Quadi besieged Aquileia and destroyed Opitergium. Marcus Aurelius spent most of his last decade at Carnuntum, Sirmium and Vindobona, writing the Meditations.
wars.detail: The war is divided into the first (bellum Germanicum, 166/167-175) and second (expeditio Germanica secunda, 177-180) phases, separated by the revolt of Avidius Cassius. Rome faced a coalition of Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges and many smaller peoples, partly pushed by movements further north (the Goths moving towards the Black Sea). The Antonine Plague crippled recruitment; Marcus enrolled slaves, gladiators and bandits and auctioned palace treasures in 169. Captured Germans were settled inside the empire, a precedent for later centuries. The chronology is highly uncertain because Dio survives only in excerpts and the Historia Augusta is muddled; the Column of Marcus, coin legends, and inscriptions such as Laugaricio and the career of Valerius Maximianus provide anchors. Whether Marcus intended to annex Marcomannia and Sarmatia (HA Marc. 24.5, 27.10) is debated.

phases.t: Incursions; Marcus and Verus go north
Failed Roman offensive; invasion of Italy; Costoboci raid Greece
Campaigns against Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges; Rain Miracle
Second expedition; Roman garrisons in Quadi lands; death of Marcus

wars.name: Civil wars of 193-197
wars.outcome: Septimius Severus defeats Didius Julianus (193), Pescennius Niger (194) and Clodius Albinus (197) and founds the Severan dynasty
wars.summary: The wars of succession after the murder of Pertinax, in which the Danubian army's candidate Septimius Severus defeated the Syrian army's Pescennius Niger and then the British army's Clodius Albinus.
wars.detail: Severus' strategy was masterly: he neutralised Albinus with the title of Caesar, seized Rome, and sent his generals against Niger while holding the Bosporus with a long siege of Byzantium. Victory at Issus (194) gave him the East. When Albinus, cut out of the succession, crossed into Gaul, Severus marched west and won at Lugdunum (197), the largest battle between Roman armies on record. The wars established the precedent that provincial armies made emperors, and Severus' purges and confiscations funded his rule. Sides: Severans versus Nigerians and Albinians (all Roman).

phases.t: Julianus overthrown; Severus takes Rome
War against Niger: Cyzicus, Nicaea, Issus
Siege of Byzantium
War against Albinus: Lugdunum

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Parthian wars of Septimius Severus
wars.outcome: Roman victory; sack of Ctesiphon; creation of the province of Mesopotamia; Hatra unconquered
wars.summary: Severus' two eastern wars: a punitive campaign of 195 against Osroene and Adiabene, and the invasion of 197-198 that sacked Ctesiphon, followed by two failed sieges of Hatra.
wars.detail: The wars added Mesopotamia (Nisibis, Singara) to the empire, which Dio criticised as a permanent cause of war. By humiliating the Arsacids they contributed to the conditions for the Sasanian takeover in 224.

phases.t: Campaign against Osroene and Adiabene
Invasion of Babylonia; sack of Ctesiphon
Sieges of Hatra

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Severus' Caledonian war
wars.outcome: Inconclusive; Caledonians and Maeatae submit and revolt; Caracalla withdraws to Hadrian's Wall after Severus' death
wars.summary: The imperial expedition of Severus, Caracalla and Geta against the Caledonii and Maeatae beyond the Antonine line, based at York, with a legionary base at Carpow on the Tay.
wars.detail: Dio reports heavy losses to guerrilla warfare in bogs and forests. The war probably aimed at conquest; it ended with Severus' death at York in 211 and Caracalla's peace, after which the northern frontier was quiet for most of the third century.

phases.t: Arrival and first campaign; submission of the Caledonians
Revolt and genocidal punitive campaign
Severus dies; Caracalla makes peace

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Parthian war of Caracalla and Macrinus
wars.outcome: Indecisive; Macrinus pays Artabanus IV 200 million sesterces
wars.summary: Caracalla's invasion of Media and Adiabene after his marriage proposal was refused, ended by his murder and by Macrinus' bloody draw at Nisibis.

phases.t: Caracalla's raid into Media; tombs at Arbela desecrated
Caracalla murdered; battle of Nisibis; peace

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: First Sasanian war (Ardashir and Severus Alexander)
wars.outcome: Stalemate; Mesopotamia preserved at heavy cost
wars.summary: The first war between Rome and the new Sasanian dynasty: Ardashir's invasion of Mesopotamia and Alexander's three-column counter-offensive of 232.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: German war of Severus Alexander and Maximinus
wars.outcome: Roman punitive victories, including the battle at the Harzhorn; Maximinus takes the title Germanicus Maximus
wars.summary: Campaigns on the Rhine against Germanic incursions of 233-234, begun by Severus Alexander (murdered at Mogontiacum) and carried deep into Germany by Maximinus, then continued on the Danube against Sarmatians and Dacians.

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Civil war of 238 (Year of the Six Emperors)
wars.outcome: Maximinus killed at Aquileia; Pupienus and Balbinus murdered; Gordian III sole emperor
wars.summary: The Senate's rebellion against Maximinus Thrax, begun by the Gordians' revolt in Africa and ending with the Praetorians installing Gordian III.

phases.t: Gordians proclaimed at Thysdrus; defeated at Carthage
Pupienus and Balbinus; siege of Aquileia
Praetorians murder the senatorial emperors

sources.w: History of the Empire after Marcus

wars.name: Persian war of Gordian III
wars.outcome: Persian victory at Misiche; Gordian III dies; Philip pays 500,000 aurei
wars.summary: After the Sasanians took Hatra, Nisibis and Carrhae, Gordian III's great expedition won at Rhesaina but was defeated at Misiche; Philip the Arab made peace.

wars.name: Gothic war of Decius
wars.outcome: Gothic victory; Decius killed at Abritus; Gallus pays tribute
wars.summary: The invasion of Moesia and Thrace by Cniva's Goths and their allies, culminating in the sack of Philippopolis and the death of Decius at Abritus.
wars.detail: Preceded by the first Gothic raid on Histria (238), the war was the first in which a Germanic people killed a Roman emperor.

wars.name: Shapur I's second and third wars against Rome
wars.outcome: Sasanian victories: Barbalissos, Antioch sacked, Dura destroyed, Valerian captured; Odaenathus' counter-offensives restore the Roman East
wars.summary: Shapur I's devastating invasions of Syria, Cappadocia and Cilicia, including the capture of Valerian at Edessa in 260, followed by Odaenathus of Palmyra's counterattacks to Ctesiphon.

phases.t: Second campaign: Barbalissos, sack of Antioch, Dura-Europos
Third campaign: Edessa and capture of Valerian; raids into Cilicia and Cappadocia
Odaenathus' counter-offensives

wars.name: Gothic and Herulian invasions
wars.outcome: After two decades of raids by land and sea, Roman victories at the Nestus, Naissus and beyond the Danube end the great invasions
wars.summary: Seaborne raids by Boranoi, Goths and Heruli across the Black Sea and Aegean (Pityus, Trapezus, Bithynia, Athens), and land invasions of the Balkans, ended by Gallienus, Claudius II and Aurelian.

phases.t: Black Sea raids: Pityus, Trapezus, Bithynia
Great Herulian raid; Athens sacked
Naissus and pursuit
Aurelian's victory beyond the Danube

wars.name: Alamannic and Juthungian invasions of Italy
wars.outcome: Invaders defeated at Milan (259), Lake Benacus (268), Fano and Pavia (271) after a defeat at Placentia
wars.summary: Repeated invasions of Italy by Alamanni and Juthungi through the Alpine passes, prompting the building of the Aurelian Walls.

wars.name: Wars against the Gallic Empire
wars.outcome: Aurelian defeats Tetricus at Châlons (274); Gaul, Britain and Spain reunited with the empire
wars.summary: The secession of the western provinces under Postumus, Victorinus and Tetricus, intermittent Roman attempts to recover them, and Aurelian's reconquest.
wars.detail: Gallienus' attempt c. 265 failed; Claudius II recovered Spain and Raetia's loyalty shifted. The Gallic regime never attacked Italy, focusing on Rhine defence. Probus' Rhine campaigns of 277-278 are included here for continuity.

phases.t: Postumus' secession; Gallienus' failed recovery
Laelianus, Marius, Victorinus; Autun sacked
Aurelian's reconquest at Châlons

scholarship: Drinkwater, The Gallic Empire (1987)

wars.name: Palmyrene war
wars.outcome: Aurelian conquers Palmyra; Zenobia captured; Palmyra sacked after a second revolt
wars.summary: Zenobia's expansion into Egypt and Asia Minor and Aurelian's reconquest of the East in 272, with the second revolt and sack of Palmyra in 273.

phases.t: Palmyrene conquest of Egypt and Asia Minor
Aurelian's campaign: Tyana, Immae, Emesa, siege of Palmyra
Second revolt; sack of Palmyra; Firmus in Egypt

scholarship: Andrade, Zenobia (2018)
Watson, Aurelian and the Third Century (1999)

wars.name: Carausian revolt
wars.outcome: Constantius I recovers Britain after the defeat of Allectus
wars.summary: The ten-year secession of Britain and parts of northern Gaul under Carausius and Allectus, ended by Constantius' capture of Boulogne (293) and the invasion of 296.
scholarship: Casey, Carausius and Allectus (1994)

wars.name: Persian war of Galerius and Narseh
wars.outcome: Decisive Roman victory; Peace of Nisibis gives Rome five Transtigritane regions and control of Armenia and Iberia
wars.summary: Narseh's invasion of Armenia and Mesopotamia, Galerius' defeat near Callinicum, and his crushing victory in Armenia in 298 followed by the Peace of Nisibis.

wars.name: Civil wars of the Tetrarchy
wars.outcome: Collapse of the tetrarchic system; Constantine controls the West and Licinius the East by 313
wars.summary: The struggles following the abdications of 305: the usurpations of Constantine and Maxentius (306), the failures of Severus and Galerius in Italy (307), the Carnuntum settlement (308), the fall of Maximian (310), Constantine's conquest of Italy (312) and Licinius' defeat of Maximinus Daia (313).

phases.t: Usurpations of Constantine and Maxentius; Severus and Galerius fail in Italy
Carnuntum settlement; Domitius Alexander; Maximian's end
Constantine invades Italy: Turin, Verona, Milvian Bridge
Licinius defeats Maximinus Daia

scholarship: Barnes, Constantine and Eusebius (1981)
Potter, Constantine the Emperor (2013)

wars.name: Wars of Constantine and Licinius
wars.outcome: Constantine sole emperor after Chrysopolis (324); Licinius executed (325)
wars.summary: Two wars between the Augusti: the first (316-317) gave Constantine the Balkans after Cibalae and Mardia; the second (324), presented by Eusebius as a holy war, ended with Adrianople, the Hellespont and Chrysopolis.

phases.t: First war: Cibalae, Mardia; peace of Serdica
Second war: Adrianople, Hellespont, Chrysopolis

wars.name: Constantine's Gothic and Sarmatian war
wars.outcome: Roman victory; treaty of 332 with the Tervingi; settlement of Sarmatian refugees
wars.summary: Constantine's reassertion of Roman power north of the lower Danube: the bridge at Oescus (328), Constantine II's victory over the Tervingi (332), the ensuing treaty and the reception of 300,000 Sarmatians (334).
scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)

wars.name: Persian war of Constantius II and Shapur II
wars.outcome: Stalemate for two decades; Shapur takes Amida, Singara and Bezabde (359-360)
wars.summary: A long war of sieges and raids in northern Mesopotamia: Shapur's three sieges of Nisibis (338, 346, 350), the night battle of Singara (344 or 348), and his offensive of 359-360 that took Amida, Singara and Bezabde.
wars.detail: Constantius' strategy was defensive, relying on fortified cities. The war was interrupted by Shapur's eastern wars and by Roman civil war (350-353), and was renewed by Julian in 363 (see julian_persian_war).

phases.t: Sieges of Nisibis; Singara
Truce in practice; Shapur fights in the east, Constantius in the west
Shapur's offensive: Amida, Singara, Bezabde

scholarship: Dodgeon and Lieu (1991)
Matthews, The Roman Empire of Ammianus (1989)

wars.name: Civil war against Magnentius
wars.outcome: Constantius II defeats Magnentius at Mursa and Mons Seleucus; sole emperor
wars.summary: The usurpation of Magnentius in the West after the murder of Constans, the brief reigns of Vetranio and Nepotianus, and Constantius' victory at Mursa (351), one of the bloodiest battles of Roman history.

wars.name: Julian's Alamannic and Frankish wars
wars.outcome: Rhine frontier restored; Chnodomar captured at Strasbourg; Frankish Salii settled in Toxandria
wars.summary: Julian's campaigns as Caesar in Gaul: relief of Cologne and Autun, the victory of Strasbourg (357), crossings of the Rhine, and treaties with Alamannic and Frankish kings.
scholarship: Drinkwater, The Alamanni and Rome (2007)

wars.name: Julian's Persian expedition
wars.outcome: Julian killed; Jovian cedes Nisibis, Singara and the Transtigritane regions
wars.summary: Julian's invasion of Persia with perhaps 65,000 men down the Euphrates to Ctesiphon, his death during the retreat, and Jovian's humiliating peace.

wars.name: Revolt of Procopius
wars.outcome: Procopius defeated at Thyatira and Nacolia and executed
wars.summary: The usurpation of Julian's relative Procopius at Constantinople, supported by Gothic troops, against Valens.

wars.name: Valens' Gothic war
wars.outcome: Treaty on the Danube between Valens and Athanaric; subsidies ended and trade restricted
wars.summary: Valens' punitive campaigns north of the Danube against the Tervingi who had supported Procopius.

wars.name: Revolt of Firmus
wars.outcome: Count Theodosius suppresses the revolt; Firmus commits suicide
wars.summary: The rebellion of the Moorish prince Firmus in Mauretania, provoked by the abuses of the comes Africae Romanus.

wars.name: Quadic and Sarmatian war
wars.outcome: Roman punitive campaign; Valentinian I dies at Brigetio
wars.summary: Invasion of Pannonia by the Quadi and Sarmatians after the murder of the Quadic king Gabinius, answered by Valentinian's campaign of 375.

wars.name: Gothic war of 376-382
wars.outcome: Roman catastrophe at Adrianople; treaty of 382 settles the Goths within the empire as an autonomous people
wars.summary: The war that began when Tervingian refugees from the Huns, abused by Roman officials, revolted in Thrace; it brought the death of Valens and most of the eastern field army at Adrianople and ended with Theodosius' treaty of 382.
wars.detail: Ammianus' narrative ends with Adrianople; for 379-382 we depend on Zosimus, Themistius and church historians. Theodosius rebuilt the army but could not defeat the Goths decisively, and the settlement of 382 created a Gothic population within the empire that produced Alaric's revolt in 395.

phases.t: Crossing of the Danube; Marcianople; Ad Salices
Argentaria; Adrianople; Goths fail before Constantinople
Theodosius' war of containment; treaty of 3 October 382

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)
Lenski, Failure of Empire (2002)
Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)

wars.name: Civil war against Magnus Maximus
wars.outcome: Theodosius defeats Maximus at Siscia and Poetovio; Maximus executed at Aquileia
wars.summary: Magnus Maximus' usurpation in Britain and Gaul (383), uneasy recognition (384-387), invasion of Italy (387) and defeat by Theodosius (388).

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

wars.name: Civil war against Eugenius
wars.outcome: Theodosius wins at the Frigidus; Eugenius executed and Arbogast commits suicide
wars.summary: Following the death of Valentinian II, Arbogast's emperor Eugenius held the West for two years with pagan senatorial support until Theodosius' victory at the Frigidus.

sources.w: Seven Books of History against the Pagans

scholarship: Cameron, The Last Pagans of Rome (2011)

wars.name: Gothic Wars of Alaric and his successors
wars.outcome: Goths settled as federates in Aquitaine (418) after sacking Rome (410); the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse is born
wars.summary: Twenty-three years of intermittent war, negotiation and alliance between the Goths led by Alaric, Athaulf and Wallia and the two Roman courts, from the revolt of 395 to the settlement in Aquitaine.
wars.detail: The Goths' goals were consistently Roman: recognised command, regular supplies, and land. The rivalry between Stilicho and Constantinople let Alaric extract concessions from each in turn; Stilicho's fall in 408 removed the one Roman able to contain him. The sack of 410 was the result of Ravenna's refusal to negotiate, not of Gothic strength. Constantius's naval blockade, not battle, finally forced the Goths into the 416 treaty.

phases.t: Revolt in the Balkans and ravaging of Greece
First invasion of Italy: Pollentia and Verona
Sieges and sack of Rome
Athaulf in Gaul and Spain
Wallia as Roman federate in Spain; settlement in Aquitaine

scholarship: Kulikowski, Rome's Gothic Wars (2007)
Heather, Goths and Romans (1991)

wars.name: Gildonic War
wars.outcome: Gildo defeated and killed; Africa and its grain restored to the western court
wars.summary: Gildo, comes Africae, transferred Africa to the eastern court and cut Rome's grain. Stilicho sent Gildo's brother Mascezel, who routed him at the Ardalio.

wars.name: Invasion of Radagaisus
wars.outcome: Radagaisus's host destroyed at Faesulae; 12,000 drafted into the Roman army
wars.summary: A Gothic-led coalition from the middle Danube invaded Italy and was annihilated by Stilicho with Hunnic and Gothic auxiliaries.

wars.name: Usurpation of Constantine III
wars.outcome: Constantine III defeated and executed; Gaul restored to Ravenna, Britain lost
wars.summary: Civil war between Honorius and the British-born usurper Constantine III, complicated by the rebellion of Constantine's general Gerontius and his emperor Maximus in Spain, and by the Rhine invaders.

wars.name: Roman-Sasanian War of 421-422
wars.outcome: Status quo; mutual religious toleration and no new frontier forts
wars.summary: Brief war triggered by Bahram V's persecution of Christians and Roman refusal to return refugees.
scholarship: Greatrex & Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars, Part II (2002)

wars.name: War against Joannes
wars.outcome: Joannes executed; Valentinian III installed with Galla Placidia as regent
wars.summary: Theodosius II's intervention to install his cousin Valentinian III against the Ravenna usurper Joannes, who was backed by Aetius and his Huns.

wars.name: Vandal conquest of Africa
wars.outcome: Vandals take Carthage (439); treaty of 442 recognises their rule over the richest provinces
wars.summary: The Vandals and Alans under Gaiseric crossed to Africa, besieged Hippo, defeated Roman and eastern armies, were recognised as federates in 435, and seized Carthage in 439.
wars.detail: The loss of the Proconsularis and Byzacena was the most damaging blow to western finances in the fifth century. The aborted joint expedition of 441 showed the empire's capacity to respond was wrecked by simultaneous Hunnic and Persian threats.
scholarship: Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)

wars.name: Aetius's wars in Gaul
wars.outcome: Burgundians crushed and resettled; Visigoths contained after the defeat of Litorius
wars.summary: Aetius's campaigns, often with Hunnic auxiliaries, against Visigoths at Arles and Narbonne, Franks on the Rhine, Burgundians, Iuthungi and the Bagaudae of Armorica.

wars.name: Wars with Attila's Huns
wars.outcome: Huge tribute extracted from the East; Attila halted in Gaul (451), withdrew from Italy (452); Hunnic empire collapses after Nedao (454)
wars.summary: Two decades of Hunnic pressure: treaties and rising tribute (435, 443, 447), devastating Balkan invasions (441-442, 447), the invasion of Gaul (451) and Italy (452), and the collapse after Attila's death.
wars.detail: Hunnic power rested on Roman gold redistributed to a coalition of subject peoples. The East paid and rebuilt its walls; the West depended on Aetius's coalition of federates. Heather argues the Huns' greatest impact was indirect, pushing other peoples into the empire before 420 and, after 454, releasing a crowd of successor groups into Roman politics.

phases.t: Treaties of Margus and rising tribute
Balkan invasions
Diplomacy and the Honoria affair
Invasions of Gaul and Italy
Death of Attila and Nedao

scholarship: Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008)
Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)

wars.name: Roman-Vandal War of 455-474
wars.outcome: Both Roman counter-offensives (460, 468) fail; Zeno recognises Vandal rule in perpetual peace (474)
wars.summary: After the sack of Rome, twenty years of Vandal naval raiding on Italy, Sicily and the Aegean, and two great Roman attempts at reconquest under Majorian and Basiliscus, both destroyed before landing in force.

wars.name: Revolt of Illus
wars.outcome: Illus and Leontius defeated and executed
wars.summary: Rebellion of Zeno's Isaurian minister Illus with the usurper Leontius and the dowager Verina, ending with the four-year siege of Papyrius.

wars.name: Ostrogothic conquest of Italy
wars.outcome: Odoacer killed; Theodoric rules Italy
wars.summary: Theodoric the Amal, commissioned by Zeno, led the Goths from the Balkans into Italy and in four years of war destroyed Odoacer's regime.
scholarship: Moorhead, Theoderic in Italy (1992)

wars.name: Isaurian War
wars.outcome: Isaurian resistance crushed; many deported to Thrace
wars.summary: Anastasius's war against the Isaurian faction expelled from Constantinople after Zeno's death, decided at Cotyaeum and ended by the capture of their mountain strongholds.

wars.name: Anastasian War
wars.outcome: Seven-year truce; Romans recover Amida by payment and build Dara
wars.summary: Kavad I's invasion to extort money, notable for the siege of Amida, poor Roman command coordination, and the building of Dara.
scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)

wars.name: Frankish-Visigothic War
wars.outcome: Visigoths lose almost all of Gaul; Ostrogoths secure Septimania and Provence
wars.summary: Clovis's attack on the Visigothic kingdom of Toulouse, decided at Vouillé, with Theodoric's Ostrogoths intervening in 508 to save Septimania.

wars.name: Revolt of Vitalian
wars.outcome: Vitalian's fleet destroyed (515); he is later rehabilitated by Justin I
wars.summary: Three marches on Constantinople by the Thracian federate commander Vitalian, demanding Chalcedonian orthodoxy and pay for the federates.

wars.name: Iberian War
wars.outcome: 'Eternal Peace' (532): status quo, Rome pays 11,000 lbs of gold
wars.summary: War sparked by the revolt of the Iberian king Gourgen against Persia, fought in Lazica, Armenia and Mesopotamia. Belisarius won at Dara and lost at Callinicum.
scholarship: Greatrex, Rome and Persia at War 502-532 (1998)

wars.name: Vandalic War
wars.outcome: Vandal kingdom destroyed; Africa, Sardinia, Corsica and the Balearics reconquered
wars.summary: Belisarius's lightning campaign that destroyed the Vandal kingdom in two battles and restored Roman rule in Africa after 94 years.
wars.detail: Justinian took a large risk against the advice of his ministers, and the speed of victory surprised everyone. Success owed much to Gelimer's divided forces (his brother Tzazon was in Sardinia), Belisarius's discipline of his troops toward the population, and the superiority of Roman and Hunnic horse archers.
scholarship: Merrills & Miles, The Vandals (2010)
Hughes, Belisarius (2009)

wars.name: Moorish Wars in Roman Africa
wars.outcome: Moorish coalition broken at the Campi Catonis; fifteen years of peace
wars.summary: Fourteen years of war against the Mauri of Byzacena, Numidia and Tripolitania, interwoven with military mutinies (Stotzas 536, Guntharic 545-546). Solomon was killed in 544; John Troglita won the final victory in 548.

wars.name: Gothic War
wars.outcome: Ostrogothic kingdom destroyed; Italy reconquered but devastated; Pragmatic Sanction (554)
wars.summary: Justinian's twenty-year war to recover Italy: Belisarius's rapid conquest (535-540), Totila's revival (541-550), and Narses's final victories (551-554), with Frankish interventions throughout.
wars.detail: Rome changed hands five times. Procopius, an eyewitness of the first phase, narrates it in books 5-8 of the Wars; Agathias continues to 554. The war, combined with plague and famine, ruined much of Italy's urban and senatorial society. Fourteen years after its end the Lombards invaded. The cost of the war, and whether it was worth it, has been debated since Procopius.

phases.t: Belisarius's conquest: Sicily, Naples, siege of Rome, Ravenna
Totila's recovery; Rome lost twice
Narses: Busta Gallorum, Mons Lactarius, the Volturnus

scholarship: Wolfram, History of the Goths (1988)
Heather, Rome Resurgent (2018)

wars.name: Roman-Sasanian War of 540-562 (including the Lazic War)
wars.outcome: Fifty Years' Peace: Lazica Roman, Rome pays 30,000 nomismata a year
wars.summary: Khosrow I's invasion of Syria and sack of Antioch (540) opened twenty years of war: Mesopotamian campaigns until the truce of 545, and a long war in Lazica on the Black Sea coast (541-562).

phases.t: Mesopotamia and Syria: Antioch, Anglon, Edessa
Lazic War: Petra, Archaeopolis, Phasis
Truce and Fifty Years' Peace

wars.name: Roman intervention in Spain and the province of Spania
wars.outcome: Roman province of Spania held on the south-east coast for seventy years, finally lost to Suinthila
wars.summary: Justinian's expedition under Liberius in support of Athanagild, leaving a Roman coastal province that the Visigothic kings gradually reconquered.

wars.name: Roman-Lombard Wars
wars.outcome: Italy divided between the Lombard kingdom and duchies and the Roman exarchate
wars.summary: The Lombard invasion of 568 and the following decades of war, Roman diplomacy with the Franks, the creation of the exarchate, and papal negotiations with Agilulf, ending in truces after 598-605.
scholarship: Christie, The Lombards (1995)

wars.name: Roman-Sasanian War of 572-591
wars.outcome: Roman intervention restores Khosrow II; Rome gains most of Armenia without payment
wars.summary: Justin II's war in support of the Armenian revolt and in alliance with the Turks; the loss of Dara drove him mad. Two decades of campaigns in Mesopotamia and Armenia ended when Maurice restored Khosrow II against Bahram Chobin.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)

wars.name: Avar and Slav Wars in the Balkans
wars.outcome: Roman victories beyond the Danube by 599-602, undone by the mutiny of 602 and the Persian war
wars.summary: From the Avar siege of Sirmium to the mutiny of 602: Avar raids, Slav settlement in the Balkans and Greece, and Maurice's offensives across the Danube after 591.
scholarship: Whitby, The Emperor Maurice and his Historian (1988)
Pohl, The Avars (2018)
Curta, The Making of the Slavs (2001)

wars.name: Heraclian Revolt
wars.outcome: Phocas overthrown; Heraclius emperor
wars.summary: Civil war launched from Carthage by the exarch Heraclius the Elder, fought in Egypt and decided by the younger Heraclius's naval descent on Constantinople.

wars.name: Roman-Sasanian War of 602-628
wars.outcome: Roman victory after near-collapse: Khosrow II overthrown; all lost territory and the True Cross restored; both empires exhausted
wars.summary: The 'last great war of antiquity'. Persia conquered Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt and reached the Bosporus; Heraclius counterattacked through Armenia and Azerbaijan, survived the Avar-Persian siege of Constantinople, and destroyed Khosrow's army at Nineveh.
wars.detail: The war devastated the cities of the Near East, ended Constantinople's free bread, forced the melting of church plate, and drove imperial ideology toward holy war and Marian protection. Its end left both empires militarily exhausted and their Arab buffer states (Lakhmids destroyed 602, Ghassanids weakened) dismantled, opening the way for the Arab conquests.

phases.t: Persian conquest of Mesopotamia under Phocas
Fall of Syria, Palestine and Egypt; Persians at Chalcedon
Heraclius's campaigns in Armenia and Atropatene; siege of Constantinople
Turkic alliance, Nineveh, fall of Khosrow

scholarship: Howard-Johnston, The Last Great War of Antiquity (2021)
Kaegi, Heraclius (2003)

wars.name: Arab conquest of the Roman Near East
wars.outcome: Syria, Palestine, Mesopotamia and Egypt lost; the empire reduced to Anatolia, the Balkan coasts, Africa and Italian enclaves (war continued after 641)
wars.summary: From the skirmish at Mu'ta (629) to the surrender of Babylon and the Treaty of Alexandria (641), the armies of Medina destroyed Roman power in the Near East: Dathin and Ajnadayn (634), Damascus (635), the Yarmuk (636), Jerusalem (637), Mesopotamia (639-640) and Egypt (639-641).
wars.detail: Explanations range from Roman and Persian exhaustion after 628, Roman inability to pay soldiers and Arab allies, the tactical mobility of Arab armies and good intelligence, the relative leniency of surrender terms, and religious motivation and cohesion. The older view that miaphysite Christians welcomed the invaders as liberators is now treated sceptically. Sources are a problem: Arabic narratives are late, partly schematic and contradictory; contemporary non-Muslim sources (Thomas the Presbyter, the Doctrina Jacobi, Sophronius, Sebeos, John of Nikiu) are fragmentary.

phases.t: First raids: Mu'ta, Tabuk
Conquest of Palestine and Syria: Dathin, Ajnadayn, Fahl, Damascus, Yarmuk
Jerusalem, northern Syria, Mesopotamia, Caesarea
Invasion of Egypt

scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Hoyland, In God's Path (2015)

campaigns.name: Lars Porsenna's march on Rome
campaigns.strength: unknown
campaigns.summary: Porsenna's army from Clusium came down the Chiana and Tiber valleys, seized the Janiculum and blockaded (or took) Rome; his son Arruns later pushed into Latium and was destroyed at Aricia.

path.t: Past Volsinii into the Tiber valley
Down the Tiber through Faliscan country

path.note: Veii regains the Septem Pagi under the peace

campaigns.note: Route reconstructed from geography; sources give only endpoints.

campaigns.name: Coriolanus' Volscian campaign
campaigns.strength: Volscian army (no figure)
campaigns.summary: Livy's list of the towns Coriolanus took on his march from Volscian country to the edge of Rome: Circeii, Satricum, Longula, Polusca, Corioli, Lavinium, then Corbio, Vetelia, Trebium, Labici and Pedum, before he camped at the Fossae Cluiliae.

path.t: Antium, Volscian base of Attius Tullius

path.note: Veturia and Volumnia persuade him to withdraw

campaigns.note: The list of towns may reflect real 5th-century Volscian conquests attached to a legendary figure.

campaigns.name: The Gallic march on Rome
campaigns.strength: perhaps 30,000 (Diodorus; guess)
campaigns.summary: The Senones crossed the Apennines from the Adriatic, besieged Clusium, then marched down the Tiber valley, routed the Romans at the Allia and sacked Rome; after seven months they departed with a ransom.

path.t: Down the Paglia and Tiber valleys
Sack of Rome; siege of the Capitol

path.note: Polybius: the Veneti had invaded their lands

campaigns.note: Varronian date 390; Polybius 387/386. Diodorus has the Gauls camp in Iapygia/Apulia after the sack; Strabo says Caere defeated them on their return.

campaigns.name: The Caudine Forks campaign
campaigns.strength: two consular armies, perhaps 20,000
campaigns.summary: The consuls concentrated at Calatia and, believing false reports that Luceria was besieged, took the short route through the Caudine pass toward Apulia, where Gavius Pontius trapped and forced the surrender of the whole army.

path.note: Samnite soldiers disguised as shepherds report Luceria under siege

path.t: Caudine Forks: army trapped and surrenders

path.note: Campanians give them clothing and arms

campaigns.note: Exact site of the Forks disputed (Arpaia-Montesarchio valley most favoured).

campaigns.name: Fabius Rullianus through the Ciminian forest
campaigns.strength: consular army, c. two legions plus allies
campaigns.summary: From Sutrium Fabius crossed the dense Ciminian forest by night, ravaged the untouched plains of central Etruria, defeated the Etruscans and brought Perusia, Cortona and Arretium to seek a truce.

path.t: Night march through the Ciminian forest
Ravaging the plains of central Etruria
Through the Chiana valley toward the northern cities

campaigns.note: Livy gives few topographical details beyond the forest and Perusia.

campaigns.name: The Sentinum campaign
campaigns.strength: four legions plus at least as many allies, c. 36,000-40,000
campaigns.summary: After a legion was destroyed near Camerinum, the consuls Fabius and Decius marched north through Umbria and crossed the Apennines to meet the Samnites and Senones at Sentinum, while diversionary attacks on Etruria drew off the Etruscans and Umbrians.
campaigns.note: Route inferred; Livy places the legion's destruction near Clusium, Polybius near Camerinum.

campaigns.name: Pyrrhus' Italian campaigns of 280-279
campaigns.strength: 20,000 foot, 3,000 horse, 2,000 archers, 500 slingers, 20 elephants (Plutarch), plus Tarentine and Italian allies
campaigns.summary: Pyrrhus crossed from Epirus, lost ships in a storm, won at Heraclea, marched up through Campania toward Rome as far as Anagnia or Praeneste, wintered at Tarentum and fought the costly victory at Ausculum in 279.

path.t: Storm-scattered landing on the Messapian coast
Battle of Heraclea on the Siris

campaigns.note: Plutarch says he came within 300 stades of Rome; Eutropius and Florus name Praeneste.

campaigns.name: Pyrrhus in Sicily and his last Italian campaign (278-275)
campaigns.strength: c. 8,000 foot and elephants crossing to Sicily; 30,000 foot and 2,500 horse with Sicilian allies (Diodorus)
campaigns.summary: Pyrrhus crossed to Sicily, relieved Syracuse, swept the Carthaginians from all but Lilybaeum, failed to take it, lost Greek support, fought his way back to Italy through a Punic fleet, was checked at Beneventum and sailed home.

path.t: Back to Syracuse amid Greek disaffection
Naval defeat in the Strait of Messina

campaigns.note: Sicilian chronology follows Diodorus 22 and Plutarch 22-24.

campaigns.name: Alexander of Epirus in southern Italy
campaigns.strength: unknown; Epirote army with Tarentine support
campaigns.summary: Invited by Tarentum, Alexander campaigned against Messapians, Lucanians, Samnites and Bruttians, from Sipontum in Apulia to Paestum and Consentia, before being killed at Pandosia.

path.t: Victory near Paestum over Samnites and Lucanians

campaigns.note: Order of operations uncertain; Livy 8.17 and 8.24 and Justin 12.2 are brief.

campaigns.name: Regulus' invasion of Africa
campaigns.strength: 330 ships at Ecnomus; 15,000 foot and 500 horse left in Africa
campaigns.summary: The first Roman invasion of Africa: the fleet fought its way past the Carthaginian navy at Ecnomus, landed at Aspis, won at Adys and reached Tunes, before Xanthippus destroyed Regulus' army in spring 255.

path.note: embarks the army of both consuls

campaigns.name: The Gallic invasion of 225
campaigns.strength: 50,000 foot and 20,000 horse and chariots (Polybius 2.23)
campaigns.summary: The Boii, Insubres and Gaesatae crossed the Apennines into Etruria, plundered as far as Clusium, defeated a praetorian army near Faesulae, and, retreating up the coast with their booty, were trapped between two consular armies at Telamon.
campaigns.note: Polybius' topography (Faesulae north, Telamon south) is hard to reconcile; many scholars move the first battle to the Clusium area.

campaigns.name: Hannibal's march to Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 90,000 foot and 12,000 horse at the Ebro; 38,000 foot and 8,000 horse at the Rhône; 20,000 foot and 6,000 horse on arrival in Italy (Polybius 3.35, 3.56)
campaigns.summary: From New Carthage Hannibal marched across the Ebro and the Pyrenees, forced the Rhône, crossed the Alps in about fifteen days in October-November, took Turin and beat the Romans at the Ticinus and the Trebia.

path.note: subdues the tribes north of the river; leaves Hanno with 10,000

path.t: Through the land of the Volcae

path.note: settles a dispute among the Allobroges
Col du Clapier, Mont Cenis or Traversette

campaigns.note: Alpine pass disputed (Col de la Traversette, Col du Clapier, Mont Cenis, Mont Genèvre, Little St Bernard); the path drawn follows a Clapier route.

campaigns.name: Hannibal's campaigns of 217-216
campaigns.strength: c. 50,000 by 216 including Gallic allies
campaigns.summary: Leaving winter quarters in the Po valley, Hannibal crossed the Apennines and the flooded Arno marshes (losing an eye), destroyed Flaminius at Trasimene, marched to the Adriatic, ravaged Campania under Fabius' eyes, wintered at Gerunium and annihilated the Roman army at Cannae.

path.note: four days and three nights in water; Hannibal loses an eye

path.t: Ravages around Cortona to provoke Flaminius
Ager Falernus and the oxen stratagem

campaigns.name: Hannibal's march on Rome
campaigns.strength: picked force, perhaps 30,000
campaigns.summary: To relieve Capua, Hannibal marched on Rome, camped by the Anio and rode to the Colline Gate, then withdrew, plundering the sanctuary of Feronia, when the besiegers of Capua stayed put. The route given follows Livy (from Coelius); Polybius sends him through Samnium.

path.t: Camp on the Anio; rides to the Colline Gate

campaigns.note: Polybius (9.5-7) and Livy (26.7-11) give different routes.

campaigns.name: Scipio's campaigns in Spain
campaigns.strength: c. 28,000 foot and 3,000 horse at New Carthage (Polybius); 45,000 foot and 3,000 horse at Ilipa
campaigns.summary: Scipio stormed New Carthage, beat Hasdrubal at Baecula and destroyed the last Carthaginian armies at Ilipa, then crossed to Africa to court Syphax and returned to punish rebels and quell a mutiny.

path.note: dines with Hasdrubal son of Gisco at Syphax's table

campaigns.name: Hasdrubal's march to Italy
campaigns.strength: perhaps 30,000 by the Metaurus, with 10 elephants and many Gauls and Ligurians
campaigns.summary: After Baecula Hasdrubal led his army north through Spain, crossed the Pyrenees, wintered among the Arverni, crossed the Alps more easily than his brother and descended into Italy, only to be destroyed at the Metaurus.

path.t: Near Sena Gallica: two consuls face him

campaigns.note: Livy and Appian give few details; the Pyrenean crossing and Alpine pass are unknown.

campaigns.name: Claudius Nero's march to the Metaurus
campaigns.strength: 6,000 foot and 1,000 horse picked men (Livy 27.43)
campaigns.summary: Having intercepted Hasdrubal's letters, Nero slipped away from Hannibal in Apulia with picked troops and marched up the Adriatic coast, about 400 km in six or seven days, fed by the towns along the way, to join Livius Salinator and destroy Hasdrubal.

path.t: Leaves the camp facing Hannibal near Canusium
Joins Livius at Sena Gallica by night
Back facing Hannibal within six days

campaigns.name: Scipio's invasion of Africa
campaigns.strength: c. 25,000-35,000 men from Sicily, later joined by Masinissa's 6,000 foot and 4,000 horse
campaigns.summary: Scipio crossed from Lilybaeum, failed to take Utica, burned the camps of Syphax and Hasdrubal, won the Great Plains, took Tunes and finally defeated Hannibal at Zama.

campaigns.name: Flamininus against Philip V
campaigns.strength: c. 26,000 at Cynoscephalae including Aetolians and 20 elephants
campaigns.summary: Flamininus forced the Aous gorge, marched through Epirus into Thessaly, wintered in Phocis, negotiated at Nicaea, and in 197 brought Philip to battle at Cynoscephalae.

path.t: Peace talks at the Vale of Tempe

campaigns.name: Cato's campaign in Spain
campaigns.strength: 2 legions plus allies, c. 25,000
campaigns.summary: Cato sailed from Luna, defeated the Iberians at Emporiae, disarmed the tribes north of the Ebro, marched south to help the praetor in Turdetania, and failed to take Seguntia in Celtiberia before returning to the north-east.

campaigns.name: The Scipios' march to Asia
campaigns.strength: c. 30,000 with Pergamene and Achaean contingents
campaigns.summary: Lucius Scipio, with Africanus as legate, marched overland through Macedonia and Thrace with Philip V's help, crossed the Hellespont unopposed after Myonessus, sacrificed at Ilium and defeated Antiochus at Magnesia.

campaigns.name: Manlius Vulso's Galatian campaign
campaigns.strength: 4 legions and allies with Pergamene troops under Attalus
campaigns.summary: From Ephesus Manlius marched through Caria, Pisidia and Phrygia extorting money from cities and dynasts, then stormed the Galatian refuges on Mount Olympus and Mount Magaba.

path.t: Defeats the Tectosages on Mount Magaba

campaigns.name: Aemilius Paullus' Pydna campaign
campaigns.strength: c. 29,000 with 34 elephants
campaigns.summary: Paullus crossed to Corcyra, visited Delphi, took over the army facing Perseus on the Elpeus, sent Nasica round by the Pythion pass to turn the Macedonian line, and won at Pydna.

path.t: Takes command on the Elpeus near Dion

campaigns.name: Scipio Aemilianus at Carthage
campaigns.strength: c. 40,000 including Numidians
campaigns.summary: Scipio restored discipline, cut Carthage off from the land with a fortified line across the isthmus, closed the harbour with a mole, destroyed the Punic field army at Nepheris and stormed the city.

path.t: Night assault on the suburb of Megara

campaigns.name: Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia
campaigns.strength: c. 60,000 including allies and Numidians under Jugurtha
campaigns.summary: Scipio drilled the demoralised army, foraged through the land of the Vaccaei to deny Numantia supplies, then built a 9 km circumvallation; the town starved and surrendered in summer 133.

path.t: Takes over the army before Numantia
Forages near Pallantia; ambushed on return

campaigns.name: Marius against the Teutones and Cimbri
campaigns.strength: c. 30,000-40,000 in 102; with Catulus c. 52,300 at Vercellae (Plutarch)
campaigns.summary: Marius trained his army for two years in a fortified camp on the lower Rhône, digging the Fossa Mariana, then shadowed the Teutones and destroyed them at Aquae Sextiae in 102. Returning to Italy, he joined Catulus, who had fallen back from the Adige, and annihilated the Cimbri at Vercellae in July 101.

path.t: Rome: Marius consul for the second time
Fortified camp near Arelate; Fossa Mariana dug
path.note: army trained 104-102 while the Cimbri were in Spain

path.t: Aquae Sextiae: Teutones and Ambrones destroyed
Rome: elected consul for the fifth time

campaigns.note: The site of Vercellae is disputed (Piedmont or the lower Po).

campaigns.name: Sulla's march on Rome
campaigns.strength: 6 legions (c. 35,000) from the army besieging Nola
campaigns.summary: Deprived of the Mithridatic command by Sulpicius' law, the consul Sulla led the army at Nola up the Via Latina to Rome and fought his way in through the Esquiline, the first Roman march on the city.

path.t: Esquiline Gate: Sulla forces his way into Rome

campaigns.name: Sulla's campaign in Greece and Asia
campaigns.strength: 5 legions, c. 30,000 men
campaigns.summary: Sulla crossed to Epirus in 87, besieged Athens and the Piraeus through the winter, destroyed Archelaus' armies at Chaeronea and Orchomenus, marched through Macedonia to the Hellespont, made peace with Mithridates at Dardanus and took over Fimbria's army at Thyatira before settling Asia from Ephesus.

path.t: Siege of Athens and the Piraeus

campaigns.name: Sulla's return and the conquest of Italy
campaigns.strength: 5 legions (c. 40,000) on landing, joined by Metellus Pius, Crassus and Pompey's three legions
campaigns.summary: Sulla landed at Brundisium in spring 83, beat Norbanus near Capua, absorbed Scipio's army at Teanum, and in 82 defeated the younger Marius at Sacriportus, entered Rome, campaigned against Carbo around Clusium, and returned to win the Colline Gate.

campaigns.name: Lucullus' campaigns against Mithridates and Tigranes
campaigns.strength: 5 legions, c. 30,000 foot and 2,500 horse; 12,000 foot and 3,000 horse at Tigranocerta
campaigns.summary: Lucullus relieved Cyzicus, invaded Pontus and broke Mithridates at Cabira, crossed the Euphrates against Tigranes and won at Tigranocerta, pushed towards Artaxata until his army refused to go on, took Nisibis, and returned to Pontus as his army mutinied.

path.t: Danala, Galatia: hands over to Pompey

campaigns.note: Tigranocerta's location is disputed.

campaigns.name: The march of Spartacus' army
campaigns.strength: 70 gladiators at the breakout; 70,000-120,000 including non-combatants at peak (Appian)
campaigns.summary: From Capua the slaves moved to Vesuvius, wintered in Lucania, marched north through Apulia and Picenum to Cisalpine Gaul, beating both consuls and the governor at Mutina, then turned south to Bruttium, where Crassus walled them in. They broke out and were destroyed in Lucania.

path.t: Rhegium: pirates fail to ferry them to Sicily

campaigns.note: The route north and back is reconstructed from fragmentary notices.

campaigns.name: Pompey's campaign against the pirates
campaigns.strength: 500 ships, 120,000 infantry, 5,000 cavalry, 24 legates (lex Gabinia)
campaigns.summary: Dividing the Mediterranean into thirteen zones under legates, Pompey swept the western seas in 40 days, returned to Rome, then sailed from Brundisium to Cilicia, where the pirates' strongholds surrendered after the battle of Coracesium; the whole campaign took about three months.

path.t: Back to Ostia and Rome (40 days)
Soli, refounded as Pompeiopolis for resettled pirates

sources.w: De imperio Cn. Pompei (Pro lege Manilia)

campaigns.name: Pompey in the East
campaigns.strength: Lucullus' army and his own, perhaps 40,000-50,000
campaigns.summary: Pompey took over from Lucullus, destroyed Mithridates' army at the Lycus, received Tigranes' surrender at Artaxata, campaigned against the Albanians and Iberians in the Caucasus, wintered at Amisus, annexed Syria, captured Jerusalem and returned to Italy in 62.

campaigns.name: Crassus' march to Carrhae
campaigns.strength: 7 legions (c. 35,000), 4,000 cavalry, 4,000 light troops
campaigns.summary: Crassus crossed the Euphrates at Zeugma and, instead of following the river or going through Armenia, struck across the Mesopotamian steppe after the Parthian army, guided by the Osrhoene Abgar. Surena caught him south of Carrhae; the survivors retreated through Carrhae towards the Armenian hills, where Crassus was killed.

path.t: Near Sinnaca: Crassus killed at a parley

campaigns.name: Caesar in Gaul, 58 BC: the Helvetii and Ariovistus
campaigns.strength: 1 legion at Geneva rising to 6 (VII-XII), with auxiliaries; c. 30,000-35,000
campaigns.summary: Caesar raced from Rome to Geneva, blocked the Helvetii, raised two new legions in Cisalpine Gaul, crossed the Alps, cut up the Tigurini at the Saône, defeated the Helvetii near Bibracte, and in September destroyed Ariovistus' Germans in Alsace.

path.t: Genava: bridge broken, wall along the Rhône

campaigns.note: Battle sites at Bibracte and against Ariovistus are approximate.

campaigns.name: Caesar in Gaul, 57 BC: the Belgae
campaigns.strength: 8 legions (two new, XIII and XIV), plus Numidian, Cretan and Balearic auxiliaries
campaigns.summary: Caesar marched north to the Remi, held the Belgic coalition at the Aisne until it broke up, received the submission of the Suessiones, Bellovaci and Ambiani, nearly lost his army to the Nervii at the Sabis, and stormed the oppidum of the Atuatuci.

path.t: Durocortorum (Reims): the Remi ally with Rome

campaigns.note: The Sabis is identified with the Sambre or the Selle; the Atuatucan oppidum is unlocated.

campaigns.name: Caesar in Gaul, 56 BC: the Veneti
campaigns.strength: 8 legions divided: Caesar against the Veneti, Labienus on the Rhine, Crassus in Aquitania, Sabinus in Normandy; a fleet under Decimus Brutus
campaigns.summary: After meeting Pompey at Luca, Caesar went to the Loire, where a fleet was built, and destroyed the Veneti in Quiberon Bay; Publius Crassus conquered Aquitania. A late campaign against the Morini and Menapii was stopped by the weather.

path.t: Mouth of the Loire: fleet assembled
Winter among the Aulerci and Lexovii

campaigns.name: Caesar in Gaul, 55 BC: the Rhine and Britain
campaigns.strength: 8 legions; 2 (VII and X) for the British expedition, about 80 transports
campaigns.summary: Caesar massacred the Usipetes and Tencteri near the Meuse-Rhine confluence, bridged the Rhine and spent 18 days in Germany, then crossed to Britain late in the season with two legions.

path.t: Massacre of the Usipetes and Tencteri

campaigns.note: The Rhine bridge site (Neuwied or Koblenz-Urmitz) and the British landing beach are disputed.

campaigns.name: Caesar in Gaul and Britain, 54 BC
campaigns.strength: 5 legions and 2,000 cavalry in Britain, c. 800 ships; 8 legions and 5 cohorts in Gaul
campaigns.summary: Caesar crossed to Britain with five legions, defeated Cassivellaunus beyond the Thames and imposed tribute. That winter Ambiorix destroyed Sabinus and Cotta's force at Atuatuca and the Nervii besieged Quintus Cicero, whom Caesar relieved.
campaigns.note: The battle of Atuatuca (battle_of_atuatuca) was fought by Sabinus and Cotta, not Caesar's column.

campaigns.name: Caesar in Gaul, 53 BC: the punitive campaigns
campaigns.strength: 10 legions (three new, one lent by Pompey)
campaigns.summary: Caesar struck the Nervii before spring, held a council at Lutetia, forced the Senones, Carnutes and Menapii to submit, crossed the Rhine a second time and turned the land of the Eburones over to plunder. At Durocortorum he had Acco of the Senones flogged and beheaded.

path.t: Devastation of the Eburones; base at Atuatuca

campaigns.name: Caesar against Vercingetorix, 52 BC
campaigns.strength: 10 legions with German cavalry, perhaps 50,000-60,000
campaigns.summary: Caesar hurried from Italy across the snow-bound Cévennes, joined his legions at Agedincum, took Vellaunodunum, Cenabum and Avaricum, failed at Gergovia, reunited with Labienus, and after a cavalry battle besieged Vercingetorix at Alesia, defeating the relief army.

campaigns.name: Caesar's campaigns of 49-48 BC
campaigns.strength: 1 legion at the Rubicon; 6 legions in Spain; 7 legions crossing to Epirus, later 11; 22,000 infantry at Pharsalus
campaigns.summary: From the Rubicon Caesar overran Italy in two months, pushed Pompey out of Brundisium, went to Spain by way of Massilia and won at Ilerda, returned to Rome, crossed the Adriatic in January 48, was beaten at Dyrrhachium, and won at Pharsalus. He pursued Pompey to Egypt.
campaigns.note: Months are by the pre-Julian calendar, which ran about two months ahead of the seasons.

campaigns.name: Caesar's campaigns of 47-45 BC
campaigns.strength: 3,200 foot in Alexandria; 4 legions at Zela; c. 10 legions in Africa; 8 legions and 8,000 horse at Munda
campaigns.summary: After the Alexandrian War Caesar went through Syria to Pontus and destroyed Pharnaces at Zela, returned to Rome, crossed to Africa and won at Thapsus, came back for his triumphs and then went to Spain, where he beat Pompey's sons at Munda.

campaigns.name: Antony's invasion of Media Atropatene
campaigns.strength: 16 legions (c. 60,000), 10,000 Gallic and Spanish cavalry, 30,000 allies: c. 100,000 (Plutarch)
campaigns.summary: Antony marched from Zeugma north through Armenia, left his siege train behind under Oppius Statianus, and besieged Phraaspa in Media. When the train was destroyed and Armenia deserted him he retreated over the mountains in 27 days of fighting, and lost thousands more to winter on the way to the coast.

path.t: Into Media Atropatene; siege train left behind
Leuke Kome on the Phoenician coast

campaigns.note: Phraaspa's location and the route of the retreat are uncertain.

campaigns.name: Octavian's Actium campaign
campaigns.strength: c. 80,000 infantry and 12,000 cavalry; c. 400 ships under Agrippa
campaigns.summary: Octavian crossed to Epirus while Agrippa raided the Greek coast, took Methone and cut Antony's supply; Antony was blockaded in the Ambracian Gulf and broke out to defeat at Actium. Octavian wintered at Samos, went back to Italy to calm his veterans, then marched through Asia and Syria to take Alexandria.

path.t: Camp at Mikalitzi, north of the Ambracian Gulf

campaigns.name: Augustus in Cantabria
campaigns.strength: Perhaps seven legions in the peninsula, with a fleet from Aquitania; numbers in the main column unknown
campaigns.summary: Augustus's only personal campaign as princeps. From Segisama three columns pushed north into the Cantabrian mountains while a seaborne force landed on the coast; the emperor fell ill and withdrew to Tarraco, leaving his legates to finish the blockade of Aracillum.

path.note: Augustus enters his eighth consulship here; winter headquarters

path.t: Pompaelo region (march through the upper Ebro)
Cantabrian coast (Portus Blendium?), seaborne landing links up

campaigns.note: Order of operations and identification of Vellica and Aracillum are debated; recent archaeology of Roman siege lines at La Espina del Gallego, El Cincho and La Loma supports a campaign in the upper Pisuerga and Besaya valleys.

campaigns.name: Aelius Gallus's expedition to Arabia Felix
campaigns.strength: c. 10,000 Roman and allied troops, including 500 Jews from Herod and 1,000 Nabataeans under Syllaeus; 130 transports
campaigns.summary: Augustus's attempt to seize the incense lands of South Arabia. Misled (so Strabo claims) by the Nabataean minister Syllaeus, the army took six months to reach Marib, failed to take it, and returned in sixty days, having lost most of its men to disease rather than battle.

path.note: Wintered here due to scurvy and disease

path.t: Battle at a river; 10,000 Arabs killed for 2 Romans (Strabo)
Crosses the Red Sea to Myos Hormos
Coptos, then down the Nile to Alexandria

campaigns.note: Strabo (16.4.22-24) was Gallus's friend and companion in Egypt and blames Syllaeus; Res Gestae 26.5 claims the army reached Mariba. Exact inland route and the location of Leuke Kome (Aynunah or al-Wajh) are debated.

campaigns.name: Petronius's campaign in Kush
campaigns.strength: Fewer than 10,000 infantry and 800 cavalry (Strabo)
campaigns.summary: Counteroffensive by the prefect of Egypt after the Kushite sack of Syene: victory at Pselchis, capture of Primis, and the razing of Napata, the old religious capital of Kush.

path.t: Relief of Primis against the Candace

campaigns.note: Strabo 17.1.54; Dio 54.5. Pliny NH 6.181 lists towns taken. Archaeology at Qasr Ibrim confirms a Roman occupation phase.

campaigns.name: Drusus's German campaigns
campaigns.strength: Perhaps 5-6 legions on the Rhine plus auxiliaries and a fleet
campaigns.summary: Four seasons of offensives that took Roman arms from the Rhine to the Elbe: the North Sea expedition and the fossa Drusiana (12 BC), the Lippe-Weser drive and the Arbalo ambush (11 BC), the Chatti (10 BC), and the great march to the Elbe (9 BC), on the return from which Drusus died after a fall from his horse.

path.t: Ems estuary; fleet stranded among the Chauci
Reaches the Weser in Cheruscan territory
Ambush at Arbalo on the return
Through Cheruscan lands to the Harz
The Elbe; apparition of a giant woman warns him back (Dio)
Fall from horse between Saale and Rhine; dies in camp 30 days later

campaigns.note: Routes are reconstructed from Dio 54.32-33 and 55.1, Florus 2.30 and the distribution of Augustan camps (Oberaden, Haltern, Anreppen, Hedemünden); the camp where Drusus died (castra scelerata) is unlocated.

campaigns.name: Varus's last march
campaigns.strength: Legions XVII, XVIII, XIX, three alae and six cohorts with camp followers; c. 15,000-20,000 soldiers
campaigns.summary: Varus left his summer camp near the Weser for winter quarters on the Rhine and was diverted, on Arminius's report of a rising, into difficult country where the army was destroyed over several days.

path.t: Summer camp near the Weser (Porta Westfalica area?)
Diversion west towards the reported rising
First attacks; marching camp with three legions' worth of entrenchment (Tac. Ann. 1.61)
Kalkriese: the trap between Kalkrieser Berg and the Great Moor
Garrison breaks out to the Rhine (Vetera)

campaigns.note: The identification of Kalkriese with the final stage is widely but not universally accepted (coins stop c. AD 9; Varus countermarks VAR). Older theories placed the battle in the Teutoburger Wald near Detmold. The location of the summer camp and of Aliso are uncertain.

campaigns.name: Germanicus's campaigns beyond the Rhine
campaigns.strength: 8 legions of the Rhine armies (c. 40,000) plus 26 auxiliary cohorts and 8 alae; in 16 a fleet of 1,000 ships
campaigns.summary: Three campaigns to avenge Varus: the massacre of the Marsi (14), the raid on the Chatti and visit to the Varian battlefield followed by the near-disaster of Caecina at Pontes Longi (15), and the amphibious invasion via the Ems that won Idistaviso and the Angrivarian Wall but lost much of the fleet to a North Sea storm (16).

path.t: Vetera; after the mutiny the army crosses the Rhine
Marsi massacred at a festival; shrine of Tanfana razed
Mogontiacum; spring raid on the Chatti
Fleet of 1,000 ships assembles at the Insula Batavorum
Return by sea; fleet wrecked by storm, Germanicus's trireme driven to the Chauci

campaigns.note: Tacitus Annals 1.49-71 and 2.5-26 is the only detailed source; topography is vague and site identifications (Idistaviso near Minden or Rinteln, the Angrivarian wall near Leese) are conjectural.

campaigns.name: Aulus Plautius's invasion of Britain
campaigns.strength: Four legions (II Augusta, IX Hispana, XIV Gemina, XX) and auxiliaries, c. 40,000; Claudius brought elephants and the praetorians
campaigns.summary: The Claudian invasion: delayed by a mutiny of troops who refused to campaign 'outside the known world', the army crossed in three divisions, defeated Togodumnus and Caratacus in a two-day battle at a river (the Medway), forced the Thames, and waited for Claudius to lead the final advance on Camulodunum.
campaigns.note: Dio 60.19-22 is the only narrative and names no rivers; the Medway and Richborough are inferences. A landing near Fishbourne in friendly Atrebatic territory has been argued (Hind, Manley).

campaigns.name: Vespasian and legio II Augusta in southern Britain
campaigns.strength: Legio II Augusta with auxiliaries, c. 10,000
campaigns.summary: As legate of II Augusta, the future emperor fought 30 battles, subdued two powerful peoples, took more than 20 oppida and the Isle of Wight (Suet. Vesp. 4), conventionally identified with the Durotriges and Belgae and the Dorset hillforts.

path.t: Hod Hill: ballista bolts concentrated on the chieftain's hut; Roman fort built in the corner
Towards the Exe (later fortress of Isca)

campaigns.note: Suetonius gives no place-names; the route is inferred from archaeology (Hod Hill, Lake Farm, Waddon Hill) and the later base of II Augusta at Exeter (c. 55).

campaigns.name: Suetonius Paullinus: Mona and the Boudican war
campaigns.strength: For the final battle legio XIV Gemina, vexillations of XX and nearby auxiliaries, almost 10,000 men (Tac. Ann. 14.34)
campaigns.summary: Paullinus was storming the Druidic island of Mona when news of Boudica's revolt came. He rode ahead to Londinium, judged it indefensible and abandoned it, then fell back up Watling Street to choose his ground, where he destroyed the British host.

path.t: Flat-bottomed boats and cavalry fording the Menai Strait
Mona: Druids and sacred groves destroyed

campaigns.note: Tacitus does not name the battlefield; Mancetter (Manduessedum) is the favourite of many, but High Cross, Church Stowe and sites near Towcester have been proposed. The year is 60 in Tacitus but often corrected to 61.

campaigns.name: Corbulo's conquest of Armenia
campaigns.strength: Legiones III Gallica and VI Ferrata, plus X Fretensis or IV Scythica in part, auxiliaries and allied kings' contingents
campaigns.summary: After a winter in tents in the Armenian highlands, Corbulo stormed fortresses with exemplary severity, took and razed Artaxata, marched across the Mesopotamian edge to Tigranocerta, which surrendered, and installed Rome's candidate Tigranes VI.

path.t: Upper Euphrates (Satala region), winter under canvas
Erzurum plain; fortress of Volandum stormed
March south through the Mardi country, suffering thirst

campaigns.note: Tacitus Annals 13.35-41 and 14.23-26; the site of Tigranocerta is disputed (Arzan near Silvan is favoured).

campaigns.name: Vespasian and Titus in Judaea
campaigns.strength: Legiones V Macedonica, X Fretensis, XV Apollinaris (from 67) with 23 auxiliary cohorts, 6 alae and allied kings' troops, c. 60,000 (Josephus BJ 3.64-69); XII Fulminata added for Jerusalem
campaigns.summary: Vespasian's methodical reconquest of Galilee in 67, Perea and the Judaean lowlands in 68, followed after his proclamation by Titus's siege of Jerusalem in 70.

path.t: Ptolemais; Titus joins with XV Apollinaris
Japha taken by Trajan (father of the emperor)
Tarichaeae and the battle on the Lake of Gennesaret

path.note: Operations halt on news of Nero's death

campaigns.note: Josephus BJ 3-6, an eyewitness for most of it (first as rebel commander, then as Roman captive and interpreter).

campaigns.name: Caecina's march on Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 30,000 from the upper German army, legio XXI Rapax as core
campaigns.summary: Caecina led the Vitellian southern column from Vindonissa, crushed the Helvetii en route, crossed the Great St Bernard in late winter and reached the Po before Valens.

path.t: Helvetii massacred near Mons Vocetius; Aventicum submits
Crosses the Great St Bernard (Poeninus) in snow
Fails before Placentia, whose amphitheatre burns

campaigns.note: Tacitus Histories 1.61-70; 2.17-45.

campaigns.name: Fabius Valens's march on Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 40,000 from the lower German army, core of legio V Alaudae
campaigns.summary: Valens's larger column marched from Cologne through Gaul, terrorising Divodurum (where 4,000 were massacred) and extorting money from Vienne, crossed the Mont Genèvre and joined Caecina at Cremona days before the battle with Otho.
campaigns.note: Tacitus Histories 1.62-66; 2.27-30.

campaigns.name: Antonius Primus's Flavian offensive
campaigns.strength: Five Danubian legions (VII Galbiana, XIII Gemina, VII Claudia, VIII Augusta, III Gallica) with auxiliaries, c. 30,000-40,000
campaigns.summary: Ignoring orders to wait for Mucianus, the legate of legio VII Galbiana led the Danube legions into Italy in a lightning campaign, won the second battle of Bedriacum, sacked Cremona and forced his way into Rome.

path.t: Fanum Fortunae; over the Apennines in snow

campaigns.note: Tacitus Histories 3.1-35; 3.41-63; 3.78-86.

campaigns.name: Agricola's campaigns in Wales and Caledonia
campaigns.strength: Up to four legions (II Adiutrix, IX Hispana, XX, II Augusta in part); 8,000 auxiliary infantry and 3,000 cavalry in the battle line at Mons Graupius
campaigns.summary: Seven seasons of campaigning that took a Roman army to the Moray Firth: Ordovices and Mona (77/78), the Brigantes and the north (79), the Tay (80), consolidation on the Forth-Clyde isthmus (81), the south-west facing Ireland (82), and the push up the east coast to Mons Graupius (83 or 84), with the fleet circumnavigating Britain.

path.t: Mona taken by auxiliaries swimming beside their horses
South-west Scotland; Ireland in view, 'could be taken with one legion'
Night attack on legio IX in camp beyond the Forth

campaigns.note: Tacitus Agricola 18-38 gives seasons but almost no place-names; reconstruction depends on marching-camp series. Whether Mons Graupius was in 83 or 84 depends on whether Agricola arrived in 77 or 78.

campaigns.name: Trajan's First Dacian campaign
campaigns.strength: Perhaps 9-12 legions in whole or part and as many auxiliaries; c. 100,000-150,000 in the theatre
campaigns.summary: Trajan crossed the Danube on pontoon bridges at Lederata, fought a bloody battle at Tapae, returned to meet a Dacian and Roxolanian counterattack in Lower Moesia over the winter, and in 102 converged on Decebalus's mountain fortresses, forcing a peace.
campaigns.note: Reconstruction depends on Dio 68.8-9, the Column, and archaeology; the Column's scenes cannot be mapped onto a single itinerary with confidence.

campaigns.name: Trajan's Second Dacian campaign
campaigns.strength: Some 14 legions were on the Danube by 105-106; perhaps 100,000+ in the field
campaigns.summary: Trajan left Rome in June 105, crossed the Adriatic, inspected his Drobeta bridge and in 106 besieged Sarmizegetusa Regia; Decebalus fled north and killed himself as Roman cavalry closed in.

path.t: Pursuit of Decebalus to the north

campaigns.note: The place of Decebalus's death (Ranisstorum on the Philippi tombstone of Ti. Claudius Maximus) is unlocated.

campaigns.name: Trajan's Parthian campaign
campaigns.strength: Up to 11 legions in whole or part, with Moorish cavalry of Lusius Quietus
campaigns.summary: From Antioch through Armenia (114), across Mesopotamia (115), down the Euphrates and Tigris to Ctesiphon and the head of the Persian Gulf (116), and back to a failed siege of Hatra (117) before Trajan, stricken by a stroke, died at Selinus.

path.t: Tigris crossed into Adiabene on a boat bridge
Babylon; sacrifices in the room where Alexander died

campaigns.note: Chronology of 115-116 (and whether Mesopotamia was taken in 115 or 116) is debated: Lepper, Trajan's Parthian War (1948), versus Bennett and others.

campaigns.name: Avidius Cassius's Mesopotamian offensive
campaigns.strength: Syrian legions (III Gallica, IV Scythica, XVI Flavia) with reinforcements from the Danube and Rhine (I Minervia, II Adiutrix, V Macedonica)
campaigns.summary: While Statius Priscus retook Armenia, Avidius Cassius, a Syrian disciplinarian, led the main army from the Euphrates crossing at Zeugma down to Dura, Seleucia and Ctesiphon, and in 166 into Media.

path.t: Battle of Europos on the Euphrates
path.note: Lucian mentions Europos; often identified as Carchemish/Jerablus area

path.t: Return to Syria; plague among the troops

campaigns.note: Fragmentary sources (Dio 71.2, HA Verus 7-8, Lucian, Fronto); the order of Dura and Seleucia and the identification of 'Europos' are uncertain.

campaigns.name: Marcus Aurelius on the Danube
campaigns.strength: Up to 16 legions along the Danube, plus the new II and III Italica
campaigns.summary: Marcus's long presence on the northern frontier: from Aquileia (168) through headquarters at Carnuntum (171-173), operations among the Quadi on the Gran (Hron), the war against the Iazyges from Sirmium (173-175), the eastern interruption of 175-176, and the second expedition based at Vindobona (178-180).

path.t: Aquileia; Verus dies at Altinum on the way back (169)
Among the Quadi on the Granua (Meditations Book 1 colophon)

campaigns.note: Chronology of the Marcomannic Wars is notoriously uncertain; this path follows Birley, Marcus Aurelius (rev. 1987).

campaigns.name: Severus' advance against Pescennius Niger
campaigns.strength: Danubian legions and vexillations; strength unknown
campaigns.summary: From Rome Severus marched overland through Illyricum and Thrace to Perinthus, while his generals crossed into Asia, won at Cyzicus and Nicaea, forced the Taurus passes and destroyed Niger at Issus.

path.note: Severus leaves Rome about a month after arriving

path.t: Antioch: Niger caught and killed nearby

campaigns.note: Severus himself remained mostly in Thrace; the Asian campaign was conducted by Anullinus and Candidus. Route through Illyricum inferred.

campaigns.name: Severus' march against Clodius Albinus
campaigns.strength: Danubian and Rhine legions; Dio's 150,000 is exaggerated
campaigns.summary: After making Caracalla Caesar at Viminacium, Severus marched west through Pannonia, Noricum and Raetia into Gaul and met Albinus north of Lugdunum.
campaigns.note: Route through Noricum and Raetia follows indications in the HA and the logic of the road network; exact itinerary unknown.

campaigns.name: Severus' Mesopotamian campaign
campaigns.strength: Probably three Parthian legions plus vexillations, Osroene archers and a Euphrates river fleet
campaigns.summary: Severus sailed from Brundisium to Syria, relieved Nisibis, then descended the Euphrates in a fleet of boats to take Seleucia, Babylon and Ctesiphon, returning up the Tigris and failing before Hatra.

path.t: Nisibis: winter quarters and organisation of Mesopotamia

campaigns.note: Dio and Herodian differ on details; Herodian has the fleet drift to Ctesiphon by chance.

campaigns.name: Severus' Caledonian campaigns
campaigns.strength: Perhaps 40,000-50,000 including the British legions, Praetorians and vexillations; Dio claims 50,000 casualties
campaigns.summary: From York, Severus and Caracalla advanced through the eastern lowlands, crossed the Forth on a bridge of boats to the new base at Carpow and penetrated Strathmore toward the north-east, building a line of large marching camps.

path.t: Cramond: supply base on the Forth
Carpow: legionary base on the Tay
path.note: Forth crossed by a pontoon bridge
Dio: Severus approached the extremity of the island

campaigns.note: Northern limit uncertain; the line of 'Severan' 63-acre and 130-acre camps is dated by association, not inscriptions.

campaigns.name: Gordian III's Persian expedition
campaigns.strength: Large army with Germanic and Gothic contingents (ŠKZ); numbers unknown
campaigns.summary: Gordian marched from Rome through the Balkans to Antioch, recovered Carrhae and Nisibis after Rhesaina, then advanced down the Euphrates toward Ctesiphon and was defeated at Misiche.

campaigns.name: Decius against Cniva
campaigns.strength: Danubian field army; perhaps 20,000-30,000
campaigns.summary: Decius relieved Nicopolis ad Istrum, pursued Cniva over the Haemus, was surprised near Beroe, regrouped and in 251 caught the returning Goths near Abritus, where he was killed.
campaigns.note: Sequence reconstructed from Jordanes, Zosimus and the Dexippus fragments; details uncertain.

campaigns.name: Shapur I's third campaign
campaigns.strength: Royal army; captured 70,000 Romans (ŠKZ)
campaigns.summary: Shapur advanced from Ctesiphon through Mesopotamia, besieged Edessa and Carrhae, captured Valerian, then raided Syria, Cilicia and Cappadocia before being harried by Odaenathus on his return across the Euphrates.
campaigns.note: The ŠKZ lists captured cities rather than a route; sequence reconstructed.

campaigns.name: Aurelian's campaign against Zenobia
campaigns.strength: Field army including Dalmatian and Moorish cavalry, Moesian and Pannonian legions, Palestinian clubmen
campaigns.summary: Aurelian crossed into Asia, took Tyana, forced the Cilician Gates, defeated Zabdas' cataphracts at Immae and Emesa, and besieged Palmyra until Zenobia's capture.

campaigns.name: Aurelian's campaign against Tetricus
campaigns.strength: Central field army
campaigns.summary: Aurelian marched from Italy over the Alps into Gaul and destroyed the Gallic army at the Catalaunian Fields.
campaigns.note: Route into Gaul not recorded.

campaigns.name: Galerius' Persian campaign
campaigns.strength: c. 25,000 picked troops, mainly Danubian (Festus)
campaigns.summary: With a new army raised in Illyricum, Galerius advanced through Cappadocia into Armenia, routed Narseh and captured his family, then pushed through Media and Adiabene and returned via Mesopotamia.
campaigns.note: Route beyond Armenia, and whether Galerius reached Ctesiphon, are uncertain.

campaigns.name: Constantine's invasion of Italy
campaigns.strength: c. 40,000 (modern estimate); a quarter of his army according to the panegyric of 313
campaigns.summary: Constantine crossed the Alps from Gaul, stormed Segusio, won at Turin and Verona, then marched down the Via Aemilia and Via Flaminia to defeat Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge.

path.t: Via Flaminia through the Apennines (Furlo pass)

campaigns.note: Alpine pass (Mont Genèvre or Mont Cenis) uncertain.

campaigns.name: Licinius against Maximinus Daia
campaigns.strength: c. 30,000 (Lactantius)
campaigns.summary: From the Milan conference Licinius hurried east, defeated Maximinus at Tzirallum in Thrace, published the Milan letter at Nicomedia and pursued his rival to Tarsus.

campaigns.name: Constantine's war against Licinius
campaigns.strength: 120,000 foot and 10,000 horse (Zosimus, inflated); fleet of 200 ships under Crispus
campaigns.summary: From Thessalonica Constantine forced the Hebrus at Adrianople, besieged Byzantium while Crispus won the Hellespont, then crossed the Bosporus to win at Chrysopolis.

campaigns.name: Constantius II against Magnentius
campaigns.strength: 80,000 (Zonaras), including heavy cavalry
campaigns.summary: Leaving the Persian front, Constantius marched west through Asia Minor and Thrace, accepted Vetranio's abdication at Naissus, and met Magnentius on the Drava at Mursa.

campaigns.name: Julian's campaign of 357
campaigns.strength: 13,000 at Strasbourg (Ammianus)
campaigns.summary: From winter quarters at Sens, Julian moved to the Rhine, rebuilt Tres Tabernae, defeated Chnodomar at Strasbourg, crossed the Rhine near Mainz and ended the year besieging Frankish raiders on the Meuse before wintering at Paris.

path.t: Across the Rhine: raid into Alamannic lands
Meuse forts: Frankish raiders besieged for 54 days

campaigns.note: Location of the Meuse forts unknown.

campaigns.name: Julian's Persian expedition
campaigns.strength: c. 65,000 (Zosimus) including Procopius' northern force of 18,000-30,000; river fleet of over 1,000 ships
campaigns.summary: Julian marched from Antioch to Carrhae, sent Procopius north, descended the Euphrates with his fleet, crossed to the Tigris by canal, won before Ctesiphon, burned his fleet, and died during the retreat; Jovian led the army home via Hatra and Nisibis.

path.t: Dura on the Tigris: Jovian's treaty

campaigns.note: Points between Ctesiphon and the retreat are approximate.

campaigns.name: Gothic movements, 376-378
campaigns.strength: Tervingi perhaps 15,000-20,000 warriors with families; joined by Greuthungi, Alans and some Huns
campaigns.summary: The Tervingi crossed the Danube, broke out after Lupicinus' treachery at Marcianople, ranged through Thrace, fought at Ad Salices, and destroyed Valens' army near Adrianople before failing at Constantinople.
campaigns.note: Order of Thracian movements in 377 is uncertain; Ad Salices location disputed.

campaigns.name: Theodosius' campaign against Magnus Maximus
campaigns.strength: Eastern army with large Gothic, Hunnic and Alan contingents
campaigns.summary: From Thessalonica Theodosius marched north-west up the Axius and Morava, crossed the Save at Siscia, beat Maximus' brother at Poetovio and took Maximus at Aquileia.

campaigns.name: Theodosius' campaign against Eugenius
campaigns.strength: Eastern army with c. 20,000 Gothic federates
campaigns.summary: Theodosius marched from Constantinople up the Balkan military road, forced the Julian Alps at Ad Pirum and won the two-day battle of the Frigidus.

campaigns.name: Alaric's march through Thrace and Greece
campaigns.strength: Gothic federates of the Frigidus campaign with families; perhaps 10,000-20,000 fighting men (modern estimates)
campaigns.summary: After revolting in 395 the Goths threatened Constantinople, moved through Macedonia and Thessaly, passed Thermopylae, extorted terms from Athens, sacked Corinth, Argos and Sparta, escaped Stilicho's blockade at Pholoe and crossed into Epirus.

path.note: Goths ravage Thrace and threaten the capital

path.t: Crossing of the Gulf of Corinth

path.note: Alaric made magister militum per Illyricum by Constantinople

campaigns.note: The order of sacks and the route are reconstructed mainly from Zosimus 5.5-7 and Claudian; exact itinerary uncertain.

campaigns.name: Alaric's first invasion of Italy
campaigns.strength: Gothic army with families, perhaps 15,000-20,000 warriors
campaigns.summary: From Illyricum Alaric crossed the Julian Alps in November 401, besieged Aquileia, cut Honorius off in Milan and Hasta, was fought to a standstill at Pollentia on Easter Day 402 and defeated near Verona, then withdrew east.
campaigns.note: Claudian's poems are the main source; the date of Verona (402 or 403) is disputed.

campaigns.name: Radagaisus's invasion of Italy
campaigns.strength: perhaps 20,000 warriors plus families (ancient figures of 200,000-400,000 are fantasy)
campaigns.summary: Radagaisus's host came from the middle Danube through Pannonia and over the Julian Alps, crossed the Po valley and the Apennines, and besieged Florence before being trapped and destroyed at Faesulae.
campaigns.note: Route unattested in detail; entry by the Julian Alps is the likeliest reconstruction.

campaigns.name: Alaric's second invasion and the sack of Rome
campaigns.strength: Gothic army swollen by c. 30,000 defectors from Stilicho's federates (Zosimus) and fugitive slaves
campaigns.summary: After Stilicho's execution Alaric marched from Noricum through Aquileia, Cremona, Bononia and Ariminum, down the Flaminia to Rome, which he blockaded in 408 and 409, seized Portus, negotiated at Ariminum, and finally sacked Rome in August 410 before marching south toward Africa.

path.note: town saved, Zosimus says, by a thunderstorm

campaigns.note: Itinerary from Zosimus 5.37 and 6.6-13 and Olympiodorus; the Ariminum-Rome shuttles are simplified.

campaigns.name: Vandal and Alan migration from the Rhine to Carthage
campaigns.strength: Hasdings, Silings and Alans; 80,000 people in 429 (Victor of Vita)
campaigns.summary: From the Rhine crossing at the end of 406 the Vandals and Alans plundered Gaul for three years, crossed the Pyrenees in 409, settled in Gallaecia and Baetica, crossed to Africa in 429 and marched east along the Mauretanian and Numidian coast to Hippo and finally Carthage.
campaigns.note: Gallic and Spanish movements are largely reconstructed from Jerome, Hydatius and Salvian; the land route through Mauretania is assumed to follow the coastal road. Gaiseric led only from 428.

campaigns.name: The Goths from Italy to Aquitaine
campaigns.strength: the whole Gothic people under Athaulf, then Wallia
