legions.summary: 'The Horned Ones', an auxilium palatinum of Germanic recruits whose horned helmets appear on the frieze of the Arch of Constantine. With the Bracchiati they held the right of the line at Strasbourg (357), raising the barritus war-cry.

legions.name: Petulantes
legions.endNote: Notitia, western auxilia palatina (seniores)
legions.summary: Gallic auxilium palatinum which, with the Celtae, refused Constantius II's order to march east in February 360 and proclaimed Julian Augustus at Lutetia (Paris).
legions.detail: Ammianus (20.4) says the soldiers feared leaving their families exposed to the Alamanni; Julian was raised on a shield and crowned with a neck torque of a standard-bearer.

legions.name: Legio I Iovia Scythica
legions.endNote: listed at Noviodunum in the Notitia
legions.summary: One of the two Diocletianic legions of the new province of Scythia Minor, sharing the name of the emperor's divine patron. Its base at Noviodunum guarded the Danube crossing used by Valens in 369.

legions.name: Legio II Herculia
legions.endNote: listed at Troesmis in the Notitia
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of Scythia Minor at Troesmis, named after Maximian's patron Hercules, pair to I Iovia at Noviodunum.

legions.name: Legio IV Martia
legions.endNote: listed at Betthorus in the Notitia; fortress abandoned after the earthquake of 551 or earlier
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of Arabia at Betthorus (el-Lejjun), a 4.6-hectare fortress excavated by S. T. Parker's Limes Arabicus Project; its smaller size reflects late legions of perhaps 1,000-2,000 men.
legions.detail: The fortress shows a reduction of the barracks in the 5th century and a church built inside; the garrison seems to have been demobilised under Justinian, who relied on Ghassanid allies.

legions.name: Legio I Illyricorum
legions.endNote: listed at Palmyra in the Notitia

stations.note: camp of Diocletian built in the western quarter of the city

legions.summary: Legion probably formed from Illyrian troops after Aurelian's destruction of Palmyra in 273 and stationed in the 'Camp of Diocletian' inside the ruined city on the Strata Diocletiana.

legions.name: Legio I Pontica
legions.endNote: listed at Trapezus in the Notitia
legions.summary: Diocletianic legion of the Pontic frontier at Trapezus, guarding the Black Sea end of the road to Satala and Armenia.

legions.name: Legio V Parthica
legions.endNote: destroyed when Shapur II stormed Amida in 359
legions.summary: Garrison legion of Amida on the upper Tigris. In 359 it held Amida for 73 days against Shapur II alongside the Magnentian legions and others; Ammianus Marcellinus, inside the city, escaped and wrote the eyewitness account.

legions.name: Theban Legion (Thebaei)
legions.endNote: Thebaei listed among the western palatine legions; the martyr legion of Agaunum is legendary
legions.summary: Late units called Thebaei appear in the Notitia. The legend of St Maurice and the 6,600 Christian soldiers of the Theban Legion massacred at Agaunum by Maximian is told by Eucherius of Lyon (c. 430-450) and is unhistorical in its numbers and details.

frontiers.name: Hadrian's Wall (Vallum Aelium)

phases.t: built: Broad Wall in stone from the east, Turf Wall west of the Irthing; forts added to the line
largely abandoned for the Antonine Wall
recommissioned; repaired under Severus (c. 205-208) and in the 4th century

frontiers.summary: Stone and turf curtain wall 80 Roman miles (117 km) from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness on the Solway, begun c. 122 after Hadrian's visit by the governor A. Platorius Nepos, with milecastles every Roman mile, two turrets between each, 14-16 forts and the Vallum earthwork behind.
frontiers.detail: Building inscriptions name II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix, each legion working in lengths. Hadrian's biography says it was built 'to separate the Romans from the barbarians' (HA Hadr. 11.2). The Vallum, a flat-bottomed ditch with mounds, marked the military zone to the south. Garrisons are documented by the Notitia's 'per lineam valli' list and by Vindolanda and Birdoswald. Late Roman occupation continued at Birdoswald into the 5th century with timber halls.

frontiers.name: Antonine Wall

phases.t: first occupation
brief second occupation, then withdrawal

frontiers.summary: Turf rampart on a stone base 60 km long across the Forth-Clyde isthmus, built from 142 under the governor Q. Lollius Urbicus, with 16-17 forts and a deep ditch. Abandoned after barely twenty years in favour of Hadrian's Wall.
frontiers.detail: The building of the wall is recorded by eighteen or more 'distance slabs', some carved with scenes of conquest, set up by detachments of II Augusta, VI Victrix and XX Valeria Victrix, each recording the paces built. Antoninus Pius took his only imperial acclamation for the campaign (HA Ant. Pius 5.4). Severus campaigned beyond it in 208-211 and reoccupied forts such as Cramond, but did not refortify the wall.

frontiers.name: Gask Ridge frontier

phases.t: towers built (early date argued by Woolliscroft and Hoffmann)
Agricolan advance, Inchtuthil built
abandoned

frontiers.summary: Line of timber watchtowers and fortlets along the Roman road on the Gask Ridge from Ardoch to Bertha on the Tay, with forts at the mouths of the Highland glens ('glen-blocking forts'). Possibly the earliest fortified land frontier of the Roman empire.
frontiers.debate: Dated either to Agricola (c. 79-83) as a temporary line, or earlier under Cerialis or Frontinus (c. 70s) as a deliberate frontier that predates the German limes; the towers show only short occupation.

frontiers.name: Stanegate frontier

phases.t: forts at Corbridge, Vindolanda, Nether Denton, Carlisle
extra forts and fortlets added (Old Church Brampton, Haltwhistle Burn, Throp)

frontiers.summary: Road and chain of forts across the Tyne-Solway isthmus, from Corbridge to Carlisle and Kirkbride, that formed the de facto frontier after the withdrawal from Scotland c. 87-105, before Hadrian's Wall was built just north of it.
frontiers.detail: The Vindolanda tablets date from the Stanegate period. Whether it was a frontier system or simply a communications road with forts is debated.

frontiers.name: Upper German-Raetian Limes

phases.t: Domitianic patrol road and timber towers in the Taunus and Wetterau
Hadrianic palisade; Odenwald-Neckar line in the south
outer line advanced 30 km east under Antoninus Pius (Walldürn-Lorch straight section)
Raetian stone wall (Teufelsmauer); Caracalla's Alemannic campaign of 213
Alemannic raids; given up c. 259-260 (the 'Limesfall')

frontiers.summary: The longest land frontier of Europe, 550 km from the Rhine at Rheinbrohl to the Danube at Hienheim near Eining, with about 60 forts and 900 watchtowers. Began as a patrol road with timber towers after Domitian's Chattan war (83-85) and grew into palisade, ditch-and-bank (Upper Germany) and stone wall (Raetia).
frontiers.detail: The 80 km straight section between Walldürn and Haghof deviates less than 2 m per km, a feat of Roman surveying. The Agri Decumates between Rhine, Main and Danube were surrendered c. 260 under Gallienus. UNESCO World Heritage (2005).

frontiers.name: Odenwald-Neckar Limes

phases.t: timber towers, then stone towers and forts
stone phase; forts moved forward c. 159-160

frontiers.summary: Inner line of the Upper German limes, from the Main at Wörth through the Odenwald and along the Neckar to Köngen, held from the late Flavian or Trajanic period until the advance to the outer limes c. 159-160.

frontiers.name: Lower German Limes (Rhine)

phases.t: Drusus's bases for the conquest of Germany
stabilised after the Varian disaster; Claudius orders Corbulo back (47)
overrun in the Batavian revolt
rebuilt in stone
Frankish pressure; Julian restores forts 358-359

frontiers.summary: The Rhine frontier of Germania Inferior from the Vinxtbach to the North Sea at Katwijk, a riverine frontier of legionary fortresses (Bonn, Neuss, Xanten, Nijmegen) and auxiliary forts every 10-15 km along the Rhine and the Oude Rijn. Caligula and Claudius fixed it; Corbulo was ordered back to it from beyond the Rhine in 47.
frontiers.detail: Wet conditions preserved timber forts, ships (Zwammerdam barges) and the Valkenburg fort sequence. UNESCO World Heritage (2021).

frontiers.name: Danube Limes: Raetia and Noricum

phases.t: Claudian and Flavian forts
Marcomannic wars; Regensburg and Lauriacum fortresses built
late-Roman reconstruction under Diocletian and Valentinian I
evacuation of Noricum ordered by Odoacer (488)

frontiers.summary: Upper Danube frontier from Eining to the Vienna Woods, with the legionary fortresses of Regensburg and Lauriacum, cohort forts such as Künzing and Passau, and late-Roman burgi. The Life of Severinus describes its last decades in the 470s-480s.

frontiers.name: Danube Limes: Pannonia (Ripa Pannonica)

phases.t: Claudian-Flavian forts
Marcomannic wars
Diocletianic and Valentinianic fortification, counter-forts on the left bank
Valeria ceded to the Huns by Aetius

frontiers.summary: The Pannonian Danube from the Vienna Woods to the Sava confluence at Belgrade: legionary fortresses at Vindobona, Carnuntum, Brigetio and Aquincum facing the Marcomanni, Quadi and the Sarmatian Iazyges of the Hungarian plain.

frontiers.name: Danube Limes: Moesia Superior and the Iron Gates

phases.t: Claudian forts; Tiberian road cut 33-34
Trajan's canal and bridge for the Dacian wars
rear line behind Roman Dacia
frontier again after Aurelian's evacuation

frontiers.summary: Danube frontier through the Iron Gates gorge, where Tiberius and Trajan cut a towpath road into the cliff (Tabula Traiana, 100) and Trajan dug a canal at Karataš to bypass the rapids (101). Apollodorus's bridge crossed at Pontes-Drobeta.

frontiers.name: Danube Limes: Moesia Inferior and Scythia Minor

phases.t: Claudian and Flavian forts; Domitian's Dacian war
Gothic invasions (Cniva, 250-251)
Diocletianic legions I Iovia and II Herculia; Constantine's bridge at Oescus (328)
Goths admitted across the river
Justinianic restoration; collapse under Avar-Slav pressure after 602

frontiers.summary: Lower Danube frontier from Ratiaria to the delta at Halmyris, with the legionary fortresses of Oescus, Novae, Durostorum, Troesmis and Noviodunum and the Moesian fleet. It faced Getae, Bastarnae, Roxolani, Carpi, Goths and finally Avars and Slavs.

frontiers.name: Dacian Limes (Limes Porolissensis and eastern line)

phases.t: Trajanic forts
Hadrianic reorganisation into three Dacias; earthworks at Porolissum
Marcomannic and Costobocan attacks
Carpic and Gothic pressure; evacuation

frontiers.summary: Frontier of Roman Dacia on the north-west (Meseș mountains, around Porolissum) and along the Eastern Carpathians, combining watchtowers, earthworks and forts. The province was abandoned under Aurelian c. 271-275.
frontiers.detail: The western section follows the Pleiades trace of the Limes Daciae; the eastern line is approximate between attested forts.

frontiers.name: Limes Alutanus (Olt line)
frontiers.summary: Fortified line along the Olt (Alutus) river, the eastern boundary of Dacia Inferior under Hadrian, which kept the Wallachian plain outside the province. Superseded by the Limes Transalutanus c. 200, and partly reused after 245.

frontiers.name: Limes Transalutanus
frontiers.summary: Earth rampart and ditch of about 235 km with 14 forts, running from Flămânda on the Danube north to Câmpulung and Rucăr near the Carpathians, 10-50 km east of the Olt. Built under Septimius Severus c. 200 and abandoned in 245-248 under Carpic attacks.
frontiers.detail: Its southern end follows the Pleiades trace (Flămânda-Băneasa); the northern part is approximate.

frontiers.name: Brazda lui Novac de Nord
frontiers.summary: Earthwork about 300 km long across Oltenia and Muntenia, north of the Danube, named in Romanian folklore after the hero Novac. Often linked to Constantine's reconquest north of the Danube (bridge at Oescus 328, Gothic treaty 332), it would have marked a Roman glacis in Wallachia.
frontiers.debate: Dating is unresolved: Constantinian (c. 330s) is the majority view, but it has also been ascribed to the 2nd century, to the Goths or to the early Middle Ages. Course shown is approximate.

frontiers.name: Lower Trajan's Wall (Bessarabia)
frontiers.summary: Earth rampart about 126 km long from the Prut near Vadul lui Isac to Lake Sasyk on the Black Sea, south of an Upper Trajan's Wall between the Prut and the Dniester near Tighina. The popular name is modern.
frontiers.debate: Attributions include Trajan (2nd century), the Gothic king Athanaric, who Ammianus says built a wall 'from the banks of the Gerasus (Prut) to the Danube' against the Huns in 376 (31.3.7), and later nomads. Course approximate.

frontiers.name: Strata Diocletiana
frontiers.summary: Fortified road built under Diocletian from Sura on the Euphrates via Palmyra to Damascus, lined with forts and road stations a day's march apart, guarding the Syrian steppe against Arab nomads and Persian raids.
frontiers.detail: Milestones carrying the name 'strata Diocletiana' and the forts of the Notitia (dux Syriae et Euphratensis, dux Phoenicis) mark its course; Justinian's ruling on a dispute between the Ghassanid al-Harith and the Lakhmid al-Mundhir concerned the lands south of it (Procopius, Wars 2.1).

frontiers.name: Limes Arabicus

phases.t: Trajanic annexation; forts on the Via Nova Traiana
Diocletianic build-up: Betthorus, Udhruh, Qasr Bshir (306)
earthquake of 363; garrisons reduced; Justinian relies on the Ghassanids from c. 530

frontiers.summary: The desert frontier of Arabia, a zone of forts, watchtowers and road stations along and east of the Via Nova Traiana from Bostra to Aila on the Red Sea, strengthened by Diocletian with the legionary fortresses of el-Lejjun and Udhruh.
frontiers.detail: Whether it was a defensive line against nomads (Parker) or an internal policing and road-security system (Isaac, The Limits of Empire, 1990) is a classic debate of frontier studies.

frontiers.name: Euphrates frontier

phases.t: Flavian legionary bases on the upper Euphrates
Trajan's provinces beyond the river
Dura held as a Roman garrison town until 256
frontier zone again after Jovian's peace; Justinian fortifies Callinicum, Sura and Circesium

frontiers.summary: The Euphrates line from the Armenian highlands at Satala past the legionary bases of Melitene, Samosata and Zeugma to Sura, Callinicum, Circesium and Dura. Rome's eastern river frontier under the Flavians; after 165 and especially 198 it became a rear line behind Mesopotamia, and again the front after 363.

frontiers.name: Fossatum Africae (Gemellae sector)
frontiers.summary: Ditch and bank up to 6 m wide with stone walls in places, controlling seasonal pastoral movement around Gemellae south of the Aurès. One of several Fossatum sectors, probably Hadrianic in origin.
frontiers.detail: The Codex Theodosianus (7.15.1, 409) mentions land assigned to gentiles to maintain the limes and fossatum. Baradez's aerial photography (1949) revealed the system. Trace from the Pleiades sector line.

frontiers.name: Fossatum Africae (Hodna-Tubunae sector)
frontiers.summary: Sector of the Fossatum running from the Hodna mountains south-east past Tubunae (Tobna) towards Mesarfelta, enclosing the Hodna basin.

frontiers.name: Fossatum Africae (limes Bazensis sector)
frontiers.summary: Eastern continuation of the Fossatum south of the Aurès and Nemencha mountains between Badias and Ad Maiores.

frontiers.name: Limes Tripolitanus
frontiers.summary: Fortified routes and forts on the desert edge of Tripolitania, from Tacapae (Gabès) through Tillibari (Remada) to the Severan outposts of Gheriat el-Garbia and Bu Njem (Golas), built 201 by detachments of III Augusta.
frontiers.detail: Ostraca from Bu Njem (c. 253-259) record the garrison's daily reports and the arrival of Garamantian guides. The system was reorganised into limitanei sectors under the comes Africae and dux Tripolitaniae. Course partly approximate.

frontiers.name: Anastasian Wall (Long Walls of Thrace)

phases.t: probably begun under Leo I and completed or rebuilt under Anastasius I (c. 503-507)
breached by Zabergan's Kutrigurs after earthquake damage
abandoned in the early 7th century

frontiers.summary: Wall 56 km long, 3.3 m thick and up to 5 m high, from the Black Sea near Evcik to the Sea of Marmara 6 km west of Selymbria, about 65 km west of Constantinople, enclosing the city's hinterland.
frontiers.detail: Procopius (Buildings 4.9) complains it was hard to man and leaked raiders. Its vicar (vicarius of the Long Walls) was abolished by Justinian. Northern trace from Pleiades fort points; southern end approximate.
frontiers.debate: Attribution to Anastasius rests on its name and the chronicles; some scholars (Croke) argue for Leo I c. 469.

frontiers.name: Theodosian Walls of Constantinople

phases.t: inner wall
outer wall and moat added under the prefect Constantine; resisted the Avar-Persian siege of 626

frontiers.summary: Triple land wall of Constantinople (inner wall, outer wall and moat) 5.7 km from the Marble Tower on the Sea of Marmara to Blachernae on the Golden Horn. The inner wall was built in 408-413 by the praetorian prefect Anthemius; the outer wall and moat were added in 447 after an earthquake, rebuilt in 60 days as Attila approached.
frontiers.detail: 96 main towers on the inner wall up to 20 m high. The Golden Gate served as the triumphal entry. The walls were breached only in 1204 (from the sea) and 1453.

frontiers.name: Aurelian Walls of Rome

phases.t: built at 6 m height
doubled in height by Honorius and Stilicho
held by Belisarius against Vitiges

frontiers.summary: Brick-faced concrete wall of 19 km with 381 towers and 18 main gates, begun by Aurelian in 271 after the Juthungi raided Italy and completed under Probus (c. 279). It enclosed all seven hills, the Campus Martius and part of Trastevere.
frontiers.detail: It incorporated existing structures such as the pyramid of Cestius, the Castra Praetoria and the Amphitheatrum Castrense. Constantine abolished the praetorian camp's separate defence in 312. Belisarius defended it for a year against the Goths.

frontiers.name: Servian Wall of Rome

phases.t: built after the Gallic sack
Hannibal rides up to the Colline Gate
last used defensively in the civil war of Marius and Cinna

frontiers.summary: Rome's republican city wall of Grotta Oscura tufa, about 11 km long, attributed by tradition to King Servius Tullius but built after the Gallic sack, from 378 BC (Livy 6.32.1). On the Esquiline plateau it was reinforced by the agger, an earth rampart with a ditch 30 m wide.
frontiers.detail: The Colline Gate saw Sulla's decisive victory over the Samnites on 1 November 82 BC. By Augustus's time the city had outgrown it and it was built over; the best surviving section stands outside Termini station.

frontiers.name: Hexamilion
frontiers.summary: Six-mile wall across the Isthmus of Corinth, with the Isthmia fortress at the sanctuary of Poseidon, built after Alaric's invasion of Greece (395-396), probably under Theodosius II (c. 408-450), and restored by Justinian.
frontiers.detail: Its builders reused blocks from the Isthmian sanctuary. It failed to stop Slavic invaders in the late 6th century and was rebuilt by Manuel II in 1415.

frontiers.name: Derbent Wall (Caspian Gates)
frontiers.summary: Sasanian fortification at Derbent where the Caucasus meets the Caspian: two parallel city walls 3.6 km to the sea and the Dagh-bary mountain wall running some 40 km inland, rebuilt in stone under Khosrow I (c. 560s) against the steppe nomads.
frontiers.detail: The Romans contributed subsidies for the defence of the Caucasus passes under several 5th-6th-century treaties, a recurrent issue in the Persian wars. Mountain wall course approximate.

frontiers.name: Great Wall of Gorgan
frontiers.summary: Brick wall 195 km long with over 30 forts and a canal-fed ditch, from the Caspian shore to the Pishkamar mountains, built by the Sasanians against the Hephthalites and other northern nomads. OSL and radiocarbon dates place it in the 5th century, probably under Peroz (459-484) or earlier.
frontiers.detail: Sometimes called the 'Red Snake' after its fired bricks. Its forts could hold a garrison of perhaps 15,000-30,000, a scale comparable to Hadrian's Wall (Sauer et al., Persia's Imperial Power in Late Antiquity, 2013). Trace from Pleiades fort points.

frontiers.name: Saxon Shore forts (Litus Saxonicum)

phases.t: early forts at Brancaster and Reculver
main building phase, perhaps under Carausius
the 'barbarian conspiracy'; count Nectaridus killed

frontiers.summary: Chain of nine or ten coastal forts from Brancaster in Norfolk to Portchester in Hampshire, built c. 260-300, placed in the Notitia under the comes litoris Saxonici per Britanniam. Matching forts stood on the Gallic coast.
frontiers.debate: Whether the forts defended against Saxon raiders or were bases for Carausius and Allectus against Rome, and whether 'Saxon Shore' means the shore attacked by or settled by Saxons, are debated.

frontiers.name: Danube-Iller-Rhine Limes
frontiers.summary: Late Roman frontier after the loss of the Agri Decumates c. 260: the High Rhine from Kaiseraugst to Lake Constance, the Iller from Bregenz to the Danube near Ulm, and the Danube to Eining, refortified under Diocletian and again under Valentinian I.

frontiers.name: Devil's Dykes (Csörsz árok)
frontiers.summary: System of earthworks some 1,260 km in total enclosing the Sarmatian lands of the Great Hungarian Plain between the Danube and the Carpathians, usually dated to Constantine's treaty with the Sarmatians after 322-334, when Rome protected them against Goths and Vandals.
frontiers.debate: The Constantinian date relies on finds and context rather than inscriptions; parts may be later. Course approximate.

roads.name: Via Appia

extended.t: to Tarentum and Brundisium (completed by c. 190 BC)
6,000 crucified slaves of Spartacus lined it from Capua to Rome (71 BC)

roads.summary: The 'queen of roads' (regina viarum, Statius). Built in 312 BC by the censor Appius Claudius Caecus from Rome to Capua, extended to Beneventum, Venusia, Tarentum and by c. 190 BC Brundisium, 540 km in all.
roads.detail: Its straight 90 km section across the Pontine marshes included a parallel canal (Horace, Sat. 1.5, travelled by barge at night). Trajan's Via Traiana (109) offered a faster alternative from Beneventum to Brundisium. Procopius (Wars 5.14) admired its fitted basalt paving still intact in 536.

roads.name: Via Latina
roads.summary: Inland route from Rome to Campania through the Sacco and Liri valleys, older than the Via Appia and following a natural corridor used in the Latin and Samnite wars; it joined the Appia at Casilinum.
roads.detail: Its date is unknown (perhaps paved in the late 4th century BC with the Latin colonies at Cales and Fregellae). Hannibal marched up it in his feint on Rome in 211 BC (Livy 26.9). The Tombs of the Via Latina park preserves 2nd-century painted tombs near Rome.

roads.name: Via Tiburtina
roads.summary: Road from Rome to Tibur (Tivoli) past the sulphur springs of Aquae Albulae and the travertine quarries; its continuation into the Apennines was the Via Valeria.
roads.detail: The Mausoleum of the Plautii at the Ponte Lucano (c. AD 10) still stands beside the road. Hadrian's Villa lies just south of it below Tibur.

roads.name: Via Valeria
roads.summary: Continuation of the Via Tiburtina across the central Apennines to the Fucine basin and Corfinium, probably begun by the censor M. Valerius Maximus (307 BC); Claudius extended it to the Adriatic at Aternum as the Via Claudia Valeria (48-49).

roads.name: Via Salaria
roads.summary: The 'salt road' along which the Sabines fetched salt from the Tiber mouth, one of the oldest routes of Italy; paved through Sabine country to Asculum and the Adriatic.
roads.detail: The Gauls marched down it in 390 BC to the Allia, a tributary on its course 18 km from Rome. Vespasian's birthplace at Falacrinae lay on it.

roads.name: Via Flaminia

extended.t: restored by Augustus; arches at Rome and Ariminum

roads.summary: Great north road built in 220 BC by the censor C. Flaminius from Rome across the Apennines to the Adriatic at Fanum and on to Ariminum, the main artery to Cisalpine Gaul. Augustus rebuilt it in 27 BC; Vespasian cut the Furlo tunnel (Intercisa) in 76-77.
roads.detail: It crossed the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge, where Constantine defeated Maxentius on 28 October 312. A later branch ran via Spoletium and Interamna. C. Flaminius died at Trasimene in 217 BC.

roads.name: Via Aurelia

extended.t: Via Aemilia Scauri from Pisae via Luna to Vada Sabatia and Genua (M. Aemilius Scaurus)

roads.summary: Coastal road north-west from Rome through Etruria to Pisae, probably built by the censor C. Aurelius Cotta in 241 BC; continued to Genua by the Via Aemilia Scauri (109 BC) and into Gaul by the Via Iulia Augusta.
roads.detail: Rutilius Namatianus sailed rather than rode home to Gaul in 417 because the road was impassable after the Gothic invasions (De reditu 1.37-42).

roads.name: Via Cassia
roads.summary: Road through inner Etruria from the Milvian Bridge past Sutrium, Volsinii, Clusium and Arretium to Florentia and Luca, named after an unknown Cassius (perhaps C. Cassius Longinus, censor 154 BC).
roads.detail: Its date is uncertain (2nd century BC); Cicero mentions it in 43 BC (Phil. 12.22-23) as one of three routes from Rome to Mutina.

roads.name: Via Clodia
roads.summary: Road branching from the Via Cassia north of Rome through the Etruscan towns of the Tolfa hills and Tuscania to Saturnia and Rusellae. Its builder and date are unknown, though it may follow an Etruscan route.

roads.name: Via Aemilia
roads.summary: Built in 187 BC by the consul M. Aemilius Lepidus from Ariminum to Placentia, a 260 km almost straight line along the Apennine foot that structured the colonies and fora of the Po plain; the region of Italy and modern Emilia take its name.
roads.detail: Its towns were founded at regular intervals as road stations (Forum Livi, Forum Corneli, Regium Lepidi). The battle of Forum Gallorum (14 April 43 BC) between Antony and the consuls was fought on it.

roads.name: Via Postumia
roads.summary: Built in 148 BC by the consul Sp. Postumius Albinus across northern Italy from Genua on the Tyrrhenian to Aquileia on the Adriatic, crossing the Po at Placentia and passing Cremona and Verona.
roads.detail: The two battles of Bedriacum in 69 were fought astride it between Cremona and Verona.

roads.name: Via Popillia (Via ab Regio ad Capuam)
roads.summary: Road of 321 Roman miles from Capua to Rhegium built c. 132 BC, recorded on the Lapis Pollae (CIL I² 638), whose builder boasts he 'first made shepherds yield to ploughmen on public land'. The builder is P. Popillius Laenas (cos. 132) or T. Annius Rufus (cos. 128).

roads.name: Via Annia and northern Via Popillia
roads.summary: Coastal route around the Adriatic lagoons: the northern Via Popillia (132 BC) from Ariminum by Ravenna to Hatria, and the Via Annia (T. Annius Luscus, 153 BC, or T. Annius Rufus, 131 BC) from Hatria through Patavium and Altinum to Aquileia.

roads.name: Via Traiana
roads.summary: Trajan's road of 109 from Beneventum across Apulia to Brundisium, shorter and flatter than the Via Appia; commemorated by the Arch of Beneventum (114) and a coin issue showing a reclining woman holding a wheel.

roads.name: Via Domitiana
roads.summary: Coastal road built by Domitian in 95 from Sinuessa on the Via Appia across the Volturnus marshes to Cumae and Puteoli, celebrated in Statius's poem on its construction (Silvae 4.3).

roads.name: Via Amerina
roads.summary: Road from the Via Cassia through the Faliscan towns of Nepet and Falerii Novi to Ameria, Tuder and Perusia, built after the foundation of Falerii Novi (241 BC). In the 6th-7th centuries it was the Byzantine corridor linking Rome with Ravenna through Lombard territory.

roads.name: Via Ostiensis
roads.summary: Road along the left bank of the Tiber from the Porta Ostiensis to Ostia, 24 km, carrying the salt and later the grain traffic of Rome's harbour. Paul was buried beside it at the site of San Paolo fuori le Mura.

roads.name: Via Portuensis
roads.summary: Road on the right bank of the Tiber from Trastevere to the Claudian-Trajanic harbour of Portus, laid out with the harbour under Claudius; a double carriageway in its imperial form.

roads.name: Via Praenestina
roads.summary: Road east from the Porta Praenestina past Gabii to Praeneste (Palestrina), originally the Via Gabina, continued to join the Via Latina near Anagnia. The Ponte di Nona (2nd century BC) is one of its best surviving viaducts.

roads.name: Via Egnatia
roads.summary: Built c. 146-120 BC by the proconsul Cn. Egnatius from Dyrrachium (with a branch from Apollonia) across the Balkans to Thessalonica and later Byzantium, 1,120 km. It carried the armies of the civil wars to Pharsalus and Philippi and later linked Old and New Rome.
roads.detail: A bilingual milestone found near Thessalonica in 1974 names Egnatius and gives the distance from Dyrrachium (Polybius in Strabo 7.7.4 describes the road measured and marked). Paul travelled it from Neapolis to Thessalonica.

roads.name: Via Militaris (Via Diagonalis)
roads.summary: The diagonal road across the Balkans from Singidunum through Naissus, Serdica, Philippopolis and Hadrianopolis to Byzantium/Constantinople, the main military artery of the late empire. Paved under Claudius and Trajan, it was the route of Attila (441-447), Theodoric and the Avars.
roads.detail: The Bordeaux pilgrim's itinerary (333) and the Antonine Itinerary list its stations. Valens marched it to his death at Adrianople in 378; the Crusaders and the Ottomans used the same corridor.

roads.name: Via Pontica
roads.summary: Coastal road along the western Black Sea linking the old Greek colonies of Thrace and Scythia Minor (Apollonia, Mesembria, Odessos, Tomis, Histria) with Byzantium and the Danube delta.

roads.name: Via Sebaste
roads.summary: Augustan military road of 6 BC built by the legate Cornutus Aquila linking the Pisidian colonies (Comama, Cremna, Antioch, Lystra) across the Taurus foothills, during the war against the Homonadenses of the Taurus.

roads.name: Via Maris (coastal road of Palestine)
roads.summary: The ancient coastal highway from Egypt through Philistia and the Sharon plain, turning inland through the Megiddo pass to the Jordan and Damascus. The name derives from Isaiah's 'way of the sea' (Isa. 9:1); the Romans paved it as part of their road network.
roads.detail: Vespasian and Titus moved their armies along it; Pompey and later Persian and Arab invaders used the same corridor.

roads.name: Via Nova Traiana
roads.summary: Road built 111-114 by the legate C. Claudius Severus 'from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea' (a finibus Syriae usque ad mare Rubrum), as Trajan's milestones say, through the new province of Arabia from Bostra by Philadelphia and Petra to Aila.

roads.name: Via Hadriana (Egypt)
roads.summary: Desert road built by Hadrian in 137 from his new city of Antinoopolis east to the Red Sea and then south along the coast to Berenice, 'through safe and level country, with plentiful wells, stations and garrisons' as its inscription says.
roads.detail: Its dedication stone (IGRR I 1142) is dated 25 February 137. Recent survey has traced stations along the coast; the inland stretch is approximate here.

roads.name: Persian Royal Road
roads.summary: Achaemenid highway of 2,500 km from Sardis to Susa with 111 relay stations, which Herodotus says a traveller took 90 days to cover while royal couriers did it in about a week (5.52-54; 8.98). Shown here as context for Rome's eastern road system; its exact course is reconstructed.

roads.name: Via Domitia
roads.summary: The first Roman road in Gaul, built c. 118 BC by Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus from the Mont Genèvre pass across Provence and Languedoc to the Pyrenees, linking Italy and Spain. Its milestone of Domitius, found near Narbonne in 1949, is the oldest in Gaul.
roads.detail: Pompey reopened the Alpine section in 77 BC on his way to fight Sertorius. The Pont Ambroix at Ambrussum and the track worn into the rock at the Col de Panissars (with the trophy of Pompey) survive.

roads.name: Via Augusta
roads.summary: Augustus's rebuilding (8-2 BC) of the old Via Heraclea along the Mediterranean coast of Spain and inland through Castulo and Corduba to Gades, 1,500 km. The Vicarello cups list its stations from Gades to Rome.
roads.detail: The arch of Janus Augustus on the Baetis marked the entry into Baetica. Scipio's and Hannibal's armies had used the same coastal corridor.

roads.name: Iter ab Emerita Asturicam (Vía de la Plata)
roads.summary: North-south road from Hispalis and Emerita Augusta through Caparra and Salmantica to Asturica Augusta, carrying the produce of the north-western gold mines. Its modern name comes from Arabic balat (paved road), not silver.

roads.name: Via Iulia Augusta
roads.summary: Augustus's road of 13-12 BC from Placentia via Dertona to the Ligurian coast and along the Riviera to Arelate, built after the conquest of the Alpine tribes celebrated at the Tropaeum Alpium at La Turbie (7-6 BC).

roads.name: Via Agrippa (Lugdunum-Arelate-Massilia)
roads.summary: The southern branch of Agrippa's road system radiating from Lugdunum (Strabo 4.6.11), down the Rhône valley through Vienna, Valentia and Arausio to Arelate and Massilia.

roads.name: Via Agrippa (Lugdunum-Rhine)
roads.summary: Agrippa's road from Lugdunum up the Saône to Cabillonum, over the Langres plateau to Tullum, Divodurum and Augusta Treverorum and down the Moselle valley and the Eifel to the Rhine army at Cologne.

roads.name: Via Agrippa (Lugdunum-Ocean)
roads.summary: Agrippa's road to the Channel coast at Gesoriacum (Boulogne), the embarkation point for Britain, by way of Augustodunum, Durocortorum and Samarobriva.

roads.name: Via Agrippa (Lugdunum-Aquitania)
roads.summary: The western branch of Agrippa's roads, across the Massif Central through Augustonemetum (Clermont) and Augustoritum (Limoges) to Mediolanum Santonum (Saintes), crossing the Charente by a bridge marked by the Arch of Germanicus.

roads.name: Via Belgica (Bavay-Cologne road)
roads.summary: Main east-west road of northern Gaul from Boulogne via Bagacum (Bavay), the hub of seven roads, and Atuatuca Tungrorum (Tongeren) to Cologne, probably laid out under Agrippa; 'Via Belgica' is a modern name.

roads.name: Via Claudia Augusta
roads.summary: Alpine road over the Reschen and Fern passes from the Adriatic to the Danube, opened by Drusus during the Alpine war of 15 BC and completed by Claudius in 46-47, as two milestones state ('from the river Po ... to the river Danube, 350 miles').

roads.name: Via Flavia (Istria)
roads.summary: Road down the west coast of Istria from Tergeste to Pola, built under Vespasian in 78-79 according to its milestones.

roads.name: Carthage-Theveste road
roads.summary: Road of 191 Roman miles from Carthage up the Bagradas valley to Theveste, paved in 123 by soldiers of III Augusta under the legate P. Metilius Secundus, joining the capital to the legionary zone.

roads.name: Watling Street
roads.summary: The Roman road from the Kentish ports through London and Verulamium to Wroxeter, the axis of Iter II of the Antonine Itinerary; the name is Anglo-Saxon (Wæclingastræt, after the people of Verulamium). Paulinus probably destroyed Boudica's army somewhere along it in 60/61.

roads.name: Fosse Way
roads.summary: Road of about 370 km in near-straight alignment from Exeter to Lincoln, never more than 10 km from a straight line, which may mark the first frontier of the province c. 47 under the governor Ostorius Scapula. 'Fosse' refers to its ditch.
roads.detail: The theory that it was a frontier road (limes) for the early province goes back to Haverfield; it remains debated.

roads.name: Ermine Street
roads.summary: Road from London north through Durobrivae (Water Newton) to Lincoln, then to the Humber at Winteringham, ferry to Petuaria (Brough) and on to York. The name is from the Anglo-Saxon Earninga stræt.

roads.name: Dere Street
roads.summary: Road from York north across the Tees and Tyne at Corbridge, over the Cheviots past High Rochester to Newstead and the Forth at Inveresk: the invasion route of Agricola, Lollius Urbicus and Severus into Scotland. Named after the Anglian kingdom of Deira.

roads.name: Stanegate (road)
roads.summary: The 'stone road' (Middle English) between Corbridge and Carlisle, laid out c. 80 under Agricola to link the Tyne and Eden river crossings, later the service road behind Hadrian's Wall.

sources.name: Quintus Fabius Pictor

works.books: Number of books unknown; c. 30 fragments and testimonia, plus a Taormina library inscription summarizing him
works.note: Ran from Aeneas and the foundation to the Second Punic War, which he lived through.

sources.reliability: The first Roman historian, a senator writing in Greek to explain Rome to the Hellenistic world during the Hannibalic war. Polybius used him for the Punic Wars and criticized his pro-Roman, anti-Barcid bias (Polyb. 1.14-15, 3.8-9). Dated Rome's founding to 748/747 BC.
sources.summary: Senator of the great Fabian gens, sent to consult Delphi after Cannae (216). Founder of Roman annalistic historiography; all later accounts of early Rome descend in part from him.

sources.name: Lucius Cincius Alimentus
sources.reliability: Praetor 210 BC, once a prisoner of Hannibal, who told him he had lost 36,000 men since the Rhône (Livy 21.38). Fragments few but valuable for eyewitness data.
sources.summary: Second Roman annalist in Greek; dated the foundation to 729/728 BC.

sources.name: Gnaeus Naevius

works.books: Saturnian epic, later divided into 7 books; c. 60 fragments
works.note: Opened with the Aeneas legend before the war itself.

sources.reliability: A veteran of the First Punic War writing epic about it; fragments are tiny and mostly grammarians' citations.
sources.summary: Campanian poet; first Latin national epic. Jailed for attacking the Metelli.

sources.name: Quintus Ennius

works.books: 18 books of hexameters; c. 600 lines survive in quotation
works.note: From the fall of Troy to the 170s BC; books 7-9 on the Second Punic War; book 16 added for the Istrian war.

sources.reliability: Epic not history, but deeply influential on Roman self-image (moribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque); Cicero, Virgil and Livy drew on it. Fragmentary.
sources.summary: Messapian-born poet brought to Rome by Cato (204), protégé of Fulvius Nobilior, whom he accompanied to Ambracia (189).

sources.name: Cato the Elder

works.note: Books 1-3 on the origins of Rome and the Italian peoples; 4-5 the Punic Wars; 6-7 down to 149, with his own speeches inserted. Famously omitted generals' names.
Oldest surviving Latin prose work: villa slave management, contracts, recipes, rituals.
Over 150 speeches known to Cicero; c. 80 attested by title, including Pro Rhodiensibus (167) and De sumptu suo.

sources.reliability: First Latin prose history; strong personal and anti-aristocratic slant. De agri cultura is a primary document for 2nd-century slave agriculture.
sources.summary: Novus homo from Tusculum, consul 195, censor 184, implacable advocate of destroying Carthage (Carthago delenda est).

sources.name: Polybius

works.books: 40 books; books 1-5 complete (to Cannae), the rest in Byzantine excerpts (Constantinian Excerpta, Codex Urbinas) and fragments
works.note: Main theme: how Rome conquered the known world in under 53 years (220-167); books 1-2 background from 264; extended to 146. Book 6 analyses the Roman constitution and army; book 12 attacks Timaeus; book 34 geography.

sources.reliability: Best surviving historian of the Middle Republic: a cavalry commander, hostage, friend of Scipio Aemilianus, present at Carthage in 146. Used documents (the Carthage treaties, the Lacinian inscription of Hannibal for troop numbers), walked Hannibal's route, interrogated eyewitnesses. Biases: pro-Scipionic, pro-Achaean; tendency to systematize causes (pragmatic history).
sources.summary: Achaean statesman from Megalopolis, deported to Rome among 1,000 hostages after Pydna (167). Livy followed him closely for eastern affairs.

sources.name: Valerius Antias
sources.reliability: Notorious for inflated casualty figures, as Livy complains (Livy 33.10, 36.38); a key Sullan-era annalist behind Livy's third and fourth decades.
sources.summary: Late annalist of the 70s BC; the archetype of rhetorical, invented 'annalistic' detail.

sources.name: Quintus Claudius Quadrigarius

works.note: Began with the Gallic sack, deliberately skipping the unverifiable earlier period.

sources.reliability: Livy used him heavily in books 6-10 and 30-45; more sober than Antias but still rhetorical. Gellius preserved his vivid Torquatus single-combat passage.
sources.summary: Sullan-era annalist.

sources.name: Posidonius

works.note: Continued Polybius; probably ended with the 80s BC.

sources.reliability: Stoic polymath from Apamea whose lost Histories underlie much of Diodorus, Strabo, Athenaeus and Plutarch on the Sicilian slave wars, the Gauls (head-hunting, druids), the Cimbri and Athenion's Athens.
sources.summary: Head of the Stoic school at Rhodes; envoy to Marius; host to Cicero and Pompey.

sources.name: Sallust

works.note: Includes speeches of Caesar and Cato in the debate of 5 Dec 63.
Background from Micipsa's death (118); war 111-105.

works.books: 5 books; c. 500 fragments, with complete speeches and letters (Lepidus, Philippus, Cotta, Macer, Pompey's letter, Mithridates' letter)

sources.reliability: Brilliant, Thucydidean stylist with a moralizing scheme of decline after 146 and hostility to the nobility; chronology and geography in the Jugurtha are loose. A Caesarian partisan, expelled from the Senate in 50, governor of Africa Nova (46) and enriched there.
sources.summary: The first great Roman historical monographer; tribune 52. His gardens (Horti Sallustiani) became imperial property.

sources.name: Julius Caesar

works.note: One book per campaigning year: Helvetii and Ariovistus (58) to Alesia (52).
Ends with Caesar besieged in Alexandria (late 48).

sources.reliability: Eyewitness commander's account in plain third-person prose; indispensable but self-serving (casualty figures for enemies, e.g. 368,000 Helvetii and 430,000 Usipetes and Tencteri, are suspect; the Gallic ethnography of book 6 is partly schematic). Cicero praised the style; Asinius Pollio doubted its accuracy.
sources.summary: Wrote the Gallic commentaries probably year by year or in 52/51 as political dispatches; the civil-war books are an apologia.

sources.name: Caesarian corpus (Hirtius and continuators)

works.note: Bellovaci, Uxellodunum.
Probably Hirtius; Alexandria, Pharnaces at Zela, Illyricum, Spain.
Anonymous officer's eyewitness account of Thapsus.
Anonymous, crude Latin; campaign of Munda (17 Mar 45); text breaks off.

sources.reliability: Completes Caesar's narrative from 51 to 45. The Bellum Africum and Hispaniense are valuable as unpolished soldiers' accounts.
sources.summary: Aulus Hirtius (consul 43, killed at Mutina) wrote BG 8 and probably the Alexandrine War; the others are by unknown Caesarian officers.

sources.name: Cicero

works.t: Letters (Ad Atticum, Ad Familiares, Ad Quintum fratrem, Ad Brutum)
works.books: c. 900 letters (some 90 from correspondents); Att. 16 books (68-44), Fam. 16 books (62-43), QFr. 3 books (60-54), Brut. 2 books (43)
works.note: Thin before 61; dense 51-43.

works.books: 58 survive complete or in part (of c. 88 known), from Pro Quinctio (81) to the 14 Philippics (44-43)
works.note: Verrines (70), Catilinarians (63), Pro Sestio (56), Pro Milone (52) and others.
Brutus (46) is a history of Roman oratory from the beginnings; De re publica (54-51, partly recovered from a Vatican palimpsest) and De legibus on the constitution; De officiis (44).

sources.reliability: The single richest body of evidence for any period of antiquity: day-by-day, unguarded correspondence for 61-43 BC. Speeches are advocacy, not fact; letters reveal motives but reflect Cicero's own vanity and anxieties. Asconius and the scholia supply context.
sources.summary: Novus homo from Arpinum, consul 63 (Catilinarian conspiracy), exiled 58-57, proconsul of Cilicia 51-50, proscribed and killed 7 Dec 43.

sources.name: Cornelius Nepos

works.t: De viris illustribus: Foreign generals; Hamilcar; Hannibal
works.note: 23 lives of foreign generals survive, including Hamilcar and Hannibal (the only ancient biography of Hannibal).
Atticus written by a friend; Cato in a short version.
Universal chronicle in 3 books, dedicatee of Catullus' poems.

sources.reliability: Uncritical and slight, but the Hannibal preserves non-Polybian material, and the Atticus is a contemporary portrait of a banker-equestrian.
sources.summary: Transpadane friend of Cicero, Atticus and Catullus.

sources.name: Varro

works.note: Written c. 47-43 BC; preserves archaic legal and religious formulae and Roman topography.
Farming, livestock, villa economics (aviaries, fishponds).
41 books; known through Augustine's City of God.

sources.reliability: The Republic's greatest scholar; his antiquarian framework (including the 'Varronian' foundation date of 753 BC) underlies later Roman chronology and religion.
sources.summary: Pompeian legate in Spain (49), pardoned by Caesar and made head of the planned public library; proscribed by Antony but saved.

sources.name: Diodorus Siculus

works.books: 40 books; 1-5 (myth and ethnography) and 11-20 (480-302 BC) complete; 21-40 in fragments and Byzantine excerpts
works.note: Books 21-40 preserve, via excerpts, the Pyrrhic, Punic and Sicilian slave wars and the late Republic to 60 BC; Roman events from the 5th-4th century in books 11-20 give an independent (sometimes earlier) consul list.

sources.reliability: A compiler who reproduces his sources (Ephorus, Timaeus, Hieronymus, Polybius, Posidonius) with little critique, which makes him valuable for lost material; chronology often confused by forcing events into single archon-consul years.
sources.summary: Sicilian from Agyrium, wrote in Rome c. 60-30 BC.

sources.name: Dionysius of Halicarnassus

works.books: 20 books; 1-10 complete, 11 mostly, the rest in excerpts
works.note: From the earliest inhabitants to the outbreak of the First Punic War. Books 1-2 on origins and the regal constitution; 3-11 the kings and early Republic in great detail.

sources.reliability: Argues Romans were really Greeks. Long invented speeches; but preserves antiquarian detail (e.g. the 'Servian' centuriate system, early census figures, the Foedus Cassianum) from Varro and the annalists. Parallel to Livy 1-10.
sources.summary: Greek rhetor who lived in Rome from 30 BC; also wrote literary criticism.

sources.name: Livy

works.books: 142 books; 1-10 and 21-45 survive (41 and 43-45 with gaps), plus a palimpsest fragment of book 91 (Sertorius, 77 BC); the rest known from the Periochae, Oxyrhynchus epitome and fragments
works.note: Ended with the death of Drusus (9 BC). First decade to 293; third decade the Hannibalic war; fourth and fifth to Pydna and 167.

sources.reliability: The main narrative of Republican Rome. For the early period he admits the unreliability of his sources (6.1) and follows the late annalists (Antias, Quadrigarius, Licinius Macer, Tubero); for 218-167 he relies on Polybius for the East, giving high reliability. Preserves annual records (prodigies, magistrates, colonies, temple dedications) from the pontifical tradition. Patriotic, moralizing, militarily vague.
sources.summary: From Patavium; wrote under Augustus, who called him a 'Pompeian' but remained friendly; encouraged the young Claudius to write history.

sources.name: Periochae of Livy

works.note: Valuable for the lost books 11-20 (293-219) and 46-142 (167-9 BC); some entries are a line or two.
Papyrus epitome of books 37-40 and 48-55 with consular dating.

sources.reliability: Uneven and sometimes garbled, but the only continuous outline for much of 293-219 and 167-9 BC, including census returns and key laws.
sources.summary: Anonymous epitome, probably 3rd-4th century; derived from an earlier digest of Livy that also fed Florus, Eutropius, Orosius, Obsequens and Cassiodorus.

sources.name: Fasti Capitolini

works.note: Marble lists of consuls, dictators, magistri equitum, censors and consular tribunes; about two-thirds survive, with gaps (e.g. much of the 3rd century BC).
Triumphs from Romulus to L. Cornelius Balbus (19 BC), the last triumph by a non-imperial general.

sources.reliability: The official Augustan version of Republican chronology (Varronian, with inserted 'dictator years'); early entries are reconstructions, not contemporary records. Found in the Forum from 1546, now in the Capitoline Museums.
sources.summary: Inscribed c. 18-17 BC, probably on the Parthian arch of Augustus in the Forum (or the Regia), with later additions.

sources.name: Res Gestae Divi Augusti

works.note: Copies from Ancyra (Monumentum Ancyranum, Latin and Greek), Apollonia and Antioch in Pisidia; the original stood on bronze pillars before the Mausoleum.

sources.reliability: Augustus' own account of his honours, expenditures (e.g. 860 million sesterces for veterans' land, 600 million in Italy and 260 million in the provinces; 170 million to the aerarium militare) and achievements. Accurate in its numbers but artful in omission (no mention of Antony by name, of the proscriptions, or of Varus).
sources.summary: Written by Augustus and deposited with the Vestals with his will; finalized AD 14.

sources.name: Strabo

works.note: Describes the oikoumene c. 20 BC-AD 23 with historical excursuses back to Homer; books 3-6 on Iberia, Gaul, Britain and Italy, 12-14 Asia Minor, 16-17 the Near East and Egypt.
Continued Polybius.

sources.reliability: Uses Polybius, Posidonius, Artemidorus and personal travel (Egypt with Aelius Gallus). Indispensable for the Augustan empire's geography and client kingdoms; dated for some regions (e.g. Spain via Posidonius).
sources.summary: From Amaseia in Pontus, of a family of Mithridatic courtiers.

sources.name: Velleius Paterculus

works.books: 2 books; book 1 has a large gap from Romulus to 168 BC; book 2 complete
works.note: Book 2 runs from 146 BC to AD 30 and dwells on Tiberius' campaigns in Germany and Pannonia (AD 4-12), in which Velleius served.

sources.reliability: Panegyric of Tiberius and Sejanus written in AD 30; eyewitness value for AD 4-12 (Pannonian revolt, Varus). Lists Roman colonies with dates (1.14-15) and digressions on literary history.
sources.summary: Equestrian cavalry prefect, legate under Tiberius, praetor AD 15.

sources.name: Valerius Maximus

works.note: Organized by theme (religion, omens, discipline, censorial severity, cruelty); epitomized by Julius Paris and Nepotianus.

sources.reliability: Rhetorical handbook of exempla dedicated to Tiberius; unreliable as narrative, but preserves anecdotes and customs from lost Republican sources.
sources.summary: Client of Sextus Pompeius (cos. AD 14).

sources.name: Asconius

works.books: Commentaries on 5 speeches survive (In Pisonem, Pro Scauro, Pro Milone, Pro Cornelio, In toga candida)
works.note: Pro Milone commentary gives the fullest account of Clodius' murder (18 Jan 52) and Pompey's sole consulship.

sources.reliability: Highly reliable scholarly commentary using the acta diurna and senatorial records; corrects Cicero's tendentious statements.
sources.summary: Paduan scholar, wrote c. AD 54-57 for his sons.

sources.name: Granius Licinianus

works.note: Covers the 160s, 105 (Arausio) and 88-78 (Sulla, Lepidus).

sources.reliability: Antiquarian epitomator; the palimpsest (British Library, discovered 1853) gives unique details for the 80s-70s BC.
sources.summary: Probably Antonine-era.

sources.name: Julius Obsequens

works.note: List of prodigies year by year (only 190-11 BC survives), excerpted from Livy.

sources.reliability: Mechanical but faithful excerpt of Livy's prodigy lists, preserving year-entries from lost books (e.g. 166-11 BC).
sources.summary: Probably a 4th-century pagan compiler.

sources.name: Lucan

works.note: Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon to Alexandria.

sources.reliability: Epic of Caesar's war, anti-Caesarian and Republican in sentiment; history bent for effect (Cato's African march, Erichtho the witch), but reflects Neronian views of the civil war.
sources.summary: Nephew of Seneca; forced to suicide after the Pisonian conspiracy.

sources.name: Silius Italicus

works.books: 17 books, the longest surviving Latin epic
works.note: The Second Punic War, following Livy's third decade.

sources.reliability: Derivative of Livy with mythological machinery; of literary rather than historical value.
sources.summary: Consul 68, the last consul appointed by Nero; proconsul of Asia.

sources.name: Frontinus

works.note: Written as curator aquarum (97): capacity, history and abuses of the nine aqueducts, with quinariae figures.
Collection of stratagems, including Domitian's Chattan war (83) in which he served.

sources.reliability: Technical and administrative document of high value on the water supply; the Strategemata is anecdotal.
sources.summary: Consul three times, governor of Britain (c. 74-77, conquered the Silures).

sources.name: Josephus

works.note: From the Maccabees to the fall of Masada (73/74); a detailed description of the Roman army (3.70-109).

works.books: 20 books; books 11-20 cover the Persian-Roman period
works.note: Books 1-10 biblical history. Long excursus on Gaius' death and Claudius' accession (19.1-273) from a Roman source.

sources.reliability: Eyewitness, first as rebel commander in Galilee (surrendered at Jotapata, 67), then on Titus' staff at the siege of Jerusalem (70). Pro-Flavian and self-justifying; numbers inflated (1.1 million dead at Jerusalem), but invaluable; quotes Roman decrees for the Jews.
sources.summary: Jewish priest and aristocrat, freed by Vespasian and given citizenship and a pension in Rome.

sources.name: Philo of Alexandria

works.note: Eyewitness of the Alexandrian pogrom of 38 and his embassy to Caligula (39/40).

sources.reliability: Partisan but vivid primary account of Caligula's court and the persecution under the prefect Flaccus.
sources.summary: Leader of the Alexandrian Jewish community and philosopher.

sources.name: Pliny the Elder

works.note: Encyclopedia with countless historical notices: provincial and city lists (books 3-6, from Augustan documents), mines, prices, metals, art, the census of AD 47 in Italy's 8th region; historical anecdotes from all periods.
Used by Tacitus.
History of his own times continuing Aufidius Bassus; a source for Tacitus' Histories and Annals.

sources.reliability: Uncritical compiler (from some 2,000 volumes), but his geographical books preserve Agrippa's measurements and Augustan administrative lists.
sources.summary: Equestrian officer and procurator; prefect of the fleet at Misenum; died at Stabiae in the eruption of Vesuvius (24 Aug or Oct 79).

sources.name: Pliny the Younger

works.note: Senatorial life, trials (Marius Priscus, 100), villas, the eruption of Vesuvius (6.16, 6.20).
Governor of Bithynia-Pontus: aqueducts, fire brigades, Christians (10.96-97).
Consular speech of thanks, 1 Sep 100.

sources.reliability: Literary letters selected for publication, but book 10 is a unique run of real administrative correspondence between a governor and the emperor.
sources.summary: Nephew and adopted son of the Elder Pliny; consul 100; died in Bithynia c. 113.

sources.name: Tacitus

works.books: 16 (or 18) books; 1-4, part of 5, 6, and 11-16 (broken off in 66) survive
works.note: Lost: Caligula, early Claudius (37-47) and the end of Nero (66-68).

works.books: Originally c. 12-14 books; 1-4 and part of 5 survive
works.note: The year of the four emperors, the Batavian revolt and the siege of Jerusalem.
Biography of his father-in-law; conquest of Britain to Mons Graupius (83/84).
Ethnography of the Germans.

sources.reliability: The greatest Roman historian; used the acta senatus, memoirs (Agrippina the Younger, Corbulo) and earlier historians (Pliny, Cluvius Rufus, Fabius Rusticus). Reliable on facts, but shapes them with insinuation and a bleak senatorial view of the principate (Tiberius' 'dissimulation'). The Lyon tablet allows comparison of his version of Claudius' speech with the original.
sources.summary: Senator from Gallia Narbonensis or Cisalpina; consul suffect 97, proconsul of Asia c. 112-113.

sources.name: Suetonius

works.books: 12 lives, Julius Caesar to Domitian; the opening of the Julius is lost
works.note: Organized by rubric (family, career, vices, death, omens) rather than chronology.
De grammaticis et rhetoribus survives; lives of Terence, Horace, Lucan and others in excerpt.

sources.reliability: As ab epistulis under Hadrian (dismissed c. 122) he quoted Augustus' letters and other archival documents; gossip-rich and unsystematic, but much detail is genuine. Later lives thinner after loss of archive access.
sources.summary: Equestrian scholar, protégé of Pliny the Younger.

sources.name: Plutarch

works.books: 22 pairs plus 4 single lives survive; the Epaminondas-Scipio pair is lost
works.note: Roman lives: Publicola, Coriolanus, Camillus, Fabius Maximus, Marcellus, Aemilius Paullus, Cato the Elder, Flamininus, Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, Marius, Sulla, Sertorius, Lucullus, Crassus, Pompey, Caesar, Cato the Younger, Cicero, Brutus, Antony; plus Romulus and Numa (legendary), and Pyrrhus, Philopoemen, Demetrius among Greek subjects of Roman relevance.
Augustus to Vitellius; only Galba and Otho survive.

sources.reliability: Moral biographer who disclaims writing history (Alex. 1), but read widely (Polybius, Posidonius, Fenestella, memoirs of Sulla, letters of Cicero, Asinius Pollio) and preserves much lost material. Chronology loose; character over cause.
sources.summary: Priest at Delphi from Chaeronea; Roman citizen with consular friends (Sosius Senecio).

sources.name: Appian

works.note: Roman wars in Spain to Numantia (133), with a brief note on Augustus' Cantabrian war.
Unique full narrative of the Third Punic War and the siege of Carthage, from Polybius.
To Octavian's Illyrian war (35-33).
War with Antiochus III and a Seleucid history to Pompey.
The only continuous narrative of 133-70 BC; ends with the death of Sextus Pompey.

works.t: Lost books (Kings, Italy, Samnites, Celts, Sicily, Macedonia, Egypt, Dacia, Arabia)

sources.reliability: Arranged by region rather than chronology; his Civil Wars book 1 is the main source for the Gracchan land crisis and Sulla. Reliability depends on lost sources (Polybius, perhaps Asinius Pollio); careless in places but often uniquely informative.
sources.summary: Alexandrian Greek who rose to procurator under Antoninus Pius through Fronto's patronage.

sources.name: Florus

works.note: Rome's wars in biological stages (infancy to old age), to Augustus and Varus.

sources.reliability: Rhetorical summary chiefly from Livy; few independent facts, many errors, but sometimes reflects lost Livian books.
sources.summary: Probably the African-born poet friend of Hadrian.

sources.name: Arrian

works.note: Report to Hadrian as legate of Cappadocia on the Black Sea forts.

works.t: Ektaxis kata Alanon (Order of battle against the Alans)
works.note: His own battle orders for repelling the Alans, unique evidence for a legionary phalanx deployed against cavalry.
Includes the Hadrianic cavalry exercises (hippika gymnasia).
Trajan's Parthian war.

sources.reliability: A serving governor's documents on frontier command; his Anabasis of Alexander is the best source on Alexander.
sources.summary: From Nicomedia; pupil of Epictetus; consul c. 129; legate of Cappadocia 131-137.

sources.name: Gaius

works.books: 4 books; the only classical legal text surviving almost intact, from a Verona palimpsest found by Niebuhr in 1816
works.note: Persons, things, obligations, actions; model for Justinian's Institutes.

sources.reliability: Primary statement of classical private law (status of slaves, freedmen, Latins, peregrines, women's guardianship, the formulary system).
sources.summary: Jurist of the Antonine age, possibly in the East.

sources.name: Cassius Dio

works.books: 80 books; books 36-60 (69 BC-AD 46) survive, with 55-60 partly only in epitome; parts of 78-80 (216-220) in a Vatican codex
works.note: The only continuous narrative for 46-229 apart from Herodian, via the epitomes.
Covers books 36-80; the books on Antoninus Pius and early Marcus were already missing in Xiphilinus' copy.
Zonaras follows Dio for books 1-21 (to 146 BC) and 44-80; between he used Plutarch.
10th-century thematic excerpts (on embassies, virtues and vices, sententiae).

sources.reliability: Senatorial historian writing c. 202-229; eyewitness of Commodus to Severus Alexander (he watched Commodus in the arena). Strongly structural (the Agrippa-Maecenas debate of book 52 as a blueprint for monarchy); reliable on institutions, uneven on the Republic.
sources.summary: From Nicaea in Bithynia, son of a consular; consul c. 205 and (ordinarius, with Severus Alexander) 229; governed Africa, Dalmatia, Pannonia Superior.

sources.name: Herodian

works.t: History of the Empire after Marcus

sources.reliability: Contemporary but vague: few names or dates, rhetorical set-pieces, invented speeches. Independent value for 222-238 (Severus Alexander, Maximinus, the Gordians), where Dio fails.
sources.summary: Probably a Syrian Greek in minor imperial service.

sources.name: Dexippus

works.note: Gothic wars. A palimpsest in Vienna (Scythica Vindobonensia, published 2014) adds Decius' campaigns of 250-251 and an attack on Thessalonica (c. 262).

sources.reliability: Eyewitness of the Herulian sack of Athens (267/268), whose resistance he claimed to have led (IG II2 3669). Used by Zosimus, Zonaras and the HA.
sources.summary: Athenian archon and priest.

sources.name: Historia Augusta

works.books: 30 biographies of emperors, heirs and usurpers from Hadrian to Carinus, ascribed to six authors
works.note: A lacuna removes 244-260 (Philip to the start of Valerian).

sources.reliability: A late-4th-century hoax by a single author (Dessau 1889) posing as six Diocletianic-Constantinian writers. The early 'major' lives (Hadrian to Caracalla) rest on a good lost source (Marius Maximus or the 'Ignotus'); the secondary lives and everything after 238 contain invented documents, people and letters. Use only with control from other sources.
sources.summary: Probably written c. 395-400, possibly by a pagan senator.

sources.name: Vindolanda tablets

works.books: Over 1,700 ink leaf-tablets and stylus tablets, found from 1973 at the fort of Vindolanda behind Hadrian's Wall
works.note: Mostly periods 2-4 (c. 92-105), the cohors IX Batavorum and cohors I Tungrorum.

sources.reliability: Unfiltered military documents: a strength report of the First Tungrians (752 men on the books, only 296 present at Vindolanda, 31 of them unfit), Claudia Severa's birthday invitation (the earliest known Latin in a woman's hand), the disparaging 'Brittunculi', supply accounts.
sources.summary: Written by the garrison and families of the fort before Hadrian's Wall.

sources.name: Oxyrhynchus papyri

works.books: Over 500,000 fragments from the city's rubbish dumps, excavated by Grenfell and Hunt from 1896; 87 volumes published by 2023
works.note: Documentary: census returns, tax receipts, contracts, petitions, letters, imperial edicts, libelli of the Decian sacrifice (250). Literary: lost works (Hellenica Oxyrhynchia, the Livy epitome P.Oxy. 668).

sources.reliability: The densest documentation of any Roman provincial community: prices, wages, liturgies and the working of government from the Ptolemies to the Arab conquest.
sources.summary: Middle Egyptian nome capital (Pemje, modern el-Bahnasa).

sources.name: Shapur I's inscription on the Ka'ba-ye Zartosht (ŠKZ)

works.note: On the 'Cube of Zoroaster' at Naqsh-e Rustam: Shapur's three Roman wars: Gordian III killed at Misiche (244) and Philip paying 500,000 denarii; destruction of a Roman army of 60,000 at Barbalissos (253) and the sack of 37 cities including Antioch; the capture of Valerian 'with our own hands' near Carrhae and Edessa (260), with lists of captured praetorian prefect, senators and the deportation of Romans into Iran.

sources.reliability: The Persian counter-narrative to Roman sources for the 240s-260s; its battle claims (Misiche) conflict with Roman accounts of Gordian's death. Also lists the provinces of the empire and the fire temples endowed.
sources.summary: Royal inscription of Shapur I, c. 262; companion to the rock reliefs of Naqsh-e Rustam and Bishapur showing Valerian kneeling.

sources.name: Antonine Itinerary

works.note: 225 routes with stations and distances in miles (leagues in Gaul); core probably compiled under Caracalla, revised under Diocletian.

sources.reliability: Register of road routes across the empire, the backbone for locating Roman road stations (including 15 British routes). Not a map; distances are corrupted in places.
sources.summary: Compiled from cursus publicus records.

sources.name: Tabula Peutingeriana

works.books: 11 surviving parchment segments, 6.75 m long; the westernmost (Britain, Spain) lost
works.note: 13th-century copy of a late antique road map, now in Vienna. Date of the original disputed (c. 300 Talbert; c. 435 Weber; with Augustan or earlier strata).

sources.reliability: Schematic diagram of the road network from Britain to India with hundreds of settlement symbols and some 3,000 named features, stretched east-west; Constantinople, Rome and Antioch shown as personifications.
sources.summary: Named after Konrad Peutinger, the Augsburg humanist who owned it.

sources.name: Panegyrici Latini

works.books: 12 speeches: Pliny's Panegyricus plus 11 Gallic speeches of 289-389
works.note: To Maximian (289, 291), Constantius (297, on the recovery of Britain), Constantine (307, 310 with the vision of Apollo, 311, 313, 321), Julian (Mamertinus, 362) and Theodosius (Pacatus, 389).

sources.reliability: Court rhetoric, but contemporary and often the only source for Tetrarchic campaigns and Constantine's shifting self-presentation (the Claudius Gothicus ancestry first appears in 310).
sources.summary: Collected at Autun/Trier rhetorical circles.

sources.name: Edict on Maximum Prices

works.books: Preamble and 32 sections, c. 1,200 items, reconstructed from over 40 fragmentary copies, almost all in the Greek east (Aphrodisias the longest)
works.note: Issued late 301 (after 20 Nov) in the names of the Tetrarchs; prices in denarii communes for grain, wine, meat, textiles, wages (farm labourer 25 denarii a day with food), freight by sea and land.

sources.reliability: Unique source for relative prices and transport costs (land carriage of wheat for 300 miles roughly doubled its price; sea transport far cheaper). The preamble blames avarice; Lactantius says it caused shortages and bloodshed and was abandoned.
sources.summary: Diocletianic legislation accompanying the currency revaluation edict of Sep 301.

sources.name: Verona List

works.note: Seventh-century manuscript list of the 12 dioceses and about 100 provinces, dated c. 314 (Barnes; Jones c. 312-320), with a list of barbarian peoples.

sources.reliability: Primary evidence for Diocletian's subdivision of provinces and the creation of dioceses; some entries reflect later revisions.
sources.summary: Preserved in a Verona chapter library manuscript.

sources.name: Lactantius

works.note: Death of persecutors from Nero to Maximinus Daza, detailed for 303-313: the Great Persecution, Diocletian's abdication, Constantine's dream before the Milvian Bridge (the chi-rho shield sign), and the text of the 'edict of Milan' (Licinius' letter of 313).

sources.reliability: Hostile to Diocletian and Galerius, but a contemporary in Nicomedia; preserves the texts of Galerius' edict of toleration (311) and the 313 rescript. His account of Diocletian's 'four rulers' and tax burdens is caricature with a factual core.
sources.summary: North African rhetor appointed by Diocletian at Nicomedia, later tutor of Constantine's son Crispus at Trier.

sources.name: Eusebius of Caesarea

works.books: 10 books, several editions (to c. 313 and c. 325)
works.note: Quotes documents verbatim, including imperial rescripts to Christians.
Constantine's oath-sworn account of the vision of the cross; imperial letters quoted.
Synchronized tables from Abraham to 325; survives in Jerome's Latin version and an Armenian translation.

sources.reliability: Founder of church history and Christian chronography; invaluable documents, but a panegyrist of Constantine who suppresses unwelcome facts (Crispus' execution).
sources.summary: Bishop of Caesarea Maritima from c. 313; at Nicaea (325).

sources.name: Anonymus Valesianus

works.note: Concise, factual account of Constantine's career, probably c. 340-390.
Odoacer and Theodoric, with the end of Boethius and Symmachus; mid-6th century, Ravenna perspective.

sources.reliability: Two unrelated texts named after their editor Henri de Valois (1636); both reliable and terse.
sources.summary: Anonymous.

sources.name: Chronograph of 354

works.note: Illustrated calendar compiled by Furius Dionysius Filocalus: consular fasti from 509 BC, Easter tables, city prefects 254-354, Depositio episcoporum and Depositio martyrum (first record of 25 Dec as Christ's birth), list of bishops of Rome, regionary catalogue of the city, Chronica urbis Romae.

sources.reliability: Survives in Renaissance copies of a lost Carolingian manuscript; key for late antique Rome's calendar and administration.
sources.summary: Commissioned by the Christian aristocrat Valentinus.

sources.name: Aurelius Victor

works.note: Written 361; Augustus to Constantius II, moralizing on the decline of senatorial standards and the army.

sources.reliability: Short imperial history from the lost Kaisergeschichte (Enmann's hypothesis) with independent interpretive views; valuable for the 3rd century.
sources.summary: African of humble origin; governor of Pannonia Secunda under Julian (361), prefect of Rome 389.

sources.name: Epitome de Caesaribus

works.note: Augustus to the death of Theodosius I; distinct from Victor and with independent information (e.g. on Constantine's birth, Theodosius).

sources.reliability: Anonymous, wrongly ascribed to Victor in manuscripts; uses the Kaisergeschichte, Marius Maximus and other lost sources.
sources.summary: Written soon after 395.

sources.name: Eutropius

works.note: Dedicated to Valens (369/370); translated into Greek by Paeanius and much used in Byzantium.

sources.reliability: Clear, neutral summary based on Livy's epitome, Suetonius and the Kaisergeschichte; reliable in outline, especially for the 3rd-4th centuries. An eyewitness of Julian's Persian campaign.
sources.summary: Magister memoriae under Valens; proconsul of Asia, praetorian prefect of Illyricum (380-381), consul 387.

sources.name: Festus

works.note: Short survey of the acquisition of provinces and the wars with Persia, written c. 370 for Valens' eastern campaign.

sources.reliability: Valuable for the provincial list and the sequence of Roman-Persian wars; otherwise thin.
sources.summary: Magister memoriae of Valens.

sources.name: Julian (writings)

works.t: Orations, letters, Caesars, Misopogon, Letter to the Athenians
works.note: The Letter to the Athenians (361) justifies his usurpation; Misopogon (363) satirizes Antioch; c. 80 letters, including religious edicts (the school law of 362).

sources.reliability: An emperor's own voice, unusual for antiquity; partisan but revealing on his pagan restoration and campaigns.

sources.name: Libanius

works.note: Funeral oration for Julian (Or. 18), On the temples (Or. 30), on patronage of villages (Or. 47), on the riots of 387 (Or. 19-23).

sources.reliability: The largest letter collection of antiquity; a pagan rhetor's view of urban life, curial decline and imperial officials in 4th-century Antioch.
sources.summary: Sophist at Antioch; teacher of John Chrysostom (by tradition).

sources.name: Ammianus Marcellinus

works.note: Gallus Caesar, Silvanus, the siege of Amida (359, which he escaped), Julian's Gallic and Persian campaigns, Valentinian and Valens, the Huns and Adrianople.

sources.reliability: The last great Latin historian and the best source for any late Roman period: an officer (protector domesticus) who served under Ursicinus and Julian. Fair-minded pagan, but with hostility to Valentinian's regime and satirical excursuses on Rome's aristocracy.
sources.summary: Greek from Antioch writing in Latin at Rome c. 390.

sources.name: Eunapius

works.note: Main source of Zosimus for 270-404.

sources.reliability: Hostile to Christians and Theodosius; Photius found him verbose. Known mainly through Zosimus and the Constantinian excerpts.
sources.summary: Sophist of Sardis.

sources.name: Jerome

works.note: Translation of Eusebius' canons with additions on Roman history and a continuation 325-378.
Letter 123 on the barbarian invasions of Gaul (406-409); Letter 127 on the sack of Rome.

sources.reliability: Annalistic notices on the 4th century (often from the Kaisergeschichte); letters give vivid if rhetorical reactions to 410.
sources.summary: Biblical translator (the Vulgate), at Bethlehem from 386.

sources.name: Symmachus

works.books: 49 official reports as prefect of Rome
works.note: Relatio 3 (384) pleads for the restoration of the Altar of Victory: 'uno itinere non potest perveniri ad tam grande secretum'.

sources.reliability: Window on the pagan senatorial elite and the administration of Rome (grain supply, games).
sources.summary: Prefect of Rome 384-385, consul 391.

sources.name: Claudian

works.note: Panegyrics on the consulships of Honorius and Stilicho; invectives against Rufinus and Eutropius; De bello Gildonico, De bello Getico (Pollentia, 402).

sources.reliability: Stilicho's court poet: the only near-contemporary western narrative for 395-404, heavily slanted.
sources.summary: Alexandrian Greek writing Latin at Milan and Ravenna.

sources.name: Vegetius

works.note: Recruitment, training, legion organization, siegecraft, naval warfare; dedicated to an emperor (Theodosius I or Valentinian III).

sources.reliability: Antiquarian idealization of the 'ancient legion' drawn from Cato, Celsus, Frontinus and Paternus, set against the decline of his own day; reliability on contemporary practice disputed.
sources.summary: Senior civil official (vir illustris, comes).

sources.name: Notitia Dignitatum
sources.latin: Notitia dignitatum omnium tam civilium quam militarium

works.note: Eastern part c. 395-401; western part revised piecemeal to c. 420s. Lists every high office, its staff (officium), insignia, and the several hundred military units under each commander, with illustrations of shield emblems and fortifications.

sources.reliability: The fundamental document for the late Roman state and army. A paper picture: some units and offices may have existed only nominally, and the western list mixes dates.
sources.summary: Copies from a lost Carolingian manuscript (Codex Spirensis).

sources.name: Codex Theodosianus

works.books: 16 books, over 2,500 constitutions from 312 to 437; books 1-5 incomplete
works.note: Promulgated 15 Feb 438, in force in the West from 1 Jan 439; book 16 on religion (heresy, Jews, pagan cults). With the Sirmondian Constitutions and post-Theodosian Novels.

sources.reliability: Laws excerpted and dated; the repetition of laws shows enforcement problems rather than mere legislative activity. Indispensable for the coloni, curiales, army and church.
sources.summary: Compiled by a commission under Theodosius II (429-438).

sources.name: Orosius

works.note: From Ninus to 417; book 7 has unique material on 400-417 (Radagaisus, Athaulf's wish to restore Rome with Gothic strength).

sources.reliability: Written at Augustine's request to show disasters were worse before Christ; poor on the distant past (from Livy and Eutropius), useful for the contemporary West.
sources.summary: Priest from Bracara (Braga) who fled the Vandals to Africa.

sources.name: Olympiodorus of Thebes

works.note: Summarized by Photius; used by Zosimus 5-6 and Sozomen.

sources.reliability: Diplomat whose memoir is the best source for the West 407-425 (Constantine III, Athaulf and Placidia, Constantius III); records Roman senatorial incomes (up to 4,000 lb of gold a year).
sources.summary: Egyptian poet-diplomat; embassy to the Huns c. 412.

sources.name: Philostorgius

works.note: Arian (Eunomian) perspective; secular material on Stilicho, the Goths and the Huns.

sources.reliability: The only heterodox church history to survive in any form; useful for secular events and Arian bishops.
sources.summary: Cappadocian layman.

sources.name: Socrates Scholasticus
sources.reliability: Careful, moderate lawyer-historian continuing Eusebius; corrected his first edition after reading Athanasius. Records Hypatia's murder (415) and secular events in Constantinople.
sources.summary: Lay advocate in Constantinople.

sources.name: Sozomen

works.books: 9 books; planned to 439 but ends c. 425
works.note: Draws on Socrates and Olympiodorus; information on Persian Christians, monasticism and the West.

sources.reliability: Literary rewriting of Socrates with additions; dedicated to Theodosius II.
sources.summary: Lawyer from near Gaza.

sources.name: Theodoret of Cyrrhus

works.note: Includes the penance of Theodosius after Thessalonica (390).

sources.reliability: Strongly anti-Arian; preserves letters and creeds. His Religious History of Syrian monks is also historical evidence.
sources.summary: Bishop of Cyrrhus, a theologian of the Antiochene school.

sources.name: Zosimus

works.books: 6 books, the last unfinished (breaks off just before the sack of Rome, 410)
works.note: Book 1 sketches Augustus to 270 briefly, then the 3rd century from Dexippus; a lacuna removes 282-305; books 2-5 use Eunapius, 5-6 Olympiodorus.

sources.reliability: Pagan answer to Orosius: Rome declined because the old gods were abandoned (blames Constantine). Quality mirrors his sources; careless with geography and names.
sources.summary: Comes and advocatus fisci in Constantinople, writing c. 498-518.

sources.name: Hydatius

works.note: Continues Jerome; eyewitness of the Suevic kingdom in Gallaecia, Visigothic campaigns in Spain and embassies to Aetius (431).

sources.reliability: Apocalyptic in tone (expecting the end in 482), chronology sometimes faulty, but unique for 5th-century Spain.
sources.summary: Bishop of Aquae Flaviae (Chaves) in Gallaecia.

sources.name: Prosper of Aquitaine

works.note: Continues Jerome from 379; own material for 425-455 including Aetius, Attila in Italy (452) and Pope Leo.

sources.reliability: Terse but contemporary in Rome for the age of Aetius; Augustinian theologian.
sources.summary: Secretary to Pope Leo I.

sources.name: Priscus

works.books: 8 books; substantial fragments in the Constantinian Excerpta de legationibus
works.note: Contains his eyewitness account of the embassy to Attila (449): Attila's wooden palace, his simple wooden cup, the Greek merchant turned Hun who praised life under Attila.

sources.reliability: Thucydidean-style history of high quality; the main source for the Huns and eastern diplomacy; Jordanes' Attila chapters derive from him.
sources.summary: Rhetor from Panium in Thrace, on Maximinus' embassy of 449.

sources.name: Malchus
