works.note: Zeno's reign, Theodoric Strabo and Theodoric the Amal, the embassy of Odoacer's senate returning the western regalia.

sources.reliability: Fragments of high quality via the Constantinian excerpts and Photius.
sources.summary: Sophist from Philadelphia (Amman).

sources.name: Sidonius Apollinaris

works.books: 9 books of 147 letters; 24 poems including panegyrics on Avitus (456), Majorian (458) and Anthemius (468)
works.note: Portrait of Theodoric II (Ep. 1.2); the defence of Clermont against Euric (471-475).

sources.reliability: The fullest picture of the Gallo-Roman elite as the western empire dissolved, in a precious style.
sources.summary: Son-in-law of Avitus; prefect of Rome 468; bishop of Clermont from c. 470.

sources.name: Victor of Vita

works.note: Includes Huneric's edict of 484 and the list of exiled bishops (Notitia provinciarum et civitatum Africae).

sources.reliability: Catholic polemic against the Vandal Arian kings; exaggerates but preserves documents and the 484 bishop list.
sources.summary: African cleric, probably bishop.

sources.name: Laterculus of Polemius Silvius

works.note: List of the provinces of the empire by diocese appended to a calendar dedicated to Bishop Eucherius of Lyon, plus lists of emperors, animals and Roman buildings.

sources.reliability: A mid-5th-century provincial list from Gaul that mixes current and outdated information; compared with the Verona List and Notitia for provincial change.
sources.summary: Compiled by Polemius Silvius in Gaul, 448/449.

sources.name: Chronicle of Pseudo-Joshua the Stylite

works.note: Edessa during the Anastasian war with Kavad I (502-506): famine, plague, prices, the sieges of Amida and Edessa.

sources.reliability: A remarkably precise local chronicle with grain prices and military detail; preserved within the Chronicle of Zuqnin.
sources.summary: Anonymous Edessene monk (not Joshua), written c. 507.

sources.name: Marcellinus Comes

works.note: Eastern perspective; continuation to 548 by another hand. Notes under 476: 'the western empire of the Roman people... perished with this Augustulus'.

sources.reliability: Official-minded chronicle; first source to treat 476 as the end of the western empire.
sources.summary: Illyrian, cancellarius of Justinian.

sources.name: Cassiodorus

works.note: Letters drafted for Theodoric, Athalaric, Amalasuntha, Theodahad and Witiges, and in his own name as praetorian prefect.
Consular list with notes to 519.
Lost; used by Jordanes.

sources.reliability: Primary documents of Ostrogothic government, cast in elaborate rhetoric; Romano-Gothic accommodation ideology.
sources.summary: Senator, quaestor, magister officiorum and praetorian prefect; founded the monastery of Vivarium.

sources.name: Jordanes

works.note: Gothic history from Scandza to 551; Catalaunian Plains from Priscus; earlier parts legendary (Goths conflated with Getae and Scythians).
Compilation from Florus, Eutropius, Jerome and Marcellinus, with original notes for the 6th-century Balkans.

sources.reliability: Abridges Cassiodorus' lost Gothic history (from memory, he says); a pro-Justinian Goth. Unique for some 5th-century events, but ethnogenesis passages are literary constructions.
sources.summary: Of Gothic-Alan descent, notarius of a magister militum, later a cleric in Constantinople.

sources.name: Procopius

works.books: 8 books: Persian (1-2, to 549), Vandalic (3-4, background from 395; to 548), Gothic (5-7, 535-551), book 8 (to 553/554)
works.note: Eyewitness as Belisarius' assessor 527-540: Dara, the Nika riot, Ad Decimum, the siege of Rome; the plague of 542 at Constantinople (2.22-23).
Written c. 550, unpublished in his lifetime: savage invective on Justinian and Theodora, Belisarius and Antonina.
Panegyric of Justinian's building programme: Hagia Sophia, Danube forts, Dara.

sources.reliability: The best historian of late antiquity and the main source for Justinian's wars; classicizing (Thucydides, Herodotus), so Christian and administrative matters are muted. The three works pull in different directions, reflecting a politically constrained author.
sources.summary: From Caesarea in Palestine; lawyer and legal assessor to Belisarius.

sources.name: Corpus Juris Civilis

works.books: 12 books, c. 4,600 constitutions from Hadrian to 534
works.note: First edition 529 (lost); second 534.

works.books: 50 books, excerpts from 39 classical jurists (Ulpian about a third, Paul a sixth), promulgated 16 Dec 533
works.note: Classical law of the 1st century BC to the 230s, edited (interpolated) by Tribonian's commission.

works.books: c. 168 new laws, mostly in Greek
works.note: Administrative reforms, e.g. Novel 8 against sale of offices, the provincial reorganizations of 535-536.

sources.reliability: The codification of Roman law; the Digest is the main source for classical jurisprudence, though interpolations must be detected; the Code shows imperial rescripts in action.
sources.summary: Compiled under Justinian by commissions led by Tribonian (528-534).

sources.name: John the Lydian

works.note: History of Roman offices from the kings, focused on the decline of the praetorian prefecture under John the Cappadocian; gives Diocletian's army figures.

sources.reliability: Embittered bureaucrat's insider view of the eastern civil service; antiquarian errors about early Rome, real knowledge of 6th-century administration.
sources.summary: Official in the praetorian prefecture 511-551, professor of Latin at Constantinople.

sources.name: Gildas

works.note: The appeal to Aetius 'thrice consul' (446-454), the invitation to the Saxons by a 'proud tyrant', Ambrosius Aurelianus, Mons Badonicus.

sources.reliability: A sermon, not a history: chronology confused and Roman Britain misunderstood, but the only near-contemporary British narrative of the 5th-6th centuries.
sources.summary: British monk, writing c. 530-545.

sources.name: Corippus

works.note: John Troglita's campaigns against the Moors.
Justin II's accession and ceremonial.

sources.reliability: Epic panegyric giving unique detail on Moorish tribes and Byzantine Africa, and on court ceremonial.
sources.summary: African grammarian.

sources.name: John Malalas

works.books: 18 books; the main manuscript breaks off in 563
works.note: World chronicle from Adam; Antioch-centred, rich for 5th-6th century earthquakes, riots, circus factions, the Nika revolt and Justinian's laws.

sources.reliability: Naïve and error-prone on early history, but contemporary for c. 500-565 and an important source for urban life and the eastern frontier; the first Byzantine popular chronicle.
sources.summary: Syrian rhetor ('malal' = orator) from Antioch, later in Constantinople.

sources.name: Agathias

works.note: Narses in Italy (Casilinum 554), war in Lazica, the Kutrigur raid of 559 repulsed by the aged Belisarius; excursus on Sasanian kings from the Persian royal annals, obtained via the interpreter Sergius.

sources.reliability: Continuator of Procopius; more moralizing, weaker on military detail, but his Persian chapters use genuine Sasanian records. Source of the army figure of 150,000 under Justinian.
sources.summary: Lawyer and poet from Myrina.

sources.name: Evagrius Scholasticus

works.note: From the Council of Ephesus to 594; personal account of the plague of 542 and its recurrences, which killed his wife, children and servants.

sources.reliability: Chalcedonian lawyer's history mixing church and state; uses Zosimus, Procopius, Priscus, Malalas and Eustathius.
sources.summary: Lawyer at Antioch, adviser to Patriarch Gregory.

sources.name: Chronicle of Pseudo-Zachariah Rhetor

works.note: Includes a Syriac version of Zachariah of Mytilene's church history (451-491), Anastasius' Persian war, the Huns and the Caucasus, and a description of Rome.

sources.reliability: Miaphysite Syriac compilation; valuable for eastern frontier events and steppe peoples.
sources.summary: Anonymous Amidene monk, 569.

sources.name: Menander Protector

works.books: Large fragments in the Excerpta de legationibus
works.note: The Fifty Years' Peace of 561/562 with its terms quoted; embassies of Zemarchus to the Turks (569) and to the Avars.

sources.reliability: Excellent diplomatic source with treaty texts and envoy reports; continues Agathias.
sources.summary: Imperial guardsman under Maurice.

sources.name: John of Ephesus

works.note: Justin II, Tiberius, Maurice; Slav invasion of 581-584; persecution of Miaphysites. Parts I-II survive partially through the Chronicle of Zuqnin (incl. the plague of 542).

sources.reliability: Miaphysite bishop with court access; vivid, partisan, written partly in prison.
sources.summary: Missionary bishop who converted thousands of pagans in Asia Minor for Justinian.

sources.name: Gregory of Tours

works.note: Books 1-2 to Clovis; 5-10 detailed contemporary history of 575-591.

sources.reliability: The main source for Merovingian Gaul; Catholic and episcopal viewpoint, story-telling over analysis; his Clovis narrative is shaped by hagiographic models.
sources.summary: Bishop of Tours from 573, of Gallo-Roman senatorial family.

sources.name: Strategikon of Maurice

works.note: Cavalry tactics, camp organization, how to fight Persians, Avars and Turks, Slavs and Franks.

sources.reliability: Practical late 6th-century field manual; key evidence for the transition of the Roman army toward cavalry archers and Avar-style equipment (stirrups).
sources.summary: Attributed to Maurice or a general of his court.

sources.name: Theophylact Simocatta

works.note: Maurice's reign: Balkan wars against Avars and Slavs, Persian war and the restoration of Khosrow II (591), the mutiny and murder of 602; with a retrospective from 572.

sources.reliability: Last classicizing historian; ornate style, chronological confusion in the Balkan narrative, but well-informed through official sources.
sources.summary: Egyptian, secretary under Heraclius; wrote c. 630.

sources.name: Isidore of Seville

works.note: Two recensions (619, 624); the latter praises Suintila's expulsion of the Byzantines.

sources.reliability: Primary source for the Visigothic kingdom to 624; Hispano-Gothic patriotism.
sources.summary: Bishop of Seville from c. 600.

sources.name: George of Pisidia

works.note: Expeditio Persica (622), Bellum Avaricum (siege of 626), Heraclias (628).

sources.reliability: Court poet and deacon at Hagia Sophia; contemporary witness to Heraclius' campaigns and the siege of 626, used by Theophanes.
sources.summary: Deacon and chartophylax of Hagia Sophia.

sources.name: Chronicon Paschale

works.note: Easter-chronicle from Adam to 628 (the text breaks off); with lacunae in the 6th century. Eyewitness record of the Avar-Persian siege of Constantinople (626) and the text of Heraclius' victory dispatch of 628.

sources.reliability: Based on consular lists and Malalas for earlier periods; primary for 600-628.
sources.summary: Anonymous Constantinopolitan cleric, c. 630.

sources.name: Sebeos

works.note: Armenia between Rome and Persia from the revolt of 572, Khosrow II's war, Heraclius' campaigns, the rise of Islam and the earliest non-Muslim account of Muhammad.

sources.reliability: Near-contemporary and well-informed, written c. 660; attribution to Bishop Sebeos is uncertain.
sources.summary: Armenian churchman.

sources.name: Chronicle of Fredegar

works.note: Own material for 584-642; earlier books abridge Jerome, Hydatius and Gregory; notes Heraclius and the Arabs, the Slav ruler Samo.

sources.reliability: Merovingian chronicle in barbarous Latin; key for 7th-century Francia and western perceptions of Byzantium.
sources.summary: Anonymous Burgundian compiler(s); 'Fredegar' is a 16th-century attribution.

sources.name: John of Nikiu

works.note: World chronicle surviving only in an Ethiopic translation (1602); a lacuna removes most of 610-639; the end gives a near-contemporary account of the Arab conquest of Egypt (639-642).

sources.reliability: Garbled in transmission but the only substantial contemporary non-Muslim narrative of the conquest of Egypt.
sources.summary: Coptic bishop of Nikiu in the Delta, writing c. 690.

sources.name: Khuzistan Chronicle

works.note: Late Sasanian civil wars, Heraclius' campaign, the Arab conquest of Iraq and Khuzistan.

sources.reliability: East Syrian Christian chronicle written c. 660; contemporary witness for the fall of the Sasanians.
sources.summary: Anonymous, Church of the East.

sources.name: Paul the Deacon

works.note: Lombard origins, Alboin's invasion of 568, the dukes, Agilulf and Theodelinda, Rothari; uses the lost history of Secundus of Trent.

sources.reliability: Late (written c. 790) but the essential narrative for Lombard Italy; folk traditions mixed with chronicles.
sources.summary: Lombard monk at Monte Cassino and Charlemagne's court.

sources.name: Theophanes the Confessor

works.note: Annalistic year-by-year chronicle (Annus Mundi) from Diocletian to 813; for 602-641 it is the main Byzantine narrative of Phocas, Heraclius' Persian war (from George of Pisidia and dispatches) and the Arab conquests (from an eastern Greek source shared with Syriac chronicles).

sources.reliability: Late, and its year-dates are often off by one or more years, but indispensable for the 7th century; compiled partly from George Syncellus' materials.
sources.summary: Monk and abbot; exiled for opposing Iconoclasm.

sources.name: al-Tabari
sources.latin: Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari

works.t: History of the Prophets and Kings (Ta'rikh al-rusul wa'l-muluk), Sasanian section
works.note: Ardashir to Yazdegerd III, from Arabic translations of the Middle Persian Khwaday-namag ('Book of Lords'); then the conquests year by year from 632.

sources.reliability: Preserves the late Sasanian court tradition, idealizing (Khosrow I as just king) and legendary in places (Bahram Gur), but with genuine administrative detail; Nöldeke's annotated translation (1879) remains fundamental.
sources.summary: Persian-born scholar in Baghdad.

sources.name: Zonaras

works.note: From creation to 1118. For Rome: books 7-9 from Dio's lost books 1-21 (to 146 BC), then Plutarch for 146-44 BC; books 10-11 from Dio to Severus Alexander; book 12 the 3rd century from lost sources (perhaps Peter the Patrician and the 'Leoquelle'); then Eusebius, Socrates, Theophanes.

sources.reliability: A careful 12th-century epitomator; our main witness for Dio's lost early books and for parts of the 3rd-century crisis.
sources.summary: Byzantine official (droungarios tes viglas) who became a monk.

glossary.def: The two chief annual magistrates of the Republic, elected by the comitia centuriata, holding full imperium and alternating the fasces monthly. They commanded armies, presided over the Senate and assemblies and gave their names to the year (eponymous dating). Opened to plebeians by the leges Liciniae Sextiae (367 BC); from 342 one consul could be, and from 172 both sometimes were, plebeian. Minimum age 42 under the lex Villia annalis (180) as revised by Sulla. Under the empire consuls became honorific, with suffect pairs every few months; the ordinary consulship survived until 541 (last private holder Anicius Faustus Albinus Basilius).

A consul elected to replace one who died or resigned during the year. From Augustus, regular suffect pairs shortened terms (often two to four months) to multiply consular rank for governorships and commands; the ordinarii of 1 January still named the year.

Magistrate with imperium below the consuls. The urban praetor (from 367 BC) administered justice among citizens; the peregrine praetor (c. 242) cases involving foreigners. Numbers rose to govern provinces (four by 227, six by 197), eight under Sulla, sixteen under Caesar. Each issued an edict setting out the remedies he would grant, the main engine of Roman private law until Hadrian fixed the edictum perpetuum (c. 130).

Two senior magistrates elected (from 443 BC) usually every five years for 18 months to conduct the census, assign citizens to tribes and classes, revise the rolls of Senate and equites (lectio senatus, with the nota censoria for moral failings), let public contracts and build public works, and close the census with the lustrum. Held almost always by ex-consuls; the pinnacle of a career. Lapsed under the empire after Claudius and Vespasian took the office; Domitian became censor perpetuus (85).

Two plebeian aediles (from 494 BC) and two curule aediles (from 367) responsible for the city: streets, temples, markets and weights, the grain supply and public games (Ludi Romani, Plebeii, Megalenses). Lavish games bought popularity for higher office, so the aedileship was costly; Caesar's aedileship of 65 bankrupted him for a time. Not a compulsory step in the cursus.

Lowest regular magistracy, managing finance: the urban quaestors ran the aerarium; others served as paymasters and deputies to consuls and governors. Eight from 267 BC, twenty under Sulla, who made it the qualifying office for automatic Senate membership; forty under Caesar, twenty again under Augustus. A bond of quasi-filial loyalty linked a quaestor to his commander.

Ten plebeian officers (two at first, from 494 BC; ten by 457) elected by the concilium plebis to protect plebeians (ius auxilii). Sacrosanct; could veto (intercessio) any act of a magistrate, election or senatus consultum, and propose plebiscites, binding on all after 287. The Gracchi, Saturninus, Sulpicius and Clodius used it as a popular weapon; Sulla gutted it (81) and Pompey and Crassus restored it (70). Augustus took tribunicia potestas without the office.

Extraordinary single magistrate named by a consul on the Senate's request for a specific task (causa), with supreme imperium for at most six months or the duration of the task, unaccompanied by appeal or tribunician veto in the early period; 24 lictors. Causae included rei gerundae (war), comitiorum habendorum (holding elections) and clavi figendi (driving the sacred nail). Disused after 202 BC; revived without time limit by Sulla (82) and Caesar (perpetual, 44), then abolished by the lex Antonia.

The dictator's deputy, chosen by him and subordinate to him, nominally commanding the cavalry. Famous clashes: Papirius Cursor tried to execute his magister Fabius Rullianus (325 BC); Minucius Rufus was voted equal imperium with Fabius Maximus (217). Mark Antony and Lepidus served Caesar in the role.

A patrician senator appointed for five days when both consulships were vacant, to hold consular elections; successive interreges followed until elections were held (the first interrex never held them). Revived in 82 BC to propose Sulla's dictatorship and used in 52 when riots prevented elections, before Pompey became sole consul.

The senator placed first on the censors' list and therefore first asked his opinion in debate; a position of great prestige (auctoritas) held by the senior patrician ex-censor in the early period. Holders included Scipio Africanus, Aemilius Lepidus, Aemilius Scaurus. Augustus was enrolled princeps senatus in 28 BC, one root of the title princeps.

Head of the college of pontiffs, overseeing state cult, the calendar, sacred law and the Vestals and flamines; residence in the Domus Publica by the Regia. Elected by 17 of the 35 tribes from the 3rd century BC. Caesar was elected in 63 BC; Augustus took it on Lepidus' death (12 BC) and all emperors held it until Gratian dropped the title (c. 379 or 383). Popes later used pontifex.

Boards of three to six (later up to six) military tribunes with consular power elected in place of consuls in 51 years between 444 and 367 BC. Ancient explanations: to admit plebeians without opening the consulship, or to provide more commanders. The number of colleges increased in the warlike years around Veii. Abolished by the Licinio-Sextian laws.

Two boards of ten men with supreme power who replaced the regular magistrates in 451-449 BC to codify the law, producing the Twelve Tables. The second board under Appius Claudius became tyrannical (the Verginia story) and was overthrown by the second secession of the plebs. Other decemviral boards included those for sacred rites and for land assignment.

Six senior officers per legion in the Republic, 24 elected by the people for the first four legions from 311 BC; young nobles began careers here. Under the empire each legion had one senatorial tribunus laticlavius (second in command) and five equestrian angusticlavii.

A promagistrate acting in place of a consul: first in 326 BC (prorogation of Publilius Philo's command at Neapolis), becoming normal for provincial governors. Sulla's system sent consuls and praetors to provinces after their year; Pompey's law of 52 imposed a five-year gap. Under the empire, governors of 'public' provinces (Africa, Asia) bore the title; Augustus held imperium proconsulare over his own provinces.
Promagistrate with praetorian imperium, used for provincial governors and subordinate commanders; legates of the emperor governed imperial provinces as legati Augusti pro praetore.

Extension of a magistrate's imperium after his year in office (prorogatio) or grant of imperium to a private individual (privatus cum imperio, like Scipio in Spain in 210 BC or Pompey in 77). The device that made provincial empire administrable and later concentrated huge commands (Pompey's under the leges Gabinia and Manilia).

An envoy or delegated officer. In the Republic, senators appointed by the Senate as ambassadors or as staff officers to commanders (Caesar's legates in Gaul commanded legions). Under the empire, the legatus Augusti pro praetore governed imperial provinces and the legatus legionis commanded a legion.

Attendants who walked before magistrates carrying the fasces and clearing the way: 12 for a consul, 6 for a praetor (2 within the city), 24 for a dictator. Lictors carried out floggings and executions ordered by magistrates.

Bundle of rods tied with red thongs, with an axe added outside the pomerium, symbolizing a magistrate's power to beat and execute. Lowered (fasces summittere) before the assembled people as a sign of the people's sovereignty; wreathed in laurel after victory.
Folding ivory stool reserved for the 'curule' magistrates (consul, praetor, curule aedile, censor, dictator), an Etruscan-derived symbol of judicial authority, with the toga praetexta.

The ordered sequence of offices in a senatorial career: quaestor, (aedile or tribune), praetor, consul, optionally censor, with minimum ages and two-year intervals fixed by the lex Villia annalis (180 BC) and Sulla (81 BC: quaestor at 30, praetor 39, consul 42). Imperial careers added military tribunates and the vigintivirate before the quaestorship and posts as legate and governor after the praetorship; equestrians had a parallel procuratorial cursus.

Twenty junior magistracies (the board of three moneyers, the three in charge of executions, four for street cleaning in Rome, ten judges of the centumviral court) that young senatorial sons held before the quaestorship under the Principate; earlier 26 (vigintisexviri).

The supreme power of command and jurisdiction held by consuls, praetors, dictators and promagistrates, conferred by a lex curiata. It included command of armies, coercion (coercitio) and capital jurisdiction outside the city, symbolized by the fasces and axe. Limited inside the pomerium by provocatio and tribunician intercession. Imperium could be greater (maius) or equal (aequum) to another's.

The right and duty of magistrates to take the auspices (consult the will of Jupiter through signs such as birds, lightning or the feeding of sacred chickens) before public acts. Patricians originally monopolized the auspices; their claim that only they could take them was a pretext against plebeian consuls. Obnuntiatio (announcing unfavourable signs) could block assemblies, as Bibulus tried against Caesar in 59 BC.

The legal power of any magistrate to act within his sphere (issue edicts, convene bodies, fine), distinct from imperium. Magistrates were classified as having greater or lesser potestas (maior/minor), which determined who could veto whom.

The citizen's right to appeal to the people against a magistrate's capital or corporal punishment inside Rome, traditionally established by a lex Valeria of 509 BC (reaffirmed 449 and 300) and extended by the leges Porciae (early 2nd century) to citizens everywhere. Gaius Gracchus' law of 123 forbade execution without trial, the basis of the debate over the Catilinarians in 63.

The right of a magistrate to block the act of an equal or lesser colleague, and of tribunes of the plebs to veto any act of any magistrate (except a dictator, in the early period). Tiberius Gracchus' deposition of his vetoing colleague Octavius (133 BC) was a constitutional rupture.

The Republican principle that every magistracy (except the dictatorship) was held by at least two equal colleagues, each able to block the other; combined with annuality to prevent a return of kingship.

(1) The 'first triumvirate' of Pompey, Crassus and Caesar (60/59 BC) was a private political alliance, not an office. (2) The triumviri rei publicae constituendae (Antony, Lepidus and Octavian), created by the lex Titia of 27 Nov 43 BC for five years with consular powers, renewed at Tarentum (37) until 33: a legal triple dictatorship that carried out the proscriptions.

In the regal and early Republic a deputy left in charge of Rome when the magistrates were away. Augustus made it a permanent senatorial post for policing Rome, with the urban cohorts; in late antiquity the prefect of Rome (and from 359 of Constantinople, the eparch) governed the city and presided over its senate.

'First citizen': the informal title Augustus preferred, signalling a magistrate-like leadership within restored Republican forms rather than kingship. The resulting system (the Principate, 27 BC to the 3rd century) rested on a bundle of powers (proconsular imperium, tribunician power, control of the army and treasury) voted to each emperor, as in the lex de imperio Vespasiani.

Name voted to Octavian on 16 January 27 BC ('revered', with augural associations), adopted by all subsequent emperors as the title of the senior ruler; from 161 (Marcus and Lucius) there could be two or more Augusti. Women of the dynasty could be Augusta (first Livia, AD 14).

Originally the cognomen of the Julii Caesares, it became part of every emperor's name, and from Hadrian's adoption of Aelius (136) the title of the designated heir. In the Tetrarchy the junior emperors were Caesares under the Augusti.

Victorious general acclaimed by his troops, a title held by Republican commanders until their triumph. Octavian used Imperator as his first name (praenomen imperatoris); emperors counted imperatorial salutations (IMP VII etc.) for victories won under their auspices, and from Augustus only members of the imperial house could be acclaimed (the last private acclamation was Junius Blaesus, AD 22).

The powers of a tribune of the plebs (sacrosanctity, veto, right to propose laws and convene the Senate) held by Augustus without the office from 23 BC and renewed annually; emperors numbered their years by it (TR P). Conferral on a colleague (Agrippa, Tiberius) marked a designated successor.

Proconsular imperium superior to that of other governors, granted to Augustus (from 23 BC) and to delegated princes such as Agrippa, Germanicus (in the East, AD 17) and Corbulo. Gave the emperor command over every army and governor.

Equestrian commander of the Praetorian Guard, created by Augustus (2 BC), usually two in office; became the most powerful official after the emperor (Sejanus, Plautianus) and acquired judicial and administrative duties (jurists Papinian and Ulpian held it). Constantine removed its military role and created regional prefectures (Gaul, Italy, Illyricum, Oriens) that ran taxation, the annona and supply, with appellate jurisdiction: the apex of the late Roman civil hierarchy.

glossary.term: prefect of the grain supply (praefectus annonae)
glossary.def: Equestrian official established by Augustus (c. AD 8) to manage the supply and distribution of grain to Rome from Egypt, Africa and Sicily, including contracts with shippers (navicularii).
Equestrian commander of the vigiles, Augustus' 7,000-strong fire brigade and night police (AD 6), with seven cohorts each covering two of the city's fourteen regions.

Equestrian governor of Egypt with legions under his command, a post closed to senators, who could not even enter Egypt without permission, because of the province's grain and wealth. The first prefect, Cornelius Gallus, fell in 26 BC.

Senatorial governor of an imperial province, appointed by and responsible to the emperor, holding delegated imperium for an indefinite term (usually three years); ex-consuls governed the great military provinces (Syria, Germania, Britain, Pannonia), ex-praetors the one-legion ones.

Senatorial commander of a legion under the Principate, normally an ex-praetor in his thirties. Gallienus excluded senators from such commands (c. 262), replacing them with equestrian praefecti legionis.

Agent managing property for another. Under the empire, equestrian (or freedman) officials managing the emperor's estates, provincial finance (procurator provinciae, who collected taxes in imperial provinces and spied on governors) or governing small provinces (Judaea, Raetia, Noricum, the Alpine and Mauretanian provinces). Pontius Pilate was praefectus, later such governors were styled procurators.

glossary.term: imperial secretariats (ab epistulis, a rationibus, a libellis)
glossary.def: The central bureaux of the Principate: correspondence (ab epistulis, split into Latin and Greek), accounts (a rationibus), petitions (a libellis), legal inquiries (a cognitionibus). Under Claudius run by powerful freedmen (Narcissus, Pallas, Callistus); transferred to equestrians from the Flavians and Hadrian. Evolved into the late Roman scrinia under the magister officiorum.

Informal advisory body of friends (amici), jurists and officials consulted by the emperor on legal and political matters, as in Juvenal's satire of the turbot council. Became the formal sacrum consistorium in late antiquity.

Title of the emperor's wife, mother or sister, first given to Livia by Augustus' will (AD 14). Augustae (Julia Domna, Julia Mamaea, Helena, Pulcheria, Theodora, Martina) could wield great influence; in the East an Augusta could confer legitimacy on a new emperor, as Pulcheria did on Marcian (450) and Ariadne on Anastasius (491).

Diocletian's system of four rulers: two Augusti (Diocletian, Maximian) and two Caesares (Galerius, Constantius) from 1 March 293, each with his own army, court and capital (Nicomedia, Milan, Sirmium/Thessalonica, Trier), bound by adoption, marriage and the divine identities Jovius and Herculius. Planned succession by merit collapsed after the abdications of 305, ending in Constantine's sole rule (324).

Modern term (from dominus, 'lord') for the autocratic late Roman monarchy from Diocletian, contrasted with the Principate: court ceremonial (adoratio, proskynesis), the emperor sacred and remote, separate civil and military hierarchies. Recent scholarship stresses continuity and treats the contrast as overdrawn.

Council of ex-magistrates (c. 300 members in the middle Republic, 600 after Sulla, 900+ under Caesar, 600 again under Augustus) that advised magistrates by senatus consulta. In practice it directed foreign policy, finance, war and provincial assignments. Under the empire it remained a court, a body of governors and the source of legitimacy; in late antiquity there were two senates (Rome and Constantinople) and the senatorial order grew to thousands of clarissimi. The Roman senate is last heard of c. 603.

The meeting place of the Senate: the Curia Hostilia, burned at Clodius' funeral (52 BC), was replaced by Caesar's Curia Julia (completed 29 BC), whose Diocletianic rebuilding survives in the Forum. Also one of the 30 archaic divisions of the citizen body (curiae) underlying the comitia curiata, and in the provinces the town council.

Oldest assembly, organized by the 30 curiae; by the late Republic represented by 30 lictors. Passed the lex curiata conferring imperium on magistrates and witnessed adoptions (Clodius' transfer to the plebs in 59 BC) and wills.

Assembly of the people in 193 centuries arranged by wealth class and age (iuniores, seniores), originally the army in civil form, meeting on the Campus Martius outside the pomerium. Elected consuls, praetors and censors, declared war, and heard capital appeals. The 18 equestrian and 80 first-class centuries held a majority of 98, so voting often stopped before the poor voted; reformed c. 241 to align centuries with the 35 tribes.

Assembly of all citizens voting in 35 tribes, presided over by a consul or praetor; elected quaestors, curule aediles and military tribunes and passed laws. Each tribe had one vote decided by majority within it; the four urban tribes were outnumbered by 31 rural ones, favouring landowners able to come to Rome.

Assembly of plebeians only, voting by tribe, convened by a tribune of the plebs; elected tribunes and plebeian aediles and passed plebiscita, binding on all citizens after the lex Hortensia (287 BC). Most Republican legislation was passed here, including the Gracchan laws.

A public meeting summoned by a magistrate to address the people, without voting; where laws were explained, debated and denounced before the voting assembly. Crucial to late Republican popular politics.

Territorial voting and census unit. Four urban and an increasing number of rural tribes (21 by 495 BC) reached 35 in 241 BC, after which new citizens were added to existing tribes; enrolment of freedmen and the new Italian citizens after 89 BC in particular tribes was fiercely contested.
Voting unit of the comitia centuriata, nominally 100 men, and in the army a company of (in the empire) 80 men under a centurion.

The five census classes of the 'Servian' system, defined by property qualifications in asses (first class 100,000 asses in Livy's account), which determined military equipment and voting weight in the comitia centuriata; below them the capite censi.

Citizens below the lowest property class, registered only by their heads; also called proletarii (contributing only offspring). Exempt from legionary service until the minimum qualification was lowered and Marius openly enrolled them as volunteers (107 BC).
Citizens without property worth registering, counted only as producers of offspring (proles). Effectively the same as the capite censi; manned the fleets in the Punic Wars.

Citizens with property above the minimum census, liable for legionary service and the tributum. The supposed shrinkage of the assidui through war and the spread of large estates was the premise of Tiberius Gracchus' land law.

A decree of the Senate: formally advice to a magistrate, in practice authoritative. Records survive in inscriptions (SC de Bacchanalibus 186 BC; SC de Cn. Pisone patre AD 20). Under the empire senatus consulta acquired the force of law.

The 'final decree' (videant consules ne quid res publica detrimenti capiat) urging magistrates to defend the state by any means, first passed against Gaius Gracchus (121 BC), then against Saturninus (100), Lepidus (77), Catiline (63) and Caesar (Jan 49). Its legality, overriding provocatio, was contested by populares.
Ratification by the patrician senators of decisions of the assemblies; the lex Publilia (339 BC) and the lex Maenia required it to be given in advance, making it a formality.
A resolution of the concilium plebis proposed by a tribune; binding on the whole people after the lex Hortensia (287 BC), and thereafter the main form of legislation.

A statute passed by an assembly on the proposal (rogatio) of a magistrate, named after its proposer's nomen (lex Iulia, lex Sempronia). Laws were posted for three market days (trinundinum) before the vote; voting became secret by the leges tabellariae (139-107 BC).

Declaration by the Senate that a citizen was an enemy of the state, outlawing him: used against Marius and his allies (88 BC), Lepidus (77), Catiline (63), Antony (43), Nero (68) and later emperors and usurpers.

First written Roman law code, drawn up by the decemvirs (451-450 BC) and displayed in the Forum. Fragments quoted by later authors cover procedure (summons, debt bondage with the debtor cut in parts, 'partes secanto'), family (a father selling his son three times loses potestas), property, burial and torts. Cicero says boys learnt it by heart.

Laws of the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius (367 BC) that ended consular tribunes, opened the consulship to plebeians (Sextius the first plebeian consul, 366), limited holdings of public land (500 iugera, probably anachronistic) and eased debts.

Law of the dictator Quintus Hortensius (287 BC), passed after the last secession of the plebs, making plebiscites binding on all citizens without patrician ratification; conventionally the end of the Conflict of the Orders.
Law of the tribune Lucius Villius (180 BC) fixing minimum ages for magistracies and a two-year interval between them, regularizing the cursus honorum.

Law of the tribune Aulus Gabinius (67 BC) giving Pompey an extraordinary command against the pirates for three years, with imperium equal to governors' up to 50 miles inland, 500 ships and 24 legates; he cleared the Mediterranean in three months. Followed by the lex Manilia (66) giving him the Mithridatic command.

Bronze tablet (found in Rome, now in the Capitoline Museums) preserving the end of the law or senatus consultum of December 69 conferring powers on Vespasian, with precedents from Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius, including a discretionary clause to do whatever he judged in the public interest.

Edict of Caracalla (212) granting Roman citizenship to virtually all free inhabitants of the empire, except the dediticii (exact meaning disputed). Dio says the motive was to extend the inheritance tax; papyri show a flood of new 'Aurelii'. Made the citizen/non-citizen distinction obsolete, replaced by honestiores and humiliores.
Law applying to Roman citizens, from the Twelve Tables, statutes and juristic interpretation, as opposed to the law of peoples.
The 'law of nations': rules applied to relations involving non-citizens, developed especially by the peregrine praetor; jurists also used it for institutions common to all peoples (sale, slavery).

The annual edict in which each praetor announced the legal remedies (actiones, exceptiones) he would grant; carried over and expanded by successors, it was codified by the jurist Salvius Julianus on Hadrian's orders (c. 130) and then frozen.

Classical civil procedure: the parties appeared before the praetor, who issued a written formula defining the issue, then a private judge (iudex) decided the case. Gradually replaced by cognitio extra ordinem.

Procedure in which an official (emperor, prefect, governor) heard and decided a case himself from start to finish; spread under the Principate and became the only procedure in late antiquity, with appeals up the hierarchy.

Permanent jury court for a particular crime, first for extortion by governors (lex Calpurnia de repetundis, 149 BC), later for treason, murder, electoral bribery (ambitus) and others under Sulla. The composition of the juries (senators or equites) was a central political issue from Gaius Gracchus (122) to the lex Aurelia (70).

Recovery of money illegally taken by Roman officials from provincials; the first standing court (149 BC). Cicero's prosecution of Verres (70 BC) is the classic case; the lex Iulia of 59 tightened the rules.

Crime of diminishing the majesty of the Roman people: originally for incompetent commanders (lex Appuleia, c. 103 BC); under Tiberius extended to words and acts against the emperor, fuelling the trials and informers (delatores) Tacitus describes.
Archaic charge of high treason, tried before the people, as in the trial of Horatius and, revived as a show, of Gaius Rabirius (63 BC).

The father's legal power over his descendants in the male line, including in principle life and death, ownership of all their property and control of marriage, lasting until the father's death unless he emancipated them. Sons could own a peculium; daughters married sine manu stayed in their father's power.

Marriage form in which the wife passed into the power of her husband (or his father), becoming legally like a daughter; created by confarreatio, coemptio or usus. Rare by the late Republic, when marriage without manus left women under their fathers or guardians.

Requirement that adult women not in potestas have a guardian to authorize certain acts; increasingly formal. Augustus' ius trium liberorum freed freeborn women with three children (freedwomen with four).

Privileges granted under Augustus' marriage laws (lex Iulia de maritandis ordinibus, 18 BC; lex Papia Poppaea, AD 9) to parents of three children: faster careers for men, release from guardianship for women, full inheritance rights. Often granted as a favour (Pliny the Younger received it childless).

Freeing of a slave, formally by the vindicta before a magistrate, by enrolment in the census, or by will, which made the freed person a citizen (unlike most ancient societies); informal manumission gave Junian Latin status. Augustus restricted testamentary manumission (lex Fufia Caninia, 2 BC) and set age limits (lex Aelia Sentia, AD 4). Tax of 5% (vicesima libertatis).

A freed slave, a citizen but bound to his former master (patronus) by obligations of respect (obsequium) and services (operae); barred from magistracies and the Senate but prominent in trade and as Augustales. Imperial freedmen (Pallas, Narcissus) ran the Claudian administration.
Property a father or master allowed a son or slave to manage as his own, legally belonging to the head of household; the basis of slave business agency and of slaves buying their freedom.

The legal distinction, crystallizing in the 2nd century and universal after 212, between the 'more honourable' (senators, equites, decurions, veterans) and the 'more humble'. Humiliores faced torture, crucifixion, the beasts and the mines; honestiores exile or beheading.

The emperor's written answer to a petition or official's query, establishing law for the case and as precedent; the bulk of the Codex Justinianus' early material. Petitions answered by subscriptio were posted publicly.

Modern term for official condemnation of a person's memory: erasing names from inscriptions (as Geta's across the empire), destroying statues, annulling acts and forbidding the praenomen. Applied to Sejanus, Caligula (in part), Nero, Domitian, Commodus (later reversed), Geta, Elagabalus, Maximian and others.

Publication of lists of citizens declared outlaws whose killers received rewards and whose property was confiscated: by Sulla (82-81 BC, some 520 named initially and perhaps 4,700 in all) and by the triumvirs (43 BC: 300 senators and 2,000 equites according to Appian, including Cicero).

Inviolability of the tribunes of the plebs, based on the oath of the plebs to kill anyone harming them; violators were sacer. Its violation in the murder of Tiberius Gracchus (133 BC) opened the age of political violence.
Archaic debt bondage in which a debtor pledged his person; abolished by the lex Poetelia Papiria (326 BC), which forbade imprisoning citizens for debt, a key plebeian gain.

Hereditary aristocracy of clans (gentes) claiming descent from the first senators (patres), who monopolized priesthoods and early magistracies. A closed order by c. 450 BC (the Twelve Tables banned intermarriage, repealed by the lex Canuleia of 445). Shrank to some 14 gentes by the late Republic; Caesar and Augustus created new patricians; Constantine's patricius was a personal honour, not a caste.

All citizens who were not patricians, including rich families who formed the plebeian nobility after 367 BC. Organized as a state within the state with its own assembly, tribunes and aediles. Under the empire plebs urbana referred to Rome's citizen population receiving the grain dole.

Modern name for the struggle (494-287 BC) between patricians and plebeians, marked by secessions of the plebs (494, 449, 287), the tribunate, the Twelve Tables, the Licinio-Sextian laws and the lex Hortensia. It produced the patricio-plebeian nobility rather than democracy; ancient accounts are retrojected from late Republican politics.
Collective withdrawal of the plebs from the city, a general strike and military refusal: to the Mons Sacer or Aventine (494 BC), against the decemvirs (449), and to the Janiculum (287).

Originally the cavalry of the 18 centuries with a public horse (equus publicus); by the 2nd century BC a wealthy non-senatorial class with a census of 400,000 sesterces (fixed under Augustus), including publicani, bankers and landowners. Gaius Gracchus gave them the extortion juries. Under the empire, equestrians staffed the procuratorships, prefectures, and the army officer corps; from the 3rd century they displaced senators in governorships and commands.

Families with a consular ancestor (by the most common modern definition, after Gelzer), patrician or plebeian, who dominated the consulship: of some 200 consuls 233-133 BC, only about 15 were 'new men'.
The first man of his family to reach the Senate, and especially the consulship: Cato the Elder, Marius, Cicero.
'The best men': senators defending the Senate's authority and property against popular legislation (Catulus, Cato the Younger, Bibulus). Not a party but a political style and self-description.

Politicians who worked through the people's assemblies and tribunes, often with land, grain or debt measures, against senatorial opposition: the Gracchi, Saturninus, Clodius, Caesar. Usually nobles themselves.

Hereditary relationship of dependence between a patron and clients, involving mutual obligations (fides): legal protection and help from the patron, political support and attendance (morning salutatio) from the client. Extended to whole communities and provinces (the Fabii as patrons of the Allobroges; Pompey in Picenum). Its political weight in elections is debated.

Protector in a client relationship; former master of a freedman; advocate in court; patron of a town or collegium. In late antiquity patrocinium of powerful landlords over villages was repeatedly forbidden by law as a way of escaping taxes.
Morning greeting ceremony at which clients called on their patron's house, ranked by status; size of the crowd measured a great man's standing.

Clan of families sharing a nomen (Cornelia, Iulia), with a praenomen, nomen and cognomen (Publius Cornelius Scipio); agnomina recorded victories (Africanus). Women bore the feminine nomen (Cornelia). The system broke down after 212 when new citizens took the emperor's nomen (Aurelius), and late Romans used single names.
The male head of a familia, the oldest living ascendant, holding patria potestas over his descendants, their spouses in manus, and slaves.
'The custom of the ancestors': the unwritten norms and exempla regarded as authoritative alongside written law, invoked by conservatives against innovation.
An edifying story of an ancestor's conduct (Horatius at the bridge, Mucius Scaevola, Cincinnatus) used in rhetoric and education; Valerius Maximus collected nearly 1,000.
A Roman noble's standing and worth derived from offices, deeds and ancestry, which he was obliged to defend; Caesar justified crossing the Rubicon as protecting his dignitas.
Influence and prestige that commanded deference without legal compulsion. Augustus claimed to have excelled all in auctoritas while holding no more potestas than his colleagues (RG 34).
Good faith and trustworthiness, the bond underlying clientship, contracts and foreign relations (deditio in fidem); deified with a temple on the Capitol.

Large estates, worked by slaves or tenants, often formed from public land; Pliny's 'latifundia perdidere Italiam' (NH 18.35). Archaeology shows medium villas and smallholdings coexisted, so the scale of the 2nd-century BC crisis is debated.

Slaves were property (res) with no legal personality; perhaps 1-1.5 million in Augustan Italy (10-20% of population; some estimate more), from war captives, piracy, birth and exposure. Revolts: Sicily (135-132, 104-100 BC) and Spartacus (73-71). Manumission was frequent. Slavery persisted through late antiquity, though agricultural labour shifted toward coloni.

Originally a farmer or tenant; in late antiquity coloni were tenants tied by law to the land they farmed (from Constantine's law of 332) to secure tax collection, the 'colonate'. Older views of a serf-like class are now nuanced: rules varied by region and class (coloni adscripticii).

Members of the town councils (curiae, ordo decurionum), usually 100 men of property, hereditarily responsible for local government and for collecting imperial taxes, making up shortfalls personally. From the 3rd century burdens drove flight into the army, clergy or imperial service, which laws repeatedly tried to stop.

Senators and their families, with a property qualification of 1 million sesterces under Augustus, the broad purple stripe (latus clavus) and privileges. Late Roman grades: clarissimi, spectabiles and illustres, with only illustres sitting in the Senate by the mid-5th century.

Late Roman honorific grades: vir clarissimus (all senators, by the 4th century thousands), spectabilis (proconsuls, vicars, duces) and illustris (praetorian prefects, magistri militum, palatine ministers); in the 6th century gloriosissimus was added above.

The giving of public benefactions (buildings, games, banquets, oil) by the rich to their cities in return for honour, the motor of urban monumental building in the empire; the term comes from euergetes (benefactor).

Association (professional, religious, burial) with officers and rules; suppressed when politically active (Clodius' collegia, 58 BC) and licensed under Augustus. Late Roman guilds of shippers and bakers were made hereditary.

The basic Roman heavy-infantry formation. Polybius' manipular legion had 4,200 infantry (1,200 velites, 1,200 hastati, 1,200 principes, 600 triarii) and 300 cavalry; the late Republican and imperial legion c. 4,800-5,500 men in 10 cohorts (the first double-strength from the later 1st century AD) with 120 cavalry, numbered and named (Legio X Fretensis). Under the empire about 25-33 legions formed the citizen core of the army; late Roman legions were much smaller units of 1,000-3,000.

Tactical unit of two centuries (120 men for hastati and principes, 60 for triarii) in the middle Republican legion, deployed in a checkerboard (quincunx) of three lines allowing relief and flexibility; adopted, by tradition, during the Samnite Wars.

Unit of three maniples (c. 480 men in six centuries of 80) which became the main tactical subdivision of the legion by the late 2nd century BC; also the standard unit of auxiliary infantry (cohors quingenaria of c. 480 or milliaria of c. 800) and of the Praetorian, urban and vigiles units.
Company of the legion commanded by a centurion: 80 men (ten contubernia) under the empire, despite the name.
Squad of eight legionaries sharing a tent (papilio) and a mule, the smallest unit of the legion; ten made a century.
First line of the manipular legion: younger men with scutum, gladius and two pila.
Second line of the manipular legion: men in their prime, equipped like the hastati.
Third line of the manipular legion: veterans with thrusting spears, kneeling in reserve; 'res ad triarios rediit' meant a desperate situation.
Light-armed skirmishers of the manipular legion, the youngest and poorest, with javelins and small round shields; abolished in the reforms of the later 2nd century BC.

Modern label for changes attributed to Marius c. 107-101 BC: enrolling the capite censi as volunteers, cohort organization, the eagle as sole legionary standard, the improved pilum and soldiers carrying their own kit ('Marius' mules'). Many changes were gradual (cohorts appear earlier; property qualifications had already fallen), and the link between volunteer armies and client armies loyal to generals is debated.

Officer commanding a century, the professional backbone of the legion: about 60 per legion, graded by cohort and seniority, culminating in the primus pilus. Paid many times a legionary's salary; promotion came from the ranks or by direct equestrian commission.

Senior centurion of the first cohort, commanding its first century and the legion's eagle; on retirement entitled to equestrian rank and a large bonus, often going on to praefectus castrorum or procuratorships.
Deputy to a centurion (or decurion), chosen by him, standing at the rear of the century.
Standard-bearer of a century, also responsible for the unit's savings bank.

The silver (later gold) eagle standard of a legion, carried by the aquilifer and kept in the shrine of the headquarters; its loss was the ultimate disgrace (the eagles of Carrhae, recovered 20 BC; the three of Varus, two recovered in AD 15-16 and 41).

(1) In the Republic, an allied contingent (ala sociorum) roughly equivalent to a legion, posted on the wings. (2) Under the empire, an auxiliary cavalry regiment of c. 500 (quingenaria, 16 turmae) or 1,000 (milliaria, 24 turmae), commanded by an equestrian prefect; the ala milliaria command was the summit of the equestrian militiae.

Non-citizen regiments (alae of cavalry, cohorts of infantry, mixed cohortes equitatae) recruited from provincials and formally organized under Augustus, roughly matching the legions in number; soldiers received citizenship on discharge after 25 years (recorded on diplomas) until the Constitutio Antoniniana. Ethnic names (Batavi, Tungri, Thracians) reflect origin, not later recruitment.
Auxiliary cohort with an attached cavalry element (c. 120 or 240 horse), well suited to frontier policing.

Generic term for a military unit; specifically irregular ethnic units of the 2nd-3rd centuries (numeri Brittonum, Palmyrene archers, Moorish cavalry) outside the standard auxilia. In late antiquity a standard term for a regiment (arithmos in Greek).

Detachment drawn from one or more legions or auxiliary units and sent on campaign under a vexillum flag, increasingly common from the 2nd century; in the late army, vexillationes were the cavalry regiments of the field armies.
Commander of a turma (about 30 troopers) in an auxiliary ala or of the legionary cavalry.
Third in command of a legion, usually an ex-primus pilus, responsible for the fortress, engineering, supplies and training.

The emperor's guard, formed by Augustus from the Republican commander's cohors praetoria: nine (later ten to sixteen) cohorts of 500-1,000 Italians with higher pay and 16-year service, concentrated in the Castra Praetoria by Sejanus (c. AD 23). Kingmakers (Claudius 41, Otho 69, the auction of 193); Severus replaced it with provincial legionaries (193); disbanded by Constantine after the Milvian Bridge (312).
Police force of Rome (three, later four cohorts) under the urban prefect, created by Augustus; detachments at Lugdunum (guarding the mint) and Carthage.
Rome's fire brigade and night watch, 7 cohorts of freedmen (later freeborn) under the praefectus vigilum, from AD 6, with buckets, pumps, axes and blankets.

The imperial navy: praetorian fleets at Misenum and Ravenna, provincial fleets (classis Britannica, Germanica on the Rhine, Pannonica and Moesica on the Danube, Alexandrina, Syriaca, Pontica), manned by provincials on 26-year service. In the Republic the fleets of the Punic Wars were built ad hoc (Rome reportedly built 100 quinqueremes in 60 days in 261 BC).

Boarding bridge with a spike used by the Roman fleet in the First Punic War (Mylae 260, Ecnomus 256), turning sea battles into infantry fights; probably abandoned because it made ships unstable in storms.

A fortified camp. On campaign legions built marching camps every night to a standard plan (Polybius 6.27-42; Pseudo-Hyginus). Permanent fortresses (castra stativa) of c. 20 ha for a legion, with principia, praetorium, barracks, granaries and baths, became the nuclei of many cities (Chester, York, Vienna, León).
Formation in which soldiers locked shields overhead and around to approach walls under missile fire, shown on Trajan's and Marcus' columns.
Heavy javelin with a long iron shank designed to bend or penetrate shields, thrown before the charge; two were carried by Republican legionaries.
The short stabbing sword (gladius Hispaniensis, adopted from Iberians in the 3rd century BC; later Mainz and Pompeii types). Replaced in the 3rd century AD by the longer spatha.
Legionary shield: curved oval in the Republic (the Fayum example), curved rectangular under the early empire, replaced by flat oval shields in the 3rd century.
Modern name for the articulated iron plate cuirass of legionaries from the early 1st to the 3rd century AD (Kalkriese, Corbridge and Newstead types); coexisted with mail (lorica hamata) and scale.

Torsion artillery powered by twisted sinew skeins: stone throwers (ballistae) and bolt shooters (catapultae, scorpiones); each imperial legion had about 60 cart-mounted carroballistae and 10 stone throwers according to Vegetius. The one-armed onager appears in the 4th century.
One-armed torsion stone thrower named after its 'kick', described by Ammianus (23.4).

Siege lines around a besieged place, with an outer contravallation against relief forces, as at Alesia (52 BC: inner and outer lines of c. 16 and 21 km), Numantia (134-133) and Masada (73/74, the circumvallation and ramp still visible).

Procession of a victorious general with his army, captives and spoils from the Campus Martius to the Capitol, where he sacrificed to Jupiter; voted by the Senate for a major victory by a magistrate with imperium (in theory 5,000 enemies killed). Some 320 triumphs in the Fasti; after 19 BC reserved for the imperial family, others receiving ornamenta triumphalia.
Lesser triumph on foot or horseback, wreathed in myrtle, for victories over unworthy enemies (slaves, pirates) or without full war; Crassus' ovation after Spartacus (71 BC).

Arms stripped by a Roman commander from an enemy commander killed in single combat, dedicated to Jupiter Feretrius; only three cases (Romulus, Cossus, Marcellus in 222 BC). Augustus blocked Crassus' claim (29 BC) by ruling that Cossus had been consul.
Punishment of a cowardly unit by executing every tenth man chosen by lot, the others beaten by their comrades; rare (Crassus against Spartacus, Antony in 36 BC).
Oath sworn by soldiers on enlistment to their commander, later to the emperor, renewed annually.

Conscription of citizens for the legions, held by consuls each year in the Republic from the assidui; under the empire mostly volunteers, with conscription in emergencies (AD 6 and 9) and in late antiquity a levy of recruits from landowners (praebitio tironum) commutable into gold.
Discharge after full service with privileges and a gratuity: from AD 6 the aerarium militare paid legionary veterans 12,000 sesterces (Augustus), later 20,000 (Caracalla).

Pair of bronze tablets certifying the grant of citizenship and conubium (right of marriage) to discharged auxiliaries and sailors, copied from the master list on the Capitol; over 1,000 known, dating from Claudius to c. 300, invaluable for unit locations.
Cash gift to soldiers on an emperor's accession or other occasions; Claudius gave the Praetorians 15,000 sesterces each (41), Marcus and Lucius 20,000 (161).

Soldiers' pay, introduced traditionally during the siege of Veii (406-396 BC). Annual legionary pay: c. 112.5 denarii in the mid-Republic (Polybius' 2 obols a day), 225 under Caesar, 300 under Domitian, 450 under Severus, 675 or 750 under Caracalla; deductions for food and kit. In late antiquity pay was largely in kind (annona) plus gold donatives. Also the fixed tribute of some provinces.
Veterans recalled to service, often as specialists or junior officers; Praetorian evocati served the emperor in administrative roles.

Originally a road or path, later the fortified frontier zone of the empire with its roads, forts and watchtowers: the Upper German-Raetian limes (palisade and wall, 550 km), Hadrian's Wall, the Antonine Wall, the Danube and Euphrates frontiers, the fossatum Africae. Modern debate concerns whether frontiers were defensive lines (Luttwak's 'grand strategy') or zones of control and exchange (Isaac, Whittaker).

Late Roman frontier troops (also ripenses on rivers) under duces, distinguished from the field armies by Constantine's time; given land and lower status, often stereotyped as peasant militia, though they remained real soldiers into the 6th century. Justinian reconstituted them in Africa (534).

Soldiers of the mobile field armies (comitatus) created by Diocletian and Constantine, under magistri militum; better paid and privileged over the limitanei. The Notitia shows regional field armies (Gaul, Illyricum, Thrace, Oriens) and two praesental armies in the East.
The senior regiments of the field armies, originally attached to the emperor's person; higher pay and precedence than comitatenses.
Frontier units transferred to the field armies, ranking below comitatenses; a symptom of the 4th-5th century drain on frontier forces.

Allies bound by treaty (foedus). In the 4th-5th centuries, barbarian groups settled or subsidized under their own leaders to fight for Rome (the Goths of 382, the Visigoths in Aquitaine 418); in the 6th century, a regular corps of mixed recruitment under Roman officers.
Private armed retainers of generals and magnates, named after the hard-tack (bucellatum) they were fed; Belisarius had up to 7,000. Took an oath to the emperor as well as their patron.
Barbarian settlers given land in Gaul and Italy in return for hereditary military service, attested from the Tetrarchy (Panegyric of 297) and in the Notitia's praefecti laetorum.

Heavily armoured cavalry with horse armour, modelled on Sarmatian and Parthian/Sasanian lancers; Roman units from Hadrian (ala I Gallorum et Pannoniorum catafractaria), expanded in the 3rd-4th centuries; clibanarii ('oven men') was a related term for fully enclosed riders.

Some 35 state arms factories listed in the Notitia under the magister officiorum (shields at Augustodunum, armour at Antioch, artillery at Augustodunum and Treveri), staffed by hereditary fabricenses.

Imperial guard cavalry regiments created by Constantine (each c. 500 men), under the magister officiorum, largely Germanic in the 4th century; by the 6th century a showpiece, displaced by the excubitors.
Palace guard of 300 founded by Leo I (c. 460), often Isaurian; their commander (comes excubitorum) became a kingmaker: Justin I and Tiberius II rose from that post.
Corps of officer-cadets attached to the emperor from the mid-3rd century, a route to command (Diocletian and Ammianus served as protectores).

College of priests (3, later 9 from 300 BC, 15 under Sulla, 16 under Caesar) supervising state cult, sacred law, the calendar and intercalation, burial and adoption law, and keeping the annual tablet of events (tabula, later the Annales maximi in 80 books). Members were co-opted, then elected by 17 tribes from 104 BC.
Priest of a single god: three major flamines (Dialis of Jupiter, Martialis, Quirinalis), patrician, and twelve minor; later flamines of deified emperors in Rome and the provinces.

Priest of Jupiter, bound by archaic taboos (no touching iron, horses or ivy, could not spend a night away from Rome or see an army), which made the post hard to fill; vacant from 87 BC (the young Caesar was designated but never inaugurated) to 11 BC.
'King of sacred rites', a patrician priest who inherited the religious functions of the kings, barred from political office; outranked even the pontifex maximus in the order of precedence.
Member of the college of augurs (9 from 300 BC, 15 under Sulla) who interpreted signs of divine will (auspices) and could declare acts vitiated; inaugurated templa. Cicero was an augur from 53 BC.

Etruscan diviner who read the entrails of sacrificial animals (especially the liver: the Piacenza bronze liver), lightning and prodigies; consulted by the Senate, not a Roman priesthood. Claudius created an ordo of 60 haruspices; Spurinna warned Caesar of the Ides of March.

Six priestesses of Vesta, chosen as girls aged 6-10 for 30 years of chastity, guarding the eternal fire and sacred objects (including the Palladium) in the temple of Vesta. Unchastity was punished by burial alive (some ten cases, e.g. 216 and 114-113 BC). Disbanded under Theodosius (c. 394).

College (2, then 10 from 367 BC, 15 under Sulla) that kept and consulted the Sibylline Books when ordered by the Senate and oversaw foreign cults (Magna Mater, Apollo); organized the Secular Games of 17 BC.

Oracular books in Greek hexameters, by legend bought by Tarquin from the Cumaean Sibyl, consulted in crises; they prescribed new cults (the lectisternium of 399 BC, the Magna Mater in 205, burial alive of Greeks and Gauls in 228 and 216). Burned with the Capitol in 83 BC and reconstituted; destroyed by Stilicho c. 408.

College of 20 priests responsible for the rituals of treaties and declarations of war (rerum repetitio, throwing a spear into enemy territory, later into a column by the temple of Bellona), ensuring a 'just war'. Octavian revived the rite against Cleopatra (32 BC).
A war declared with the proper fetial forms after a demand for reparation, so assured of divine favour; a principle Cicero theorized (De officiis 1.36) and Augustine later Christianized.
Leaping priests of Mars (and Quirinus) who danced through the city in March and October with the sacred shields (ancilia), singing the archaic Carmen Saliare.

College of 12 priests of Dea Dia revived by Augustus; their inscribed records (Acta Fratrum Arvalium, 21 BC-AD 304) at the grove at La Magliana record sacrifices for the imperial house, the archaic Carmen Arvale, and dates of accessions.

Purificatory sacrifice (suovetaurilia: pig, sheep, bull) performed by a censor on the Campus Martius to close the census, then the five-year period between censuses; not every censorship ended in a lustrum.

Registration of citizens, their families and property by the censors, determining tribe, class, military liability and tax; returns were reported in totals (130,000 in 508 to 910,000 in 70 BC; 4,063,000 in 28 BC, see the debate on the change). Provincial censuses under Augustus (the census of Quirinius in Judaea, AD 6) assessed tribute; late Roman censuses assessed capitatio and iugatio.

(1) The calendar of days on which legal business was permitted (dies fasti) or forbidden (nefasti), with festivals and market days; published by Gnaeus Flavius in 304 BC, reformed by Caesar (the Julian calendar of 365.25 days, from 1 Jan 45 BC, after the 'year of confusion' of 445 days in 46). Painted and inscribed calendars survive (Fasti Antiates maiores, pre-Julian; Praenestini by Verrius Flaccus). (2) Lists of magistrates (fasti consulares) and triumphs (fasti triumphales), the backbone of Roman chronology, above all the Augustan Fasti Capitolini.

Note placed by the censors beside a citizen's name for moral or civic failings, with consequences such as expulsion from the Senate, loss of the public horse or transfer to an inferior tribe (aerarii).

The sacred boundary of the city, marked by stones, within which imperium militiae lapsed, armies could not enter (except for a triumph), burial was forbidden and the auspices were urban. Extended by Sulla, Claudius (49) and Vespasian; Aurelian's walls did not follow it.
Space inaugurated by augurs for taking auspices or holding meetings (the Senate had to meet in a templum, so the Curia was one); by extension a temple building (properly aedes).

Ritual by which a Roman commander vowed himself and the enemy army to the gods of the underworld and charged to his death, as the Decii Mures did at Veseris (340 BC) and Sentinum (295), and reportedly the grandson at Ausculum (279).
Ritual summoning of an enemy city's tutelary god to Rome with the promise of a new temple, as Camillus did with Juno Regina of Veii (396 BC); also reported for Carthage (146).

Greek-style feast in which images of gods were laid on couches before food, first ordered by the Sibylline Books in 399 BC during a pestilence, and on a grand scale for twelve gods in 217 after Trasimene.
Public prayer and thanksgiving at all temples, decreed by the Senate in crises or for victories; Caesar received unprecedented supplications of 15 (57 BC), 20 and 50 days.

Unnatural event (talking cattle, rains of blood or stones, lightning strikes, monstrous births) reported to the Senate as a sign that the pax deorum was broken, expiated on the advice of pontiffs, Sibylline Books or haruspices. Livy's annual prodigy lists and Obsequens preserve hundreds.
The 'peace of the gods', the right relationship between Rome and its gods maintained by correct ritual, whose breach was revealed by prodigies and defeats.

Annual rite of driving a nail into the wall of the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Ides of September, said to mark the years; in crises a dictator clavi figendi causa was appointed to perform it to avert plague (363, 331, 313?, 263 BC).
Italic vow dedicating everything born in a spring to the gods; children born then were sent out as adults to found new communities (Sabellian migrations). Rome vowed one in 217 BC (performed 195).

Worship of the emperor, his genius or numen, and deified predecessors (divi), with temples (Rome and Augustus at Pergamum and Ancyra, the altar of the Three Gauls at Lugdunum), provincial priesthoods and the Augustales; refusal to sacrifice became the test in persecutions.

Title of an emperor (or empress) deified by vote of the Senate after death (consecratio), with temple, flamen and cult: Julius Caesar (42 BC), Augustus, Claudius, Vespasian, Titus and most later emperors until Constantine (deified 337). Funeral eagles released from the pyre symbolized the ascent.
The divine guardian spirit of a man (and the paterfamilias); oaths by the emperor's genius and offerings to the genius Augusti were core acts of loyalty.

Household gods: Lares of the house and crossroads (Lares compitales, reorganized by Augustus with his genius in the 265 vici of Rome in 7 BC) and Penates of the storeroom; the public Penates were associated with Aeneas.

Phrygian mother goddess brought from Pessinus (or Pergamum) in 205/204 BC on Sibylline advice during the Hannibalic war, as a black stone; temple on the Palatine (191). Her castrated priests (galli) were foreigners, with Romans barred until Claudius.
The 'Unconquered Sun', elevated by Aurelian (274) with a temple, a college of pontifices Solis and games on 25 December; prominent on Constantine's coins until c. 325.

Persecution of Christians launched by Diocletian and Galerius with four edicts (Feb 303 to early 304): destruction of churches and scriptures, arrest of clergy, universal sacrifice. Enforced unevenly (lightly in Constantius' west, harshly in the east under Galerius and Maximinus) until Galerius' edict of toleration (311) and the settlement of 313.
Certificate that its holder had sacrificed to the gods before commissioners, required by Decius' edict of 249/250; some 46 survive on papyrus from Egypt, including one for a priestess of Petesouchos.

Conventional name for the agreement of Constantine and Licinius at Milan (Feb 313), known from Licinius' letter to the governor of Bithynia (Lactantius DMP 48; Eusebius HE 10.5), granting freedom of worship to all and restoring confiscated church property. Not an edict, nor issued at Milan.

Theology attributed to Arius of Alexandria (c. 318), that the Son was created and subordinate to the Father; condemned at Nicaea (325) but favoured in various forms (homoian) by Constantius II and Valens, and adopted by the Goths through Ulfilas, becoming the faith of most Germanic kingdoms until Reccared's conversion (587/589).

Creed of the Council of Nicaea (325) declaring the Son 'of the same substance' (homoousios) as the Father; reaffirmed and expanded at Constantinople (381) and made the test of orthodoxy by Theodosius' edict Cunctos populos (380).
Empire-wide council of bishops convened by the emperor: Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431), Chalcedon (451), Constantinople II (553); later councils continued (680-681, 787).

The Council of Chalcedon (451) defined Christ as one person 'in two natures'. Opponents (Miaphysites, called Monophysites by their enemies) held to 'one nature' after the union, dominant in Egypt, much of Syria and Armenia; repeated imperial compromises (Henotikon 482, Justinian's Three Chapters, Heraclius' Monoenergism and Monotheletism 638) failed to reunite the churches.

North African schism from 311 over bishops who had handed over scriptures in the persecution (traditores); the Donatist church rejected sacraments by such clergy, became the majority in Numidia, and was condemned by Constantine and repressed after the Conference of Carthage (411), with Augustine its chief opponent.

Title of the bishops of the major sees: Rome, Constantinople (second in rank by canon 3 of 381, equal privileges by canon 28 of Chalcedon, contested by Rome), Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem (from 451), the later 'pentarchy'.

Head of the Christian community of a city; after Constantine bishops gained judicial powers (episcopalis audientia), exemptions and wealth, and became civic leaders who negotiated with invaders (Leo with Attila in 452) and ran cities in the post-Roman West.

Bronze unit of account and coin. Originally a pound of bronze (aes grave, cast from c. 280 BC), reduced to sextantal (2 oz) around the introduction of the denarius c. 211 BC, uncial (1 oz) c. 141 and semuncial (lex Papiria, 91). Imperial as in copper, a quarter of a sestertius, 1/16 denarius.
Early Roman bronze money: aes rude (raw lumps), aes signatum (cast bars with designs, c. 300-250 BC) and aes grave (heavy cast round coins of the libral as and fractions, from c. 280 BC).

Rome's first silver coins, struck in the Greek standard from c. 310-300 BC for southern Italy, culminating in the quadrigatus (Janus and Jupiter in a quadriga) of the First and Second Punic Wars, replaced by the denarius.

Rome's main silver coin, introduced c. 211 BC (the date established from the hoard at Morgantina) at 1/72 pound (c. 4.5 g), reduced to 1/84 (c. 3.9 g) by the 190s-170s, tariffed at 10 asses then 16 (c. 141 BC). Nero reduced it to 1/96 pound and lowered fineness (64); progressive debasement from Marcus to Severus (c. 50% by 211), superseded by the antoninianus in the 240s. Diocletian's denarius communis was a unit of account.
Silver coin (c. 3.4 g) issued alongside the early denarius, valued at three-quarters of a denarius, probably for trade with Greek southern Italy; discontinued c. 170 BC and revived as the quinarius.
Silver half-denarius, struck intermittently from 211 BC, regularly from 101 BC (the lex Clodia) for Gallic trade.

Originally a small silver coin worth 2.5 asses (a quarter denarius); the standard unit of account in which large sums and fortunes were reckoned (HS). Augustus made it a large orichalcum (brass) coin worth 4 asses, the great medium of imperial portraiture; struck until the 260s.
Brass coin worth two asses (half a sestertius), distinguished from the as from Nero by the radiate crown on the emperor.

Gold coin worth 25 denarii, struck occasionally in the Republic (emergency issues of 211-209, Sulla, Pompey) and regularly from Caesar (c. 8 g, 1/40 pound); reduced to 1/45 (Nero), 1/50 (Caracalla), and unstable in the 3rd century; reset at 1/60 by Diocletian, replaced by the solidus.

Silver coin introduced by Caracalla in 215, a double denarius with radiate portrait but only about 1.5 times its silver; revived in 238, it collapsed under Gallienus to c. 2-5% silver with a surface wash. Aurelian's reformed radiate (274) bore XXI. Ancient name unknown.
High-purity silver coin (c. 3 g, 1/96 pound, c. 90% silver) introduced in Diocletian's reform of c. 294, intended to restore Neronian standards; issued only briefly in quantity.

Modern name for the large silver-washed bronze coin introduced in Diocletian's reform (c. 294, c. 10 g, GENIO POPVLI ROMANI), repeatedly reduced in the 4th century. Anastasius' reform of 498 created a new large copper follis of 40 nummi marked M, with denominations of 20 (K), 10 (I) and 5 (E).
Generic 'coin'; in late antiquity the smallest copper coin, of which the 5th-century West and East struck vast numbers of tiny pieces; the unit of the Anastasian follis system (40 nummi = 1 follis).

Gold coin introduced by Constantine (c. 309-312) at 72 to the pound (c. 4.5 g), kept stable for seven centuries as the 'dollar of the Middle Ages' (nomisma). Taxes, salaries and subsidies were reckoned in solidi and pounds of gold; the tremissis (one-third) and semissis (half) were fractions.
Gold third of a solidus, introduced c. 383; the main gold coin of the Germanic successor kingdoms.

Late Roman silver coins: the siliqua (1/24 of a solidus by value, c. 2-3 g, named from the carob seed weight) and the heavier miliarense (1/1000 of a pound of gold in theory). The Hoxne hoard (buried after 407) contained over 14,000 siliquae.
Heavy silver coin (c. 6.5 g, two grammata) introduced by Heraclius in 615 to pay the army, partly struck from church plate requisitioned for the Persian war; inscribed DEUS ADIUTA ROMANIS.

Greek unit of weight and money (Attic talent c. 26 kg = 6,000 drachmas, roughly 6,000 denarii), used for indemnities: Carthage paid 3,200 talents after 241 BC and 10,000 after 201; Antiochus III 15,000 at Apamea.

Roman pound of c. 327 g, divided into 12 unciae; coin standards were expressed as fractions of the pound (aureus 1/40, solidus 1/72), and large payments in pounds of gold (Rua's 350 lb a year, Attila's 2,100).
Dry measure of about 8.7 litres (c. 6.5 kg of wheat); a grain ration of 5 modii a month was standard for the frumentationes and soldiers.
Land measure of 28,800 square Roman feet (c. 0.25 ha), 'what a yoke of oxen could plough in a day'; colonists received 2 to 10 iugera in early colonies and Gracchan allotments up to 30.

Division of colonial or allotted land into square grids (centuriae, usually 20 x 20 actus, c. 710 m on a side, = 200 iugera) by surveyors (agrimensores), still visible in the Po valley, Tunisia and around Orange (whose marble cadastres survive).

Public land of the Roman people, mostly confiscated from defeated Italian communities, let to occupiers for a rent or leased by the censors; much was occupied by large holders. Tiberius Gracchus' law (133 BC) reclaimed holdings over 500 iugera (plus 250 per son) for allotment to the poor; the lex agraria of 111 privatized most of what remained.

The year's grain harvest, then the grain supply of Rome (and from 332 Constantinople) organized by the state, from Sicily, Sardinia, Africa and Egypt (Egypt alone sent some 20 million modii a year under Augustus, according to the Epitome de Caesaribus 1.6). In late antiquity also the system of taxes and rations in kind (annona militaris).
Requisition in kind for the army's food and fodder, regularized from the 3rd century into the annual assessment of the late Roman state (indiction); rations were later commuted into gold (adaeratio).
