Distribution of grain to Roman citizens: subsidized by Gaius Gracchus' law (123 BC), free from Clodius' law (58 BC), with recipients fixed at about 200,000 by Augustus (2 BC) who received tickets (tesserae) for 5 modii monthly. Severus added oil, Aurelian bread, pork and wine.
Shippers who carried state grain under contract; from the 4th century a hereditary corporation compelled to serve, compensated with land and privileges.

Companies of equestrian contractors (societates publicanorum) who bid for state contracts: public works, army supply, mines and especially tax farming (the decuma of Asia let at Rome from 123 BC). Their extortion embittered the provinces (the 'Asian Vespers' of 88 BC); Caesar and Augustus curtailed tax farming of direct taxes.

Direct tax on Roman citizens' property, levied as a war tax until 167 BC, when the booty of Pydna allowed its suspension; thereafter tribute was paid by provincials (tributum soli on land, tributum capitis on persons), assessed by census.

Indirect taxes and revenues: customs dues (portoria, often 2.5% inland and 25% on the eastern frontier), rents from public land, mines, salt, the 5% manumission tax, and the 1% sales tax (centesima rerum venalium).

Tolls on goods crossing boundaries and harbours, collected at stations in regional districts (the quadragesima Galliarum, 2.5%; the 25% tetarte at the eastern frontier); the customs law of Asia (lex portorii Asiae, 62 AD inscription at Ephesus) survives.
Augustus' 5% inheritance tax on citizens (AD 6), with exemptions for close kin and small estates, earmarked for the aerarium militare; Caracalla doubled it to 10%.
State treasury in the temple of Saturn under the quaestors (under Augustus, praetors or prefects); progressively eclipsed by the emperor's fiscus.
Military treasury founded by Augustus in AD 6 with 170 million sesterces of his own money, funded by the 5% inheritance and 1% sales taxes, to pay veterans' discharge bonuses.
The emperor's treasury (originally 'basket'), receiving provincial revenues of imperial provinces and confiscations; by the 2nd century the main state treasury, managed by the a rationibus.
The emperor's private estates and their revenues, organized by Severus (managed by the comes rerum privatarum in late antiquity), swollen by confiscations and later by temple lands.

Diocletian's tax assessment system (from c. 287-297), measuring land in fiscal units (iuga, by quality and use) and labour in heads (capita), with an annual rate set by the praetorian prefects (indiction), collected in kind and later in gold; regional variations were large.

The annual tax assessment declared by the praetorian prefect; from 312 indictions ran in 15-year cycles beginning 1 September, becoming a standard dating system (Justinian made it obligatory in documents, 537).

Tax in gold and silver on merchants and craftsmen (including prostitutes), introduced by Constantine and levied every five years; notoriously oppressive (Zosimus); abolished by Anastasius in 498, who burned the records.
Commutation of taxes, rations or levies in kind into gold, increasingly common from the later 4th century as the solidus spread, notably for military rations and recruit levies.

Compulsory public services imposed on citizens and decurions (supplying transport, collecting taxes, maintaining roads or baths, funding games), the Roman counterpart of Greek liturgies; exemptions were a valuable privilege.

Three junior magistrates who supervised coinage in the Republic, increasingly signing coins with family types (from c. 140 BC); under Augustus their names disappeared (c. 4 BC) and the emperor controlled the mint.

The state transport and post system created by Augustus, with relay stations (mansiones, mutationes) and requisitioned animals and vehicles for officials with permits (diplomata, evectiones); burdensome to provincial communities, reformed by Nerva and Hadrian, run in late antiquity under the praetorian prefects and the agentes in rebus.

Originally the sphere of command assigned to a magistrate, then a territory under a Roman governor: Sicily (241 BC) and Sardinia-Corsica (238/227), the Spains (197), Macedonia and Africa (146), Asia (133), Narbonensis (c. 121), Cilicia, Bithynia, Cyrene, Syria and Crete in the 1st century BC. Some 45 under Hadrian, about 100 after Diocletian, around 120 by c. 400.

Augustus' settlement of 27 BC divided provinces into those governed by the emperor through legates (mostly the frontier provinces with legions) and the 'public' ones assigned by lot to senatorial proconsuls (Africa and Asia for ex-consuls, the rest for ex-praetors). Egypt was under an equestrian prefect. The terms 'senatorial' and 'imperial' are modern.

Judicial districts of a province, where the governor held assizes on a circuit (Asia had 13 by the early empire); also associations of Roman citizens resident in a provincial town (conventus civium Romanorum).
A self-governing community (city or tribe) with its territory (territorium), the basic unit of provincial administration and taxation; also citizenship (civitas Romana).

Self-governing community whose inhabitants held Roman citizenship (originally civitas sine suffragio) or Latin rights, with its own magistrates (duoviri or quattuorviri) and council; the Flavian municipal law from Spain (lex Irnitana) shows their charters.

Settlement of Roman or Latin citizens founded on conquered land: small citizen colonies guarding coasts (Ostia, Antium), large Latin colonies with independent status (Cales 334, Venusia 291, Aquileia 181), Gracchan and veteran colonies (Narbo 118; Caesar's and Augustus' foundations of perhaps 100 colonies). Later the title was a privileged rank granted to existing cities.

Status shared by members of the Latin league and later Latin colonies, with rights of trade (commercium) and intermarriage (conubium) with Romans and, for magistrates, Roman citizenship (from the later 2nd century). Extended to Transpadane Gaul (89 BC) and by Vespasian to all of Spain.
Roman citizenship without the vote, imposed on communities incorporated after the Latin War (338 BC), such as Capua and Caere, with obligations of military service and tax but internal autonomy.

The Italian communities bound to Rome by bilateral treaties, supplying troops (usually more than Rome's own legions) without paying tribute; their demand for citizenship produced the Social War (91-88 BC) and the enfranchisement of Italy south of the Po.

Formal treaty sworn with fetial rites: equal (aequum), like the Foedus Cassianum with the Latins (493 BC), or unequal, requiring the ally to respect the majesty of the Roman people. Late Roman foedera settled barbarian groups.

Unconditional surrender of a community into the power (in fidem or in dicionem) of the Roman people, after which Rome decided its fate; the Carthaginian deditio of 149 BC preceded the order to abandon the city.

glossary.term: friendship (amicitia) and 'friend of the Roman people'
glossary.def: Relationship of mutual goodwill between individuals or between Rome and kings and states (amicus et socius populi Romani), recorded on the Capitol, the basis of client-king relationships.

Dependent monarchy ruled by a 'friend and ally' of Rome (Numidia, Galatia, Cappadocia, Judaea, Mauretania, Thrace, Commagene, the Bosporus), offering frontier security and local knowledge; most were annexed in the 1st century AD, often on the ruler's death.

Late Roman administrative group of provinces under a vicarius, created under Diocletian (by c. 314 there were 12: Oriens, Pontica, Asiana, Thracia, Moesiae, Pannoniae, Italia, Africa, Hispaniae, Viennensis, Galliae, Britanniae). Later the church adopted the term for a bishop's see.

The largest late Roman administrative division, run by a praetorian prefect: by 395 Oriens, Illyricum, Italy-Africa and Gaul; Justinian added Africa (534). The prefecture handled taxation, the annona, supply, public works, the cursus publicus and appeals.
Governor of a diocese, deputy of the praetorian prefect, hearing appeals and supervising provincial governors; Justinian abolished several vicariates (535).

Common title of late Roman provincial governors (equestrian, later clarissimi), alongside consulares and correctores; civil only, since Diocletian and Constantine separated civil and military command.

'Companion' of the emperor: from Constantine a formal rank in three grades and a title for many offices: comes sacrarum largitionum (finance), comes rerum privatarum, comes domesticorum, comites rei militaris commanding regional armies, comites civitatum governing cities in the successor kingdoms (the origin of medieval counts).
Late Roman finance minister in charge of mints, mines, the precious-metal taxes (chrysargyron, aurum coronarium), state factories for luxury goods, and donatives to the army.
Late Roman commander of the troops (mainly limitanei) of a frontier region (dux limitis), often covering several provinces; ranked below the comites rei militaris. Origin of the medieval duke.

Supreme late Roman military commander, created by Constantine (magister peditum and magister equitum); later regional magistri (per Orientem, per Thracias, per Illyricum) and praesental magistri in the East. In the West the magister utriusque militiae (Stilicho, Constantius, Aetius, Ricimer, Gundobad, Orestes) dominated the emperor; in the East Leo I and Zeno broke the power of Aspar and the Isaurian generals.

'Master of the offices', a palatine minister created by Constantine controlling the secretariats (scrinia), the scholae, the agentes in rebus, the state arms factories, court ceremonial and reception of foreign embassies; John Lydus traces his rise at the expense of the prefects.
Late Roman chief legal minister who drafted imperial laws and replies to petitions; Tribonian held the office under Justinian.

Grand chamberlain, a eunuch heading the imperial bedchamber staff, often immensely influential (Eusebius under Constantius II, Eutropius under Arcadius, Chrysaphius under Theodosius II, Narses' early career).

Corps of imperial couriers and inspectors (successors of the frumentarii) under the magister officiorum, who carried messages, controlled the cursus publicus and served as heads of governors' staffs; widely feared as spies.
Imperial shorthand secretaries who kept records of the consistory and were sent on confidential missions; their chief was the primicerius notariorum (Joannes, usurper of 423, held the post).
The late Roman emperor's formal council, where members stood ('consistere') in the emperor's presence; included the chief palatine ministers.

An official register of offices and units, above all the Notitia Dignitatum (c. 395-420s), listing every senior office, its staff and insignia and the military units under each commander; also notitiae of provinces and bishoprics.

Late Roman official list of provinces or offices: the Verona List (c. 314), the Laterculus of Polemius Silvius (449) and Hierocles' Synekdemos (c. 527-528), the key evidence for provincial subdivision.
Greek title of the urban prefect of Constantinople (from 359), responsible for order, guilds, markets and the city's senate.

Governor combining civil and military authority over the remaining Byzantine territories of Italy (exarchate of Ravenna, attested from 584) and Africa (Carthage, from c. 591), created by Maurice to defend against Lombards and Moors. Heraclius' father was exarch of Africa and launched the revolt of 608-610 from there.

Honorific personal dignity created by Constantine for the highest officials; in the 5th-century West 'the patrician' became the title of the dominant generalissimo (Constantius, Aetius, Ricimer), and was granted to barbarian kings (Odoacer, Theodoric, later Clovis' successors).

The billeting system by which Roman landowners hosted soldiers; used to describe how barbarian federates were settled in Gaul and Italy (thirds of land or of tax revenue), a much-debated question (Goffart's tax-share theory vs land division).

The Blues and Greens (with lesser Reds and Whites), organizations that ran chariot racing and claques in the hippodromes of Constantinople and other cities; their riots culminated in the Nika revolt of 532 (some 30,000 killed) and played roles in the fall of Phocas (610).

Greek for general, used for Roman magistrates and commanders (strategos hypatos = consul) and in the 6th-7th centuries for army commanders; in the later themes the strategos combined military and civil authority. Precursors include the exarchs and Justinian's combined governors (e.g. the praetor of Thrace, 535).

Military-administrative districts of the middle Byzantine empire (Anatolikon, Armeniakon, Opsikion, Thrakesion), named after the field armies withdrawn to Anatolia after the Arab conquests of the 630s-640s. Older views (Ostrogorsky) credited Heraclius with creating the themes and soldiers' land-holdings; most scholars (Haldon, Kaegi) now see a gradual development from c. 640-660s, with civil and military powers merged under strategoi only later.

series.title: Roman census figures, 5th-3rd centuries BC
series.note: From Livy and the Periochae. Fifth-century figures are generally regarded as unreliable or inflated; those from 293 onward are broadly accepted. Servius Tullius' legendary 80,000 (Livy 1.44, citing Fabius Pictor) is omitted.
sources: Brunt, Italian Manpower 225 BC - AD 14 (1971) 13-14

series.title: Silver content of the denarius (traditional Walker figures)
series.note: Rounded mean fineness as established by D. R. Walker's surface XRF analyses (1976-78) and widely reproduced (e.g. Harl 1996). Republican issues c. 95-98%. Walker's method measured silver-enriched surfaces, so post-64 values are now thought too high (see denarius_silver_bp). Key steps: Nero's reform of 64 (weight from 1/84 to 1/96 lb and fineness cut); Domitian's restoration of 82 and retreat of 85; Trajan's reform; Severus' heavy debasement from 194; the denarius gives way to the antoninianus in the 240s.
sources: Walker, The Metrology of the Roman Silver Coinage I-III (BAR 1976-78)
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy, 300 B.C. to A.D. 700 (1996)
Duncan-Jones, Money and Government in the Roman Empire (1994)

series.title: Silver content of the denarius, AD 54-117 (Butcher & Ponting revision)
series.note: Butcher and Ponting drilled cores and analysed the interior metal rather than the enriched surface. Their findings: pre-reform Neronian denarii were essentially pure; the reform of 64 cut fineness to c. 80%, a far sharper debasement than Walker's 93.5% (late Neronian issues c. 90%); Rome kept c. 80% under Vespasian and Titus while western and Syrian mints struck finer coin; Domitian's 82 reform restored pure silver and his 85 retreat set c. 90%, maintained by Nerva; Trajan reduced to c. 80% in a reform they date c. AD 100 (following Woytek) rather than 107. Values are bullion, not elemental silver, so not strictly comparable with Walker.
sources: Butcher & Ponting, The Metallurgy of Roman Silver Coinage: From the Reform of Nero to the Reform of Trajan (Cambridge 2014)
Woytek et al., 'The Denarius under Trajan', NC 2007

series.title: Silver content of the antoninianus (radiate), 215-294
series.note: Introduced by Caracalla in 215 as a double denarius containing only about 1.5-1.6 times the silver of one; dropped by Elagabalus c. 219, revived by Pupienus and Balbinus in 238, it became the main silver coin. Collapse under Valerian and Gallienus (financial strain, loss of mines and the Persian ransom/military crises) to a silver-washed bronze. Aurelian's reform of 274 marked coins XXI/KA, usually read as 1 part silver in 20 (5%). Diocletian's reform of c. 294 replaced it with the argenteus (c. 90% silver) and the silvered nummus. Figures are indicative means from several analytical programmes and vary by mint.
sources: Walker, Metrology III (to 253)
Cope et al., analyses of radiate coinage
Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy (1996)
Estiot, 'The Later Third Century', in Metcalf (ed.), Oxford Handbook of Greek and Roman Coinage (2012)

series.title: Census returns of Roman citizens, 508 BC - AD 47
series.note: Figures as transmitted (mostly Livy and the Periochae, with Dionysius, Pliny, Eusebius-Jerome, Phlegon, the Res Gestae and Tacitus); the early 5th-century numbers are probably annalistic constructions. Republican figures count adult male citizens (iuniores and seniores, or capita civium), owners of property, possibly excluding proletarii in some periods. Dips track war losses (209 BC after Cannae: 137,108) and enfranchisement drives jumps (70 BC: 910,000 after the Social War grants). The leap from 910,000 (70 BC) to 4,063,000 (28 BC) is the central crux of Roman demography: the 'low count' (Beloch, Brunt) holds that Augustus counted women and children, giving Italy c. 6-7 million free people; the 'high count' (Frank, Lo Cascio, Kehoe) holds that the method was unchanged and Republican censuses were badly incomplete, giving Italy 12-14 million or more. Scheidel and Hin propose intermediate solutions.
sources: Brunt, Italian Manpower 225 B.C.-A.D. 14 (1971), App. IV
Lo Cascio, 'The Size of the Roman Population', JRS 84 (1994)
Scheidel, 'Roman population size: the logic of the debate' (2008)
Hin, The Demography of Roman Italy (2013)

series.title: Number of legions under arms
series.note: Republican figures are modern reconstructions (Brunt) from Livy's annual dispositions; the early figures are schematic (two consular legions, four from 311 BC per Livy 9.30). Civil-war peaks combine both sides. Imperial counts follow attested creations and losses: 3 lost with Varus (AD 9); XV and XXII Primigenia (Caligula); I Italica (Nero); the legions of 68-69; Vespasian's cassation of four Rhine legions and creation of IV and XVI Flavia (70); I Minervia (83); losses of V Alaudae (86?) and XXI Rapax (92); II Traiana and XXX Ulpia; disappearance of IX Hispana and XXII Deiotariana under Hadrian or later; II and III Italica (165); I-III Parthica (197). After Diocletian legions multiplied but shrank to c. 1,000-3,000 men, and the Notitia lists over 150 units styled legio, so the count is not comparable.
sources: Brunt, Italian Manpower (1971), Table XIII and ch. 22-26
Keppie, The Making of the Roman Army (1984)
Farnum, The Positioning of the Roman Imperial Legions (2005)
Le Bohec, The Imperial Roman Army (1994)

series.title: Estimated total size of the Roman army, Augustus to Heraclius
series.note: Points are central estimates; 'range' gives scholarly low/high. Principate totals combine legions (paper strength c. 5,000-5,500) and auxilia (Tac. Ann. 4.5 implies roughly equal numbers in AD 23). Diocletian: John Lydus (De mens. 1.27) gives 389,704 soldiers and 45,562 in the fleets. c. 395: Notitia Dignitatum paper strengths; Agathias' 'old' figure of 645,000 is taken by Treadgold as the late 4th-century establishment, while Elton, Whitby and Coello argue for much lower real strengths. 559: Agathias (5.13) says Justinian's army had fallen to 150,000. 641: Treadgold's reconstruction after the Arab conquests; Haldon prefers lower figures.
sources: MacMullen, 'How big was the Roman imperial army?', Klio 62 (1980)
Holder, 'Auxiliary deployment in the reign of Hadrian' (2003)
Treadgold, Byzantium and Its Army 284-1081 (1995)
Elton, Warfare in Roman Europe AD 350-425 (1996)
Whitby, 'Recruitment in Roman armies from Justinian to Heraclius' (1995)
John Lydus, De mensibus 1.27
Agathias, Histories 5.13

series.title: Population of the Roman Empire: Beloch
series.note: Karl Julius Beloch's pioneering estimate for the empire at Augustus' death (Italy c. 6 million on the low count).
sources: Beloch, Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886)

series.title: Population of the Roman Empire: Frier
series.note: Bruce Frier's regional table in the Cambridge Ancient History: 45.5 million in AD 14 rising to 61.4 million by 164, on the eve of the Antonine plague.
sources: Frier, 'Demography', CAH XI (2nd ed. 2000) 811-816

series.title: Population of the Roman Empire: Scheidel and successors
series.note: Scheidel accepts c. 45 million for AD 14 on the low count and argues for growth to roughly 60-75 million by the mid-2nd century (Scheidel and Friesen use c. 70 million for c. 150-165; Harper c. 75 million). The Antonine plague (from 165) and the 3rd-century crisis cut this; the eastern empire under Justinian is put at c. 26-27 million before the plague of 541.
sources: Scheidel, 'Demography', in Scheidel, Morris and Saller (eds.), Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World (2007)
Scheidel and Friesen, 'The size of the economy and the distribution of income in the Roman Empire', JRS 99 (2009)
Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
Treadgold, A History of the Byzantine State and Society (1997)

series.title: Population of the city of Rome (estimates)
series.note: All figures are modern estimates with wide uncertainty; 'range' gives the spread. Archaic and early Republican figures rest on the area within the walls (c. 285-427 ha). The Augustan 'million' is inferred from the 200,000+ grain recipients plus women, children, slaves, foreigners and the elite households (Lo Cascio argues higher, Storey lower). Late-antique estimates use the pork-dole figures of 419 and 452 (Durliat). After the Gothic War (535-554) the city may have fallen below 50,000.
sources: Ampolo, in La formazione della città nel Lazio (1980)
Cornell, The Beginnings of Rome (1995)
Hopkins, Conquerors and Slaves (1978)
Morley, Metropolis and Hinterland (1996)
Lo Cascio, 'Le procedure di recensus' (1997)
Durliat, De la ville antique à la ville byzantine: le problème des subsistances (1990)
Krautheimer, Rome: Profile of a City 312-1308 (1980)

series.title: Recipients of the Roman grain dole (frumentationes)
series.note: Gaius Gracchus' lex frumentaria (123 BC) introduced monthly sales at 6 1/3 asses per modius (numbers unknown). The lex Terentia Cassia (73 BC) fixed 5 modii a month; c. 40,000 recipients is inferred from Cicero's figures. Cato's law of 62 widened the list at a cost Plutarch gives as 1,250 talents a year. Clodius' law (58) made the grain free, and numbers swelled to 320,000 before Caesar's recensus cut them to 150,000 (Suet. Iul. 41.3). In 5 BC 320,000 of the plebs urbana took Augustus' cash gift (RG 15); in 2 BC he fixed the list at 'a little over 200,000' (RG 15; Dio 55.10.1), the approximate level for the next two centuries. Severus added oil, Aurelian baked bread, pork and wine. The 419 figure is for pork recipients (CTh 14.4.10) and is not strictly comparable.
sources: Suetonius, Divus Iulius 41.3
Res Gestae 15
Cassius Dio 55.10.1
Rickman, The Corn Supply of Ancient Rome (1980)
Garnsey, Famine and Food Supply in the Graeco-Roman World (1988)
Erdkamp, The Grain Market in the Roman Empire (2005)

series.title: Length of emperors' reigns
series.note: Derived from rulers.json: point = [accession year, length in years, name, how the reign ended, office]. Reigns that began and ended in the same year are shown as 0.5. Co-emperors are counted from their elevation to Augustus. Note the 3rd-century trough: between 235 and 284 the median reign is under three years and most ended in murder or battle.
sources: Derived from rulers.json (Kienast, Römische Kaisertabelle; PLRE)

series.title: Area of the Roman state (Taagepera)
series.note: Rein Taagepera's estimates of territory under control. 326 BC: Rome with its Latin and Campanian holdings; 200 BC after the Second Punic War; 146 BC after Carthage and Corinth; 50 BC after Pompey and Caesar; 25 BC; peak under Trajan (117); 250-350 roughly 4.4; western empire c. 2.0 at 395; eastern empire 2.7-2.8 (c. 450 and again under Justinian c. 555). The 641 value is a rough estimate after the loss of Syria, Palestine and most of Egypt, not Taagepera's.
sources: Taagepera, 'Size and duration of empires: growth-decline curves, 600 B.C. to 600 A.D.', Social Science History 3 (1979) 115-138
Taagepera, 'Expansion and contraction patterns of large polities', International Studies Quarterly 41 (1997)

list.name: Augustus
list.note: Sole master of the Roman world from Actium (2 Sep 31 BC) and Alexandria (Aug 30 BC); name Augustus voted 16 Jan 27 BC. Died at Nola 19 Aug AD 14 after 40 years 7 months of sole rule.

list.name: Tiberius
list.note: Died at Misenum 16 Mar 37 aged 77. Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio report rumours that the prefect Macro smothered him or Caligula poisoned him.

list.name: Caligula
list.note: Stabbed in a palace passage 24 Jan 41 by the praetorian tribunes Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus; wife Milonia Caesonia and infant daughter killed the same day.

list.name: Claudius
list.note: Died 13 Oct 54. Tacitus, Suetonius and Dio say Agrippina had him poisoned (mushrooms, with the poisoner Locusta and doctor Xenophon); a minority of modern scholars allow natural death.

list.name: Nero
list.note: Declared hostis by the Senate; stabbed himself in the throat with the help of the freedman Epaphroditus at Phaon's villa outside Rome, 9 Jun 68. Last of the Julio-Claudians.

list.name: Galba
list.note: Proclaimed by his troops in Hispania Tarraconensis Apr 68, recognized by the Senate Jun 68; cut down in the Forum near the Lacus Curtius 15 Jan 69 by praetorians who had hailed Otho.

list.name: Otho
list.note: Stabbed himself at Brixellum 16 Apr 69, two days after his army's defeat at the first battle of Bedriacum, reportedly to spare further civil war.

list.name: Vitellius
list.note: Proclaimed by the Lower German legions at Colonia 2 Jan 69; dragged through the Forum and killed at the Gemonian Stairs 20 Dec 69 as Flavian troops stormed Rome.

list.name: Vespasian
list.note: Proclaimed at Alexandria 1 Jul 69 (his dies imperii); died of fever and diarrhoea at Aquae Cutiliae 23 Jun 79, joking 'I think I am becoming a god'.

list.name: Titus
list.note: Died of fever 13 Sep 81 at the Flavian villa near Reate after a reign of 26 months marked by Vesuvius (79) and the fire and plague at Rome (80).

list.name: Domitian
list.note: Stabbed 18 Sep 96 by the steward Stephanus in a plot involving the chamberlain Parthenius and probably Domitia and both praetorian prefects; damnatio memoriae followed.

list.name: Nerva
list.note: Senatorial choice on Domitian's death; humiliated by the praetorian mutiny of Casperius Aelianus (97), he adopted Trajan in Oct 97; died 27 Jan 98 of a fever.

list.name: Trajan
list.note: First emperor born in a province (Italica, Baetica). Died at Selinus in Cilicia c. 8 Aug 117 after a stroke on the way home from Mesopotamia; Hadrian's adoption was announced by Plotina, and Dio doubted it.

list.name: Hadrian
list.note: Died at Baiae 10 Jul 138 after long illness (probably heart failure), having adopted Antoninus on condition he adopt Marcus and Lucius.

list.name: Antoninus Pius
list.note: Died at Lorium 7 Mar 161, giving the watchword 'aequanimitas'. Never left Italy as emperor.

list.name: Marcus Aurelius
list.note: Died 17 Mar 180 at Vindobona or Sirmium on campaign against the Marcomanni and Sarmatians, probably of the Antonine plague.

list.name: Lucius Verus
list.note: First formal joint Augustus with Marcus; nominal commander of the Parthian War (161-166). Died of a stroke at Altinum early 169.

list.name: Commodus
list.note: Augustus 177, sole ruler 17 Mar 180. Strangled in his bath on 31 Dec 192 by the athlete Narcissus in a plot of his mistress Marcia, chamberlain Eclectus and prefect Laetus.

list.name: Pertinax
list.note: Reigned 87 days (1 Jan to 28 Mar 193); speared by mutinous praetorians in the palace after attempting to restore discipline and finances.

list.name: Didius Julianus
list.note: Won the praetorian 'auction' with 25,000 sesterces a man (Dio 74.11); condemned by the Senate and killed in the palace 1 Jun 193 as Severus neared Rome. Reigned 66 days.

list.name: Septimius Severus
list.note: Proclaimed at Carnuntum 9 Apr 193; defeated Niger (194) and Albinus (197). Died at Eboracum 4 Feb 211 during his Caledonian war.

list.name: Caracalla
list.note: Augustus 198, sole ruler from Dec 211. Stabbed while relieving himself on the road from Edessa to Carrhae 8 Apr 217 by the guardsman Julius Martialis, at the instigation of the prefect Macrinus.

list.name: Geta
list.note: Augustus 209; killed in his mother Julia Domna's arms by centurions on Caracalla's orders, 26 Dec 211. His name was chiselled off monuments across the empire.

list.name: Macrinus
list.note: First equestrian emperor and first never to visit Rome as emperor. Defeated near Antioch 8 Jun 218 by Elagabalus' army; caught at Chalcedon/Cappadocia and executed.

list.name: Diadumenian
list.note: Son of Macrinus; Caesar 217, Augustus May 218; seized at Zeugma fleeing to Parthia and killed.

list.name: Elagabalus
list.note: Hereditary priest of the Emesene sun god; proclaimed at Raphanaea 16 May 218. Killed with his mother Julia Soaemias by the praetorians 11 or 12 Mar 222; bodies dragged and thrown in the Tiber.

list.name: Severus Alexander
list.note: Killed with his mother Julia Mamaea by mutinous troops at Vicus Britannicus (Bretzenheim) near Mogontiacum, Mar 235, ending the Severan dynasty.

list.name: Maximinus Thrax
list.note: First emperor risen from the ranks; never visited Rome. Killed with his son Maximus by soldiers of Legio II Parthica during the siege of Aquileia, spring 238.

list.name: Gordian I
list.note: Proconsul of Africa, proclaimed at Thysdrus by rebels against the procurator, aged about 80; hanged himself at Carthage on news of his son's death after about 21 days (date Jan or Mar 238 disputed).

list.name: Gordian II
list.note: Co-Augustus with his father; killed at Carthage fighting Capelianus, governor of Numidia, with Legio III Augusta.

list.name: Pupienus
list.note: Elected by a senatorial commission (vigintiviri) with Balbinus; both tortured and killed in the palace by the praetorians after about 99 days.

list.name: Balbinus
list.note: Co-emperor with Pupienus; murdered with him by the praetorians, who proclaimed the 13-year-old Gordian III.

list.name: Gordian III
list.note: Died Feb 244 on the Persian front. Shapur's ŠKZ claims he was killed in battle at Misiche (renamed Peroz-Shapur); Roman sources blame his prefect Philip; a cenotaph stood at Zaitha.

list.name: Philip the Arab
list.note: From Shahba in Trachonitis; bought peace from Shapur for 500,000 aurei; celebrated the millennium of Rome 21 Apr 248. Killed at or after the battle of Verona against Decius, c. Sep 249.

list.name: Philip II
list.note: Caesar 244, Augustus 247; killed by the praetorians in Rome on news of Verona, aged about 12.

list.name: Decius
list.note: Ordered the universal sacrifice of 250 (libelli survive from Egypt). First emperor killed by a foreign enemy, in the marsh at Abritus against Cniva's Goths, c. Jun 251.

list.name: Herennius Etruscus
list.note: Augustus May 251; killed by an arrow at Abritus shortly before or during the battle.

list.name: Hostilian
list.note: Younger son of Decius, co-Augustus with Gallus; died of the plague of Cyprian (Aurelius Victor) or was killed by Gallus (Zosimus), late 251.

list.name: Trebonianus Gallus
list.note: Governor of Moesia, proclaimed after Abritus; made peace paying the Goths. Killed with his son by their own troops at Interamna, c. Aug 253.

list.name: Volusianus
list.note: Son of Gallus, Augustus late 251; killed with his father at Interamna.

list.name: Aemilianus
list.note: Governor of Moesia proclaimed after a victory over the Goths; reigned about 88 days; killed near Spoletium by his own men as Valerian's army approached.

list.name: Valerian
list.note: Captured by Shapur I in the campaign of Edessa, spring/summer 260, the first emperor taken alive by a foreign enemy; died in captivity. Lactantius' tale that he was used as a mounting block and flayed is Christian polemic.
list.death: died in Persian captivity, date unknown

list.name: Gallienus
list.region: west 253-260; all 260-268 (minus Gallic and Palmyrene territories)
list.note: Co-Augustus 253, sole ruler 260. Killed outside Milan c. Sep 268 while besieging Aureolus, in a plot of his staff (Heraclianus, Marcianus, Cecropius; Claudius and Aurelian implicated).

list.name: Saloninus
list.note: Son of Gallienus, raised to Augustus at Colonia Agrippina while besieged by Postumus; surrendered by the garrison and killed.

list.name: Claudius II Gothicus
list.note: Won the great victory over the Goths at Naissus (269); died of plague at Sirmium Aug/Sep 270. Later claimed as ancestor of Constantine (a fiction of c. 310).

list.name: Quintillus
list.note: Brother of Claudius; reigned between 17 days and a few months at Aquileia; suicide or killed by his troops when the army chose Aurelian.

list.name: Aurelian
list.note: Reunified the empire (Palmyra 272-273, Gallic Empire 274), built the Aurelian Walls, reformed the coinage (274). Killed at Caenophrurium near Perinthus c. Sep/Oct 275 by officers duped by forged lists from his secretary Eros.

list.name: Tacitus (emperor)
list.note: Elderly general proclaimed in late 275; died at Tyana mid-276 after defeating Goths in Asia Minor, of fever (Victor) or murdered (Zosimus). His supposed descent from the historian is HA fiction.

list.name: Florianus
list.note: Tacitus' praetorian prefect and half-brother; killed by his own men near Tarsus after about 88 days when Probus' army avoided battle in the summer heat.

list.name: Probus
list.note: Restored the Rhine frontier; settled barbarians in the provinces. Killed by soldiers at Sirmium Sep/Oct 282, reportedly over forced labour draining marshes, as Carus was proclaimed.

list.name: Carus
list.note: Took Ctesiphon in 283; died near the Tigris Jul/Aug 283, officially struck by lightning; murder by the prefect Aper is suspected.

list.name: Carinus
list.note: Augustus spring 283; won at the river Margus against Diocletian (spring 285) but was killed by his own officers in or after the battle.

list.name: Numerian
list.note: Died Nov 284 near Nicomedia; the stench from his closed litter revealed the corpse. The army chose Diocletian, who killed the prefect Aper with his own hand.

list.name: Diocletian
list.note: Proclaimed at Nicomedia 20 Nov 284; created the Tetrarchy (Maximian Augustus 286; Caesars 293). Abdicated at Nicomedia 1 May 305 and retired to Spalatum; died there c. 311-312.

list.name: Maximian
list.note: Caesar 285, Augustus 1 Apr 286; abdicated with Diocletian 1 May 305, resumed the purple 306-308 with his son Maxentius, and tried again in 310 against Constantine. Forced to hang himself at Massilia 310.
list.death: forced suicide (or executed) at Massilia after his third bid for power

list.name: Constantius I
list.note: Caesar 1 Mar 293, Augustus 1 May 305; recovered Britain from Allectus (296). Died at Eboracum 25 Jul 306.

list.name: Galerius
list.note: Caesar 293 (victor over Narseh 298), Augustus 305; chief driver of the Great Persecution. Died of a gangrenous illness at Serdica c. May 311, days after his edict of toleration (30 Apr 311).

list.name: Severus II
list.note: Caesar 305, Augustus 306. His troops deserted to Maxentius; surrendered at Ravenna and was put to death (or forced to open his veins) at Tres Tabernae, 307.

list.name: Maxentius
list.note: Proclaimed at Rome 28 Oct 306 by praetorians and people; never recognized by the eastern Augusti. Drowned in the Tiber at the Milvian Bridge 28 Oct 312.

list.name: Constantine I
list.note: Proclaimed at Eboracum 25 Jul 306; sole ruler after Chrysopolis (324); founded Constantinople (dedicated 11 May 330). Baptized by Eusebius of Nicomedia and died at Achyron near Nicomedia 22 May 337.

list.name: Licinius
list.note: Made Augustus at the conference of Carnuntum 11 Nov 308. Defeated by Constantine at Adrianople (3 Jul 324) and Chrysopolis (18 Sep 324); abdicated on promise of his life; hanged at Thessalonica 325.
list.death: executed at Thessalonica on a charge of plotting

list.name: Maximinus Daza
list.note: Caesar 305, Augustus 310. Routed by Licinius at Tzirallum 30 Apr 313; died at Tarsus summer 313, by poison he took (Lactantius) or illness.

list.name: Constantine II
list.note: Augustus 9 Sep 337 after the purge of his cousins; killed in an ambush near Aquileia while invading his brother Constans' territory, early 340.

list.name: Constans
list.note: Overthrown by Magnentius at Augustodunum 18 Jan 350; caught and killed by Gaiso at Helena (Elne) at the foot of the Pyrenees.

list.name: Constantius II
list.note: Defeated Magnentius at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353). Died of fever at Mopsucrenae in Cilicia 3 Nov 361, marching against Julian, whom he named heir on his deathbed.

list.name: Julian
list.note: Proclaimed by his troops at Lutetia Feb 360; sole ruler from Nov 361; attempted pagan restoration. Wounded by a spear in a rearguard action near Maranga/Samarra 26 Jun 363 and died that night.

list.name: Jovian
list.note: Chosen by the army on Persian soil; ceded Nisibis, Singara and five Transtigritane regions to Shapur II for safe passage. Found dead at Dadastana 17 Feb 364, from charcoal fumes or bad food.

list.name: Valentinian I
list.note: Proclaimed at Nicaea 26 Feb 364; made his brother Valens eastern Augustus (28 Mar 364). Died of a stroke at Brigetio 17 Nov 375 while raging at Quadic envoys.

list.name: Valens
list.note: Admitted the Gothic Tervingi across the Danube (376). Killed at Adrianople 9 Aug 378; body never found.

list.name: Gratian
list.note: Augustus 24 Aug 367 aged 8; dropped the title pontifex maximus and removed the Altar of Victory (382). Deserted by his army near Paris to Magnus Maximus; killed at Lugdunum by Andragathius 25 Aug 383.

list.name: Valentinian II
list.note: Proclaimed aged 4 at Aquincum 22 Nov 375. Found hanged at Vienne 15 May 392 after quarrelling with his magister militum Arbogast: suicide or murder.

list.name: Theodosius I
list.note: Made Augustus at Sirmium 19 Jan 379; Nicene Christianity made the state creed (Cunctos populos 380); victor over Maximus (388) and Eugenius at the Frigidus (Sep 394). Died at Milan 17 Jan 395, the last emperor to rule both halves.

list.name: Honorius
list.note: Augustus 393 aged 8; ruled through Stilicho (executed 408). Rome sacked by Alaric 24 Aug 410. Died of oedema at Ravenna 15 Aug 423.

list.name: Constantius III
list.note: Magister militum, husband of Galla Placidia; co-Augustus 8 Feb 421, unrecognized by Constantinople; died 2 Sep 421.

list.name: Valentinian III
list.note: Installed aged 6 by an eastern army after the suppression of Joannes (23 Oct 425). Murdered Aetius with his own hand (Sep 454); killed on the Campus Martius 16 Mar 455 by Optila and Thraustila, Aetius' Hunnic retainers.

list.name: Petronius Maximus
list.note: Twice consul, prefect of Rome; proclaimed 17 Mar 455. Killed by a mob or imperial servants (stoned, by tradition) fleeing Rome 31 May 455 as Gaiseric's fleet approached; the Vandal sack followed (2-16 Jun).

list.name: Avitus
list.note: Gallo-Roman aristocrat proclaimed at Arelate with Visigothic support 9 Jul 455. Defeated near Placentia by Ricimer and Majorian 17 Oct 456 and consecrated bishop of Placentia.
list.death: died 456/457, possibly killed, on his way to Gaul

list.name: Majorian
list.note: Acclaimed 1 Apr 457 (formally 28 Dec 457). His invasion fleet was destroyed at Portus Ilicitanus near Carthago Nova (460); arrested by Ricimer at Dertona and beheaded 7 Aug 461.

list.name: Libius Severus
list.note: Ricimer's puppet, never recognized by Leo I. Died at Rome 14 Nov 465; Cassiodorus and Sidonius hint Ricimer poisoned him.

list.name: Anthemius
list.note: Eastern aristocrat sent by Leo I and proclaimed 12 Apr 467; married his daughter to Ricimer. Besieged in Rome by Ricimer and beheaded by Gundobad 11 Jul 472.

list.name: Olybrius
list.note: Husband of Placidia, daughter of Valentinian III; proclaimed by Ricimer Apr 472; died of dropsy 2 Nov 472.

list.name: Glycerius
list.note: Comes domesticorum proclaimed at Ravenna 3 Mar 473 with Gundobad's backing; deposed by Julius Nepos at Portus Jun 474 and consecrated bishop of Salona.

list.name: Julius Nepos
list.note: Magister militum of Dalmatia, nephew of Marcellinus, installed with Leo I's backing 19 Jun 474. Driven from Ravenna by Orestes 28 Aug 475; kept the title in Dalmatia, recognized by Zeno and named on some of Odoacer's coins, until murdered in his villa near Salona 9 May 480.

list.name: Romulus Augustulus
list.note: Son of the magister militum Orestes, proclaimed 31 Oct 475, never recognized by Constantinople. Deposed by Odoacer at Ravenna 4 Sep 476 and pensioned off to the Castellum Lucullanum near Naples.

list.name: Arcadius
list.note: Augustus 383; ruled through Rufinus, Eutropius and Anthemius. Died 1 May 408.

list.name: Theodosius II
list.note: Augustus 402 aged 9 months. Theodosian Walls (413), University of Constantinople (425), Codex Theodosianus (438). Died 28 Jul 450 after a riding fall near the Lycus.

list.name: Marcian
list.note: Thracian officer who married Pulcheria; stopped tribute to Attila, convened the Council of Chalcedon (451). Died 27 Jan 457, leaving a large surplus.

list.name: Leo I
list.note: Thracian officer raised by Aspar; the 468 armada against the Vandals under Basiliscus cost some 64,000 lb gold and 700,000 lb silver (Lydus). Had Aspar killed (471). Died 18 Jan 474.

list.name: Leo II
list.note: Grandson of Leo I, aged about 7; crowned his father Zeno co-emperor 9 Feb 474; died Nov 474.

list.name: Zeno
list.note: Isaurian chieftain (Tarasis); driven out by Basiliscus Jan 475 to Aug 476. Henotikon (482); sent Theodoric to Italy (488). Died 9 Apr 491.

list.name: Anastasius I
list.note: Palace silentiarius chosen by Zeno's widow Ariadne. Isaurian war (492-497), copper reform (498), abolished the chrysargyron, Anastasian Wall; left 320,000 lb of gold. Died 9 Jul 518.

list.name: Justin I
list.note: Illyrian peasant who rose to command the excubitors; ended the Acacian schism (519). Died 1 Aug 527.

list.name: Justinian I
list.note: Co-emperor 1 Apr 527, sole 1 Aug 527. Corpus Iuris Civilis, Nika riot (532), Hagia Sophia (537), reconquest of Africa (533-534) and Italy (535-554), plague of 541-542. Died 14 Nov 565.

list.name: Justin II
list.note: Nephew of Justinian; refused tribute to the Avars and Persia; lost Dara (573) and went insane; Tiberius ruled as Caesar from 7 Dec 574. Died 5 Oct 578.

list.name: Tiberius II Constantine
list.note: Comes excubitorum, Caesar 574, Augustus 26 Sep 578; famously lavish. Died 14 Aug 582 (by tradition after eating bad mulberries).

list.name: Maurice
list.note: Restored Khosrow II (591) and won the Balkan wars against Avars and Slavs. Overthrown when the Danube army mutinied over wintering north of the river; made to watch five sons beheaded at Eutropius' harbour, Chalcedon, then killed 27 Nov 602.

list.name: Phocas
list.note: Centurion of the Danube army. Khosrow II's war of revenge opened in 603. Beheaded 5 Oct 610 when Heraclius' fleet reached Constantinople.

list.name: Heraclius
list.note: Son of the exarch of Africa; survived the loss of Syria, Palestine, Egypt and the siege of 626, destroyed Persian power at Nineveh (Dec 627), restored the True Cross (630), then lost Syria to the Arabs (Yarmuk 636). Died of oedema 11 Feb 641.

list.name: Constantine III
list.note: Co-emperor since 613; ruled jointly with his half-brother Heraclonas from Feb 641; died of tuberculosis 25 May 641 (rumours blamed Martina).

list.name: Heraclonas
list.note: Son of Heraclius and Martina, co-emperor 638; deposed Sep/Oct 641 after pressure from the army and Constantinopolitan crowd; nose slit and exiled with Martina to Rhodes.

list.name: Constans II
list.note: Son of Constantine III, crowned 641 aged 11. Moved his court to Syracuse (663); killed in his bath there by a chamberlain 15 Jul 668.

list.name: Lucius Arruntius Camillus Scribonianus
list.note: Governor of Dalmatia who called on Claudius to abdicate; his two legions (VII and XI, thereafter Claudia Pia Fidelis) deserted within five days. Killed himself or was killed on Issa.

list.name: Gaius Julius Vindex
list.note: Aquitanian senator who rose against Nero (Mar 68) and offered the throne to Galba; defeated by Verginius Rufus near Vesontio and killed himself. Did not claim the purple.

list.name: Lucius Clodius Macer
list.note: Legate of Legio III Augusta; raised Legio I Macriana liberatrix and cut Rome's grain supply; killed by the procurator Trebonius Garutianus on Galba's orders, Oct 68.

list.name: Gaius Nymphidius Sabinus
list.note: Praetorian prefect who abandoned Nero, then bid for the throne against Galba; killed by the guard in the camp, autumn 68.

list.name: Terentius Maximus (pseudo-Nero)
list.note: One of at least three false Neros (68/69, 79/80, 88); found support in Asia and with the Parthian Artabanus III before being surrendered.

list.name: Lucius Antonius Saturninus
list.note: Seized the savings of two legions at Mogontiacum (1 Jan 89); his Chattan allies were cut off by a thaw on the Rhine and he was defeated by Lappius Maximus. Domitian thereafter forbade double-legion camps.

list.name: Gaius Avidius Cassius
list.note: Victor of the Parthian War, governor of Syria with command over the East; proclaimed himself on a false report of Marcus' death (perhaps with Faustina's encouragement); killed by a centurion after about three months.

list.name: Gaius Pescennius Niger
list.note: Governor of Syria proclaimed Apr 193; beaten at Cyzicus, Nicaea and Issus (194); caught fleeing towards the Euphrates and beheaded.

list.name: Decimus Clodius Albinus
list.note: Governor of Britain; Caesar under Severus 193-195, then Augustus. Defeated at Lugdunum 19 Feb 197 in one of the largest Roman battles; killed himself or was killed, his body trampled by Severus' horse.

list.name: Gaius Petronius Magnus
list.note: Consular accused of plotting to destroy Maximinus' Rhine bridge; possibly a fabricated conspiracy (Herodian 7.1).

list.name: Titus Quartinus
list.note: Proclaimed by Osrhoenian archers loyal to Severus Alexander; murdered by their commander Macedo.

list.name: Sabinianus
list.note: Proclaimed at Carthage; crushed by the governor of Mauretania and handed over by his own followers.

list.name: Tiberius Claudius Marinus Pacatianus
list.note: Proclaimed by Danube troops in 248 (coins with ROMAE AETER AN MILL ET PRIMO); killed by his own men, which led Philip to send Decius to the Danube.

list.name: Marcus Fulvius Rufus Iotapianus
list.note: Claimed kinship with Severus Alexander; revolted against Philip's brother Priscus' exactions; killed by his own troops.

list.name: Julius Valens Licinianus
list.note: Proclaimed in Rome while Decius campaigned against the Goths; killed within days.

list.name: Titus Julius Priscus
list.note: Governor of Thrace who sided with the Goths at the fall of Philippopolis (250); declared hostis; probably died in 251.

list.name: Silbannacus
list.note: Known from two antoniniani (one found 1937); context and date (perhaps 253) uncertain.

list.name: Uranius Antoninus
list.note: Emesene priest-dynast (Sulpicius Antoninus) who repelled Shapur's attack on Emesa (253) and struck gold and silver coins; fate unknown.

list.name: Ingenuus
list.note: Governor of Pannonia proclaimed after news of Valerian's capture (or 258); defeated at Mursa by Gallienus' cavalry commander Aureolus; drowned himself or was killed.

list.name: Regalianus
list.note: Proclaimed by Ingenuus' surviving troops; coins struck at Carnuntum over Severan denarii; killed by his men or the Roxolani.

list.name: Macrianus Minor
list.note: Proclaimed with his brother Quietus after Valerian's capture, backed by their father Macrianus Major and the prefect Ballista; father and son defeated and killed in Illyricum by Aureolus, 261.

list.name: Quietus
list.note: Brother of Macrianus Minor, left in command at Emesa; killed there by the citizens with Odaenathus besieging, 261.

list.name: Postumus
list.note: Founder of the Gallic Empire (consuls, senate and mint at Colonia/Treveri). Killed by his own troops at Mogontiacum after refusing them the sack of the city, which had backed Laelianus.

list.name: Lucius Mussius Aemilianus
list.note: Prefect of Egypt who backed the Macriani then claimed the purple; defeated by Gallienus' general Theodotus, strangled in prison.

list.name: Aureolus
list.note: Gallienus' cavalry commander; declared for Postumus, then himself, at Milan. Surrendered to Claudius II after Gallienus' murder and was killed by the soldiers.

list.name: Laelianus
list.note: Rose against Postumus at Mogontiacum; defeated and killed.

list.name: Marius
list.note: Former smith (by tradition) who briefly succeeded Postumus; killed with a sword of his own making according to the HA; coinage implies a reign of some weeks.

list.name: Victorinus
list.note: Praetorian prefect of Postumus; besieged and sacked Augustodunum (270), which had appealed to Claudius II. Killed at Colonia by an officer (Attitianus) whose wife he seduced.

list.name: Domitianus II
list.note: Known from two coins (the second found at Chalgrove, Oxfordshire, 2003) and a literary mention; brief reign after Victorinus.

list.name: Tetricus I
list.note: Governor of Aquitania raised by Victoria; surrendered to Aurelian at the battle of Catalaunian Fields (Châlons) in 274, possibly by prior arrangement; walked in Aurelian's triumph and was made corrector Lucaniae.

list.name: Septimius
list.note: Proclaimed in Dalmatia during the Juthungian invasion of Italy; killed by his own troops.

list.name: Vaballathus
list.note: Son of Odaenathus; styled 'King of Kings' and corrector totius Orientis, then Augustus in 272 with his mother Zenobia as Augusta; fate after Aurelian's capture of Palmyra unknown.

list.name: Tetricus II
list.note: Son of Tetricus I, Caesar 273, perhaps Augustus 274; spared and later a senator.

list.name: Firmus
list.note: Merchant-supporter of Palmyra who allegedly held Alexandria against Aurelian (HA Firmus); possibly a corrector misrepresented as a usurper.

list.name: Bonosus
list.note: Rhine commander who rebelled after Germans burned the Rhine fleet; defeated by Probus and hanged himself ('an amphora hanging, not a man', HA).

list.name: Proculus
list.note: Rose at Lugdunum with Bonosus; betrayed by the Franks and killed.

list.name: Julius Saturninus
list.note: Moorish-born commander proclaimed in the East; killed at Apamea by Probus' troops.

list.name: Sabinus Julianus
list.note: Corrector Venetiae proclaimed on Numerian's death; defeated and killed by Carinus near Verona.

list.name: Carausius
list.note: Menapian commander of the Channel fleet; seized Britain c. 286, styled himself 'brother' of Diocletian and Maximian on coins (CARAUSIUS ET FRATRES SUI). Killed by his finance officer Allectus after losing Bononia (293).

list.name: Allectus
list.note: Carausius' rationalis and murderer; killed in battle against Constantius' prefect Asclepiodotus, who landed in fog past the British fleet off the Isle of Wight (296).

list.name: Lucius Domitius Domitianus
list.note: Proclaimed in Alexandria amid unrest over Diocletian's tax census; papyri show his regnal years; died during the revolt, succeeded by his corrector Achilleus.

list.name: Aurelius Achilleus
list.note: Led the Alexandrian resistance to Diocletian's eight-month siege; executed after the city fell (spring 298).

list.name: Eugenius
list.note: Tribune of 500 soldiers forced to dig the harbour; proclaimed, marched on Antioch, killed with his men by the citizens.

list.name: Lucius Domitius Alexander
list.note: Vicar of Africa who refused to send his son as hostage to Maxentius; cut off Rome's grain; strangled after Maxentius' prefect Rufius Volusianus took Carthage, which was sacked.

list.name: Valerius Valens
list.note: Dux limitis Daciae raised to Augustus by Licinius during the war of Cibalae; executed at Constantine's demand in the peace of Serdica (1 Mar 317).

list.name: Martinian
list.note: Licinius' magister officiorum raised to Augustus before Chrysopolis; spared at first, then put to death in Cappadocia 325.

list.name: Calocaerus
list.note: Magister pecoris camelorum who rose on Cyprus; suppressed by Constantine's half-brother Dalmatius and burned alive at Tarsus.

list.name: Magnentius
list.note: Germanic-born comes of the Ioviani and Herculiani, proclaimed at Augustodunum 18 Jan 350. Defeated at Mursa (28 Sep 351, among the bloodiest battles of the century) and Mons Seleucus (353); killed himself at Lugdunum 10 Aug 353.

list.name: Vetranio
list.note: Elderly magister peditum proclaimed at Mursa 1 Mar 350, perhaps at Constantina's prompting to block Magnentius; abdicated before the troops at Naissus 25 Dec 350 and retired to Prusa on a pension.

list.name: Julius Nepotianus
list.note: Nephew of Constantine; seized Rome with gladiators 3 Jun 350; killed after 28 days by Magnentius' officer Marcellinus, his head paraded on a lance.

list.name: Decentius
list.note: Brother or cousin of Magnentius, Caesar 351; hanged himself at Senones on news of Magnentius' death, 18 Aug 353.

list.name: Claudius Silvanus
list.note: Frankish magister peditum framed by forged letters; proclaimed at Colonia, killed after 28 days by men suborned by Ursicinus, whose staff included Ammianus (Amm. 15.5).

list.name: Procopius
list.note: Maternal relative of Julian; proclaimed at Constantinople 28 Sep 365 with Constantina's daughter displayed to the troops. Betrayed by his generals at Thyatira and Nacolia (May 366) and beheaded 27 May 366.

list.name: Marcellus
list.note: Procopius' relative and officer who claimed the purple after his execution; captured and killed by Equitius.

list.name: Firmus
list.note: Moorish prince (son of Nubel) who rebelled against the comes Romanus; his supporters may have proclaimed him; hunted down by Count Theodosius and hanged himself.

list.name: Magnus Maximus
list.note: Spanish-born commander in Britain, proclaimed 383; killed Gratian; recognized for a time by Theodosius; invaded Italy 387. Defeated at Siscia and Poetovio, executed at Aquileia 28 Aug 388. Welsh legend remembers him as Macsen Wledig.

list.name: Flavius Victor
list.note: Son of Magnus Maximus, co-Augustus; killed at Treveri by Arbogast after his father's death.

list.name: Eugenius
list.note: Rhetor made emperor by Arbogast 22 Aug 392; patron of the last pagan revival under Nicomachus Flavianus. Defeated at the Frigidus 6 Sep 394 and beheaded; Arbogast killed himself.

list.name: Gildo
list.note: Comes Africae who transferred allegiance to Arcadius and cut Rome's grain; defeated by his brother Mascezel and strangled himself or was killed at Tabraca. Did not claim the purple.

list.name: Marcus
list.note: Proclaimed by the British army in 406; killed by the troops.

list.name: Gratian (usurper)
list.note: British municipal (municeps) proclaimed after Marcus; killed after four months.

list.name: Constantine III
list.note: Soldier proclaimed in Britain for his name; crossed to Gaul after the Rhine crossing of 406 and was recognized by Honorius (409). Besieged at Arelate by Constantius, he surrendered on promise of life, was ordained, and executed before reaching Ravenna (Sep 411).

list.name: Constans (son of Constantine III)
list.note: Former monk made Caesar then Augustus by his father; killed at Vienne by Gerontius' troops 411.

list.name: Maximus of Hispania
list.note: Puppet of the general Gerontius 409-411, fled to the barbarians; re-emerged 420-422; displayed and executed at Ravenna at Honorius' tricennalia (422).

list.name: Priscus Attalus
list.note: Prefect of Rome made emperor by Alaric (Nov 409), deposed by him (Jul 410); raised again by Athaulf at Burdigala (414). Captured 416, paraded in Constantius' triumph, a finger cut off, exiled to Lipari.

list.name: Jovinus
list.note: Gallic noble proclaimed with Burgundian and Alan support (Gundahar, Goar); made his brother Sebastianus co-emperor; captured by Athaulf's Visigoths and beheaded at Narbo by the prefect Dardanus.

list.name: Sebastianus
list.note: Brother and co-Augustus of Jovinus; killed by the Visigoths.

list.name: Heraclianus
list.note: Comes Africae who executed Stilicho; consul 413; invaded Italy, was beaten at Utriculum, fled to Carthage and was beheaded there.

list.name: Joannes
list.note: Primicerius notariorum proclaimed at Rome on Honorius' death, refused recognition by Theodosius II. Betrayed at Ravenna to Aspar's army; hand cut off, paraded on an ass in the Hippodrome of Aquileia, beheaded (mid-425). Aetius arrived with 60,000 Huns three days late.

list.name: Basiliscus
list.note: Brother of Empress Verina; commander of the failed 468 Vandal expedition. Seized Constantinople Jan 475; his Encyclical alienated Chalcedonians. Surrendered to Zeno Aug 476 on promise of no bloodshed and was walled up in a dry cistern at Limnae in Cappadocia to die of starvation and exposure.

list.name: Marcianus
list.note: Son of the western emperor Anthemius and husband of Leo I's daughter Leontia; attacked the palace; ordained priest and exiled to Caesarea.

list.name: Leontius
list.note: Crowned at Tarsus by Verina at the instigation of the Isaurian general Illus; besieged at the fortress of Papyrius; beheaded with Illus 488.

list.name: Vitalian
list.note: Comes foederatorum who led a revolt of Bulgar and Hunnic foederati in the Chalcedonian cause, three times threatening Constantinople; his fleet burned in the Bosporus (515, by tradition with 'sulphur' devised by Proclus). Later consul (520), murdered in the palace in 520, Justinian suspected.

list.name: Hypatius
list.note: Nephew of Anastasius, crowned by the Nika rioters in the Hippodrome (18 Jan 532) against his will; executed the next day after Belisarius and Mundus massacred some 30,000 in the Hippodrome.

list.name: Stotzas
list.note: Leader of the great army mutiny in Byzantine Africa (from Easter 536); defeated by Belisarius and Germanus, fled to the Moors; killed at Thacia 545, mortally wounding the magister militum John.

list.name: Guntharic
list.note: Dux Numidiae who murdered the magister militum Areobindus and seized Carthage; killed at a banquet by the Armenian Artabanes after 36 days.

list.name: Hamilcar son of Mago
list.note: Magonid commander in Sicily; killed at Himera (480) by Gelon; Herodotus says he threw himself into the sacrificial fire.

list.name: Hannibal son of Gisco (Mago)
list.note: Grandson of Hamilcar; destroyed Selinus and Himera (409), took Acragas; died of plague in the siege camp (406).

list.name: Himilco son of Hanno
list.note: Took Acragas and Gela; besieged Syracuse (397-396), army struck by plague, abandoned his mercenaries; starved himself at Carthage.

list.name: Mago (fl. 396-375)
list.note: Fought Dionysius I; killed at Cabala (c. 375).

list.name: Hanno the Great (4th c.)
list.note: Leading statesman who attempted a coup; crucified with his family (c. 350, Justin 21.4).

list.name: Hamilcar son of Gisco
list.note: Defeated Agathocles at the Himeras (311) and besieged Syracuse; captured in a night attack and beheaded (309).

list.name: Bomilcar
list.note: Commander against Agathocles in Africa; attempted to seize sole power (308); crucified in the agora.

list.name: Hanno (264)
list.note: Commander who surrendered the Messana citadel to the Romans; crucified at Carthage.

list.name: Hanno son of Hannibal
list.note: Commanded at Agrigentum (262), defeated and fined.

list.name: Hamilcar (First Punic War)
list.note: Victor at Thermae (260) and commander at Ecnomus (256).

list.name: Xanthippus
list.note: Spartan mercenary who reorganized the army and destroyed Regulus at the Bagradas (255), then left Carthage.

list.name: Adherbal
list.note: Admiral who destroyed Publius Claudius Pulcher's fleet at Drepana (249), Carthage's greatest naval victory.

list.name: Hamilcar Barca
list.note: Commander in Sicily (247-241), victor of the Mercenary War (241-237), conqueror of southern Iberia (237-229); drowned crossing a river near Helike while retreating from the Oretani (229/228).

list.name: Hanno (Aegates)
list.note: Admiral defeated by Lutatius Catulus at the Aegates Islands (10 Mar 241); crucified.

list.name: Hanno the Great (3rd c.)
list.note: Leader of the landed faction opposed to the Barcids and to the war with Rome; commander in the Mercenary War.

list.name: Gisco
list.note: Commander at Lilybaeum who evacuated the army; tortured to death by the rebel mercenaries Spendius and Mathos.

list.name: Hasdrubal the Fair
list.note: Barcid son-in-law; founded Carthago Nova (c. 227); the Ebro treaty with Rome (226/225); killed by a Celtic slave whose master he had executed.

list.name: Hannibal Barca
list.note: Commander in Iberia 221, invaded Italy 218, recalled 203, lost at Zama 202; suffete 196 (reformed the court of 104 and state finances); fled 195; poisoned himself at Libyssa in Bithynia c. 183.

list.name: Hasdrubal Barca
list.note: Commander in Iberia; crossed the Alps 207; killed at the Metaurus, his head thrown into Hannibal's camp.

list.name: Mago Barca
list.note: Commander at Trebia and Cannae, then in Iberia and Liguria (205-203); died of wounds at sea on recall.

list.name: Hanno son of Bomilcar
list.note: Hannibal's subordinate in southern Italy; defeated at Beneventum (214).

list.name: Hasdrubal son of Gisco
list.note: Commander in Iberia, defeated at Ilipa (206); father of Sophonisba; routed at the Great Plains (203); poisoned himself (202) or was killed by a mob.

list.name: Hasdrubal the Boeotarch
list.note: Commander in the Third Punic War; surrendered to Scipio Aemilianus at the Byrsa; his wife killed their children and threw herself into the burning temple of Eshmun.
list.death: survived as a captive in Italy

list.name: Gelon
list.note: Deinomenid tyrant of Gela, then Syracuse; victor of Himera (480).

list.name: Hieron I
list.note: Victor over the Etruscans at Cumae (474); patron of Pindar and Aeschylus.

list.name: Thrasybulus
list.note: Expelled after 11 months; democracy restored.

list.name: Dionysius I
list.note: Fought four wars with Carthage; extended Syracusan power into southern Italy and the Adriatic.

list.name: Dionysius II
list.note: Expelled by Dion 357; regained the city 346; surrendered to Timoleon (344) and retired to Corinth.

list.name: Dion
list.note: Plato's friend; murdered by Callippus.

list.name: Timoleon
list.note: Corinthian liberator; defeated Carthage at the Crimisus (341); retired as a private citizen.

list.name: Agathocles
list.note: Tyrant from 317, king from 304; invaded Africa (310-307). Died 289, possibly poisoned.

list.name: Hicetas
list.note: Tyrant expelled by Thoenon.

list.name: Pyrrhus
list.note: King of Epirus invited as king of Sicily against Carthage; abandoned the island in 276.

list.name: Hieron II
list.note: General, then king (c. 270 after defeating the Mamertines at the Longanus); Rome's loyal ally from 263; Archimedes' patron. Died aged about 90.

list.name: Gelon II
list.note: Co-ruler with his father Hieron II; predeceased him.

list.name: Hieronymus
list.note: Grandson of Hieron II; switched to Carthage; assassinated at Leontini aged 15.

list.name: Hippocrates and Epicydes
list.note: Carthaginian-born brothers who led Syracuse against Rome until Marcellus took the city (212); Hippocrates died of plague, Epicydes fled to Agrigentum.

list.name: Pyrrhus (Epirus)
list.note: Earlier reign 307-302. Defeated Rome at Heraclea (280) and Asculum (279) at heavy cost, checked at Beneventum (275). Killed in street fighting at Argos, struck by a roof tile thrown by an old woman.

list.name: Antigonus I Monophthalmus
list.note: Took the royal title with Demetrius in 306; killed at Ipsus.

list.name: Demetrius I Poliorcetes
list.note: King of Macedon 294-288; surrendered to Seleucus 285.
list.death: drank himself to death in captivity in Syria

list.name: Antigonus II Gonatas
list.note: Claimed the title from 283; secured Macedon after defeating the Gauls at Lysimachia (277).

list.name: Demetrius II Aetolicus
list.note: Died fighting the Dardanians.

list.name: Antigonus III Doson
list.note: Regent then king; crushed Cleomenes III of Sparta at Sellasia (222).

list.name: Philip V
list.note: Allied with Hannibal (215); lost the Second Macedonian War at Cynoscephalae (197); executed his son Demetrius (180).

list.name: Perseus
list.note: Defeated at Pydna 22 Jun 168; walked in Aemilius Paullus' triumph.
list.death: died in custody at Alba Fucens, c. 166 (Diodorus says by sleep deprivation)

list.name: Andriscus (Philip VI)
list.note: Pretender claiming to be Perseus' son; defeated by Metellus (148), led in triumph and executed (146). Macedonia became a province.

list.name: Seleucus I Nicator
list.note: Satrap of Babylon 321/311 (Seleucid era from Oct 312); took the royal title 305; murdered by Ptolemy Keraunos near Lysimachia.

list.name: Antiochus I Soter
list.note: Co-king from 294; 'Elephant Victory' over the Galatians.

list.name: Antiochus II Theos
list.note: Died at Ephesus, allegedly poisoned by his first wife Laodice.

list.name: Seleucus II Callinicus
list.note: Lost the Third Syrian War and the east to the Parni; died falling from his horse.

list.name: Seleucus III Ceraunus
list.note: Killed by his officers on campaign in Asia Minor.

list.name: Antiochus III the Great
list.note: Eastern anabasis (212-205); took Coele-Syria at Panium (200); defeated by Rome at Thermopylae (191) and Magnesia (190); Peace of Apamea (188): 15,000 talents, Taurus frontier. Killed robbing the temple of Bel in Elymais.

list.name: Seleucus IV Philopator
list.note: Paid the Apamea indemnity; murdered by his minister Heliodorus.

list.name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
list.note: Hostage at Rome; invaded Egypt (170-168) until Popillius Laenas drew the circle at Eleusis; persecution of Judaism provoked the Maccabean revolt. Died at Tabae in Persis.

list.name: Antiochus V Eupator
list.note: Boy king killed on the orders of Demetrius I.

list.name: Demetrius I Soter
list.note: Escaped from hostage in Rome with Polybius' help; killed against Alexander Balas.

list.name: Alexander I Balas
list.note: Pretender backed by Attalus II, Ptolemy VI and Rome; beaten at the Oenoparas, murdered in Arabia.

list.name: Demetrius II Nicator
list.note: Captured by the Parthians 138, released 129; killed at Tyre (125). First reign 145-138, second 129-125.

list.name: Antiochus VI Dionysus
list.note: Child king set up by Diodotus Tryphon, who killed him.

list.name: Diodotus Tryphon
list.note: General who made himself king; besieged at Apamea, killed himself or was killed.

list.name: Antiochus VII Sidetes
list.note: Took Jerusalem (134) and reconquered Babylonia; killed in a Parthian counter-attack in Media.

list.name: Alexander II Zabinas
list.note: Ptolemaic-backed pretender; executed by Antiochus VIII.

list.name: Cleopatra Thea
list.note: Queen of three kings; ruled alone 126-125; forced by Antiochus VIII to drink the poison she had prepared for him.

list.name: Seleucus V Philometor
list.note: Killed by his mother Cleopatra Thea.

list.name: Antiochus VIII Grypus
list.note: Killed by his minister Heracleon.

list.name: Antiochus IX Cyzicenus
list.note: Rival king in Coele-Syria; killed himself after defeat by Seleucus VI.

list.name: Seleucus VI Epiphanes
list.note: Burned alive in the gymnasium at Mopsuestia by the populace.

list.name: Demetrius III Eucaerus
list.note: Captured by the Parthians.

list.name: Antiochus X Eusebes
list.note: Killed fighting the Parthians or Philip I (date 92 or 88).

list.name: Antiochus XI Epiphanes
list.note: Drowned in the Orontes fleeing Antiochus X.

list.name: Antiochus XII Dionysus
list.note: Killed fighting the Nabataeans at Cana.

list.name: Tigranes II (in Syria)
list.note: The Armenian king held Syria until Lucullus' victory at Tigranocerta.

list.name: Antiochus XIII Asiaticus
list.note: Restored by Lucullus, rejected by Pompey; killed by the Emesene dynast Sampsiceramus.

list.name: Philip II Philoromaeus
list.note: Last claimant; Pompey annexed Syria (64/63).

list.name: Ptolemy I Soter
list.note: Satrap from 323; king 305/304; seized Alexander's body.

list.name: Ptolemy II Philadelphus
list.note: Co-regent 284; Museum and Library, Pharos; sent the first embassy to Rome (273).

list.name: Ptolemy III Euergetes
list.note: Third Syrian War; reached Babylon.

list.name: Ptolemy IV Philopator
list.note: Raphia (217), first large-scale use of Egyptian phalangites; native revolt in the Thebaid.

list.name: Ptolemy V Epiphanes
list.note: Lost Coele-Syria at Panium (200); Rosetta decree (196). Died possibly poisoned.

list.name: Ptolemy VI Philometor
list.note: Saved by Rome's ultimatum to Antiochus IV (168); died of wounds after the battle of the Oenoparas.

list.name: Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II (Physcon)
list.note: Co-king 170-164; king of Cyrene 163-145; willed Cyrene to Rome (155) in a famous inscription; civil war with Cleopatra II (132-124).

list.name: Ptolemy VII Neos Philopator
list.note: Killed by Ptolemy VIII at his own wedding to Cleopatra II (numbering disputed).

list.name: Cleopatra III
list.note: Co-ruled with her sons; killed by Ptolemy X (Justin).

list.name: Ptolemy IX Soter II (Lathyros)
list.note: Expelled 107 to Cyprus; restored 88-81.

list.name: Ptolemy X Alexander I
list.note: Killed in a naval battle off Cyprus after expulsion; reputedly bequeathed Egypt to Rome.

list.name: Berenice III
list.note: Murdered by her husband Ptolemy XI after 19 days of joint rule.

list.name: Ptolemy XI Alexander II
list.note: Installed by Sulla; lynched by the Alexandrians.

list.name: Ptolemy XII Neos Dionysos (Auletes)
list.note: Bought Roman recognition (6,000 talents to Caesar and Pompey, 59); expelled 58-55, restored by Gabinius.

list.name: Berenice IV
list.note: Ruled during her father's exile; executed on his return.

list.name: Cleopatra VII
list.note: Last Ptolemy; ally and lover of Caesar and Antony; killed herself in Alexandria c. 10/12 Aug 30.

list.name: Ptolemy XIII
list.note: Drowned in the Nile after defeat by Caesar.

list.name: Ptolemy XIV
list.note: Probably poisoned by Cleopatra (Josephus).

list.name: Ptolemy XV Caesarion
list.note: Son of Caesar and Cleopatra; killed on Octavian's orders ('too many Caesars').

list.name: Philetaerus
list.note: Eunuch commander who defected from Lysimachus with 9,000 talents.

list.name: Eumenes I
list.note: Defeated Antiochus I near Sardis.

list.name: Attalus I Soter
list.note: Took the royal title after defeating the Galatians (c. 238); Rome's ally against Philip V; brought the Magna Mater stone to Rome (205).

list.name: Eumenes II Soter
list.note: Gained most of Seleucid Asia Minor at Apamea (188); built the Great Altar.

list.name: Attalus II Philadelphus
list.note: Founded Attaleia; Stoa of Attalus at Athens.

list.name: Attalus III
list.note: Bequeathed his kingdom to Rome, which Tiberius Gracchus sought to use for his land programme.

list.name: Aristonicus (Eumenes III)
list.note: Claimed the throne and rallied slaves and the poor ('Heliopolitans'); captured by Perperna, strangled in Rome (128).

list.name: Pharnaces I
list.note: Took Sinope (183), his new capital.

list.name: Mithridates V Euergetes
list.note: Roman ally in the Third Punic War; assassinated at Sinope.

list.name: Mithridates VI Eupator
list.note: Fought three wars with Rome (89-85, 83-81, 73-63); massacre of Romans in Asia (88). Deposed by his son Pharnaces, poison failed (mithridatism), had his Gallic bodyguard Bituitus kill him at Panticapaeum.

list.name: Pharnaces II
list.note: King of the Bosporus; defeated by Caesar at Zela ('veni vidi vici', 2 Aug 47); killed by Asander.

list.name: Darius son of Pharnaces
list.note: Installed by Antony.

list.name: Polemon I
list.note: Antony's appointee kept by Augustus; also king of the Bosporus; killed fighting the Aspurgiani.

list.name: Pythodorida
list.note: Queen; granddaughter of Antony.

list.name: Polemon II
list.note: Pontus annexed by Nero (64) to Galatia/Cappadocia.

list.name: Zipoetes I
list.note: Ruler from c. 326, king 297; resisted Lysimachus and Antiochus I.

list.name: Nicomedes I
list.note: Invited the Galatians into Asia; founded Nicomedia (264).

list.name: Ziaelas
list.note: Killed by Galatian chiefs he had planned to murder.

list.name: Prusias I Cholus
list.note: Sheltered Hannibal; founded Prusa.

list.name: Prusias II Cynegus
list.note: Greeted Roman envoys dressed as a freedman; killed by his son Nicomedes.

list.name: Nicomedes III Euergetes
list.note: Told Marius that Roman tax-farmers had enslaved his subjects (104).

list.name: Nicomedes IV Philopator
list.note: Expelled by Mithridates twice (90-89, 88-84); his raid on Pontus at Roman urging triggered the First Mithridatic War; bequeathed Bithynia to Rome. Rumoured lover of the young Caesar.

list.name: Gaia
list.note: Father of Masinissa; Carthaginian ally.

list.name: Oezalces
list.note: Brother of Gaia, by agnatic succession.

list.name: Capussa
list.note: Killed by the rebel Mazaetullus.

list.name: Lacumazes
list.note: Puppet of Mazaetullus, expelled by Masinissa.

list.name: Masinissa
list.note: Regained his kingdom with Roman help, see numidia.

list.name: Syphax
list.note: Married Sophonisba and joined Carthage; captured by Laelius and Masinissa at Cirta (203).
list.death: died in Roman captivity at Tibur

list.name: Vermina
list.note: Son of Syphax; made peace with Rome (200).

list.name: Masinissa
list.note: United Numidia after Zama; reigned until about 90, constantly encroaching on Carthaginian land and provoking the Third Punic War.

list.name: Micipsa
list.note: Joint king with Gulussa and Mastanabal (Scipio Aemilianus divided the royal functions); sole king from c. 140; built up Cirta.

list.name: Gulussa
list.note: Held the military command.

list.name: Mastanabal
list.note: Held judicial functions; father of Jugurtha.

list.name: Hiempsal I
list.note: Killed by Jugurtha's agents at Thirmida.

list.name: Adherbal
list.note: Besieged in Cirta by Jugurtha; killed with the Italian traders of the city, provoking Rome's war.

list.name: Jugurtha
list.note: Betrayed by Bocchus I to Sulla (105); led in Marius' triumph.

list.name: Gauda
list.note: Half-brother of Jugurtha; Marius' client.

list.name: Hiempsal II
list.note: Expelled by the Marians (81-?) and restored by Pompey; author of Punic books used by Sallust.

list.name: Hiarbas
list.note: Marian-backed usurper; killed after Pompey's African campaign.

list.name: Juba I
list.note: Destroyed Curio's army at the Bagradas (49); after Thapsus he and Petreius fought a suicide duel at Zama. Kingdom became Africa Nova.

list.name: Baga
list.note: Provided Masinissa with 4,000 men (206).

list.name: Bocchus I
list.note: Father-in-law of Jugurtha whom he betrayed to Sulla; gained western Numidia.

list.name: Bogud
list.note: King of western Mauretania, Caesarian; fled to Antony when Tingis rebelled.

list.name: Bocchus II
list.note: East, then all Mauretania from 38; bequeathed it to Rome.

list.name: Juba II
list.note: Son of Juba I raised in Rome; married Cleopatra Selene; scholar-king at Iol Caesarea; wrote on Libya and Arabia (used by Pliny).

list.name: Ptolemy of Mauretania
list.note: Grandson of Antony and Cleopatra; summoned to Lugdunum and killed by Caligula, provoking the revolt of Aedemon and the annexation of two provinces (c. 42).

list.name: Artaxias I
list.note: Former Seleucid strategos; founded Artaxata (with Hannibal's advice, per Strabo and Plutarch).

list.name: Tigranes II the Great
list.note: Built an empire from the Caucasus to Syria; founded Tigranocerta; defeated by Lucullus (69) and submitted to Pompey (66).

list.name: Artavasdes II
list.note: Abandoned Crassus; seized by Antony (34) and led in his Alexandrian triumph.

list.name: Artaxias II
list.note: Killed by his courtiers as Tiberius approached.

list.name: Tigranes III
list.note: Crowned by Tiberius.

list.name: Tigranes IV and Erato
list.note: Anti-Roman sibling-spouses; Tigranes killed in war c. AD 1.

list.name: Ariobarzanes
list.note: Median prince installed by Gaius Caesar.

list.name: Vonones
list.note: Ex-king of Parthia; removed under Parthian pressure.

list.name: Artaxias III (Zeno)
list.note: Son of Polemon I, crowned by Germanicus at Artaxata.

list.name: Arsaces
list.note: Son of Artabanus II.

list.name: Mithridates (of Iberia)
list.note: Reigned 35-37 and 42-51; murdered by his nephew Rhadamistus.

list.name: Rhadamistus
list.note: Iberian prince; expelled twice by the Armenians.

list.name: Tiridates I
list.note: Brother of Vologases I; crowned by Nero in Rome (66) after the compromise of Rhandeia (63): Parthian prince, Roman investiture. Reign interrupted by Tigranes VI (60-62).

list.name: Tigranes VI
list.note: Roman nominee imposed by Corbulo.

list.name: Axidares
list.note: Deposed by Osroes, provoking Trajan's war.

list.name: Parthamasiris
list.note: Laid his diadem at Trajan's feet at Elegeia; killed by his Roman escort. Armenia made a province (114-117).

list.name: Sohaemus
list.note: Roman senator and consul of Emesene/Arsacid descent; expelled by Vologases IV (161), restored by Statius Priscus (164).

list.name: Pacorus
list.note: Parthian appointee.

list.name: Khosrov I
list.note: Lured and imprisoned by Caracalla.

list.name: Tiridates II
list.note: Resisted the Sasanians.

list.name: Hormizd-Ardashir (Sasanian)
list.note: Shapur I's son as 'Great King of Armenia' during Persian occupation.

list.name: Narseh (Sasanian)
list.note: Later shahanshah.

list.name: Tiridates III
list.note: Restored by Rome; converted by Gregory the Illuminator (traditionally 301, more probably c. 314), making Armenia the first Christian kingdom. Dates disputed (some put the reign 298-330).

list.name: Tiran
list.note: Blinded by the Persians.

list.name: Arshak II
list.note: Wavered between Rome and Persia; imprisoned by Shapur II in the Fortress of Oblivion.

list.name: Pap
list.note: Installed by Valens; murdered at a banquet by the Roman general Trajanus (Amm. 30.1).

list.name: Arshak III
list.note: Ruled Roman Armenia after the partition of c. 387.

list.name: Khosrov IV
list.note: Persian Armenia.

list.name: Vramshapuh
list.note: Patron of Mesrop Mashtots and the Armenian alphabet (c. 405).

list.name: Artaxias IV (Artashir)
list.note: Deposed by Bahram V at the request of the Armenian nobles; Persarmenia became a marzpanate.

list.name: Arsaces I
list.note: Leader of the Parni; Arsacid era begins 247.

list.name: Arsaces II
list.note: Submitted to Antiochus III (209).

list.name: Mithridates I
list.note: Conquered Media and Mesopotamia; took Seleucia (141); captured Demetrius II.

list.name: Phraates II
list.note: Defeated and killed Antiochus VII (129); killed fighting Saka nomads and mutinous Greek captives.

list.name: Artabanus I
list.note: Killed fighting the Tocharians.

list.name: Mithridates II
list.note: Restored Parthian power; first contact with Rome at the Euphrates meeting with Sulla (96), whose seating humiliated the envoy Orobazus.

list.name: Phraates III
list.note: Dealt with Pompey; murdered by his sons.

list.name: Mithridates IV
list.note: Fled to Gabinius; executed by his brother Orodes.

list.name: Orodes II
list.note: Destroyed Crassus at Carrhae (53) through his general Surena; murdered by his son Phraates IV.

list.name: Pacorus I
list.note: Co-ruler; overran Syria with Labienus (40); killed by Ventidius at Gindarus.

list.name: Phraates IV
list.note: Defeated Antony (36); returned the standards of Carrhae (20); sent four sons to Rome as hostages; poisoned by his Italian wife Musa and son Phraataces.

list.name: Tiridates II
list.note: Pretender who fled to Augustus.

list.name: Phraates V (Phraataces)
list.note: Co-ruled with his mother Musa; agreed the Euphrates frontier with Gaius Caesar (AD 1).

list.name: Vonones I
